en: Preface:
The Gautama clan appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition. For forty-nine years, he extensively proclaimed the sublime truth.

To peer into its profound significance is almost like entering the ocean to count its sands; yet among the various vehicles of the teachings, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* are particularly preeminent.
It is a supreme treasure. Now, while the Lotus Sūtra represents the Buddha’s entire body, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is the crown of the Buddha.

Thus, because this sūtra is ultimately firm and solid, everything from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) proceeds by means of cultivation through the crown;
one directly treads upon the crown of Vairocana. It is the most honored and sublime dharma of Great Awakening, serving as the bridge for becoming a Buddha—just as the lotus flower...
This is the essential core [of the teachings]. To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, there is no way other than this.

Therefore, since the time of Tiantai, successive sages have followed one after another, each generation elucidating and expounding [the doctrine]. Although their expositions differ in length—some being detailed and others concise—their compassionate intent remains the same.

In brief, by serving as the unifying source that penetrates all doctrines and encompassing all categories of beings to bestow their grace, [this work] ensures that the teachings of the Lord Gautama are not lost.
This is the essential purport [of the teachings]. When the *Separate Transmission* (Chán) came to the East, the religious and doctrinal schools began to disparage one another.

Upon meeting Longtan, Master Xuánjiàn burned his commentaries on the *Qīnglóng Sūtra*, considering that all profound dialectics were like a single hair placed in the vast void, and all the world’s pivotal mechanisms were like a single drop cast into the great ocean.
Thus, as soon as one enters the realm of verbal expression, it becomes nothing but superfluous meaning.

Yet, regarding the profound cause, the cultivation and realization, and the ultimate meaning of the Bodhisattva’s myriad practices as perfected in unison—the wondrousness that transcends what can be said—there have been many who have treated these [teachings] like discarded scrap paper. Alas! Capacities vary between sharp and dull; spiritual faculties differ in their speed and slowness.

If you claim that by simply "upholding the single phrase" (dantí biéchuán) one may completely abolish the study of doctrinal learning (yìxué), then as soon as Gautama left Tuṣita Heaven, he should have directly shown his "double-legged" kōan to Kāśyapa.
Why, instead, did he speak crosswise and vertically, repeatedly turning the Wheel of the Buddha?
If this were truly because he did not disdain the trouble, then why would the former masters of old have spoken of "dwelling in the void day after day"?
Is this not a profound analogy? The merit of propagating the sutras far surpasses that of the sands of the Ganges. Whether monastics or laypeople, those involved are manifold;

in brief, they have personally received the transmission of the prophecy and manifest their presence wherever they encounter the Dharma, ensuring that the torch of wisdom burns eternally and the banner of the Buddha does not fall.

Were it not for the power of long-accumulated vows, how could one possibly utter a single word? To employ the refined reflections and swift brushstrokes of a literary man to expound the profound discourses of the Tamer (the Buddha),
and to use the chapters and sections of worldly books to analyze the structural threads of the *Pitaka*,
is like comparing the constant flow of a river returning to the sea, or like the fine threads of a loom entering their respective slots— such is the power of his eloquence.
Unimpeded, both Exoteric and Esoteric teachings were fully revealed. Seeking such a person today, one finds none other than Mr. Yan. Mr.
Yan was a scholar of long-standing learning and a great master who lived in seclusion to compose his works; he was particularly profound in the essential tenets of the Five Houses of Chan.

He subsequently compiled the work *Lengyan Guanshe* (The Comprehensive Integration of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra), which took twenty-seven years to complete. This was because he applied himself with singular diligence, desiring— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
With the vigor of a single individual, he has cleared the way for the myriad species from the ford of delusion. How benevolent was his application of mind, truly that of the Master Gautama!
Within these chapters, he uses the Buddha’s words to verify the Buddha’s wisdom; neither identical nor separate, they possess both order and backbone.
Truly, there is nothing they do not penetrate and nothing they do not encompass. It is here that the Master has finally attained a comprehensive understanding of this sutra.

I understand. Subsequently, I saw that our paths converged; furthermore, through Master Li, I was able to read the *Zhengmo* (The Correct Pulse). Ultimately, however, I drew my materials from Jingling’s *Rushuo* (As It Is Spoken).
This may be called gathering the fur from many armpits to make a robe, or intermingling five colors to create a painting.

As for its ability to streamline the concise and eliminate the redundant, threading them directly together to dissect the subtle and profound—opening the scroll, one understands clearly. I, this humble youth, have read it.
I was delighted by it, as if beholding a blue utpala flower; though I wished not to feel joy or offer praise, it was impossible to refrain.
Thus, following the command of my elder brother, I have composed this preface for it.
In the fifth month of the Jiyou year of the Kangxi era, Xu Yuanwen, a junior friend from Kunshan, respectfully prostrates himself and composes this preface.

Now, as for those who preach the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be preached; as for those who interpret the sutras, they rely on interpretation to preserve the sutras. That there is no dharma that can be preached—this is not... [text continues]
This prevents the horizontal and vertical modes of exposition. Borrowing explanations to preserve the sutra, the primary value lies in one interpretation that encompasses all interpretations.
Since the sutras first flowed into China, many have commented upon them; indeed, those who have commented on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* are especially numerous.
Yet, some dissect the text into minute fragments and provide indirect proofs or peripheral citations, which conversely deviates from its pervasive unity. Others cling to the literal phrasing and...
When commentaries proliferate and follow the text, they eventually lapse into fragmentation and frivolous elaboration;
thus, it may even be better to have no interpretation at all. This is why Master Da encouraged people to read the original text alone.

Since the time of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* commentaries were first produced, only the *Shi-jia-huijie* (Commentary by Ten Houses) by Tianru has been widely circulated in the world. However, with the emergence of Master Yiyu’s *Hezhe*, a new perspective was revealed.
A separate edition was opened. When Master Jiaoguang’s *Zhengmai* (Correct Pulse) appeared, its profound meanings were fully elucidated;
thus, the Elder Master Yunqi Lianchi donned his ceremonial robes and prostrated before it, setting aside his brush and refraining from further commentary—this was for good reason.

Subsequently, Zhong Bojing and He Zhongnan, drawing upon the principles of the *Zhengmai*, composed the *Rushuo* (As Spoken), which introduced many novel insights. Layman Liaohan then compiled these various [works].
He compiled it according to the method of our Confucian lecture commentaries. Initially titled *Guanshe*, it was later renamed *Shuotong*. Alas, how complete it is!

Having obtained this work, I have read it through to its conclusion. Therein I see that he has thoroughly swept away the entanglements of scholastic pedantry and uniquely highlighted the wondrous meaning of directness and simplicity;
his spirit is entirely focused on the seamless transition between sections, making ten volumes appear as one.
One fascicle is like one sentence; one sentence is like one character.

Those who, in the past, would yawn and stretch upon opening a scroll as if wishing for sleep, now find themselves increasingly savoring its flavor the more they read, as if fearing it might end too soon.

Is this not what is meant by "borrowing an interpretation to preserve the sutra," wherein a single interpretation encompasses all interpretations? As for the Layman, being a [Buddha] returned to this world...

This person propagates the legacy of the Three Teachings. He bathes his person like the branches of a tree and the trunk of a pine amidst frost and snow; he refines his character like the moon in a deep pool, the wind through pines.
As for his profound cultivation and secret refinement that lie beyond words and letters, the two masters Gao and Xu have already spoken of them;
why should I add anything superfluous?
Written by Xiong Zhao, younger brother of the family,
who is a Graduate of the Jinshi Degree conferred in the autumn of the辛亥 year of the Kangxi era,
serving as an Imperial Censor of the Yunnan Circuit and currently dispatched on inspection duty for the salt administration of Liangzhe and Guanzhong. Respectfully inscribed.

This preface to the *Lengyan guan she* was not written by me to instruct those who have already attained realization, but rather to serve as a bridge for later students. There are already many commentaries on this sutra;
why then trouble myself with this again? I reply: A sutra is a book in which the Sages of the West discourse upon the Way. However, the Sage...
The writings of men are originally the words of the sages. That which the sages spoke is truly different from that of ordinary people;
yet their speech possesses order and backbone, with calls and responses, such that every character and phrase has a definitive resolution.
Several sections and chapters interlock with one another; if these were the same as the words of ordinary people, they would surely be even more detailed.
This is the ultimate limit. Thus, those who read the scriptures in future generations must fully comprehend the words of the Sage before they can grasp the Sage’s intent;
furthermore, they must be as if hearing the Sage’s speech face-to-face before they can truly harmonize with the Sage’s words.
Therefore, the craft of the literary man is far removed from the Way, yet it occasionally employs its own excellence in wondrous ways.
Resounding like bells and drums, and as bright as the sun and moon—this must indeed be what the Great Awakened One meant by breaking into a subtle smile.
Yet, if this is so, one might ask: do the various interpretations of the ancient masters and contemporary worthies still leave something insufficient? I say: it is because their applications differ.
For carriages and boats diverge according to the needs of Yan and Wu, while furs and葛 (gé) garments are distinguished by cold and heat; it is not that [the principle] itself...

Superiority and inferiority exist therein; yet, as for what is appropriate, they are indeed worlds apart. The commentaries of various masters dissect the subtle and unravel the profound, each possessing its own specialized strengths;
however, some may elaborate upon the meaning while failing to embody the literal phrasing.

To find one whose call-and-response is clear and whose structural logic is thoroughly penetrating is truly not easy to encounter frequently. Yet, in this compilation by the Master, every glance evokes emotion, and it is truly...

This concerns the meaning of "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*). It is intended to transcend the views of various masters, supplementing what they have failed to reach and clarifying what they have not yet understood.
Although there are many *sūtras*, the *Buddhapiṭaka* (the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*) alone is most honored and supreme. It does not merely refute and reveal;

it exhaustively reaches the inner sanctum and thoroughly investigates the profound depths, making clear, point by point, the distinctions between the *pāramitā* and *mantra* vehicles, as well as the provisional and the ultimate, and the heterodox and the orthodox. This is truly because of [Master] Fang...
The Master’s calligraphy was sublime, and his brushwork entered the realm of the wondrous. Consequently, the profound mysteries of India have now been brought into the light of day.
Thus, this compilation by the Master is truly the fulfillment of the Tamer’s (the Buddha’s) entrustment and a meritorious achievement for Qinghe.

Now, while it is certain that writing conveys the Way, there are nonetheless two aspects when the Way has not yet been fully clarified. As for those who are "dragon-elephants" in the study of doctrine, they are certainly not lacking.
However, because my extensive study of external classics has not yet been profound, there are occasional stammers when I take up the pen.

If one were to examine each instance to ensure that the phrasing is compliant and smooth, that the reality and the fiction are both appropriate, then even the ancient masters would often have criticisms to offer.

As for the direct pointing of the Chan school, which prides itself on not falling into verbal explanations, I fear that by leaning toward language, it would immediately become a mere doctrinal sign (*śāstra-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, I have not deigned to compose [this work].
In his *Longshu Chao* (Commentary on the Dragon Draft), he instead applied his mind to the works of Li Bai, Du Fu, Han Yu, and Ou-yang Xiu, busily contending for preeminence with mere literary men;

this is truly lamentable. If one were to claim that brush and ink exist outside of True Suchness (*tathatā*), then since earth, water, fire, and wind are already fully encompassed [within it], why would one claim that Prajñā exists outside of language? This is the pure essence of the true teaching in this land.

Purity resides in hearing the sound. To govern oneself in this regard, would one not fall into the error of silence? Now, if a stream flowing for a thousand li is blocked at a single bend, it will not flow through;
if a performance of a single piece fails to reach its full expression through modulation and resonance, the piece remains incomplete.
How much more so with the subtle and profound words of the Sage—how could they ever be treated with negligence, while merely relying on superficial brilliance to grasp the general meaning?
Is it not to avoid the reproach of "losing one's resolve through playthings"? The arguments of those gentlemen were surely made with a specific purpose in mind.
Indeed, there are those who find resonance with the rare endowments of the ancients and their teachings that transcend words;
there are those who grasp the meaning by taking a single chapter or passage; and there are indeed those for whom a single word or phrase strikes home like a blow. There are certainly...
This is like the case of the "Ying-script and Yan-explanation," where great benefit was gained. It does not stop at this alone.

Even taking the present scripture itself as an example, there are indeed those who have attained realization by misinterpreting the punctuation and phrasing of the phrase "establishing knowledge through knowledge.
Furthermore, speaking in terms of the Chan school, there are indeed those whose "bottom of the bucket" has fallen away upon hearing dirges or erotic poetry. It does not stop at this alone. By...
Speaking of other worlds, there are indeed those who perform the Buddha-work through the fragrance of food and incense.
Even the use of staffs and shouts is considered blunt and inadequate; how much more so the case of verbal discourse?

Nevertheless, while it may be possible to speak of the methods of different regions for the sake of an individual’s awakening, if one wishes to reach the capacities of beings in this Sahā world and expound the Dharma of the Great Hero, one must first...

The words of the Sage, spoken with ear-to-ear and face-to-face intimacy, cause each and every person of a thousand or ten hundred years hence to follow them with their ears and permeate them to their hearts.
Thus, they may savor the waves of the ocean of nature and behold the brilliant radiance of the sky of meaning;

it is clearly evident that this must lie herein and not elsewhere. This humble servant, having completed his studies of this compilation, could not help but rejoice and join his palms, saying: "Buddha!"
The light from the crown [of his head] again illuminated the four continents. Regarding the meaning of *sūtra*: in China it is translated as "Scripture in Accordance with Truth" (*qijing*).
This is because, above, it accords with the principle of all Buddhas, and below, it necessarily accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

As for the meaning of "scripture" (*jing*), it signifies "pervasion" and "gathering. It pervades and penetrates the supreme path that has been taught, and it gathers and sustains the sentient beings who are to be transformed.
Furthermore, this compilation by the Master follows the model of the lecture commentaries on the Confucian classics.

Taking "faithful resemblance" and "penetrating clarity" as its standard, he has already selected and adopted the sublime interpretations of various masters that accord with the principles of the Buddhas of the past.

As for the language, it is as vivid as life itself; it is truly pervasive and truly comprehensive, designed to conform to the diverse capacities of sentient beings. This has been achieved through [his] previous...
There has never been one to surpass him. His *Zichai jianglu* (Lecture Records of Purple Firewood) is particularly perfect;

it will undoubtedly stand alongside the *Jingang jing yiqu guangyan* (Extensive Exposition on the Meaning of the Diamond Sutra) by the Grand Secretary Zhang Dayuan for a thousand autumns. Following Jiaoguang, he once again achieved extraordinary merit.
This is truly a cause for rejoicing. I, your humble servant, have often marveled that the ancestral teachings have not declined in this land of Jingluo.

Great Master Zhaojue manifested in the form of a bhikṣu; Prime Minister Neijiang manifested in the form of a lay official; and now you, sir, manifest as a Vimalakīrti or a Layman Pang, standing as a third pillar among them.
All of these may be called the udumbara flower and the kalaviṅka’s song. May this compilation circulate widely.

Throughout the world, it is common knowledge that the Golden-Colored Dhūta is currently at Mount Kukkuṭapāda, guarding the Buddha’s robe and awaiting the face-to-face transmission to the Bodhisattva who will succeed him.
Who would have known that the Venerable Ānanda was likewise at that very moment upon the lion throne, presently compiling the Buddha’s words?
I cannot bear to add further annotations, yet out of compassion for sentient beings in this Dharma-ending age, I have done so.
On the day of the winter solstice, the first month of the Yang cycle, in the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era,
by Zongrenfu Cheng, formerly Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel and concurrently Academician of the Court of Imperial Annals.
Dongmeng Gao Heng composed this preface on the origins and process of compilation.

In the year of Gengchen, while I was a guest in the capital, I first read the *Lengyan jing huijie* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra). I read it twice, barely managing to glimpse its general outline.
This was all I could grasp. In the Dinghai year, I sought refuge from the chaos at the Jincheng Pass of Liangshan.
There, I obtained a commentary (*huìjiě*) and read it; gradually, my understanding became clearer. At that time, I harbored a secret aspiration:

"How might I achieve such comprehensive and lucid mastery, so that I may expound upon the meaning for the benefit of later students, as the Confucian scholars do? In the winter of the Wuzi year, I followed my elder brother Jixian to Daxu.
In the Han City Garrison of this province, I suddenly obtained a single fascicle of the *Hezhe* (Compendium) from among a collection of fragmented sutra scrolls. Taking it up, I recited it;
my mind opened and my spirit leaped with joy, thinking, "This may serve as a resource for the conceptual framework of my lectures. However, I had not yet seen the complete text.
In the year Jichu (1469), I arrived at Jialing and visited Master Lizhi, who told me that he possessed the complete version of the *Hezhe*. Then, in the year Gengyin (1470)...
Having obtained it, I completed my studies and was once again filled with a sense of leaping joy, exclaiming that such a thing had never been encountered before.

My Upādhyāya said to me, "While following the same track is certainly good, it is not as excellent as the *Zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse). I then sought out the *Zhengmai* and read it; at first, I found its categorization and analysis to be overly complex and fragmented, and though I read it repeatedly, I remained in the dark regarding its meaning.
However, upon observing its concise insights and its method of grasping the fundamental source, I saw that it did not rely on the Tiantai system of *śamatha*.

Observing these various outstanding insights, which rise far above the multitude of commentaries, it is truly for this reason that tradition says when Master Padmasambhava first beheld this text, he faced north, burned incense, adjusted his robes, and prostrated.

My intention in lecturing on this may now be compiled. Thus, I have taken the *Zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse) and *Heyue* (Concordant Tracks) as my primary guides, scrutinizing and comparing them through the method of "fivefold investigation," and following the precedent of scriptural lecture notes, I have harmonized and integrated them.

I have compiled this work. In dividing it into chapters and tracing the flow of the pulse [of the teaching], I have ensured that every connection and correspondence perfectly mirrors the lips of the Buddhas of the past and penetrates the minds of future students.
Consequently, all fragmented and redundant classifications have been eliminated. Generally, I have adopted six-tenths of the orthodox lineage and followed four-tenths of other traditions;
furthermore, I have appended one-tenth of my own limited insights as a humble contribution. This undertaking began in the year of Xin... (辛).
It began in the first month of the Year of the Hare (Mao) and was completed in the ninth month of the Year of the Dragon (Renchen). The work consists of ten volumes in total.
I respectfully submitted it to Master Li, who did not consider it erroneous and instructed that the manuscript be preserved to await the right conditions for its publication.
In the Gengzi year of the Shunzhi era, I went to my parents’ home and returned to the capital; this copy remained behind in Jialing and was not brought along.
I happened to obtain one volume of the *Rushuo* (As Spoken) at Baoguo Temple and read it. It was composed by the two lay practitioners Zhong Bojing and He Keshang;
for the most part, it is based on the *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Lineage), yet interspersed with new interpretations. Often, these harmonize wonderfully with the intent of the Buddha.
In the spring of the Dingwei year, my second son, Ruhuai, arrived from Jialing and brought me the manuscript of my own draft.
It is as if meeting an old friend again; the joy is beyond description. Thereupon, I further revised and finalized it, cross-referencing it with the original teachings.
Thus, over a period of twenty-seven years, my great vow has finally been fulfilled, and I may do so without regret.
As for the carving of the woodblocks and their distribution, I did not dare to take it for granted. My fellow countryman, Mr. Bai Tian, the Magistrate of Gaoping, read [the work].

He approved of it and was the first to donate one hundred pieces of gold to initiate the carving of three volumes. Two gentlemen, Tang and Xie, followed his lead, and my son finally brought it to completion.
Within half a year, the ten volumes were finished. The preface was written with a masterful brush by Mr.
Gao Niandong, the Junior Minister of the Court of Astronomy; he is the Zhang Wujin of our day. Entrusting this sacred scripture to him, I have had him compose this narrative.

Is this not a great fortune? Thus I have recorded its beginning and end in this manner, so that future readers may reflect upon the difficulty of propagating the Great Sūtra and refrain from treating it with negligence or irreverence.
On the first day of the eighth month of autumn in the seventh year of the Kangxi era of the Great Qing, the year Wushen (1668),
Liu Daokai, a lay disciple who observes the precepts, inscribed this at Hongxuetang in Yantai.
The Preface to the Repentance Ritual:
I humbly submit that the Buddha-dharma is vast and expansive; even the most eminent sages have been unable to fathom its depths or its limits.

The meaning of the sutras is profound and subtle; how could one of inferior intelligence dare to provide an exegesis or commentary? I have merely relied upon the discursive arguments of former scholars to offer this modest contribution of my own meager talent in compilation.
Now that the work has been inscribed into a book, it is fitting to issue a formal announcement.
I humbly address myself to [the authorities].
Lion Throne.

Looking down with compassion upon the humble sincerity of this ant-like being, I reflect that your disciple Liu Daokai is but a dull-witted ordinary person, lost in the vast expanse of karmic consciousness.
Fortunately, having planted roots of goodness in past lives, he has now attained the opportunity to behold [the Buddha].

Regarding this wondrous scripture in my present life, I first recalled reading the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* in the year of Gengchen. As for the compilation of this direct commentary (*zhíjiě*), it was undertaken in the year of Xinmao;
after two years of study, it was finally completed, having entirely eliminated the trivialities of the interlinear annotations (*dié kē*).
He synthesizes a multitude of teachings to extract their essence, striving to ensure that the underlying principles flow through them with seamless coherence.

Discerning the fundamental roots, he does not employ the *Tiantai* system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* to prune away the complex for the sake of simplicity; rather, his style resembles the commentaries of Confucian scholars. Upon opening the volume, everything is clear at once.
Thus, beginners find it easy to understand, and as they progress, they encounter unobstructed clarity; even those of dull faculties will not suffer from its difficulty.
I understand. This collection has resided in its casket for many years, awaiting the convergence of conditions for carving.
Relying upon the power of the Vedas’ vows, it silently opened the way for the lay patron’s faith. The patron Xian Guan Bai Liangyu initiated the carving of three volumes previously;
the patron Xian Guan Xie Shudu assisted in carving two volumes subsequently. As for the remainder, it is the work of his disciples.

Dào Kāi, together with his sons (Xìn Guān Rúhàn and Gòngshēng Rúhuái), contributed according to their means to assist in its completion. Calculating the labor costs, they expended over three hundred taels of gold.
They produced one case containing ten volumes of this excellent edition. Once the carving of the woodblocks was finalized, they prostrated themselves to announce its completion.
Thereupon, on the first day of this month, they respectfully proceeded to Miaoxi Ān to invite monks to perform a memorial offering. (Thus it is said.)
I humbly pray that your vast compassion may clearly discern this,
and that your power of wisdom may protect and sustain it, so that it does not fall into great error.
I humbly entreat Your Holiness to further guide its dissemination, so that all sentient beings throughout the heavens may together traverse the gate of the One and Six,
and all spirits throughout the land may ascend together to the realm of Perfect Penetration. Your disciple Daokai cannot overcome the utmost sincerity of his longing and trepidation.
Respectfully submitted.
Compiled by the layman of Bajun, Liu Daokai (pen name: Feiyuan), for the first fascicle of the *Lengyan shuotong*.
The śramaṇa Lishi of Chengdu points out that the three characters "Dafoding" (Great Buddha-Crown) in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—
the Definitive Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas—
should, according to other scriptures, be understood as referring to one of the thirty-two marks of a Buddha’s body.

This refers to the mark of the invisible crown of the head. If one relies on the scriptures to clarify its meaning, it denotes the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*, the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa.
From this essential body of mind, the ten voids are encompassed and all phenomena are pervaded.
This is the supreme and most excellent pinnacle-dharma of Great Awakening. Regarding the "Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning":
"Unchanging" is named *tathā* (Thusness), and "following conditions" is *āgata* (come). In the Lesser Vehicle, there is Thusness but no coming; in ordinary beings, there is coming but not Thusness.
Only I, the Great Awakened One, am both Thusness and come; therefore, I am called the Tathāgata. It is that which is known and seen by me alone.

This refers to the Secret. That which gives birth to the noble fruit is called the cause (*hetu*). That which involves refinement, cultivation, and practice is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

That which is realized through the silent resonance of a mind that has forgotten itself is called realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). That which leaves nothing uninvestigated or exhausted is called completion (*pariniṣṭhita*). That which does not fall within the realm of words or thought is called the meaning (*artha*).

It means that the Great Awakened One takes this "Crown Dharma" as the cause, and through actual cultivation and actual realization, exhausts all hindrances and empties all delusions, reaching the ultimate limit of the cause.
The fruit is fulfilled; the task is completed; there is nothing further to be done. This single meaning is fully realized, and no other meaning remains.
Therefore, it is called "The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization. As for the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the foremost of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas:

Śūraṅgama: This is translated as "Ultimate Firmness. It means that from the stage of Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment, one takes this "Crown Dharma" as the cause to cultivate the myriad practices, gradually severing ignorance and partially realizing the True Principle.
Thus, one ascends through the stages of the sages, treading the rungs of the Buddha’s ladder, until every matter is accomplished with firm stability—except for the Buddhas themselves.

As for Bodhisattvas and other world-transcending beings of lesser fruition, as well as worldly sages and worthies, although they each possess their own realization and entry, seeing but a single glimpse in a hazy and indistinct manner, they all remain seated within a semblance of awakening.

This is because they are unable to empty the five aggregates, dissolve the six sense faculties, exhaust the five abodes of ignorance, or transcend the two deaths; they have not yet surpassed the measure of the mind and have not reached perfect consummation.
Therefore, "Sūtra" (Jing) means "constant. It establishes the eternal norms for all time and serves as the final flame of the Buddha’s lamp.
[The titles are: 1. The Great One; 2. The Buddha-Crown; 3. The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata; 4. The Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization;
5. The Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas; 6. Śūraṅgama; 7. The Sūtra. Regarding the first, "The Great One," this is a term of praise.
It possesses eight meanings: vastness, inclusiveness, pervasiveness, multiplicity, profundity, primordiality, constancy, and transcendence.

Regarding the "two Buddha-uṣṇīṣas": while the *Lotus Sūtra* is the complete body of the Buddha, this sūtra is the crown of the Tathāgata; this reveals that this sūtra contains the essential meaning within the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Third, regarding the "secret cause of the Tathāgata": "Tathā" (如) refers to fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

The "coming" refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). When the fundamental and the initial reach their ultimate fulfillment, one is called a Tathāgata. Regarding the term "mysterious cause" (*guhyahetu*):

it refers to when the Tathāgata, while still an ordinary person, suddenly realized at the gateway of the six sense faculties the perfectly湛 (pure and tranquil), non-arising, and non-ceasing, wondrously luminous true mind.
This mind is the fundamental, real nature of the four categories and the seven elements; it fully possesses the three Tathāgatagarbhas.
The essence is the great function; it is fundamentally the Buddha. How could it be merely the causal nature?
It is also precisely the resultant nature, for there is no separate realization for the Tathāgatas, nor is there even a hair’s breadth of addition at the time of realization.
This is what is meant by attaining perfect enlightenment from the very first moment of generating the bodhicitta. It is called the most esoteric because this is so.
Between these two roots, the true root is what is called the "essence of the clarity of consciousness" (*vijñāna-prasāda-mūla*). It is the original pure substance of the Bodhisattva’s *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha said that all sentient beings fail to achieve unsurpassed *bodhi* precisely because they do not penetrate this root and instead practice in a confused and erroneous manner.
Furthermore, in the subsequent verse, it is stated that [the Buddha] "never reveals it," which sufficiently demonstrates its presence within the sense faculties (*indriya*).
The Tathāgatagarbha nature possessed by all is a most profound and esoteric teaching, difficult to fathom and difficult to know.

From the opening request for formal instruction in the sutra until the fourth fascicle’s passage on the body and mind attaining lightness and ease and experiencing what has never been experienced before—this is precisely that secret cause.
Furthermore, this section constitutes the "wondrous śamatha" among the three names requested by Ānanda.

By means of these three *tathāgatagarbhas*, which are the self-nature primordially settled, one who suddenly awakens to and thoroughly penetrates this state does so through subtle and secret contemplation. Fourth, regarding the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization:

since the preceding section has fully revealed that the self-nature is inherently endowed and spontaneously perfected by nature, yet as it is called the "secret cause," how could it obstruct cultivation and realization? This is...
Therefore, although one may have already tasted the nature of the treasury, it is still likened to not yet having entered the magnificent mansion.

For this reason, the gateway of definitive meaning is opened to demonstrate the sequence for untying the knots. One must untie the six knots and transcend the three emptinesses before it constitutes the cultivation of the definitive meaning;
one must attain the two excellences and manifest the three functions before it constitutes the realization of the definitive meaning. However, it is said that...

Regarding the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), there are two senses. First, it is because one employs the faculties (*indriya*) rather than the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). For if one employs the consciousnesses, one takes that which is subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation;
this is like steaming sand to make rice—it will ultimately fail to produce the eternally abiding Bodhi. Therefore, it is not the definitive meaning.
To employ the faculties, however, is to take the nature that is neither born nor extinguished as the mind of the causal ground. This is like relying upon...
Gold is used to fashion vessels because it is certain to achieve unsurpassed bodhi; thus, it is definitive (nītārtha).

Furthermore, among the sense organs already established as definitive, the ear-faculty is specifically selected as the most definitive of the definitive, for it transcends the twenty-four noble ones and is uniquely sublime as the single path to nirvāṇa for all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.
This is the essential gate. Second, cultivation arises from the nature (*dhātu*), for the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition.

This is because, based on the secret cause, within the ocean of fruition where there is no cultivation or realization, one does not hinder illusory cultivation or illusory realization. Thus, there is cultivation without cultivation; it is not the defiled cultivation of phenomenal characteristics.
There is realization without realization; it is not a newly achieved actual realization. Therefore, it is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and not [otherwise].

This is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). From the latter half of the fourth fascicle, where the request for the "Gate of the Flowered Hall" begins, up until the "Dhāraṇī Protected by a Hundred Spirits" at the beginning of the seventh fascicle, this constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Now, this section is precisely the "Sublime Samādhi" requested by Ānanda; it takes this "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Faculty" as the foremost among the "Illusion-like Samādhis."

This is because of [the stage of] Maitreya. Regarding the "five classes of bodhisattvas and ten thousand practices": the "bodhisattvas" refers to the fifty-five stages of partial realization attained by the various sages as categorized in the original scripture.

The "ten thousand practices" refers to the specific practices cultivated sequentially throughout these stages, such as the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and so forth, up to the stage of equality (*samatā*).
Awakening—its practice should be immeasurable. These myriad practices build upon the previously explained definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and advance further into the profound and mysterious.
In essence, their root and foundation lie in the three *tathāgatagarbhas*, culminating in the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*.
This section of the sutra extends from the latter half of the seventh fascicle, where Ānanda requests his station, until the conclusion at the end where the title of the sutra is established.
This refers precisely to these myriad practices. This section corresponds to what Ānanda requested as the third name among the three:

"Wondrous Samādhi" (Miao Chan-na). The "Sixfold Śūraṅgama" is the general name for the Great Samādhi; it encompasses the three aforementioned specific titles within itself as the totality of a single samādhi.
One should know that this samādhi is fundamentally different from the common paths of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. For the common...
In the path of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one belongs entirely to the realm of effort; this, however, is not so. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha himself explains the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, saying:
"All phenomena are ultimately firm and solid. Yet the ancient masters immediately clarified that it penetrates to the very source of all dharmas.
It is immovable and indestructible. To examine its purport in detail: it is clearly established that taking the self-mind’s inherent nature as the Śūraṅgama-samādhi is primary;

how could it ever take the cessation and contemplation (śamatha-vipaśyanā) of a mind arising in response to objects as the definitive state? As for the "Seven Scriptures," this is the general title for these various sūtras.
Regarding the excellence of their phrasing, it is rooted in the Tathāgata’s refined meaning and skillful discernment, further augmented by [the commentary of] Fang...
The artisan who polished and embellished these [inscriptions] has rendered them exceedingly ornate and elegant, wondrously containing inexhaustible meaning.

Those who contemplate them and savor their flavor shall surely grasp this for themselves. ○ He Zhongnan said: "In the sutras it is said: 'Even seeing is already transcended by seeing; seeing cannot reach it.'"
The Great Buddha-Crown [Sūtra]. Attaining the nature of primordial luminous awareness that is neither born nor extinguished serves as the mind for the causal ground; this is the "Secret Cause.

The Samādhi of Illusory-like [Reality], by which one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning with a mere snap of the fingers, is the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization. The twenty-five perfect penetrations and the fifty stages constitute the true path of Bodhi; these are the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas. *Da foding* (The Great Buddha-Crown). To attain the nature of original enlightened awareness, which is neither arising nor ceasing, is to take it as the mind of the causal ground; this is the "Esoteric Cause. The "Illusory-like Samādhi," by which one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning in the snap of a finger, is the definitive teaching on cultivation and realization.
The twenty-five perfect penetrations and the fifty stages are the true path of Bodhi; these constitute the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas. *Da* (Great).
Samādhi has three meanings. First, it is called "wondrous" because this is a sublime samādhi that is inherently possessed by one's original nature;

it is spontaneously unmoving and does not depend on cultivation for its completion. Even while remaining entirely within the state of delusion amidst movement, its essence is fundamentally as it is; therefore, it is termed "wondrous."
Otherwise, how could it be the ultimate source of all dharmas, the samādhi that is immovable and indestructible?
Based on this, any practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā that does not accord with the nature itself but seeks effort elsewhere is a samādhi that is not sublime.

The second point is: This is perfect concentration (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*). It is precisely because of this concentration that not only one's own mind alone is unmoving, but all phenomena and all affairs are likewise fundamentally unmoving, constituting the single essence of concentration.

Otherwise, how could it be called the concentration in which all things are unmoving and indestructible? Based on this, anything that does not encompass the myriad existences [is not true concentration].
Those who merely control the mind alone possess concentrations that are not yet perfected. Third, it is said: This is the Great Samādhi.

Precisely because of this samādhi, even while one remains in a state of delusion, the fundamental nature has never wavered; after awakening and understanding, how could there be any further emergence or regression?

One should know that from the moment this samādhi spontaneously gives rise to understanding and the commencement of practice, until the attainment of Buddhahood through traversing the stages, [this samādhi persists].
It never withdraws; how much less could it be destroyed? If this were not so, how could it be called a samādhi that is ultimately firm and solid?
Based on this, any state involving entering, abiding, and withdrawing—even if it lasts for a long time—does not constitute a Great Samādhi.
The sutra is divided into three sections: first, the Introduction; second, the Main Body; and third, the Dissemination. Section One:
The Introduction (which includes both the General Introduction and the Specific Introduction).
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in the city of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
Together with a multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty people, all of whom were great Arhats free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
The intent of the prologue to the sutra is as follows: "Thus have I heard this Dharma from the Buddha at one time.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, where gold had been spread upon the ground. Together with the Great [Kāśyapa]...
The assembly of the Bhikṣus numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty. These individuals were all free from the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance;
they were great Arhats who had turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], and were not to be compared with those Śrāvakas of fixed destiny.

The sons of the Buddha dwell in the maintenance of the Dharma, skillfully transcending all realms of existence. They are able to perfect majestic deportment within the lands, turning the wheel of the Dharma following the Buddha and being worthy of his sublime entrustment.
They strictly purify the Vinaya and establish a grand model for the three worlds; manifesting infinite response-bodies, they deliver and liberate sentient beings.
They rescue those of the future and transcend all worldly burdens.
To speak of their virtue as great arhats in terms of their self-benefit:

they dwell securely in the palace of the Tathāgata, grasp the Dharma-seal of the Tathāgata, are able to carry out the commands of the Dharma King, and are able to succeed to the throne of the Dharma King.
This is called the Buddha-son’s abiding maintenance. Regarding the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the formless existence, he has skillfully transcended them.
Generally, in the Hinayana, transcendence is defined as exiting the three realms; thus it is not called "skillful. Now, however, one exits the three realms while remaining within them;
this is not like the fear of the three realms as if they were a prison in the past. This is the virtue of self-benefit.
Thus, regarding his benefit for others: he is able to accomplish the three thousand modes of dignified conduct within the lands of the ten directions.

Having accomplished these, he also brings beings to accomplishment; this is not like those of former times who were addicted to the tranquility of nirvana and refused to bring sentient beings to maturity.
Furthermore, he is able to assist in propagating the Buddha’s transformation, turning the Great Wheel of Dharma, and shouldering the family legacy.
He was a worthy recipient of the Tathāgata Miaokan’s final entrustment; he was not like those of former times who were incapable of receiving this Dharma.

Furthermore, his body was adorned and his mind purified by the three groups of precepts (tri-skandhaka-śīla); his words served as a model for the world, and his conduct became a standard for the world.
Thus, he establishes a great model for the three realms; it is not like the precepts of former times, which possessed leaks and deficiencies and could not serve as a standard for the three realms.
Furthermore, he can manifest immeasurable response-bodies to deliver sentient beings;
it is not like the approach of former times, which was like tuning a lute with fixed pegs—lacking skillful means. By this, he rescues future sentient beings who have fallen into [wrong] views.
Those who are pierced by thorns, he extracts them; those drowning in the mud of desire, he rescues them.

He causes them to transcend the dust of defiled roots and the burdens that weigh upon the mind, so that they do not fall into the pitfall. This is not like the practice of former times, which concerned only the single person.
It is like the solitary leap of a gazelle. Such is the virtue of benefiting others. This refers to the Great Arhat who has turned his mind toward the Buddha Vehicle.
○ Zhong Bojing’s commentary states: "The single phrase 'strictly purifying the *vinaya*' encompasses the meaning of the preceding and following passages.
*Vinaya* refers to the precepts and discipline. To be 'strict' in body and 'pure' in mind—this is the teaching of the six fascicles."
The four purities and clear instructions, as well as the seven-fascicle *Anlidaochang* (Establishment of the Path of Practice), both rely entirely upon this [text].
Phrases such as "seeing that one excellently transcends all realms of existence" and "establishing a broad model for the three worlds" all take this as their fundamental basis.
This is because this sutra regards the precepts as paramount.
Their names were: the greatly wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upāli, and Śāṭha, who served as the leaders.
What are their names? They are Mahāmati Śāriputra, here called Śāriputra; Mahāmaudgalyāyana, here called Kauṣṭhila;
Mahākauṣṭhila, here called Mahāpārśva, who was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and formerly the brahmin Dīrghanakha; and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Here...
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is translated as "Cloud-Filled Compassion. Subhūti is translated as "Born of Emptiness. Upāli Śata is translated as "Dust-Nature Emptiness.
These arhats each possessed superhuman abilities that placed them above the heads of others; thus, they served as leaders.
In the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is stated that they receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood, yet they originally followed the path of the two vehicles.

To speak of it: it culminates ultimately in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Therefore, when opening the sutra and extolling its virtues, it first mentions the *śrāvakas* and subsequently addresses the *bodhisattvas*.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* speaks of the "initial expedient" (*ādikarmika-upāya*), setting aside the two vehicles of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*, and directly denouncing them as "confused practice," placing them at the end of the ten types of false views. This is because the *Śūraṅgama* begins...

The discussion of the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna) concludes here, with nothing further remaining to be said. Therefore, in this section on praising his virtues, the discourse begins directly from the perspective of the untainted Great Arhat;
this is already a talk of the ultimate pinnacle. The *Lotus Sūtra* is like a prime minister who, having accomplished his task, withdraws from office.
To recount his background as a *xiucai* and *xiaolian*: it was by way of taking a detour and entrusting himself to these roles that he reached his goal.

The *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* is like the initial cultivation for a beginner; his father and teacher immediately instructed him to resolve to become a prime minister, forbidding him from harboring thoughts of being a *xiucai* or *xiaolian*.
This is what is meant by the "definitive meaning of cultivation and realization."
Furthermore, there were immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas, both those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those at the initial stage of the path, who together came to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the bhikṣus had concluded their summer retreat and were performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; meanwhile, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions sought to resolve their doubts and perplexities, reverently honoring the Buddha’s compassionate yet majestic presence as they sought the profound meaning of the Dharma.

Immediately, the Tathāgata arranged his seat and sat in tranquil composure, proclaiming the profound and abstruse Dharma for those within the assembly. The pure multitude at this Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before.
His kalaviṅka-like celestial voice resounded throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī was the foremost among them, yet it did not end there.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable pratyekabuddhas—those who had exhausted their ignorance and reached the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)—along with those at the initial stage of investigating reality and severing delusions; all came together to the Buddha’s presence without prior consultation.
They arrived and were drawn together by a natural affinity. At that time, it happened that the bhikṣus had completed their ninety-day summer retreat (*varṣā*).

As the days were fulfilled and the retreat concluded, they were permitted to speak freely, a day set aside to examine the virtuous deeds accomplished during those ninety days. The Bodhisattvas from the ten directions...
I shall ask freely to resolve the doubts in my mind, reverently receiving the Tathāgata’s compassion that gathers sentient beings and his majestic severity that subdues them,
while further seeking the definitive meaning of secret cultivation and secret realization. At that moment,
the Tathāgata spread out his sitting mat and dwelt in tranquil composure, proclaiming for those in the assembly the profound and esoteric Dharma.
This assembly at the pure Dharma-seat has all heard what they have never heard before and attained what they have never attained before.
Like the celestial voice of the kalaviṅka bird, it pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, hearing the Tathāgata’s voice, have all gathered at the site of enlightenment, with Mañjuśrī as their leader; for this bodhisattva—

This represents fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and serves as the eye for the discernment of dharmas (*dharma-pravicaya*). Regarding "the end of summer and the invitation to confession" (*pravāraṇā*):

when a bhikṣu reaches the beginning of the summer season, he immediately enters the retreat (*varṣā*), binding his feet to remain in seclusion and abstaining from begging for alms; this is called "the end of summer.

It is also known as "sitting in wax. As for the "invitation to confession," it refers to the day at the conclusion of the period when the retreat is lifted—specifically the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day of the seventh month.

The sixth day is the *tri-rātra* (the third day). If one knows of one's own transgressions, one may freely present them oneself; if one does not know of one's transgressions, one leaves it to the Sangha to raise the matter.
This is precisely the meaning of strictly purifying the *vinaya*, and it further demonstrates that the precepts are of paramount importance.
At that time, King Prasenajit was observing a fast on the anniversary of his father’s death and had invited the Buddha to the inner palace.

He personally went out to welcome the Tathāgata and prepared an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors. Furthermore, he personally extended invitations to the great bodhisattvas.

Within the city, there were also elders and lay devotees who were simultaneously feeding the Sangha, waiting for the Buddha to come and respond to their offerings. The Buddha then commanded Mañjuśrī to lead a portion of the bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattvas and Arhats were all invited by the various masters of the feast.
At that time, King Jayasena of Śrāvastī was observing the memorial day for his deceased father;
he invited the Buddha into the inner palace and personally went out to welcome the Tathāgata, providing a vast array of exquisite and unsurpassed delicacies.
This was the height of his devotion. Furthermore, he honored both his teachers and his disciples; moreover, he personally invited various great bodhisattvas.

At that time, there were also elders in the city whose merit and virtue flourished together, as well as lay practitioners (*gṛhapati*) who dwelt in purity, all simultaneously providing meals for the Saṃgha.
Because the Buddha could not attend to them all, he commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the bodhisattvas and [distribute the offerings].
The Arhats should attend to the various hosts of the feast to comfort the hearts of the assembly. This concludes the general introduction.
Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation; having traveled far, he had not yet returned and was unable to join the ranks of the Sangha.
Since there were neither elders nor preceptors with him, he returned alone from the road. On that day, no offerings were provided. Thereupon, Ānanda took up his alms-bowl.
As he wandered through the city, begging from door to door in sequence, he initially sought out the final donor to serve as his host for the midday meal;
whether they were pure or impure, of noble Kṣatriya lineage or even Caṇḍālas, he practiced universal compassion equally, making no distinction between the lowly and the humble.
He has resolved to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings.
Since the disciples have already been assigned their respective roles as masters of the feast, only Ānanda remains;

however, prior to the *pravāraṇā*, he had accepted an invitation from another region and, being on a distant journey and not yet returned, has no leisure to take his place among the ranks of the assembly. At that time—
Since he had traveled far away, there was neither an elder (sthavira) nor a preceptor (ācārya) to provide him with restraint and guidance.
Furthermore, as he returned alone along the way, he was not included in the ranks of the Saṃgha; thus, on that day, there would be no alms-offering for him.
Thereupon, Ānanda took up his standard begging bowl and went from door to door to beg in the city where they were traveling, his mind initially seeking the most [excellent offering].
Furthermore, regarding those donors who have never before provided meals for the Sangha or practiced giving, they shall serve as the hosts for this fast.
Whether they be pure or impure—ranging from the families of Kṣatriya kings down to the families of Caṇḍālas and butchers—I shall exercise my impartial compassion toward them all.
I do not discriminate against the lowly or the humble; I only intend to bring to full completion the immeasurable [merit] of all sentient beings.
This is a matter of merit. Yet one does not realize that as soon as there is a seeking mind, there is discrimination;
once there is discrimination, there is purity and defilement, and there is nobility and meanness. How can one then view all things with the single eye of equality?
Therefore, know that the two characters "initially seeking" are precisely where Ānanda went astray.
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for their minds not being impartial as Arhats;
he deeply revered the Tathāgata’s exposition of the unobstructed truth to resolve all doubts and slanders, and thus they passed through the city moat.
He walked slowly toward the city gates, maintaining a solemn and dignified demeanor, and prepared reverently for the ritual of the alms-gathering.

Why did he resolve to go forth on this begging tour? It was because Ānanda already knew that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, had once rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa—both of whom were Arhats—for one having abandoned the poor to follow the wealthy, and the other [having done the same].
First, [if one] abandons the wealthy to follow the poor, it would not be equitable. Now, out of my deep reverence for the Tathāgata’s words from days of yore, I have conceived this intention:
first, to expound the compassion that is equal, unobstructed, and without hindrance; second, to prevent the masses from giving rise to doubt or slanderous speech.
For if one were to direct oneself exclusively toward the poor, the wealthy would harbor suspicion. If one were to...
When he approaches wealthy households, the poor ones slander him. Because it is thus, he hangs his bowl from a high gate and begs in due order;
passing through the moats outside that city, he walks slowly within the gates of the capital, maintaining a solemn and dignified demeanor.
Thus, one should maintain solemnity and reverence in accordance with the rules of purification (*śīla*). Observing this conduct, it is clear that such a person may enter the pure but not the defiled;
they may enter the realm of the Buddha but not that of Māra; they may be a *bhikṣu* but not a *bodhisattva*.

When one views the movements of the Tathāgata as described in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*—how he puts on his robes, takes up his bowl, and enters the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food—it is naturally so.
To act with moderation and naturalness is entirely effortless; the difference between these two states is as vast as that between heaven and earth.
At that time, Ānanda, while on his almsround, passed by a brothel and was encountered by the greatly illusory Mātangī.
Using the *pāvikāra* mantra of the former Brahmā, she drew him into the chamber of lust; as his body was caressed and fondled, he was on the verge of destroying his precept-body.
At that time, Ānanda, while on his alms-round, made no discrimination and unwittingly passed by the courtesan.
In his chamber, he encountered Mahā-māyāvatī, known here as Mātangī, a woman of the "original nature" (prakṛti).

She employed a *brahmā-vidyā* mantra transmitted by the Kāpālika heretics to draw him into her bedchamber. As she drew near and touched him with her body, she sought to destroy the purity of his precepts.
Because the Venerable One’s aspiration for the Dharma had not yet ceased and his resolve remained undimmed, his mind was not [overcome].
Zeng Ping saw He Zeng and others; he intended to practice universal compassion, yet in the end he met with a murderous hand.
Thus we know that one who has not attained unimpeded mastery in all matters can never enter the mud or the water to practice universal compassion.
○ Zhong’s Commentary says: The mind aroused by Ānanda was precisely one of feeling shame for the Small Vehicle and admiring the Great; it is exactly like the Vaipulya [teachings].
Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): it is like a person who, upon leaving his house, ought to raise himself up and aim for the foremost place in the competition.

Even if he encounters bandits along the way, the encounter with bandits is simply an encounter with bandits; being the foremost is simply being the foremost. How can one claim that because of the encounter with bandits, he was not fit to be the foremost in the competition?

The Tathāgata knew that she had employed the arts of seduction; having finished his midday meal, he returned. The king, along with the great ministers, elders, and lay devotees, all came to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.
From within the light, a thousand-petaled precious lotus emerged, upon which a transformation-body Buddha sat in the full lotus posture and proclaimed a divine mantra.

He commanded Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go forth to protect [the assembly], so that malevolent spells might be extinguished. He then exhorted Ānanda and the daughter of Matanga to return to the presence of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata was then still in the royal palace, where he had been subjected to the arts of seduction; Ānanda faced a difficult situation.

Having finished his meal, he returned in haste. When the King, the ministers, the elders, and the householders saw that the Buddha did not take the time to preach the Dharma, it seemed contrary to his usual custom;
therefore, they all followed the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma. Thereupon, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred jewels from the crown of his head.
It is the light of fearlessness. There is no goodness it does not possess; hence it is called "Hundred Treasures. There is no evil it does not crush; hence it is called "Fearless.
Within this light, thousand-petaled jewel lotuses arise, manifesting this wisdom-light as the root of the myriad practices.
There is an emanation body of the Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture, who reveals this light of wisdom as the mother of all Buddhas.
The Buddha does not himself recite the mantra, but causes the emanation Buddha to proclaim this divine spell, revealing this heart of the mantra as the immovable wisdom.
This must have been spoken by the Immovable Buddha (Aksobhya). He then commanded Mañjuśrī, a person of great wisdom, to go forth bearing the mantra.
By the power of this mantra, it was applied to Māraṇḍa’s lustful faculty, just as boiling water melts ice or light dispels darkness;
thus, he caused Māraṇḍa’s fire of lust to cease instantly, and Ānanda’s precept-body returned to its original state. [The Buddha] roused and encouraged him, and he returned.
