One knows its location, yet one simply requests the true mind. Because one habitually employs the deluded mind, one protects it with all one's might;
seeing the Tathāgata point it out as a thief, though one does not speak the words, the heart nonetheless refuses to believe.
[The Buddha] clearly points out its seven locations. If one says, "Since it has a location, how can it be hastily called a thief?"—observe what follows.
The text states: "In performing all difficult practices and dharmic deeds, one employs this very mind. It further says:

"To manifest the 'conditioned mind' (yuanxin) as that which is worthy of veneration is, in fact, to secretly protect the deluded mind; it is the fundamental sentiment of mistaking a thief for one's own son, which has now been brought forth.
The Buddha explicitly stated that such a thing is impossible, and later in the text, he directly rebukes him, saying: "This is not your mind."
It is precisely because this mind is a thief and not a son that one need not seek its location.

If it were the eternally abiding true mind, then it could exist within the seven locations, it could not exist within the seven locations, and it could also be neither existing nor non-existing therein.
The old commentary does not speak of "breaking the mind" (poxin), but rather of "seeking the mind" (zhengxin); this refers to the three [aspects of] suchness.
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) likewise cannot be added beyond these seven locations.
Therefore, that which is being investigated is precisely the eternally abiding true mind. Such seemingly plausible words constitute no small betrayal of the Sūtra. ○ He said:

"The refutation of the mind in the seven locations is still called the refutation of consciousness in the seven locations; it does not mean that this consciousness actually has a fixed location. Ānanda—
I know it; yet the Buddha alone knows it. It is precisely because this consciousness fundamentally has no location that sentient beings are deluded into thinking it has one.

Therefore, as they cling to it, I shatter it at every turn, desiring them to realize in each instance that this consciousness fundamentally has no location, thereby causing them to doubt this false consciousness.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike take their conscious mind to reside within the body.
Even when observing the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they are seen to be on the Buddha’s face;
yet when I now observe these four sensory objects of the floating roots [the eyes], they are found only on my own face. Thus, this conscious mind must truly reside within the body."
This was the Venerable One’s first demonstration of the spear-method, maintaining his mind within. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, among the twelve modes of birth in all the worlds, excluding the formless realm because it is empty and dispersed and lacks corporeal characteristics, and excluding the realm of non-perception because it is like earth or wood and lacks mental characteristics—of the remaining ten types of beings,"
Those who possess the perception of a body and mind likewise maintain that the conscious mind resides within the body.
Furthermore, even when I observe the Tathāgata’s eyes—bright, pure, cultivated, and expansive like the petals of a blue lotus—they too are situated upon the Buddha’s face.
Now, as I observe this coarse and superficial faculty of the physical eye, which is daily entangled with the four objects of form, sound, smell, and touch, it resides only here.
My face—thus, from the sages down to the commoners, it is none other than that the eyes are on the outside while the mind is within.
How could I not know that such a discerning mind truly dwells inside my body?
Although you, Venerable Sir, possess such clever and sharp wit, acting as if no one else exists, you do not realize that your crown has already touched the ground. Even now, three...
"O Child, let us test his mind. He immediately pointed to his chest and said, "That which resides within.

This arises from the very beginning of receiving form within the parents' womb; by absorbing the two drops of red and white, the body is formed, and this grasping occurs spontaneously without waiting for instruction.
It is called co-emergent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*), and it is also called the stubborn delusion.
Because of this perception, one firmly clings to this body as the dwelling place of the mind. Like a goose in a jar or a frog in a well, one is ultimately unable to emerge;
furthermore, one does not realize that the body is actually within the mind, like a single bubble upon the great ocean. Thus, the Venerable One also holds this same view.
If the Venerable One were to direct his mind toward the location where the mind resides and inquire into it, he would recognize [the truth].
Dītóu then took the World-Honored One’s hand and walked together with him, strolling freely through the ocean of awakening.

How could there be the various subsequent deluded attachments? It is precisely because of this single calculation that all sentient beings are imprisoned within the womb-prison, shackled by their physical bodies, and even submerged in the three miserable realms, undergoing immeasurable suffering as they transmigrate.
That they cannot liberate themselves all stems from this. The false teachers of the world even say that the body is the dwelling and the mind is the master;

how truly lamentable! Zong said: "The mind is within the body" is the habitual attachment of all sentient beings, whereby they take what is called the state of confused turmoil to be the nature of the mind. Thus, through a single delusion, it becomes the mind.

It is precisely this that constitutes the delusion regarding the physical body as being within [the self]. As for the other six [elements], they were merely driven by the Buddha at one time to abandon their positions and forced to adopt alternative calculations.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You are now here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall; look at the Jeta Grove—where is it now?"
“World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion, the Pure Lecture Hall, is located in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, which is now the Jeta Grove;
yet it is actually outside the hall. “Ānanda, what did you first see within the hall? “World-Honored One, while inside the hall, I first saw the Tathāgata, and next I observed the great assembly.
Only after looking out in this manner did my gaze fall upon the grove and garden. “Ānanda, as for your gazing at the grove and garden...”
"For what reason was there a view? World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall were wide open, I, while inside the hall, was able to look out from afar.
The Venerable One held his mind within and took it for granted, like a strong man bristling with spirit as he soars upward toward the Ox and Dipper constellations."

The World-Honored One is the Omniscient One. He perceives the innermost depths of one's heart with penetrating clarity; he does not merely analyze words and phrases or elaborate upon commentaries and sub-sections.
Instead, he employs commonplace and easily understood matters before one’s eyes to cross-examine them, compelling others to answer with their own mouths, leaving no room for evasion.
Thereafter, using the claws of the Dharma-cave, he captures them alive and in hand. Therefore...
First, having carefully determined the boundaries of the internal and external, he addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda, you are currently sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall.
Look at the Jeta Grove; where is it now located? Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall is within Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
As for the Jeta Grove, it is actually outside the hall; the hall is situated within the grove."
The grove is outside the hall; thus, the distinction between the internal and external realms is established. Next, one must further examine and determine the sequence of perceptions.
He asked: "Ānanda, within this hall, what do you first see? He replied: "World-Honored One, while I am inside the hall, I first see the Tathāgata, and next I observe the great assembly.
Only when looking out in this manner do my eyes finally fall upon the gardens and groves. Thus, he first saw [the internal].
Only after perceiving the internal does one perceive the external; thus, the sequence of perception must not be disordered. Next, he further examines the cause for perceiving the external. He asks:
"Ānanda, when you gaze upon the grove and garden, by what cause is there seeing? He replies: "World-Honored One..."
This great lecture hall has its doors and windows wide open; therefore, while I am within the hall, I am able to see far off.
Because the doors and windows are wide open, one is able to see the outside; thus, seeing is not without a cause. The World-Honored One asked three times, and the Venerable One answered three times;
in each instance, he fell into the World-Honored One’s trap. Below, [the text] uses those very words to refute them.

This is what is meant by "taking up your spear to pierce your shield. The World-Honored One raised many difficult questions concerning the seven locations, which also contained the implication that the nature of seeing is the mind and not the eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden-hued arm and stroked the crown of Ānanda’s head. He then informed Ānanda and the entire assembly:
"There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices."

"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all transcend through a single gate upon the path of wondrous adornment. Listen attentively now, Ānanda! Ānanda prostrated himself and humbly received the compassionate instruction.
This first demonstrates the essence of the Great Samādhi as the foundation for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. At this point, Ānanda—
He asked about the initial expedient means for wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna.
The World-Honored One, in turn, questioned him regarding his initial aspiration to examine whether his understanding and vision were true or delusory.

Consequently, Ānanda employed the consciousness-mind to grasp at a Tathāgata with perceptible characteristics, yet he remained confused regarding his own true Buddha, which is without perceptible characteristics.

When the Tathāgata further questioned him regarding the conditions for the thirty-two marks, asking whom he saw and whom he delighted in, the Venerable One replied that it was with his eyes that he saw and with his mind that he delighted.
The Tathāgata then further inquired as to the place from which the mind and the eyes arise.
The Venerable One was certain that this mind resides within the physical body.
At this point, Ānanda’s criminal nature had been exposed; the evidence was present, leaving no room for concealment.
Now, wishing to advance and refute him, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm from amidst the great assembly and stroked Ānanda’s head, manifesting compassion and gathering him in.
Accept this meaning. Announce it to Ānanda and the great assembly: there is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices.
It is the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.
Listen attentively now. This Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is all-pervasive and all-encompassing; there is no dharma that it does not contain.
There is no practice that is not perfected. Yet, it cannot be known through cognition, nor can it be seen through vision.
It is the father of Bodhisattvas and the mother of all Buddhas; indeed, my thirty-two marks are all manifestations appearing within this very state.
Why, then, do you mistakenly identify it as being inside the physical body? Now, you wish to investigate supreme enlightenment and open [the way].
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision must first recognize this mark of the invisible crown of the head; then, without practicing *śamatha*, one spontaneously achieves *śamatha*;
without practicing *samādhi*, one spontaneously achieves *samādhi*; without practicing *dhyāna*, one spontaneously achieves *dhyāna*.
This is called the Samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*), also named the Samādhi of One Practice (*ekavyūha-samādhi*), and further termed the King of All Samādhis, Śūraṅgama. Among all samādhis...
Among all samādhis, this is the most supreme. When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, the myriad practices are fully perfected;
in every thought-moment they can realize the true and eternal, and in every instance they can reach the ultimate.

All Tathāgatas of the ten directions rely upon this single gateway to transcend to the wondrously adorned ocean of fruition, without encountering bypaths or further detours. What cause for concern could there be?

"Is this not due to the fault of my failure to accumulate learning, or the incompleteness of my power of the Way? Thereupon, Ānanda prostrated himself in worship and humbly received the compassionate instruction.
Question: Why is it that in this passage *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (dhyāna) are not specifically mentioned, while only *samādhi* is singled out?
Why is this? The answer is: this samādhi is precisely the "Great Dhāraṇī Gate" (Mahādhāraṇīmukha) referred to in the subsequent text;
it is the sublime path of practice for all samādhis. Through it, śamatha is awakened to, and through it, dhyāna is realized. Therefore, it is called the "Illusion-like Samādhi.
By snapping one's fingers, one transcends the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa); for apart from this single gate, there is no other cultivation.
The path of practice is precisely that of the ancient Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata; it is also called "entering samādhi through hearing, contemplating, and cultivating.

*Samādhi* here is translated as "equanimous holding" (*samādhāna*). Since this is a common name for all meditative concentrations and a general designation for the entirety of such states, it does not refer to the *samādhi* among the three names requested by Ānanda; that [latter] is a specific category within the general class.

This is the distinction. Titles such as "The Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*) are specifically the names of this samādhi. What is taught throughout the entire sutra is entirely for the sake of this samādhi;
these [other titles] are merely incidental designations attached to it. Zhong said: Ānanda requested instruction on the Great Samādhi, and the Buddha first demolished his "conditioned mind.
This was the first instance of demolishing the mind. Before the question-and-answer session had concluded, [the Buddha] urgently revealed [the truth].
"Because there is samādhi," and so forth. This is intended to suppress the soul that has suddenly returned and to comfort the mind that first raised the inquiry.
It is like a destitute son who, upon seeing his father, is first told of the family treasures so that he may know in advance where food and clothing are provided;
once his alarm is settled and his breath is calm, the father then gradually questions him, concluding the text with the seven refutations. Hereafter...
Examining the Great Samādhi in detail: it is not only that his heart and mind are profoundly compassionate, but also that his words are most wonderful.
There is not a single character that fails to evoke deep reflection; for instance, when he said, "The samādhi you have requested already exists here;

there is no need for haste," this corresponds to the "wondrously adorned path of transcending through a single gate. This "transcending through a single gate" is the cause, while "entering deeply through a single gate" is the effect.
"Transcending through a single gate" refers to the fruit [of realization]. Because one enters by means of the Great Samādhi, it is called the "path.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is as you have said: while the body is in the lecture hall, with doors and windows wide open, one gazes afar at the groves and gardens."
"Furthermore, there may be sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata, yet see those outside the hall.
Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, it is impossible for one to be inside the hall and not see the Tathāgata, yet be able to see the groves and springs.
"Ānanda, you are just like that. Your mental essence is all-encompassing and clearly aware. If the mind that is currently clearly aware before you were truly [located elsewhere]..."

Within the body. At that time, one must first thoroughly understand the internal mind. Are there any sentient beings who first perceive within their own bodies and only afterwards observe external objects?
Even if they cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, they certainly ought to clearly perceive the growth of nails and hair, the shifting of tendons, and the throbbing of the pulses.
How could they not know this? If they do not know what is within, how can they know what is without? Therefore, you should understand that what you said—
That the mind capable of cognition and awareness dwells within the body—this is impossible.
This refutes the notion that the mind does not reside within. The Buddha again reiterated his inquiry and addressed Ānanda:
"According to what you say, the body is in the lecture hall, with doors and windows wide open, and only then can one gaze afar at the gardens and groves; there are also many [people]..."
“Śāriputra, while inside this hall, have you not seen the Tathāgata? Have you instead first seen what is outside the hall?
Ānanda replied, “World-Honored One, it has never happened that one could see the groves and springs while being inside the hall and failing to see the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda, what you are now considering is precisely the case of being inside the hall and failing to see the Tathāgata, yet being able to see what is outside.”

This is the nature of forests and springs. Why is this so? If your spirit of enlightened awareness were located at the gates of the six sense organs—vividly clear and unclouded, constantly cognizant and fully aware—and if the mind that you currently perceive with such clarity actually resided within your body, then you ought first to be able to perceive the things inside your body.
Could there be any sentient being who first perceives their own body...?
Is it that one first dwells within the viscera and only thereafter observes external objects? Indeed, the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach are the most profound parts of the body;
it might be permissible for these to remain unseen. Yet, as for the growth of nails and hair, the turning of tendons and the throbbing of vessels—how can these be ignored?
That which is superficial within the body should indeed be clearly understood; how is it that you know nothing of either the deep or the shallow?
If your mind cannot know what is internal, how can it also know what is external?
To know the external without knowing the internal—how is this different from being inside a hall and not seeing the Tathāgata, yet being able to see the forests and springs outside?
This is different. I certainly do not perceive it internally, yet I know for certain that this mind does not reside within the body.
Therefore, you should understand that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious awareness dwells within the body—is impossible.
This single refutation alone will cause those with the karmic affinity to be startled into awakening and fall prostrate in realization.

Apart from the sublime scriptures of the Buddha, how could one ever have heard such a teaching in other books—that the mind does not reside within the body? How extraordinary! This is truly the Lion’s Roar.
The heart, liver, spleen, and stomach are the deep recesses. Yet, as the nails grow and the hair lengthens, the tendons shift and the vessels quiver. To compare...
[The Master replied: "Superficially so. However, they are all things belonging to the body.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and said to the Buddha: "Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, I have realized that my mind truly resides outside the body.
Why is this? It is like a lamp burning within a room; that lamp must certainly be able to..."
First it illuminates the interior of the room; then from the door of that room, it reaches the courtyard.
All sentient beings do not see within their own bodies, but see only outside their bodies, just as a lamp placed outside a room cannot illuminate the interior. This principle is necessarily clear.
"May there be no further delusion; may this accord with the Buddha’s definitive meaning (nītārtha) and not be false?
This second attachment holds that the mind resides outside. Ānanda bowed his head and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, I now realize that my mind indeed does not reside within; it truly dwells outside the body."
Why is this? Let us take the analogy of a lamp. For example, if a lamp is lit within a room, that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room;
then, through its doorway, it subsequently reaches the courtyard, illuminating gradually as it proceeds.
This is just like the mind, which dwells within the body and must first perceive what is internal before perceiving what is external. Now, all...
Sentient beings do not perceive [the light] within their own bodies, but see it only outside the body.
This is just like a lamp placed outside a room, which cannot illuminate the interior of that room. This principle is decisively clear and free from doubt;
is it not identical to the Buddha’s discourse on the definitive meaning? Could there be any error or delusion in this?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "These bhikṣus have just now followed me from Śrāvastī, begging for alms-food along the way and returning to the Jeta Grove.
I have already finished my meal. Look at these bhikṣus: when one person eats, are all the others satisfied?"
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are all arhats, their bodies and lifespans differ;
how could one person cause the multitude to be satiated?"
The World-Honored One is a great master of the Great Hand (Mahāmudrā). If it comes from the left, he turns to the left; if it comes from the right, he turns to the right.
Whether on this side or that, there is nothing acceptable and nothing unacceptable. Whether within or without, all may be swept away. I shall also offer a parable in response:
what is called "plum for peach" or "returning an ox for a horse. The Buddha told Ānanda: "These bhikṣus have just..."
"Come with me to the city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms from house to house for food.
Upon our return to the Jeta Grove, I shall have already finished my meal. Observe this bhikṣu:
when one person eats, can it cause all these people to be fully satiated? Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus..."
All of them are arhats. Although their fetters as sons are exhausted, the fetters of the fruit still remain;
they cannot merge with the multitude into a single entity. How then could one person eat and cause the multitude to be satiated?

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If the mind that perceives, knows, and sees were actually located outside the body—existing externally to both the body and the mind, such that they were mutually unrelated—then what the mind knows, the body would not perceive; and what the body perceives at its own boundaries, the mind would not know."
"I now show you my hand of tūla-cotton. When you see it with your eyes, does your mind not discern it?
Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, "If they are mutually cognizant, why would one be 'external'? Therefore, you should know this."
Your claim that the mind which perceives and knows dwells outside the body is impossible.
This is precisely to refute the notion that the mind does not reside within. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If the mind that perceives, knows, and sees were truly located outside the body, then since the body and mind would be external to one another, they would have no mutual connection whatsoever."
That which is to be known by the mind cannot be perceived by the body; that which is perceived by the body cannot be known by the mind.
It is like the physical bodies and life-forces of Arhats, which are distinct: what satisfies one does not satisfy another, and what satisfies another does not satisfy this one.
I now show you my hand, as fine as *tūla* cotton, with the color of fragrant frost; when your eyes see it, your mind discriminates it as "this is a hand."
"No," Ānanda replied, "it is so, World-Honored One. When my eye sees, the mind discriminates. The Buddha told Ānanda, "Seeing with the eye is the cognition of the body;
discriminating with the mind is the cognition of the mind. These two cognitions occur simultaneously."
There has never been a duality of substance; this is not like the distinction made between an Arhat and others, separating one from another.
Since it is precisely this consciousness that knows, how can you judge that the mind which perceives and knows resides outside the body? Therefore, you should know:
your claim that the mind capable of awareness and cognition dwells outside the body is impossible. Ānanda, light a paper lamp for the world...
The Venerable One saw it, but it was instantly extinguished by the World-Honored One’s single breath.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, because one does not see within, it does not dwell inside the body;
yet because the body and mind know each other and are not separate, it is not outside the body. As I now reflect, it must reside in a single location. The Buddha—

[The Buddha] asked, "Where is its location now? Ānanda replied, "This cognizant mind, since it does not know what is within yet can see what is without, as I have reflected upon it, must be hidden deep within the sense organs.
It is like someone taking a crystal bowl and placing it over both eyes;
although something covers them, there is no obstruction. That organ follows what is seen and immediately makes distinctions. Thus, I perceive and understand."
The mind capable of knowing does not perceive the internal because it resides within the sense organs; it clearly gazes outward without obstruction because it is hidden within the organs.
This is the third hypothesis: that [the mind] is hidden within the organs. Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said...”
"Because it perceives the internal, it does not reside within the body; yet because the mind and body are mutually aware, it is not outside the body.
Since neither 'internal' nor 'external' is established, I now reflect that it must reside in a single location. The Buddha said, "Where, then, is this location?
Ānanda replied, "This cognizing mind, being unable to know the internal while yet being able to see the external, as I ponder it, seems to be hidden within the faculty of the eye."
It is like this: suppose there were a person who took a lapis lazuli bowl and placed it over both eyes. Although something was covering them, it did not obstruct their vision.

That faculty of sight saw whatever was before it and immediately made distinctions accordingly. Here, the lapis lazuli is used as a metaphor for the eye, and the eye is used as a metaphor for the mind.
Just as the lapis lazuli covering the eye does not hinder the eye from seeing or from making distinctions, it is the same as with the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
The mind unites with objects, yet the mind’s vision is not obstructed by its mental discrimination.

Now, as for this mind of mine that is aware and capable of cognition—why is it that it does not see within but sees without? Since it already resides in the sense organs, and the organs themselves are not located within, it is only natural that it does not see within.
Furthermore, since it is latent within the organs, and the organs are like lapis lazuli, it is only natural that...
It gazes outward without obstruction. Thus, it is simply this single submerged faculty (*āyatana*), and with respect to the two preceding meanings, there is no error whatsoever.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said, that which is submerged within the faculty is like beryl (*vaidūrya*); that person should, by means of it..."
If one were to cover the eyes with a lapis lazuli cage and look at mountains and rivers, would one see the lapis lazuli? "Yes, World-Honored One;
that person would truly see the lapis lazuli because of the lapis lazuli cage covering the eyes. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your mind were united with the lapis lazuli in this way,"
One constantly sees mountains and rivers; why does one not see the eye? If one were to see the eye, the eye would be identical to its objects, and thus could not function as that which follows them.
If it cannot be seen, how can you say that this cognizing consciousness lies hidden within the sense organ, like being enclosed in crystal?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious cognition dwells hidden within the sense organs like a crystal vessel—is untenable.
This directly refutes the notion that the mind is latent within the roots. The World-Honored One, taking their error as a point of departure, addressed Ānanda, saying: "As for..."
"As for what you said regarding the sense organs being hidden within, it is like beryl.
When that person covers their eyes with a beryl lens, do they see only the mountains and rivers, or do they also see the beryl? Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One.
When that person covers their eyes with a beryl lens, they indeed see the beryl. The Buddha then refuted him, saying, "Your mind..."
If it were joined with the eye-faculty in the same way that [a mirror] is joined with lapis lazuli, one should see mountains and rivers; why then does one not see the eye?
In the analogy, the eye sees both the mountains and rivers and the lapis lazuli. In the dharma-reality, since the mind sees the mountains and rivers, it should likewise see the eye.
Why, then, is it not seen? If the mind were able to see the eye, the eye would, in turn, become...

If the object of focus for the mind is not the faculty that produces [cognition], then your thesis—that those faculties see and immediately differentiate—cannot be established; this constitutes the fault of contradicting one's own words.
Furthermore, if the mind does not see the eye, why then does the eye see lapis lazuli? This also commits the fault of the dissimilarity between the principle and the illustration.

This is erroneous. If this were so, both [theories] would fail to be established. How can you maintain that the mind capable of cognition and awareness dwells hidden within the sense organ like a crystal vessel?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind which perceives and knows dwells hidden inside the organ like a crystal—is untenable.
Ānanda then took up the crystal bowl and held it out to challenge the World-Honored One.
"Furthermore, that wealthy man was ground into fine powder by the World-Honored One.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have now reflected in this way: within the body of a sentient being, the internal organs reside inside while the orifices are situated on the outside.
Where there are organs, there is darkness; where there are orifices, there is light. Now, as I stand before the Buddha, I have opened [my eyes]."
Seeing light with the eyes is called seeing the external; closing the eyes and seeing darkness is called seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?

This is the fourth pair of calculations regarding the internal and external. First, he calculates that [the seer] is within; the Buddha refutes this by stating that one does not see the internal organs.

Next, he calculates that it is outside; this again invites the difficulty of the body and mind being separated. Furthermore, he calculates that it is hidden within the sense organ; yet this too deviates from the truth.
Regarding the analogy of the lapis lazuli cage for the eyes, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected in this way:
within the body of these sentient beings, the internal organs reside inside while the orifices are situated outside.

It is because there are internal organs that it is dark; it is because there are orifices that it is bright. Now, as I face the Buddha, it is by virtue of having orifices that it is bright; therefore, I open my eyes."
When one sees light, one should immediately see what is external; it is not necessary to insist that this is outside the characteristics of the body and mind.

Because there is darkness due to the internal organs, seeing darkness when the eyes are closed is equivalent to seeing the interior; it does not necessarily mean one is seeing the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach.
If the internal and external were established as such, and it were not merely hidden within the roots [of the eyes], then one might avoid the three aforementioned faults.
However, I do not know whether this principle is correct or not; because I have failed three times, I have not yet dared to be self-confident.
○ Zhong said: "Because there is an aperture, there is brightness; therefore, when the eyes are opened, one sees brightness. Because there is...
The internal organs are dark; therefore, when one closes the eyes, one sees darkness. Seeing light is called seeing the external, while seeing darkness is called seeing the internal.

Although "internal" and "external" are presented as a pair, this merely borrows the perception of external forms to perceive the internal; it nonetheless remains rooted in the original attachment to an internal locus.
Thus, in the following passage, the Buddha refutes only the notion of seeing the internal.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and see darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye or not?
If it faces the eye, the darkness is in front of the eye; how then can it be considered 'internal'? If it were internal,"

Dwelling within a dark room where there is no sun, moon, or lamp—this dark room is entirely composed of your own internal organs. If these were not present before you, how could seeing be established?
This destruction of the darkness of views is called "seeing internally. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As you have said, when you close your eyes and see darkness, does this objective realm of darkness face the eye, or does it not face the eye?
If this appearance of darkness faces the eye, then that appearance of darkness would be in front of your eyes; how then could it be considered 'closing the eyes'?"
To see darkness is called "seeing internally. If you were to grant that the darkness before one's eyes is indeed the internal viscera, then there would be no need to close one's eyes;

simply by staying in a dark room where there is no light from the sun, moon, or lamps, this darkness before the eyes would be your *trijaṭharāgni* (the three *jiaos*) and six *fu* organs. But how could such a thing be possible? If...
This characteristic of darkness does not confront the eye. How then can one see darkness before the eyes?
Thus, whether the eye confronts the characteristic of darkness or does not confront it, neither case establishes an internal [organ].
If you set aside external vision and consider what is established through internal confrontation: when you close your eyes and see darkness, you call this "within the body";
when you open your eyes and see light, why do you not see your own face? If you do not see your face, then internal confrontation is not established.

If seeing your face were established, then this cognizing mind and the eye-faculty would reside in empty space; how could they be said to be within? If they were in empty space, they would not be your own substance.
The Tathāgata now beholds your face; this is also your own body. Your eyes already know [the face], yet your body should not perceive it.
If you insist that both body and eyes perceive, there would have to be two cognitions; thus, your single body would become two Buddhas.
Therefore, you should know this: your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal" is untenable.
Furthermore, regarding your statement that seeing darkness constitutes seeing the internal, could it not be asked:
is the darkness you perceive not external darkness facing the body from without, but rather internal darkness facing the viscera within the body? If it were separate from external [darkness]...
[Objection: It is seen. That which is accomplished through internal confrontation is precisely the eye’s ability to look back upon itself.

Since it can look back, it ought to be able to do so both with eyes closed and with eyes open. Now, when the eyes are closed and one sees darkness, one is uniquely able to look back at the body within;
yet when the eyes are open and one sees light, why cannot one likewise look back at one's own face? If, at the time when the eyes are open, [it is not so]...
If one were able to look back at one's own face, then even when the eyes are closed, one would still be able to look back at the interior of the body;

yet this internal facing does not occur. If you claim that when the eyes are open and seeing light, one can also see the face, then this cognizing mind and the eye faculty must both reside within empty space. Yet you originally reckoned that the mind remains inside. Furthermore...
How can it be said to exist within? Furthermore, since the eye and mind already abide in empty space, then empty space itself must be your own substance;

conversely, your body would no longer be your substance. If you insist that seeing the face while separated from the body does not preclude it from still being one's own substance, then the Tathāgata would likewise be separated from your body, yet he too sees your face—and by that logic, he too should be you.
Is it your body? Furthermore, since your mind and eyes are already in empty space and possess sensation and cognition, this body of yours ought to be devoid of sensation and cognition.

If you insist that the body itself possesses sensation while the eyes in the air also possess their own cognition, then your single body would have two cognitions: one in empty space and one in your own person. Since...
If there were two cognitions, then your single body would have to become two Buddhas; is such a principle possible?

Therefore, you should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing within" is without foundation. [The Master] concludes the section on "seeing within" alone, which is sufficient to show that this calculation [of seeing darkness] is likewise situated within.
One must understand the distinction between calculating it as being within, calculating it as being without, calculating it as hidden within the sense organ, and calculating both together as within.
Externally, it has never not been so; however, because Ānanda clung to the traces and gave rise to emotional attachments, every word he asked became a sickness.
The World-Honored One, according to the situation, untied his bonds, so that every word in his response became medicine. An ancient worthy said: "If you can understand this..."
Thus, dead phrases all become living phrases; if one does not understand, living phrases all become dead phrases.
The marvelous and divine transforms into the putrid and corrupt, and the putrid and corrupt again transforms back into the marvelous and divine. Truly, there is no fixed dharma.

These four preceding reckonings were all because the World-Honored One’s question, "How do you know that which is external? acted as a hook to stir Ānanda. Therefore, the Venerable One abandoned one [view] while grasping another.

It is said that those who rely on words lose [the truth], and those who cling to phrases are deluded. Regarding the three subsequent calculations, their views and knowledge have already reached their limit.

Yet they further cite the profound meaning of the nature and characteristics spoken by the World-Honored One, drawing out branches from the vines and giving rise to false speculations, not realizing that "if it is correct, it is entirely correct;
if it is incorrect, it is entirely incorrect."
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. As I now reflect—this very act of reflection is my own mind-nature.
Wherever it conjoins with something, the mind appears accordingly; yet it does not abide in any of the three locations: within, without, or in between."
"This fifth calculation holds that the mind resides wherever it happens to conjoin with an object. Ānanda said, "All that I have previously stated was merely my own speculative view.
I have often heard from the Buddha himself as he formerly revealed to the fourfold assembly: 'Because the mind arises...'"
Various phenomena arise; because phenomena arise, various states of mind arise.
As I now reflect upon the arising of mind and phenomena as taught by the Blessed One, that which is capable of this reflection is truly my own nature of mind.
This mind, in conjunction with whichever phenomenon it encounters, arises in accordance with that very phenomenon. Why must it necessarily exist internally, externally, or in between?
"Does this mean there is an interval between the three locations? You do not understand what the World-Honored One meant by 'the arising of mental dharmas from the mind.

This simply means that all mental dharmas arise through the transformation of the karmic consciousness; they are simultaneously and falsely existent, like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
There are no dharmas apart from the mind, and no mind apart from dharmas. It does not mean that the mind can produce dharmas, nor that dharmas can produce the mind, Venerable Sir."
You have mistakenly recognized the mutual arising of mind and phenomena; thus, you calculate that they arise in conjunction with one another.
You first cite what the World-Honored One has said as evidence, wishing thereby to silence the Tathāgata. Little do you know that the Tathāgata is a sword from head to toe—touch him and you die;
he brooks no sentimentality at all. ○ Nor does Ānanda mean to say that the mind must possess a physical substance. It is precisely...
This means that although the mind has no substantial entity, it is capable of conjunction. Conjunction is precisely where the mind resides.

The following text correctly argues that whatever possesses conjunction must possess a substantial entity; that which lacks an entity cannot conjoin, and if there is no conjunction, there is no place of residence.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have now said—that because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise, and that wherever there is a point of conjunction, the mind follows and exists—this mind has no substance;
thus, there would be nothing with which to conjoin. If it were possible to conjoin while having no substance,"
Thus, the claim that nineteen elements arise from the conjunction of seven objects is incorrect.

If they possess a substantial entity, then when you prick your own body with your hand, does the consciousness that perceives this emerge from within, or does it enter from without? If it emerges from within, [how could it perceive the external object?]
If it were to come from outside, one should first see [the mind] within the body.
This directly refutes the notion that the mind does not accord with its point of contact. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Now you say that because of the arising of dharmas, various minds arise; wherever there is a point of contact, the mind exists accordingly. As for what is called 'contact,' it is like a lid."
To join two things together, they must both possess substantial existence; only then can they be joined. Now, the mind that you contemplate is fundamentally a floating thought;
it truly has no self-substance. Since it lacks self-substance, there is no place for it to join.

If you claim that something without substance can still join with another, then you would have to add a nineteenth realm beyond the eighteen realms, and add a seventh sense-object beyond the six objects.
A single speck of dust—all these lack substance and are mere empty names, identical to the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. Upon what basis could one discuss their conformity?
If they possessed substance, it would be like you using your own hand to poke your own body. As for this mind that you know: does it emerge from within, or does it enter from without?
If there were emergence and entry, there must necessarily be an internal and an external. Since there is already an internal and an external...

If one were to see the internal simply by meeting with the external, one would again fall back into the error previously refuted; how could perception arise merely in accordance with such conjunction?

To claim that things exist in accordance with their conjunction, rushing headlong in confusion and agitation, is no different from a wild fire. Yet you still mistake this for the True Mind—this exhaustively describes the deluded state of worldly people.
Ānanda said, "I see with this eye; I know with the mind that it is not the eye. Therefore, 'seeing' is not the function of the eye.
The Buddha said, "If the eye were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see? Furthermore, among those who have already died, their eyes still remain;
they should all be able to see objects. If they could see objects, how could they be called dead?"
Upon hearing the statement that "the internal face sees," Ānanda immediately gave rise to doubt and difficulty, thinking:
"The eye may be called 'seeing,' and the mind may be called 'knowing. That which sees is the eye; the mind’s cognition is not the eye.

Now, to take the mind as the seer seems inconsistent with the meaning. The Buddha refuted this, saying: "That which is seen is the object; that which is able to see is the mind. For now, let us consider..."
You represent the mind, and the door represents the eye. Although the door allows for seeing, there must first be "you" within the door before seeing occurs.
If you claim that the eye can see by itself, then even if you were inside the room, it would be as if you did not exist at all.

Can the gate itself see? Thus we know that although the eye has the capacity for universal vision, it must have consciousness within the locus of the eye before seeing occurs. If there were no consciousness, how could the eye possibly see?
If one were to claim that the eye alone can see, then all those who are already dead—since they still possess eyes—should likewise perceive objects. If they do perceive objects, [then...]
Furthermore, it cannot be called "death. This means that it is merely a case of not seeing with the eyes; both what can be seen and what is known through vision all belong to the mind.
How could one falsely divide vision and attribute it solely to the eyes?
Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that perceives and is capable of knowing: if it must have a substantial body, does it have a single body or many bodies?
Now, while residing within your own person, does it pervade the entire body or not pervade it?

If it were a single body, then when you prick one limb with your hand, your other three limbs should feel it. If all of them felt it, then the location of the prick would be indeterminate. If [you say] the prick...
If it has a location, then your single body could not be established as such. If it were multiple bodies, then you would become many people; which body, then, would be "you"?
If it were an all-pervading body, it would be the same as the previous case of being pricked. If it were not all-pervading, then when you touch your head, you would also be touching your feet;
yet while the head experiences sensation, the feet should remain without cognition. But this is not the case for you. Therefore, you should know that according to where [the sensation occurs]...
It is impossible for the mind to exist wherever [the body] is joined.
Indeed, dharmas have fixed characteristics, whereas the mind has no fixed substance; it is just like a gourd on water: press it down and it turns.
The sun is a jewel among stones; its color has no fixed form—how could it have a fixed substance?
Ānanda, furthermore, if that mind of yours which perceives and knows must necessarily have a substance, I shall ask you: does it have a single substance or many substances?
If it has a single substance, then the four limbs share one and the same mental substance. If it has many substances, then each of the four limbs would have its own separate substance.
This is the substance of the mind. Furthermore, as for your mind now within your body, does it pervade the entire body or not pervade the entire body?
If it pervades the entire body, then the single mind fills all four limbs. If it does not pervade the entire body, then the single mind does not fill the four limbs.
If the four limbs share one common substance of the mind, then plucking out a single hair should cause all the other hairs to move.
When one limb is touched, the entire body perceives it. If the entire body perceives it, then the point of contact would have no fixed location.
If the point of contact had a fixed location, then the body could not constitute a single entity.
If there were multiple entities, then there would be many people, for a single person possesses only a single mind; multiple minds would constitute multiple people. Because there are many...
If each person were to divide their own mind and divide their own body, then among these many bodies, which one would be you?
If it were the entire body, then as before, when one limb is pricked, all four limbs should feel it.
If it were not the entire body, then when you touch your head, you would simultaneously touch your feet; yet if the head perceives while the feet do not, how could that be called [a single self]?
"It is not all-pervasive. Yet, you are not like that either. When the head is touched, the head knows; when the foot is touched, the foot knows. Can this be called 'not all-pervasive'?
Therefore, the substance of the mind is neither one nor many, neither pervasive nor non-pervasive; it fundamentally has no fixed substance."

Since it has no fixed substance, it can be known that it does not conform to things that possess fixed existence. Therefore, one should know: wherever there is conformity, the mind would likewise exist;
such a thing is impossible. Ānanda, taking his "pumpkin seal" and flaunting his cleverness, was once again cast by the World-Honored One into the depths of the great ocean.
—Zhong (Note: The character "鍾" [zhōng] at the end likely serves as a signature or a mark of the compiler/annotator.)
It is said: It is not a single entity, nor many entities; it is not a pervasive entity, nor a non-pervasive entity. It is, in all cases, without entity.
How can that which is without entity have conjunction?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have also heard the Buddha discourse with Mañjuśrī and other Dharma-princes on the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One also said: 'The mind is neither within nor without.

As I reflect upon this, there is nothing seen within, and there is no mutual cognition without. Because there is no cognition within, its existence within is not established. [Yet] body and mind cognize one another..."

The external is not the object [of cognition], because they are mutually cognizant; yet, since there is no seeing within, it must exist in between. (Note: The character "bu" [not] in the phrase "wai bu xiangzhi" is likely an error for the character "you" [also/furthermore]).
This is the sixth consideration regarding the intermediate state. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, in the past when I heard the Buddha and Mañjuśrī and the other Dharma-Princes discussing the true nature of reality, the World-Honored One also said that the mind is neither within nor without.
To say it is not within means it does not reside in the sense organs; to say it is not without means it does not reside..."
It exists within the dust of the world. As I contemplate it, according to the first hypothesis, there is nothing seen within; according to the second hypothesis, there is mutual cognition externally.
Because there is no cognition within, luminosity does not reside inside. Because the body and mind cognize one another, luminosity does not reside outside.
Since there is mutual cognition externally yet no seeing internally, it is neither internal nor external. I suspect this must be the mind.

Is it then to be found in the space between the sense organs and their objects? You do not realize that when the World-Honored One said the mind is neither internal nor external, he was precisely stating that the mind has no fixed location;
he did not mean that the mind resides in the interval. As soon as one calls it "the middle," it is already a fabrication.
Thus, there is indeed a fixed location. Since the deluded mind has no substance, it has no location; since the true mind is all-pervasive, there is nowhere it is not.

It does not linger in a single place; fundamentally, these are the "three non-locations. Ānanda, by citing the two absences from among these, establishes his own argument, which accords with the Buddha’s intent.
The Buddha said, "Regarding what you call 'the middle,' the middle must not be confused; it cannot be without a location. Now, as you investigate this middle, where does it reside?

Does it reside in space, or does it reside in the body? If it resides in the body, then residing at the periphery would not be the middle, and residing in the center would be the same as the interior.

If it resides in space, is it something that can be indicated, or is it something that cannot be indicated? That which cannot be indicated is the same as non-existence. As for that which can be indicated..."
There is no fixed [direction]. Why is this? For example, when a person uses a gnomon to mark the center, looking toward the east makes it west, and observing from the south makes it north.
Since the substance of the gnomon is thus indeterminate, the mind should likewise be confused and disordered.
This investigation determines that [the mind] neither resides in the body nor in the object; thus, both are refuted as having no location at all. The Buddha said:
"If you claim that the mind is in the interval, then that interval must be definite and unmistakable, and it could not be without a specific location.
Now, examine for yourself where this so-called 'interval' is: does it reside within the body, or is it in a place outside the body?"
Should it reside within the body? If it resides within the body, there would be the two distinctions of center and periphery. If it is at the periphery, it cannot be considered the center;
if it is at the center, it is the same as being "inside" previously mentioned, and one ought to perceive that interior. If, on the other hand, it resides in a location...
It is like constructing a house: one must necessarily set up a marker pole to indicate the central position. Now, does this marker indicate something, or does it indicate nothing?
If there is nothing indicated, then there is no center. If there is a marker, then the center has no fixed location.

For example, when a person uses a marker to indicate the center, looking from the east it is west, and observing from the south it becomes north. Since the substance of the marker is thus confused, how can the mind be at peace?
"If there were a fixed 'middle' that was not subject to confusion, then wherever one is situated, it would never constitute a middle.
Ānanda said: 'The "middle" I speak of is not these two kinds. As the World-Honored One has said, with the eye and forms as conditions, [consciousness] arises.'"
Regarding visual consciousness: the eye possesses discrimination while the object of form is devoid of cognition;

when consciousness arises between them, it is then said that "the mind resides therein. Ānanda spoke again: "In what I have explained, this is not the two-fold notion of 'residing in the body' or 'residing in a location.
As the World-Honored One has taught, with the eye and form as conditions, visual consciousness arises. Now, the eye is the faculty (*indriya*), and form is the object (*viṣaya*)."
Furthermore, the eye possesses discrimination and thus belongs to the internal faculties; visible forms are insentient and thus belong to external objects.
When the faculties and objects face each other internally and externally, consciousness arises between them and performs the function of discrimination. Is this not precisely where the mind resides?
The examples cited by Ānanda are the teachings of the Buddha’s *lakṣaṇa-yāna* (Characteristics School), spoken in accordance with worldly conventions. They are not...

This is also of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Furthermore, the Blessed One’s intention was that the two factors of the eye and visible form serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness;
it does not mean that the eye and visible form themselves can produce consciousness. This is because consciousness possesses its own seeds capable of producing it.

Moreover, both the sense faculty and the object are of the nature of material seeds (*rūpa-bīja*); how could material seeds give rise to mental active states (*citta-pravṛtti*)? Furthermore, it is said:

To say that the eye possesses discrimination is likewise a mistaken interpretation. One fails to realize that while the eye can illuminate objects and consciousness can discriminate, the eye itself is actually devoid of discrimination.
Thus, the text below states: "When the eyes look about, they are merely like a mirror;
there is no separate analysis. It is within this that your consciousness sequentially points and identifies. This is the proof. Master Zhong said: "By means of..."
When the eye encounters form, the form is without consciousness; when the mind encounters the eye, the eye is likewise without consciousness. The Buddha said:
"If your mind were located between the faculty and the object, would this essence of the mind be inclusive of both, or not inclusive of both?

If it were inclusive of both, then the substance of the object and the essence of the mind would be intermingled and confused. Since the object is not conscious of the essence, they would stand as two opposing entities. How could this be?"
If it were the Middle, it would simultaneously fail to be both; being neither known nor unknown, it would lack any essential nature. What, then, would constitute the characteristic of the Middle?
Therefore, one should know that for it to exist in the middle is impossible.

The Buddha said: "If your mind were within the sense organs and their objects, would this essence of the mind encompass both the organs and the objects—like a child born from the union of a father and mother—or would it not encompass both—like a child born of itself without depending on parents?
Now, 'objects' (chen) refer to external things, while 'organs' (gen) refer to the physical bodies. If it encompasses both..."

In that case, the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) would be conflated, and their respective entities would become confused. Objects are not conscious, while the substance [of the mind] is conscious;
thus, being half-conscious and half-unconscious, it stands opposed to its counterpart and falls into the two extremes. How could this be the Middle Way?
If neither of these two combined is established, then this essence of the mind is neither the consciousness of the faculties nor the [consciousness] of the objects.
"I do not know. Since its essential nature does not even exist, what characteristic could there be for the 'middle'?
Thus, whether one includes both extremes or does not include them, neither can establish a 'middle. Therefore, you should know that to claim there is a 'middle' is impossible.
Ānanda presented to the World-Honored One this sand-pot that clings to no boundaries; he has smashed it once again. (The two extremes together).

"Those who do so" are those who give rise [to the mind] between the sense organs and their objects by grasping both simultaneously. "Those who do not embrace both" are those who stand alone and independent, with both the sense organs and their objects set apart.
Some become mired in this term "body" (tǐ) in "the body of the mind," and consequently take the term "body" used for physical objects to mean the "body of the mind"; this is incorrect.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma.

He constantly spoke of how the nature of the mind, through which one awakens to and discerns, is neither within, nor without, nor in between; it has no location whatsoever and is entirely free from attachment."
To name it "mind" is for me to be without attachment; to not name it "mind" is likewise for me to be without attachment.
This is the seventh reckoning of non-attachment. When the World-Honored One was in the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he expounded the true doctrine of non-attachment.
"It does not exist within, without, or in between; to speak precisely, the mind has no location. Since there is no place for the mind to dwell, one should not further cling to anything.
The Venerable One, having misunderstood the Buddha’s intention, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha..."
Together with the four great disciples, such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he turned the wheel of the Dharma. He constantly said:
"This mind that perceives and discriminates is not internal, not external, and not in between; it has no location whatsoever. Being entirely unattached, it is called 'mind.
Now, I shall take this mind and not allow it to become attached to any phenomena. In this way, it may be attained."
Is this what is called "the mind not being attached"? Little do you realize that the very act of "not attaching the mind" is already an attachment.

Thus, the former masters said: "To call it 'Suchness' (Tathatā) is already a transformation. Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking of it; if you speak of it, then horns will grow upon your head. Question:
The locus where the Buddha manifests is fundamentally the manifestation of no-locus. Now that there is no locus, why [is there still a manifestation]?

"Must it not further be refuted? He replied: "The Buddha’s point of reference is precisely the manifestation of no-place. By manifesting no-place, the Buddha causes one to realize the absence of intrinsic substance.
Now, you take this very non-attachment to be the essence of the mind; thus, while there is indeed no-place, you persist in clinging to the existence of a substantial essence."
This is why it is refuted. Master Zhong said: "The three are not present" means non-attachment; yet, by taking "non-attachment" as the name for one's mind, one is again attached to non-attachment.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: "As for your statement that the nature of the mind which perceives, knows, and discriminates has no location whatsoever—if all the phenomena in the world, including empty space, water, land, and flying creatures, are called 'all things,' then when you are not attached to them, do they exist or do they not exist?"
If it were non-existent, it would be identical to a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; how then could there be non-attachment? That which is non-attached cannot be called non-existent.

If it lacks characteristics, it is non-existent; if it is not non-existent, it possesses characteristics. If characteristics exist, then [the entity] exists; how then can there be non-attachment? Therefore, one should know this.
"It is impossible that the mind which perceives and knows all things without attachment is non-existent.
The World-Honored One, unable to find a way to open his mouth [to refute him], pressed him further, saying:

"Ānanda, you say that the nature of the mind which perceives, knows, and discriminates has no location, yet you reckon that the absence of attachment to all things constitutes the mind. This so-called 'one'..."
"‘All things’ refers to the various phenomena of the world—those in space, on water, on land, or in flight.
As for your non-attachment to them, does this mind of yours inherently possess a location yet remains unattached to all dharmas?
Or does it inherently lack a location and thus remain unattached to all dharmas? If your mind inherently lacks a location..."
Yet, if you do not cling, this mind is identical to the fundamental non-existence of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns;

how could you further add "non-clinging"? If your mind originally possessed a location but did not go on to cling to all phenomena, then your mind would have merely departed from clinging and added another instance of non-clinging—how could this be called "non-attachment"? Furthermore...
This being so, attachment arises from signs (*nimitta*). If you truly have no mental signs, then this is genuine mindlessness (*acittatā*), and there would certainly be no attachment.
If it is not genuine mindlessness, then there must certainly be mental signs. Since there are mental signs, there must certainly be a locus;
since there is a locus, there is certainly attachment. How then can you say that all things are without attachment? To speak to the ultimate extent, it is not...

Only having characteristics cannot be called non-attachment; even the absence of characteristics cannot be called non-attachment, for as soon as one speaks of "no-characteristics," one immediately falls back into the realm of characteristics.
Therefore, you should know that it is impossible for all non-attachment to be named the "awakened knowing mind. Ānanda was about to present a dead cat’s head—utterly useless—to the World-Honored One.
World-Honored One, he has also been cast by the World-Honored One into other worlds. The Dharma-body has no fixed location, yet there is nowhere it is not present.
In the previous six instances, you reckoned that the mind was either within or without, or doubly reckoned it as being hidden in the sense organs, or as conforming to their union.
In the interim, he regarded the mind as having existence; therefore, the World-Honored One refuted this by means of non-existence.
Upon reaching the seventh stage, he again reckoned the mind as being non-existent; therefore, the World-Honored One refuted this by means of the existence of characteristics.
Although this is a temporary shattering of attachments, it truly reveals the principle of being neither in existence nor non-existence.
This is what the former masters meant when they said: "Do not dwell where there is a Buddha; run swiftly past where there is no Buddha.

This is the fundamental tenet of the entire scripture. The Buddha told Ānanda:

They do not know that practitioners are like this.
