"Good friend, it is by means of this mind that one gives rise to great courage and performs all those difficult dharmic practices.
Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it would still be because of this mind.
If what I have now revealed were not the mind, I would be without mind, identical to earth or wood; apart from this awareness, there would be nothing else. How then could the Tathāgata say..."

"This is not the mind. I am truly terrified, as are this entire assembly; there is none among us who does not harbor doubt and confusion. We pray that you will bestow your great compassion and reveal the truth to those who have not yet awakened.

This attachment to the delusive and refusal to let it go has given rise to alarm and suspicion. The World-Honored One’s single-minded heart of maternal care has, instead, resulted in our being left bewildered and frustrated.
Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am indeed the Buddha’s beloved younger brother. It was because my heart loved and delighted in the Buddha that I left the household life;
it was my own mind that caused me to renounce the world. Yet, why should my mind offer sustenance to the Tathāgata alone?
I shall travel throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve all Buddhas and [cultivate] goodness."
Knowledge. One must arouse great courage and vigor to perform all those difficult dharmic practices, all of which rely upon this mind;
thus, it is this mind that can be made virtuous. Even if one slanders the Dharma and forever loses their roots of goodness, it is still because of this mind.
"This mind is capable of committing evil. Whether performing good or evil, all these manifold functions are this very mind.
If, as you have now revealed, it were not the mind, then I would indeed be a person without a mind."
To be without mind would be equivalent to being like earth or wood. Why? Because apart from this mind of cognition and awareness, there is no other mind whatsoever.
How then can the Tathāgata say that this is "non-mind"? This is a vast discrepancy; it does not accord with human sentiment.
I am truly terrified, as are this great assembly, including those in the heavens and among humans, as well as all ordinary beings, outsiders, and those of provisional or limited capacity.
There is no one who does not say this is the mind. Now that we have heard this teaching, there is no one who does not harbor doubt; nor can we help but be afraid, nor can we help but be perplexed.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow great compassion and mercy, and reveal to me and the great assembly what we have not yet understood.
For we did not realize that those who perform good and evil deeds originally belong to the ignorance that gives rise to karma (ālayavijñāna), which is termed...
It is said: "As for 'neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil,' this is precisely the Venerable One’s original face.
Yet you abandon that which is inherently present without realizing it, and cling to delusive thoughts without relinquishing them—how can you be so alone in this?
A former master said: 'Suddenly, amidst a clear sky, the sound of a thunderclap; at the Three-Level Rapids of Yumen, the waves roar and crash. With such many horns and heads, one becomes a dragon.'"
"Go. The crab still stared with its eyes wide open. This is what the Venerable One meant.

At that time, the World-Honored One revealed this teaching to Ānanda and the great assembly, desiring to cause their minds to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
From his lion throne, he stroked Ānanda’s head and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always taught that all phenomena which arise are manifested solely by the mind.
All causes and effects, the worlds, and even the finest motes of dust—all take their substance from the mind.

Ānanda, if one were to examine the root source of everything that exists within all these worlds, down to the smallest blade of grass, leaf, thread, or knot, they would all be found to exist [only as manifestations of the mind]."

As for its essential nature, even empty space possesses name and appearance; how much more so this pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind, which is the nature of all minds, yet lacks a self-substance of its own?
This verse demonstrates that the true mind possesses a substantial essence, thereby resolving the doubt regarding it being as insentient as wood or earth.

At that time, the World-Honored One revealed this to Ānanda and the great assembly, desiring to cause their minds to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena).
One who abides in this patience perceives not even the slightest dharma arising, nor perceives the slightest dharma ceasing, within or without the three realms.
Transcending emotion and departing from views, it is the very essence of true wondrousness—the substance of a mind that is neither good nor evil.
This is precisely the ultimate solidity of all phenomena. While on the lion throne, he rubbed Ānanda’s head;
when the latter grasped at delusion as truth, he roared with majestic authority, and when Ānanda was startled and filled with fear, he again rubbed his head to comfort him.
This is what is meant by "sometimes a ball of cotton wrapped in iron, sometimes iron and stone wrapped in cotton"—feigning anger and feigning joy.
This means he was able to both emit and retract [the light]. Having rubbed the crown of his head, he addressed him, saying:

"Have you not heard the Tathāgata constantly teach that all phenomena which arise are manifested solely by the mind? Sentient beings are deluded and falsely claim that each of the myriad things has its own source of origin;
they do not know that the single true mind-body manifests through conditions. If there were no single mind, then..."

All phenomena have been thus for a long time. Reaching the ultimate source from which all phenomena arise, extending to all causes and effects, the provisional and the real of both ordinary beings and sages, the vastness of worlds and the minuteness of atoms—since these are all manifestations of the mind alone, they likewise take their substance through the mind.
To say that the mind has no substance must mean that all phenomena have no substance; only then would it be possible. Ānanda!

In all worlds, whatever exists—even down to the most minute forms such as blades of grass, leaves, or strands of thread—if one investigates their ultimate source, they all possess an essential nature (svabhāva). This holds true even for empty space.
This is the greatest of all formless things. Although it lacks substantiality, it nevertheless possesses name and appearance. Since it has name and appearance, it must also have substance.
One can observe that whether sentient or insentient, whether large or small, there is nothing that does not possess substance;
how much more so for the mind that is pure, stainless, wondrously clean, untainted, profoundly tranquil, and fundamentally luminous? And...
If the mind, which takes all phenomena as its nature, were itself devoid of substance, it would be most unreasonable.
For all phenomena are but images manifested within the ocean of the true mind;
if even the objects manifested possess substance, it is certainly not the case that the manifesting mind itself lacks substance. Thus, the true mind must necessarily possess substance.
It is simply because you cling to that deluded mind that you are confused regarding this true essence. How could it be that apart from this awareness there is nothing else?
○ He said: "The patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) means to understand that dharmas do not arise and to maintain this realization within the mind.

In various sutras, one realizes the patience of non-arising at the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). However, according to the *Avataṃsaka*, it is only after the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) that it is designated as the patience of non-arising.

This sutra states that even before entering the stage of the Ten Faiths, one immediately attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is what is meant by the necessity of sudden enlightenment through principle.
Master Zhong said: "The character 'patience' (*kṣānti*) does not refer to the exertion of effort; it already signifies being as-it-is and immovable.
If one contemplates deeply, both 'Great Samādhi' and 'Ultimate Solidity' are fully contained within this single character 'patience. Thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is established."
Regarding patience—this is precisely that patience.

If you maintain that the nature cognized by the conceptualization of vitarka and vicāra must necessarily be the mind, then this mind should exist as a complete, distinct entity apart from all objects of the senses, such as the elements of form, odor, taste, and touch, as well as their various activities; it would be just like [the self] you currently [assert].

To listen to my Dharma involves making distinctions based on sound. Even if you were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere shadow of conceptualization regarding mental objects (*dharmas*). I am not commanding you to insist that this is not the mind.
However, you must subtly examine the mind: if the nature of discrimination exists apart from external objects, then that is truly your mind;

if the nature of discrimination has no substance apart from objects, then it is merely a reflected phenomenon of the discrimination of external objects. Since external objects are not permanent, [the reflection is likewise impermanent].
If, at the time of transformation and cessation, this mind were like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, then your Dharma-body would likewise be subject to transformation and cessation;
who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
This was intended to lead the Venerable One to discern and infer that this [faculty] is delusory, thereby removing his attachment to it as being delusory.

The Buddha further said: "If you stubbornly cling to and do not relinquish this nature—which is capable of discrimination, possesses applied and sustained thought, and is aware and unclouded—and insist that it is your true mind, then this mind should be able to exist apart from all forms."
Regarding the activities of the various objects—such as fragrance, flavor, and touch—there exists a distinct, non-outflowing, and perfectly complete essence.

(The mention of "form, fragrance, flavor, and touch" cites four to encompass all six; "various objects" refers to the six sense-objects; "activities" is synonymous with the affairs and karma of the objects, as seen in the subsequent passage concerning the "four objects of the floating faculties").
Just as you are now seated here, receiving my teaching, this mind that listens to the Dharma likewise arises because of my speaking.
To give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the sound of the Dharma is a leaking mind; it is not the perfect essence. How could it be considered true?

Not only do you currently possess the functioning discrimination of the six consciousnesses, which cannot be called true, but even if you were to completely extinguish all these seeds and manifestations of the six consciousnesses—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—and attain the state of an Arhat...
Han: (Briefly citing what is seen, heard, sensed, and known—combining smelling and tasting into one for a total of six, with the four as the basis.

If one were to guard the inner state of profound seclusion and indulge in the bliss of cessation, refusing to let go, then this very guarding of profound seclusion still belongs to the faculty of mind (*manas*). This is because the mind encounters mental objects (*dharma*).

This is like the relationship between mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and discrimination: they appear as reflections of one another, being merely light and shadow, utterly devoid of substantial reality, and thus cannot be considered true.
How much more so now, while the present seeds have not yet been emptied, would you wish to recognize this as the truth?

(The *Zhengmo* says: "All provisional vehicles possess meditative states with entry and exit; these are all subtle discriminations. This is because they entirely rely upon the suppression of the subtle mind of discrimination to maintain that state of quiescence. If one does not discriminate at all, the state of quiescence immediately [manifests]. )

This is called "emerging from concentration. How could such a thing exist within the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama? Even today, I am not forcibly insisting that these [mental activities] are not the mind.
Rather, you should take this discriminative observation and subtle reflection and examine them minutely:
whether they exist or do not exist, whether they are real or false. If this nature of discrimination exists apart from external objects, then it is truly your own mind.
If the nature of discrimination has no substance apart from objects, then it is merely a reflected image of the preceding objects;
it is not your true mind. What you now grasp as discrimination, reflection, and observation all exist because of external objects.
It relies entirely upon the various sense-objects to manifest the shadows of discrimination. These objects are not permanent; they change and perish in an instant.
When they change and perish, how could the mind possibly remain? It would be like a shadow vanishing when its form is destroyed.
Is this mind not, then, like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit? Since the mind perishes along with the objects, your Dharma-body would likewise perish along with the ashes.
[If you] sever [them], what further thing could serve as the mind of the causal ground to realize this *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*?
To know that there is arising and ceasing is the deluded mind conditioned by sensory objects; to know that there is neither arising nor ceasing is the eternally abiding true mind.
Master Zhong said: "Even if one extinguishes all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and internally maintains [the mind] within the profound stillness..."

Even in a state of stillness, one is merely engaging with the reflected images of the mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*). These mental objects correspond to the mind-faculty (*manas*), which is what is called the sixth consciousness.
This is what this sutra refers to as the confused practice of non-Buddhists and others; it arises from failing to realize the true nature of the eight consciousnesses.

The application of such learning and study ceases with the sixth consciousness. One may either mistake the restless, proliferating mind that chases after objects—its state of turbid agitation—as the "void, luminous, and unclouded" mind, such as Ānanda described as the "discerning mind";

or one may mistake the inwardly maintained state of profound stillness and the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) for true "calm concentration. This refers to those practitioners who...
To achieve unsurpassed bodhi, the root of the illness lies precisely here. ○ Master Padmasambhava said:
"When I first entered the Way, I recalled Mencius’s thought that the state where joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused is the 'Centrality.

I took this Centrality to be the self prior to the kalpa of emptiness. Subsequently, upon studying the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it says: 'Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing...'"
To know this: though one may dwell inwardly in profound seclusion, it is still but a shadow of the discrimination of *dharmas*.

Now, when seeing and hearing have ceased and perception and cognition are cut off, it resembles the state before joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure have been manifested; yet why is it called "the discrimination of *dharmas*"?
It is because the mind is the faculty and *dharmas* are the objects. When the faculty and the object confront each other, a favorable condition is stimulated, and joy and pleasure are manifested.
Thus it is. When one encounters adverse conditions, anger and sorrow arise; this is the faculty of mind (*manas*) discriminating among mental objects (*dharmas*).

Before they have arisen, the objects have not yet interfaced with the external, and the faculties have not yet emerged within; it is tranquil and unmoving, which should be the fundamental substance (*tattva*).
One was unaware that previously one moved toward conditioned objects; now one conditions a state of stillness. Previously, one was certainly engaged in the coarse discrimination of mental objects.
It is also the subtle discrimination of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). All are matters of reflected images; they are not real. They are called "profound and secluded" (*youxian*);
"profound" simply means superior to the manifest, and "secluded" simply means superior to the noisy. This is one's own nature prior to the empty kalpa.
"It is still far from being reached.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and lost in thought.

The Buddha said to Ānanda, "All practitioners in the world who have attained the nine successive meditative absorptions (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) in the present life may yet fail to exhaust their outflows and become Arhats."

"All this arises from grasping at these deluded thoughts of birth and death and mistakenly taking them to be real. Therefore, although you have now acquired much learning, you have not attained the fruit of sainthood.
This passage breaks the deluded mind that clings to attachments. At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha’s opening [of the teaching].
[The Master] showed [him this]: that which one has habitually relied upon as the mind suddenly becomes utterly devoid of essence and nature, leaving nothing to be pursued.
Furthermore, one does not know what constitutes the mind. It is like a person who has lost a cherished treasure;

they wish to cling to it but cannot, and wish to let it go but cannot. Thus, they fall into silent self-frustration. The World-Honored One, seeing his lingering attachment and stagnation, [said: "Or..."
Furthermore, he rebuked Ānanda with the utmost severity, saying:

"Regarding those practitioners in the world who have attained the three fruits and below—though they may currently achieve the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), and the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*)—in the Śrāvaka vehicle, the first eight are accomplished at the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the ninth is accomplished at the stage of the untainted noble one (*anāsrava-ārya*). One who attains these nine attainments..."
It would have been appropriate for him to transcend birth and death, realize nirvana, and attain the fruit of arhatship.

That he did not exhaust his outflows and become an arhat was entirely due to his attachment to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and his refusal to relinquish it. Even this meditative absorption of cessation is but a shadow-like phenomenon;
even this attachment is but a delusive thought (*vikalpa*). It is because he clung to this delusive thought of birth and death that he failed to achieve liberation.
Because you have mistakenly taken what is not the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to be so, you fail to achieve the state of a true Arhat despite your cultivation;

how much less so for you, who have not yet mastered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), nor maintained profound stillness, but instead cling to the false appearances and conceptions of external objects, mistaking them for reality and refusing to relinquish them?
Thus, although you possess extensive learning, the power of the Path remains incomplete, and you do not attain [liberation].
This constitutes the realization of the fruit of sainthood. Regarding what was previously called "maintaining" (shǒu), it means to embrace firmly without shifting;

regarding what is here called "grasping" (zhí), it means to hold fast without relinquishing. Both the characters for "maintaining" and "grasping" are afflictions. To eliminate the character for "maintaining" is to depart from the realm of shadows.
To set aside the grasping at words is itself the reality. Furthermore, the preceding text states:
"The continuous cycle of birth and death for all sentient beings arises entirely from the employment of various false imaginings; because these imaginings are not true, there is transmigration.

This concludes by returning to the previous judgment. The World-Honored One’s two instances of speaking with urgent and piercing words were like deep probes and painful pricks, all intended to reach the very bottom.
For the sake of others, one must cause the Venerable One to abandon deluded consciousness and seek the true mind. In the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
since the ninth stage is already judged to be the untainted (anāsrava) rank of the sage, yet it is further said that one cannot become an Arhat by exhausting the outflows (āsrava),
one should know that what they call the "untainted rank of the sage" is entirely a provisional concession intended to guide and encourage those who progress toward it.
Thus it is said. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "You should observe and deliberate that what is called nirvāṇa is not the ultimate reality.

Since it is not the true nirvāṇa, how could it be termed the true exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)? Therefore, Changshui’s assertion that those of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are arhats who have exhausted their outflows is beyond doubt.
Furthermore, the Hīnayāna teachings permit that all four fruits are noble (*ārya*). Ānanda had already attained [the first fruit].
To claim that the first fruit (srotāpanna) is not yet "noble" (ārya)—how could one destroy the first fruit while alone preserving the [remaining] four?

It is certain that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) alone constitute the noble fruits of partial realization (*pradeśaprāpti*). For in this sutra, even the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the four preparatory stages (*catasraḥ prayogabhūmayaḥ*) are still termed "worldly.

Within this, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*) are called the nine concentrations (*navasamāpatti*). These are the internal...
To maintain the ultimate state of profound stillness is still merely a matter of the shadows of dharma-dust; therefore, it does not constitute the fruit of sainthood.

To cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death and mistake them for reality is not only said of those non-Buddhists whose six consciousnesses grasp at external objects, but also includes those of the Two Vehicles who take the essence of cognition to be the fundamental luminosity, yet have not yet shattered their karmic consciousness. This applies to them as well.
[This was] correct. ○ Having finished refuting the grasping at the deluded mind to open the path of *śamatha*, Ānanda, having heard this, again shed tears of grief.
Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Ever since I followed the Buddha to leave the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and constantly thought to myself that there was no need for me to practice.
I presumed that the Tathāgata would bestow samādhi upon me, unaware that body and mind can never substitute for one another; thus, I lost my original mind.
Although one has left the household life in body, if the mind does not enter the Path, it is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees;

only today do I realize that even if one possesses much learning, if one does not practice, it is equal to having heard nothing at all—just as a person who speaks of food can never be satiated by such talk alone.
World-Honored One, we are now entangled by the two obstacles precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us, who are destitute and exposed, and by giving rise to his wondrously luminous mind, open our eye of the Way.
This is precisely the request for instruction regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha himself.

Generally, it is only after one has attained deep awakening that compassion arises—either through awakening to the illusory nature of things and grieving for long-standing suffering, or through awakening to the Reality and grieving for its long-term loss. Having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda...
Only then did he realize that the mind capable of such reasoning was illusory. Thereupon, he wept once more with deep sorrow;
prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since I followed the Buddha and resolved to leave the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to constantly reflect within myself that there is no need for me to practice. I presumed that the Tathāgata was my own kinsman, and surely—"

Yet you have bestowed upon me the samādhi of right reception; how could I have known that the bodies and minds of this person and that person are fundamentally incapable of substituting for one another?
It is just as when a father and son climb a mountain: each must exert their own effort; substitution is impossible.
Now, hearing your reproach, I realize that the Tathāgata allows no room for sentimentality, and my single heart of hope has fallen entirely into emptiness. Pray, look upon me!
Hitherto, you have mistakenly identified the deluded mind as your own, thereby losing your original mind. Though you have left the household life in body, you have never truly entered the Way.
How is this different from one who dwells in a fertile land yet cannot nourish himself, instead rushing outward in pursuit?
Is it not like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees, begging for food from others? Only today do you realize what was being said.
To gain one *zhang* is not as good as practicing for one *chi*. Although one may possess much learning, if one does not practice, it will ultimately be of no benefit;
it is equal to having heard nothing at all. It is like a person speaking of food who can never be satiated, for a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger.
World-Honored One, we have not yet exhausted the two delusions of views and cultivation. (Ānanda, it is only upon attaining the first fruit that one is freed from the delusion of views.)

If the afflictions of thought (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) are not yet exhausted, one is entangled by the obstacle of affliction. If the craving for the phenomena that constitute objects of perception has not been emptied, one is entangled by the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

Since one cannot sever the afflictions to realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), nor can one sever the obstacle to the knowable to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the reason one remains entangled in these two obstacles and cannot liberate oneself is precisely because one does not understand [this].
It is because one clings to these deluded thoughts as being real, despite the nature of the mind being unshakeable, devoid of arising or ceasing, tranquil, and eternal.

I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for my wretchedness—lacking the flavor of the Dharma to nourish my spirit and lacking the garment of the Dharma to cover my body—will manifest his wondrously luminous mind and open my eye of the Way. For although I possess this wondrous mind...
I have been consistently concealing [the truth], failing to distinguish between good and evil, and mistakenly taking my own fallacious reasoning to be reality.
I pray that the World-Honored One will lift this veil and reveal it to me. Although I possess the eye of the Way, I have remained perpetually blinded and unable to discern right from wrong.
He merely recognizes his physical eyes and considers them capable of seeing. He prays that the World-Honored One will scrape away the cataracts and open his vision.
One should know that this request differs significantly from the previous one made after the eye was pierced;

the former concern arose because he was immersed in a brothel due to not knowing where the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) leads, and thus he still took deluded consciousness for the true mind—this was a matter of self-reproach.
Not knowing the locus of truth, one merely seeks a locus. Now it is said that being entangled by the two obstacles arises precisely from not knowing the nature of the mind as quiescent and eternal;
only then does one reproach oneself for not knowing the true mind and seek a "true mind" elsewhere.
The commentary states: "The wondrously luminous mind is the principle of suchness; the eye of the Way is the wisdom of suchness. 'To bring forth' means to bring forth its treasury;
'to open' means to open its light. The two characters 'mind' and 'eye' implicitly respond to the preceding passage:
'It is only the mind and the eyes—where are they now?'"
At that moment, from the *svastika* on the Tathāgata’s chest, a precious light surged forth.
This light was brilliant and radiant, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors, which simultaneously pervaded Buddha-worlds as numerous as the motes of dust in the ten directions.

It completely drenched the crowns of all the Tathāgatas in the precious lands throughout the ten directions, then returned to Ānanda and the great assembly. Addressing Ānanda, the Buddha said: "I shall now, for your sake..."
They shall erect the great Dharma-banner and cause all sentient beings to obtain the wondrous, subtle, and esoteric mind of pure intrinsic brightness, thereby attaining the eye of purity.
(Above the word "pure brightness," one should remove the character "wondrous.")

This indicates that the Tathāgata first silently manifested signs of light and only then granted permission to speak. At that moment, from the *svastika* on his chest, the Tathāgata emitted a precious radiance.
This clearly demonstrates that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision must flow forth from within his own breast before they can encompass heaven and earth;
it is not a light produced by the attachment to delusion. That light was brilliant and resplendent, possessing a hundred...

The thousand colors manifest the accomplishment of myriad virtues. Simultaneously pervading Buddha-worlds as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, they universally drench the crowns of all Tathāgatas in every precious land of the ten directions, and then descend upon Ānanda.
Together with the great assembly, he manifested that both sentient and insentient beings, as well as the noble and the ordinary, all emerge from within the light of equality.
Thereupon, he addressed Ānanda, saying: "Your own nature, the Dharma Banner, has long been cast to the ground;
I now establish it for you so that it shall no longer fall or lean, and likewise cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to attain [it]."
The wondrous, subtle, and secret nature; the wondrously pure and luminous mind—these are indeed the ultimate truth of the *dharmadhātu*.
It is but a single essence: from the perspective of its primordial quiescence, it is called "nature" (*prakṛti*); from the perspective of its primordial awakening, it is called "mind" (*citta*).

The nature is wondrous because of its subtlety and secrecy; the mind is wondrous because of its purity and luminosity. This is what is meant by the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). Attaining purity...

"Pure Eye. The former, the deluded mind, takes the entirety of its being as an object of sensory dust; therefore, it is not pure. This eye is far removed from discrimination and is not defiled by any sensory objects.
It accords with principle and pervades the Dharma-realm; thus, it is called "pure. This is what is meant by "Tathatā-wisdom" (suchness-wisdom).
Ānanda sought the nature of the quiescent and constant mind, yet the Buddha granted him the nature of the wondrous, subtle, and secret; he sought the wondrous, but [received]...
He requested the "mind of wondrous purity and clarity," and was granted it; he sought to have his "path-eye opened," and was granted the attainment of the "pure eye.
Thus, the request and the granting were indeed in accord. ○ Hei said: "The emission of light on the previous occasion symbolized the aspect of shattering delusion."
Light is emitted from this place to manifest the characteristic of truth. The two characters "mind" (xīn) and "eye" (yàn) correspond to what Ānanda requested:
the "mind-eye. The character "obtain" (huò) corresponds to the "arise" (fā) mentioned above; the character "attain" (dé) corresponds to the "open" (kāi) mentioned above.

The old commentary states that from this point onward, the text as a whole is intended to refute false views, thereby causing students not to dare to directly identify the substance of seeing as the mind. This [interpretation] contradicts...

The Buddha’s established fundamental intent reaches no further than this. One must recognize that the most extraordinary feature of this sutra lies entirely in its rejection of the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) and its exclusive reliance upon the root-nature (*indriya-prakṛti*) as the causal mind.

This nature of seeing is not affected by anything. Thus, all myriad phenomena, as well as all worlds, may be disordered, moving, or still at will;

they all have no bearing upon the nature of seeing. If a person, amidst these myriad phenomena, suddenly perceives this unmoving nature—constant and never obscured—how could it ever be seized by external objects? This is the ultimate in wondrousness.
Furthermore, when the masters of our school raise a finger or extend a fist to enlighten others, they mostly conceal this meaning to cause people to awaken to it themselves;
the only difference lies in the fact that the teachers of other schools explain it clearly and thoroughly.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single jewel-light from his palm marked with the wheel; it rested to Ānanda’s right, whereupon Ānanda immediately turned his head to look to the right.
He then emitted another light to Ānanda’s left, and Ānanda likewise turned his head to look to the left.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "For what reason does your head shake today? Ānanda replied, "I saw the Tathāgata emit wondrous jewel-light that came to my left and right;

therefore, as I looked to the left and right, my head moved of its own accord. "Ānanda, when you gaze at the Buddha’s light and move your head to the left and right, is it your head that moves, or is it what you see that moves? "World-Honored One, it is my head that moves of its own accord."
"The nature of my seeing has no cessation; who could cause it to waver? The Buddha said, "It is so.
This proceeds from the distant to the intimate, and is further verified by the head. While external objects move, the nature of seeing remains unmoved."
It may be easy for people to understand this; however, it is truly difficult to discern that while the head moves, the nature of seeing remains unmoving.
This is because worldly people identify "seeing" with the eyes; thus, when the head shakes and the eyes turn, it appears as though the nature of seeing also moves.
Therefore, one must test it by means of the head. Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single jewel-light from his wheel-marked palms, which hovered before Ānanda.
To the right. Immediately Ānanda turned his head and looked to the right. Again, a light flew out on the left, so he looked to the left.
Then [the Buddha] examined him and said: "Today you look to the left and look to the right; why does your head shake about like this?"
The Venerable One was not left alone with his question; he replied, "Because I saw light flying to my left and right, I looked around and my head moved.
The World-Honored One’s compassionate heart was sincere and profound, seeking to bring people to realization to the very bottom;

therefore, he further examined him, saying, "When you looked at the light and your head moved, did it move because of your head, or did it move because of what you saw? Ānanda, having no place left to evade, exerted himself to the utmost.
Take this up. Answer afresh: when the head moves, one sees that which is unmoving. As it is said:
"Though there may be a thousand kinds of grass, in the end there is but one kind of wind. Therefore, the World-Honored One again certified him, saying: "So it is.
This means that if one knows the head moves while what is seen remains unmoving, this is precisely the principle of adventitious dust versus the fundamental void. Since one already knows the head...
When movement is seen as constant non-movement, then although this body may travel back and forth for thousands or tens of thousands of miles,
even reaching worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, dying here and being born there, this seeing-nature remains ever like empty space, without any movement whatsoever.

If a person awakens to this constancy and does not follow the fluctuations of the body, then throughout daily life—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—they will always abide within the samādhi of their own nature.
Master Zhigong said: "Without giving rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation or study, one is eternally sovereign within the light of formlessness.
This is what he meant. How could this be compared to those who close their eyes and imagine emptiness, thereby falling into the shadows of mental objects (*dharmas*)?
The gap between heaven and the abyss is vast indeed. Furthermore, the followers of our school have gone from east to west, even to the point of dancing;
their intention was to manifest this very truth, yet those who are deluded imitate them, merely playing with their spirits and never attaining the essential meaning.

When the World-Honored One wished for Ānanda to know the location of the true mind, Ānanda became repeatedly confused and distressed; had this occurred within the secular classics, it would have been considered indignation.

When one’s hesitation reaches its ultimate limit, one must be enlightened by the contemporary [master]. Although the World-Honored One repeatedly opened and guided them, he did not fully reveal the truth for them;
rather, he waited for them to bring it forth from within themselves, merely corroborating it with the two words "thus" (evam). This is what is meant by "seeking the jewel in one's own robe.
These two instances of "thus" stand in direct contrast to the statement that "there is no such place" (naitad sthānam vidyate) found in the *Saptavastuka*.

"Indeed. Therefore, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly: 'If there are sentient beings who designate that which is in motion as "dust" (rajas) and that which does not abide as "guest," you should observe Ānanda’s head as it moves back and forth; though the head moves, what you perceive is actually without motion.'"
Furthermore, observe my hand as it opens and closes; you see no actual stretching or rolling up. Why, then, do you now take movement to be the body and movement to be the object?
From beginning to end, moment by moment, things arise and perish; thus you have lost the true nature and act in delusion.

"The fundamental nature and mind have lost their truth; one recognizes external objects as the self. One revolves within this cycle, taking upon oneself the process of wandering through birth and death.
Although this passage ostensibly places the blame on the great assembly, it actually employs the assembly to bring Ānanda to realization.

Seeing that the Venerable One had understood the principle of the immovability of the emptiness of the subject, the World-Honored One stirred and inspired him from within the crowd—what is known as "striking [the student] with a blow."
"Grass startling a snake. This means: I have now revealed this teaching layer upon layer; it may be called clear and explicit.

Yet, if there were still sentient beings who would regard that which moves as "dust" and that which does not abide as a "guest," unable to comprehend the emptiness that is the unmoving host—then you should simply observe Ānanda: at the place where the head moves, he attained awakening.
In seeing, there is no movement. In the place where the hands open and close, one sees that seeing itself has neither expansion nor contraction;
it is already present before you right now, possessing its own form. Why is it that you all take only that which moves to be the body, failing to understand the unmoving Lord?
You take that which moves to be the object, failing to recognize the tranquil void. Furthermore, from beginning to end, you have merely...

To take that which clings to objects moment by moment, arising and ceasing in restless fluctuation, as the mind, while instead neglecting the unmoving true nature (the true nature being precisely this unmoving seeing-nature)—is this not acting in a state of total inversion?

Since that which you rely upon as the nature of the mind is not the unmoving true essence, you will see that the cause is mistaken and the result will be erroneous; you will inevitably encounter only external objects.
For the sake of one's own suffering, one wanders in saṃsāra within the realm of this body; the flow of birth and death continues without ceasing.
Yet this wandering does not descend from heaven, nor does it emerge from the earth, nor is it bestowed by others; it is taken up solely by oneself. Is this not tragic?
It has been said that as soon as one begins to study the Way, one should know to seek the master of the house. However...
One merely recognizes and clings to the transient guest that cannot abide, while failing to realize that the nature of seeing, which is bright and eternally present before one,

is the true master. As soon as they hear the term "prajñā," they speak of "empty vacuity," yet they close their eyes and engage in mental fabrications regarding shifting sensory objects (dharmas), remaining ignorant of the vast and immovable reality before them.

To see one's nature is precisely to realize true emptiness. How wonderful is this subtle instruction of the Dharma King! If a practitioner reflects upon and realizes this through repeated practice, there will surely be those who attain sudden and great enlightenment.
To mistake external objects for oneself is precisely to undergo the bitter fruit of receiving a body and becoming attached to sensory realms.
It is like ordinary people who falsely claim that the body is the self and that external realms belong to the self; thus, the body becomes heavy.
However, the object is light. Those of provisional and small capacity mistakenly identify the mind that realizes [enlightenment] as the "self," which is the "body";
they also take the *nirvāṇa* realized as "mine," which is the "object. Here, the object is heavy while the body is light. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says:
"Even realizing pure *nirvāṇa* is all the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*). Guifeng’s commentary explains: "The mark of self grasped by ordinary beings is..."
The objects of the deluded consciousness are the marks of a self grasped by provisional sages; these are objects of deluded wisdom.

Although they differ in being coarse or subtle, both are termed "recognizing external things as oneself. Viewed from this perspective, even the nirvana of provisional sages is still recognizing external things as oneself.
Thus, is it not the case that the body and objects of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) consist of recognizing external things as oneself?

This is no different from the various spirits and monsters who rely upon grass and wood, seizing them as their own bodies; they are equally subject to delusion. How can one fail to awaken to this with urgency and give rise to weary detachment?
○ Zhong said: "That which moves is called 'dust' (*rajas*); that which does not abide is called a 'guest' (*ātithi*). Ānanda...
The head moves of its own accord. That which moves is adventitious; it is dust. To see that there is no movement is the Tathāgata. The hands open and close of their own accord.
That which opens and closes is adventitious; it is dust. To see that there is no movement is the Tathāgata.

How is it that you now clearly know movement to be the body and movement to be the environment, yet from beginning to end, moment after moment, you fail to realize that they arise and perish? You have lost sight of this.
The true nature is immovable. Yet you take external objects to be yourself and pursue these objects as if they were yourself; is this not how you bring about your own cycle of birth and death?
Since you already know that movement constitutes the realm of the body, you ought to realize that the body and its realm are entirely adventitious dust.
One should not follow after [phenomena] and thereby lose the emptiness of the subject. Regarding "beginning and end":
from a distant perspective, the beginningless is the beginning and this present life is the end; from a proximate perspective, birth is the beginning and death is the end.

This perversion applies not only to worldly affairs, but all various forms of cultivation are likewise termed "perversion," because they involve movement by clinging to the body and its objects, while remaining still by relying on sensory dharmas.

Regarding "according to the objects of the senses," this is identical to the case of the body's sensory fields; one has never awakened to the knowledge that the fundamental seeing-nature is inherently unmoving.
"Within this" refers to within the sensory fields of the body. Thus ends the second demonstration that seeing is unmoving.

Then Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil and at ease. They reflected back upon the beginningless past.

Having lost my original mind, I mistakenly identified with the shadows of conceptualization arising from conditioned objects. Today I have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering her again.

With palms joined, I pay homage to the Buddha and pray to hear the Tathāgata reveal the true and the false within body and mind, and the nature of illumination that manifests both the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing before us.

This third section clarifies that seeing is not extinguished. At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having been rebuked by the Buddha for mistaking what is not the mind for the mind, were immediately seized by alarm and doubt.
Upon hearing that it was detached from dust and subject to cessation, they became even more unsettled.

This was because, apart from consciousness, they had seen nothing else as "mind"; now, having been pointed out by the Buddha within his own faculties, they perceived it as clearly existing as something distinct.
Tranquil and unmoving, his alarm and doubt were instantly stilled; thus, his body and mind became serene. He thought to himself:
"Since beginningless time, I have lost my original, unshakeable true mind and instead identified with the illusory phenomena of conditioned perceptions and discriminations.
Today I have finally attained awakening, just like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encounters her again. [The text continues: "The impoverished son of former days abandoned..."

"Father, today this nursing infant has encountered its mother; how joyful it is! Yet, although this nature of quiescent permanence—neither arising nor ceasing—has been granted by your seal of approval, if we rely on the common perception that 'this is the eye,' then both the eye and the seeing belong to the realm of arising and ceasing.
If we rely on today’s observation where the hand opens and closes while the seeing has no opening or closing, and the head shakes while the seeing does not..."
As he was shaking [the bowl], it became clear that within this body of birth and extinction there exists a nature of non-birth and non-extinction.
Although he has now attained an understanding of the principle that the vision is unmoving, he has not yet clarified its underlying cause and still harbors doubts.

Thereupon, he joined his palms, prostrated before the Buddha, and prayed to hear from the Tathāgata how to manifest the true nature of body and mind: who is real and who is false? What is empty and what is substantial? He sought this essential point...

Within this body that is presently subject to movement, agitation, arising, and ceasing, one must directly point out the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, so that these two natures—the true and the false—become as clear as the stars and the moon;
only then will one reach the ground of self-confidence free from doubt. Master Zhong said:

Regarding the second point, "revealing the nature" (*fāmíng xìng*): the two characters "reveal" (*fāmíng*) should be understood as having the meaning of manifesting and making evident from the standpoint of principle (*lǐ*).
This refers to the fact that within the principle of true nature (*zhēnxìng lǐ*), there inherently exists that which is neither arising nor ceasing.

The nature that is revealed and manifested is precisely this: the one becoming the infinite, the infinite becoming the one; the small appearing within the large, and the large appearing within the small, and so forth. As for the phrase "delusory revelation of principle" (*wàngmíng lǐ*):
The nature manifested therein is as follows: "That which is below, obscured and dark, becomes space; within the darkness of space, the coagulation of darkness becomes form;

form mixed with deluded thought, and the characteristics of thought become the body," and so forth. There are those who interpret this by viewing it through the lens of the two natures of manifestation and obscuration.
This was indeed an elucidation through speech. However, the phrasing and meaning were not consistent.

At that time, King Prasenajit rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha: "In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I encountered Kātyāyana and Ajita Keśakambalin, both of whom said that after this body dies, its cessation and extinction is called Nirvana. Although I encountered them..."
"World-Honored One, I still harbor doubts. How can you manifest and provide proof that this mind is a ground neither arising nor ceasing?
Now, all those in this great assembly who still possess outflows long to hear this."
This King Ajātaśatru personally confessed his nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) in order to inquire about non-arising and non-ceasing.
In the past, the King had served non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*), and the seeds of heterodox thought had once entered the depths of his heart.

Now, having been seized by Ānanda at his most sensitive point, he took the opportunity to pose his question—just as one who encounters peach and plum trees suddenly recalls the springtime of his old garden. Kātyāyana...
Yan (延) means "to cut hair. Vīrāṭi (毗羅胝) means "non-action"; he was one of the six heterodox teachers. Their doctrines all take annihilation as their primary tenet.

Because they do not understand that the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*—which departs later and arrives first—is the root of birth and death, they fail to realize that the transformation of this eighth consciousness is what is called *nirvāṇa*. Instead, they falsely calculate it [as something else].

"To regard the annihilation of the body as *nirvāṇa*—to calculate that birth in this world consists merely of a seven-foot frame, and that upon death it becomes but a coffin of earth, subject to crushing, burning, pounding, grinding, or being of no further use—all such views are included in this category.
How could they know that there exists one who dies but does not perish? At that time, King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha, "In the past, I..."

Before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I once encountered two kinds of non-Buddhists who both claimed that after the death of this body, there is annihilation, and that this very annihilation is what is called Nirvana.
Although I have now met the Tathāgata, I still harbor doubts and have not reached a resolution;
I must certainly have a manifest proof before me in order to be able to believe that this mind is indeed [Buddha-nature].
“Arising and ceasing. World-Honored One, how do you manifest and bring about the realization of this mind’s ground of non-arising and non-ceasing?
Now, the great assembly gathered here, those who have not yet reached the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), all desire to hear this.

If one judges by the elimination of the coarse delusions of the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*), then these "outflows" seem to refer only to ordinary worldlings within the realms and to those of the two vehicles who are still in training (*śaikṣa*). However, if one discerns the views...
Since the nature is true and eternal, even those at the four fruits of the Small Vehicle or the three stages of worthiness of the Separate Teaching must be universally pointed toward it;
for they have not, from the outset, clearly perceived that the nature is the true and eternal mind.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body is present now. I ask you again: Is this physical body of yours eternal and indestructible like a diamond, or is it subject to decay and transformation?
"World-Honored One, this body of mine will ultimately undergo change and perish. The Buddha said: "Great King, you have not yet perished.
How do you know it will perish? "World-Honored One, this body of mine is impermanent and subject to decay and transformation."
"Although it has not yet been extinguished, I observe that before my eyes every moment passes away; it is ever-new and never-abiding.
Like fire turning to ash, it gradually wastes away and perishes without ceasing. I know for certain that this body must eventually come to total extinction. The Buddha said, "It is so."
Because I wish to demonstrate the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, I first examine its arising and ceasing. The Buddha said to the Great King:
"You harbor doubts regarding the place where you will be reborn after death in the future; I shall question you only concerning the place where you are currently born.
Your body exists right now. I ask you: is this physical body a diamond-like, eternally abiding, and indestructible thing, or..."
"Furthermore, is it ultimately a thing subject to transformation and decay? King Nigaṇṭha replied, "World-Honored One, this body of mine is not a permanent entity;

it will ultimately end in transformation and extinction. The Buddha questioned him again and again with great care, seeking to draw out his understanding like extracting a fox's saliva from a hook, and then said, "Great King, while your body is currently present and has not yet perished, on what basis do you presume to know its future cessation?"

"Will it perish? King Ajātaśatru replied, "World-Honored One, although this impermanent and decaying body of mine has not yet perished, I observe that before my eyes, every moment passes away; it is ever-new and never abides, like fire turning to ash."
Gradually wasting away and approaching death, there is not a single moment of rest. One must realize that this body will ultimately perish;
only then can one attain true liberation. The Buddha said: "Your body must perish; it is truly as you say.
With these few words alone, one may be alerted to impermanence. How could those who are intensely preoccupied with worldly affairs not be struck with trepidation?
"Great King, you have now reached an age of decline and old age. How does your countenance compare to that of your youth?
"World-Honored One, when I was once a child, my skin and flesh were moist and lustrous. As I grew into adulthood, my blood and vital energy were full and robust.

But now, advanced in years and pressed by decrepitude, my physical form is withered and emaciated, my spirit is clouded and dim, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled; it will not be long before I am gone."
"How do you see him compared to when he was in the prime of his vigor?
Furthermore, examine closely whether his spirit and complexion from youth until old age are the same or different.
The Buddha spoke again: "Great King, at this present age of yours, you have already passed into senility. As for your countenance—"
"How was it when you were a youth? King Bimbisāra replied, "World-Honored One, in the past, when I was a mere infant, my skin and flesh were moist, supple, and radiant.
As I grew to maturity, my essence was complete and my spirit vigorous; my blood and qi were full.
But now that my years have declined, pressed by old age and decrepitude, my appearance is withered and haggard, and my spirit..."
Then one is shrouded in darkness and confusion. With skin like that of a rooster and hair as white as a crane, walking with a tottering gait, the sun is already setting behind the mulberry trees;
one’s end is surely near. How can you compare this state to a time when the spirit was full, robust, and overflowing?
The Buddha said, "Great King, your physical form should not have decayed so suddenly. The King replied, "World-Honored One, transformation shifts secretly;
I truly do not perceive it. Yet as cold and heat pass and flow, I have gradually reached this state. Why is this?
When I was twenty, though I was called young, my countenance was already aged compared to when I was ten. At thirty, I was further declined than at twenty."
"I am now sixty-two. When I observed myself at fifty, I was still quite robust. World-Honored One, I perceive this subtle shifting;
although there is this falling away, as it flows and changes over the course of ten years, if I were to contemplate it with minute attention, would the change be limited to a decade or two?
In truth, it is the change of years. But is it only the change of years? It is also accompanied by months."

It transforms; not only does it change with the months, but it also shifts daily. Contemplating deeply and observing with discernment, one sees that from moment to moment, between every thought, nothing remains stationary.
Thus, one knows that this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.

This, moreover, is a subtle examination of the suddenness or gradualness of arising and ceasing. The Buddha said: "Great King, a single breath is not exhausted all at once; a single form is not diminished all at once.
Your physical appearance must not have decayed all at once in a single day; it must have decayed gradually. The King said:
"World-Honored One, the transformations of the world shift so subtly and secretly that I truly do not perceive them. However—"
I observe the sun setting and the moon rising, and how cold and heat alternate and shift, gradually arriving at this present state. Why is this so?
The span of human life is sometimes long and sometimes short; let us take ten years as a standard measure. For instance, consider when I was twenty years old.
Although I am called young, my countenance has already aged by ten years from what it was; having reached the age of thirty, I have further declined from when I was twenty.
Now that I have reached sixty-two, looking back at fifty, I appear as if I were still in the prime of youth.
Is this not a transformation occurring every ten years? World-Honored One, I observe this subtle shifting; though I am strong...
Physical form declines day by day until it perishes; the signs of old age hasten its fall.
Yet even within this interval of flux, it is still limited to ten years; this is merely stated in broad terms.
If I were to engage in subtle contemplation to investigate the nature of these changes, how could it be limited to a single cycle of twelve years, or even two cycles of twenty-four years?
The record states: "In truth, there is indeed a transformation once every year; yet it is not only a transformation by the year, but also a metamorphosis by the month.

It is not merely a metamorphosis by the month, but furthermore, a shift occurs every day. If one were to further deepen their contemplation and examine with meticulous observation, then within this very single thought—which comprises ninety *kṣaṇas*—in each and every *kṣaṇa*, and in every moment of thought, all..."
In its constant flux, it never remains still for a moment. Its substance is neither metal nor stone; how could it endure such a state?
From the longest span of years down to the briefest instant of a *kṣaṇa*, transformation shifts so subtly and secretly that only those who are naturally indifferent to it fail to perceive it.
Through mental attention and inferential deliberation, one first comes to know this; thus, one knows that my own body must ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.
In the teachings, it is said that piercing ninety sheets of paper with a sharp blade constitutes a single *kṣaṇa*; therefore, a single *tatkṣaṇa* (moment) comprises ninety *kṣaṇas*.
The Buddha said to the Great King, "You see that transformations and changes ceaselessly proceed; you have realized this cessation.
At the time of such cessation, do you know that within your body there is something that does not cease? King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, "Truly, I do not know."
The Buddha said, "I shall now demonstrate to you the nature of non-arising and non-extinction.

Because the World-Honored One saw that King Bimbisāra had recounted the phenomena of transformation and extinction without omitting even the slightest detail, he gave a sudden, direct challenge at this critical juncture, saying:
"Great King, you see that transformations do not cease; realize and know that you yourself are subject to extinction. He also [said]: "At the same time..."
"When it ceases, do you know that there is something within your body that does not cease? The King joined his palms and said to the Buddha, "I truly do not know.
An ancient said, "The place where one does not know is most intimate"—this is what is meant by "using it daily without knowing it."

"By causing him to know this, he will certainly not be deluded by the view of annihilation. The Buddha said, "Since you do not yet know it, I shall now demonstrate to you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished."
"Great King, at what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges? The King replied, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīvaka;
as we passed by this stream, I immediately recognized it as the water of the Ganges. The Buddha said to the Great King:
It is as you have said. From the age of twenty one declines from that of ten, and so on until sixty; days, months, years, and seasons change and pass away moment by moment.
Thus, when you were three years old and saw this river, what was its water like when you reached the age of thirteen?
The King said, "It is exactly as it was when I was three years old; there is not the slightest difference. Even now, at the age of sixty-two, there is likewise no difference.
This is because, while the perception of the river has changed over the years, my vision remains unchanged. The Buddha then began another topic.
The Buddha asked, "Great King, how old were you when you first saw this River Gaṅgā?
The King replied, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother carried me in her arms to visit the deity Dīrghāyu.
As we passed by this water, I immediately recognized it as the Gaṅgā. The Buddha said, "Great King, it is as you have said; from the age of ten until sixty..."
"Years pass; as time shifts and changes from moment to moment, your vision should likewise shift and change.

Yet you do not know whether, from the time you were three years old when you saw this river until you saw it again at age thirteen, the water during those intervening ten years has changed in any way.
The King said, "When I observed the river at thirteen, it was exactly as it was at age three; it was perfectly unchanged."
It is not merely thirteen years; it has now reached sixty-two. Behold this river water;
it is no different from what it was when I was three years old.
The Buddha said, "Now you lament that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled; indeed, your face must have become wrinkled compared to your youth.
As you now look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between this vision of yours and the vision you had when looking at the river as a child—any distinction between childhood and old age?
The King replied, "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face is wrinkled, the essential nature of this seeing-essence has never been wrinkled."

That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change. That which changes undergoes cessation. As for that which is unchanging, it fundamentally has neither birth nor death.
How could birth and death be experienced therein? Yet you still cite Makkhali Gosāla and others who claim that after this body dies, there is total extinction.
Upon hearing these words, the King came to believe that after death one abandons this life to take up another, and together with the great assembly, [he attained realization].
He leaped for joy, having attained what he had never experienced before.
This further confirms that there is neither childhood nor old age; by destroying and severing views, the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is revealed.
The Buddha spoke again: "Now you lament that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled. Let me ask you about this single matter of facial wrinkles."
Your face must surely be wrinkled compared to your youth; thus, your face possesses both childhood and old age.
But I do not know whether the vision you have now when viewing the river is subject to childhood or old age, just as it was when you viewed the river in your youth.
The King replied, "No, World-Honored One. Having thus examined each point with clarity until there was no room for evasion, the Buddha spoke to him:
"Great King, do you not yet recognize the nature that is neither born nor extinguished?

Although your face has grown wrinkled, this vision that observes the river is precisely your vision-essence (*darśana-vijñāna*). This vision-essence of yours has never, in its true nature, been wrinkled."
That which is wrinkled is subject to change; that which is not wrinkled is not subject to change.
That which changes is subject to extinction; that which does not change is fundamentally without birth or extinction.
Since it is without birth or extinction, how could it again follow your present body to undergo your birth and death? This very [unchanging nature] is precisely what constitutes birth.

When the body is extinguished, the nature of non-arising and non-extinction remains. Yet, you still cite those who do not see the Way, such as the non-Buddhists, who all claim that after this body dies, it is completely annihilated—is this not a grave error?
Upon hearing these words, the King came to believe and know that the nature is without arising or extinction;
that after this body dies, one abandons this life to be born elsewhere, like moving from one dark room to another dark room.
Emerging from one wheel of suffering and entering another wheel of suffering, it has never been severed or extinguished.

Together with the great assembly, they leaped for joy and attained what they had never experienced before. ○ In this chapter, because King Bimbisāra observed within his own body, he perceived cessation and extinction;
whereas the World-Honored One illuminated the matter from the perspective of vision, thus there is neither arising nor ceasing. This is what is meant by "not departing from beneath the flower."
This leads one into the midst of the cave-heaven. This not only shatters King Prasenajit’s view of annihilationism, but also fulfills Ānanda’s two-fold request.
Question: Formerly, National Teacher Zhong asked a Zen guest from where he had come.
The guest replied, “From the South. The Master asked, “How do the teachers of the South instruct people? The guest said:
The spiritual teacher of that region directly points out to the student that the very mind is Buddha; apart from this, there is no other Buddha.
This body indeed undergoes birth and death, but the nature of the mind has never been subject to birth or death.

As for the birth and death of the body, it is like a dragon shedding its bones, a snake sloughing off its skin, or a person leaving an old house. The Master said: "If that is so, then how does this differ from the non-Buddhists?"
What is the distinction? They say: "Within this body of mine there is a divine self (*ātman*). This self is capable of knowing pain and pleasure.
When the body perishes, the self departs, just as when a house is burned, the owner of the house departs;
the house is impermanent, but the owner is permanent. If one examines it in this way, then the false and the true cannot be distinguished. Now, the Buddha says that what is wrinkled...
[The questioner asks: "Is it a transformation? Or is it that which does not wrinkle, thus not a transformation? Might this not conflict with the National Preceptor? [The Master] answers:

"The National Preceptor shattered the attachments of a particular moment; the Tathāgata opened up the provisional means of a particular moment. Both are subtle eloquence. You must grasp them through the meaning;

you must not recklessly give rise to conjecture, for then you will incur the displeasure of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Furthermore, the masters of our school often say that [the truth] is not separate from within the body."
There is, then, an indestructible essential nature; this refers precisely to the nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth within the sense organs.

It does not mean that there is a separate life-force or nature existing apart from them within the heart or inside the viscera—this would be identical to the "consciousness-mind within the body" that Ānanda clung to.
○ Zhong says: The previous instance of bending the fingers and chasing the light pointed out the [indestructible nature] within a single moment and a single event.
The nature of arising and ceasing. This demonstrates the vision of one observing a river; it points out the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing within the span of a single lifetime.
Reaching the analogy of the sound of the pestle in the fourth fascicle, it says:
"Even if your physical form dissolves and your life-force and radiance pass away, how could this nature be extinguished for you? Thus, the nature that does not arise or cease after death is revealed.
[The Master] brought it forth from the depths. ○ The third section, revealing that seeing is indestructible, is concluded.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated to the Buddha with palms joined, and knelt long before the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of delusion?"
"I pray that you will give rise to compassion and wash away my defilements.
This fourth instance clarifies that seeing is not lost. Above, only "seeing" was mentioned; here, it is further combined with "hearing.
The character "hearing" (聞) is likely an error for the character "nature" (性). Since King Ajātaśatru’s insight was not extensive, his mind-ground [was transformed] by these few words.
[The Buddha] explained it clearly. [Ananda] should simply believe directly. Ānanda possesses much knowledge and has seen much; thus, when encountering matters, he gives rise to emotional attachments.

Therefore, while he was just beginning to believe, he suddenly became doubtful. At that moment, he rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if this seeing-nature were necessarily subject to arising and ceasing, it could be called lost. Since this seeing-nature is certainly not..."
Arising and ceasing are themselves quiescent and eternal; they are equal to all Buddhas, without any distinction.
Why, World-Honored One, do you say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of delusion, while you do not say that the Buddhas have lost their nature or act in delusion?
My mind is shrouded and obscured, like being stained with dust and grime. I pray that you will arouse your compassion and wash it clean for me.
How could one know that when the Buddha speaks of "losing the true nature," he is speaking of loss due to delusion and inversion, rather than loss due to annihilation?
Therefore, the subsequent text fully demonstrates the characteristics of inversion in order to interrogate this point.
At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm; with his wheel-marked hand pointing downward, he showed it to Ānanda, saying:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted? Ānanda replied: "The sentient beings of the world consider this to be inverted, yet I do not know which is upright and which is inverted.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If the people of the world consider this to be inverted, then..."

"What do people of the world consider to be upright? Ānanda replied, "If the Tathāgata raises his arm, which has hands as soft as *tūla* cotton, pointing it upward toward the sky, that is what they call upright.

The Buddha then raised his arm and said to Ānanda, "If this [arm] were inverted, with head and tail swapped, and all people of the world looked at it twice over, then you would know that your body and those of all the Tathāgatas are equally pure."
The Dharma-body. To elucidate this through analogy: the body of the Tathāgata is named "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), whereas your bodies are designated as "inverted by nature.
As you observe them with discernment, where in your own bodies or in the Buddha’s body is there a name that can be called "inversion"?
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha; their eyes did not blink, and they were unaware [of anything else].
"The locus of the inversion of body and mind.
This indicates the characteristics of inversion in order to verify the nature of that inverted state.
At that moment, the Tathāgata lowered his hand and pointed downward, saying to Ānanda: "Ānanda, as you now see my *mudrā* hand, is it upright or inverted? Ānanda—
Having once suffered at the hands of poison, I did not dare to take responsibility for this myself, fearing it would bring misfortune upon others.
I said, "I observe that all sentient beings in the world consider this downward orientation to be 'upside-down,' yet I do not know who is actually upright and who is actually upside-down.
The World-Honored One then pressed him with a single question: "If worldly people consider this to be upside-down, then what do they take to be upright?"
Ānanda twisted the straight into a curve, saying, "If the Tathāgata were to raise his arm and point this hand upward, then it would be called 'correct.
The World-Honored One, taking error for error, immediately raised his arm and said:
"If you truly consider pointing upward to be correct, then this is precisely like placing a crown on one's feet and shoes on one's head—turning the head into a tail and the tail into a head."
How could one seek inversion elsewhere? Moreover, this single arm is fundamentally neither inverted nor upright;

it is only worldly people who distinguish between inversion and uprightness, viewing it with a biased perspective. How could they know that hanging down constitutes inversion? Indeed, it is inversion.
Pointing upward is considered upright, yet it is also inverted. How can you claim that pointing upward is upright while hanging downward is inverted?
It is because you have given rise to this dualistic view that the Tathāgata does not hold such a view.

Therefore, by using your own body as a comparison to illustrate the pure Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas, it is seen that the body of the Tathāgata is called the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
Your bodies are inverted in accordance with their nature; thus, your claim that you are no different from the Buddha and therefore not inverted is an error.

Since I have already elucidated the nature of inversion, I further apply the probe to cause you to follow the name in search of the reality, so that you may examine for yourselves the actual locus of inversion.
Therefore it is said: "Now, furthermore, I shall follow you in careful and thorough investigation."
"Compared to the Buddha’s body, yours is called 'perverse' (*viparyāsa*). Since you bear the name 'perverse,' there must be a reality to that perversity.
From what reality did you receive this name? When Ānanda was thus questioned by the World-Honored One, he was as if blind though possessing eyes, and as if mute though possessing a mouth;
he had no words with which to respond and no principles by which to defend himself. He could only—
The great assembly stared blankly at the Buddha; they were dazed and motionless, their eyes not blinking, unaware that their bodies and minds were in a state of inversion.
Is it not so that even those of great wisdom have a darkness of three feet before their faces?
Master Zhong said: "Inversion and correctness are the same arm; it is merely a matter of exchanging head and tail. This is correctness.
Universal knowledge and the inversion of nature share this same body; they differ only in that one is deluded and the other is awakened.

To know this is to realize that even while losing oneself, the inversion does not hinder the fact that one is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished. ○ *Mudrā* means "Seal of the Hand" in this context.
The Buddha gave rise to compassion and, out of pity for Ānanda and the great assembly, uttered a voice like the tide of the ocean, addressing all the good sons gathered there:
"I have often said that the various conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all objects of cognition,"
All is manifested by mind alone. Your bodies and your minds are all objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence—the wondrous mind.
Why, then, do you all lose this original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, and instead recognize delusion within awakening? You fail to perceive the wondrous nature of the mind’s clarity.
From here below, the text correctly elucidates the actual locus of inversion. Ānanda, may you give rise to compassion; the Buddha likewise gives rise to compassion.
Out of pity for Ānanda and the great assembly, He utters the voice of the ocean tide, which never fails its appointed time, addressing all the virtuous sons gathered here:
"I have often said that there are eleven material dharmas and eight consciousnesses."
