The mental dharmas: the four conditions for the arising of the mind, the two conditions for the arising of form, and the fifty-one mental factors that accompany the mind—
ranging extensively from the wholesome, unwholesome, and the heterodox or orthodox, to all mundane and supramundane activities, causes and effects, and all objects of cognition—
all these five categories are manifestations of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, just as [images appear] in a clear mirror.
As a mirror manifests images, one can see that all phenomena are the mind itself.

Your present body of the five sense organs and your mind of the eight consciousnesses are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous true essence, the wondrous mind; thus, one can see that the mind encompasses all phenomena.
Now, as for "mind" (citta) and "nature" (prakṛti), they are mutually designated as essence and function. The mind arises from the wondrous as its luminosity.
Perfectly interfused and illuminating, it is like the light of a mirror; its nature is intrinsically luminous and wondrous, pure, clear, firm, and solid, like the substance of a mirror.

This mind and this nature have been yours from the very beginning. Why, then, do you all neglect and lose this original, self-evident, and wondrously perfect, luminous mind and precious, brilliant, wondrous nature that does not depend on cultivation to be realized?

Yet you recognize the delusions within original enlightenment; you do not know that the myriad dharmas are the mind and that the mind encompasses the myriad dharmas, but instead claim that all dharmas exist outside the mind and that the mind falls within the dharmas.
This is to falsely conceive of inversion where there is no inversion, and to be functionally equivalent to having lost what has never been lost. Question: Previously, it was said that one sees...
The "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the substance of the *ālayavijñāna*; it is the mind of the Tathāgatagarbha, and it is also the substantial reality of all phenomena.

It appears as the "agent of manifestation. Now, since the "mind" within the phrase "matter and mind" (*rūpa-citta*) encompasses all eight consciousnesses, the *ālayavijñāna* has already become the "object manifested.
Therefore, the "mind" referred to in the phrase "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) must be a distinct, purely authentic mind. How can one still take the mind of the Tathāgatagarbha [as this]?

To explain this: the answer is that while the preceding seven [consciousnesses] serve only as the manifested (*pratibhāsa*) and the true mind serves only as the manifestor (*pratibhāsaka*), this *ālayavijñāna* functions as both.
When contrasted with the true mind, it descends to the status of the manifested; when contrasted with the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*), it ascends to the status of the manifestor.
This is because it is fundamentally non-dual in essence with the true mind, differing only in that it carries along delusion (*moha*).

Obscurity and darkness constitute emptiness. Within this obscure emptiness, the gathering of darkness forms matter. Matter is intermingled with false conceptualization; these conceptual appearances form the body. As it gathers conditions, it stirs within;
as it pursues external objects, it rushes outward. This state of confused turmoil is taken to be the nature of the mind. Thus, through a single delusion, it becomes the mind.

You have determined that delusions reside within the physical body. You do not know that everything from the physical body outward—to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is all a thing within the wondrously luminous true mind.

It is like discarding a hundred thousand vast oceans of clear water and recognizing only a single floating bubble, taking that bubble to be the entire tide and exhausting the whole expanse of the sea. You all are people who are doubly deluded.
"Just as my hanging hand is equal and without distinction, the Tathāgata calls such a person one who is to be pitied.
This section below elucidates why the body and mind constitute delusion within awakening. Now, regarding this wondrously luminous mind-nature:
Originally, there were no signs of body or mind. It was all due to the initial lack of awakening (*abodha*), which suddenly gave rise to ignorance (*avidyā*).

This took that primary emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and, through its obscuration, turned it into a dull emptiness devoid of knowledge or awareness—what is called "the void arising from delusion.
Because this transformed dull emptiness and the transforming ignorance unite as these two dharmas, within that dull...
Yet, within this state of obscurity and darkness, it coagulates to form the colors of the four great elements—what is called "the clarity of thought forming the land.
Thus, the colors of the four great elements mingle with the deluded mind; this deluded mind and deluded color, along with their perceived characteristics, combine in harmony.
The five aggregates and the root-body are thus formed; what we call perception is the sentient being.

This is precisely why the body is delusion within awakening. Since the four great elements of the root-body exist, they combine internally and externally to produce a false, conditioned vapor that accumulates therein.
Consequently, one is stirred incessantly by internal conditions—reflected phenomena—and by external conditions—real objects.
It races and gallops without ceasing; it is dark and turbulent, neither clear nor pure.
Furthermore, one clings to this state of darkness and turbulence, taking it to be the perfectly wondrous and luminous mind, the precious, luminous, and wondrous nature.
This is precisely why the mind is deluded within its own awakening. Having once mistaken this dark and turbulent state for one's own mind, one becomes definitively confused.
You think this mind resides within the physical body, dwelling upon the mass of flesh;

yet you fail to realize that not only is this physical body of yours a manifestation within the wondrously luminous mind, but even the external mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth are all manifestations within the wondrously luminous mind. Now, you abandon this vast [mind]...
With such a wondrous mind, you falsely identify the four elements as the characteristics of your own body and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of your own mind.

How is this different from abandoning the clear and vast ocean extending for hundreds of thousands of li, only to instead identify a single floating bubble in the sea as being the entirety of the tide within that ocean?
Even if one were to exhaustively search the entire expanse of the sea, it would still be found only here [in the bubble].

Ah! Viewed from this perspective, you will know that your own body and the body of the Tathāgata, when compared and illuminated through analogy, are of one and the same substance and fundamentally without distinction.
However, the Tathāgata has fully realized that the ocean is the ocean and the bubble is the bubble;
he does not abandon the ocean to identify with the bubble, and thus it is called "right knowledge. He does not mistake the bubble for the ocean, and thus it is called "universal knowledge. You all...
Having already abandoned the ocean to recognize the bubble, you further recognize the bubble as the ocean; therefore, it is called "inversion of nature.
This is why I address you all as people who have added a double layer of delusion upon their existing delusion. It is just like when I hang my hand down:
in reality, there is no distinction between "upright" and "inverted," yet you take the downward-pointing position to be inverted and the upward-pointing position to be upright. This is precisely...
You abide in perversion; therefore, know that you originally have nothing lost. It is because of perversion that you speak of loss.
This is what the Tathāgata calls those who are to be pitied. For if you were truly lost, [you would not be here].

This alone is not yet sufficient grounds for deep compassion. Now, because of perversion (*viparyāsa*), one is constantly as if having lost it—just like one who holds a jewel yet acts as a beggar, needlessly enduring poverty.
Is this not also deeply pitiable? Question: Previously, you stated that seeing the nature is the substantial reality (*dravya*) of the eight consciousnesses;
now, you further describe the gathering of conditions as the functional capacity (*vṛtti*) of the eight consciousnesses. How are the merits and faults to be distinguished? Answer:
This consciousness is a fusion of the true and the false. Therefore, when the nature of seeing perceives, it takes a portion of the True Principle;

when it gathers conditions, it takes a portion of deluded sentiment. All statements regarding the eight consciousnesses—such as "departing after" or "arriving before"—are spoken solely in terms of deluded sentiment.
○ Furthermore, it says: "Once deluded, one takes this as the mind and is certain to be confused by it as being within the physical body. How profound these words are!

Indeed, were it not for the Buddha’s teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), who would not reckon that life and nature reside within the body, and that the myriad phenomena are merely external to the mind?
Yet, the reckoning of life as residing within the body has been especially prevalent in the Daoist tradition for a long time.
Sentient beings do not believe that within their own bodies there is fundamentally no life or destiny. [The Master] asked again:
"To take a single floating bubble and call it the entire tide—how does this differ from claiming that a single pore contains the entirety of the ocean of worlds (*kṣetrasamudra*)?

He replied: "That person has realized that the nature of all phenomena is the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, a single hair, being in accord with that nature, encompasses everything without exception. It is like speaking of a true *maṇi* jewel."
"A pearl worth an entire kingdom" is indeed not false. This [person], however, does not understand the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
they merely take their deluded and agitated conceptualizations to be within the body, and furthermore, perversely cling to it as being able to encompass empty space and the great earth.

Since this [body] has no essence that can be found, upon what could it possibly rely to be so vast and all-encompassing? To say that a bubble on the water is worth an entire kingdom is truly a great delusion.

How can they be the same? ○ Previously, when Ānanda heard the rebuke that [the mind he identified was] not the true mind, he was startled and thought that apart from this, there was nothing else—regarding it as being like earth or water.
The Tathāgata comforted him by merely granting that the true mind has a substance; it was not yet a formal revelation of the true mind.
It is like promising someone an object and only giving it to them on a later day. Changshui, in his commentary on... [text truncated]
That place refers precisely to the revelation of the true mind. Although it was permitted as being given, there was still a lack of actual realization.
It is only upon reaching this chapter that it constitutes the main text for the revelation of the true mind;
at this point, Ānanda finally understands that beyond the objects of the senses, there exists such a vast essence of mind, and that what the Tathāgata promised is indeed not false.
The fourth section, clarifying that seeing is not lost, concludes.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms, addressing the Buddha:

"Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the fundamental ground of the heart that is perfect, eternal, and abiding—I have now awakened to the Buddha..."

You now manifest the sound of the Dharma; you now manifest with the mind that conditions it. We truly look up to you in reverence, yet though we have obtained this mind, we do not yet dare to recognize it as our fundamental, original mind-ground.
We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim the perfect sound to uproot our doubts and lead us back to the Unsurpassed Way.

This fifth section clarifies that seeing has no place of return. Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction—having been suspended head-downward for ten thousand kalpas and remaining in delusion for a lifetime—was suddenly enlightened. Moved by the Buddha’s deep compassion, he came to weep profusely.
Yet, my mind still harbors doubts; therefore, I again join my palms and address the Buddha, saying:

"Although I have received this wondrous voice from the Buddha and realized that this wondrously luminous mind is precisely my own originally complete and perfect, unborn and undying, eternally abiding ground of the heart, we have nonetheless consistently neglected this vast nature of the mind."
To recognize this state of dullness and agitation as the nature of the mind (cittatā) is indeed why it is appropriate to call us "perverted in nature" (viparyasta).
However, at present, when we see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, we do so entirely by means of this very mind of discursive thought (ālambana-citta).

Although the World-Honored One does not wish for us to recognize this, he has rejected it as being "not the mind. If it were a different kind of mind that perceives objects, it might be possible to discard it.
Now that I have awakened to the Buddha’s Dharma-sound, I have received and internalized it; I am only now relying upon its application. How could I suddenly abandon it?
Because I have attained its utility, I cannot but acknowledge it. World-Honored One, that which I acknowledge is the perfect and wondrous mind.
Although it is vast and great, at present I do not yet attain its utility; I have merely acquired this in vain. Therefore, I—
I venture to claim this as my original mind-ground. To recognize this, one ought to abandon that; yet now, since I cannot bear to abandon that, I also do not dare to claim this.
Furthermore, if one were to discard the mind that engages with conditioned phenomena, what would there be to receive and uphold the Buddha-Dharma hereafter?
Even if one does not begrudge this conditional mind, does one not nonetheless hold the Buddha-Dharma in high regard? I pray—
The Buddha, out of compassion, proclaimed the perfect sound to uproot my doubts and lead me to the stage beyond doubt, whereby I may return to the Unsurpassed Way.
○ He [Heshang] said: "Zhengmo claims that Ānanda did not abandon the mind of conditions and therefore did not recognize the true mind;

he fears that if one recognizes this, one must abandon that. However, he does not realize that the original text says, 'I have not yet dared to recognize it,' and is not [saying that he has already recognized it]."
This means they are unwilling to acknowledge it. Holding onto this mind they have first attained, they have not yet made use of it and do not yet dare to finally acknowledge it as their own master.
They must seek the World-Honored One to reveal it thoroughly, so that they may personally see their original face;
only then will they dare to acknowledge it. Therefore it is said: "Uproot my root of doubt. This is precisely the true inquiry and actual practice of the ancients.
The Place of Realization. Zhong said: "Faculties have their stages of ripening and rawness.

For Ānanda, throughout his daily life, he was accustomed to the mind that perceives conditions (*yuán-xīn*), while he remained unaccustomed to the nature of seeing (*jiàn-xìng*). Where one is unaccustomed, one cannot suddenly employ it;

where one is accustomed, one cannot easily abandon it. This is simply human nature. However, in this instance, the emphasis lies in seeking the Truth, rather than in abandoning the delusion. This is precisely...

While the Venerable was still swaying and had not yet found stability, and while his provisional mind and true mind were held in a state of indecision—like a person bewildered at a fork in the road, dazed and unsettled—an ancient master said:
"It is easy to open a mouth for the beginning and the end, but difficult to preserve a heart through the winter's cold.
The Venerable took these words to heart. From that point on, he proceeded directly until each and every one came to know for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions.
Only when you have attained the fundamentally wondrous mind and abide in the state of eternal non-extinction will you finally be willing to accept it as such.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is also a condition and is not equal to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)."
It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another. That person, by means of the finger, should look toward the moon.
If, however, they gaze at the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar orb, but also lose the finger itself?

Why is this? Because they have taken the finger used as a signifier to be the bright moon. Would they not only lose the finger, but also fail to distinguish between light and darkness? How could this be?

For this reason, one takes the substance of the finger itself to be the nature of the moon’s brightness; yet because the two natures of light and darkness cannot be discerned [as distinct], you are likewise so.
This rebukes him for recognizing the sensory object of sound while failing to penetrate the Dharma-nature. The Buddha told Ānanda: "I now, like..."
In this moment, I have laid bare my heart and soul, lingering among the weeds to desire that you abandon delusive conditions and realize the nature of mind.
Yet, I did not expect that your views and understanding remain, in every detail, no different from those of the past, and that you still employ a mind of grasping and attachment.
"Listen to me as I explain the Dharma of the perfect, eternally abiding mind. Yet, this very Dharma of the perfect, eternally abiding mind also becomes an object of perception (*ālambana*).
How, then, can you possibly realize this nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? You do not know that the one who preaches the Dharma is merely like a person pointing at the moon.
Suppose there were someone here who, with his finger, pointed at the moon to show it to another person; that person, by means of the finger, would then—"
"Look at the moon! If you take the finger pointing at it to be the essence of the moon, how foolish you are! You not only fail to recognize the moon, you also fail to recognize the finger.
Not only do you fail to recognize the finger, you likewise fail to recognize light and darkness, for the moon is bright while the finger is dark.
If, after hearing the Dharma, you cease all speech, cast aside your cleverness, and become one..."
Relinquish everything completely. Silently investigate your own mind. This is like using a finger to point at the moon; it is for those who do not cling to the appearance of the finger.

If you continue as before with much knowledge and understanding, refusing to resolve [all things] back into yourself, you are merely chasing words and phrases—a person who mistakes the finger for the moon.
Now, you cling to the sound of the Dharma while failing to penetrate the nature of the Dharma. Why?
To mistake a pointing finger for the moon is to fail to distinguish black from white and remain unaware of the difference between dusk and dawn.

Thus it is said: "You are also like this. Zhong says: "The mind that conditions" refers to the subjective mind capable of conditioning. "Conditioning by phenomena" refers to the objective objects being conditioned.
Since the sound of the Dharma is a sensory object (the dust of sound), it too is not the truth. "Dharmatā" refers to ultimate reality. This is the selection of the teaching.
Truth. Principle is the mind of sentient beings; how can one mistake the teachings for the mind? The finger is a metaphor for the Dharma;
the moon is a metaphor for the listener’s own mind. The preaching of the Dharma reveals the mind; upon hearing the teachings, one should naturally turn inward to contemplate the mind.
If one clings to the sounds of the teachings and fails to understand the practice of reflecting back upon one's own mind, such a person not only fails to realize their own mind, but furthermore—
One does not understand the intent of the teaching. Why is this? Because one takes the sounds of another’s teaching as one’s own mind, failing to distinguish between self and other.
Not only does one fail to understand the intent of the teaching, but one also fails to comprehend the essence and characteristics of the mind that gives rise to the teaching.

Why is this? The teaching belongs to the sensory object of sound and lacks the capacity for awakening or illumination; the essence of the mind is numinous awareness, fully possessing the capacity for awakening and illumination. [How can you take] an object that lacks illumination...

This is because there is a mind that illuminates; since there is no distinction between the state of illuminating and not illuminating, Ānanda’s delusion of the mind and his delusion regarding the teaching—and even the characteristics of the essence of the mind that is deluded by the teaching—are likewise just this.

According to [the commentary], as for Ānanda’s refusal to abandon the conditioned mind out of his deep reverence for the Buddha-Dharma: how could he have known that this Dharma itself is also a condition, and thus ought to be abandoned along with it? Zhong says:

If you wish to study the Buddha-vehicle and explore the precious treasury, you must, point by point, resolve each teaching within yourself, and word by word, cause them to merge in silent accord with the true mind.
Do not merely cling to the literal phrasing and give rise to understanding based on words;

you must directly probe for the underlying intent beneath the text, so as to harmonize with the fundamental and realize the source. In this way, the Way of innate truth will not be obscured, and you will require no teacher.

This wisdom manifests before one. If you consistently turn your back on yourself to pursue the literal text, clinging to study and engaging in disputation, it is like seeking speech from a wooden man or expecting a stone woman to give birth to a child;
you will pass through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in vain, for there is ultimately no principle to be attained.

The "conditioning" of the "conditioned mind" refers to *ālambana* (grasping at objects). The "conditioning" of the "conditioning of dharmas" refers to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*). This is because the sound of the Dharma is itself the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*).
Therefore, it too is not the ultimate reality. If it falls upon paper and ink, it becomes yet another object of the sensory realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).

Now, the School of the Patriarchs does not permit the exposition of doctrinal principles, for as soon as one involves oneself in principles, one again falls into the objects of the mental faculty (*dharma-dhātu*), which can likewise become an object of cognition.
If you take this discriminative sound of my teaching on the self to be your mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from the discriminative sound.
It would be like a guest staying at an inn who halts only briefly before departing, never remaining there permanently.
Yet the attendant of the pavilion has nowhere to go; he is called the "master of the pavilion. This is also like that:
if your true mind has nowhere to go, how could it be devoid of the nature of non-discrimination regarding sound? Thus, this is not merely a matter of the discriminating mind regarding sound.

Discriminating one's own appearance, one is detached from all marks of form; this is the nature of non-discrimination. Thus, even up to the point where discrimination is entirely absent, it is neither form nor emptiness.
Kauśika and others mistake this for the obscure principle (tattva); it is the nature of non-discrimination, detached from the conditions of all phenomena.
"Then your mind-nature would each have its own place of return; how could it be the master?
This rebukes him for identifying with the deluded mind rather than the true mind.

"If you now do not abandon the conditioned mind—that which grasps at the sounds of my preaching as being 'I'—then that very grasping mind shall be your true mind. Since he has identified this discriminating mind [as the self],...
If one considers the mind that takes sounds to be real, this mind ought naturally to be free from the discrimination of sounds; yet it possesses a definitive nature of discriminating sounds.
Why is this? The deluded mind is like a guest, while the true mind is like the host. This may be observed through a provisional analogy.
It is like a traveler who stays at an inn; having stayed for one night, he departs and never remains permanently, and thus he is called a guest.
As for the master of the inn, he does not go anywhere at all, and thus he is called the host. This is also like that.
If this were truly your mind, it should be like the innkeeper, remaining without departing.
Why, then, does it lose its discerning nature when separated from sound? Is it merely like a guest who stops for a while and then departs?
By reasoning from this, it is evident that this is not only the discerning mind regarding sound; even the mind that discerns my own appearance departs [when separated].
My physical form also lacks intrinsic nature; all these belong to the conceptualization of the first six deluded consciousnesses and are not the true mind.

Not only this, but even up to the point where the conceptualizations of the first six have no locus at all to be considered as having a separate self-nature—neither belonging to form nor to space—this is precisely the seventh [consciousness] perceiving the eighth, which belongs to and carries [the seeds].

The objective realm is both a conceptual construction and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because the Sāṃkhya teachers were ignorant of this, they mistakenly grasped it as the "Primal Darkness" (*avyakta*) which is the intrinsic nature.
This is because the non-Buddhists establish twenty-five principles (*tattva*), the first of which is designated as the "Principle of Darkness" (*tama-tattva*).
They claim that the Primordial Darkness gives rise to consciousness (*buddhi*), which is the origin of all phenomena and the supreme principle.
Now, their view that it is neither form nor emptiness is precisely identical to this [view]. How could they know that discrimination is entirely absent?

They have merely abandoned coarse discrimination; as for the subtle, continuous flow, they certainly have not awakened to it. That both form and emptiness are utterly exhausted is likewise merely the abandonment of...
Within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), one half gives rise to the dust of sensory objects, while the other half extinguishes that dust; it is truly impossible to be separated from them.
If one were to separate from the conditions of this half that extinguishes the dust of all phenomena, there would be no nature of non-discrimination.
This is of one kind and no different from the aforementioned absence of nature when separated from sound and form. Indeed, the six sense bases condition the mind, each following its own [object].
They arise following their respective objects and likewise perish following those same objects.
Just as a shadow follows a person, so too does that which comes from a certain person also depart following that same person. Thus, your mind-nature belongs entirely to the realm of the transitory;
each has its own place of return. How can it then be the permanent host that neither comes nor goes? Zhong said: "The preceding..."
Using the guest as a metaphor for the body and its objects, this uses the guest to metaphorize the conditions of the mind, while the nature of seeing is the host.

Taking sound as an analogy for form, they are explained in succession: not only does the discriminating mind of sound lack an inherent nature apart from sound, but the discriminating mind of form likewise lacks an inherent nature apart from form.
This applies even when extending the analysis to include fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.

There is nothing else; it is what is called "internally maintaining a state of profound stillness. Because there is nothing else, it exists yet is not form; because one continues to maintain this state, it is non-existent yet is not emptiness.
Being neither form nor emptiness, it is a dark, unified consciousness. This is precisely the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) of the six consciousnesses.
The six consciousnesses have a point of return and cannot serve as the sovereign master. If it is the eighth consciousness, then it is the essential brightness of the consciousness-essence.
"If there were nothing to which it could return, then it would be able to act as the sovereign.
Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature each had something to which it returned, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has no place to return?
I pray only that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

This reason refers to returning that which is borrowed, not returning that which is not borrowed. "Returning" is like an object borrowed from someone else; it must necessarily be returned to its owner.
If it were an object belonging to one's own household, there would be no place to return it. Ānanda said:

"If my conditioned mind has various things to which it must return, why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has no place to return? I pray that you will deign to explain."

Out of compassion, please explain this for me. Long ago, Zhang Wugou went to visit Chan Master Qing of Shanquan and asked, "Is it true that everyone has their share of this matter, and that each person is fully perfected? Qing replied, "Indeed. Gong said, "..."
"Why is it that there is no point of entry? Qing took several prayer beads from his sleeve and showed them to him, asking, "Whose are these?
The official lowered his head and had no reply. Qing then tucked them back into his sleeve and said, "If they were yours, you would have picked them up and taken them with you.
As soon as one engages in conceptual thought, they are no longer yours. The official was struck with awe. Thus, one knows that as soon as there is discrimination, [the truth is lost].
Thus, there is that which can be returned.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for your seeing me—this clarity of seeing is the fundamental source. Although this seeing is not yet the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind,"
"Just as the second moon is not the reflection of the moon, you should listen attentively. Now I shall show you the ground from which there is no returning.

Hereafter, the text borrows the visual essence (*jian-jing*) to demonstrate the true nature that does not return. This is because the wondrously pure, luminous mind—the precious, luminous, wondrous nature—possesses the three great aspects:
essence (*ti*), characteristic (*xiang*), and function (*yong*). Due to the non-awakening of ignorance, a single moment of delusion arises.

Movement: This fundamental substance is transformed to become the *karmic consciousness* (*ālaya-vijñāna*). This luminous wisdom is transformed to become the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*), which is called the "transforming consciousness.
Furthermore, this true object is transformed to become the "image-portion" (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is called the "seen-consciousness.

Within this context, the essence of seeing is precisely the seeing-portion produced by the transformation of that light. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for your seeing my thirty-two marks..."
At that time, before this vision has fallen into conceptual discrimination, is it not the essence of seeing? It is fundamentally and originally possessed;
it is not borrowed from the light of the sun, moon, or lamps. Is it not the primordial clarity?

Since this vision is one of the six essences, and furthermore is clear and unclouded wherever it is located, it already inherently possesses the substance of brilliant clarity. It is only due to two kinds of inversion...

Because delusive views have not yet been eliminated, the subject and object still persist and cannot function interchangeably; thus, although it possesses clarity and brilliance, it merely lacks subtlety.
Nevertheless, though it is not the subtle, brilliant, and pure mind, it is like a second moon produced by pressing on the eye—it is fundamentally no different in essence from the true moon.
It is not like the reflection of the moon in water, which has a gap between it and the true moon.
This separation by a deep abyss is precisely because one has not yet attained the first moon; one must urgently recognize the second moon.
It is like one who has not yet attained the wondrous, pure, and bright mind, and must urgently recognize the fundamental source of the clarity of seeing.
You should listen attentively as I demonstrate to you the reality of that which is non-returnable. The moon has three aspects. The first is the sky.
First is the pure moon. Second is when a person presses on their eyes with their hands and looks at the moon, whereby two discs appear;
that which is produced by the pressing is taken as the second moon. Third is the reflection of the moon in water. Now, the first moon is used as a metaphor for the pure, true mind;
the second moon is a metaphor for the luminous essence of seeing; and the third moon is a metaphor for the conditions of sensory objects.
[The Master] discriminates [the months] with the intention of causing people to resolutely abandon the third month and resolutely recognize the second month;
then, the first month will not be far off, for it is immediately present. Question: Why do you not directly point to the pure, true mind, but instead employ this indirect indication?
Answer: The pure, true mind is possessed only by the Buddhas and those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi).

Since even this state still carries the aspect of ignorance (*avidyā*), how much more so for the stages prior to the [first] ground, and even for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) throughout the five stages?
What pure and true mind could possibly be present before them? Nevertheless, although the truth is not yet pure, its essence never changes.
It is like gold in ore: apart from the ore there is no gold; it is only that the ore may be genuine or counterfeit, and none but a skilled goldsmith can distinguish between them. Therefore:
The Buddha points directly to the fundamental nature as the mind, just as one points to ore and speaks of gold. The gold is already within the ore;
it does not exist separately apart from the ore. At this stage, because ignorance has not yet been pierced, there remains a lack of the single word "subtle" (*miao*).
Therefore, the Buddha briefly employs suppression and praise, intending merely to manifest its earnestness. It is not like...

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by objects" (*yuan chen*), [the Master] rebukes the notion that the mind has no substance. Various commentaries on this point have gone too far in their fabrication of delusions;
for instance, they lightly apply the name "conditioned by objects," thereby conflating it with the "third moon" [illusion].

They insistently seek a place where [the light] returns, which seems to openly contradict the Buddha’s words and merely leads people into hesitation, such that they dare not directly recognize the nature of seeing as the mind.
The error of this is no small matter. One does not realize that the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of sentient beings is none other than this nature within the sense organs;

apart from this, there is nothing else to be pointed out. Therefore, when the Patriarchs gave instruction, they mostly took it from the gateway of the six sense organs, following the secret mandate of the Buddha.
During practice, one need only request to recognize this nature, and there will never be even a single failure. It is like purchasing goods.
Regarding the gold ore: although it is not pure gold at the time of extraction, true gold can ultimately never be obtained apart from the ore.
If one were to discard the ore in search of the gold, not only would the gold be lost along with it, but one would surely become confused by brass, and true gold would remain forever unseen.
Is this not a great pity? ○ Zhong said: Although the second month is not yet the true [spring],...
The moon. Yet, apart from the true moon, a second moon can never be found. Although the essence of seeing is not the true mind, apart from the true mind, the essence of seeing can never be found.
For it arises from the true [mind] and is in its entirety the true [mind]. One should simply seek the true mind through the essence of seeing;
one must not mistake the essence of seeing for the true mind. [Remove] the essence of seeing...
The delusion is precisely the true mind; the grasping at the moon is precisely the true moon.
Certainly they cannot be divided into two, yet they must not be hastily conflated into one.
Ānanda, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east. When the sun rises in the sky, there is bright radiance;
at midnight, during the dark fortnight when clouds and mist obscure the heavens, it is again shrouded in darkness. Through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives openness;
amidst the walls and buildings, one observes obstruction. Where there is distinction, one perceives conditions; throughout the empty void, it is all-pervasive.
Emptiness is like a place of turbidity where dust swirls in the gloom; yet when it clears and the sky becomes bright, the miasma subsides and one perceives purity once more, Ānanda.
"You all observe these various transformed appearances. I shall now each return them to their original causes. What are these original causes? Ānanda, these various transformations:
clarity returns to the sun; why is this? Without the sun there would be no clarity, for clarity is dependent upon the sun, and therefore it returns to the sun.
Darkness returns to the dark moon; penetration returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and buildings; and conditions return to the divisions [of space]."

They are distinct. When the stubborn void returns to emptiness, the thick clouds return to dust, and the clear brightness returns to a cloudless sky, then all that exists within the world does not fall outside these categories.
Of the eight kinds you perceive, which of the essential nature of the seeing-clarity would you wish to return? Why is this so?

If light were to return [to its source], then when it is not light, one would no longer perceive darkness. Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the perception itself has no distinction.
Those things that can return are naturally not you; as for that which does not return to you, if it is not you, who else could it be?

Thus you should know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, bright, and pure. It is you yourself who have become deluded and distressed, losing your original nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth;
within this birth and death, you are constantly adrift and submerged. For this reason, the Tathāgata calls you "one worthy of compassion."
This is a comprehensive enumeration of the characteristics of objects that have a "return" (reversion), intended to demonstrate that the nature of seeing does not revert along with them.
Ānanda, what is it that I call "that which has no return"? Consider the objects in the world that can be returned; their substance consists of eight types.

Its characteristics are also eight, like the solar disc, the night’s darkness, a door or window, a wall or building, differentiation, emptiness, turbid dust, and clear, cloudless weather. These eight are its substance:
luminosity, darkness, penetration, obstruction, conditions, vacuity, congestion, and purity. These eight are its characteristics. Ā.
[Ananda] replied, "It is difficult. "Observe these various manifested forms; each has its own cause. I shall now restore each of them to its original causal source for you.
What is this original cause? Ānanda, just as the sun is the cause of light, so too do these various manifestations return to the solar orb.
Why is this? Because without the sun there is no light; the cause of light belongs to the sun. Therefore..."
This refers to the process of returning. By extension, darkness returns to the dark moon; openings return to doors and windows; obstructions return to walls and buildings;

conditions return to discrimination; rigidity and emptiness return to the void; turbidity and dust return to the fine particles; and clarity returns to a cloudless sky—all may be understood through such analogies of returning.
To extend this further, all things within the world that possess form and can be returned are likewise included.

None of them fall outside this category. If you perceive the essential nature of the clarity and precision of these eight kinds of views, within these eight manifestations, with which manifestation would it return? Let me cite one manifestation for the sake of inquiry.
If this nature of seeing were to return together with light, then this seeing would depart along with the light; when there is no light, by what means would one see darkness?
Know that once the single characteristic is understood, all characteristics are understood. Now, let all characteristics shift as they may.
One sees each and every thing, clearly discerning the characteristics of light, darkness, and so forth.

Within this nature of seeing, various distinctions arise—things coming and going, things competing and usurping one another—but this essence of seeing remains bright, eternally abiding, unmoving, and unchanging;
fundamentally, it is without differentiation. By this, one knows that all things which can be returned [to their source] do so because they are borrowed from external objects.

Yet it exists. This spontaneity is not your own possession. If this "non-returning" of yours were not due to a borrowed state, and were not something belonging to yourself, to whom else would it belong? It is simply that you recognize this nature of seeing as non-returning;
thus you know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, fundamentally luminous, and fundamentally pure. For the nature of seeing is the host within the guests, and the true mind is...
This is because you are the Lord of Lords. Due to your confusion and delusion, you have not awakened;
since you do not recognize the Lord of Lords, nor do you recognize the Lord of Guests, you have lost your original nature and suffer in vain through saṃsāra.
Within the cycle of birth and death, you emerge and submerge like the tide, with no time of escape in sight. Therefore, I say that you all are objects of compassion.
...Thus it is. These eight objects form four pairs; each pair is formed by taking those characteristics that are mutually opposite.
Only the object of empty space is turbid, such that its essence and appearance are inverted; however, this will be seen clearly in the section on "Returning to the Place" below.
"Discrimination" refers here to the discrimination of various objects, such as places where pines and thorns, cranes and crows are mixed together.
"Conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to various distinct characteristics, such as the traits of straightness, curvature, whiteness, or blackness.
"Rigid void" (*yuanxu*) refers to a place where all things are entirely absent. "Pervasive emptiness" (*bian shi kongxing*) means that one perceives only a single, solitary characteristic of space.
This is because conditions are of diverse colors, whereas emptiness is of a uniform color; since the uniform and the diverse are opposites, [the former] gives rise to [the latter].
This forms a pair. In the old commentary, "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) is taken as the mind that discriminates;
if so, how does the word "object" (*ālambana*) below differ from what precedes it? Furthermore, with what would the "space" (*ākāśa*) below form a pair? Thus, a single phrase has been misinterpreted.

This would cause the entire text to become a mere accumulation of redundancies. Furthermore, the "Eightfold Return" was used to distinguish seeing, in contrast to the preceding "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations.
Now, the seven investigations were already somewhat superficial remarks; yet to single out this "Eightfold Return" as the means for distinguishing seeing is even more like the babble of a dream.
Throughout the ten successive sections, all were intended to demonstrate the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), yet you have singled out only the eighth.
[The text] returns. As for the rest, in what dharma are they all distinguished? Furthermore, the preceding seven locations constitute seven major sections;
how could they possibly correspond to this single section? Now, I shall revise them collectively, stating: "Seven locations to refute the mind; ten rounds to reveal the seeing.
In this way, not only will the number of dharmas be symmetrical, but the essential principles of the mind's delusion and the seeing's truth will also be clearly distinguished. Section One.

The fifth section on revealing that seeing has nothing to return to is concluded. Master Zhong said: "If you simply understand that this nature of seeing has nothing to return to, then you will know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure.
This was intended to lead him to awaken to his own fundamentally wondrous, luminous mind by means of the nature of seeing.

It is not that the nature of seeing itself is the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind. This is because the nature of seeing belongs to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which still carries the traces of karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
The fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind belongs to the ninth consciousness, for it is the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place to return, how can I know that it is my true nature?

This sixth turn clarifies that seeing is not intermingled with other things. Ānanda said, "Now, having received the Buddha’s instruction, although I know that this seeing does not return along with various forms, it is nonetheless always associated with objects such as those moving in water, on land, or through the air."
They are so intermingled that they are difficult to distinguish. Now, among all these things, how shall we discern which is the nature of my seeing and which are the characteristics of objects?
It is not easy to analyze and clarify this. Zhong said: "Ānanda’s intention is that the nature of seeing is mixed within the myriad things;
there is no seeing that is not an object, and no object that is not seeing. How can one distinguish them?"

"What is this nature of seeing that belongs to me? The Buddha’s intention is that although the cognitive capacity of seeing differs among all ordinary beings and sages, the nature of seeing is the same.
Now, based solely on the objects you perceive, those various distinctions are merely external things."
"That which is able to see is you. You have your own seeing; it does not concern my affairs. I have my own seeing;
it does not concern your affairs. This may be called the ultimate in clarity. Why do you not recognize this for yourself?
Why do you come to me in such distress to seek it out? How could my seeing become your seeing? This question emphasizes only the word "I. It does not... [The text ends here].
The character "true" (zhen) is emphasized. Examine the meaning of the answer below; it naturally corresponds [to the truth]. Wu-xing’s interpretation is incorrect.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "I now ask you: at present, you have not yet attained the untainted purity (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*). It is by relying on the Buddha's spiritual power..."

In the first dhyāna, one attains unimpeded vision; Āniruddha, for instance, saw Jambudvīpa (it is likely that "Jambudvīpa" is a scribal error for "Sahā world") as clearly as observing an *āmala* fruit upon the palm of one's hand.

The various bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds, while the Tathāgatas of the ten directions perceive all pure lands, as numerous as motes of dust, without anything escaping their gaze. As for sentient beings, their clear vision does not exceed these limits.

[This concludes the previous section. This first sets forth the five kinds of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the essence of vision (*darśana-śakti*) in order to introduce the following text. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"I now ask you: you have just now realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), yet you have not yet attained the untainted purity (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*). You rely in vain upon the Buddha..."
Through the empowerment of supernatural power, one is able to see a single set of four continents within the first dhyāna without obstruction;
such is the range of vision for the wisdom-eye of those still in training (śaikṣa).
As for Aniruddha, he sees this Sahā world as if looking at an amala fruit in the palm of his hand; such is the range of vision for the divine eye (divyacakṣus) of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is so. If bodhisattvas and others can see hundreds of thousands of worlds, is this not the scope of vision of the Dharma-eye?
As for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, who perceive every pure land as vast as the atoms of dust, is this not the scope of vision of the Buddha-eye?
As for all sentient beings, they see only what is before their eyes; as for that which...
To see through a hole is limited to a mere inch or two; this is likewise the range of vision for the physical eye.

Now, these five types of vision range from the vastness that exhausts the entirety of all lands to the narrowness of no more than an inch or two. Although their ranges of vision differ, they are all equally the nature of seeing itself.
○ *Amala* (菴摩羅) means "difficult to distinguish. It resembles a peach but is not a peach; it resembles a crabapple...

This is not something that occurs elsewhere. Aniruddha was the Buddha’s maternal cousin; though he was rebuked for sleeping during his painting practice, through his diligent effort he lost his physical sight, subsequently realized the four fruits of arhatship, and attained the divine eye.
Ānanda, let us now, together with you, observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings reside, and survey everywhere within them—those moving upon water, land, and in the air.
Although there are various forms, both obscure and bright, they are none other than the obstructions left behind by the discrimination of external objects.
You should, in this regard, distinguish between what is self and what is other. Now, I shall lead you to select from within this seeing: which is my true essence, and which is...?
Regarding the characteristics of phenomena: this is intended solely to have Ānanda, based on what he has personally witnessed, examine and discern for himself.
Ānanda, set aside the five views for a moment; let me first lead you upward from the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell, and observe from there. In the middle...

Those who look about and see what is in the water, on the land, or moving through the air—though there may be various forms that are either obscure or clear and not uniform—all of these are nothing other than the perceptions of the mind’s discrimination regarding external objects (*pūrvadhara*). They are merely places where [the mind] lingers and encounters obstructions.
Within this very realm of the seer and the seen, you should distinguish for yourself what belongs to the self and what belongs to the other.
The self is the nature of seeing; the other consists of all external objects. Even if you are unable to do this yourself, you must certainly rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom.

I shall then lead you to discern, within this mutual seeing of "me" and "you," who is my substance that is able to see objects, and what constitutes the characteristics of objects that are seen. In this way, it will become perfectly clear;
there must be a distinct and unmixed differentiation between what is the object and what is the seeing. This very capacity for seeing is what is called my substance.
This is precisely what you perceive, namely, objective phenomena.
Ānanda, exhaust the source of your vision: from the palaces of the sun and moon—these things are not you—to the Seven Golden Mountains, observe them thoroughly and completely.
Although there are various kinds of light, these too are objects and not you. Gradually continue to observe: clouds rising, birds flying, and the wind moving.
Dust arises; trees, mountains, rivers, grasses, shrubs, humans, and livestock—all these things are not you.
This correctly states that objects are not the seeing. As for the source of seeing, it is the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
Ānanda, exhaust the power of your eyes and observe from the palaces of the sun and moon; these most excellent objective forms are indeed objects, yet they are not you. Furthermore,

He proceeded to the Seven Golden Mountains and surveyed them thoroughly and with clarity. He observed that although the appearances of these objects in the center possess various kinds of light, they are still material things and not you.
Gradually descending, he further observed the rising of clouds and the flight of birds.
The movement of the wind, the rising of dust, trees, mountains, rivers, weeds, and humans and livestock—these are the most inferior manifestations of phenomena (*dharmas*).
They are indeed phenomena, yet they are not you. Thus, that which is called "who is it that possesses these phenomenal characteristics?
is precisely this [point]. As for the Seven Golden Mountains, they surround Mount Sumeru in seven tiers on its exterior, all composed of pure gold.
Gold is its substance; it possesses the greatest radiance. Even the rising clouds and soaring birds, when viewed from the Golden Mountain, appear to be at the very bottom.
Ānanda, although these various natures of things, near and far, differ from one another, they are all equally pure like your own faculty of seeing.

That which is gazed upon consists of various categories of things, each with its own distinctions; yet the nature of seeing is without difference. This subtle and wondrous clarity is truly your own nature of seeing.
This statement correctly asserts that seeing is not a thing. Ānanda, whether these various things are near or far, they all possess [their own] entities.
Phenomena appear in a thousand forms and myriad states; though they differ from one another, they are all equally what is beheld by your pure essence of vision.
Thus, while the objects themselves vary, the nature of seeing is simply a single, luminous illumination, without any distinction.
This lack of distinction is pure and unmixed; it is precisely that "wondrously pure and bright mind" mentioned previously. This wondrously pure and bright...
"Mind, truly, your seeing-nature has never been mixed with the differentiated characteristics of material objects.
Thus, that which you asked, 'Who is my essence?'—this is it."
If you see this object, then you can also see my seeing. If we see the same thing, it is called "seeing me.
When I am not seeing, why do you not see the place where I am not seeing? If you see that which is not seeing, then it is naturally not the characteristic of "not seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my not seeing, then it is naturally not an object; how could it not be you?
This is a counter-argument to clarify that the aforementioned "seeing" is not an object. Now, I maintain that seeing is not an object; do you perhaps still not believe this?

Let me explain it further. If my nature of seeing were no different from the objects seen, then when seeing perceives the distinct characteristics of various objects, this seeing would be identical to those objects.
In that case, the nature of seeing would itself become something visible—just like your own eyes.
One may also perceive my seeing. Why is this? Since seeing is itself an object, it ought to manifest as a distinct characteristic;
how could it not be clearly visible? Yet when I observe objects, they are in reality not fixed. At times, when I cast my gaze to grasp characteristics, I see the object;
at other times, when I withdraw my vision and depart from characteristics, I do not see it. If you were to take my seeing as [an object],...

Regarding the timing of objects: when one relies on other objects perceived in common and falsely claims to see my seeing, suppose I withdraw my vision and detach from appearances so that I do not see those objects;
why then would you not also see the very substance of my non-seeing?
And how could one point out its location? When it is not being seen, it cannot be seen; even when it is seen by others, how can that truly be seeing it?
Furthermore, if you insist on saying, "I have already seen the place where you do not see," [you are mistaken].
Indeed, precisely at the time when one does not see, the seeing-nature is the substance of my non-seeing, and all phenomena are the marks of that non-seeing.
Now, since my seeing has already departed from objects, you also see my own substance.
This need not be expounded through further effort; this non-seeing of mine is naturally not the mark of those objects of non-seeing. Furthermore:
If you are unable to perceive the ground where I do not see, there is no further need to exhaust your efforts in debating this.
This "not seeing" of mine is naturally not a thing. Why is this? If that which is visible is already not a thing, how much more so that which cannot be seen;
could it possibly still be the same as the characteristics of a material object? Indeed, when the visible and the invisible are joined together...
Yet, as each of these is successively found not to be that object, how can it not be your own self-nature?
Furthermore, at the very moment you now see an object, since you see the object and the object also sees you, their essential natures become intermingled and confused.
In that case, you, I, and all the world would fail to be established. Ānanda, when you see, it is you who see and not I;
this nature of seeing is all-pervasive—if it is not you, then who is? Why do you doubt your own true nature, claiming that your nature is not real, and instead seek the truth from me?
This is a counter-argument to refute the previous claim that objects are not the seeing itself.
Now, you say that objects are not the seeing; yet do you not yourself still fail to believe this? Let us investigate it further.

Furthermore, when you now see these various distinct objects, if those objects were themselves the seeing, then that object would be one thing and this [seeing] would be another. Since you have already seen the objects, [how could they be the seeing?]

Objects, too, should see you; the natures of the sentient and the insentient would become so chaotic and intermingled that there would no longer be any distinction between the vessel-world and its contents. This is what is meant by "the confusion of things.

When even the sentient and the insentient cannot be distinguished, sentient beings and sentient beings become all the more impossible to differentiate. Thus, when you see me, it would conversely become my seeing you. In the world...
All people are without exception like this: they destroy the worldly distinctions between self and other, yet fail to establish a stable foundation;
such a person is confused. Ānanda, when you see me, it is certainly only your own seeing, and not my seeing.
That self and this [object] are distinct and clear; they have never been confused or disordered—this is the portion of the person.

Now, if sentient beings do not even intermingle with one another, then your seeing-nature, though pervasive throughout all things, remains utterly distinct from both the sentient and the insentient—this is the portion of the object. Thus, objects cannot be mixed together, for they are not your true nature.
Who is it? Furthermore, this true nature is something you inherently possess. Why do you lack self-confidence and instead harbor doubts?

The true nature resides within you; yet you do not believe it to be true, but instead seek clarification from the corners of my mouth, asking, "How can I know that this is my true nature? Is this not delusion? (From the *Zongjing*).

It is said: "At the moment of entering through faith, one naturally attains penetrating clarity and perfect illumination. Even at the stage of full realization, this does not depend upon mental conceptions;
how much less could one seek one's own Dharma from another, taking another's eye as the means to achieve universal penetration?"
Counting jewels will never relieve poverty; speaking of food can never satisfy hunger. One must personally arrive at the gate of ultimate learning;
only through illumination can one reach the principle of non-action (*wuwei*). This concludes the sixth section, clarifying that the seeing-nature is unmixed.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing must be me and nothing else, then when I and the Tathāgata were observing the magnificent treasure-palace of the Four Heavenly Kings and dwelling in the palaces of the sun and moon, this seeing was all-encompassing, pervading the entire Sahā world-system.
Yet, when we returned to the vihāra, I saw only the monastery; entering the hall with its pure mind, I beheld only the eaves and corridors. World-Honored One, this seeing is like..."
"It is so. Its substance is originally all-pervasive throughout the entire realm; yet now, being within this room, it fills only this single room.
Is it that this vision has contracted from the large to the small? Or is it that the walls and roof have constricted it and severed it? I do not know where the truth of this matter lies.
I pray that you will grant me your great compassion and explain this for me."

This seventh section clarifies that seeing is unimpeded. Because Ānanda had heard the words regarding the pervasiveness of the nature of seeing, he doubted that what was great could become small again, or that what was open could become obstructed again; thus, he initiated a question and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing is fundamentally pervasive, it must be my true nature, unmixed with external objects."
If that were so, it should remain unchanging regardless of one's location.

Now, when I and the Tathāgata observe the Jewel Palace of the Four Heavenly Kings' Supreme Treasury, or sometimes dwell within the palaces of the sun and moon and look down upon a single set of four continents, this vision is all-encompassing, filling the entire Sahā world-system; how vast it is! Yet, upon returning to the vihāra, we see only—
"Entering this garden further into the hall, I observed with a clear mind; yet looking only at the eaves and corridors, how small it was!
World-Honored One, if this seeing-nature is fundamentally all-pervasive throughout the entire Sahā world, then that which is great should not become smaller.
For what reason is it now within this room, filling only the room? Why is its size so indeterminate?"
Is it that this vision itself contracts its vastness to become small? Or is it that it is partitioned by walls and buildings, which constrict it and cause it to be severed?
Whether it is contracted or severed, there must be a definitive principle behind it; yet for now, I do not know where this principle lies.
Therefore, I pray that you will bestow your compassion and expound its meaning for me. ○ Within the Hall of the Heavenly Kings, all manner of jewels are present;

hence it is called the "Victorious Treasury" (Jin-zang). The palaces of the sun and moon are both composed of *maṇi* jewels. Their palaces, terraces, ponds, and pools are filled with devas and humans.
Although the solar palace is formed from fire-*maṇi* jewels, it is likewise cool like the moon; however, its radiance is superior to that below.
This refers to the "hearing" becoming heated. Ānanda followed the Buddha and sometimes resided with him.
Gu Shan states that in the first dhyāna, one sees only a single four-continent world-system; thus, the Sahā world-realm must refer here to a single minor *kṣetra*.
*Gā-lán* (伽藍) translates as "garden" (*ārāma*). ○ Zhong says: "The seeing-nature must be myself and nothing else; knowing is oneself and not another. Since this is...
If it were not dependent on another, it would be able to act as its own master. Why then would its large and small dimensions depend on another, such that it lacks autonomy?
If it can still act as its own master when shrinking the large to become small, then it is clear that once it is pinched and severed by an object, it can no longer be its own master.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All worldly activities, whether great or small, internal or external, each belong to the preceding sense objects.
One should not say that the faculty of seeing expands or contracts."
This clarifies that expansion and contraction, as well as largeness and smallness, reside in the characteristics [of objects] and not in the seeing itself. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Your statement that this seeing contracts and becomes small is erroneous. For all things in the world—whether large or small, internal or external—"

Furthermore, brightness and darkness, penetration and obstruction—all such activities belong to the external objects (*viṣaya*). The faculties, the body, and the physical world are matters pertaining to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Since the objective aspect has form, one may speak of its expansion and contraction. But seeing (*darśana*) is fundamentally formless;
how could it be said that seeing undergoes expansion and contraction? As for the claim that "contraction includes expansion," if there is contraction, then there must be expansion.
It is like seeing a square void within a square vessel. I ask you again: Is this square void seen within the square vessel fixedly square, or is it not fixedly square?
If it were fixedly square, then when a round vessel is placed there instead, the void should not become round.

If it were not fixed, then when placed within a square vessel, there would be no "square space. You say that you do not know where this principle resides; yet the nature of principles is such—how could they have a location?
Ānanda, if you wish to cause [the space] to enter into a state without squareness or roundness, you need only remove the squareness of the vessel;
the essence of space itself has no directionality. One should not say that one must further remove the directional characteristics of empty space itself.
To clarify this through an analogy: the nature of seeing is fundamentally neither large nor small; it appears as large or small according to the space within its boundaries.
It is just as empty space is fundamentally neither square nor round, yet it appears square or round according to the vessel that contains it.
Suppose there were a square vessel here; within it, one would see only square space. Now I ask you: does this square space within the square vessel...
Is it fixed in shape? Or is it not fixed in shape? If it were fixed in shape, then when placed in a round vessel, the space within should not be round;
yet the vessel is round and the space is round—thus it is not fixed in shape. If it were not fixed, then when inside a square vessel, there should be no square space;
yet the vessel is square and the space is square—thus it is again fixed in shape. Whether fixed or not fixed, both are untenable.
It can be determined. In short, it is simply so as long as the vessel exists. You say that you do not know where this principle resides.
Now, the nature of this principle of expansion and contraction, whether large or small, is likewise without fixed location. If there is no fixed location, then there is no place of residence.
Why, then, do you wish to seek its location? Ānanda, if you further wish to cause it to enter into the formless—neither square nor round—you need only...

Except for a square vessel: when the vessel is removed, the square characteristic immediately vanishes; it should not then turn toward empty space to seek out and remove that square characteristic, for the substance of emptiness has no directionality.
Thus one should know that if one wishes to cause the vision to appear neither large nor small, one need only remove the external objects before it;
one should not say that one must further remove the characteristics of largeness or smallness within the nature of vision itself.
This is because the essence of seeing is fundamentally without size; squareness and roundness merely depend on the vessel.
When the vessel is removed, squareness and roundness vanish. What more could be removed from empty space? Size merely depends on objects; when objects are forgotten, size vanishes.
What more could be removed from the nature of seeing? The practice of forgetting objects lies in the causal stage of initiating action.
This is merely visualization; it is simply realizing that the elemental chamber is fundamentally empty, thereby suddenly ceasing all grasping and maintenance.

Even if one becomes proficient in such contemplation and the mind-ground suddenly opens up, such that the body vanishes into vast emptiness and the elemental chamber is no longer seen, this is only a semblance of non-obstruction, not the reality.

One must wait until the power of contemplative practice reaches its peak and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is completely exhausted, so that the ten directions open wide and there is no longer any darkness.
In the darkness, the internal and external spheres of the body appear with distinct shadows, as clearly as seeing fruit in the palm of one's hand; this is the true state of non-obstruction.
However, this is merely non-obstruction of the essence (*tǐ*), not non-obstruction of function (*yòng*). As for the non-obstruction of great function, it is further explained in the text below.
If it were as you ask—that when entering a room, one contracts the vision to make it small—then when looking up at the sun, would you not have to stretch your vision to match the face of the sun?
If you build walls and houses that can enclose and sever it, or pierce it with small apertures, how could there be no trace of such continuity?
This argument is not correct;
it is precisely to refute that your question was inappropriate.
If, as you suggest, one could contract [the eyes] when entering a room, then when looking up at the sun, one should likewise be able to contract them.
If one attempts to lift it upward, there is no one in the world who can pull their vision so that it aligns with the surface of the sun.

If you claim that because a wall can be broken by being pried apart at its foundation, a hole in a wall should likewise allow vision to be drawn through and restored, there is no such person in the world who can restore their sight through a hole in a wall. Since one cannot pull it upward, [it follows that it cannot be restored].
Furthermore, how could one contract it to make it small? Since one cannot extend it to make it continuous, how could one also constrict it to make it severed?
Therefore, it is said that this interpretation is not tenable. Although it was stated above that the nature of meaning is indeterminate, we still allow for the establishment of such meanings.
Now it is said that this interpretation is incorrect, and thus the proposed thesis is rejected.
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded by taking themselves to be external objects; they have lost their original mind and are driven about by those very objects.
Therefore, within this state, one contemplates the great and the small. If one can master external objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata;
body and mind are perfectly luminous, unmoving from the site of enlightenment, and within the tip of a single hair, one can universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
This refers to his delusion and the subsequent re-clarification [of the truth]. Now, the seeing is inherently unobstructed, and objects are inherently incapable of obstructing it.

Yet, that sentient beings ultimately encounter obstruction is not due to the obstruction of objects; rather, it arises solely from the fact that, since beginningless time, they have failed to realize that all things are themselves.
Thus, they mistake themselves for objects and consequently lose sight of the oneness of all things.
The Original Mind. Since objects do not belong to one's own mind, they not only fail to follow the mind’s movements, but instead turn the mind against itself.
Because the mind is turned by objects, it becomes obstructed by them;

thus, within the sensory realms before one, whether observing the large or the small, there is no longer any freedom. One thereby realizes that objects are fundamentally the mind, yet through delusion—
When these things exist as objects, they obstruct the mind, just as ice—though originally water—obstructs water when it freezes.
The cause of this obstruction lies precisely in one’s own delusion and being turned by objects. Those who are turned by objects are sentient beings;
if one can turn objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata. For when deluded, the body is but a tiny fragment. Furthermore...
When the shell of stagnation is sealed, the mind becomes dark; as it pursues objects with partiality and limitation, it is consequently turned around and becomes an obstruction.
Now, if one can turn things around, then the myriad things are of one body—perfect and not partial. When one realizes that all things are already [complete], one is luminous and not obscure.
Body and mind are perfectly luminous; the six sense organs function interchangeably. Thus, these ephemeral objects and the world itself, upon a mere thought, are transformed into supreme awakening.
Then the body becomes the Dharma-nature body, and the land becomes the Dharma-nature land. The entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions becomes a single eye;
the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions becomes a single Buddha-land. With such an eye, one contemplates.

In such a land, numerical limitations are dissolved and principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused. Thus, one can remain unmoved within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) while the body pervades the ten directions;
within a single hair-tip, one contains entire lands. That a hair-tip contains the ten directions is the small encompassing the large;
that the ten directions reside within a hair-tip is the large entering the small. When one observes the lands within a hair, the lands do not become small.
Thus, the small manifests the large; though the country appears vast from the outside, the hair is not large. Likewise, the large manifests the small.
This is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena, the profound gateway of sovereign freedom regarding breadth and narrowness.

How could there be any expansion or contraction, or any distinction of large and small? The subtlety of perceiving one's nature is unsurpassed. This compares with the previous state of forgetting sensory objects.
It is even more profound. That [refers to] illuminating in all directions; this is the perfect function.

Illumination and function are fully perfected and harmoniously integrated—is this not the ultimate realization of the essential nature? Zhong says: "Object" refers to the "object recognized as self" mentioned in the preceding text;
it points to the mind of arising and ceasing, not to external objects (*pratyaya*). "Delusion" refers to what is called the "original ignorance" in the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*.
It is due to a lack of awakening. One’s own true nature is originally all-pervasive, yet sentient beings fail to realize this themselves;

consequently, it transforms into the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and the two divisions of subject and object (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*). Thereupon, the original true mind is completely lost, and one is instead driven by the three divisions of the ālaya-vijñāna.
Thus, regarding the objects of the sensory fields, one perceives them as large or small; this is simply because of [this deluded] seeing.

Furthermore, [the mind] is obstructed by its own perceived objects (*nimitta-bhāga*). If one can internally detach from body and mind, externally cast off the world, and internally reverse the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), then one will be identical to the Tathāgata, wherein body, mind, and all phenomena are a single entity. It is perfect and without partiality;

it penetrates all things and is luminous rather than obscure. Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), a single hair contains the ten directions; within the small, the great is manifested. The great...
The large appears small within; it is sovereign and unimpeded. Furthermore, how could there be any expansion or contraction of the large and the small?
When one speaks to this point, this nature of seeing has already been integrated into the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
○ Daokai said: According to secular classics, the *Daxue* says "investigate things" (*gewu*), and the *Zhongyong* says "the myriad things are nurtured. It also says that one can...

"To exhaust the nature of things. Mencius said, "Shun was clear-sighted regarding all phenomena," and again, "The myriad things are all complete within me," and further, "When one thing encounters another, it is merely drawn along by it. In all these cases, he was not turned by external things.
As for those who seek to "transform things," they simply do not know its power and function, nor whether it can truly transform things.
If one can indeed transform things, then one is identical to the Tathāgata. Thus, the *Zhao Lun* says: "Is there anyone who unifies the myriad things into a single body?
It is surely only the Sage. The seventh section, clarifying that seeing is unimpeded, is concluded.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature, then this wondrous nature is now present before me;

since it sees, it must be my true self. But what, then, are my current body and mind? My current body and mind possess the capacity for discrimination and are real, yet that vision has no such power to distinguish my own body. If it were truly my mind, it would cause me to see. [He continued: "Seeing..."
If the nature is truly the self, yet the body is not the self, how does this differ from what the Tathāgata previously refuted—the claim that an object can see the self?
We pray that you will deign to show great compassion and reveal the truth to those who have not yet awakened.
