This eighth section clarifies that seeing is undivided. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if we follow the present intent of the Buddha, this pervasive essence of seeing must be my own profoundly still and wondrous nature."
Now, this wondrous nature is present before our eyes upon external objects.
Since that which is present before our eyes is my true self, then what is this thing within my current body that is capable of discrimination?
While the mind within the body indeed performs the function of discriminating external objects, as for that seeing-nature which pervades those external objects—

In reality, there is no separate agent that distinguishes my body. If that seeing-nature were truly my mind, acting as a sovereign over me to cause me to see external objects and internally see my own body, then it would follow that there is no other distinct discriminator;
thus, it would truly be "I. Conversely, if there is a real entity that performs this discrimination, then that [entity] is not "I. Furthermore, consider this: seeing...
Since the nature (xing) already exists prior to body and mind, and yet it can internally perceive itself, it would be the same as an external object being able to see the self.
However, that an object can see the self was already refuted by the Buddha as an error; why then is this not an error? To pursue this through successive reasoning, I truly do not understand it.

Therefore, I pray that you will bestow your compassion and once again provide me with enlightenment. Question: Since [it is]... with... (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "既與," which translates to "Since [it is]... or "Because [it is]...". As the source text is incomplete, the translation reflects the available portion.)
If things were not differentiated, they would immediately become the myriad phenomena; this is precisely what is meant by "views. Why, then, does the text further state that there are no such views?
Answer: In the parable of Mañjuśrī, it is explicitly stated that if there is "is-ness," then two distinct entities are formed, and it is impossible for them to become a single entity.
One must be without "is" and without "is not" before one can realize the wondrousness of the single essence. For this single essence is precisely non-differentiation;
one should know that this non-differentiation is the principle of the simultaneous severance of both "is" and "is not. ○ He said: This is the point where Ānanda harbored doubt.
It is merely that you recognize the nature of seeing and the body-and-mind as two. Furthermore, what is this "thing" (vastu)?

From the beginning, it has always been a thing arising within the wondrously luminous true mind. You simply suspect that there is actually a distinct thing existing within the wondrous luminosity, and thus cannot harmonize them into one.
You do not realize that the body, the mind, and the physical world are, in their very essence, fundamentally empty; they are entirely...
First is True Vision. It is like a reflection in a mirror; it is merely what the mirror manifests. How could there truly be a single thing residing within the mirror?
Therefore, the Buddha interrogated him with both "it may be" and "it is not," causing him to reach an impasse on both paths.
Only then did he tell him directly: "Originally there is nothing at all; it is fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous Bodhi."
This may be called an exhaustive disclosure of the truth. ○ Zhong says: In the preceding passage, because the true mind could not be employed, the conditioned mind could not be abandoned.
Here, because the deluded mind cannot be dissolved, the true mind cannot be employed.
Although you have heard that your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous mind, yet this one—
The word "thing" has no place to be established. From the aggregates, sense bases, and elements down to all phenomena, they are all the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
thus, the delusory is itself the real. The body and mind employed [in practice] are precisely this seeing-nature, which from the beginning has never had two distinct entities.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have just said—that what you see is right before you—is not true.
If it were truly before you, and if you truly saw it, then this essence of vision would have a specific location and could not be said to be without a point of reference."
Although the questions are many, this one stands foremost as the root of the error; therefore, by refuting this single preceding characteristic alone, all doubts are completely resolved.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have just said—that the seeing is right before you—is truly a false statement and possesses no real meaning at all.
If this essence of seeing were actually present before you, you would truly perceive its form."

As for "having a form," since it possesses characteristics and appearances, it must have a specific location; and since it has a specific location, it can certainly be pointed out as being in such-and-such a place.
Furthermore, as we now sit together in the Jeta Grove, you may survey the groves, the streams, and the halls;
from above, up to the sun and moon, and before you, facing the Ganges River. Now, in my presence upon this lion throne, point with your finger and describe these various features.

The "obscured" refers to a forest; the "illuminated" refers to the sun; the "obstructed" refers to a wall; the "unobstructed" refers to empty space. Thus it extends even to grass, trees, and the finest hairs;
though they differ in size, as long as they possess form, there is nothing that cannot be pointed out. If one were to insist upon seeing [the nature of] these things:
It is now before you; you should point it out clearly with your hand: what is seeing? Ānanda, you should know this:
if space were seeing, then since it has already become seeing, what would be space? If material objects were seeing, then since they have already become seeing...
"What constitutes a 'thing'? You may minutely peel away and analyze the myriad phenomena to extract the essence of pure, bright, and wondrous fundamental vision;
point it out and show it to me, so that it is as clearly understood as those other things, without any doubt."
This is intended to cause him to point out the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) from among the myriad phenomena before him.

Now, that which is "before one" must necessarily be pointable out. Furthermore, as you and I sit here in the Jeta Grove, looking all around at the groves, streams, halls, the sun and moon, and the Ganges River, you might raise your hand before the Lion Throne and point to these various forms. [If] they are obscured...
The forest is the object; light is the day; the obstruction is the wall; the passage is space.
Even down to grasses, trees, and the finest hairs—whether large or small—there is nothing that possesses form which is not pointed out.

If this nature of seeing were necessarily located before you, you should likewise point it out with your hand with certainty, saying: "Which of these is seeing? Ānanda, you should know: if you point to space as being [seeing]...
Regarding "seeing-nature": since it has already been established as seeing, what else could be empty?
If one points to an object, since seeing-nature is already seeing, what else could be the object? By citing both emptiness and objects, the myriad phenomena are fully present.
You should apply subtle and refined effort to peel away these myriad phenomena; you must [penetrate] within the myriad phenomena.
Within this, analyze and extract this essence of vision—vivid, pure, and wondrous—and point it out to me.
Like those other objects, it should have its characteristics and forms clearly manifest, free from any doubt.

Ānanda said: "In this multi-storied lecture hall, from here as far as the Ganges River, looking up at the sun and moon, pointing with my hand, and surveying with my gaze—everything I point to is an object; there is nothing that is the faculty of seeing.
World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, how much less can I, a defiled beginner Śrāvaka, or even a Bodhisattva, perceive the nature of the myriad phenomena?"
Previously, when the essence was dissected and examined, it was seen to have a distinct self-nature apart from all other things. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
This seal demonstrates that the nature of seeing is free from all marks. Ānanda received the Buddha’s command to provide this definitive exposition.
Indeed, he directed his gaze toward all phenomena and observed his own fingers. Yet, as he raised his hand and cast his eyes about, everything was but a phenomenon;
he could not perceive the nature of seeing that stood before him. Thus it is said: "There is no such seer.
Furthermore, having received the Buddha’s command for a subtle and minute dissection, he indeed performed a thorough analysis amidst the myriad phenomena. However—
He wished for it to be clear, yet it became increasingly unclear. Therefore he said:
"Even a Bodhisattva cannot immediately discern the essential seeing from within objects and cause it to stand apart from them, so that its own nature is revealed in its nakedness.
If even a Bodhisattva cannot do this, how much less can I, a mere beginner? Thus, the perception I had previously was truly not real. The Buddha immediately confirmed this.
The Master said: "So it is, so it is. I grant that there is not a single thing, yet there is seeing.
In this section, only the phrase "separated from all things" is difficult to comprehend. This is because it precisely indicates that the nature of seeing is detached from all marks (lakṣaṇa).

Furthermore, if one were to say that the nature cannot be extracted to make it separated from all things, would this not be nearly contradictory? Upon careful examination of the meaning of the words, it means that—

If one seeks to see things through their manifestations, there is fundamentally no such seeing. Even if one were to dissect things to reveal them, so that they might be clearly displayed apart from their material forms, there would still be no such seeing.
Only in this way is one truly free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Let the reader examine this carefully.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda: "As you have said, there is no seeing-essence that exists apart from all objects with a distinct self-nature;
thus, among the objects you point to, there is no such thing as 'the seer. Now I tell you further: you and the Tathāgata are sitting in the Jeta Grove.
Observe once more the groves and gardens, even up to the sun and moon and their various distinct forms; yet, necessarily, there is no seer."
"I have carefully accepted what you have pointed out. You have further clarified that among all these objects, which one is not seeing?
Yet, there is not a single object that is seeing; the nature of seeing certainly does not reside within them. Furthermore, there is not a single object that is not seeing;
how then could the nature of seeing reside within those objects either? The Buddha feared that Ānanda might understand the nature of seeing as being separate from all phenomena, and...
He did not realize that this was identical to all phenomena. Therefore, he spoke again, saying:

"Since you are definitively unable to point out, before the myriad phenomena, which among them is your nature of seeing that is distinct from objects—because among all those objects pointed out, none is the seer—I now ask you again: You and the Tathāgata are still sitting [here]."
From groves, gardens, and parks, up to the sun and moon—though these various objects differ, the essence of seeing (*darśana-vidhā*) certainly does not undergo such distinctions.
How could it be that all these things are truly not the faculty of seeing? Furthermore, you must clarify: among all these objects, which one is not the seeing?
Ānanda said, "I truly see this entire Jeta Grove. I do not know what within it is not seen. Why is this?
If the tree is not the seeing, how can one see the tree? If the tree is the seeing, then how can it be a tree? This applies even unto the sky:
if the sky is not the seeing, how can one see the sky? If the sky is the seeing, then how can it be the sky? Furthermore, I...

He reflected: "Within these myriad phenomena, there is nothing that does not manifest through this subtle illumination; it is none other than the faculty of seeing. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.

This seal of the nature of seeing is itself all dharmas. Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s elucidation on the principle that the nature of seeing is not [a conditioned] seeing, [understood its meaning].
He then said: "I have indeed perceived this Jeta Grove and even all phenomena; yet among these various things, I do not know which one is not seeing.
Why is this? If one says that the tree is not seeing, how can seeing reside within the tree?
If one says that the tree is itself seeing, why then is it still called a 'tree'? Thus, throughout [all things]..."

He traversed all things, even unto emptiness, and there was nothing that was not thus. I further reflected that within these myriad phenomena, through subtle illumination, there is truly no thing that is not of seeing. The Buddha again confirmed this, saying: "So it is, so it is."
It is permitted that there is not a single thing that is not seeing. The former masters said, "This is one who has attained it.

To say "it is" also has a path of emergence; to say "it is not" also has a path of emergence. Therefore, the World-Honored One neither affirmed seeing nor non-seeing, granting his seal of approval to both.
According to this, the original intent was clearly to clarify that there is no "non-," so it should simply have been stated as "if..."
The tree is not the seeing. How then can it suffice to say "seeing the tree"? Furthermore, it is said: if the tree were identical to the seeing, how then could there be a tree?

Moreover, to negate this identity is to fear that by hearing "not-identity," one will instead fall back into "identity. To demonstrate this dual transcendence, there is indeed the subtle purport of the skillful means of the Honored One.
Now, the measure of the nature of seeing encompasses the ten directions, and its substance contains all phenomena. Its...
It is with all phenomena neither identical nor separate. Precisely because it is not identical, its numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects;
the physical body and its realms do not interfere with it, and it is not bound by birth and death.

If sentient beings do not comprehend this principle, they will confuse the true with the false and sink into the cycle of saṃsāra. Since they lack the wisdom to distinguish for themselves, how could they ever attain liberation?
Indeed, because it is not something separate, it is able to blend the dust-motes and lands into a single unity, such that the myriad things constitute one body.

Its function pervades the entire Dharma-realm, and its existence or disappearance is entirely free. If sentient beings do not realize this principle, they will remain submerged in darkness, stagnate in stillness, become extinguished like ashes, or be entangled in emptiness.
Having themselves failed to recognize their own family treasure, how could they possibly make use of it? Therefore, I have previously pointed to it for them to see.
From [the section] "Since then" onwards, up to the first half of "Unimpeded," all sections are based on the principle of non-identity;
they distinguish the true from the false to resolve upon the essence that stands independently apart from sensory objects.
Now, this present section on "Non-differentiation" is based on the principle of non-separation; it dissolves the false to merge with the true, thereby manifesting and revealing [the essence].
The subtle mystery of the interpenetration of all things is intended to lead sentient beings to clarify the principle of non-identity, whereby they do not sink into birth and death;
and to clarify the principle of non-separation, whereby they do not stagnate in nirvana. Though these may appear to be contradictory, in reality they mutually complete one another.
Thereupon, the great assembly—those who were not yet free from training—hearing these words of the Buddha, were utterly bewildered and did not understand the beginning or end of their meaning;
at once they were struck with terror and lost their composure. The Tathāgata, perceiving that their spirits were agitated and cowed, gave rise to a heart of compassionate pity.
He comforted Ānanda and the great assembly, saying: "O sons of good family, the Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth;
he teaches according to reality, without deception or falsehood. This is not like the fourfold confused and evasive discourse on immortality of Makkhali Gosāla."
Reflect upon this with careful attention; do not fail in your sorrowful longing.
Because [the Buddha] had granted two successive permissions, the entire assembly was left in a state of bewilderment.
Then, among the great multitude, the śrāvakas still in training heard these words of the Buddha and were utterly bewildered, not knowing what constituted "no view" or "no non-view."
Regarding these two meanings: if one pursues the latter, its end remains unfathomable; if one traces back the former, its beginning cannot be found.
Their words are as vast as the Milky Way, and their original steps have been lost. If one were to decide upon either "it is so" or "it is not," then it could serve as a basis for adherence.

Now, however, both are permitted and yet both are absent; there is no single certainty at all. Therefore, one is struck with trepidation and loses that which was once held as a standard. It is like this:
Upon learning that his spirit was trembling with fear, he conceived a heart of compassion and comforted Ānanda and the great assembly, saying:
"O sons of noble family, do not be alarmed or doubtful. The Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth; he speaks in accordance with the principle of True Suchness (tathatā).
His speech is free from the deception of error and free from the falsehood of pretension. It is not like that of the heterodox Makkhali."

The Path. There are those who rely on the pretext of an "Immortal Heaven" (*amara-vimāna*), claiming that one who does not give a confused answer to a question during their lifetime shall be reborn in that heaven.

They establish four kinds of evasive discourse (*vibhramśa-vāda*): namely, "both changing and constant," "both arising and ceasing," "both existent and non-existent," and "both increasing and decreasing.
All of these maintain two possibilities and ultimately lack any certainty. Now, there is neither such a view nor its negation.
[The Master] saw [the truth]. He decisively dispatched both [extremes], so that neither was established. How could this be the same as that deceptive and indeterminate confusion?

It is simply that your minds are coarse and your reflections shallow; you have not contemplated with earnest attention. If you were willing to contemplate with earnest attention, there would surely be a point of entry.
I shall certainly not fail the sincerity of your mournful longing. ○ He said: "Previously, I used a shout to startle Ānanda."

However, this [approach] employs both [affirmation and negation] to leave the great assembly bewildered. This is because delusion must be shattered all at once; thus, it sweeps it away with a single stroke that cuts in two.
Since the Truth is difficult to speak directly, it is pursued through a process of indirect maneuvering—seizing and releasing—to exhaust its depths.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, this great assembly does not yet understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s clarification regarding the two kinds of refined vision—the seeing of form and the seeing of emptiness, and what is correct and what is incorrect. World-Honored One, if these people before us...”
If these objects such as form and emptiness are what is seen, they should have something pointed out [as their locus]. If they are not what is seen, there should be nothing gazed upon.
Yet now, I do not know where this principle leads; therefore, I am filled with alarm and fear. It is not that my past roots of goodness were meager or slight.
I only pray that the Tathāgata’s great compassion will illuminate this: what are these various objects and this essence of seeing fundamentally?
Regarding these matters, there was nothing that could be judged as right or wrong.
Because the great assembly was thus bewildered, it was necessary for one of great wisdom to intercede on their behalf to resolve their doubts.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat, prostrated with reverence, and addressed the Buddha.

He said: "World-Honored One, this great assembly does not understand the two meanings of the Tathāgata’s clarification regarding the refined vision that perceives both form and emptiness as being neither 'is' nor 'is not.

World-Honored One, if these preceding objects—the forms, emptiness, and so forth—were themselves the seeing, then one should be able to point out those very objects within the myriad phenomena; why is it that they cannot do so? If they are not..."
As for "seeing," one should see that within the myriad phenomena there is nothing at all to be seen. Why is it that in a single glance, there is nowhere that is not so?

Now, this great assembly, precisely because they have heard this profound Dharma—whose meaning is abstruse and remote, and which leaves no place for attachment—finds it difficult to comprehend at first;
thus they experience alarm, doubt, and fear. This is not as it was in the past during the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
In this assembly, our roots of goodness are slight and meager; hearing the Great Dharma, we are unwilling to take it upon ourselves.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, in his great compassion, will once again clarify these various phenomena and this essence of seeing: what kind of entity are they originally?
Why do they reside between the two pillars—neither being existent nor yet non-existent? Is it right or wrong?
"Is" refers to the two meanings of "is" and "is not. "Is" means the absence of the view that [something] is; "is not" means the absence of the view that [something] is not.
Two instances of the character "wu" (absence/non-existence) are omitted; this is merely an abbreviation of the expression.

The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly: "The Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, while abiding in their own samādhi, perceive that the seer and the conditions for seeing, as well as all conceived appearances, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent."
This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be "is" or "is not" within it?
This passage shows that seeing and objects merge into the one true essence, thereby elucidating the principle that there is neither "is" nor "is not.

"Seeing" refers to the essence of seeing; "seeing-objects" refers to the six sense-fields, such as form, emptiness, and so forth; and "conception" refers to the consciousnesses of the six sense-bases.
"Mind and appearance" refers to the appearances of the six sense organs and their physical bodies, as well as the mind and body themselves. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī and the great assembly:
"Because you have not yet attained the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi, you differentiate between objects and self within the myriad phenomena, distinguishing 'this' from 'that' and 'right' from 'wrong.
However, the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas have personally realized the Śūraṅgama Samādhi."
What is meant by "the Nāga is always in samādhi; there is no time when he is not in samādhi"?

Abiding within this samādhi, one perceives that the seeing-essence (*darśana-vijñāna*) of the perceived portion (*nimitta-bhāga*), as well as the objects of perception (*ālambana*) of the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), along with the body and mind of conceptualized appearances, are all like the vision of floating flowers in the sky by one suffering from an eye disease—they fundamentally do not exist. This is truly because these two divisions of seeing and appearance are originally Bodhi.
He extracts the essence of the wondrous, pure, and luminous body. That which is called the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is like empty space; therein all Buddhas abide.
Abiding in this *dharmatā*, one does not even perceive the existence of form, emptiness, or the subtle faculty of seeing. How could there be "is" within it, let alone "is not"?
At this point, the World-Honored One has laid out the entire matter upon the platter. Question: At the beginning, the Buddha spoke only of "seeing."
It is taken as the nature [of the mind], yet it is explained in a circuitous manner that it does not associate with the body, the mind, or the myriad phenomena.
This seems to suggest that seeing alone is real while all else is false. Now, if one discusses the false, then even the seeing-nature is equal to empty flowers; if one discusses the real...
Thus, all phenomena ascend to share the same true essence; this is indeed a discourse on the ultimate principle.
Yet, how can one avoid being at a loss as to where to apply it? Answer: Although the subsequent text is naturally clear, I shall now provide an additional analogy.

The One Truth is like the water in the great ocean; the seeing-essence is like the luminosity of the water; and all objective forms and images are like reflections within the water. Specifically, because of...
The fool mistakes the reflection for reality and, conversely, forgets the water. Now, one wishes to cause him to abandon the recognition of the reflection and recognize the water;
however, because the substance of the water is limpid and transparent, its form is not seen. Therefore, for the time being, one causes him to recognize the light upon the surface of that water.
Therefore, each instance refutes the shadow as false and praises the light as true, desiring that one recognize the water through the light itself.
Yet those deluded ones further cling to the idea that the light and the shadow each possess their own substantiality, groundlessly giving rise to disputes of right and wrong.
Thus, it is clarified once more that both the light and the shadow lack any self-nature, and that the sole reality is the water itself. Therefore, one knows the light...
Although both shadow and light are said to be entirely empty, when comparing light to shadow, the shadow undergoes arising and ceasing while the light has no coming or going;
the shadow is partial and localized, whereas the light is pervasive and all-encompassing.

Furthermore, although both light and shadow are equally present in the water, taking hold of the shadow entails the danger of drowning, whereas recognizing the light brings the benefit of gaining the water. Moreover, the shadow is itself an external object.
Although it is reflected therein, the light itself remains entirely unchanged in its essence.

Thus, by examining this analogy in detail, one sees that while the essence of vision and the myriad phenomena are equally both false and true, the distinction between their respective gains and losses remains perfectly clear.
“Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: Is there another Mañjuśrī like you who is also Mañjuśrī, or is there no such Mañjuśrī?
“Thus it is, World-Honored One. I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no such Mañjuśrī as that. Why is this?
If there were such a one, there would be two Mañjuśrīs. Yet, today I am not without being Mañjuśrī; within this, there is truly neither ‘is’ nor ‘is not.’”
[The interlocutor] asked about the characteristics [of these phenomena]. The Buddha said: "This wondrous clarity of vision and these various empty objects are likewise thus.
They are originally the wondrously clear, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind. Through delusion, they appear as form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing.

It is like a second moon: who can say which is the real moon, and which is not? Mañjuśrī, there is only the one true moon; between them, there is naturally neither 'this is the moon' nor 'this is not the moon.'"
The Moon.
Having already provided this illumination, the World-Honored One feared that [the disciples] might still be unable to believe and understand it;
he therefore required Mañjuśrī to add annotations from the side. Thus he asked him: "Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: is this very body of yours the true Mañju?"
Mañjuśrī, would it be permissible to add another Mañjuśrī outside of this present Mañjuśrī and call him "this Mañjuśrī"?
Would it be permissible to subtract one Mañjuśrī from within this present Mañjuśrī and call him "no Mañjuśrī"?
Mañjuśrī is a person of great wisdom; as their natures are harmonious, they naturally resonate with one another like corresponding sounds. Therefore...
He said: "This very 'I' is the one true Mañjuśrī; nothing else can be added to this as being Mañjuśrī.
Why? If one were to add another 'I' as being Mañjuśrī, then I would have two Mañjuśrīs.
Yet, while I possess this one true Mañjuśrī, it is also not the case that there is no Mañjuśrī at all. Thus it is.

If there were something additional to the fundamental substance, only then could it be called "is. If it were entirely absent along with the fundamental substance, only then could it be called "is not.
Now, since it is neither existent nor non-existent, how could there be the two characteristics of "is" and "is not" within it?

This analogy correctly states that apart from the one true substance, one cannot perceive the existence of the myriad things by adding anything to it, nor can one perceive their absence by subtracting anything from it.
Objects are neither seen nor perceived, because the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) does not possess even a single dharma in excess, nor lack even a single dharma;
it is perfectly identical to the Great Void, being without deficiency and without surplus. The Buddha said:

"Since you know that in the true Manjushri above, there is fundamentally no right or wrong, then this wondrously luminous seeing and all these empty objects of the senses are likewise so. This is because—
This seeing and these objects are originally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind.

Due to the initial lack of awakening, a single thought arose; thus, one became deluded into the karmic consciousness, which then transformed into the two divisions of subject (seeing) and object (phenomena).

That which is subsumed under the objective division consists of form and emptiness; that which is subsumed under the subjective division consists of hearing and seeing. This is truly because form, emptiness, hearing, and...
[This] seeing arises based on the True [Nature], like a second moon. Since it is like a second moon, one knows it is fundamentally non-existent;
how then could one, regarding this second moon, give rise to false conjectures, asking, "Who is the true moon, and who is not?
To be unaware of whether something is produced as true or false is simply to have not yet seen the True Moon. Mañjuśrī, if one sees only one...
The moon is the reality; thus, one does not falsely establish right and wrong. As for the "second moon," it differs from the former:
the former solely serves as a metaphor for seeing, whereas this simultaneously serves as a metaphor for both form and emptiness.

Therefore, when you now perceive and observe the various manifestations of the sense objects, these are called deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*). You are unable to discern within them what is real and what is not.
It is because of this true, essential, wondrously enlightened, and luminous nature that you are able to distinguish between the pointing finger and that which it points to.
(The word "you" here refers to Ānanda.
This further uses the Dharma to correspond with the metaphor, reiterating and clarifying the point. "Seeing" refers to the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddha*).
"Dust" (*rajas*) encompasses everything, both internally—the body and mind—and externally—the myriad phenomena. The mind is also included among the dusts because it is itself an object of perception.
It is because it is a shadow. Since you have never dwelt in this Śūraṅgama Samādhi, your eye of wisdom has not been clear;

thus, upon dharmas that are dependent on others, you give rise to various kinds of parikalpita (imagined) constructions. Speaking in terms of body and mind, you say that the nature of seeing is before you;
speaking in terms of the myriad things, you say that some are seen and some are not. Both are false and deluded thoughts; they do not attain the reality, and therefore [it is not so].

Within this state, one may distinguish right from wrong, yet it is like observing a second moon— indulging in arbitrary conjecture that ultimately does not transcend the false discourse of "this is the moon" or "this is not the moon.
If one attains the wondrously arising true samādhi, one will clearly realize that the essence of seeing, the body and mind,
and all myriad phenomena are fundamentally one true essence, the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity, originally and solely one.
Only when one realizes this essence can one suddenly awaken to the fact that all phenomena are entirely without distinction between self and other.

How could one then still propose to perceive the nature within the body and mind and claim it is pointable, or measure the perception of the nature within the myriad things and claim it is unpointable?
It is like a person with clear vision who, having seen the true moon, would never point to this [reflected] moon as being it.

This moon is not a moon. It is because at first one’s stubborn attachment was foremost; it seemed as if it could be pointed out falsely, yet when examined in detail against the object, it again seemed as if it could not be pointed out.
Both of these are delusions caused by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), leading to a state of confused conjecture.

Now, having realized the single truth, this doubt is suddenly severed. Therefore it is said: "The pointing finger is not the pointing. Thus we know that when one is deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then...
Right and wrong arise adventitiously. When one awakens to the true nature, it is empty, luminous, vast, and penetrating—just this.

The eighth section, "Revealing that Seeing and the Seer are Not Distinct," concludes. "Emerging" means transcending. "Pointing and not pointing" refers back to the previous statement that since there is a location, it is not the case that there is no indication.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has said:
that the awareness which conditions objects pervades the ten directions, remaining profoundly still and eternally abiding, its nature being neither arising nor ceasing.

How does this differ from the 'Dark Principle' (Tattva) discussed by the former Brahmin Śāṇḍilya, and from the 'True Self' that pervades the ten directions as taught by the various non-Buddhist sects such as the ash-smearing ascetics? World-Honored One...

The World-Honored One also once, on Mount Laṅkā, expounded this meaning for the sake of Mahāmati and others. Those heterodox teachers constantly speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), whereas I speak of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);
it is not within their sphere of experience. I now observe that this nature of awakening is spontaneous, neither arising nor ceasing, and far removed from all false delusions;
it appears as if it were not a matter of causes and conditions, and thus seems identical to their notion of spontaneity. How is this so?

What is being revealed? It is that one does not enter among the various heterodoxies, but attains the true mind—the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous nature (the character "yu" [with] is similar to the character "lei" [like]).

This is the ninth instance clarifying that seeing transcends the realm of the emotions. Whether [conceived as] spontaneous or through causes and conditions, these are all merely deluded attachments of the emotional mind.
Now, this nature of seeing does not belong to any of these; therefore, it is said to "transcend the emotions. To be aware of conditions is precisely the nature of seeing.
Because the nature of seeing can see light and see darkness, see obstruction and see openness, pervading and conditioning all things, it is designated as "awareness of conditions" (*jueyuan*).
Ānanda, when you saw the Tathāgata manifest his essential clarity and see both form and emptiness, that was originally *bodhi*.
Only when one realizes the essence of wondrous purity and clarity can one truly comprehend the teaching that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive;
yet, one may still doubt that this view conflates with non-Buddhist teachings and contradicts one's own school. Therefore, [the interlocutor] addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if it is indeed as the Dharma King has taught—that the conditions of awakening are truly all-pervasive, truly eternally abiding, and truly neither arising nor ceasing—then previously..."

Among the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) established by the non-Buddhist Brahmin followers of the Golden Head (*Suvarṇaśiras*), the first is the *avyakta-tattva* (the Unmanifest Principle), which they erroneously claim to be the eternal primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, those non-Buddhists who practice asceticism such as smearing themselves with ashes postulate a *puruṣa* (Self) that pervades the ten directions.
The "enlightened object" (*bodhyālambana*) now being discussed, which pervades the realms of the ten directions, is [identical to] what they postulate as the *avyakta-tattva* and the *puruṣa*.
"What difference is there between my [claim] that I pervade the worlds of the ten directions and this?
It is no different from mistaking fish eyes for bright pearls, or mistaking a mountain pheasant for a colorful phoenix.

Furthermore, in the past, the World-Honored One also, at Mount Laṅkā, extensively distinguished for Mahāmati and others the meaning of why the internal teachings differ from those of the non-Buddhists."

The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others constantly proclaim spontaneity (*svabhāva*). They claim that both internally, as for the nature of the mind, and externally, as for the myriad things, all are fundamentally without cause;
they exist spontaneously and naturally. As it is said: "Who opened the rivers and seas and heaped up the mountains? Who pared down the thorns and painted the birds and beasts?
There is nothing in the world capable of producing anything. Therefore, all phenomena are eternally spontaneous. This [view] is a repudiation [of causality].

There is no cause and effect; cultivation and realization are not established. Therefore, the Buddha extensively expounded upon causes and conditions to refute it, because the realm realized by me is not the realm realized by them.
I now observe this awareness that perceives objects as the nature of seeing.
It is also spontaneous. Being originally present and leaving nothing behind, it is not born. Being ultimately indestructible, it does not perish.
Being the single truth and the single essence, it is far removed from delusion. Having no self and no other, it is far removed from inversion.
Within the midst of a thousand differences, it is manifest and perfected everywhere; amidst the ten thousand phenomena, it stands preeminent at every point. Thus, it is not merely...
The causal conditions taught by the Tathāgata contradict [your position] and instead accord with the spontaneous origination (*svabhāva*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

This violates your own school’s tenets and conflates them with external teachings; once one has fallen into error, one further becomes hypocritical and enters into darkness, failing to understand what other skillful means the World-Honored One might employ for instruction. What the Tathāgata has taught differs from that of those non-Buddhists.
In calculation, each is different. Only when we first succeed in not entering among the various heterodoxies do we then attain the true mind and the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity.
As for "cause" (*hetu*), it refers to the seeds produced by causes. As for "condition" (*pratyaya*), it refers to the auxiliary conditions that assist in their development.
For example, in the case of the hundred grains and other such things, they must take the root-seed as the cause and soil and water as the conditions; only then can they produce sprouts.
It is like a sprout. When the Buddha teaches the Dharma for those of the provisional vehicles, he speaks entirely in terms of causes and conditions.

Master Zhong says: "In the Perfect Teaching of the *Śūraṅgama*, all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) are entirely the nature (*dharmatā*). Ānanda, however, divided nature and phenomena into two; therefore, he suspected that the 'True Self' of the non-Buddhists was confused with Wondrous Enlightenment.
As the preceding text states: "I must see my own True Self. Now, as for this body and mind of mine, what are they? This refers to the body.
To claim that there is a nature of seeing distinct from the mind is the very root of doubt. This immediately results in two characteristics:
conjunction and non-conjunction. How is this clarified? It is said that if a single true self exists within the ten directions, this constitutes conjunction;
if the essence of the true self does not intermingle with the ten directions, this constitutes non-conjunction. Thus, O Worldly One...
The Honored One did not provide a detailed analysis, but merely cited the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve spheres, and the eighteen elements;
as well as the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness, and the seven great elements in their perfect interfusion and omnipresence.

These are far removed from both combination and non-combination, as well as from causes and conditions or spontaneity. Thus, all speculative views are extinguished, including the "True Self" of the non-Buddhists.
This has been clearly distinguished and resolved. Regarding the character "yǔ" (with) in the phrase "yǔ pǐ zìrán" (similar to that spontaneity), it means "like" or "of the same kind.
As for what is meant by "explaining and revealing": Ānanda truly believed [the world] was spontaneous (*zìrán*), yet he merely sought to distinguish it from the non-Buddhists (*wàidào*).
He did not realize that while it might differ from them, it nonetheless lacked entirely the meaning of true spontaneity. Dàodào said: "In the teachings of this land..."
This refers to the path of the celestial dharma. The nature of the path is spontaneous;
it is truly reckoned as spontaneous. The Buddha told Ānanda: "I have now thus revealed these skillful means and have truly informed you. Yet you still have not attained awakening."
"Delusion is considered natural, Ānanda. If it were necessarily natural, one must clearly distinguish that there is a substantial entity of nature.
You should observe this wondrously luminous vision: what constitutes its self?
Does this vision take light as its self, darkness as its self, space as its self, or obstruction as its self? Ānanda, if light were its self, it should not perceive darkness."
If, moreover, emptiness were taken as its own essence, one would not perceive obstruction.

Likewise, if even such characteristics as darkness and so forth were taken as its own essence, then at the time of light, the nature [of the visual faculty] would be severed and extinguished; how then could it perceive light?
This refutation of "naturalness" is self-evident. The Buddha told Ānanda: "I have now thus refuted the deluded mind to reveal the nature of seeing.
I do not know how many twists and turns it has required, nor how many skillful means I have employed, for your true benefit. Yet you still do not awaken;
instead, you are once again deluded into thinking it is 'natural. Ānanda, if you insist that the nature of seeing is natural..."
This must be clearly distinguished and discerned. That which possesses its own substantial reality—neither shifting nor changing—is precisely what is "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).

Now, observe this wondrous, luminous nature of seeing. Amidst all the various phenomena you perceive—within light and darkness, emptiness and obstruction—which specific dharma do you definitively designate as the spontaneous body? If you take "light" to be the spontaneous, then this seeing...

The nature [of things] should only perceive light; it should not perceive darkness. If one further considers emptiness to be self-existent (*svabhāva*), then it should only perceive emptiness and ought not to perceive obstruction.
This applies even to various characteristics such as darkness: if one takes them to be self-existent, then one will no longer perceive light.
Because it exists as a self-existent entity here, it should likewise exist as a state of annihilation there. Now, since there is light...
When coming here, it perceives light; when darkness comes, it perceives darkness. Since it changes according to what it perceives, one knows that the nature of awareness is certainly not inherent.
Why, then, do you cling to it as being inherent? Zhong said: "Inherent" means that its own essence is naturally so.
If its own essence were naturally so, it would not change according to objects. Now, since it changes in accordance with them, it is not inherent.
Ānanda said, “If this wondrous nature of seeing is certainly not spontaneous, then I now understand it to be produced through causes and conditions.
Yet my mind is still not clear; I consult the Tathāgata: how does this meaning accord with the nature of causes and conditions?

The Buddha said, “Regarding what you call ‘causes and conditions,’ I shall ask you further. Now, because of seeing, the nature of seeing manifests before you. Does this seeing exist because of light?”
Seeing. Seeing exists because of darkness; seeing exists because of space; seeing exists because of obstruction. Ānanda, if seeing existed because of light, one should not see darkness.
If it existed because of darkness, one should not see light. This applies likewise to space and obstruction, which are identical to light and darkness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, this seeing also depends on light to exist, depends on darkness to exist, and depends...
There is the perception of emptiness and the perception of obstruction. Ānanda, if one perceives emptiness as the object, one should not perceive obstruction;
if one perceives obstruction as the object, one should not perceive emptiness. This applies likewise, even to the perceptions of light and darkness, which are the same as emptiness and obstruction.

This refutes [the notion of] causes and conditions. Ānanda said: "If this wondrous vision is certainly not spontaneous, it must surely belong to the category of borrowed [conditions], such as the production of consciousness through the four conditions. I now declare that it is produced by causes and conditions.
Yet my mind is still not clear; I must consult the Tathāgata. This nature of awakening is originally pervasive and eternal; its nature is not born."

[The afflictions] are extinguished. How, then, can one attain accord with the principle of causes and conditions? The Buddha said: "Regarding what you call 'causes and conditions,' I shall ask you further:

Since you now have the seeing-nature manifest before you because of seeing light, darkness, space, and obstruction, from among this light, darkness, space, and obstruction, by what cause does this seeing-nature exist? Ānanda, if you take light as [the cause]..."
That which arises from seeds, when darkness replaces light, is like exchanging grain for sand; how could the sprout grow?
One should not perceive darkness [as the cause], and it is the same regarding darkness. This applies even to space and obstruction, which are identical to light and darkness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within this nature of seeing of yours, upon what do you rely among light, darkness, space, and obstruction?

It is so, Ānanda. If emptiness serves as a contributing condition for the arising of vision, then when that which is obstructed replaces the empty space—just as if one were to substitute water for fire—how could the sprout emerge? One ought not to see the obstruction; yet the same applies to the condition of obstruction.
This extends even to the conditions of light and darkness, which are identical to emptiness and obstruction. Now, since you can see light and also see darkness, you must likewise see emptiness.
Furthermore, because one can see obstruction, it is clear that the essential nature (svabhāva) is unchanging, does not arise from causes, and does not arise following conditions.
Master Zhong said: "Taking objects as causes and following objects as conditions—since there is no fixed destination, this is not [the operation of] causes and conditions.
According to this, the seeing-nature is the self-body, while light, darkness, form, and emptiness are external dharmas. The self-body is able to follow these external dharmas.
Dharmas are not self-existent. Other dharmas cannot transform their own essence; they are not produced by causes and conditions.
You should know that this wondrously bright, subtle awakening is neither caused nor conditioned, yet it is neither self-existent nor not self-existent.
There is neither non-being nor being; there is neither right nor wrong. It is free from all marks and is identical with all dharmas.
How can you now attempt to apply your mind within it, using the conceptual names and marks of worldly frivolity to make distinctions?
It would be like trying to grasp and rub empty space with your palms—this only increases your own fatigue. How could empty space ever be seized according to your grasping?

From this point downward, the text repeatedly brushes away [dualistic traces] to clarify that the nature of awakening is both unchanging while following conditions and follows conditions while remaining unchanging.
Those who cling to "spontaneity" do not understand following conditions; those who cling to "causality" do not know its unchanging nature.

Thus, there arise the distinctions between non-Buddhists and followers of the Lesser Vehicle. As for the principle that it is unchanging while following conditions and follows conditions while remaining unchanging—this is the teaching of the World-Honored One.
This is the grand standard for expounding the Dharma and the profound discourse for entering into principle. Therefore, the conclusion states:

"One should know that such subtle, wondrous, and luminous awareness does not belong to causes and conditions, nor does it belong to spontaneity; yet it is not non-spontaneous, nor is it not caused by conditions."

Fundamentally, there is neither right nor wrong, nor is there correctness or incorrectness. By means of this essence of wondrous, luminous, and primordially pure perfect awakening, one is detached from all marks;
therefore, that which is "not" is entirely "not. Yet, because it is identical with all dharmas, that which is "is" is entirely "is.
To direct the mind toward it is already a deviation; to stir a thought is already a separation. How can you, within this wondrous awakening, point to...?

To apply mental attention by means of worldly conceptual proliferation and names and marks—specifically, to speculate upon the Tathāgata’s wondrously enlightened and luminous nature by means of "spontaneity" or "causes and conditions"—is no different from trying to grasp empty space with one's hand.
How could empty space ever be seized according to your grasping? The *Zongjing* says: "Causes and conditions, as well as spontaneity, are all merely worldly discourses."
Existence and non-existence, as well as the ultimate and the conventional, are all merely the discriminating consciousness-mind.

If one does not directly perceive the reality of things, yet wishes to seek it through intellectual understanding and emotional striving, it is like taking a bow made of rabbit horns, mounting an arrow of tortoise hair, and attempting to shoot Mount Sumeru with a person who has no hands;
it is but a vain exertion of worldly toil, for such a thing can never happen. Furthermore, the former masters said: "It is neither from causes and conditions, nor is it self-existent..."

Indeed. The most subtle within the subtle, the most profound within the profound—the myriad phenomena of the universe manifest within its radiance; yet though one seeks them, their source cannot be found.
This [text] and that [reality] mutually unfold and clarify one another. Regarding "the various worlds":

in the Abhidharma school (Lakṣaṇayāna), there are the world of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and the world of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). As for "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), it is the doctrine followed by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); thus, it is not [the state of] training.
These are the worldly conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the provisional vehicles; they are the worldly conceptual proliferations of those who study.
[End of the ninth section, clarifying that the seeing transcends the emotions. This is not a case of mixing the subtle clarity of essential awakening with the nature of seeing.
Nevertheless, the principle that "while following conditions it does not change, while not changing it follows conditions" is likewise realized from the nature of seeing.
The World-Honored One’s words were clear and self-evident.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the nature of wondrous enlightenment must be neither caused by conditions nor dependent on conditions.

Why then does the World-Honored One constantly proclaim to the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions—namely, space as a condition, light as a condition, the mind as a condition, and [the eyes as a condition]?"
"The eye. What is the meaning of this?

This tenth section clarifies that seeing is distinct from the act of seeing. Now, since the essence of seeing is said to be a union of the true and the false, one may, according to its significance, distinguish between the two types of seeing:
the true and the false. However, when the true seeing is accompanied by falsehood, it is then designated as "false."
Seeing. When one is free from delusion, it is called true seeing. What is now termed "leaving seeing" means that true seeing merely leaves behind a portion of deluded seeing within its own substance;
it does not mean leaving behind views such as those concerning the self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) or extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi). Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"As for the negation of spontaneity, I have already received your instruction, World-Honored One. If you say this wondrous..."

If you claim that the nature of seeing is not produced by causes and conditions, why does the World-Honored One constantly teach the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions—namely, space, light, the mind, and the eyes?
If there were no space and no light before one’s face, how could there be seeing? If my mind were without eyes, how could I see? Therefore, it must fall under the category of having causes.
[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, I have now shown that the essence of seeing does not at all rely upon these [conditions]. Is it that what is present is right while what was past was wrong?
Or is it that the meaning is the same for both present and past, yet I have not yet understood? The nature of seeing cited by Ānanda is likely the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
That which the Tathāgata has pointed out is the nature within the sense organ (*indriya*). In the Mahāyāna, visual consciousness arises through nine conditions; in the Hīnayāna...
Within the Dharma, these four conditions are roughly complete; none may be lacking. Yet all are the conditions for the arising of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

"Mind" (*citta*) here refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna do not realize that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are one with the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*). As the Confucians say:

"When the mind is not present, one looks but does not see. This is precisely it. "Ruler and square" refers to the ignorant Śrāvakas who do not distinguish between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects.

"Consciousness. Do you believe this? ○ Zhong said: Both "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) have been refuted. Yet, one does not inquire about spontaneity because it is not our own teaching.

Since causes and conditions are our own teaching, the question is raised again. Within the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang-zong*), it is only taught that consciousness arises from causes and conditions;
it has never been taught that the wondrous enlightened nature (*miao-jue-xing*) arises from the four conditions, for the wondrous enlightened nature is not...
Because it is that which is produced by productive causes, Ānanda mistakenly identifies the wondrous enlightened nature as being born from causes and conditions;

his confusion is profound indeed. Therefore, the subsequent text first refutes that the nature of seeing belongs to the four conditions, thereby revealing by contrast that the wondrous enlightened nature is beyond the reach of the nature of seeing and certainly does not belong to causes and conditions.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "What I have spoken regarding the characteristics of worldly causes and conditions is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This clarifies that the former teaching and the present teaching are fundamentally different. The Buddha said:

"Ānanda, when I previously spoke of causes and conditions, it was merely for the purpose of counteracting the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and to entice those of the Lesser Vehicle; it was a provisional teaching suited to a particular time, not [the final teaching]."
What has been taught is the foremost teaching of the definitive meaning regarding cultivation and realization. How can you take that [teaching] to challenge this one?

As for the frequent past discourse on consciousness arising from the four conditions, it was precisely because non-Buddhists falsely cling to spontaneity (*svabhāva*) that he borrowed the principle of causes and conditions to refute them—what is called "using a wedge to extract a wedge," a matter belonging to the second gate.
"Ānanda, I ask you again: when people of the world say, 'I am able to see,' what do they mean by 'seeing' and what do they mean by 'not seeing'?
Ānanda replied: 'People of the world rely upon the light of the sun, the moon, and lamps to perceive various forms;
this is called "seeing. If these three kinds of light were absent, one would be unable to see. Ānanda, if it were dark..."
Regarding "not seeing": one should not see darkness. If one necessarily sees darkness, this is merely the absence of light; how could it be called "not seeing"?

Ānanda, if during the time of darkness one does not see light, it is called "not seeing"; now, during the time of light, one does not see the characteristic of darkness, and this is likewise called "not seeing.
Thus, these two characteristics are both termed "not seeing. Furthermore, if these two characteristics were to mutually suppress one another...
"It is taken away; it is not that your nature of seeing is temporarily absent therein. Thus you should know that both [states] are called 'seeing. Why then do you say you do not see?
This was to investigate and refute the conditions upon which he relied. The Buddha said, "Ānanda, I shall ask you again."
"Just as people in the world each say of themselves, 'I am able to see,' by what means is this seeing accomplished?
Once seeing has been accomplished, by what further means does one fail to see? Ānanda replied, "People rely on the light of the sun, the moon, and lamps to see various forms;
therefore, it is called 'seeing. If there were no light from the sun, the moon, or lamps, then [one would not see]."
"One can see. This clarifies that both seeing and not seeing belong to causes and conditions;
thus, one knows that the nature of seeing arises from causes and conditions. The World-Honored One used his words to refute this, saying:
"Ānanda, if this nature of seeing were called 'not seeing' because it lacked these three kinds of light, then it should not fail to see darkness. If you say that although it does not see light..."
"One who is certainly able to see darkness—this is simply ignorance (*avidyā*). Why, then, is it called 'not seeing'?
"Ānanda, if you say that not seeing light while in the dark is called 'not seeing,' then one should also be called 'not seeing' when one does not see darkness during the bright day.
If this were so, then both seeing darkness and seeing light would equally be called [not seeing]."

"It is not seen. Is there such a principle? If you say that when light comes, darkness departs, and when darkness comes, light departs—this being merely the mutual displacement of the two characteristics of light and darkness, and having nothing to do with the seeing-nature which would thus be temporarily present and temporarily absent—then you must know that seeing darkness and seeing light are both called 'seeing.
Why, then, is it called 'not seeing' at the time one sees darkness?"
One should know that according to worldly conventions, clear vision is permitted while dark vision is not; the latter requires many conditions.
Now, from the very moment one points to the sense organ itself, one perceives seeing within the darkness.

Thus, if even the seeing within the darkness does not employ the eye, how much less could it rely upon empty clarity or the discriminating mind? This demonstrates that within the darkness— Output format: ... (as requested) ...
If one perceives [this], then all four conditions are simultaneously refuted. ○ Ānanda mistakenly identifies the wondrous enlightened nature as a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions.
However, not only does the wondrous enlightened nature not belong to causes and conditions, how could the nature of seeing ever have belonged to causes and conditions?
Therefore, for the time being, he borrows the name of "the seer" to refute this.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should now know this: when seeing light, the seeing is not the light; when seeing darkness, the seeing is not the darkness;
when seeing emptiness, the seeing is not the emptiness; and when seeing obstruction, the seeing is not the obstruction.
The four meanings are thus accomplished. You should further know this: when the seeing sees, that seeing is not [itself] seeing; seeing is already apart from seeing, and seeing cannot reach it.
How, then, can you speak again of causes and conditions, spontaneity, or the characteristics of their combination?
This citation uses the fact that the self-substance is independent of conditions as an analogy for the true seeing being independent of what is seen. Therefore, Ānanda, you should now know:

from what I have previously taught—that this seeing sees light yet is not light, sees darkness yet is not darkness, sees emptiness yet is not emptiness, and sees obstruction yet is not obstruction—it is clear that the nature of the capacity to see is not identical to the objects that are seen. All of these...
This is the ultimate truth that transcends conditions; it has already surpassed the tenet of dependent origination.
Since the four meanings of light, darkness, space, and obstruction have been established as the analogies, you should further understand that within this essence of vision:
The union of the real and the false consists of the fundamental substance of true seeing, which is nonetheless accompanied by a portion of the false seeing of ignorance.
When this true seeing suddenly manifests, one is able to penetrate and see the very substance of the false.

However, at the very moment it is seen, the substance of this true seeing has already detached itself from the false seeing and no longer falls within its sphere; therefore, it is called "seeing the seeing."

At this time, "seeing that which is not seeing" is truly because, according to the four preceding meanings, the nature that is able to see perceives the objects that are seen; yet that nature is itself not the object.
Now, by analogy with this, the true seeing that is able to see perceives the deluded seeing that is seen; yet true seeing is itself not deluded seeing. Indeed, this true...
Even when one has abandoned the essence of vision that is mixed with delusive views such that the essence of vision can no longer reach [the object],
how could there still be a simultaneous vision that is likewise detached, yet still said to depend upon causes and conditions?
Why, moreover, do you employ worldly frivolous discourse to falsely speculate, speaking of causes and conditions as if they were in opposition to the nature of causes and conditions?
This is the natural state and the characteristic of the harmonious conjunction of causal conditions.

This is where the World-Honored One led the Venerable One to a precipice ten thousand fathoms high and gave him one more push, intending to force him to let go and take full responsibility. Zhong said:
"By using light and darkness, form and emptiness as points of inference, he establishes the meaning of realizing the nature of seeing as being detached from these four sensory objects."

Thus, it is clear that the nature of seeing does not belong to dependent origination. Nevertheless, although the nature of seeing does not belong to dependent origination, it still belongs to the manifestation of one’s own karmic consciousness;
it remains separated from the wondrous enlightened nature by yet another layer. Therefore, taking this opportunity to refute it, [the Buddha] said: "You should further know (etc.).
At the moment of seeing the seeing, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing; even seeing is already detached from seeing."

Three phrases. The three instances of the character "see" (*jiàn*) above refer to the essence of nature (*xìng-tǐ*). The three instances of the character "see" below refer to the seeing-essence (*jiàn-jīng*).
This is because the seeing-essence is taken as false while the essence of nature is taken as true. Thus, when the nature is within seeing, it is called the seeing-essence;
when the nature is apart from seeing, it is called the "seeing of seeing. The meaning of the words is as if to say: "seeing light and seeing darkness."

To see emptiness or to see form is merely to see; it is false seeing. Only when one sees this very act of seeing can it be called true seeing, for once true seeing has been attained, one is already free from seeing.
It is beyond the reach of those [ordinary] forms of seeing; how much less could such things as the characteristics of causes and conditions, spontaneity, or harmony possibly reach it?
○ The essence of seeing belongs to the eighth consciousness; because it contains delusion within its midst, it is therefore... [as follows].
In the "Wenju" (Chapter on the Distinctive Activities), the shared portion explains two kinds of false views, clarifying the three instances of the character "view" (*jian*) that follow.

This refers to such statements as "the eye disease is itself the fatigue of seeing" and "the shadow and the seeing are both eye diseases. The wondrously enlightened nature belongs to the ninth consciousness;
it is purely true and without falsehood. Therefore, the subsequent text further states that because "that seeing is the true essence and its nature is not an eye disease," it is not so named.

"Seeing. To explain the three instances of the word "seeing" mentioned above: the pure real mark (*dharmatā*) is precisely true seeing; it is the same as the "subtle, wondrous clarity of essential awareness" mentioned previously.
This corresponds to what is described in the *Awakening of Faith* as "entering the subtle from the equal" and employing ultimate awakening to contemplate the ignorance of the phase of arising.
It is at the moment when the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been exhausted that one enters the stages of a bodhisattva.
This is beyond the reach of the partial awakening of the Śrāvakas; it is no wonder that Ānanda was bewildered and distressed.

Furthermore, it says: "When seeing sees, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing. Seeing is already apart from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. This directly reveals the true nature as being devoid of the essence of seeing.
Recently, Jiaoguang has argued that the Tathāgata’s intention was to emphasize the manifestation of seeing, exerting great effort [to clarify this].
This refutes the doctrine of "seeing. One does not realize that prior to the "eight returns," what is called "manifest seeing" is like gold within ore;
as long as one cannot remove the ore, the true nature remains solitary while the essence of seeing naturally dissolves.
It is like the single moon being the reality, with no second moon existing at all. Thus, it is seeing itself that is destroyed, not a person destroying seeing.
"You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and lacking in discernment; you are unable to penetrate the pure true reality. I now instruct you:
you should contemplate well and must not grow weary on the wondrous path to bodhi."
This is an extremely earnest exhortation. It is because you śrāvakas are confined and submerged in what you have previously heard; you take a little as sufficient.
Being both narrow and inferior, you lack the wisdom of discernment and consistently dwell only upon the imagined and dependent natures, seeking a livelihood therein.
You are unable to penetrate the reality that all things are untainted and that all marks are non-marks.
[The Buddha said: "I have now already instructed you, and you have heard it. You should contemplate it more deeply and examine it minutely;
exert yourself and practice diligently. Do not be lax or negligent, nor stop halfway through, allowing yourself to become weary and indolent.
This is because, in the desire to reach Bodhi, this single path of the essence of seeing is the most wondrous. [This concludes] the tenth section: Revealing the Seeing.

The discussion on "Transcending Views" concludes. ○ To discuss these collectively according to the ten sections: the first section reveals that it is detached from the faculties and detached from objects, standing aloof as the numinous light shines uniquely.
The second section reveals that it is detached from the body and detached from the environment, remaining concentrated and fundamentally unshakable.
The third section reveals that it persists until the end of the future, ultimately never ceasing. The fourth section...
The first section reveals that from time immemorial, its fundamental existence has never been omitted.

The second section reveals that it neither departs nor returns, standing preeminent beyond all things and eternally abiding. The third section reveals that it is neither mixed nor confused, transcending the realm of forms with solitary distinction.
The fourth section reveals that its nature is fundamentally sovereign; as it transforms the myriad things, what "large" or "small" could there be?
The eighth section reveals that its essence is fundamentally interpenetrating and harmonious, like the single moon where distinctions between right and wrong cannot be discerned.
The ninth section reveals that all sensory perceptions do not fall into error, far transcending external calculations and provisional doctrines.

The tenth section reveals that even its own characteristics are detached, entering into pure truth free from delusion. When the manifestation reaches this point, it may truly be called "manifestation."
This is the ultimate point. Previous commentaries have taken this manifest meaning as a whole and treated it entirely as a refutation of views; why is this so?
It is simply because, within the state of delusion of sentient beings, two kinds of false views still remain unremoved; therefore, it is said that "the true is revealed while accompanied by delusion.
[The section on] "Revealing the True While Accompanied by Delusion" is concluded.
○ From here below begins the section on "Discerning Delusion to Reveal the True. The two kinds of inverted views are delusions, like jade hidden within its raw matrix.
Yet the true essence perceived therein is like the jade existing within that matrix; therefore, the true is shown while accompanied by delusion, just as one points to the matrix to speak of the jade.
Although it is precious and not empty, the coarse stone has not yet been split open and the beautiful jade has not yet been polished. This section "discerns delusion to reveal the true," just as...

When the raw ore is split open, the jade emerges; its brilliance then shines forth. Thus, when prior [teachings] destroy consciousness until it reaches the state of having no substance, that constitutes a "true destruction.

However, this present [approach] splits through delusion so that the actual reality is revealed; this is what is called "not a final destruction," for while it appears to be a destruction, in truth it is a manifestation. Can this be generally categorized as "destruction"?

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has for our sakes proclaimed the characteristics of the conjunction and non-conjunction of causes and conditions as well as self-conditions, our minds have still not been opened.

Now, having further heard of ‘seeing seeing’ and ‘not seeing seeing,’ our confusion and distress have increased all the more. We prostrate ourselves, entreating Your Great Compassion to bestow upon us the eye of great wisdom and reveal to us awakening.”
His mind became clear and pure. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with tears of grief and received the holy command.
This was because, due to views born of doubt—seeing what is not seeing—he earnestly requested further clarification. Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, regarding the teachings on causes and conditions and spontaneity that the Buddha has proclaimed for us, these are all matters I have already asked about."

Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of conjunction and those of non-conjunction—these four points which I have not yet asked about—I see that their nature is entirely detached from them, yet my mind remains unenlightened;
I am already bewildered and distressed. Moreover, I have heard the teaching that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing.
Now, World-Honored One, since you say that the nature of seeing is unmoving and undying, neither expanding nor contracting, then...
If the seeing and the objects of seeing are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi, then this seeing-essence is clearly the nature of wondrous enlightenment.
Yet, you suddenly say that when one sees the seeing, that seeing is not seeing; that the nature of seeing is one.
Why do you speak of the true and the false, alternating between suppression and exaltation without fixed consistency? This leaves me bewildered and distressed.

[My doubts] increased all the more, and I remained utterly ignorant of why this was so. I prostrate myself and pray that Your Great Compassion will bestow upon me the eye of great wisdom, revealing to us how the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) is luminously pure.
For if even a slight doubt lingers in the mind, the awakening will not be luminously pure;
it is essential to dispel this confusion and open what has not yet been opened, so that thereafter the awakened mind may be entirely luminously pure. Having spoken these words—
Having finished, he wept with compassion and prostrated himself, thereby receiving the holy command.

Since the Buddha had revealed the pure *dharmatā*, and Ānanda further requested the eye of wisdom, it is certain that from this point onward, the *tathāgatagarbha* will be fully developed as emptiness. ○ Zhong says:
The refutation of the combined and the non-combined occurs later; since this is a restatement (*nidāna*) of what has already been heard, the subsequent text should be placed here.

Following the previous refutation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), we shall now refute spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and combination (*sāmagrī*). These are all categories of imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
since they belong to the same class of meaning, they are grouped together in one place for refutation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, was about to expound the path of sublime cultivation for the various samādhis of the Great Dhāraṇī.
This is the scribe’s narration of the Buddha’s intent. *Dhāraṇī* means "total retention" (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇa*);
it refers to the totalizing of all phenomena and the upholding of immeasurable meanings. "All *samādhis*" is a general term for the twenty-five perfect paths of penetration.

"The wondrous path of cultivation" cryptically points to the gateway of the ear. With these two phrases, the text explains the aforementioned *dhāraṇī*, revealing that among the gates of cultivation, the ear is the primary one.

The "Root Perfect Penetration" (*mūla-pariśuddha-samādhi*) is the Great Total Retention (*mahā-dhāraṇī*). It does not rely on the conventional commentaries that categorize [the path] into fixed divisions of wisdom and skillful means, or cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
Generally, for those who wish to engage in wondrous cultivation, they must first seek true wisdom; the extensive opening of true wisdom serves as the ground for wondrous cultivation.
Therefore, while the Buddha was about to speak of the subtle and secret contemplative observation, the compiler of the sutra first described it from a distance.
If one contemplates the two characters "about to" (jiāng yù), their significance is profound; it is found within the fifth and sixth fascicles.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those present and the great assembly, was about to elaborate upon the Great Door of Dharani—the most concise and essential among all samādhis, the wondrous path of practice.
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "Although you possess a powerful memory, it merely increases your erudition;

yet regarding the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*, your mind has not yet fully realized it. Listen attentively now, and I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that all future beings subject to outflows may likewise attain the fruit of Bodhi."
The Buddha’s intention was thus. He then addressed Ānanda, saying: "Though you possess a powerful memory, you merely indulge your mouth and ears;

you have not yet realized the true meaning.
