Regarding the nature of *śamatha*, which is endowed with fundamental concentration, and its subtle, secret contemplation and observation—the luminous manifestation of the inherently present essence of illumination—your mind has still not fully understood it. Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal it for you. Furthermore:
It causes all future beings with outflows (*sāsrava*) to fully attain the ultimate fruit of Bodhi.

If even those with outflows are made to achieve Buddhahood, it goes without saying for those without outflows (*anāsrava*). To direct the mind toward the mirror and contemplate is a coarse observation; it is not subtle.

Restraining the body and sitting in stillness, entering and emerging from the signs of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), is not "mysterious" (*mi*). It is distinguished from this [ordinary state] and is therefore called "subtle and mysterious" (*weimi*).
Furthermore, to be free from delusion and cut off from signs is called "subtle" (*wei*); to realize that signs are signless is called "mysterious" (*mi*).

What is now explained—the seeing of seeing as non-seeing, up to the seven elements being all-pervasive—is precisely the severing of delusion and the cutting off of signs; it is subtle observation and illumination. The following text [continues with] "fulfillment" (*man*).
Maitreya answered: "The 'correct' is precisely the signless within signs; it is the secret contemplation and illumination. This intent illuminates the three Tathāgatagarbhas to their full extent;
this is called true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*). Only by means of this true wisdom can one subsequently engage in the wondrous cultivation. ○ Zhong said:
"Subtle and secret observation" is spoken in contrast to "coarse and superficial"; therefore, it is called subtle and secret.

Since discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are considered coarse and superficial, the wisdom of reverse observation is termed subtle and secret. By employing this [wisdom], one perceives darkness and perceives light.
This is called vitarka and vicāra. By employing these to reflect back upon one's own nature, one shatters the karmic consciousness and directly perceives the awakened nature;
this is precisely what is termed "subtle and secret contemplation," for it is not two separate things.
Ānanda, all sentient beings transmigrate through the world due to the delusive discriminating views of two types of inversion.
These arise from their own respective states and cause them to revolve according to their respective karma. What are these two views? First, the delusive view of individual karma;
second, the delusive view of commonality.
This is about seeing the nature, which is further elaborated as two kinds of deluded seeing. Ānanda, when I say that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing," is there not a reason for this?
It is simply because within true seeing, there are fundamentally two kinds of deluded seeing.
All sentient beings, from ordinary worldlings up to those of the Two Vehicles, cannot yet escape birth-and-death through the stages of segmentation or transformation. And...
Those who transmigrate through the world all do so because of the initial single thought of non-awakening.

Through the deluded movement of ignorance, this awakened nature is turned, thereby forming the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*). Because there is a seeing-part, there is consequently a "perceived-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*), resulting in two kinds of inverted, discriminative, and delusive views.
Because one turns one's back on the awakened nature and unites with ignorance, it is called "inversion. Because [there is...]

Subtly flowing and circulating, it discriminates the sense organs, the body, and the physical world; therefore, it is called "discrimination. These two views are delusions that turn their backs on pure awakening, arising abruptly;
they merely manifest as confusion and have not yet reached the point of being summoned by karma. Therefore, it is said they "arise in their own place.
That is to say, within the very realm of delusion where they arise, one grasps and creates karma, and according to that karma, one receives retribution. Next...
Next is the transition of flux; therefore, it is said that one revolves through karma. This demonstrates that deluded views can summon such great calamities;
thus, one must not fail to awaken to this truth and distance oneself from them. Now, as for what are called the "two views," what are these two?
The first is the deluded vision of the individual karma of sentient beings, which pertains to the root-body and the vessel-world perceived by a single person’s single consciousness.
This refers to the realms (*dhātu*). Second, there is the deluded vision of the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) among sentient beings;

this refers to the sense organs, bodies, and the physical world as perceived by many people and many consciousnesses. One must know that the nature of seeing is the medicine that prevents hands from cracking;
it depends entirely on whether one uses it skillfully or not. If one uses it skillfully, then the deluded is itself the true; if one does not use it skillfully...
Thus, the entirety of the real is but delusion. How, then, could there be any doubt regarding the principle that the "seeing of seeing" is not seeing? Question:
Since Ānanda had already doubted that the "seeing of seeing" is not seeing, why did the World-Honored One not answer directly, but instead extensively clarify the two kinds of delusive seeing?
Answer: Had he not extensively demonstrated that delusive seeing possesses [the quality of] seeing, he would have been unable to bring forth the true seeing.
There is no seeing. Therefore, the subsequent passage extensively analyzes this by contrasting the case of a single person with that of many.

It should be understood that as long as one has not yet abandoned the eye-disease of ignorance—whether they be an ordinary being, a follower of the Small Vehicle, or even a Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment—they are still said to have "deluded seeing.

Only the Buddha alone, having completely eliminated the eye-disease, is called "True Seeing. Regarding the phrase "arising in its own place": "in its own place" indicates that [it does not come from elsewhere].
The movement of the mind is like the immeasurable and manifold objects seen in a dream; there is immeasurable rushing about, yet one does not leave the bed or pillow, nor does one move a single step.

This is precisely the fundamental state of namelessness—the three subtle aspects of consciousness—which serve as the cause for the transformative birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*) of the two vehicles.
That which revolves through karma is the arising of the two kinds of ignorance—projecting and moistening—which constitute the six coarse aspects of consciousness.
These are the marks. They serve as the cause for the segmented birth-and-death of ordinary beings.
What is meant by "deluded vision resulting from individual karma"? Ānanda, it is like a person in the world who has a red film over the eye;
at night, they see the light of a lamp and perceive a separate circular shadow with five overlapping colors. What do you think? Is this what is manifested by the light of the lamp at night?
"Is this circular radiance the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the vision? Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, then it would not belong to the person with the cataract;
why then would they not see it together? Yet this circular shadow is seen only by the one with the cataract. If it were the color of the vision, then the vision itself would have become color."
Then, as for that person with the eye disease who sees the circular shadow, what would you call him?

Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow existed separately from the lamp, then when one looks sideways at a screen, a curtain, or a table, a circular shadow should likewise appear; it would have to exist independently of the act of seeing.

It should not be within the range of visual perception. How then can a person with cataracts see a circular shadow? Therefore, one should know that while the color actually resides in the lamp, the visual ailment perceives it as a shadow.
Both the shadow and the perception are the ailment; the perception of the ailment itself is not the ailment. Ultimately, one should never say that this is the lamp or that this is the vision.
Within this, there is that which is neither lamp nor vision, just as the second moon is neither a substantial entity nor a reflection. Why is this?

Because the perception of a second moon is produced by pressing [the eyes]. No wise person should say that the source of this pressed organ is either a shape or not a shape, or something apart from vision or not apart from vision.
This case is also like this: it is produced by an eye disease. Now, whom do you wish to name as being [this]?
The lamp is the seeing; how much more so when one discriminates between what is neither lamp nor seeing?
This is an analogy established to clarify the deluded vision of individual karma. What is meant by "deluded vision of individual karma"?
Ānanda, it is like a person in the world whose eyes have a red cataract (*rakta-piṭaka*); at night, they see a circular shadow appearing as something distinct from the light of a lamp.
The five colors are layered one upon another. What do you think? Is this circular light manifested by the lamp the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the visual faculty?
Ānanda, if it were the color of the lamp, then those without the visual impairment should see it just as well;
why do they not all see it, such that only those with the impairment perceive it? If it were the color of the visual faculty...
Once the color has been formed, by what means does that person with the visual disorder perceive this circular shadow?

Thus, the circular shadow exists without being identical to the lamp or the vision. Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow existed separately from the lamp, then when one looks sideways at a screen, a curtain, a table, or a seat, a shadow should appear on all of them; why then does it appear only for the lamp?
There is. If this circular shadow existed separately from the vision, it should not require the gaze of the eyes.
How then can one see the circular shadow? It is still due to the diseased eye. Thus, the circular shadow does not exist apart from the lamp and the vision.
Since it is neither produced from the lamp and the vision, nor does it exist apart from the lamp and the vision, then from—
From where does it arise? Therefore, you should know that there is only radiance upon the lamp; it is the eye disease (*taimirika*) that produces the circular shadow.
Not only is the perceived circular shadow produced by the red eye disease, but even the faculty capable of perceiving that circular shadow is likewise produced by the red eye disease.
Thus it is said: "The shadow and the perception are both eye diseases. However, the essence of the seeing that perceives the eye disease has, in truth, never [been affected].

This falls within the realm of visual defects and illnesses. Therefore, it is said that seeing the defect is not itself the illness. Thus, the circular image arises from the red defect; it has no relation to the lamp or the act of seeing.
One should not insist that this [image] is produced from the lamp and the seeing, and claim "this is the lamp" or "this is the seeing.
Nor should one claim that it exists apart from the lamp and the seeing, and say "this is neither the lamp nor the seeing. It is just like a second moon: it is not the substance of the true moon.
Nor is it the reflection of the moon. Why? Because this second vision is produced by pressing the eyes;
since it arises from such pressure, how could one maintain that it is the actual form of the moon? It is not the form of the moon, for it arises apart from the view of self.
It does not arise apart from the view of self; this case is also like that. "Visual impairment" (*miṅ*) refers to the pressure on the eye; the "perfect circle" refers to the second moon.
Since it is produced solely by the visual impairment, it has no connection whatsoever with the lamp or the act of seeing.

How much less could one designate who is the lamp and who is the seeing, let alone differentiate between what is not the lamp and what is not the seeing? This is what is called the false vision resulting from individual karma.
One should know that the eyes are a metaphor for the noble wisdom of self-awakening; the lamp is a metaphor for the truth of original awakening;
the red cataracts are a metaphor for the karmic consciousness of ignorance; and the circular reflections are a metaphor for the body-faculties and the objective world.

When the wisdom of suchness accords with the principle of suchness, wisdom and principle are one and the same, fundamentally devoid of subject and object. Yet, when ignorance stirs even once, subject and object are thereby divided. Therefore...
The body with its sense organs and the vessel-world arise from seeing. As the Sūtra says: "Whatever has marks is entirely illusory.
How profound! This chapter merely expresses metaphors; it does not yet express the Dharma, for the Dharma will be clarified through the subsequent sections on advancing and retreating.
In various expositions, the metaphors have become intermingled with the literal meaning, thereby increasing entanglement and making it difficult to proceed with the subsequent text. ○ Zhong said:

"The distinct karma and the common portion are both transformations of the karmic consciousness within the *ālayavijñāna*, consisting of the two divisions of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*) and perception (*darśana-bhāga*).
However, when observing the circular reflection in a lamp, it is neither the lamp itself, nor is it separate from the lamp; it is neither the visual faculty itself, nor is it separate from it."
Seeing is thus. That which can be seen—the illusory appearance—is fundamentally without cause; that one sees a circular shadow is due to nothing else but a cataract in the eye.
That one is startled and runs about is due to nothing else but a deranged mind. When the cataract is removed, it is simply the pure eye.

When the madness ceases, it is precisely this wondrously luminous mind. Throughout the entire *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, it is clarified that not only is the true mind neither conditioned by causes and conditions nor spontaneous, but even the deluded mind is neither conditioned by causes and conditions nor spontaneous. As it is said: "Awareness in its confusion has no cause;
delusion has nothing upon which to rely. Since there is not even arising, what could there be to cease? These words do not go beyond this.
What is meant by "common deluded vision"? Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands upon the level lands in between.
In the central great island, measuring from east to west, there are two thousand three hundred large countries.
As for the remaining small islands scattered among the various seas, some contain two or three hundred countries, while others contain only one.

Or two, up to three, four, five, or ten. Ānanda, if among these there were a small continent containing only two countries, and the people of that single country collectively experienced adverse conditions, then the sentient beings of that land on that small continent would [suffer].
They beheld all manner of inauspicious omens: sometimes two suns were seen, or two moons;
within them appeared halos, solar spots, rings, crescents, comets, meteors, shooting stars, double halos, and rainbows—various such evil signs, which were seen only in this country.
The sentient beings of that land have never seen this before, nor have they ever heard of it;
this clarifies the deluded vision shared by those of a common lot (*sabhāga-viparyāsa*). What is meant by "deluded vision shared by those of a common lot"?
Ānanda, here, to the south of Mount Sumeru, in the continent of Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there is a level land consisting of three [parts].
There are one thousand continents. The central great continent measures two thousand three hundred large countries from east to west.
As for the remaining two thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine continents situated within the various oceans, their lands consist of either three hundred or two hundred countries;
the smallest comprise one or two countries, extending up to three, four, five, or ten. All are thus included.
All such arguments are set aside. Ānanda, suppose among them there were even the smallest continent, and upon that continent there were but two kingdoms.
In one of those kingdoms, the inhabitants collectively experienced adverse conditions;

the sentient beings of that land beheld various omens of ill fortune—such as seeing two suns or two moons, or even halos of evil vapors encircling them, eclipses, and malevolent miasmas approaching the sun.
Yet, like a jade pendant or ring, there are comets with star-like rays pointing in all directions; there are *bṛhat* (meteors) with radiating vapors spreading in the four quarters;

there are flying objects moving crosswise and flowing currents pouring downward; there are halos surrounding the sun like ears upon ears, and rainbows formed by vapors reflecting the sun—such various evil omens are seen only by the people of this one country, while those in other lands do not see them.

They are born; not only do they not see it, they also do not hear it. Those who see do so because of what is induced by their collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*). Those who do not see do so because they lack such common karma.
Such is the nature of deluded vision regarding the "commonality" (*sabhāgatā*). This is compared to [the case of] individual karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*).

Having already briefly addressed the two meanings of "detachment" (*li*), there is still a lack regarding the "cause of delusion. "Briefly" means that the intention is to follow the preceding section;
"lacking" means that it shall be presented by way of example within the subsequent discussion on "advancing and retreating" (*jin-tui*).
Ānanda, I shall now, for your sake, clarify these two matters through their progression and regression.
The two matters are the two metaphors of identity and difference, and the two principles of identity and difference. Regarding progression and regression:
first, I advance the metaphor of distinct karma to clarify the principle of distinct karma; next, I regress from the principle of distinct karma and again advance the [metaphor of] distinct karma.

"Metaphor" (*dṛṣṭānta*) refers to using an example of a particular individual (*pratyekasabhāga*) to illustrate the principle of shared characteristics (*sabhāgatā*), and subsequently using the case of one person’s distinct karma to advance toward the principle of a nation’s shared characteristics,

thereby illustrating the shared characteristics of a great trichiliocosm. "Synthesis" (*yoga*) means to clarify the matter by comparing the similarities and differences between the dharma and the metaphor,
employing analogy to bring it forth.
Who is it? It is like the deluded vision resulting from the individual karma of those sentient beings, who perceive a circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light.

Although it appears as if it were an external object, it is ultimately produced by the visual defect of the observer. This defect is simply the fatigue of seeing; it is not created by the visible forms themselves.
Yet, for one who perceives this defect, there is ultimately no fault in their vision. By analogy, when one uses the eyes today to observe mountains, rivers, nations, lands, and all such things...

Sentient beings are all formed by the disease of views that has no beginning. The view and its conditions appear as present objects; originally, they are my enlightened clarity. The view and its objects are but a cataract;

the awareness of the view is itself the cataract. When the fundamental enlightened mind is aware of the conditions, it is not a cataract; when it is aware of that which is perceived, it is a cataract.
Since this awareness is not within the cataract, this is truly the seeing of seeing. How, then, can it again be called awareness, hearing, knowing, or seeing? Therefore...
That you now see me, yourself, and all the ten classes of beings in the world—all this is seeing a visual impairment (*taimirika*).
It is not the seer of the impairment who sees it; that which sees the true essence has a nature that is not impaired, and therefore it is not called "seeing."
This serves as an analogy for the distinct karma of individuals, clarifying the principle of distinct karma.

Ānanda, it is like the false vision of distinct karma experienced by those sentient beings, wherein they gaze upon the circular reflection appearing within a lamp’s light. Although this reflection manifests with form, it is not truly existent;
it is called a "semblance-object. Ultimately, it is produced by the cataract of the observer's own eyes—the cataract being the very sickness of seeing.

These deluded signs of exhaustion arise falsely; they are truly not produced by the light of the lamp. Yet, one who perceives this red cataract ultimately bears no blame for the ailment of the cataract itself.
This is because the cataract does not see the cataract; rather, it is the one who sees the cataract who perceives the true essence of seeing.
He is indeed free from ailment. I shall now employ a metaphor to illustrate the principle, taking your present experience as an example.

When you observe with your eyes the vessel-world of mountains, rivers, lands, and nations, as well as the root-bodies of all sentient beings, these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.

Your visual observation is the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part); the lands and sentient beings are the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-part). This "disease of vision" has been present since the beginningless past.
This is precisely the karmic consciousness of ignorance. Due to that ignorance, the karmic consciousness first forms and subsequently gives rise to the two divisions of seeing and appearance.

Thus, seeing is like a cataract, and appearances are like the circling lights seen by one with blurred vision. From this point on, for vast eons, there has been no further purification; hence it is said, "accomplished by the ailment of seeing.
This perfectly accords with the conclusion that the seer is accomplished by the cataract of the eye. Now, as for seeing and the seer...

The two divisions of the conditions arise together based upon self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*). Because they depend on the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), which is not substantially real, they are also said to be "semblances.

This precisely accords with the fact that although they appear, they are like objects [that are not truly external]. Nevertheless, these two divisions—subjective seeing and objective appearance—are originally the wondrously luminous essence of my own fundamental awakening.
Suddenly, a single thought arises, forming a delusion of eye-disease (*taimira*), whereby there subsequently come to be the seer and the seen.
It is conditioned by the ears. This conjunction with the cataract is what constitutes the exhaustion of seeing; it is not something produced by external forms.

If, by means of the luminous mind of original enlightenment, one realizes that this essence of seeing arises from the red cataract, then this luminous mind of original enlightenment—though engaged in daily activities and universally aware of all conditions—is truly not comparable to the deluded vision of one who possesses a cataract. This is how it should be understood: the one who perceives the cataract ultimately...

There is no fault in this seeing. Once one realizes that the conditions are not the cataract itself, one knows that the nature of awareness is fundamentally real, while the cataract is fundamentally illusory.
When one has not yet realized the cataract, awareness constantly falls within it; as soon as one realizes it is a cataract, awareness has already emerged outside of it.
This is precisely what was previously described as the principle that "at the time of seeing the seeing, the seeing is not [the true] seeing."

Indeed. For if one realizes that the cataract is itself a delusion, one is immediately liberated from the cataract; likewise, if one realizes that seeing is itself a delusion, one is immediately liberated from seeing.
How can you take this "seeing that is free from seeing" and equate it with, or place it alongside, ordinary perception, hearing, cognition, and vision?
What difference is there between valuing the jade of Mount Jing at the same price as common pebbles? Is this not a grave error? Therefore, you should know: as for your present seeing...
Both you and I alike perceive the twelve classes of living beings. This perception has both a subject that perceives and an object that is perceived;
it is entirely a vision produced by the presence of a cataract within the eye, rather than a vision that clearly perceives the disease of the cataract itself.
It resembles a vision that clearly perceives the disease of a cataract—true and unmixed with delusion, pure and unmixed with the cataract—just as a mani jewel reflects colors.
It is like a bright mirror manifesting forms; though one looks at it all day long, one does not perceive any signs of the phenomenal world.
Therefore, it cannot be characterized by a vision impaired by cataracts. Thus it is said: "Even seeing is free from seeing," for seeing cannot reach it.
Why are you so bewildered and distressed by this? ○ When it says that seeing is further accompanied by hearing, awareness, and cognition, it means they are of one essence and equally possessed.
That which is directly perceived by the eyes is called "seeing" (*darśana*). That which is heard from others is called "hearing" (*śruta*).

That which is mentally constructed through the movement of one's own mind is called "cognition" (*vijñāna*). That which is internally experienced and personally realized is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Huangbo said: "Practitioners of the Way must not identify with seeing, hearing, cognition, and knowledge; rather, within the very state of seeing, hearing, cognition, and knowledge, recognize the fundamental mind. By means of this fundamental...
The mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, yet it is also not separate from seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing.
The *Renwang jing* states: "Prior to the adamantine concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), all knowledge and vision are not clear visions;

only when the Buddha suddenly realizes his omniscience (*sarvajñā*) can all knowledge and vision be called 'vision. Therefore, it is said that false knowledge has knowledge, and there is that which is not [knowledge]."
To know is to truly know non-knowing; thus there is nothing that is not known. To see falsely is to have seeing, whereby there is something not seen.
True seeing is non-seeing; thus there is nothing that is not seen. Therefore, it is only when the knowing and seeing of sentient beings are exhausted that the Buddha’s knowing and seeing manifest.
Ānanda, just as those sentient beings share a commonality of false vision, so too may one person with a distinct karmic lot be compared to that false vision.
A single person with diseased eyes is like that entire country; the circular shadow he perceives is produced by the delusion of his cataract.
This inauspicious sight perceived by this collective multitude arises from the pestilential evil within their shared karma. Both are produced by the beginningless false vision of seeing.
This section uses the analogy of individual karma to further clarify the principle of shared karma (*sabhāgatā*). Individual karmic illusions are illusory yet easy to understand;
shared karmic illusions are substantial yet difficult to believe. The intention is to show that even what is substantial is identical to what is illusory.
Ānanda, it is like the shared karmic illusions of those sentient beings. [The text here indicates a transition from the discussion of] "regression" (*hāni*)...
Regarding the analogy of individual karmic delusions, consider a person with diseased eyes who is like the inhabitants of that country.
The circular shadow seen by that person with diseased eyes arises from the false manifestation of a cataract (*taimira*);

likewise, the inauspicious sights seen by the people of that country arise from adverse conditions within their collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*). Although there is a difference between the illusory and the real, what is seen [in both cases] is not...

It is the same. Yet both belong to that which is produced by beginningless delusive views. If one advances the lamp-wheel to merge it with the phenomena of the calamity, then the phenomena of the calamity are certainly the visual impairment of an entire nation.
If one withdraws the phenomena of the calamity to merge them with the lamp-wheel, then the lamp-wheel is likewise the miasma and evil of a single person.
For example, within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans, the Sahā world, and extending to all the realms of outflows throughout the ten directions,
as well as all sentient beings therein, are equally this enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind. Yet, due to the conditions of false illness— seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—
they falsely conjoin to give rise to birth and falsely conjoin to undergo death.
This uses the analogy of an individual’s distinct karma retreating to illustrate the principle of the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of the great trichiliocosm.
Just as what is seen as inauspicious in one country arises from pestilence and evil, so it is in all countries within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa in the south.
As it is with the countries of the southern continent, so it is with the countries of the other three continents. This applies to a single sun and moon.
Since the worlds under his governance are thus, so too are the billion suns and moons and the great trichiliocosm (mahāsāhasralokadhātu) governed by Śākyamuni.

Since the great trichiliocosm is thus, so too are all the worlds governed by the various Buddhas who are the emanations (nirmāṇakāya) of Śākyamuni throughout the ten directions, as well as all the realms of outflows (sāsrava).
This is truly because these sentient beings are equally characterized by awakened clarity (bodhi-prakāśa) and lack... [the text continues].
The outflow of the wondrous mind: its initial single thought of deluded movement transforms into seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
From within these four faculties, beginningless empty habits accumulate over successive lifetimes, even down to their specific proportions and numerical categories.
These converge in one place to become the conditions for the disease of delusion; they are born together and die together. The very root of birth and death is truly based upon this.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The union of the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing, which is neither identical nor different, is called the ālayavijñāna;

it serves as the cause for the cycle of birth and death. Question: Why is the analogy of individual karma (*bipakṣa*) not applied by way of example to the great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*)? Answer:
Because the great trichiliocosm and a single world-system are both equally subsumed within the deluded vision of the same common lot (*sabhāgatā*). It is only that...
Fearing that [the reader] might not be able to grasp this all at once, he clarifies the commonality of a single country through the use of a metaphor;

that is, he uses the commonality of a single country as an analogy for the commonality of the trichiliocosm. Having thus completed the clarification through both progressive and regressive application.
If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction, then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death.
Thus, the nature of bodhi, which is beyond arising and ceasing, is perfected; the fundamental mind is purified, and original enlightenment abides eternally.
This clarifies that the two kinds of deluded views are transformed into the fundamentally pure essence of *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*.

As for the various "conjoined conditions," these refer to the two kinds of ignorance (*avidyā*)—namely, the "arousing" and the "moistening"—which arise through conjunction by taking objects as conditions;

that is, the six coarse consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), which serve as the cause for birth-and-death with distinct segments (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*). This refers to what was previously called "karmic action."
That which revolves is this very thing. The non-concordant conditions are the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which turns its back on pure awakening and arises abruptly;
these are the three subtle aspects of consciousness that serve as the cause for the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*).
This is what was referred to in the preceding text as "arising in its own place. If one employs this subtle and secret contemplation to illuminate and shatter the two kinds of non-existence...
When there is clarity, the causes of the two deaths are forever abandoned, and the fruits of the two deaths are forever severed. Reaching this state, it may be called the fulfillment of Bodhi;
it may be called the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; it may be called the pure original mind; it may be called the eternally abiding fundamental awakening.
Now, you have not yet eliminated the delusions of the two kinds of views, nor have you emerged from the two deaths; your karmic consciousness remains vast and murky.
Having no basis upon which to rely, you wish to take this very root of birth and death for the nature of wondrous enlightenment; is this not too premature a calculation?
If you contemplate skillfully and can employ subtle and secret observation and illumination, you will be able to clearly perceive the root of birth and death.
From the life-faculty downward, with a single stroke of fierce power, one cuts it all at once;
only then does one correspond to the designation of "Pure Wondrous Enlightenment. The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* verse says: "The Tathāgata’s Pure Storehouse is the worldly ālaya."
It is like gold and a finger-ring: they are mutually indistinguishable. Because the Buddhas have realized this, it becomes the Pure Treasury (*viśuddhagarbha*);

because sentient beings cling to it, it becomes the *ālaya*. Just as true gold, depending on the conditions of the furnace fire, receives the various names of "finger-ring" and so forth, so too does the True Mind, depending on the conditions of defilement and purity, receive the various designations of "saint" and "ordinary being. To recognize these as mere provisional names—
Yet, two views suddenly arise; by awakening to the true essence, one realizes perfect enlightenment within the single mind.
○ He said: This is precisely what is meant by "transcending views. "Harmonious conjunction" refers to the six harmonies mentioned below.
"Non-conjunction" refers to "serenely entering and merging with serenity, returning to the limit of consciousness" mentioned below. Both types belong to the essence of seeing.
Only that which is in combination constitutes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); that which is not in combination constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

This corresponds to the two kinds of roots mentioned in the first fascicle. Previously, it was stated that the mind that grasps at objects is the root of birth and death, while the original luminosity of the essence of consciousness is the fundamentally pure substance of bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Here, however, it is further explained that within this essence of consciousness, a single portion of deluded vision constitutes birth...
It is the root of death. One must depart from these false views; only then can the root of birth and death be extinguished.
This is purely the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana. Therefore it is said: "Even seeing must be left behind by seeing; seeing cannot reach it.

This precisely corresponds to the character "depart" (離) in the phrase "departing from all conditions of conjunction" in this section. According to the two kinds of false views, although they are called inverted...
It is a distorted discrimination (*viparyāsa-vikalpa*). However, this discrimination is merely a spontaneous, vivid, and unobscured state;
it is what is called "subtle, continuous-flowing discrimination" (*sūkṣma-nisyanda-vikalpa*), not the coarse discrimination of intentional conceptualization (*manasikāra-parikalpa*).

What is generally termed "delusive seeing" (*dṛṣṭi-moha*) has its essence in the subtle consciousness of the *ādāna-vijñāna*. Within its aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), there is a portion of deep affliction integrated therein. [The following text...]
What the Buddha refers to as "co-nascent ignorance" is precisely the root of the fetters of birth and death. The truth revealed through the ten stages is that which is inherently possessed;
how could it have anything to do with delusion? That which is eliminated by the two views is precisely that which is inherently possessed as delusion.
What obstructs the Truth? The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha revealed by the four subsequent sections and the seven elements has no separate substance;
it is simply this very nature of vision, merely renamed as the "garbha-nature. Thus ends the refutation of the two kinds of false views.
Ānanda, although you have previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of fundamental enlightenment is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature,
you have not yet clarified that this source of enlightenment is neither born from combination nor from non-combination.

Having seen this, his vision was clarified; his confusion and distress were resolved. Yet Ānanda’s original inquiry regarding the nature of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), as well as the characteristics of conjunction and non-conjunction, remained unilluminated in his mind.

Although the two meanings of causes and conditions and spontaneity had already been clarified within the previous section on "Transcending Emotion," the specific points of conjunction and non-conjunction had not yet been explained. Therefore, he called out:
And he addressed him, saying: "Ānanda, this wondrously enlightened awareness is neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it spontaneous;
this is what I have already explained, so there is no need for you to labor over what you have previously realized.

As for this enlightened awareness as an object of conditions—whether it arises from a combination of factors or not—it is something you have truly not yet realized, and it is something I have not yet spoken of. How could it be now..."
I shall now reveal this to you. Ānanda, I shall now again question you regarding the objects before you.

You still harbor doubts because you take all the worldly, delusory natures formed by the conjunction of causes and conditions to be the very nature of the Bodhi-mind arising from a combination of factors. Thus, you—
Now, as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing: does it blend with light? Does it blend with darkness? Does it blend with openness? Or does it blend with obstruction?
If it blends with light, then when you observe light and that light appears before you, where within it is the seeing mixed? The characteristics of the seeing and the light can be distinguished;
what kind of form would their mixture take? If it is not the seeing itself, how could it see the light? If it is identical to the seeing, how...
Seeing sees. Seeing must be complete. Where would seeing and clarity be in harmony? If clarity were complete, it could not be in harmony with seeing. Seeing must be distinct from clarity;
if they were mixed, one would lose the name of its inherent nature as clarity. If their natures as clarity were lost through mixing, then "harmony" and "clarity" would have no meaning.
This is likewise true for darkness, openness, and all various obstructions. Furthermore, Ānanda, you who are now so wondrously pure...
Consider this essence of seeing: does it unite with light, or does it unite with darkness? Does it unite with openness, or does it unite with obstruction?
If it united with light, then when darkness arrives and the appearance of light has already ceased, this seeing would not be uniting with the various forms of darkness;
how then could it see the dark? If it did not unite with darkness when seeing the dark, yet it did unite with light, then it should not be seeing the light. Since this is not the case...

Seeing light. What is meant by "conjunction with light"? It is the clear realization that light is not darkness. That darkness, as well as the open spaces and all the various obstructions, are likewise so.
This refutes conjunction. Conjunction means to blend all things into one. If there were indeed such a conjunction, [then...]
"There would then be no Bodhi. Therefore, he refutes this, saying: "Ānanda, I now ask you again about the objects before you that I have seen.
You still harbor doubts based on the nature of worldly false thoughts and various causes and conditions, clinging to this pure awakened mind as something that also arises through combination.
If that were so, then your wondrously pure faculty of vision, when in light..."
Within the intermingling of darkness and obstruction, with whom does it harmonize? Furthermore, what is meant by "harmony"?

It refers to the state where water and earth are blended together and cannot be distinguished. If you claim that the essence of seeing harmonizes with light, then at the very moment you raise your eyes and see light—when the appearance of light is manifest before you—from what location does this essence of seeing mix with it to become one?
Is it their blending? Furthermore, clarity and seeing are two things that do not intermingle; thus, they can be distinguished one by one.
If the two were to intermingle, then clarity would lose its clarity and seeing would lose its seeing—what form or image would there be then? How could you know that seeing and clarity blend?
Moreover, in the case of any objects that blend together, they must first be separate before they can come into contact. If...
This means that when the appearance of light manifests, it is not itself the seeing. Thus, the appearance resides in its own place of appearance, and the seeing resides in its own place of seeing;
each is unaware of the other, and there should be no seeing. How, then, can one see the light?

If you claim that the manifestation of the appearance of light is itself the seeing, then seeing does not see itself. Now, how can seeing see seeing? This is the simultaneous cessation of both confusion and identity.

Furthermore, by what means could harmony be achieved? If one insists that the nature of seeing (*darśana*) must be complete, then there would be no empty space for it to harmonize with clarity (*āloka*).
If one insists that the characteristic of clarity must be complete, then there would be no gap to accommodate the nature of seeing.

If one claims that seeing must necessarily be seeing and clarity must necessarily be clarity, such that they are each distinct from one another, then if they were now mixed and harmonized, seeing would lose its [distinctive] nature.
As for the term "seeing": if its name is lost, how can its essential nature not be lost? It is not merely that its name is lost;
furthermore, if they are intermingled, one simultaneously loses both the fundamental nature of seeing and that of clarity.

When both name and nature are lost, to say that "seeing and clarity are blended" is absolutely impossible. Thus, the principle of their blending is not established. This applies equally to darkness and penetration.
It is the same for all other clusters; one may know by analogy that they are not in harmony.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for this essence of seeing within you, which exists amidst brightness, darkness, penetration, and obstruction—with what does it unite?
What is called "uniting" refers to being joined like a lid to a box, attached and inseparable. If this essence of seeing were already [united] with brightness...
[The opponent] says: "When it reaches the time of darkness, the light-phase has already ceased; this vision likewise ceases along with the light and will certainly never again unite with darkness.

How then can it see darkness when darkness arrives? If you claim that although it sees darkness, it does not actually unite with darkness, then since it does not unite at the time of seeing, it must not see at the time of uniting. As for what was previously said regarding its union with light..."
Regarding "conjunction": it should not be seeing light. Since you do not see light, how could you, at the time of conjunction with light, clearly know that "this is light and not darkness"?
Now, since you can both see light and see darkness, one knows for certain that this seeing does not conjoin with light;
thus, the principle of "conjoining with light" is not established. This applies equally to darkness, openness, and all other [objects].
The same applies to the various obstructions; by this analogy, one may know that they do not combine.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, as I contemplate it, is this wondrous source of awakening not in harmony with the various conditioned objects and the mind's thoughts?"
The "wondrous awakening source" (miao jue yuan) is the nature within the faculties. The various conditions and objects are the "objects" (chen). Mental deliberations are "consciousness" (shi).

This precisely distinguishes the faculty-nature as being linked with objects and consciousness; if they are not [the true nature], then all are equally non-existent. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
Union is not established; thus it is non-union. As I contemplate this, is this wondrous enlightenment fundamentally not in union with the various sense objects and mental deliberations?
Yet, as soon as one departs from this [position], one falls once again into the error of negation.
Zhong said: "Erroneous conceptualization and discrimination do not exceed the four natures: self, other, both, or causelessness. 'Spontaneity' is causelessness; 'causes and conditions' is the 'both.
As for Ānanda’s attachment to the void, the light, and the mind's eye: the void and the light are 'other,' while the mind and the eye are 'self.
Furthermore, the Buddha spoke of two kinds of objects of vision: the seeing and the seen. The seeing is 'self,' and the object is 'other. Since...
The existence of self and other necessarily implies their commonality. Because this commonality is difficult to refute, they further employ the concept of "conjunction" (saṃyoga) to explain it.
However, even the meaning of conjunction is derived from self and other; it is merely a circuitous elaboration intended to prevent the persistence of harmful habitual tendencies.
The Buddha said, "You have now further stated that awakening is not a composite. I shall ask you again:

regarding this wondrous essence of vision which is not a composite—is it not in conjunction with light? Is it not in conjunction with darkness? Is it not in conjunction with openness? Is it not in conjunction with obstruction?
If it were not in conjunction with light, then there would necessarily be a boundary between vision and light. You should observe closely: where is the light, and where is [the vision]?"
This is seeing. It exists within seeing and within light. From what does its boundary arise? Ānanda, if within the limit of light there were no seer, then they would not reach one another;
since one would not know where the characteristic of light resides, how could a boundary be established? This applies equally to darkness and to openness.
It is likewise with all various obstructions. Furthermore, this wondrous seeing-essence is not something that comes into combination;

does it not combine with light? Does it not combine with darkness? Does it not combine with openness? Does it not combine with obstruction? If it did not combine with light, then the seeing and the light—
Their essential natures and characteristics are mutually incompatible. It is like the ear and clarity not touching one another;

since seeing does not even know where the characteristic of clarity resides, how can it discern the principle of conjunction versus non-conjunction? The same applies to darkness and openness, as well as all various obstructions.
This refutes the notion of non-conjunction. To be "non-conjoined" means not to act as a companion to the myriad dharmas.
If it were truly non-conjoined, there would be no birth and death; therefore, he further refutes it, saying: "You now further claim that this awakened nature is not conjoined. I ask you again:
does this wondrous essence of vision exist within brightness and darkness, or within penetration and obstruction?"

With whom would it not be in harmony? Furthermore, when substances interpenetrate one another, this is called harmony; conversely, when substances do not interpenetrate, this constitutes a lack of harmony.
For example, when bricks and stones are stacked side by side, their two substances do not merge, and there must necessarily be boundaries between them;
this is what is meant by discordant harmony. If this faculty of vision were not in harmony with light, then the vision—
Light and seeing each have their own boundaries. You should carefully observe these two kinds of boundaries:
where does light belong, and where does seeing belong? Within seeing and within light, what serves as the demarcation? Ānanda, if you say that it is within the limit of light—
If there were necessarily no one to perceive them, then that [darkness] and this [light] would each have their own boundaries; they would not reach one another.
Thus, one would not know where the light resides, nor at what point it is divided. If the meaning of a boundary cannot be established, then the meaning of non-harmony is likewise not established.
The same applies to that darkness, its transgressions, and all various obstructions. This is so. Can it be?
From this example, one can know that it is not a state of disharmony. Furthermore, this wondrous seeing-essence is not something produced by combination;

yet, while existing amidst light and darkness, penetration and obstruction, with whom would it not be in union? Moreover, that which is not in union is precisely separate; therefore, they remain utterly distinct and do not encounter one another.

This would constitute a lack of conjunction. If you claim that the nature of seeing does not conjoin with light, then seeing and light would be like the two horns of an ox—mutually opposed and incompatible.
Furthermore, it would be like using the ear to hear light; there would be no connection whatsoever.
Since they do not touch, this essence of seeing would be unable to know where the characteristic of light resides; how, then, could it discern or distinguish conjunction?
If one cannot discern whether they are in conjunction or not, then it does not itself constitute the meaning of non-conjunction.
This is likewise true for "darkness" and "pervasion," as well as what is called "the multitude of obstructions"; by analogy, one can know that these are not cases of non-conjunction.

Regarding the absence of a concluding summary hereafter: this is because it originally belongs to the remaining points within the preceding section on "Transcending Sentiment," and therefore is not treated separately.

[The section on] Binding. If you insist on binding it, you may refer to the preceding text which says: "You should know that this wondrously luminous, essential awareness is neither conjoined nor separate, yet it is not non-conjoined.
This continues until: "even as you grasp and seize it. From this point onward, the manifestation of seeing has reached its ultimate limit.
Furthermore, as śamatha reaches its culmination through the expedient means of pointing directly from the faculty to the mind, it subsequently transforms and is named the *tathāgatagarbha* nature;
it is no longer referred to by the general term "seeing the nature. The direct investigation of the true nature of the faculties to point directly at the true mind is hereby concluded.
According to the traditional exegesis, the above corresponds precisely to the "Contemplation of Returning Form to Emptiness" within the *Dharmadhātudarśana*.
○ From here below, the four categories are harmonized; this is the eternality of the nature itself.

The preceding category spoke of the mind that is quiescent, eternal, and wondrously luminous—the most intimate point—which is currently fully present within the faculties. Therefore, by focusing specifically on the nature of the faculties, the true mind is directly pointed out.

Although it is proximately present within the faculties, its actual measure encompasses the entire Dharma-realm, universally serving as the substantial essence of all phenomena. Now, regarding this...
Within the myriad phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), one discerns each phenomenon to reveal its inherent nature (*dhātu*). For this reason, we no longer employ specific names for the realization of this nature;
instead, we cite its general name, calling it the "Tathāgatagarbha-mind" or the "Wondrous True Suchness-nature" (*tathatā-svabhāva*).
Although these general and specific designations differ, their essence is but one.
Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all these superficial, floating, illusory, and transformative phenomena arise from their very place and perish at that same place.
These illusory fictions are called "phenomena," yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. This is true even for the five aggregates and the six sense bases;
from the twelve bases to the eighteen elements, they arise falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions. Through causes and conditions...

Separation is a false name for cessation. One is utterly unable to know that birth and death, coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—permanently abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading;
the nature of wondrous True Suchness. Within this true and eternal nature, if one seeks coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found.
The aforementioned "seeing as delusion" refers to the delusory nature of the appearance of seeing. "The essence of seeing" refers to the true nature of seeing.
This follows from what was said above: Ānanda, it is not only that the appearance of the essence of seeing is delusory while its nature is true;
you have still not clearly understood all the mundane, floating, and illusory transformations of the world—such as mirages, flowers in the sky, cities of the gandharvas, and dreams.
Objects, dust, and the "wild horses" (mirages) are rootless things. They arise where they are; they come from nowhere. They perish wherever they go; they stop at nothing.
These floating phenomena possess only false names and appearances; in reality, they have no self-nature.
If one discusses their true nature, it is simply the substantial essence of the sentient beings' wondrous, enlightened clarity. This is because:
The essence of wondrous enlightenment and clarity is like a mirror; floating dust and illusory transformations are like reflections upon that mirror.

Although reflections are utterly void, the substance of the mirror is fundamentally real. Thus, while all phenomena are utterly void, their substance is entirely real, because they are identical to the essence of wondrous enlightenment and clarity.
If even those utterly void phenomena are the substance of true awakening, how much more so are the aggregates (*skandhas*) and sense bases (*āyatana*)?
The sense bases and elements are the very things that sentient beings cherish and protect; could they not be the substance of true awakening itself?
Furthermore, consider the various worldly dharmas discussed in daily life, such as the five aggregates of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The six sense bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the twelve spheres consisting of these six faculties and their six corresponding objects;
and even the eighteen elements comprising the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—regarding these four categories, everyone knows that they arise through the combination of causes and conditions.
Falsely, there is birth; through causes and conditions, there is separation. Falsely, there is cessation.
Yet, one does not realize that since this arising and ceasing, coming and going, are all false and lack intrinsic substance, what exactly is it that manifests them?
One should know that their fundamental nature is the Tathāgatagarbha—eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading. Wondrous!

The nature of True Suchness (tathatā) merely manifests momentarily according to conditions. Failing to realize that delusion is itself True Suchness, one perceives delusion as having a substantial body.
Now, since it is the substance of true permanence, then coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, and birth and death—even within this true permanence—are but illusory designations;
they are utterly void and no real entity can be found therein. It is like looking at an image in a mirror.

An object is not recognized as a reflection within a mirror; thus, one erroneously claims it possesses substantial reality. As soon as one realizes it is a reflection within a mirror, there is only the mirror—how could there be any further object to be found?
Regarding the four lines on the harmony of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*), I shall now explain only the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
the others may be understood by analogy. This applies, for example, to the five sense organs (*indriya*) and the six sense objects (*viṣaya*). When they combine...
These constitute the eleven material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), which are termed the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
In a previous life, one must have grasped at and perfumed seeds with respect to these various phenomena, storing them within the *ālaya-vijñāna*; this is what is called the "cause" (*hetu*).

Upon reaching the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and seeking out parents, the parents then become the objective field (*ālambana*), triggering feelings of aversion and attachment; this is what is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*). This, indeed, is the cause.
Through the conjunction of conditions, the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are formed while in the womb; upon emerging from the womb, one dwells amidst the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
This is called birth. If one investigates this birth deeply, it is likewise like a dream and so forth: it comes from nowhere, yet it arises right where it is.
Therefore it is said that there is birth from the false and illusory. Yet these causes and conditions are fundamentally dharmas subject to arising and ceasing;

they determine the limits of longevity and brevity according to the power of prior karma. When those limits are exhausted, they naturally disperse. This is indeed the separation of causes and conditions.
Due to these five faculties and six sense objects, they are all simultaneously lost; this is termed "extinction. If one investigates this extinction deeply, it is likewise like a dream:
having no place to go, it is extinguished wherever it arises. Therefore, it is said that what is falsely designated as extinction is merely a name.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is thus; all other phenomena are also thus. As for the *tathāgatagarbha*, it refers to the mind of sentient beings.
It conceals the Tathāgata within; therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is precisely the "one mind" (*ekacitta*) of the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The one mind opens into two gates: first, the gate of the true suchness of mind (*cittatathatāmukha*); second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind (*cittotpādanirodhamukha*).

Because sentient beings follow the flow of birth and death, the aspect of arising and ceasing is fully manifest while true suchness is entirely concealed. Nevertheless, this arising and ceasing has no inherent substance.

Yet its essence is entirely *tathatā* (suchness). Therefore, the Buddha clarifies that this arising and ceasing, coming and going, is precisely the wondrous nature of *tathatā* within the *tathāgatagarbha* of sentient beings;
it is eternally abiding and immovable, transcending the birth and death of ordinary beings.
"Wondrously luminous and all-pervading" distinguishes [this state] from the nirvana of the two vehicles; these eight characters all describe the virtues of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Although it is called the "wondrous nature of True Suchness," it is none other than the entire substance of the seeing-nature revealed in the preceding ten sections.
○ He said: The above text refutes the deluded mind and the two kinds of deluded views; this is the ultimate point of refuting delusion.

Not even a hair’s breadth of the false can be mixed with the true. It is said that what is seen is not seeing; it is neither through causes and conditions, nor is it spontaneous, nor is it a combination, nor is it a non-combination.
This is the ultimate manifestation of the true. Not even a hair’s breadth of delusion can be admitted here. Having reached this point—
Ānanda has now discerned and understood clearly; he no longer mistakes the bubble for the ocean.

However, I fear that Ānanda perceives the true and the false as being too distinct, and thus inevitably seeks the water apart from the waves. Therefore, it is said: "You have not yet attained clarity," and so forth.

This is intended to make him know that the entire manifestation is the nature, and the entire bubble is the ocean; that the dependent and the perfected are fundamentally of one essence. Only then is it so.
The non-obstruction of all phenomena is the One True Dharma-realm. ○ It is further said:

"The original intent here is not to lead people to know that [phenomena] are false, but rather to lead them to know them as true. This is because falsehood has no self-substance; it is entirely the One True.

It is not a matter of speaking of the falsity of appearances in contrast to the truth of nature. ○ According to the subsequent detailed analysis of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus):

The realms are illusory; they are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This passage of nearly five thousand words is voluminous and its language profound, making it difficult for beginners to grasp quickly.

One should simply take these one hundred-odd words—from "taking this as the general heading for all floating, dust-like, and illusory manifestations" to "seeking [the truth] in coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, birth and death, yet finding nothing to be obtained"—and read them repeatedly until they are mastered.
The meaning is clear and evident; this is the concise method for studying the sutras.
Ānanda, how is it that the five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?

This first section raises a critical inquiry. Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): in ancient translations they were rendered as *yin* (aggregates), while in new translations they are rendered as *yun* (heaps).

A "heap" (*yun*) signifies accumulation; an "aggregate" (*yin*) signifies covering. To fully encompass both meanings—that which accumulates conditioned phenomena and that which covers the true nature—the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is employed.
The four categories that follow do not, in total, transcend the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Here, form is subsumed and mind is expanded for the sake of those with deluded minds.
This is the teaching of one who is not deluded regarding form. The meaning is that the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth are fundamentally worldly, conditioned phenomena.
Now, if it is suddenly granted that they are the very nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*), how could there not be a teaching for this? Master Zhong said:

"If the aggregates possessed a self-nature, they would stand in direct opposition to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Precisely because they lack self-nature, they are entirely True Suchness. Therefore, in the subsequent explanation:
This merely clarifies that it has no inherent nature.
Ānanda, suppose there is a person who, with clear eyes, gazes at the bright, cloudless sky; there is only the vast, empty clarity, utterly devoid of anything.
For no reason, this person does not move their eyes but stares fixedly until they become fatigued, whereupon they perceive various things within that very emptiness.
"Mad flowers. Furthermore, there are all manner of delusory, non-existent appearances; you should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is likewise so.
This first clarifies the aggregate of form. Form takes substantial obstruction as its defining characteristic.

Since the five sense organs and the six sense objects are combined into a single aggregate of form, it comprises not only the physical body but also the external environment. "Staring" refers to the manner of gazing straight ahead. Ānanda, [listen well].

What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)? It is like a person with clear vision who gazes at a bright, cloudless sky. The sky is vast and empty, devoid of anything whatsoever. Without cause, that person does not move their eyes but stares fixedly until they become fatigued; they then see wild flowers falling in confusion within the void, as well as all manner of other delusive, non-existent forms, such as the appearance of floating hairs.

The moon, flying flies, hanging hair, and so forth—the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) should be known to be likewise. Through the wondrously enlightened clarity, one perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm;

it is pure and fundamental by nature, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended. Yet, through failing to perceive this, one stirs thoughts, which transform into the perceived and the perceiver.
Yet these eleven material dharmas arise in chaotic profusion; how are they different from seeing flowers in the empty sky?

Regarding the four heavens of formlessness and the Śūnyatā-devas, as well as the two vehicles who falsely understand nirvana as the extinction of matter—if this refutation were not present, they would conclude that they have transcended the aggregate of form.
Ānanda, these illusory flowers do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes.
Within the Dharma, ordinary people and those of limited capacity reckon that form exists outside the mind; the provisional teachings reckon that form arises from within the mind.
Therefore, in this parable, two meanings are established and both are refuted. Ānanda, although these illusory flowers appear in space...
It is neither from space that it comes. Although it belongs to what is seen by the eyes, it does not emerge from the eyes.
Thus, Ānanda, if it were to come from space, having come from space, it would return to space. If there were such coming and going, [it would not be empty].
It is not, then, empty space. If space were not empty, it could not by itself accommodate the arising and ceasing of these floral forms, just as Ānanda’s own body cannot accommodate another Ānanda.
This refutes the notion that the flowers come from space. Thus, Ānanda, if these delusive flowers came from space...
Since you came from space and return to space, if there were coming and going, there would be internal and external. If there were internal and external, it would not be empty space.
If space were not empty, it would be a substantial entity. A substantial entity cannot by its own nature allow for the arising and ceasing of its manifestations.
Thus, if you, Ānanda, were a substantial entity, you could no longer give rise to the manifestation of "Ānanda. How so?

Why then do you say that flowers grow from empty space? If, within the context of the dharmas, one calculates that form exists externally to the mind, it is likewise said that all form-dharmas emerge together from emptiness.

For example, the ordinary and inferior practitioners of the Western Regions (India) infer and analyze the formation and destruction of the physical realm as being merely the aggregation and dispersal of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
When these atoms are broken down until they can no longer be divided, they necessarily reach emptiness; thus, they cling to [the notion of] various...

All forms emerge from emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Although the Confucian and Daoist scriptures of this region are diverse, their essential intent is that emptiness gives rise to vital energy (*qi*), and vital energy forms shapes;
thus, the myriad phenomena are fundamentally rooted in the single vital energy, which in turn originates from the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).
When compared with the teachings of the Western Regions (India), the underlying principles are largely identical. Generally speaking, worldly wisdom fails to comprehend the Great...
One wonders from where emptiness comes; one merely sees that the myriad phenomena all arise from non-being, and thus concludes that non-being is the source of being.
How could one know that it is not its source? ○ He [Hegeluo] says: "The character 'return' (huan) in 'returning from emptiness' is identical to the character 'revolve' (xuan)."
This refers to "extinction. Since it has emerged from within space, then at the time of extinction, it must certainly have drilled back into space.
To have emergence and entry is to be a substantial entity. Being a single entity, how could it allow another entity to arise and cease within it?
For instance, within Ānanda’s own body, how could it allow another Ānanda to drill in and drill out?

For example, if this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) were to come from the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), then when the aggregate of form is destroyed, it ought to drill its way back into the pure dharma-realm.
If there were such coming and going, the pure dharma-realm would then be a substantial entity.
Since it is a substantial entity, how could it possibly allow the aggregate of form to enter or exit within it?

If it emerges from the eyes, then having emerged from the eyes, it must also enter back through the eyes. Since this nature of the flower emerges from the eyes, it ought to possess the faculty of vision.

If it possesses vision, then as it departs into the empty space of the flower, it should, upon returning, see the eye itself. If it lacks vision, [then what has emerged cannot be the same as that which sees].
If it emerges and obscures the sky, it must subsequently obscure the eyes. Furthermore, when one sees the flowers, the eyes should be free of obscuration;
how then can the clear sky be called "clear and bright eyes"?

This refutes the notion that these flowers emerge from the eyes. Furthermore, if these empty flowers were to emerge from the eyes, then since they have emerged from the eyes, they ought to return back to the eyes.
If they were to emerge from the eyes, then the nature of these flowers should possess the faculty of vision.
If there is seeing, then once it has gone out, being like a flower in the sky, upon returning it should allow one to see one's own eyes.
If there is no seeing, then its obstruction is in vain; for if it can obscure the sky when it goes out, it should likewise obscure the eyes when it returns.
Furthermore, if the flower issues from the eye, then once the flower has issued from the eye, at the very moment the flower is seen, the eye should be non-existent.
When there is no cataract, it may then be called a clear and bright eye. Why must one see a cloudless sky devoid of flowers before it can be designated a clear and bright eye?
Thus, the calculation that [the eye] issues from the eyes is untenable.
If we consider this in terms of the Dharma, regarding the refutation of form as arising from within the mind: when deluded, form already issues from the mind; when awakened—
Forms should enter the mind. If there were knowledge that enters, one should see the mind; if there were no knowledge that enters, it would constantly obstruct the mind.
Furthermore, for the deluded, forms emerge, yet the mind should be unobstructed; for the awakened, forms enter, yet the mind should be obstructed.
How can it be unobstructed, and only then be called the pure mind? Question: If all phenomena are but mind, why do you further refute the arising [of phenomena] within the mind?
Answer: Although phenomena are but mind, they in fact never arise; therefore, they ultimately have nothing that can be extinguished.

For those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, once they realize non-arising, delusion is entirely identical to truth. Those of the Provisional Teaching do not forget that phenomena arise from the mind, yet they must first extinguish delusion before truth appears;
thus, it is necessary for them to break through [delusion].
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is empty and false; fundamentally it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This binding of delusion is itself the truth. When sought in both places [the internal and external], it has no source from which it emerges;

this is sufficient proof that the aggregate of form is empty and false. That it fundamentally lacks a body of arising is called "empty" (*śūnya*); that it falsely manifests according to karma is called "false" (*mṛṣā*). Since its characteristics are already empty and false, yet it is able to...
What, then, is that which manifests? It is fundamentally the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā), which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
Because it is eternally abiding and immovable, its essence is forever without change; thus, it is not produced by causes and conditions.

Because its wondrous luminosity is all-pervading and perfect, it manifests transformations in accordance with conditions; thus, it is not spontaneous. Since this nature is fundamentally not external, how could it arise from outside the mind?
Yet it exists; its nature is fundamentally unborn. How could there ever be birth within the mind? For these two reasons, both positions are incorrect.
This is what is meant by saying that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā).

Ānanda, it is as if there were a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose entire frame is in harmony, such that they suddenly forget their very existence and their nature is free from both opposition and compliance.
For no apparent reason, this person rubs his two palms together against the empty air, and within those two palms, various illusory sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat falsely arise.
You should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exactly like this, Ānanda. These are all illusory contacts.
It does not come from space, nor does it emerge from the palm. It is thus, Ānanda: if it came from space, and since it can touch the palm, why does it not touch the body?
Space ought not to select [a specific spot] to touch. If it emerged from the palm, it should not depend upon contact.

Furthermore, because it emerges from the palm, when the hands are joined, the palm perceives it; when they are separated, it enters through the point of contact. The arm, the wrist, and even the marrow of the bones should likewise perceive the traces of its entry.
There must therefore be a conscious mind that knows its emergence and its entry, such that there exists an independent entity that travels back and forth within the body.

What need is there to wait for their conjunction? It is essential to understand that contact is what constitutes [the condition]. Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of sensation is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

Below this, the single mental dharma is divided into four aggregates (skandhas), and herein it is clarified that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is precisely the wondrous nature of true thusness (*tathatā*).

"Sensation" (*vedanā*) has the meaning of experiencing or receiving; that is to say, in response to objects that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neutral, the three types of sensation—pain, pleasure, and equanimity—arise.
All four [mental] aggregates are mind, yet sentient beings mistakenly identify them as their own spirit; they are not like the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

In calculating [the nature of things], one considers them from both the internal and external perspectives; yet one merely calculates them as being substantially existent. Now, by showing that they have no source in either of these two locations, it is revealed that they are empty and not real.

Ānanda, what is called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)? It is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose hundred bones are in harmony, suddenly feeling as if they have forgotten their very life.
With neither opposition nor compliance, they do not even perceive the existence of a body—how then could they know there is sensation?
Suppose a person, for no apparent reason, rubs the palms of both hands together; within those two hands, various sensations such as roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat falsely arise.

You should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exactly like this. The nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is devoid of sensation, like a person in a state of tranquil rest.
Delusion gives rise to various sensations, just as one perceives roughness and so forth when rubbing the hands. Ānanda, these [sensations of] roughness, smoothness, cold, and...
These are the characteristics of heat, namely, illusory touch. These illusory touches do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm.
Thus, Ānanda, if one were to say that this touch comes from space, then since it can touch the palm, it should also be able to touch the body;
space should not exercise such discrimination as to come and touch the palm alone. Therefore, it does not come from [space].
It comes from empty space. If you claim that this touch emerges from the palm, then the palm alone should arise by itself;

why must it wait for contact? Furthermore, if it necessarily emerges from the palm, one should perceive its emergence when the palms join; one should likewise perceive its entry when the palms separate.
If there were such an entry, then the bones and marrow of the adjacent arm and wrist should also perceive its entry.
