How could one not know its traces at that time? If the marrow within the arm and forearm truly possessed a conscious mind that knew its coming and going, then there would already be a distinct entity within the body that moves back and forth and touches itself.
Why then must it wait for the joining of the palms to know its departure, only then being called "contact"? In that case, it would not have departed from the palm. Since...
Knowing that both positions are untenable, one should understand that this aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and false; it originally lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Fundamentally, it is the wondrous *tathatā* (suchness), which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously. This is what is meant by saying that the aggregate of sensation is, in its essence, the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Thus ends this section. Since the metaphors used here are themselves the Dharma, there is no need to explicitly correlate them with specific teachings.
This is correct. One need only understand the falsity of the analogy to realize the falsity of the phenomena themselves.

Furthermore, within all consciousnesses there are aspects of sensation (*vedanā*), yet these are most prevalent in the first five consciousnesses; thus, they should properly be attributed to the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
This is because the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth necessarily arise from the contact (*sparśa*) between their respective faculties and objects.
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who, upon speaking of sour plums, has water flow from their mouth; or one who, thinking of treading on a precipice, feels a stinging ache in their feet.
You should know that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is likewise. Ānanda, such talk of sourness does not arise from the plum itself.
"It does not enter through the mouth. It is thus, Ānanda: if the plum were to arise [of itself], the plum should speak for itself; why wait for someone else to say it?
If it entered through the mouth, the mouth itself should hear it; why need one wait for the ears? If it were heard by the ears alone, why would this water not emerge from within the ears?
Your imagining that you are treading on a precipice is similar to what has been said. Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false."
"It is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is itself the wondrous true *tathatā* nature. Perception takes "discursive contemplation" as its meaning;

that is, after apprehending a preceding object, one retains it in memory without forgetting. It should properly be categorized as belonging primarily to the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Ānanda—
Question: What is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)? For example, suppose there is a person who speaks of eating sour plums, and water flows from their mouth;

or one who thinks of treading upon a precipice, and their feet feel a stinging ache. Though they have not eaten a plum, water flows from their mouth; though their feet have not reached the cliff, they feel that sensation.
As for the tingling numbness and aching in the feet, is this not due to perception (*saṃjñā*)? You should know that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is likewise.

All that is currently perceived, maintained, and conceptualized by the faculties, the body, and the objective world—such as the sour taste within a memory or the precipice within a thought—is fundamentally non-existent, yet it is stubbornly clung to and not forgotten; this is the obscuration of the aggregate of perception.
...it is so, Ānanda. This water produced by such talk of vinegar does not arise from the plum, nor does it enter through the mouth.
In this way, Ānanda, if this water arose from the plum, the plum ought to speak for itself;
why wait for someone else to speak before the water comes forth? If this water entered through the mouth, the mouth ought to hear it first; why then wait...
"Ear! If it were heard by the ear alone, why would this water not immediately emerge from the ear? Yet it emerges from the mouth. If Mei had not spoken, it would not have been produced by Mei;
if the mouth had not heard, it would not have entered the mouth; if the ear had not emitted it, it would not have been caused by the ear.
When one traces this water back, there is nowhere from which it comes. This is sufficient to know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is not real. Thus he stamped [the ground].
The hanging cliff is similar to this explanation. If the cliff does not think, it is not produced by the cliff; if the feet have not yet touched it, it is not entered by the feet;

if the mind does not feel a sense of bitterness or distress, it is not brought about by the mind. Since this bitterness and distress come from nowhere, they clearly reveal the emptiness of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of perception is false and illusory, fundamentally lacking self-nature, and is originally [empty].
This is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā), which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
This is what is meant by the statement that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. The *Tanzi Huashu* says:

"When one speaks of the appearance of putrid things, one involuntarily gags; when one hears the names of rare delicacies, one falsely swallows in anticipation. Yet the putrid has never actually arrived, nor have the delicacies..."
To feel shame for never having seen such a thing, yet to experience belching and swallowing—is this anything other than delusion?
In conjunction with this, Ānanda, it is like a torrential stream where waves succeed one another, such that the preceding limit and the succeeding limit do not overlap;
you should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is likewise. Ānanda, the nature of this flow does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water.
Nor is it of the nature of water, yet it is not separate from space and water. It is thus, Ānanda:

if it were produced because of space, then the inexhaustible space of the ten directions would become an inexhaustible flow, and the worlds would naturally all be submerged. If it existed because of water...

Then this nature of the torrent would not be water; it would possess some characteristic that must now be present. If it were identical to the nature of water, then when the water is clear and still, it would not be the substance of water.
If it were separate from space and water, space would not exist externally [to it], and there would be no torrent outside of water.
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the aggregate of formations is itself the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Formation" takes the meaning of flux and transition;

it is precisely the volition (*cetanā*) among the universal mental factors (*caitta*), which is able to drive and employ its own mind to create what is wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth. Thus, it is this very [volition].
Regarding the category of karmic formations (*saṃskāra*), it subsumes the greatest number of dharmas among the one hundred dharmas.
Although all eight consciousnesses involve flux, the *manas* (seventh consciousness) is the most predominant in its flux because it continues uninterruptedly from moment to moment.

Although all eight consciousnesses possess volition (*cetanā*), the volition of the *manas* is the most predominant because its intrinsic nature is that of deliberation (*manana*). Therefore, it should be specifically assigned to the seventh consciousness.
Ānanda, what is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)? It is like the water of a torrential stream, where waves succeed one another;
the preceding and succeeding moments do not overlap, yet the former does not wait for the latter, nor does the latter reach the former. Day and night it flows on incessantly without interruption.
You should know that the aggregate of formations is likewise: mind after mind does not abide, and every thought-moment flows on in transition. Furthermore...
It is like a torrent that cannot be dammed. Ānanda, such is the nature of this torrent: it does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water;
yet it is not the inherent nature of the water. Thus, it is not identical to space and water, yet it is not separate from space and water;
thus, it is not apart from space and water. In this way, Ānanda, if this torrent were to [arise] because of space...
If [the world] were produced from space, then the infinite voids of the ten directions would become an infinite torrent, and all worlds would be submerged and drowned together;
yet such a principle does not exist. Thus, it can be known that the world is not produced from space.
If this torrent exists because of water, then its substance should not be identical to the water, but should have a separate location and a separate [existence].
There are characteristics present in both simultaneously, like a father giving birth to a son; each possesses its own essential nature.
However, if [the water] were non-existent, it could not be known to exist by reason of the water.

If this torrential flow, when turbid, were the very essence of water, then when it is clear and still, it would conversely not be the essence of water. Since the clear and still state is indeed the essence of water, then the torrential...
Furthermore, the nature of the torrent cannot be known apart from water; thus, both the sense of identity and the sense of difference are unestablished.
If this torrent were to have a separate self-nature apart from space and apart from water, then since space is not something external, how could it be apart from space?
Outside of water there is no torrent, so how could it be apart from water? Thus, even the sense of difference is unestablished. Therefore, neither identity nor difference is tenable.
Investigate this torrent: from what does it originally arise? Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is empty and false;
it fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). From the beginning, it is the wondrous *tathatā* (suchness) which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.

This is what is meant by saying that the aggregate of formations is, in its essence, the *tathāgatagarbha*. If explained according to the dharmas: emptiness is a metaphor for external objects, and water...

This is a metaphor for the inner mind. "Flow" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). That it does not arise from empty space is a metaphor for how this aggregate of formations does not arise from external objects.

That it does not exist because of water is a metaphor for how this aggregate of formations does not exist because of the mind. Furthermore, that it is not the nature of water is a metaphor for how this aggregate of formations is also not the nature of the mind.
Finally, that it is not separate from empty space and water is a metaphor for how this aggregate of formations is not separate from the mind.
It is the object. If you reckon that it arises from the object, then the object should possess cognition; in that case, all insentient things would be capable of mindfulness.

If you reckon that it is caused by the mind, then it should have a distinct self-substance. If you reckon that it is identical to the nature of the mind, then those for whom the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted would, conversely, lose their mental nature. How then could formations be identical to the mind and its objects? If you reckon...
If one is detached from the mind and its objects, then objects are truly boundless, yet there is no movement apart from the mind. Thus, how could movement be separate from the mind and its objects?
Ānanda, it is like a person who takes a *piṅgala* jar, plugs both its openings, fills it with space, and carries it for a thousand li.
It travels far away to provide provisions for another land. You should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is likewise.
Ānanda, just as this empty space does not come from that place nor enter into this place, so it is, Ānanda. If it had come from that place, it would have remained in the original flask.

Once the emptiness has been stored and departed, there should be a slight void in the location where the original bottle stood. If it enters from this side, then as the hole is opened and the bottle is overturned, emptiness should emerge.
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of consciousness is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is none other than the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Consciousness takes "discernment" as its essential meaning.

Although all consciousnesses are capable of discernment, this specific consciousness fully encompasses the eight seas and seven waves; it is also called the *karma-vijñāna* because it is the very source of arising and ceasing;
and it is also called the *ālaya-vijñāna* because it is the very substance of True Suchness. Thus, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness is particularly...
This belongs to the eighth consciousness. Ānanda, what is called the aggregate of consciousness?

It is like a person who takes a bottle shaped like a *piṅgala* bird, plugs its two openings, fills it with empty space, and carries it on a journey of a thousand *li* to present as a gift to another country.
You should know that the aggregate of consciousness is exactly like this: deluded karma is like the bottle, and deluded consciousness is like the space within.
It is like empty space. Driven by karma, consciousness wanders, like a vessel carrying empty space as it travels. There is no place among the three realms and six paths that it does not go.
Like traveling a distance of a thousand li, it discards one body and receives another, as if sending provisions to another country.
Ānanda, just as this empty space does not come from that direction nor enter from this direction, so it is, Ānanda, if one were to say...

If this space were to come from that other direction, then since the original bottle was already filled with space when it was taken away, the place where the original bottle stood in that other direction should now lack one portion of spatial void. Yet, the space in that other direction has not diminished.
Thus, although it seems to have come, in reality it has never come. If you claim that this space enters here from this direction, then it should...
When one opens the hole and turns the bottle upside down, one should see empty space emerging from the bottle. Yet this space within the bottle has not emerged;
rather, it enters this very place. Thus, although it enters, in reality it has never entered. It comes from nowhere.
Reaching that which is nowhere to be reached—all this is brought about by the shifting of karma. One falsely perceives coming and going, yet in reality there is no coming and going.

Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is empty and false; it fundamentally lacks self-nature. From the beginning, it is the wondrous nature of *tathatā* (suchness), which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
As for what is called "the aggregate of consciousness being fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha," it is as follows:
This. ○ If explained according to the Dharma: when one abandons the body as if coming from that place, the consciousness of the previous body has never diminished;
when one receives a body as if entering this place, the consciousness of the subsequent body has never arrived. One should know that when the body dies, it does not go away;
prior to death, it was originally not restricted to this [place]. When the body is born, it does not come from elsewhere; prior to birth, [it was not yet here].

Originally, it has always been pervasive throughout this. However, because one does not understand it, they mutually produce clarity and obscurity. When deluded, one is led away at will; when awakened, they share the same essence.
The essence is eternally unmoving, yet its function can be led and shifted. The Buddha precisely desires for sentient beings to awaken to the whole essence so as to encompass the great function.
○ The metaphor of the vase refers to the karma that leads consciousness, which is the seventh manas-consciousness. Furthermore...
This is called the activity of karma. Blocking its two apertures is a metaphor for the afflictive and cognitive hindrances obstructing the two kinds of emptiness.

This is because True Suchness is immovable; however, due to the shifting and unstable flow of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, it appears as if there is coming and going, and thus there is "this" and "that.
Now, if one does not see emptiness diminishing in that direction, nor see emptiness emerging here, then one knows the nature of consciousness.
Since the aggregates (*skandhas*) lack intrinsic nature, the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is revealed in its absolute solitude.

○ Yongjia clarifies that within a single thought-moment, the five aggregates are fully present: that which obstructs and limits the true nature is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); that which is experienced and received within the mind is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*);

that which the mind takes as its object through this principle is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*); and that which continues in an uninterrupted succession is... [the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)].
This aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is distinct and clear; it is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

These five aggregates, in their entirety, are but a single thought-moment; this single thought-moment, in its entirety, is the five aggregates. If one contemplates with subtle and profound insight, and thus perceives the five aggregates:
then since the form of a mass of foam is empty, how could there be the sensation of a bubble? [The perception of] a mirage...

Perception is not real; the nature of the plantain tree is merely emptiness. Illusory and delusive consciousness has no abiding place, yet the ultimately firm and solid essence is attained without departing from what is directly before one. ○ The section on the five aggregates is concluded.

Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
The following section reveals that the Tathāgata-garbha is not separate from the six faculties (*indriya*). As for why he speaks of "bases" (*āyatana*) rather than "faculties," it is because...

Because "penetration" (tong) refers to both that which enters and that which is entered. For example, when the faculty of the eye flows outward and rushes toward forms and so forth, it acts as the "enterer";
the eye, by receiving forms and so forth in a state of emptiness, acts as the "entered. Observe the character "xu" (to suck in/absorb) below;

it corresponds precisely with the character "ru" (to enter), for the six faculties each have the capacity to suck in and absorb their respective objects. Originally, this section was not present in the "Opening and Closing" [commentary]. It is essential.
This refers to the six internal sense bases. First, it raises the inquiry: "Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the six entrances the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?"
"Ānanda, that very act of the eyes staring until they become fatigued—both the eyes and the fatigue—are equally the *bodhi* (awakening) of the staring-induced fatigue.
This clarifies that the eye-faculty is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, as I previously said, it is like a clear eye staring—"
Because of the exertion, one perceives illusory flowers; thus, these illusory flowers are the signs of that exertion.

However, it is not only the illusory flowers that are signs of exertion; even this eyeball and the very act of staring with such exertion are likewise signs of exertion arising upon the Bodhicitta. Just as a son is indeed born from a father, yet he is also [identical to] the father.
"And you—both are likewise born from the Patriarch. ○ Zhong says: "In the previous analogy, 'staring' was taken as the sign of weariness and the 'eyes' as the sign of purity;
here, even the pure eyes are taken as a sign of weariness. Taking both the eyes and the weariness together constitutes the four characters 'shadow,' 'seeing,' 'together,' and 'defect.
'Seeing' and 'the conditions for seeing' [refer to this]. ○ He further says: "Both are the same: the staring that arises from Bodhi..."

The "sign of weariness" (*láoxiàng*) is precisely a gloss for the "essence of consciousness" (*shìjīng*) and the "original luminosity" (*yuánmíng*). "Bodhi" is the essence; it is the original luminosity.

The character "staring" (*dèng*) and the character "weariness" (*láo*) are consciousness itself. Both types of deluded vision—the individual karma (*biéyè*) and the common lot (*tóngfēn*)—are produced therein.
For Bodhi is True Suchness (*zhēnrú*); the character "staring" is the ignorance (*wúmíng*) produced within True Suchness; and "weariness" is the karmic consciousness (*yèshì*).

The two lines beginning with "The manifestation arises and dwells within" refer to the two aspects of transformation and appearance. The statement that "immediately upon these words, weariness ceases, which is itself bodhi" contains two meanings:
first, even if one has not yet ceased their weariness, bodhi is never forgotten; second, [the cessation of weariness is itself bodhi].
Based on the two kinds of false objects—light and darkness—the faculty of vision arises within them; it absorbs these objective images and is called the "nature of seeing.
Yet this seeing has no ultimate substance apart from those two objects, light and darkness.
There is this faculty of the eye. Within the two kinds of delusive objects—light and darkness—it clings to the profound stillness and gives rise to seeing.
The essence of seeing reflects these forms and immediately absorbs their characteristics; thus it is called the "nature of seeing. This is merely the faculty grasping its objects to acquire a name.
As for visibility, it possesses only a name. Indeed, when one leaves light and sees darkness, that seeing does not follow the light.
When darkness ceases and one leaves it behind to see light, the seeing does not perish along with the darkness; it seems as though it possesses a substantial body.

Now, if both light and darkness are left behind, what shape or form would the nature of seeing ultimately take? You should know that this is merely a false manifestation based upon sense-objects, and in reality, it has no substantial body.
Question: Previously, you stated that the conditioned mind has no substance when separated from its objects, in order to reveal the nature of seeing.
"It has substance. Furthermore, why is it said that the nature of seeing is ultimately without substance when separated from objects? The answer is:
previously, because Ānanda insisted on identifying the mind that conditions objects and refused to let go, I pointed out the nature within the sense organs to lead him to recognize the true mind.
Now, because he has already understood the true nature yet still clings to the six sense organs as having distinct substantial characteristics, he has not yet integrated them into a single nature.

Therefore, it is stated again that the nature of seeing has no substance. Although "the nature of seeing" is mentioned here, it refers to the self-nature of localized attachment within the sense organ;

it is not the same as the previously mentioned nature of seeing that is detached from the eye and all-pervasive. The former was intended to reveal the nature, whereas this is intended to dismantle its phenomenal characteristics.
This is why they differ. Delve deeper into this: this "shattering of marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) also intends for one to leave behind marks and realize the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Thus, the principle of revealing the nature remains fundamentally the same. How could it be like the deluded mind of conditions (*pratyaya-citta*), which is truly shattered because it certainly lacks any substance?
Zhong says: When comparing the seeing of nature to the mind of conditions, then the mind of conditions is...
Delusion. When the Tathāgatagarbha is contrasted with the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), then the nature of seeing also carries delusion.
Delusion has no self-substance and ultimately reverts to the True. The two characters "ultimate" (*atyanta*) refer to that which is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness; it does not emerge from the sense organ; nor is it produced from space. Why is this?

If it came from light, then it would cease when darkness follows, and one should not see darkness. If it came from darkness, then it would cease when light follows, and there should be no seeing of light.
If it were produced from the sense organ, then light and darkness would necessarily be absent. Thus, this essence of seeing is fundamentally—

It lacks intrinsic nature. If it emerges from emptiness, then when you first gaze at external objects, you should instead see the sense organ itself. Furthermore, since emptiness observes itself, what concern is it to your sense-faculty?
Therefore, you should know that the eye-faculty is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Thus it is, Ānanda. According to the false calculations of worldly sentiment, all say that this seeing either emerges from the sense organ, or else arises from the objects, or arises from space.
You should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness, nor does it emerge from the organ, nor does it arise from space.
Why is this? If one were to say that this seeing comes from light, then it would [not exist] in darkness.

At that time, since [the faculty] has already followed the light in its extinction, it should not perceive darkness; the same applies when following from darkness. Yet, why is it that one perceives both darkness and light?

This, then, does not arise from external objects (*viṣaya*). If you claim that this seeing arises from the sense organ (*indriya*), then if the single organ could produce the nature of seeing, why would it require both light and darkness to do so? Thus, this essence of seeing is fundamentally without self-nature.

In that case, it would not arise from the sense organs. If you claim that this seeing emerges from space, then since space is distinct from the organs and their objects, both the organs and the objects would equally become visible.
Consequently, when moving forward, one could observe the objects, and when withdrawing, one could observe the organs; furthermore, space itself would be capable of seeing.
What, then, would have to do with your organ of sight? Thus, it does not arise from space. Therefore, you should know this.
This is the single sense-base of the eye. It has no substantial reality; therefore, it is empty. It comes from nowhere; therefore, it is illusory.

However, the reason it lacks a real self-nature is that its essence is precisely *tathatā* (suchness). As for the reason it does not arise from the three locations [of organ, object, and consciousness]: [it is because its essence is suchness].
Because they arise from the *tathāgatagarbha*, their fundamental nature is that of a wondrous essence which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously;
they merely manifest momentarily as the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*). Such is the meaning of "the sense-base of the eye is fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It was through this realization that Aniruddha exchanged his physical eyes for the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). [The four aggregates and the seven elements] are, in total, all...
He instructs Ānanda: "In the midst of daily life—where you see forms and hear sounds, where you put on clothes and eat meals—seek out the core essence.
This is precisely the intent behind the Patriarchs’ teaching of people to 'contemplate the critical phrase' (huatou). However, the Patriarchs were unwilling to easily reveal the truth to others;
instead, they caused them to speculate for themselves, doubt for themselves, confront it for themselves, and seek it for themselves. Ultimately, this is the vision."

From where does it arise? After enduring the pressure for a long time until one’s practice reaches maturity, one suddenly sees it face-to-face in the midst of the "cold ground" (the state of non-conceptual clarity), thereby attaining complete and total realization.
One will certainly not lightly utter the four characters "eye enters falsehood. Thus, Xiangyan said:
"I do not value my former master’s Buddha-dharma; I only value that my former master did not give it to me."
He exposes it directly. The Tathāgata’s compassion is truly excessive; he urgently thrusts his sincere heart into the belly of others.
Therefore, as soon as he opens his mouth, he explains it for the sake of people. This is precisely what distinguishes the Zen of the Tathāgata from the Zen of the Patriarchs.
Zhong said: "In terms of worldly sentiment, the 'root-source' approach is the primary strategy; the other two are defensive strategies against potential deviations."
Ānanda, it is like a person who, with two fingers, tightly plugs their ears. Because the faculty of hearing is strained, sounds arise within the head.

Both the ear and the strain are equally manifestations of *bodhi* arising from a state of fixed gazing. Due to the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises within;
it draws in these objective phenomena, which is called the nature of listening. This hearing is distinct from those movements and stillness.
The two objects of dust are ultimately without substance. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing does not come from movement or stillness;
it does not emerge from the faculty, nor is it produced from space. Why is this? If it came from stillness, it would cease as soon as there is movement, and one should not hear the movement.
If it came from movement, it would cease as soon as there is stillness, and there should be no perception of stillness. If it were produced from the faculty, there would necessarily be no movement.
"Quiet! Thus, the essence of hearing is fundamentally without self-nature. If it were to emerge from emptiness and possess the nature of hearing, then it would not itself be empty space.

Furthermore, if empty space itself were to hear, what would that have to do with your faculty of hearing? Therefore, you should know that the auditory faculty is illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions, nor is it of a spontaneous nature."
This clarifies that the ear-base is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. Ānanda, when the eye is fixed in a stare, one sees flowers in the sky;

when the ear is plugged, one hears sounds in the head. Both are equally forms of fatigue. Together with the ear and its fatigue, they are all but the signs of fatigue arising from the staring of Bodhi.
For while the fatigue of the eyes results only in seeing flowers in the sky, when Bodhi gives rise to fatigue, then—
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing arise simultaneously. Possessing this faculty of hearing, there is sound when there is movement and silence when there is stillness.
Within these two kinds of delusive objects, the arising of hearing that draws in the objects is called the nature of listening.
Yet, if this nature of hearing were separated from these two objects—movement and silence—it would ultimately have no substance. Thus, Ānanda, you should know:
This hearing does not come from stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced by space. Why is this?
If one were to say that this hearing arises from the state of stillness, then when the state of movement appears, this hearing would immediately cease along with the stillness;
thus, it should not hear the movement. Yet, who is it that hears the myriad apertures roaring in fury? If one were to say that this hearing arises from the state of movement, then...

When the state of stillness manifests, this hearing immediately ceases along with the movement; thus, there would be no awareness of the stillness, and one could not know who it is that perceives this silence and absence of sound.
If [hearing] were produced from the sense organ (*indriya*), it would not depend on movement or stillness, and furthermore, there would be no hearing.
If it emerged from space (*ākāśa*), then since space itself could hear, it should be called "the ear" and not "empty space. Moreover, if space were to hear by itself, how...

The ear enters [the object]. Therefore, one should know that the ear-faculty is empty and false; its fundamental nature is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously, but is the wondrous nature itself.
This is what is meant by saying that the ear-faculty is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara exchanged the new, rolled leaves for the faculty of perfect penetration, and from this he attained awakening and entry. ○ This is only...

The passage "Hearing constitutes the nature, which is not empty space" differs slightly from the text concerning "returning to see the root. All other points are to be understood according to the above.
"Staring" (*deng*) is a delusive manifestation of the eye; however, the five faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind all borrow this term metaphorically.
Ānanda, it is like a person who forcefully pinches their nose; after pinching it for a long time, they become fatigued, and within the nose they perceive a sensation of coldness.
Because of that sensation, they distinguish between openness and obstruction, emptiness and solidity, and so on, even extending to various fragrant and foul odors.

Together with the nose and its fatigue, these are all the same as Bodhi—they are merely the signs of fatigue produced by staring fixedly. Based upon the two kinds of false objects, openness and obstruction, the faculty of hearing arises.

Abiding in the center, it inhales these sensory objects; this is called the nature of smelling and hearing. This hearing is separate from the two sensory objects of penetration and obstruction, and ultimately has no intrinsic substance.
You should know that this hearing does not come from penetration or obstruction, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.

Why is this? If it came from penetration, then when there is obstruction, hearing would cease; how then could one perceive obstruction? If it exists because of obstruction, then when there is penetration, it would be absent.

[Śāriputra] asked: "How do you explain the manifestation of fragrance, stench, and other tactile sensations? If they arise from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no distinction between openness and obstruction.
Thus, this faculty of hearing has no inherent nature of its own. If they emerge from space, then that hearing would naturally turn back to smell your own nose;

space itself would possess the power of hearing—what concern would it have with your sensory faculty? Therefore, you should know that the olfactory faculty is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions, nor is it spontaneous."
Nature. This clarifies that the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇāyatana*) is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. Ānanda, it is like a person who suddenly contracts their nose;

after contracting it for a long time, fatigue arises, and they perceive a sensation of coldness within the nostrils. Based on this sensation, they discriminate between what is open and obstructed, or empty and solid.

Second, regarding the two characteristics: by analogy with all fragrant and foul odors, as well as the nose and its fatigue, these are likewise the appearance of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.
Possessing this olfactory faculty, it arises due to the two kinds of false objects—permeability and obstruction. Its capacity for hearing is situated therein;

when it draws in these objective phenomena, it is called the nature of smelling and hearing. Yet, if this nature of hearing were separated from those two objects of permeability and obstruction, it would ultimately...
It has no substance. You should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.
Why is this? If it came from openness, one should not perceive obstruction. If it existed because of obstruction, there should be no hearing when open.
Furthermore, how could one then smell fragrance or stench? If it were produced from the sense organ, it would not depend on openness or obstruction, and it would likewise lack the nature of hearing.
If it were to emerge from space, since the hearing is already in space, it should also turn back to smell your own nose; this would be like returning to see one's own root.

Furthermore, if space itself possessed the faculty of hearing, what would it have to do with the nasal faculty? Since it cannot be traced to any of these three locations, you should know that the nasal faculty is empty and false;
its essence is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously—it is simply the wondrous nature. As it is said:
That the nose-faculty is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha is like this. This Paṇḍaka exchanged his pair of hanging claws for the place where the heavens pierce through his nostrils.
○ Master Zhigong said: "All day long one adds incense and changes the water, yet does not know that the body is the site of enlightenment (dōjō).
If one can truly, while smelling fragrance or stench, strike away the nostrils, then one is equal to all Buddhas of the three periods."
The Buddha and [the patriarchs] breathe through the same nostrils. Su Ziyou said: "If you preserve the nose, you will see the true face;
shaking the head, one does not accept other tongs and hammers. Thus, while worldly people labor by hurriedly preserving [their breath], Mahākāśyapa attained the Way by regulating his breath.
Coldness exists because of preservation; without preservation, it is fundamentally non-existent. The delusion of the nose entering [the breath] is of this nature.

"Indeed. 'Empty' and 'substantial' are also synonymous with 'open' and 'obstructed. Therefore, one distinguishes them solely by means of openness and obstruction. Furthermore, 'fragrance' and 'stench' depend on what is being smelled at the time.
Ānanda, suppose there is a person who licks their lips with their tongue; if they lick them repeatedly until they become fatigued, and that person is ill, then..."

Regarding the taste of bitterness: for a person who is free from illness, there is a subtle sensation of sweetness. Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, it is revealed that when this tongue-faculty is unmoving, its nature of neutrality is ever-present.
Furthermore, both the tongue and its fatigue are equally the Bodhi-mind; the appearance of fatigue arises from staring fixedly.

Because of these two kinds of false objects—sweetness and bitterness—the faculty of cognition arises within them, absorbing these objective images. This is called the nature of knowing tastes. This cognition...
The nature of taste, when separated from those two objects of the senses—sweetness and bitterness, as well as blandness—is ultimately without substance.

In this same way, Ānanda, you should know that this cognition of bitter and bland tastes does not come from sweetness and bitterness, nor does it exist because of blandness, nor does it arise from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?
If the cognition came from sweetness and bitterness, then when blandness is present, that cognition would cease; how then could one perceive blandness? If it were to arise from blandness...

When it emerges, sweetness is known to perish. Furthermore, how can you know the two characteristics of sweet and bitter? If this knowledge arose from the tongue, there would necessarily be no objects of sweetness, blandness, or bitterness.
Thus, one knows that the essence of taste fundamentally lacks self-nature. If it emerged from space, then space itself would possess the flavor; it would not be known by your mouth.
Moreover, if space were to know itself, what would that have to do with your sense-faculty? Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is empty.
False imagination. It is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature;
this clarifies that the tongue-sphere is originally the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, it is like a person who uses their tongue to lick their own lips;
by licking incessantly, they cause the tongue to become fatigued. Whether they are ill or healthy, a sensation of sweetness or bitterness arises. If...
Discussing the faculty of the tongue: it possesses only the nature of taste. Together with the tongue and its fatigue, these are all manifestations of the exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.
By means of this faculty of the tongue, one gives rise to cognition and absorbs objects within the two kinds of false sensory fields—sweetness, bitterness, and blandness.
This is called the nature of knowing taste. This nature of knowing taste, if separated from those two objects—sweetness, bitterness, and neutrality—is ultimately without substance.
Ānanda, you should know that this consciousness which tastes sweetness and neutrality does not arise from sweetness, nor does it exist because of neutrality;
furthermore, it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this? If sweetness or bitterness were to come, [the consciousness] should cease.
If it arises from the bland, it should cease when the sweet is gone; how then could one know both the characteristics of sweet and bitter?
If it arises from the tongue, then even without the external objects of sweet, bland, or bitter, there would be no nature of cognition.

If it arose from empty space, then empty space itself would naturally know the taste without necessarily requiring the mouth; yet this is not what occurs. Furthermore, empty space does not possess self-cognition.
What concern is this to your tongue-faculty? Being free from dust, it has no substance; it comes from nowhere.
Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is empty and false, being fundamentally nothing other than the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
This is what is meant by saying that the tongue-faculty is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Such was the Dharma realized by Kauṇḍinya while he was in the midst of chewing his food.
This is the gate. Now tell me: with what do you drink tea and eat rice?

If you can find the place where the tongue falls within this, you will know that the broad and long tongue-mark which covers the great trichiliocosm has never, from the very beginning, departed from the edge of the licking lip or the place of chewing rice.
Zhong said: "Sweet and bitter are the flavors of movement; blandness is the flavor of stillness."
The third samādhi concerns the two objects of motion and stillness.
Ānanda, it is like a person who touches one warm hand with a cold hand. If the power of the cold is greater, the warm hand follows the cold;
if the efficacy of the warmth prevails, the cold hand becomes warm. In this way, through the contact of these joined perceptions, [the nature of touch] is revealed.

It is detached from cognition. When it encounters conditions and appears to arise, it is caused by the contact of fatigue; both the body and this fatigue are equally *bodhi*. It is like staring until the signs of fatigue appear.
Because of the two kinds of false objects—separation and conjunction—the faculty of awareness abides in the midst and absorbs these objective images; this is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
Yet this essence of cognitive awareness, when separated from those two objects of separation and conjunction, as well as opposition and compliance, ultimately has no substance. Thus it is.

Ānanda, you should know that this perception does not come from conjunction or separation; it does not exist through opposition or compliance; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it born from space. Why is this?
If it came when there was conjunction, it would have already ceased upon separation; how then could one perceive separation? The two characteristics of opposition and compliance are likewise so.
If it emerged from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of conjunction, separation, opposition, or compliance; thus, your body—
Know that [the sense bases] have no self-nature from the beginning; they necessarily emerge from emptiness. Emptiness itself possesses self-awareness; what concern is this for your "entrances"?
Therefore, you should know that the body and the entrances are false and illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the body-sphere (*kāyāyatana*) is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Touch is the object-field corresponding to the body;

both hands are equally the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Yet, by mentioning only the cold and heat of the two hands, it is shown that all instances of false cognition within the body-sphere are of this same nature.
Ānanda, it is like a person who touches one cold hand against a hot hand; when the cold is predominant...
Thus, that which is hot follows the cold; when the heat prevails, the cold becomes hot.

These two tactile sensations of cold and heat are known to be conjoined when they meet, and known to be disjoined when they separate. By means of this perception of conjunction, the cognition of disjunction is revealed.

Alternatively, one may apply heat to the cold so that the cold becomes hot, or apply cold to the heat so that the heat becomes cold. If the force of such application is established, [the transformation occurs].
It is all merely due to the exhaustion of contact. Furthermore, both the body and this exhaustion are equally the signs of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.
Based upon this faculty of the body, which arises from the two kinds of false objects—separation and union—it gives rise to awareness within itself and absorbs these objective images.

This is termed "knowing the nature of contact. Yet this essence of the awareness that perceives contact—if separated from the union and separation [of the sense organ and object], as well as from the two objects of resistance and non-resistance within that union and separation—is ultimately without substance.

Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this awareness which perceives contact does not come from union and separation, nor does it exist through resistance and non-resistance; it does not emerge from the sense faculty, nor is it...
Śūnyatā-janman. Why is this? If one claims that this cognition comes when it joins [with its object], then at the time of separation, this cognition has already ceased;

how then could there be a separation of cognition? This applies even to the two characteristics of opposition and compliance: when there is opposition, compliance ceases; when there is compliance, opposition ceases—it is likewise so.
If one claims that this cognition arises from the sense-faculties, then there would necessarily be no joining or separating, nor opposition or compliance.

Regarding these four characteristics: even when one seeks to know the body, it likewise lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If you claim that this cognition arises from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then emptiness itself must possess self-cognition;
what concern would that have with your sense-faculties? Apart from sensory objects, it has no substance and comes from nowhere. Therefore, you should know this.
The body enters into falsehood; fundamentally, it is nothing other than the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
This is what is meant by "the body entering the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha. This is the Dharma-gate realized by Pindola Bharadvāja at the place where he endured pain.
Regarding "contrariety and conformity": it is like seeing heavy furs when it is hot, or obtaining fine linen when it is cold.

To oppose [the wind] is contrary; to obtain cool breezes in summer and warm fires in winter is harmonious. Although four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are opened up, they ultimately consist of only two objects (*viṣaya*).
Regarding touch (*spraṣṭavya*), there is contact-touch (*saṃyoga-sparśa*) and separation-touch (*viyoga-sparśa*). However, without contact, separation cannot be manifested.
It is necessarily because the two [objects] intersect that one perceives them as being in contact; only after that, when the two no longer intersect, does one know them to be separated. Therefore...

It is said: By means of this, the sensation of contact is conjoined with cognition to manifest the awareness of separation. Both the cognitions of conjunction and separation arise through the process of manifestation.
Yet, by what cause is the momentum of this process produced? It arises solely from the friction resulting from the rubbing of two hands together.
Ānanda, it is like a person who sleeps when exhausted and awakens from deep slumber; upon encountering sensory objects, there is recollection, and the loss of recollection is forgetfulness.

These are the stages of arising, abiding, change, and cessation born of inversion. They absorb and accumulate within the mind, never exceeding one another, and are designated as the faculty of mental cognition (*manas*).

Together with the mind and its exhaustion, they are all equally the Bodhi-nature, yet they manifest as the symptoms of exhaustion due to staring. This is because of the two types of arising and ceasing.

Regarding false objects: the faculty of cognition abides in their midst, drawing in and grasping internal objects. When seeing and hearing flow against the current, reaching a state where the flow no longer extends outward, this is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
This nature of cognitive awareness, when separated from the two objects of waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing, ultimately has no substance.
This clarifies that the entrance of the mind (manāyatana) is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, the exhausted aspect of the faculty of the mind is difficult to describe.
For example, suppose there is a person whose body and mind are weary; they then fall into sleep. Once their sleep has become deep, they awaken and wake up.
Upon waking, they perceive sensory objects and thus remember them; while asleep, they lose this memory and it becomes forgetfulness. Having forgotten, they remember again; having remembered...
Furthermore, there is forgetting. Thus, through such inversions, they circulate in a cycle from beginning to end. In the span of a single *kṣaṇa*, there is arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
Just as initial recollection is arising, the act of recollecting is abiding, the beginning of forgetting is change, and the total loss of memory is cessation.
Once ceased, it arises again; once arisen, it ceases again. Arising and ceasing never stop; all of this is nothing but beginningless habituation.

Vital energy (*vāyu*). Inhaling this habitual energy, it returns to the faculty of the mind (*manas*), where the four phases of change flow on; though they precede [the breath], they are not separate from it.
Taking these four phases as an example, all instances of the mind’s entry into false cognition are of this same nature; therefore, it is called the "mind-faculty of cognition" (*manovijñānendriya*).

Furthermore, both the mind and its toil are equally the appearance of fatigue produced by the staring of *bodhi*. Nevertheless, although the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing exist...
Fourth: These are collectively termed "dharma-objects" (*dharmaviṣaya*). In reality, they consist only of the two objects of arising and ceasing.
The faculties are able to grasp objects because of these two kinds of false objects—arising and ceasing—which gather cognition within them; thus, the five faculties are said to "issue forth.

Here, "gathering" refers to seeds, while "issuing forth" refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*). This is because the active manifestations of the first five faculties all derive from the seeds within this [storehouse consciousness].
Thus they arise. Thereupon, they draw in and seize internal floating dust, such as the drifting toward forms and the drifting toward sounds.
However, the five sense faculties can only take their own respective objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as conditions; they cannot mutually condition one another.
Therefore, seeing does not reach smelling; hearing does not reach tasting; tasting does not reach tactile sensation; and tactile sensation does not reach mental cognition.
This faculty of mental cognition is able to perceive and know all of them. Sometimes seeing flows back toward hearing, and sometimes hearing flows back toward seeing.
Thus, these five faculties often flow toward objects beyond their respective reaches; this is what is called clarity (*zhāo*).
The nature of awakening and cognition is brilliantly manifest; yet this nature of awakening and cognition is fundamentally not true knowledge.
If one separates it from those two objects—the arising of waking and the ceasing of sleep—it ultimately possesses no substantial reality.
○ "Dharmas" are called internal objects (*antarviṣaya*); they are the receding images of all phenomena. They are also called "fallen-away objects" (*luoxie chen*).

Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this faculty of cognitive awareness does not come from waking, nor does it exist through arising and ceasing; it does not emerge from the sense-faculties, nor is it born from space. Why is this? If it came from waking, it would cease upon falling asleep; what then would constitute sleep? If it must exist at the time of birth, it would be non-existent upon ceasing; who then would experience its cessation? If it existed through ceasing... [upon arising... it would be non-existent. Who then would experience its arising? Therefore, you should know that this cognitive faculty is neither born nor ceasing; it has no location and no origin. It is simply called the "faculty of cognitive awareness" because it is provisionally established based on the conditions of the six objects and the six consciousnesses. It is like the empty space within a house: when the house exists, space appears; when the house is destroyed, space remains. Space is neither born with the house nor does it perish with the house; it is merely named "house-space" based on the conditions of the house. Thus, you should know that this cognitive faculty is neither born nor ceasing; it has no location and no origin. It is simply called the "faculty of cognitive awareness" because it is provisionally established based on the conditions of the six objects and the six consciousnesses. It is like the empty space within a house: when the house exists, space appears; when the house is destroyed, space remains. Space is neither born with the house nor does it perish with the house; it is merely named "house-space" based on the conditions of the house. Thus, you should know that this cognitive faculty is neither born nor ceasing; it has no location and no origin. It is simply called the "faculty of cognitive awareness" because it is provisionally established based on the conditions of the six objects and the six consciousnesses. It is like the empty space within a house: when the house exists, space appears; when the house is destroyed, space remains. Space is neither born with the house nor does it perish with the house; it is merely named "house-space" based on the conditions of the house. Thus, you should know that this cognitive faculty is neither born nor ceasing; it has no location and no origin. It is simply called the "faculty of cognitive awareness" because it is provisionally established based on the conditions of the six objects and the six consciousnesses. It is like the empty space within a house: when the house exists, space appears; when the house is destroyed, space remains. It is immediately extinguished and non-existent. Who then knows that which arises? If it emerges from the sense organs, then its two states of waking and sleeping would open and close along with the body;
yet apart from these two physical forms, this conscious knower is like a flower in the sky—ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature.

If it arises from space, it is simply the knowing of space itself; what concern does it have with your sense bases? Therefore, you should know that the mind-base is false and illusory; its fundamental cause is not a condition. It is not...
Its nature is spontaneous.
It not only lacks substance, but it also has no place from which it comes. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this faculty of awareness does not come from waking or sleeping;
it does not exist through arising or ceasing; it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space. Why is this?
Therefore, if you claim that this nature of awareness comes from the waking state, then at the time of sleep it would have already perished along with the waking state;
who, then, is it that now, while in a deep and heavy slumber, manifests so many dreamscapes? If, on the other hand, it comes from the sleeping state...
It is also like this. If one claims that this nature of awareness exists at the time of its arising, then it would perish immediately upon arising as soon as it ceases;
who, then, is it that undergoes this cessation? If it were to exist from the state of cessation, then at the time of its arising, it would likewise be non-existent, having already perished.
Furthermore, as for that which knows the arising [of consciousness], who is it? It does not come from the sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

If one were to claim that it emerges solely from the sense organs (*indriya*) themselves, it would have no relation to waking and sleeping. One fails to realize that within the human body, the flesh-heart is shaped like a lotus flower:
when it opens, there is clarity; when it closes, there is darkness. Waking is its opening, and sleeping is its closing. Therefore, these two states of waking and sleeping are constant.
It opens and closes along with the body, never for a moment departing from it.

If this faculty of awareness were to depart from these two objects, then this aware knower would be like a flower in the sky—ultimately devoid of self-nature. Yet among the people of the world, they are either awake or asleep;
has there ever been anyone who was apart from waking and sleeping? Thus, [this awareness] does not emerge from the sense-faculties. If you say this...
The nature of cognition arises from emptiness. Emptiness itself possesses intention; it is the emptiness that knows. What concern does this have with your sense-faculty?
Thus, it is not produced from emptiness. Having no substance and no source, you should know that the faculty of mind is illusory;
its fundamental nature is the wondrous *tathatā* (suchness), which is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, yet momentarily manifests in accordance with conditions.
It is simply this. What is called "the mental faculty (*manas*) entering the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha" is as follows:

this is the Dharma-gate realized by Mahākāśyapa when he entered the ocean of the jewel-bright void through the faculty of the mental consciousness (*manovijñānendriya*). The term "mental faculty" (*manas*) is a synonym for the mind (*citta*).
Among the five sense-faculties that grasp objects, it is only this mental faculty; among the eight consciousnesses that evolve into awakening, it is only this mental faculty. The three realms...
It is mind-only. It is this very faculty of mentation (*manas*). All phenomena are consciousness-only; it is this very faculty of mentation.
One should know that this faculty of mentation is not only the root of heaven and earth, but the root of all things, the root of ignorance, and the root of all consciousnesses.
It is the root of birth and death, and yet it is also the root of nirvana; it is the root of bodhi. That the ordinary person is transformed into a sage depends precisely upon this.
If one breaks through this barrier, it is called Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and it is called Initial Awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) as well as Original Awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

Perfect Enlightenment, Wondrous Enlightenment, Unsurpassed Enlightenment, Universal Enlightenment, and Ultimate Enlightenment—this is the great pivotal point for opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This chapter excels in describing the locus of the mental faculty (*manas*). It describes it exhaustively through the four phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;

yet, it is particularly through the two states of waking and sleeping that it reaches its full expression. Consider the human being within this world: *The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* Translated by Taishū Yamaguchi, translated into English by Yoshito S. Hakeda, 1967, p. 108.

**Note:** The original Chinese text contains the character "想" (xiǎng), which here functions as a verb meaning "to consider" or "to contemplate," rather than the noun "thought. The phrase "寤寐二境" refers to the two conditions of waking and sleep, which serve as the primary metaphors for the activity of the *manas*. The commentary emphasizes how these specific states fully illustrate the nature of the mental faculty.
Except during deep sleep, there is no moment when consciousness does not flow, nor any moment when it does not undergo the transformations of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

Even within deep sleep, when one is disoriented and deluded, creating dream-objects through illusion, this is still the activity of the *manas-vijñāna* (solitary mental consciousness); its arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing never cease for even an instant.

This is why it cuts short and delivers all people from being submerged in birth and death. Yet, those who are deluded take it to have a substantial body (*tattva*), while those who have awakened know it to be without a substantial body.
It is not that there is no substance; rather, it takes the *tathāgatagarbha* nature as its very substance. How profound is the meaning of this realization!

Regarding the entry into the three categories of aggregates, elements, and sense bases, there are three kinds of distinctions in the method of refuting phenomena (*dharmapratibheda*). The first is: [The text continues with the specific distinctions.]
The refutation by way of conditions does not restrict itself to the primary dharma, but extensively refutes external conditions. It is like extinguishing a fire:
one does not strike the flame directly, but rather removes its fuel, and the fire extinguishes of its own accord, because fire has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Second, the mutual refutation states that since two dharmas are established in mutual dependence, they must be mutually refuted. This is like a water-snake and water, which depend upon one another for their existence.
Both are sources of affliction. To eliminate them: "driving out the *jiao*" means cutting off the source of the water; "discharging the water" means destroying the dwelling of the *jiao*.
These three methods are applied according to their essentials, and there are two ways to do so. First, eliminating two factors according to the essential:
it is like two pieces of wood standing leaning against one another; if one simply pushes one over, both will fall. Second, eliminating three factors according to the essential...
It must be dismantled. For example, it is like a bow made from the combination of three things—sinew, glue, and horn—wherein the glue is the essential element.

If one merely removes the glue, the sinew and horn will no longer constitute a bow. These six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are entirely dismantled by way of their conditions; the "objects" (*viṣaya*) are those very conditions.
The following twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) involve dismantling through mutual interaction as well as the two factors arising from the essential [condition], such as the eye and form.

The four bases of ear and sound are mutually sublated. The remaining eight bases are sublated by means of two dharmas. The subsequent eighteen elements are all entirely sublated by means of three dharmas.
Although the text follows this method of essential sublation, the underlying intent is actually to sublate them all together;
this is not the same as the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), where the primary intent lies in the faculties themselves. Let the student examine this carefully. [End of] the Six Sense-Bases.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the twelve bases (*āyatana*)? Fundamentally, they are the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is explained for those who are deluded regarding form while not being deluded regarding mind: by opening up form and combining mind, it is taught. Form is originally one;

when opened, it becomes the five sense organs and the six sense objects, thus forming eleven bases. Therefore, it is said that "form is opened. As for mind, if it is contrasted with the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandha*), [it constitutes the twelfth base].

Thus, the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are combined; and in contrast to the eighteen realms below, the seven—comprising the six consciousnesses and the faculty of mind—are collectively subsumed under the single locus of "mind.
Therefore, it is said that they are "combined into the mind-locus. A "locus" (*āyatana*) refers to a place or site, and it also implies being fixed in a specific position.
These twelve loci are originally one perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening; they are merely separated by the various sensory objects.
The Yue people were lawless and distinct from other tribes, each dividing their own territories like those of the six feudal states;
they could not be merged into a single unified realm. Therefore, Ānanda attacked them in various places.

If one location was destroyed, the remaining eleven locations would submit of their own accord without waiting for an invitation to surrender. Consequently, in all his attacks, he employed no clever stratagems nor set up scaling ladders.
I merely borrow the staff held in the present moment to drive them straight away. In the first fascicle, the "Destruction of the Mind in the Seven Bases" destroys the mind as having no location;
these "Twelve Bases" destroy the bases as having no location. ○ First, the inquiry is raised as follows:
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature (tathatā-svabhāva) of the Tathāgata-garbha?
Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. What do you think?

Do these forms arise to be seen by the eye, or does the eye arise from the appearance of forms? Ānanda, if it were the case that the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) gives rise to the appearance of forms, [then...]

Seeing emptiness as not being form, the nature of form should be dissolved. Once dissolved, it is revealed that everything is utterly non-existent. Since the characteristics of form no longer exist, who can perceive the substance of emptiness?
Emptiness is likewise so. Furthermore, if the sensory object of form were to produce visual perception, then one would observe emptiness as not being form.

Upon seeing, it immediately perishes; when it perishes, it is entirely non-existent. Who then can clarify the relationship between emptiness and form? Therefore, one should know that both seeing and the emptiness of form have no location.
Thus, both form and seeing are dual locations that are illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the two locations of seeing form are originally the Tathāgata’s own age. The Dharmalakṣaṇa school uses the two horns of a snail as a metaphor:
when extended, they form a pair; when retracted, they become one. This is because both arise from the manifestation of the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga).
Therefore, the World-Honored One questioned him regarding the location of the presently manifest seeing of form, saying: "Furthermore, you..."
"Ordinarily, it is simply said that all phenomena arise by relying on causes and depending on conditions. Consider this:
when you now open your eyes and see the Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds, what do you think?
Is it because of the Jeta Grove that the vision within your eyes arises and sees this Jeta Grove? Or rather, is it because of the vision within your eyes that [the Jeta Grove] arises?"
"The Jeta Grove—do you see it? These two phrases constitute the "Vajra Ring" and the "Thorny Jujube.
Even the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot provide an explanation for them.
If you say that this Jeta Grove arises from your own visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and that you therefore see it, then when your visual faculty sees empty space, you would not see the Jeta Grove.
If the Jeta Grove were to perish, then the grove would simply vanish; once vanished, all manifested forms would be utterly non-existent.

Now, emptiness is manifested at the boundary of form and its characteristics. Since the characteristics of form no longer exist, what further thing could there be to manifest the substance of that emptiness?

It is the same with the arising of the appearance of emptiness in the eye. If you claim that this Jeta Grove arises within your visual faculty to cause you to see the Jeta Grove, then when your eye contemplates emptiness, it would not be contemplating form.
Since there is no form capable of arising, there is naturally no seeing that arises from it. Once seeing has vanished, what remains is the seeing of emptiness.
What further thing is there as form? It is said that empty space arises and is seen by the eye; it is likewise so in this case.
Therefore, you should know that seeing and the emptiness of form both lack any fixed location, whether internal or external. Form does not give rise to the eye, for the eye is itself quiescent;
the eye does not give rise to form, for form is itself quiescent. Yet, those who cling to the arising of form and seeing as having two real locations are mistaken.

All are false and illusory. This is because the perception of form is, in its single essence, fundamentally nothing but the wondrous nature that is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous. This is the point of realization for Upānanda.
First it says, "both have no location," and next it says, "the two locations are false. This clearly constitutes a direct refutation, which differs from the previous "correct" [refutation].
He breaks through the six sense bases; the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are merely words. Zong said: "The eye does not produce form, for form has no location.
Form does not produce the eye, for seeing has no location. That which is false and illusory has no substance. Having no location means having no substance;
having no substance, it takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its substance. Therefore, it is said that fundamentally it is neither caused by conditions nor produced by itself."
This is the wondrous true nature. The remaining five [elements] are to be understood in this same way.
Ānanda, listen further to this: when food is prepared in this Jeta Grove, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled.
The sounds of the bell and drum continue one after another. What do you think? Do these sounds come to the side of the ear, or does the ear go toward them?

"Ānanda, as for the sense-sphere of sound: if this sound comes to the side of the ear, then just as when I am begging for alms in the city of Śrāvastī while staying in the Jeta Grove, I am not there; so too, this sound must come to Ānanda’s ear.
Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together, let alone the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas who, upon hearing the sound of the bell, all hear it at once."

They come together to the place where food is eaten. Now, if your ear were to go to the location of that sound, then just as I have returned to dwell in the Jeta Grove and am not elsewhere in the city of Śrāvastī, so too when you hear the sound of a drum, your ear would already have gone to the place where the drum is being struck.
When the sounds of bells ring out all at once, they cannot be heard simultaneously; how much more so for the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within them?
If there were no coming or going, there would likewise be no hearing. Therefore, one should know that both the faculty of hearing and the sounds have no location.
Thus, both hearing and sound are in two locations that are false and illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the two locations of the ear and sound are, from the beginning, the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ānanda, listen further to this Jeta Grove: when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled. As for the sounds of these bells and drums, before—
It continues thereafter. What do you think? Do these sounds come to the vicinity of your ears so that you hear them?
Or does your ear go to the place where the sound is so that you hear it? Or is it heard without any coming or going?
Ānanda, if one were to say that the sound comes to the vicinity of the ear, a single sound could not reach many [ears].

Furthermore, just as a single body cannot go to two places simultaneously—just as when I beg for alms in the city of Śrāvastī, I am not present in the Jeta Grove at that same time—so too, since this sound has reached Ānanda’s ears, how could it also reach the ears of many people?
If that were so, Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together; how much less those within the crowd!
This assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty people, upon hearing the sound of a bell, all come together to the place where they eat.
Since the entire group hears it simultaneously, it cannot be that the sound has traveled to their ears. If one were to claim that the ear travels to the location of the sound...
A single ear cannot go simultaneously to many sounds, just as a single person cannot arrive at two places at once.
For instance, when I have returned to the Jeta Grove, I am no longer present in the city of Śrāvastī.
Furthermore, when you hear the sound of a drum, if that ear has already gone to the place where the drum is being struck, how could it also reach the location of other sounds?
If the sounds of the bells were to emerge all at once, they would not be heard simultaneously, for there are no ears within the location of the bells.
How much more so regarding the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within them, which are heard all together? It must be that the ear does not travel to the place where the sound is.
Calculating it as either coming or going is incorrect; one can only turn to the reckoning that there is neither coming nor going. If you say there is none—
Regarding this coming and going: the faculty of hearing and the object of sound each abide in their own respective positions and do not reach one another.
If this were so, then when a sound arises, the ear should no longer hear it; yet, it is not that there is no hearing. Thus, it cannot be that there is no coming and going.
Since both of these two calculations are incorrect, what is the reason for this? It is simply because the characteristics are false while the nature is true.
This is a false claim regarding their own characteristics. You should know that both hearing and sound are each all-pervasive and neither has a fixed location.
Thus, the intrinsic natures of these two locations—hearing and sound—are likewise unobtainable. The provisional and limited views of the Lesser Vehicle are entirely devoid of real meaning.
Since the locations are illusory, there are not even two locations; so whom can one speak of as coming and going, or as not coming?
Go forth! Regarding the mantra of self-nature, you should know that hearing and sound are not ultimately non-existent phenomena;
they are merely the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
This is the point of realization for Kauṇḍinya. Master Padmasambhava said: Suppose there is a bell tower at the center of a city. If a south wind blows, then [the sound] reaches the north.
When the wind blows from the south, the city within hears it, but those to the north do not; when the wind blows from the north, the city to the south hears it, but those to the north do not.
It is the wind that carries the sound so that people may hear it; how could it ever be that the sound does not come to the side of the ear?

It is only because sentient beings cling to stillness and give rise to the faculty of hearing that they lose their fundamental wondrous perfection. They confine it and obstruct it, binding it and making it small. Therefore, when the wind is favorable, [the sound is heard].
Then one hears it; if the wind is contrary, one does not. This occurs because [the sense organ] is turned toward its object and lacks autonomy;
this is the fault of the ear, not the fault of the sound. Furthermore, when one listens to sounds through a wall, they can be heard both from afar and nearby.
Since the wall does not obstruct the sound, why is it that when one person inside the city speaks facing the wall, while another person outside the city leans against the wall... [he cannot hear it]?
Listen. Is it not that you then hear nothing at all? This, too, is a failing of the ear; it is not due to the walls or the city.
Therefore, those whose ears are unimpeded can hear through them; they may hear a single world-system, or even as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
And yet it is inexhaustible. ○ The Immortal of Poshan said: "If you say the sound resides upon the strings of the lute, why does it not ring when placed inside its case?
