If you say the sound resides on the fingertips, why do you not listen for it upon your own fingers?
From this he attained awakening.

Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner. If this fragrance were burned from only a single *zhu* (a small weight), its scent would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* within the city of Śrāvastī. What do you think?
Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space? Ānanda, if this fragrance were to arise from your nose...
If it is said that [the fragrance] is produced by the nose, it should then emerge from the nose; yet the nose is not sandalwood—how then could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose?

If it is said that you "smell" the fragrance, it should then enter through the nose and the fragrance should emerge from within the nose; thus, to speak of "smelling" is meaningless. If [the fragrance] were produced in empty space, [it would not depend on the nose].
If emptiness were eternal, then fragrance should also be eternally present. Why then rely upon burning this withered wood in an incense burner?

If the fragrance arises from the wood, then this fragrant substance, having been burned, becomes smoke. If the nose perceives it, it ought to encounter the scent of that smoke; yet as the smoke rises into the air, [the fragrance is not perceived there].
It is not yet very far; within forty li, how can it already be heard? Therefore, one should know that the nose and the smelling, as well as the hearing, both lack a fixed location.
Thus, the two locations of the olfactory organ and the fragrance are both illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

This clarifies that the two bases of the nose and fragrance are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Throughout the day one smells fragrance, yet one does not know the source from which the fragrance comes;
it is simply because one has never investigated in detail from where it emerges. Therefore, it is said: "Ānanda, you now smell this sandalwood in the incense burner;
though only a single *zhu* is burned, throughout the forty *li* within the city of Ruo-cheng, everyone shall smell it."
"Regarding this fragrance, what do you think? Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, or does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space?

Ānanda, if you say that this fragrance arises from your nose, then since it is said to arise from the nose, it ought to emerge from the nose. However, the nose is not sandalwood; the physical flesh is not fragrance."

As for the substance, how could it exercise the function of emitting fragrance such that there is the scent of sandalwood within the nose? Furthermore, what is called "smelling fragrance" refers to the fragrance entering through the nose.
If one were to say that fragrance issues forth from within the nose, then since it is issuing forth, it cannot be described as being "smelled."
Furthermore, to say that it is heard is also inconsistent with reason; thus, it is not produced within the nose.

If one were to claim that this fragrance is produced from space, then since space is eternal, the fragrance would also exist eternally; why then must it depend on being burned within an incense burner before it comes to be?

This would mean that the fragrance is not produced from emptiness. If you claim that this fragrance is produced from the sandalwood tree, then the substance of this fragrance must become smoke through burning so that the nose may perceive it. If the nose perceives it, it ought to be enveloped by the scent of that smoke.
Yet, although that smoke rises into the air, it has not yet reached a great distance; how then could it reach as far as forty *li*?
"I have heard it. Thus, it is not produced from the wood. Upon detailed investigation, even the fragrance-particle has no place of origin;
how much less could the nature of smelling have a location? Therefore, one should know that fragrance and the nose’s act of smelling both lack a locus.
Consequently, the essential natures of both smelling and fragrance are utterly unobtainable; fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor self-existent."
It is simply the wondrous nature of that which is ignited. This is the point where Xiangyan attained the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body.
This [verse] singles out the sense-object of fragrance to demonstrate that it has no place of arising; it is what is called the essential refutation of the two dharmas.

The old commentary suspects that this violates the knowledge within the synthesis of dharmas, yet it fails to realize that this is the definitive meaning of the Dharma-nature, which is precisely the refutation.

Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), how could one instead use that [example] to challenge this? Based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), both the sense faculties and their objects are each all-pervasive; they are a single essence without division.

Thus, to speak of "separate cognition" or "unified cognition" is in every case mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). However, in the case of ordinary fragrance, the nose must be enveloped by smoke for it to manifest;
thus, "unified cognition" is shown to be of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Only in the case of this extraordinary fragrance does it not depend upon being enveloped by smoke.

"Waiting for the union of cognition" is of definitive meaning; therefore, the Buddha adopted it, as there is a profound intention behind it. "Fragrant nose" and "hearing" should be understood as an error for "fragrance" and "nose-hearing.
To speak of the "nose" and "hearing" seems to encompass both the physical organ (the *tuccha-rūpa*) and the primary sense faculty (*indriya*).
Nevertheless, when the faculty is contrasted with its object, they remain two distinct locations; there are not three factors involved.
"Ānanda, you regularly carry the alms bowl among the assembly twice a day. During that time, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called superior flavors.
What do you think? Does this flavor arise from space, does it arise within your tongue, or does it arise within the food?
Ānanda, if this flavor were to arise in your tongue, since there is but one tongue within your mouth..."
At that time, the tongue has already formed the perception of the flavor of ghee. If it encounters black rock honey, it should not shift;
if it does not shift, it cannot be said to know the flavor. If it does shift, the tongue would not be a single entity. How, then, could many flavors be known by a single tongue?
If the cognition of food arises from the food itself, since food is not conscious, how could it know itself? Furthermore, if food knows itself, that would be identical to another eating;
what concern would that have for you? As for the cognition of names and flavors, if it arose from space, then as you consume empty space, what flavor would it produce?
If it were certainly empty space that acted as a salty taste, then since it would salt your tongue, it would also salt your face;

consequently, the people of this world would be like sea fish, constantly experiencing saltiness and never knowing what it is to be bland. If they did not recognize the bland, they would likewise have no awareness of the salty.
There would necessarily be no object of cognition. What, then, would be called "taste"? Therefore, you should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting all lack a fixed location;
thus, both tasting and taste are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature of their own.
This clarifies that the two bases of tongue and taste are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. There is no one who does not eat and drink, yet few are able to know the true flavor.
Therefore, he directs him toward the side of the alms bowl to seek the source of this "taste. Thus he says:
"Ānanda, you regularly partake of two meals a day, holding the bowl among the assembly to beg for food. In the midst of this, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter..."
Ghee is called the supreme flavor. What do you think? Does this flavor arise from empty space, does it arise within the tongue, or does it arise within the food?
Ānanda, if you say that this flavor arises from your tongue, then your single tongue should perceive only a single flavor;
thus, once the taste of ghee has been formed, when you encounter black rock honey, [it should likewise remain as one].
It does not shift. However, if it were to know a single flavor without shifting or changing, then it could not be called "knowing flavor.
If it were to know distinct flavors through shifting, then since the tongue is not a plurality of entities, how could there be many flavors known by a single tongue?
Thus, it is clear that this flavor does not arise within the tongue. If you claim that this flavor arises from...
Regarding food: food itself possesses no consciousness. How, then, could it know for itself whether it is sweet or bitter?

Even if food were able to know for itself, that food would be the same as anything belonging to another; it would have nothing to do with you. For what reason, then, do you claim to be the "knower of taste"?
Thus, it is clear that this flavor does not arise from the food. If you claim that this flavor arises from empty space, then when you eat empty space, what kind of flavor do you experience?
If it were salty, then all of space would be salty; since your tongue is salty, [the rest of you must be so as well].
It would also have to salt your face; then the people of this realm, experiencing that salty taste, would all become like sea fish.
Since they constantly experience saltiness, they would certainly not know sweetness. If they do not recognize sweetness, they cannot be said to perceive saltiness.
Being entirely without such knowledge, they could not be called people who know flavors; thus, perception would not arise from emptiness and clarity.
Since it is not in these three places, the nature of flavor has no location; how then could the nature of tasting have a location?
Therefore, you should know that both flavor and the tongue’s act of tasting are devoid of any fixed place. Thus, both tasting and flavor are equally illusory.
While their mutual appearance is false, their fundamental nature is true—a wondrous nature that is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous. It is simply this.
One must know that this flavor does not depart from its present location. If one truly recognizes the fundamental ground, there is no need for chewing;
the hundred flavors are fully present. This is the place where the Medicine King attained the Chan of a single flavor.
Ānanda, you have often in the early morning rubbed your head with your hand. What do you think? Regarding this sensation known through the rubbing, who is it that performs the touching?
Does the capacity to touch reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head? If it resides in the hand, then the head would be without cognition;

how, then, could there be contact? If it resides in the head, then the hand would be without function; how, then, can it be called contact? If each were to possess [the capacity] separately, then your...
Ānanda, there must be two bodies. If head and hand were produced by a single contact, then hand and head would have to be one entity.
If they were one entity, contact could not be established. If they were two entities, with whom would the contact reside? It cannot reside in the agent, nor can it reside in the object.
It is not possible for empty space to enter into contact with you. Therefore, you should know that [the nature of] sensation and contact...
The body and [the object] have no location; thus, both the body and touch are equally illusory. Fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the two bases of body and touch are, from the beginning, the Tathāgatagarbha. The World-Honored One constantly exhorts his disciples:
One day, [the Buddha] rubbed his head three times, reciting aloud: "Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let not the body transgress;
the practitioner who acts thus shall transcend the world. Therefore, my disciple has followed this method by rubbing his head. Thus it is said:
"Ānanda, you should rely on my teaching and, every morning, rub your own head with your hand. This refers to that very act of rubbing.
As for the location of the head, one does not even know how much has been missed.

Furthermore, at the very moment you are stroking your head with your hand, the hand knows there is a head, and the head knows there is a hand. Who is it that acts as the agent of contact and gives rise to this cognition?

Is it that when the hand touches the head, the hand itself becomes the agent of contact and gives rise to this cognition? Or is it that when the head touches the hand, the head itself [becomes the agent]?

It is the faculty of touch that produces this cognition. If it were the hand that acts as the toucher to produce this cognition, then the cognition of touch would reside in the hand, and the head would become an insentient object. How then could the head know that the hand is touching it?

And how is contact established? If it is the head that acts as the agent of contact and gives rise to this cognition, then the cognition of contact would reside in the head, and the hand would become a useless object. How then could you know that the head’s contact is with my hand and call it "contact"?
If there were a separate cognition for both the head and the hand, then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies. If the head...
If there were only a single cognition of both [the hand and the head], then the hand and the head would have to constitute a single entity. If they were a single entity, contact could not occur.
If they were two distinct entities, to which of these two would this contact belong? Would it belong to the agent of contact (*spraṣṭṛ*) or to the object of contact (*spraṣṭavya*)?
If the contact belonged to the agent, then both the hand and the head would be agents of contact, and there would be no object of contact.
Since there is no object of contact, how could empty space become the object of contact for you?

If contact belongs to the category of the "object," then whether it is in the hand or in the head, both would become objects of contact, and there would be no subject of contact. Since there is no subject of contact, how could empty space become the subject of contact for you?
Regarding these two types of contact, whether one considers them as one consciousness or two consciousnesses, they cannot be definitively established. Regarding...
When one touches, there is neither a single substance nor two substances, leaving one with no basis for recourse.
Therefore, you should know that the touch which is perceived and the body which perceives it both have no location; thus, both the body and the touch are equally illusory.
Since these two characteristics are illusory, their single nature is inherently real. This fundamental nature is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous.
This is where Bhadrapāla stood while bathing, marking the spot with his heels. One should know that the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) differs from all other objects.
While all other objects face their respective sense organs, here, at the tip of the hand, there is only the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and no external object of touch.
It is only through mutual friction that the characteristic of touch is produced; yet, the faculty and the object are ultimately not distinct from one another.

[This is] a division. Although it is not a mere hypothesis, it nevertheless carries the intent of providing an analogy. By taking all other instances of contact as examples, one sees that they are all likewise illusory;
this naturally reveals that there is no duality of location, but rather a single nature. ○ He said: "The two entities of head and hand have one as the agent and one as the object.
If contact resides in the agent, what serves as the object of contact? If contact resides in the object, who serves as the agent?"
If there is a capacity [to touch] but no object [to be touched], contact is still not established. How could space possibly constitute the object for you?
If there is an object but no capacity [to touch], contact is likewise not established. How could space possibly constitute the capacity for you?

Ānanda, regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral natures that you constantly take as objects of your mind, which constitute the laws of arising and ceasing—do these phenomena arise from the mind itself, or do they exist separately from the mind in some other location? Ānanda, if they were identical to the mind...

Dharmas are neither objects of the senses nor objects of mental apprehension; how, then, can they constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)? If they existed as distinct locations apart from the mind, then would the self-nature of dharmas be cognizable or non-cognizable?
If it were cognizable, it would be called "mind"; if it were different from your [mind] yet not an object of the senses, it would be identical to the mental constructs of others.
That which is you is precisely the mind. How could your mind be dualistic with respect to you?

If it were not consciousness, then since these objects are neither form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, nor the characteristics of union, separation, cold, warmth, or empty space, where would they exist? Now, within form and emptiness—
There is no indication whatsoever. It cannot be that there is space outside of the human realm. Since the mind is not an object of perception, from what could its location be established?
Therefore, one should know that both phenomena and the mind are without location; thus, both the mental faculty (*manas*) and phenomena are equally illusory.
It is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature;
this clarifies that the two bases of mind and mental objects are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Ānanda, whenever your mind is constantly bustling and agitated, whatever it takes as its object—whether good, evil, or neither-good-nor-evil, which is termed "indeterminate"—this [is the Tathāgatagarbha].
These three natures are all shadows manifested from the falling away of the active states (pravṛtti) perceived by the preceding five sense organs.
Each possesses its own rules and serves as an object of perception for the mind (manas), and is thus called the "dharma-object" (dharmāyatana).
Does this dharma arise from the very mind of the mental organ itself? Or does it exist apart from the mind, having a separate location? Ānanda!
If this dharma-object (dharmāyatana) were identical to the mind, then this dharma would not be an object;
it would not be an objective sphere for the mental faculty (manas). How, then, could it be established as the objective sphere of the mental faculty?
If this dharma-object exists separately from the mind at a distinct location, does the self-nature of the dharma-object possess cognition, or is it devoid of cognition?
If you consider this to be "knowing," it should be called the mind (*citta*) and not the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*).
Since it is distinct from your sense-faculties and discernment (*vijñāna*), and yet is not an object, it must be a separate mind. Is this not then the same as the mental capacity of another person?
If you claim that it is not different from another's mind but is indeed your own mind, then it should not be subject to mutual opposition, nor should there be two distinct characteristics.
Now, how can mind and objects face one another? Are they not manifest as two distinct entities to you?
If you consider them to be non-cognizing, then they must be external objects; as such, they should have some defining characteristic.

Yet these objects are neither form, sound, smell, taste, nor the sensations of contact—such as separation, union, cold, or warmth—and they lack the characteristics of space and so forth. Apart from all these objects, where could they possibly exist?
Where? Now, within the interval between form and emptiness, there is absolutely no indication. It cannot be among human beings;
nor can there be a place outside of emptiness that could be accommodated as a mental object (*dharmāyatana*). Even if it were situated outside of emptiness, it would still not be an external object;

thus, it would not be something capable of being perceived by the mind. It is only by depending on what is perceived by the mind that a location for phenomena is established. Since this is not perceived by the mind, then—
From whom is the locus of dharmas established? To calculate them as being separate by combining what is known and what is unknown is incorrect.

To calculate them as being separate or identical by combining separation and identity is likewise incorrect. Thus, these dharmas ultimately have no locus. Since dharmas have no locus, how could the mind have a locus?
Therefore, one should know that dharmas and the mind are both without a place; thus, the mind and dharmas [are non-dual].
Both are equally false; fundamentally, they are nothing other than the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
This is the point of entry for the realization of emptiness. Therefore, one should know that the six sense organs have no opposition; they are all gates to the Dharma of non-contention.
All objects contain emptiness and are entirely merged within the Way of non-duality. Thus, the present realm of sentient beings is truly [the manifestation of] the Unconditioned.
How can one conceive of this? Why seek the functions of the various sages from afar while disparaging oneself as inferior? ○ Hege said:
"The previous statement—that dharmas are not objects and are not what the mind takes as its object—means that they are near yet cannot be taken as objects.

The subsequent statement—that there should be no further 'mind beyond emptiness' in the human realm that is not an object of cognition—means that they are distant and thus cannot be taken as objects. This is not so.
The mind takes an object as its condition; because it is a single entity, it cannot take itself as an object. It is like the eye, which cannot see the eye itself. The mind is not an object;
because it lacks a substantial entity, there is nothing that can be taken as an object. It is like the eye not seeing a rabbit’s horn. [End of the Twelve Bases.]
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for how the eighteen *dhātus* (realms) are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*):

this is taught for those who are deluded regarding both form and mind, taking them to be distinct from one another. "Realm" (*dhātu*) carries the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) and the meaning of "boundary" (*sīmā*).

Here, it is taken in the sense of the characteristics of realms not being confused with one another; that is, the faculties (*indriya*) which correspond to their respective objects (*viṣaya*), each according to its own faculty.

The object is the *dhātu* (element). That which discriminates in the interval is consciousness (*vijñāna*). As each has its own distinct boundary, the three [groups of six] combine to form the eighteen *dhātus*.
Although there are eighteen *dhātus*, their essence is one; therefore, he first raises a question, saying: "Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the eighteen *dhātus*?
Fundamentally, they are the wondrous *tathatā*-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. [The *dhātus* encompass the hundred...]

The Dharma Verse says: "The faculties and objects each comprise five elements; ten material [elements] follow their own names. Eight kings return to the seven consciousnesses; eighty-two are all *dharma*.
Thus, the faculty of mind (*manas*) is the seventh consciousness; since the seventh and eighth are mutually dependent, the eighth is also subsumed under the faculty of mind.
As for the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of mental objects), it is ordinarily considered to belong only to the category of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). Some say: 'The *dharmāyatana*..."
Being formless yet possessing a shadow, half would be mind and half would be matter; thus, it should follow that ten parts are half-matter and seven parts and a half are mind.
Ānanda, as you understand it, with the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises. Does this consciousness arise because of the eye?
That which arises [from the eye] takes the eye as its constituent element (*dhātu*). That which arises because of form takes form as its constituent element.

Ānanda, if it arises because of the eye, yet there is no form and no space, there would be nothing to distinguish. Even if your consciousness were present, what would you have it serve? Your vision is not blue, yellow, red, or white;
since there is nothing to indicate it, how could a constituent element be established? If it arises because of form, then when space is devoid of form—how could it arise?

Your consciousness should cease [with them]. How then can your consciousness cognize this nature of space? If form undergoes change, you likewise cognize that the characteristics of form are subject to transformation; yet your consciousness does not itself migrate.

From what basis could the realm [of consciousness] be established? If it were to follow the change [of its objects], then it would itself change, and the characteristic of the realm would naturally cease to exist.

If it were unchanging, it would be permanent. Since it arises from form, it should not be able to cognize the location of space. If it were a combination of both, then the eye and form would arise together;

yet when they combine, they would be separated in the middle, and when they separate, they would join as two. Their essential natures would thus be confused and disordered; how, then, could they constitute a sense-field (*dhātu*)?
Therefore, you should know this: the eye and forms serve as conditions to give rise to the visual consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).

Since these three locations are all non-existent, then the eye, forms, and the visual consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature. (The term "visual consciousness-element" refers to the element of consciousness regarding form; the word "consciousness" is omitted for brevity, and the other five cases follow this pattern.)

This clarifies that the eye, form, and consciousness are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, although I have previously provided various instructions and exhortations, I fear you may not yet have attained full clarity.
Therefore, I shall now further explain this for you by means of what you already understand:
namely, the ordinary way you comprehend the faculty of the eye and its objects, which stand in mutual relation between the internal and the external. Within this interval...
It arises within the eye-consciousness, between the internal and the external; thus, the three realms are established.
Yet, one does not know whether this consciousness is produced from the eye and is therefore called "consciousness produced by the eye," taking the eye as its boundary;
or whether it is produced from form and is therefore called "consciousness produced by form," taking form as its boundary? Ānanda, if one were to say this—
Consciousness arises from the eye-faculty; that which takes the eye-faculty as its boundary is consciousness, which functions to cognize objects.

Since there are neither the two objects of form nor emptiness, there is nothing to be distinguished. Even if your consciousness were to arise, what would it be used for? Because there are no objects, consciousness is not employed.
Furthermore, it is through the mutual correspondence of the faculty and the object that "internal" and "external" are indicated; only then can the realm of consciousness be established.
In the interim, there is now no solitary sense-faculty devoid of dust; yet the sense-faculty you perceive is fundamentally invisible.
Furthermore, it does not possess the color-characteristics of blue, yellow, red, or white, but is a single entity without further internal or external manifestations by which it could be represented.
By what, then, would you define "the middle" in hearing, such that you establish it as a "consciousness-element"? For a solitary sense-faculty cannot establish an element. This, then, is the element.

The principle of self-arising is not established. If you claim that this consciousness arises from the object of form and takes that form as its boundary, then when the appearance of emptiness manifests, this consciousness would have already perished along with the form;
it would no longer be in contact with emptiness. How, then, could the consciousness cognize the nature of space? If you claim that when various forms undergo transformation, your consciousness—
Furthermore, you recognize that the characteristics of form undergo change and transformation; thus, your consciousness does not perish along with the changes in form.
While form perishes, your consciousness does not shift; this consciousness exists alone, without further opposition. With what other phenomenon could it then be delimited?
And how can one establish its boundaries? It is not merely because it does not migrate that boundaries cannot be established;
even if one were to follow its migration and transformation, it would have already returned to change and extinction, such that both the entity and its boundary-phenomena would be non-existent.

Since the boundary-phenomena themselves are non-existent, one cannot say that form constitutes the boundary. Not only can emptiness not be cognized through transformation and extinction, but even if it were to remain unchanging—then...
It would establish a permanent nature, eternally identical with form and having no relation to emptiness. Who could then recognize emptiness?

Now that emptiness is recognized, it is certainly not by means of form as a constituent element (*dhātu*). Thus, the meaning of "constituent element" cannot be established for that which arises from another.
If it is claimed that this consciousness arises simultaneously from these two—namely, the eye-faculty and the object of form—merging together, then this faculty and...

If the sense-object (*viṣaya*) and the sense-organ (*indriya*) were joined together as one, there would naturally be no space between them to accommodate consciousness (*vijñāna*) and divide them into a middle boundary.
If consciousness were thus separated and situated on the side, how could it constitute a middle boundary?

Furthermore, if these organs and objects were separated and existed in two distinct places, then the consciousness produced by them would likewise have to be divided and exist in two places, joining each [factor] individually—half joining the organ and half [joining the object].
When the sense organ and the object meet, they cannot constitute a middle realm; for when two things meet, they are joined, and when the middle is absent, there is separation.

Since their essential natures would thus be confused and disordered, how could they form a realm? Therefore, the definition of a "realm" cannot be established through co-arising. Thus it is sought through analysis.
Furthermore, this visual consciousness does not arise from itself, nor does it arise from another, nor does it arise from both together.

According to your understanding that the eye and forms serve as conditions to give rise to the element of visual consciousness, since the visual consciousness thus produced cannot constitute an "element," how could the eye and forms subsequently constitute conditions?

This is because, since the intermediate element does not exist, the internal and external are unobtainable; that which is called "the arising of consciousness through conditions" [is therefore untenable].
However, these are merely established through worldly convention and possess no ultimate reality; their characteristics are thus illusory.
That being so, from where do the three—the eye faculty, the form object, and the visual consciousness element—ultimately come?

Fundamentally, they are nothing other than the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously. How could there be any three characteristics to be found? This is what Śāriputra realized.

This is the point of entry. Third, the investigation and interrogation focuses on consciousness (*vijñāna*). This accords with the previous analogy of the bow, wherein the three factors are refuted according to their essential requirements.
It is also like three households living in close proximity; if one were to demolish the boundary walls on both sides of the middle house, [the other two would collapse].
Then the boundaries of the three houses would all fail to be established. ○ He said: "The sutra text refutes the dharma through two modes:
refutation by opposition and refutation by succession. This section employs refutation by succession, which is what is called 'the club that strikes the body.

First it says: 'If one were to say that form exists, then one should not recognize emptiness. It then immediately follows up on the word 'recognize,' saying: 'If one says that one can recognize [it]...'"

The realm is not established. Why? Because while form undergoes transition, consciousness remains; thus it stands isolated and without companion. Furthermore, following closely upon the term "non-transition," it says:
"If one says it follows transition, the realm is likewise not established. Why? Because consciousness returns to transition and perishes.
Furthermore, following closely upon the character for "transition" (*bian*), it says: "If one says it does not transition, it should be subject to the same difficulty as before. Why?"
"Because the nature of consciousness is constant. ○ Zhong says: Both "changing" and "unchanging" should not establish the realms; yet they are interwoven to form the text.
Previously, it was because of following change that it was said "emptiness is not known"; subsequently, it is because of not following change that it is said "emptiness is not known.

Previously, it was because of unchanging that it was said "the realms are not established"; subsequently, it is because of following change that it is said "the realms are not established. This is the text.
"Excellent, Ānanda!

Furthermore, regarding what you have clarified: when the ear and sound act as conditions to produce the ear-consciousness, does this consciousness arise because of the ear and thus take the ear as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of sound and thus take sound as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the ear..."

When the two characteristics of motion and stillness do not manifest before one, the faculty does not constitute cognition; there is necessarily nothing known. Since even cognition itself is not established, what form or appearance could consciousness have?
If one were to take "hearing" as the ear's function, since there is neither motion nor stillness, hearing would not be established. How, then, could there be the form of the ear?
The aggregate of tactile objects of various colors is called the element of consciousness. From what, then, is the ear-consciousness element established?

If it arises from sound, such that consciousness exists because of sound, then it would have no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would vanish. Thus, consciousness would arise solely from sound.

If it is granted that sound exists because of hearing and possesses the characteristic of sound, then hearing itself should be the consciousness of hearing. If there is no hearing, it is not a constituent element (*dhātu*). If there is hearing, it is identical to sound;
once consciousness has been heard, who knows the consciousness of hearing? If there is no knower, one would ultimately be like grass or wood.

It is not logical that sound and hearing should intermingle to form a middle constituent element. Since a constituent element has no middle position, from what then could the characteristics of "internal" and "external" arise? Therefore, you should know this.

With the ear and sound as conditions, the auditory consciousness element arises. Since these three locations are all non-existent, then the triad of the ear, sound, and the auditory consciousness element are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the ear, sound, and auditory consciousness are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the ear and sound acting as conditions to produce auditory consciousness: does this consciousness arise because of the ear, such that the ear constitutes its constituent element (dhātu)?

Furthermore, is it produced because of sound, taking sound as its objective realm? Ānanda, if you say this consciousness is produced from the ear, then it would arise solely from the primary sense organ (indriya).
In that case, both of its two aspects—the movement of sound and the stillness of no-sound—would not manifest before it.
Since there would be no external object, the organ itself would be devoid of cognition. If it were truly devoid of cognition, [how could it perceive?]
Furthermore, what consciousness could there be? For if there is no object, there is no hearing; and if there is no hearing, there is no consciousness.

If you claim that the physical ear can hear—that even the peripheral sensory organ (*bu chen gen*) can produce consciousness—then since the two characteristics of motion and stillness are absent, hearing cannot be established.
If the superior sensory organ (*sheng yi gen*) itself cannot produce consciousness, how much less so this [physical ear] which lacks...

If you claim that the ear’s form, the various types of dust-particles (visibles), and the tactile objects—all equally comprised within the category of insentient matter—are collectively designated as the "consciousness-element" (*vijñāna-dhātu*) and thus give rise to consciousness, this is untenable.

Since it is impossible from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and impossible from the perspective of conventional, superficial reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one must certainly conclude that ear-consciousness does not arise from the ear.
Ultimately, from what then could the element be established? If you say that this consciousness arises from sound...

Consciousness exists because of sound; it does not depend upon the auditory faculty. How then could one know that if there were no hearing, the sound would not exist, and from what would consciousness arise?
Even if one grants that consciousness arises from sound, one must also grant that the characteristic of sound exists because of the auditory faculty.
Since consciousness is identical with the sound, at the time of hearing the sound, one should also hear the consciousness. If one does not hear the consciousness, then...

Sound and consciousness—these two should not be the elements that give rise to consciousness. If it is the case that consciousness is heard, then consciousness, like sound, would be entirely devoid of cognition.
Since consciousness is itself without cognition, it has already been "heard" by the ear. What, then, is that which knows and hears this consciousness?
If you claim there is no further knower who knows and hears this consciousness, then you must be the same as grass and trees.

Furthermore, since the single sense organ does not emerge [from its location] and the solitary object does not arise [independently], it is illogical that the organ and object should intermingle to form an intermediate realm.
Indeed, if they are said to intermingle, then an intermediate realm cannot be established. Now, it is only when there is a middle position that one can distinguish between "inside" and "outside.
Since there is currently no intermediate realm, how can one distinguish between internal and external boundaries? Investigating in this manner, this ear-consciousness...
It is not born of itself, not born of another, and not born of both together. Therefore, you should know that with the ear and sound as conditions, the sphere of auditory consciousness arises.
Since these three locations are entirely non-existent and their characteristics are wholly illusory, then the ear, sound, and the sphere of auditory consciousness—these three—are likewise so.
The nature is entirely true; it is fundamentally the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
This is the point of entry for Samantabhadra’s realization.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have understood: with the nose and fragrance as conditions, the nose-consciousness arises. Does this consciousness arise because of the nose?

That which is produced takes the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*). That which is produced because of fragrance takes fragrance as its constituent element. Ānanda, if it is produced because of the nose, then within your mind, what constitutes the nose?
Is it the physical form of the two nostrils, or is it the nature of the vibrating faculty that perceives odors?
If you take it to be the physical form, then that fleshy substance is merely the body; the cognition of the body is contact (*spraṣṭavya*), and it is called the body, not the nose.

What is called "contact" is simply the object. Since even the nose lacks a name, how can you establish a sense-field? If you take the act of smelling as the cognition, then within your mind, what constitutes that cognition?
If the flesh constitutes the cognition, then the cognition belongs to the flesh; it is originally contact and not the nose. If space constitutes the cognition...
If space were itself conscious, then flesh would not be sentient. If this were so, then empty space would be you, and your body would not be the knower.
In that case, Ānanda, you would have no place of existence today. If you take fragrance to be consciousness, then consciousness would belong to the fragrance; what concern would it have for you?
If fragrant and foul odors necessarily arise within your nose, then those two types of flowing air—fragrance and stench—would not exist in the *eranda* tree or the sandalwood tree.
Even when these two substances do not come near you, if you smell your own nose, would it be fragrant or foul? If it is foul, then it is not fragrant.
Fragrance should not be foul. If both fragrance and foulness could be smelled [by the same organ], then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses.
When I questioned you, there were two Ānandas; which of them was your true self? If the nose were one, then fragrance and foulness would not be two distinct things.
What is foul becomes fragrant, and what is fragrant becomes foul; since these two natures do not truly exist, from whom could the realms be established?
This clarifies that the nose, fragrance, and consciousness are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding what you understand as the nose and fragrance acting as conditions to produce nasal consciousness: does this consciousness arise because of the nose, such that the nose constitutes its realm?

Or does it arise because of fragrance, taking fragrance as its boundary? Ānanda, if you say that this consciousness arises because of the nose and takes the nose as its boundary, then within your mind, what do you take to be the nose?
Is it the physical form of the two nostrils—the superficial root (*bu chen gen*)—that you take to be the nose? Or is it the act of smelling and the movement of cognition that you take to be it?
Regarding the nature of the supreme sense-faculty (indriya), is it the nose? If you take it to be the physical form of flesh, then that fleshy substance is the body;
since bodily cognition is contact, the nose would then become the body and cognition would become contact. This would be to lose the reality of the nose.
Furthermore, what is called "body" is not the nose, and what is called "contact" is an object (viṣaya). Thus, both its name and its reality would be lost. It is neither in name nor in reality.
Thus, since the nose itself has no name, from what could a constituent element (dhātu) be established? This shows that clarity does not arise from the peripheral sense organ (the fleshy part).
If you take the nature of that which perceives by smelling, then within your mind, what constitutes the faculty of knowing?

If you say the flesh at the tip of the nose is what knows, then it is the same as the previous case where bodily consciousness is simply tactile contact. If you say the emptiness within the nostrils is what knows...
If emptiness were to possess cognition, then the flesh at the tip of your nose should be devoid of sensation.
Furthermore, if the emptiness within the nostrils already possesses the nature of cognition, then the emptiness in all places should likewise be the flesh upon your nose.

Since it lacks the nature of cognition, then the flesh throughout your entire body should likewise not be cognition. If emptiness is you, then empty space— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.*
If [the body] has no location, then you, Ānanda, should likewise have no location.
Since the body is devoid of cognition, even if the body were to have a location, it should not perceive where that location is. Now, ultimate cognition does not rely upon the flesh.
Furthermore, it does not depend on emptiness. In that case, does it take fragrance as its substance?

If fragrance were the nature of olfactory cognition, then once it has transformed, it would know itself and become the cognition of another's fragrance. Since that [other] possesses its own cognition, what concern is it to you?
Moreover, the two gases of fragrance and stench do not originally arise from the nose; therefore, they are not the nature of olfactory cognition. If you claim that the two—fragrance and stench—...
As for the fragrance that arises from your nose, those two kinds of diffusing scents would, conversely, not arise from the *eranda* (castor plant) or the sandalwood tree.
When neither the sandalwood nor the *eranda* are present, you should simply smell your own nose.
Whether it be fragrant or foul: if your nose were originally foul, you would certainly not simultaneously perceive fragrance;
if your nose were originally fragrant, you would certainly not simultaneously perceive foulness. If you perceive both fragrance and foulness, you must possess two noses.
If you have two noses, then you have two bodies. When I question you, which of these two Ānandas is your true body?
If the nose were held to be only one, then the fragrances and stenches it produces would likewise have to be blended together without distinction.
In that case, the nose would become fragrance, and fragrance would turn into stenches; they would mutually cancel each other out until both natures ceased to exist.
Thus, since even the sense organ lacks an intrinsic nature, from what could the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) be established?

By pursuing this line of inquiry, it becomes clear that [consciousness] does not arise dependent upon the primary sense organs (paramārthendriya). It is further evident that neither the secondary sense organs (tuccha-indriya) nor the primary ones can give rise to consciousness.
Therefore, it is even clearer that this consciousness does not arise dependent upon the nose. This section is not a place for the cognition of fragrance; it must not be so.

This is an instance of erroneously citing the passage concerning the arising of fragrance. It proceeds by first breaking down the nose as the source from which consciousness arises, and then tracing back to determine what constitutes the "nose.
Having already dismantled the coarse, physical organ (*pudgala-śarīra*), it further investigates the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of cognition: upon what does its substance depend?

Thus, by deconstructing both the flesh and space, it eventually reaches the fragrance; this merely deconstructs the cognition of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) that possesses fragrance, and is not the same [as the original context].
This refutes the notion that consciousness arises from fragrance. Those with subtle minds discern this:

if consciousness were to arise because of fragrance, then consciousness would exist because of fragrance; just as the eye possesses the faculty of seeing yet cannot perceive the eye itself, so too, because consciousness exists because of fragrance, it cannot perceive that very fragrance.

It should not know fragrance; if it knows it, that is not fragrance. If it does not know it, it is not consciousness. Fragrance does not exist because of knowing; thus, the realm of fragrance is not established.
If consciousness does not know fragrance, then the realm [of fragrance] is not established from fragrance. Since there is no middle, neither internal nor external can be established.
That nature of hearing is ultimately illusory. Therefore, you should know that the nose and fragrance act as conditions to give rise to the element of nose-consciousness;

yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the nose, the fragrance, and the element of fragrance—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

If you claim that this consciousness is produced by fragrance and takes fragrance as its constituent element (*dhātu*), then this consciousness exists because of fragrance, just as seeing exists because of the eye.
Since one cannot turn back and perceive the eye itself, how could consciousness—which exists because of fragrance—possibly turn back and know the fragrance?
If it can know it, then it is not produced by fragrance; if it does not know it, then it is not [consciousness].
It is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). However, if one does not perceive fragrance, it would not merely fail to be consciousness;

rather, both the realm of fragrance and the realm of consciousness would necessarily fail to be established. Why is this? For fragrance is not known through cognition; fragrance is not manifested by means of consciousness.
Based on this, the realm of fragrance (*gandhadhātu*) should be considered unestablished, because fragrance must depend upon cognition for its manifestation. Apart from [cognition]...
How could cognition (vijñāna) possibly establish itself? Cognition does not cognize fragrance; this means that cognition does not arise without being conditioned by fragrance.
Based on this, the element of cognition (vijñānadhātu) should not be established, for cognition must rely upon fragrance to exist. Without fragrance, how could it establish itself?

(The "element" [dhātu] here refers specifically to the element of cognition, as the term *dhātu* carries the meaning of a causal basis. If cognition were lost and the element destroyed, the resulting faults would be endless. This is therefore...

It is now even more evident that consciousness does not arise because of fragrance. Since the intermediate realm of consciousness cannot be found, the internal faculties and external objects likewise do not come into being.
When the internal and external do not exist, that which could co-arise with them lacks reality.

If the middle element (the nose) were not established, then that which arises together with it would not be real. Would the nature of the consciousness that smells and perceives not be ultimately false?

Therefore, one should know that although the nose and fragrance act as conditions to produce the element of nose-consciousness, these three locations are entirely non-existent and their characteristics are wholly illusory.
Thus, the nose, the fragrance, and the element of fragrance-consciousness—these three—are in their fundamental nature entirely real.
It is solely the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously; this is the point of realization for Sundarananda.
From here on, the various realms differ from the preceding ones, as they merely refute consciousness and demonstrate its non-arising.
Although this [argument] now also relies upon consciousness (*vijñāna*), it ultimately refutes both the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) such that neither can be established.

Only afterwards does it conclude by stating that no *dhātu* (elements) can be posited. The intent of this comprehensive refutation is made even clearer here. The following sections shall all follow this pattern. Zhong says:
According to the two nostrils as a single nose, they receive the arrival of fragrance and stench. Regarding these two vapors of fragrance and stench, one takes fragrance as the object of cognition.
It comes. Is it known by means of fragrance? Or is it known by means of flesh? Or is it known by means of space? If one takes up olfactory cognition, by what is that cognition known to come?
If one takes up olfactory cognition, is it given as the grasping of the form of flesh? Or is it received because it arises dependent on the nose?
By what does the nose come to be? It arises dependent on the nose; the nose is its constituent element (*dhātu*). Or is it received because it arises dependent on fragrance?

Fragrance constitutes the objective field (*dhātu*). With the nose as the support and fragrance as the condition, olfactory consciousness arises. One root gives rise to two branches; from those branches, further branches emerge.
As this process unfolds, it becomes increasingly complex and entangled, difficult to disentangle. One should contemplate this minutely.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the tongue and thus take the tongue as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of flavors and thus take flavors as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it were to arise because of the tongue...
Then all things in the world—sugarcane, *ume* plums, *citratus* (*yellow-root*), rock salt, *acorus calamus*, ginger, and cinnamon—would have no taste at all.
You should taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste the tongue? The tongue does not taste itself.
What constitutes cognition? The nature of the tongue is not bitter; flavor does not arise of itself. How, then, can a realm [of consciousness] be established?

If consciousness arises dependent on flavor, then consciousness itself would be the flavor, just like the tongue-organ; it should therefore not taste by itself. How then could consciousness discern whether something is a flavor or not a flavor?

Furthermore, no single taste arises from a single substance. Since tastes arise from many [substances], consciousness should likewise consist of multiple entities. If the entity of consciousness were one, then that single entity would necessarily arise from tastes;
yet how could the various transformed characteristics produced by the combination of salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors all become a single taste?
It should be without discrimination. Since discrimination is absent, it cannot be called consciousness. How, then, could it be called the tongue-flavor-consciousness-element?

It is not from empty space that your consciousness (the character "tongue" is an error here) arises. When the tongue and flavor are in conjunction, within that very state there is fundamentally no self-nature. How, then, could an element arise?
Therefore, you should know that with the tongue and flavor as conditions, the tongue-consciousness-element arises; these three locations [are thus established].
If all these are absent, then the tongue, the taste, and the tongue-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
This clarifies that the triad of tongue, taste, and consciousness is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the tongue and taste serving as conditions to produce tongue-consciousness: does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its element?
"Furthermore, is it produced because of taste, and does it take taste as its realm?

Ānanda, if you say that this consciousness is produced because of the tongue, then it would not depend on the external object of taste, but the substance of the tongue itself would be able to distinguish and form tastes.
Thus, throughout the world, [the tongue would perceive] the sweetness of sugarcane, the sourness of the *ume* plum, the bitterness of *hōryaku* (coptis), and the saltiness..."
Rock salt, black pepper, fine zingiber, ginger, and cassia—these would all become tasteless [in comparison]. This is because taste resides in the tongue.
Since taste resides in the tongue, you should taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter? Let us consider one taste for a moment.
If the nature of the tongue were bitter, then your tongue would already be a bitter flavor; who then would come to taste the tongue? Since it cannot taste itself...
One tastes with the tongue. How is it that one perceives the tongue as having a bitter taste?
If the nature of the tongue is not bitter, then this tongue cannot even produce its own taste; how then can a constituent element (*dhātu*) be established to give rise to consciousness?
Thus, it is clear that this consciousness does not arise from the tongue. If it is claimed that this consciousness arises because of the taste, then it is...
Without relying on the internal faculty of the tongue-root, consciousness itself constitutes flavor. Consciousness is itself the flavor;
yet flavor does not taste flavor, just as the tongue does not taste the tongue. How, then, can one know whether it is flavor or non-flavor?
Furthermore, all flavors originally do not arise from a single substance. Since the flavor that produces them arises from many substances, that which is produced...

The consciousness [of these tastes] should likewise consist of multiple entities, just as a mother with many children must also be many. Therefore, the multiplicity of tastes destroys the singularity of consciousness.

If one were to say that the substance of consciousness is one and that this substance arises from taste, such that the resulting consciousness is not manifold, then the producing tastes should also be one.
However, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine in different ways.
If those that arise through transformation were each distinct, they ought to be of a single flavor and devoid of discrimination; just as the child is one, the mother would likewise have to be one.
Therefore, the oneness of consciousness destroys the multiplicity of flavors. Furthermore, consciousness receives its name precisely because it is capable of discrimination.
Since discrimination is absent, it cannot be called "consciousness. If consciousness itself lacks a name, how [can one speak of its objects]?
Why, then, would you further divide taste and the tongue into three separate realms? This would clearly demonstrate that this consciousness does not arise from taste.
It does not arise because of the tongue, nor does it arise because of taste. Apart from the tongue and taste, it cannot arise from empty space to produce your tongue-consciousness.
Thus, the calculation that it arises without a cause is also incorrect. If you claim it arises from the conjunction of the tongue and taste—
Since the sense faculty and its object have already merged into one, there are no two separate natures;
how could there be an intermediate gap to accommodate the arising of the element of consciousness? Thus, the theory that they arise together is also incorrect. Nor do they arise from themselves.
It is not born from another, nor born from both together, nor born without cause. From where, ultimately, does it come?

Therefore, you should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the realm of tongue-consciousness arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent, their characteristics being wholly illusory.

Thus, the tongue, the flavors, and the realm of tongue-consciousness—these three—are in their nature entirely true. Fundamentally, they are one, neither caused by conditions nor arising of themselves.
It is simply the wondrous nature of this. This is the point of entry for Pūrṇa’s awakening.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: when body and touch serve as conditions, body-consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because of the body and thus take the body as its realm, or does it arise because of touch and thus take touch as its realm? Ānanda, if it arises because of the body...

If there were necessarily no conditions for the two types of mental application—conjunction and separation—what would the body perceive? If it arises because of contact, then there would necessarily be no such thing as "your body";
who then, apart from the body, could know conjunction and separation?
This clarifies that the body, touch, and consciousness are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have understood—that the body and touch serve as conditions to give rise to body-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the body, such that the body constitutes its realm?

"Is it produced by contact, and does it have contact as its constituent element? Ānanda, if you say that this consciousness is produced from the body, then that contact which is perceived through conjunction would manifest as knowledge even when separated.
Since there are these two conditions—separation and conjunction—there is then the bodily consciousness of perception and observation.
If these two, conjunction and separation, were not present as the conditions for perception and observation, what would this body be?"
Is this not so? Thus, the single sense-faculty cannot be established on its own, nor does it arise from itself.

If you claim that this consciousness arises because of contact (*sparśa*), then generally speaking, "contact" refers to an object coming into contact with the body, whereby the body perceives it as cold, warm, rough, or smooth.
However, there must first be my body before one can perceive these qualities of cold, warmth, roughness, or smoothness.
The characteristics [of contact] consist of conjunction and separation. If these arose solely from touch, then your body would necessarily not exist.
Furthermore, who—apart from the body—could perceive conjunction and separation? Thus, it follows that the object does not arise independently, nor does it arise from anything other than itself.
Ānanda, objects do not touch cognition; it is the body that knows there is contact. To know the body is itself contact; to know contact is itself the body.

Yet, that which is contact is not the body, and that which is the body is not contact. These two characteristics of body and contact originally have no location. When combined with the body, they constitute the very nature of the body itself;

when separated from the body, they are merely the characteristics of empty space. Since neither the internal nor the external can be established, how could a middle be posited? A middle does not exist.
Furthermore, if both the internal and external natures are empty, from whom would your consciousness arise? From what could the realms (dhātus) be established?

Therefore, you should know that although body-contact serves as a condition for the arising of the body-consciousness realm, these three locations are all non-existent; thus, the triad of body, contact, and the body-realm are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, if you say that an object alone cannot produce cognition by itself through contact, but must join with the body for there to be the knowledge of contact—does this mean that only after the body and the object have joined does this consciousness arise together?
Yet, since it is said that the body knows there is contact, this nature of knowing is certainly manifest and evident. You should now examine this nature of knowing.
Does one know the body, or does one know touch? If you say one knows the body, then this knowing is itself the knowledge of touch.
Why is this so? Touch is the counterpart of the body; the nature of this knowing must be one with touch before it can be known as being in relation to the body.
If you say one knows touch, then this knowing is itself the knowledge of the body. Why is this so?
The body is the counterpart to touch. This cognitive nature must be one with the body before it can cognize touch as its counterpart.
Since this [cognition] belongs to only one side, how could it be co-arisen? Furthermore, as for this cognition:
If it belongs exclusively to contact, it cannot simultaneously belong to the body; thus, contact would not be the body.
If it belongs exclusively to the body, it cannot simultaneously belong to contact; thus, the body would not be contact.
Since it ultimately cannot belong to either one, how can they be said to arise together? Therefore, this cognition resides neither in the body nor in contact; fundamentally, it has no fixed location.
If it were to leave the touch and join with the body, then this cognition would be the very nature of the body itself.
If it were to leave the body and join with the touch, then this cognition would be a characteristic such as empty space. Thus, this cognition of touch exists both internally and externally.
All are without fixed location; neither internal nor external is established. How, then, could the middle be established?

Since the sense organs and objects that produce [consciousness] are not established, the consciousness produced by them is likewise not established. The middle no longer stands; internal and external natures are empty.
Since the consciousness produced is not established, the sense organs and objects that produce it are also not established. All three lack a position; the realms have no source.
[Objection: How can there be a principle of co-arising? [Response: It is not self-born, not other-born, and not co-born.

Therefore, you should know that with the body and touch as conditions, the body-consciousness-element arises. In all three locations, there is nothing at all; their characteristics are entirely illusory.
Thus, the triad of body, touch, and body-consciousness-element are in their nature entirely true. Fundamentally, they are one, neither caused by conditions nor self-born.
It is simply the wondrous nature of this. This is the point of awakening and entry for Upāli.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the mental consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the mind, taking the mind as its realm? Or does it arise because of mental objects, taking mental objects as its realm? Ānanda, if it arises because of the mind...
Within your mind, there must be something you are contemplating. To clarify your intention: if those preceding dharmas did not exist, the mind would have nothing from which to arise.

Being devoid of conditions, it would have no form; what then would consciousness be used for? Furthermore, your conscious mind, along with its various modes of deliberation and its nature of discernment—
Are they identical or distinct? If they are identical, then the mind is itself the mental faculty (*manas*). How, then, could there be that which is produced?

If they are distinct, then the mind would not be identical [to the faculty], and there would be no cognition. If there is no cognition, how can the mind arise? If there is cognition, how can one cognize the mind?
Thus, neither identity nor difference is established as a nature. How, then, can the realms (*dhātu*) be established?
This clarifies that the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand:
the mind takes mental objects as conditions to produce mental consciousness. Does this consciousness arise because it is produced by the faculty of the mind, and thus has the mind as its realm?
Or does it arise because it is produced by the dust of mental objects, and thus has mental objects as its realm? Ānanda, if you say this—

As for the statement that "consciousness arises because of the mind": within your own mind, there must first be some mental object (*dharmāyatana*) upon which you reflect, and only then does the characteristic of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) manifest. When the object exists, the mind exists;

if the previously reflected-upon mental object were absent, the mental faculty would likewise have nothing from which to arise. When the object perishes, the mind perishes. Furthermore, apart from this mental object...

As for the conditions (*pratyaya*), the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) likewise lacks any discernible form or characteristic. Even if the mind were able to produce consciousness, what would it have to use?
Furthermore, your "consciousness-mind" (*vijñāna-citta*) and the mental faculty that performs deliberation both take "discrimination" as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Yet, when distinguishing between the producing faculty and the produced consciousness, ultimately, what is the difference between the faculty and the consciousness?
Are they identical or distinct? If you claim that consciousness is identical to the mind, then consciousness would simply be the mind;

how then could the mind be designated as the producer and consciousness as the produced? If you claim that consciousness is different from the mind and not identical to it, then it must fall into the category of insentient matter and should therefore lack the capacity for cognition. Since it lacks the capacity for cognition, it cannot be said to arise from the mind.
If there is that which is produced, and if there is that which cognizes, then consciousness and the mind would share the same nature of discernment. What, then, would be consciousness?
And what would be the mind? If they are identical except for their difference in name, then even the two natures of the faculty and the consciousness cannot be distinguished.
Upon what basis, then, could the sphere of the arising of consciousness be established? Thus, it is clear that this consciousness does not arise from itself.
If worldly phenomena arise from causes, they do not exist apart from the five sense objects.
Observe that the phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch have distinct characteristics; they correspond to the five sense organs and are not subsumed under the mental faculty.
Your consciousness is determined to arise in dependence upon dharmas. Now, observe closely: what is the nature of each dharma?

If you set aside form and emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, conjunction and separation, and arising and ceasing—if you transcend all these characteristics, ultimately nothing can be apprehended.

When they arise, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together; when they cease, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together. Since their causes do not exist, how can there be a consciousness produced by them?
What form does it take? It has no characteristics or marks. How, then, could a realm arise? Therefore, one should know that with the mind and phenomena as conditions, the consciousness-realm arises.
Since these three locations are entirely non-existent, the mind, phenomena, and the mind-realm—these three—are fundamentally not causes and conditions.
It is not of a spontaneous nature.
If it is claimed that this consciousness arises from dharmas, then among all worldly dharmas, none are apart from the five sensory objects—form, sound, odor, taste, and touch.
These five objects are clearly and distinctly perceived as they confront the five sense organs; they are all not the mental organ (manas).

...is what is subsumed [by consciousness]. If you claim that your consciousness does not arise from the mind-faculty (manas), but is determined to arise based on the objects of phenomena (dharmas), then you should carefully observe these dharmas:

what shape do they take? If, apart from external objects such as form and emptiness, motion and stillness, openness and obstruction, sweetness and blandness, union and separation, this shadow of arising and ceasing were to have a distinct substantial reality of its own, transcending...

It exists alone, having transcended all prior characteristics; it cannot be apprehended. Therefore, when we speak of "arising," it is merely the arising of the shadows of the various phenomena of form and emptiness.
Apart from those characteristics, there is absolutely no further substantial essence of arising. When we speak of "ceasing," [it is likewise].
Thus, the shadows of the various phenomena of form and emptiness perish; apart from those various marks, there is certainly no further substantial essence of extinction.
Therefore, the arising and ceasing of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is precisely the arising and ceasing of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Apart from the five sense-objects, no separate arising and ceasing of mental objects can be found. Furthermore, as for the nature and characteristics of these causal mental objects, even when sought...
It cannot be apprehended; how much less can there be any visible form or characteristic of the consciousness produced from the dharma-object?
Since the characteristics of the dharma-object itself do not even exist, how could one establish a sense-field (*dhātu*) to give rise to consciousness?
This is clearly evident: this consciousness does not arise from another. It does not arise from itself. It does not arise from both. It is finished.
Ultimately, from where does it come? Therefore, you should know that with the mind and dharmas as conditions, the consciousness-element arises.

Since these three locations are entirely non-existent, their characteristics are wholly illusory; yet, as for the mind, the dharmas, and the consciousness-element—these three, their nature is wholly true.
This is simply the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā), which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.

This is the point of entry for Maudgalyāyana’s awakening. To speak of them collectively: within the eighteen realms (dhātus), all are fundamentally established by the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Since the very locus of establishment is empty, how could there be any branches or leaves produced from it? As no such location can be found, furthermore—
There is no boundary to rely upon; phenomena are deceptive and principles are empty. Sentiments are precarious and conditions are weak.
The root-stumps of evil views are entirely uprooted, and the nests of deluded consciousness are all overturned together. The true mind alone shines brightly, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "If one can directly realize the internal mind and harbor no doubt regarding external objects, once the mind is realized, all external objects..."
In emptiness, everything that meets the eye and evokes emotion is none other than the wondrous nature; even mud, soil, tiles, and rubble are entirely the family treasures.

○ This section on the union of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is missing. I, the fool, maintain that the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) are inherently without characteristics, unlike the first five sense organs and their objects, which possess real natures and realms.
Furthermore, within the analysis of their constituent parts, it is made exceedingly clear that they are void and non-existent. Therefore—

There is no longer any characteristic of co-arising to be refuted; it is not a case of a missing passage. ○ Zhong says: Within this text, the analysis is restricted to the triad of *manas*, *dharma*, and *vijñāna*.

Yet, various commentaries invariably cite other sources to divide the mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), further subdividing consciousness itself into the first consciousness, the seventh consciousness, and the eighth consciousness. This is truly fragmented and confused. Furthermore, the "consciousness-mind" is simply consciousness.

That "deliberation" and "discrimination" both refer to the *manas* (mental consciousness) follows the Master [Huiyuan] of the Lotus School; this differs from the old commentaries. Let the reader not harbor doubts.
○ The aforementioned old explanations may be taken as corresponding to the contemplation of "emptiness is identical to form" within the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.
○ Regarding the *Tathāgatagarbha* pointed out among the four categories: it is like pointing to firewood to indicate that there is fire, or pointing to a well to indicate its [water].
There is water. Pointing to the bellows, he indicates that there is wind. Pointing to the pores of the mustard seed, he indicates that there is space.
Subsequently, regarding the seven great elements revealed as the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*: it fills the volume of the firewood and the fire;
it is equal in volume to the trichiliocosm. It fills the volume of the well-water; it is equal to the ocean of fragrant waters. It fills the wind of the bellows.

The measure [of their capacity] is equal to that of the Vairambha wind; it fills the space within a mustard seed, equaling the extent of infinite empty space, and even extends to fill the realm of all crawling and wriggling creatures—all of these are equal and without distinction from the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
[The Eighteen Elements are concluded.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often said that all the various transformations of the world arise through the combination of causes and conditions, and are manifested by the conjunction of the four great elements.
How is it, World-Honored One, that the Tathāgata [speaks of] both causes and conditions and spontaneity?"

We have both been cast out. We do not now know to which category this meaning belongs; we only pray that you will take pity on us and reveal to sentient beings the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.

Previously, the World-Honored One refuted that wondrous enlightenment belongs to causes and conditions. Ānanda had already understood that the essence of nature is not caused by conditions and so forth;

yet, his attachment to all phenomena as being produced by causes and conditions remained as before. Now, having heard that the aggregates, bases, and elements are all not produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions, he again gives rise to this doubt.
It is because his previous doubt concerned the single nature, whereas this present doubt concerns the myriad phenomena.
