This means: "The nature of wondrous enlightenment is the dharma of quiescent extinction; it is the primary meaning (paramārtha) and does not belong to causes and conditions.

I have already heard Your Majesty’s command regarding this. As for the aggregates, bases, and elements, these are dharmas of arising and ceasing; they are the secondary meaning (saṃvṛti) and certainly belong to causes and conditions.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One exclude them all equally? Furthermore, in Your Majesty’s ordinary discourses, you always..."

The thesis is that all things arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions. That is to say, all things in the world—sentient and insentient, including the sense organs, the physical body, and the vessel-world of the environment—each possess various kinds of transformations;
all of these appear through the conjunction of the four great elements: earth, water, fire, and wind.
Then one should reject spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and not reject dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
How is it that the Tathāgata rejects both dependent origination and spontaneity? If what was not rejected yesterday is right, then what is rejected today must be wrong.
If today’s expulsion is correct, then yesterday’s non-expulsion was incorrect.
Furthermore, yesterday’s non-expulsion seems to fall into the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*), while today’s expulsion seems to fall into the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*).

Since both have fallen into one extreme, they are certainly not the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*) and appear to belong to mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), rather than being of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). I do not now understand the underlying intent of this expulsion.

Ultimately, to which category of teaching does this belong? We pray that you will take pity on us sentient beings and reveal to us the Middle Way of definitive meaning, the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation. Now, all phenomena arise through causes and conditions.

This precisely belongs to the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the gate of existence (*bhava-mukha*). It was a provisional response to Ānanda’s initial words, yet Ānanda conversely clung to it as definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Now, this sutra distinguishes characteristics from nature; and since this wondrous nature does not stagnate in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not produced by causes and conditions;
nor does it fall into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), so it is not spontaneous (*svabhāva*). This is the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, yet Ānanda—
Seeing all these [views] as mere refutations, they instead suspect them to be biased, nihilistic, and frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

This is indeed the delusion and inversion of ordinary people, caused by their habitual immersion in existence and their flight from emptiness; therefore, the Buddha severely rebukes them in the subsequent passage.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Because you previously felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi, I shall now reveal the ultimate truth for you."
Why do you further entangle yourself with the causes and conditions of worldly frivolous discourse and delusive thoughts?
Although you are learned, you are like a man who knows about medicine but cannot distinguish it when the actual medicine appears before him; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly to be pitied.
"I shall now analyze and explain this for you, so that those who practice the Mahāyāna in the future may also penetrate the true reality.
Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command.
This was said after first sternly rebuking those who are deluded and ignorant, and only then permitting the teaching. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In the past, you cherished and delighted in the Hīnayāna; therefore, I taught you the various Hīnayāna dharmas of the conjunction of causes and conditions."

This is the teaching of provisional meaning. Now that you have grown weary of and renounced the various Hinayana vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and have earnestly entreated me for unsurpassed Bodhi, I shall today reveal to you the supreme and ultimate truth.

Since you are unable to take up this burden, why do you instead entangle and ensnare yourself with the worldly frivolities and the causes and conditions of deluded thoughts that you heard in the past, refusing to let them go? Furthermore, all people in the world have proclaimed you to be foremost among the learned;
yet, upon hearing the True Dharma, you are unable to believe or understand it—just like someone who is... [well-versed in] worldly matters.
They record the names of medicinal herbs but do not recognize the true medicine; when it is brought forth and shown to them, they cannot distinguish it and instead give rise to doubt and confusion.
This is precisely what the Tathāgata calls those who are truly pitiable.

Yet this primary truth (paramārtha-satya) is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects; fundamentally, it cannot be distinguished and cannot be demonstrated. Now that you have already—
Enveloped by the causal conditions of frivolous discourse and deluded conceptualization, I have likewise employed skillful means to analyze and reveal this for you.

However, this present revelation not only enables you to penetrate the true reality (*tattva*), but shall also enable future seekers of the Mahāyāna to penetrate the true reality and together traverse the ocean of the Tathāgatagarbha. Thereupon, Ānanda—

He could not remain silent and spoke, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command. The sutra itself, from the point where the Buddha and Ānanda resolved their confusion, immediately rebukes him for his failure to comprehend the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Now, as the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are about to be clarified, it is further indicated that the *tathāgatagarbha*—the nature of the treasury—which emerges within the three great categories, is precisely this true mark.
Residing within the six sense faculties, its essential substance is the wondrous, subtle essence (*miāojīng*) inherent therein.
The "clarity" (ming) in the four categories refers to the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) which is the very essence of all phenomena.

The "origin" (yuan) in the seven elements refers to the Tathāgata-garbha mind which is the fundamental source of their substance. Being fundamentally pure and inherently pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, this alone is the true mark of all dharmas.
One who knows thus has attained penetration of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"Ānanda, it is as you have said: the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world.
Ānanda, if the essence of those great elements were not itself a combination, they could not intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not blend with various forms.
If they were indeed combined, they would be identical to transformations—arising through initial conditions and succeeding one another through birth and cessation."
Birth and death, death and birth; life and death, death and life—like a whirling firebrand, they never cease.
Ānanda, it is like water becoming ice, and ice returning to become water again.
Ānanda questioned only regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), yet the Buddha answered by addressing both their nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics.

This was because, although the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*) explain characteristics based upon nature, that "nature" is spoken of with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*); they do not state that [characteristics] are identical to nature.

Having long practiced those teachings, Ānanda was deluded by emptiness and followed after characteristics; thus, he calculated whether they were harmonious or disharmonious, unable to let go of these thoughts through successive turns.
Now the Buddha washes away their former habitual views; thus, he presents both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*) together, yet uses nature to dissolve characteristics.

This is because only when characteristics attain the dissolution of nature can the two dualistic attachments be simultaneously eliminated. The "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) are precisely these characteristics.
The nature of the great elements is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha-mind. The Buddha said:

"Ānanda, as you have stated, that the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world implies that these elemental natures and the substantial forms of the four elements blend together to produce these transformations. Yet, is this essential nature itself something that undergoes such combination?"

"Is it not a combination, Ānanda? If those great elements were not in combination, they would be unable to intermingle with their various characteristics, just as empty space does not combine with material forms.

How could one know that the nature of these elements follows conditions to form characteristics that are eternally distinct from the inert and discontinuous nature of empty space? Therefore, it is not that they do not combine. If those great..."
If nature were a composite entity, it would necessarily undergo change along with its characteristics. It would begin because of causes and end because of causes;
as it ends, it begins again, such that beginning and ending mutually constitute one another. From birth to extinction, and from extinction back to birth, birth and extinction continue in succession.

They arise in regular sequence—death following death and birth following birth—or they arise with intervals—birth and death followed by death and birth. (Like the transformation of a molting insect, there is birth followed by further birth; hence it is said:)
Life after life, at the end of the life in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one dies and then dies again; thus it is said that death follows death like a whirling firebrand, with no rest.
How could one know that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) truly cannot transform the nature (*dharmatā*), as the firebrand does not cease? Therefore, this is not a harmonious union (*saṃyoga*).

(Question: What is it that now manifests as the cycle of birth and death? Answer: It is like the moon’s shore, which does not move, while the cloud-boat appears to move. If reality were truly moving, how could one awaken to it and bring it to sudden rest?

Furthermore, essence and appearance are fundamentally not two separate things; there are merely the two aspects of "changing according to conditions" and "remaining unchanging. I shall provide you once more with an analogy.

Ānanda, although their nature is fundamentally one, they can manifest various characteristics according to conditions. Since this is not like empty space, which remains uniform and does not combine with others, you should know what this is like:
it is like water freezing into ice. For although water is of a single substance, [it takes on different forms].
When cold, it congeals and becomes ice; though there is no actual conjunction, it manifests the appearance of conjunction.
How can this be said to be definitively non-conjoined? Although appearances may differ in ten thousand ways, they can be melted back into their fundamental nature.
Since this is not like a whirling firebrand that never ceases, how should one regard it? It should be regarded as ice returning to water. For indeed...
Although water may freeze into ice, when it melts, it remains as water. It merely appears to be a combination, yet in the end, there is no change.
How can it be said that it definitely belongs to the category of "combination" (one should contemplate the word "yet" [還]; if it were truly a combination, it would undergo change.

For example, if blue and yellow were combined, they would transform into green; how could they ever return to being blue and yellow)? Question: Ānanda clung solely to the notion of "combination. Why did the Buddha...?
"Neither [of these views] are harmonious, and both are refuted. Response: "The two positions are mutually dependent.
If they were not both refuted, then after refuting their harmony, one would inevitably still regard them as non-harmonious. To refute them simultaneously is to block further conceptual shifts."

Zhong said: "If the nature of the four great elements were not in harmony with the characteristics of the four great elements, then nature would exist outside of characteristics, and the two would not intermingle, just as empty space is not in harmony with various forms.

This would be a partiality toward spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and a falling into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), because one knows that [nature] is unchanging while failing to know that it follows conditions (*pratyaya-anuvidhāna*). Now, True Suchness follows...
To form characteristics through conditions—how could this be the same as inert emptiness? It certainly cannot be so.

If it were a matter of conjunction, then the nature of True Suchness would undergo transformation along with these characteristics, subject to arising and ceasing from beginning to end, birth and death, death and birth, and birth, death, and birth again, like a whirling firebrand that never rests.
This would be a partiality toward causes and conditions, falling into the view of annihilationism. Because...
This is because they know [the mind] follows conditions, yet do not know its unchanging nature. Now, True Suchness (tathatā) remains constant while maintaining its own nature;
how could it be the same as the various marks of transformation and change? Furthermore, this is not so.
Observe the nature of earth: that which is coarse constitutes the great earth, while that which is subtle becomes minute dust, down to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal particle).
If one analyzes the boundary of the form of that ultimate atom, it is composed of seven parts; if one further analyzes that *paramāṇu*, it is simply the nature of true emptiness.

Ānanda, if these *paramāṇus* were analyzed until they became empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form. As for your current question regarding [the elements] arising from harmony—
Through their conjunction, the various transformative manifestations of the world arise. You should observe this single atom (paramāṇu): by how much empty space does it exist through conjunction?
It cannot be that atoms conjoin to form an atom. Furthermore, when an atom is analyzed and enters into emptiness, by how many material forms (rūpa) is empty space itself formed through conjunction?
If it were a conjunction of matter, then that which is conjoined would be matter, not emptiness; if it were emptiness...
Regarding "conjunction": conjunction with space is not a material form (*rūpa*). While material form may still be analyzed, how can space be conjoined?
This clarifies that the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) does not exist through the process of aggregation.

Furthermore, as for what is called "not non-conjoined" yet in reality "not conjoined," let us clarify this by taking the earth element as our example. To observe the earth element, one should observe the earth.
"Nature. You should first investigate the fundamental root and essential nature of earth. Whether it be the coarse great earth or the subtle motes of dust, all are the locus of the nature of earth.
By analyzing from the coarse, one proceeds through successive stages until reaching the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal particle).
This *paramāṇu* is that which is formed by dividing the limit of the extreme minute form into seven parts."
This may be called the subtlest of the subtle and the ultimate of the ultimate. By further analyzing even the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom), one eventually arrives at emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
[The "limiting characteristic of form" refers to the boundary of material phenomena; beyond this, there will be no further characteristics of form.
Ānanda, if these *paramāṇus* could be analyzed into empty space, you should know that empty space, in turn, can give rise to the characteristics of form and transform back into *paramāṇus*.

It is like seeing flowers in the sky vanish into the void, and then calculating that the flowers emerged from within the void. Generally speaking, as long as one does not understand that the true source of the myriad phenomena arises from the *ālayavijñāna*, no one will be able to escape this calculation. Therefore, among the ordinary and inferior of the Western Regions, [this remains the case].
This is no different from the theories of the "Limitless" (wuji) and the "Supreme Ultimate" (taiji) in this land; they are all nothing more than such erroneous attachments.
You have now asked how, through combination, the various transformed phenomena of the world arise; this is precisely what you mean by empty space giving rise to a *paramāṇu* (the smallest particle).
However, for there to be combination, there must be quantity—either two or three combining to form one. You should observe this single *paramāṇu* dust mote.
By how many spaces (*ākāśa*) are they combined to exist? If they do not combine with space, could it be that one *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal atom) is formed by combining [other] *paramāṇus*?
We have heard of the idea that by combining with another, something becomes itself; however, there has never been a case where something becomes itself by combining with itself.
Thus, if one maintains that various characteristics combine, this *paramāṇu* must also be a product of combination. If this *paramāṇu* already...
This is "harmony" (saṃghāta). It must be formed by uniting with emptiness; only then can it be called true harmony.

Furthermore, since the boundaries of form (rūpa) border upon emptiness, and form must unite with emptiness to be formed, so too must the boundaries of emptiness border upon form, and emptiness must unite with form to be formed.
If one were to analyze a minute particle (paramāṇu) that borders on emptiness until it enters into emptiness, how much form would it take?

Do the characteristics combine to form empty space? If you say that form only combines with form and cannot combine with emptiness, and that combining with form does not constitute emptiness, then one must also know that emptiness only combines with emptiness and cannot combine with form, and that combining with emptiness does not constitute form.
How, then, can empty space give rise to the characteristics of form? Furthermore, it is by entering into emptiness through the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) that it is so named.
It is said: "Analysis. Material forms possess substance; thus they may still be broken down. If space were like clouds gathering, it would not lack substance;
how then could it gather? Knowing that space cannot gather, one knows that the *paramāṇu* (the smallest particle) is not formed through combination.
Since the neighboring atoms (*paramāṇu*) are not themselves composite, the earth element is fundamentally not something that exists through combination.
How could this notion of combination be the ultimate reality? According to Ānanda, he relied solely upon coarse appearances; the Tathāgata, however, investigated down to the most subtle dust.
This is because, having already clung to the idea that all phenomena are composed of combinations, one must take the most subtle dust as the primary origin. Yet, even this subtle...
Dust and space are neighbors; one must inevitably fall into the error of their merging with space.
Therefore, if one clearly understands that space alone cannot be joined, then the calculation of their harmonious union will naturally be overturned and utterly destroyed.
"You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This establishes his own doctrine to demonstrate that both form and emptiness emerge from the Tathāgatagarbha. [He] transformed the earth and called it...
Regarding form (*rūpa*): earth is indeed the foundation of all forms. Now, form does not emerge from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), nor does emptiness unite with form.
Ultimately, from where does the great element of earth arise? If one investigates its source and course, it is originally nothing other than a thing within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
You usually know only to analyze form into emptiness and to combine emptiness to form matter, yet you do not know [the *tathāgatagarbha*].
Within the *ālayavijñāna*, the color that is inherently complete is the emptiness of the true substance;
the emptiness that is inherently complete is the color of the true substance. Emptiness and color are mutually fused, encompassing all in their unmanifest state.

Pure and unstained, they are primordially and naturally possessed, reaching to the limit of the non-external and penetrating to the limit of the non-internal, pervading the entire dharma-realm. Such is the nature of its total embodiment.
This Tathāgatagarbha is identical in principle to what was previously mentioned, yet its meaning differs. One should savor the significance of the word "middle" (or "intermediate").
To clarify this through an analogy: it is like a wealthy elder whose storehouse contains limitless treasures;

whenever he has a residence, he invariably brings out the treasures from the storehouse and displays them extensively throughout the halls and pavilions. Nevertheless, these are but one part in ten million of the total.
It is merely divided. Those that are deeply hidden and have not yet manifested are truly infinite in measure.
Thus, the four preceding categories are like pointing only to the treasures within a hall and pavilion, stating that they are all items stored therein.
Now, these seven great elements are like saying that these are but a small portion within the storehouse, while those that have not yet manifested fill each and every place at all times.

In every instance, its application is inexhaustible. Regarding the two phrases "nature" (xing) and "form" (se), because the two terms "nature-true" (xing-zhen) are non-different, they are used interchangeably as reflections of one another. If they were not used interchangeably, there would have to be four phrases, such as:

"nature-form is true emptiness," "true emptiness is nature-form," "nature-emptiness is true form," and "true form is nature-emptiness"; only then would the meaning be complete. Question: This and the *Prajñāpāramitā*...
If one asks: "Is it the case that what is spoken of as form is itself emptiness, and what is emptiness is itself form? Are they the same, or not? We reply: "In truth, they are vastly different.

For while the Prajñāpāramitā and other such teachings speak solely of the various manifested phenomena currently confronting us, the present teaching does not concern these phenomena currently before us;
rather, it speaks profoundly of the unmanifested principle within the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, this 'form'..."

The word "emptiness" (kōng) does not merely distinguish it from substantial form; it truly reveals its difference from the form that is itself emptiness within the conventional truth of phenomenal characteristics.
This word "emptiness" does not merely distinguish it from an emptiness of annihilation;

it truly reveals its difference from the emptiness that is itself form within the ultimate truth of phenomenal characteristics. ○ Zhong said: Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature is inherently empty. It is not...
It awaits the analysis of form to become emptiness; yet its nature is fundamentally identical to form, not awaiting union with emptiness to become form.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of their cognition, and manifests according to their karma.
Once the whole body is established, its wondrous function manifests. The ocean of nature contains all in profound depth, flowing forth all phenomena.

It is only because the minds of sentient beings within the nine realms have defilement or purity, their capacities are large or small, and their karma is good or evil, that each follows according to its own mind.
Each arises according to its measure; each manifests through the activation of its respective karma. Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* is transformed into the *ālayavijñāna*;
the body of *dharmatā* is transformed into the physical sense-faculties (*indriya-kāya*); and the realm of *dharmatā* is transformed into the material world (*bhājana-loka*).

This is called "the arising of characteristics from nature," wherein the characteristics are entirely identical to the nature. Therefore, it is said that the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is itself the nature within the *garbha*.
Furthermore, "sentient beings" encompasses all beings within the nine realms. "Mind" refers to their faculties and natures; "measure" refers to the scope of their cognitive awareness.
Faculties and natures vary in superiority and inferiority, while cognitive awareness varies in magnitude and smallness.
If one were to approach them solely with an inferior mind and a limited measure, and respond with coarse and meager forms, it would certainly not fail to accord with their minds.

It fulfills its measure. If one can bring it forth with a superior mind and a vast capacity, then that which responds with expansive and wondrous forms will likewise never fail to correspond to that mind and fulfill its measure. Regarding "manifesting according to karma":
first, as for all pure and wondrous forms in both the mundane and supramundane realms, if they do not follow those various kinds of pure karma, [they would not manifest].

Although one may wish for them to manifest, they cannot be made to appear. Second, regarding the various defiled forms of the three evil realms and the four miserable states—all of which are tainted by suffering—if one does not refrain from those various defiled karmas, although one may wish for them not to manifest, they cannot be prevented from appearing.
Question: Since an awakened person must follow karma, does the Buddha follow karma as well? Answer: While the Buddha was in the causal stage, he followed it; [in the stage of fruition...]
Once it has been initiated, it merely follows the mind; since there is not even a measure of what can be responded to, how could there be karma to be followed?
Apart from mere manifestation, there is no real karma.

The world is ignorant, deludedly regarding causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature; all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and devoid of any real meaning.
Now, since it is said that "karma manifests according to its activity," the arising of karma appears to have a source or basis.

Consequently, sentient beings of shallow wisdom in the world cling to these proximate causes of arising and are thus deluded into regarding them as the nature of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
They never realize the essence of following conditions without changing, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm; what need would there be for causes and conditions? As for karma—

It is established. It appears difficult to alter or shift; thus, ignorant sentient beings in the world cling to this unalterable direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and consequently delude themselves into regarding it as an inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
They never realize its function of remaining immutable while following conditions (*anuparivartana*), responding to the mind and adapting to circumstances.
How could they remain mired in the notion of "nature"? If one relies on causes and conditions, one calculates them as a combination; if one relies on "nature," one calculates it as non-combination.
"Harmony. However, all of these are merely the conceptualization, calculation, and inference of the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings;
when expanded, all verbal expressions are like this category of "harmony," "is," or "is-not," and possess no real meaning whatsoever.

If one follows the principle that "from nature arise appearances, such that appearance is entirely identical to nature," how could it be as you say? That which is called the *tathāgatagarbha* manifests as the earth.
Such is the greatness [of this teaching]. This is the Dharma-gate realized by the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (Dharaṇīdhara).

One should know that when the World-Honored One preached the Dharma, he never from the beginning departed from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*); he merely skillfully employed causes and conditions and spontaneity.
How could he have ever discarded them? Furthermore, one should know that regarding the four categories, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), he first dissected and shattered their false appearances.
Thereafter, he concludes by manifesting the reality of the nature. These seven great elements now serve to awaken one to the profound ocean of self-nature, from which all phenomena flow forth;
therefore, they exclusively characterize the reality of the nature, being utterly devoid of any deceptive terminology. This is truly the unique discourse of the Dharma-nature school.
This not only transcends the *prajñā* [discourse], but is also vastly different from the preceding text.
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions. Observe, Ānanda, those households within the city that have not yet eaten:
when they wish to cook, they hold a magnifying lens (*ādityamaṇi*) in their hands and seek fire before the sun. Ānanda, that which is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is like me and you.
There are one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus who now constitute a single assembly.
Although the assembly is one, when their origins are examined, each has his own body, and all have their respective clans and names of birth; for example, Śāriputra is of the Brahmin caste.
The lineage of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, down to Ānanda of the Gautama clan.

Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists through the coming together of causes, when one holds a mirror in the hand and seeks fire from the sun, does this fire come forth from within the mirror, or does it come from the tinder, or does it come from the sun? Ānanda, if it came from the sun, it would burn you yourself.
As for the moxa in your hand, the trees from which it originated should all be consumed by fire. If it emerges from within a mirror, it should naturally emerge from the mirror and ignite the moxa;
why then does the mirror not melt? Since there is no sign of heat even when you hold it in your hand, how could it possibly liquefy?
If fire arises from mugwort, why must it depend on the meeting of the sun and the mirror’s radiance before the fire is produced? You should observe this closely again:
the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the heavens, and the mugwort grows naturally from the earth; from what direction does the fire come to travel here?
The sun and its reflection are mutually exclusive; they neither blend nor unite. It is not possible that the fire of the lamp should exist spontaneously without a source.

You still do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire—pure and fundamental by nature, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of their cognition. Ānanda, you should know that when people hold a mirror in one place, fire arises in that one place;

yet if they were to hold it throughout the entire Dharma-realm, fire would arise filling the entire world. Since it arises pervading the whole world, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.
The world is ignorant of this and is deluded into thinking it is caused by conditions or is of a spontaneous nature; all such views are merely the discriminations of the conscious mind.
Such conceptual deliberations are merely verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
This clarifies that the great element of fire fundamentally arises from the *tathāgatagarbha*. Ānanda, among the four great elements, only the nature of fire is without self (*anātman*).
It takes form by dwelling within objects, just as it relies upon firewood or charcoal; being entirely dependent on various conditions, it lacks any intrinsic essence.

"It can indeed be grasped. Ānanda, observe the households within the city that have not yet eaten. When they wish to cook their food, they hold a *sūryakānta* (sun-crystal) in their hands and seek fire by turning it toward the sun.

Ānanda, if you say this fire is called 'conjunction' (*saṃyoga*), there must first be a characteristic of separation as the basis for that conjunction—just as there is between me and you, or between the one thousand two hundred [monks]."
Fifty bhikṣus are designated as a single assembly; this is true harmony. Yet, although the assembly is one, if one speaks of its fundamental basis, each has their own body, birth, clan, and name.
For example, Śāriputra emerged from the lineage of the Viśvāmitras, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana from the Kauṇḍinyas, down to Ānanda, whose family name was Gautama. If these were not [distinct],...

"From what does it originate? Who comes to provide its harmony? "Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of a combination [of conditions], then it should be like Śāriputra and others, each having their own clan and place of birth.
When that person holds a mirror and seeks fire from the sun, does this fire emerge from within the mirror, taking the mirror as its root? Or does it come from the tinder?"
[The fire] emerges. Is it from the sun? Or does it take the moxa and the sun as its basis?

Ānanda, if it were from the sun, since it can burn the moxa, all the trees in the place where it comes from should have been burned first. Yet why are they not burned? Therefore, it does not come from the sun.
If it were produced from the mirror, before the moxa has even caught fire, the mirror should have melted first; yet not only does it not melt—
If you hold it in your hand, it still shows no sign of heat; how then could it melt? If that were the case, it would not have emerged from the mirror.
If it were produced from the moxa, the moxa should produce it of its own accord; why would it depend on the sun and the mirror?
If it is produced only after the light of these things meet, then it is not produced by the moxa. Not only this: even the three objects—the sun, the mirror, and the moxa—each have their own origins.
Come! It is like a mirror held by a hand, the sun coming from the heavens, and moxa growing from its own base;
yet from which direction alone does the fire come to travel here? Since it has no point of origin, how can it serve as the basis for conjunction?
Furthermore, that which is called "conjunction" must consist of things meeting and intermingling in a single location. Today, [the sun] is in the heavens.
The mirror is in someone's hand; it is suspended at a great distance. How could there be such a union? When opened, there is no place from which it arises;
when closed, there is no characteristic of union. How could it be that the fire-light exists of its own accord, coming from nowhere?
You should understand this with a start. I have already clarified it for you, yet you still do not know.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Thus, it follows the mind and responds to measure. If ordinary people were to hold mirrors in one place, fire would arise in that one place;
it is too small to be broken. If held throughout the Dharma-realm, it arises filling the world; it is too large to be carried. Up to this point...
When it arises pervading the entire world, can one still say that it has a location that can be delimited?
It is simply the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā) manifesting according to karma. The world is ignorant and deludedly regards this as being caused by conditions or arising spontaneously;
these are all mere conjectures of the mental consciousness. All such verbal explanations lack any real meaning—how could they be worthy of discussing this principle with?
Ah! This is the Dharma-gate realized by Acala (Ucchuṣma). ○ Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* states:
"The *yangsui* (sun-crystal lens) is made of copper and shaped like a mirror. When it reflects an object, the image appears inverted; when directed toward the sun, fire emerges.

○ The distinctions between opening and closing closely resemble [the principle that things] are not born from themselves, not born from another, not born from both together, and not born from no cause.

Both concern arising; yet, though the phrasing appears similar, their underlying meanings differ. The former [text] addresses those who, due to attachment, maintain that all phenomena have an arising, and thus it provides a detailed refutation of the characteristic of arising to reveal that there is no arising at all.
This [text], however, addresses those who, being ignorant of the true source of dharmas, falsely claim they emerge from a combination of conditions;
therefore, it meticulously examines their origin so that they may awaken to the true primordial source before concluding. Thus...
That [text] focuses on refutation, whereas this one emphasizes examination.
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing have no constancy.
For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the mahāsiddhas Kāpiḷa, Jāṅgala, and Padma-Hrasvaja, among other great illusionists, who sought the essence of the moon to use for their concoctions.

It is like a magical elixir. When these masters, during the daytime of the bright fortnight, hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon, does this water emerge from within the gem, or does it exist of its own accord in the air, or does it come from the moon? Ānanda, if it comes from the moon, [how could there be such a thing as] "water"?
Yet it can still cause the pearl to draw water from afar; the trees and forests it passes by all respond by discharging streams.

If they discharge [water], what need is there to wait for that which comes from the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror used for drawing dew)? If they do not discharge [water], it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon. If it emerges from the pearl, then within this pearl—
It should flow constantly; why wait for midnight? If it were produced from the white moon during the day, and since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless.
If this were so, both humans and devas would all be submerged together. How, then, could there still be those who travel by water, on land, or through the air?
Examine this further with careful attention: the moon ascends from the heavens; the pearl is held by a hand; the water-basin that receives the pearl was originally set out by a person.
From what direction does the water flow here? The moon and the pearl are far apart; they neither blend nor unite. It cannot be that the water-crystal has arisen of itself from nowhere.
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water.

Pure and inherently luminous, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. According to the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of their cognition. If one person grasps at a pearl in one place, water appears in that place;
if the entire Dharma-realm grasps at it, water arises throughout the entire Dharma-realm. When its arising fills the world, how could there be any fixed location?
They manifest according to karma. The world is ignorant of this and is deluded into regarding them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature;
all of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and devoid of any real meaning.
This clarifies that the great source of water originates from the *tathāgatagarbha*. Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed;
it follows the presence or absence of rain and dew, and the filling or emptying of streams and sources, such that its flow and cessation are never constant.
For example, within the city of Śrāvastī, there were the sages Kapila (Blue), Cakravāka (Mandarin Duck), and Padma (Red Lotus). Kṣa... [text truncated]
Many great illusionists, desiring to obtain the essence of the moon to compound with their magical elixirs, falsely calculate that water issues forth from the moon.
Thus, on a night during the waxing phase of the moon when the moon is at its zenith at midday, its light is as bright as day.
Holding a *fangzhu* (the "dark mirror," a water-crystal bead used as a sun-gem), one catches the water from the moon. Does this water emerge from within the bead?
Does it exist of its own accord in the air? Or does it come from the moon? Ānanda, if it were to come from the moon...
If a jewel is in a distant place, it can still cause water to emerge; likewise, all the trees and forests through which it passes should be made to discharge their flow.
Just as when the moon is directly south, all the trees and forests to the south of the jewel are places through which it travels;
or, if the jewel is on level ground, then all the trees and forests upon the high elevations are likewise [its domain].
In all places where it has passed or flowed, it ought to discharge as a stream. If it flows, why wait for it to emerge from the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror)?
If it does not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon. If it were to emerge from the pearl itself, then within this pearl—
It should constantly emerge from the water; why wait for the middle of the night to receive the moon before the water arises?
If it were produced from space, then as space is boundless, the water would likewise be limitless. From humans to devas, all would be submerged together.

How then could there still be creatures that travel by water, land, or air? This further fails to establish a logical principle. You should observe this more closely: the moon [descends] from heaven...
The water rises; the pearl is held in the hand; the basin that receives the pearl is set out by people.
These three things all have their origins. From what direction alone does the water flow here? (Excluding the empty basin, for emptiness has no origin and thus cannot serve as an example.
Furthermore, the moon and the pearl are separated by a vast distance; they do not occupy the same place, nor are they blended or joined. Whether open or closed, they remain distinct.
[The questioner] was at a loss. [The Buddha said: "It should not be water-crystal. It comes from nowhere, yet it suddenly exists of itself. If that is so, then ultimately from where does it arise?

I have already explained this to you twice, yet you still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, following all sentient beings."
The mind arises; one should know that which is to be measured. Therefore, when one grasps a pearl in one place, water emerges in that same place.

When grasped throughout the entire Dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire Dharma-realm. It arises filling the world—how could there be any fixed location? If one carefully investigates, all are merely manifestations following karma.
Those in the world who lack knowledge delude themselves into thinking these things are caused by external conditions or arise spontaneously; they are all...
From the six consciousnesses arises pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*); it exists in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) but does not exist in terms of principle (*tattva*).
It is merely empty talk; how could there be any real meaning? This is the Dharma-gate realized by the youth Candraprabha.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.
When you regularly adjust your robes to enter the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī robe moves and reaches a person nearby, whereupon a subtle breeze brushes that person’s face.
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, arise from empty space, or is it produced on that person’s face? Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*...

When you were wearing your wind-cloak, its garment fluttered and swayed; it ought to have separated from your body. Now that I am preaching the Dharma, my robe hangs down within this assembly. Look at my robe: where is the wind?
It cannot be that there is a place for the wind to be hidden within the robe. If it were produced in empty space, [it would have to be so].

Your robe does not move; for what reason is there no waving? If the nature of emptiness were eternally abiding, wind should be constantly produced. If there were times when there was no wind, empty space would have to perish.
If the perishing of wind could be seen, what would be the appearance of the perishing of empty space? If it possessed arising and ceasing, it could not be called empty space.
It is called "empty space. How could the wind emerge? If the wind were produced from the face that it brushes against, then it should brush against you as you adjust your robe yourself;
why then do you brush it away? Examine this closely: it is you who are adjusting your robe.
The face belongs to that person; empty space is quiescent and does not participate in movement. From which direction does the wind come to stir here?
The natures of wind and space are distinct; they neither blend nor unite. It cannot be that the nature of wind exists spontaneously without a source.

You simply do not realize that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, it is like when you, as a single person, slightly move your robe and a subtle breeze arises;
it sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm, fills the lands, and pervades the world. How could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.
The ignorant of the world are deluded, taking it to be caused by conditions or by a nature of spontaneity; all such views are merely the discriminations of the conscious mind.
Such conceptual deliberations are merely words; they possess no real meaning whatsoever.
This clarifies that the wind-element fundamentally originates from the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substantial body;
its movement and stillness are not constant. It is like a fan: it moves when shaken and is still when not shaken. When you regularly adjust your robes and enter a great [assembly]...
"O assembly, when the corner of your saṃghāṭī (the great robe) suddenly moves, and a bystander is present, a slight breeze brushes that person's face.
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the saṃghāṭī? Or does it arise from empty space?
Or is it produced from that person's face? Ānanda, if one were to say that this wind emerges from the corner of the saṃghāṭī..."
The *kāṣāya* is itself wind. When you don the *kāṣāya*, you are merely donning wind. The nature of wind is movement;
thus, your robe should also flutter and separate from your body. Furthermore, if your robe is wind, then my robe must also be wind.
As I now preach the Dharma, my robe hangs down within this assembly. Look at my robe: where is the wind? It cannot reside within the robe.
This is a place where the wind is stored; thus, it does not arise from the clothing.
If you claim that this wind arises from empty space, ordinary people hold such a view even more frequently, as when they say, "emptiness gives rise to wind.
However, if it is said to arise from space, it ought to arise spontaneously; why then rely on the movement of clothing as a condition? If your clothing does not move, then [the wind]—
Nor is there any wiping away. Furthermore, emptiness takes permanence as its essential nature, while wind takes arising and ceasing as its essential nature.
If wind were to follow emptiness, then wind should also be permanent; if emptiness were to follow wind, then emptiness should also cease.
While the cessation of wind can be perceived, what would be the form of the cessation of emptiness? Thus, that which possesses arising and ceasing cannot be called [emptiness].
Since space is called the space that is neither born nor extinguished, how could the wind of birth and extinction emerge from it?

If that were so, it would not have emerged from space. If you claim this wind arises from the surface being brushed, then since it would arise from that surface, it should blow favorably toward you; why then must you wait for you to adjust your robes?
At that time, the whisking motion was directed toward him and did not strike you; therefore, it did not arise from your face.
Examine this again with careful scrutiny: the adjustment of the robe belongs to you, the face belongs to that person, and empty space remains unmoving.

From which direction does the wind come, stirring itself to arrive here? If you insist that it comes from space, then the wind is moving while space is still; their essential natures are thus discordant and separate.
Being separate, they cannot be in harmony or union. It is certain that space does not give birth to wind; therefore, the nature of wind should not be non-existent [within space]. (Note:

This passage speaks specifically of the discordance between the essence of wind and the essence of space. It differs slightly from the previous two sections on the great elements, which primarily clarified that they are not in harmony or union.)
"I have already explained this three times from my own perspective, yet you still do not clearly understand the true meaning within the Tathāgatagarbha (and so forth).
Do you not seek what is called the 'true meaning'? This is the Dharma-gate realized by Vairocana-prabhā.
Furthermore, suppose there were a wind inside a sealed room; if one says there is wind, why does it not move?"
It is said that there is no wind; it arises only when meeting with conditions. Thus we know that the wind-element is itself unmoving, while movement belongs to the various conditions.
Furthermore, when one examines these conditions, each is found to be non-existent. Within the interplay of conditions, none possess self-nature (*svabhāva*); it is merely the movement of the mind.
When one turns back to examine the mind itself, the mind is likewise unmoving, for the mind has no form and its point of origin cannot be apprehended. Thus one knows that all [is empty].
It arises from the true nature (*dharmatā*). If it did not arise from the true nature, one would only see the true nature pervading the worlds of the ten directions.
Because the nature is unified with the true void, it is said that "the nature-wind is the true void," and "the nature-void is the true wind.
What is meant by "nature-void"? The *He Lun* states: "If the nature of earth were substantial, it could not be changed. Yet Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body can transform the great earth."
When it becomes gold, the earth element is suddenly lost. How could what preceded it have been real? If the nature of water were real, it could not be changed.
When devas and humans see water, they call it lapis lazuli; when hungry ghosts see water, they call it fire; when fish see it, they call it their dwelling. How then could it be real?
If the nature of fire were real, it could not be changed. Thus, the *śigru* tree grows from within the fire. [West...]
In a certain country there is a cloth called "fire-washing. How can that be real? The nature of wind is real, yet it cannot be altered.
When Li Zhi rides upon it and travels, how can that be real? Furthermore, earth has the nature of solidity, yet when melted it falls away and becomes the nature of moisture;
water has the nature of moisture, yet when cold it transforms into the nature of solidity. Therefore, Nāgasena said: "Earth, water, fire..."
The elements of wind and so forth possess no substantial reality; they exist merely as names.
Ignorant people claim that earth and the other elements are real, but when the noble ones observe them with the eye of wisdom, they see them as nothing but deceptive illusions.

It is like a child who, seeing a reflection in a mirror, joyfully desires to seize it, while an adult observes that it merely deceives the eyes. Thus, one knows that earth, water, fire, and wind have no substantial reality.
Therefore, Panshan said: "The three realms have no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The four great elements are originally empty;
upon what does the Buddha dwell? The celestial sphere is unmoving; it is silent and wordless. Face-to-face presentation—there is nothing more.
This may serve as a general commentary on this matter. Zhong said: "What is meant by 'brandishing the whisk upside down'? It means that wind arises from there."
As for the face: when you adjust your robe, there is originally no wind within the robe itself. While your robe has no wind, that face has wind;
it brushes against you as a favorable breeze. Now, this wind produced at that face instead brushes back against that very face—is this not a perverse brushing?

Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form. For example, in a place far from the river in the city of Śrāvastī, various Kṣatriyas (the royal caste), Brāhmaṇas (the pure-living caste), Vaiśyas (merchants and farmers), Śūdras (laborers), as well as Pahlavas and Caṇḍālas (butchers), have recently established a residence.
While digging a well to seek water, when they have removed soil one foot deep, within that [space] there is...
A cubit of empty space; likewise, even when one has excavated soil to the depth of one zhang, one obtains one zhang of empty space in its midst.
Whether this space is shallow or deep follows the amount excavated. Is this space produced because of the soil being removed, or does it exist because of the act of digging?
Or is it born of no cause and arises spontaneously? Ānanda, if this space were born of no cause and arose spontaneously, why did it not exist before the soil had been excavated?
Obstructed; one sees only the great earth, with no passage through it at all. If space emerges because of the earth, then when the earth emerges, one should see space entering.

If the earth emerges first and there is no space entering, how can empty space emerge because of the earth? If there is no such entering or emerging, then space and earth must originally have no different causes.
If they are not different, they are the same; if they are the same, then when the earth emerges, why does space not [emerge] as well?

[The space] emerges. If it emerges because of the digging, then the empty space would emerge from the digging and should not emerge from the earth. If it does not emerge because of the digging, then the digging itself emerges from the earth;

how then can you see the empty space? You must examine this again with the utmost precision and observe carefully: the digging proceeds from the person's hand and revolves according to its direction, while the earth shifts because of the ground.
As for this empty space, from what does it emerge? Is the digging and the empty space real or unreal? They do not act as one another's cause.
It is neither a product of combination nor of union. It cannot be that empty space arises from nowhere on its own.
This directly points to the Great Element of Space as merging with the preceding four great elements to return to the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, the nature of emptiness has no form;
whether square, round, large, or small, it has no fixed definition, but is merely manifested through the presence of substantial matter. For example, like a room...
In the city, at a place far from the river, various kṣatriyas down to the caṇḍālas established a summer retreat.
They dug a well to seek water; when they first excavated soil one foot deep, there was one foot of empty space within it.
Even when they had excavated soil ten feet deep, they obtained ten feet of empty space. The depth of the empty space corresponded exactly to the amount of soil that had been excavated.
If it is small, it is shallow; if much, it is deep. Yet both depth and shallowness are empty.
Does this emptiness arise because of the earth? Is it due to the digging? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
Ānanda, if this emptiness arose spontaneously without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth was dug? And why is the great earth so vast [only now]?
If there is no penetration [of space], then this clarity must arise from the excavation of the earth; how then could it be established as being causeless?
If this emptiness were to emerge because of the earth, then the earth would have to emerge first and the emptiness enter afterward, like digging a pond and then drawing water into it.

However, while the emergence of the earth can be seen, what is the characteristic of the entry of emptiness? Since there is no characteristic of emptiness entering, one must conclude that it emerges because of the earth.
To claim that there is emptiness [apart from the earth] is an error. Since it is said that emptiness has no coming or going, then emptiness should have existed even before the earth emerged.

Now, emptiness and earth are of one essence and fundamentally lack any cause for difference. If they are not different, they are identical; if they are identical, then when the earth emerges, emptiness must emerge along with it.
Thus, at the very moment the earth emerges, why does emptiness not emerge as well? This further demonstrates that it is not the case that [emptiness] emerges because of the earth.
Furthermore, if this emptiness were produced by digging, it would follow that one was merely digging at emptiness and never at soil;

thus, what emerged would be emptiness and should not have been soil. If, because it was not produced by digging, you instead argue that it was not produced by digging and has no connection with the act of digging, then the digging itself would produce soil and one should not see emptiness. Why is this so?

Is it that as you dig, you see space? If so, then it would be caused by digging and not by the absence of obstruction; such a thing is simply impossible. You should examine this further with precision.
Examine it thoroughly and observe it with extreme care: the digging proceeds from the hand, effort is applied to the ground, and the earth is displaced because of that ground.
All that is moved out from within the earth does not act as a condition for space. And yet, it is thus.
From what does empty space arise? (Since that which lacks a cause is not a real dharma, it is not taken as an example.

If you insist that it emerges from the excavation, then the excavation must excavate something real, whereas space remains empty. These two dharmas—the real and the empty—cannot function as one another's support.
Their functions are mutually opposed; they cannot establish the principle of arising through harmonious conjunction. Whether opening or closing, both possibilities are exhausted.
It should not be that space arises from nowhere of its own accord.
If this space were by nature perfectly pervasive and fundamentally immovable, then one should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind manifesting before us—
All are equally named the five great elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing.

Ānanda, your mind is clouded and deluded; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should contemplate whether space emerges or enters, or whether it neither emerges nor enters.

That being so, from where does this empty space ultimately come? All people in the world know that earth, water, fire, and wind are called the "four great elements," yet they do not realize that space is also a "great" element.
If the nature of this empty space is perfectly round and all-pervasive, fundamentally unshakable, what should it be named?
You should know that it is designated by the same name as the earth, water, fire, and wind currently before you.

Regarding the five great elements: these five great elements are of one identical nature, truly perfect and harmonious; they are all simply the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing.
While you may have no doubts when it is said that space is the Garbha, you might still hesitate when it is said that all four [elements] are the Garbha.

I fear that your mind is darkened by ignorance and delusion; you stubbornly cling to the notion that the four great elements are a mere combination, refusing to abandon your old habits and failing to realize that these four elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. If you do not awaken to this, you should simply observe the element of space:
examine whether it has coming and going, or whether it is without coming and going. If you realize that the element of space is immovable and all-pervading...

It is perfect, neither emerging nor entering, and not that which neither emerges nor enters; this is precisely the realization that the four great elements are neither compounded nor conjoined, yet not non-compounded and non-conjoined.
Yet you still doubt whether they are not all the Tathāgatagarbha.
"You do not know at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. According to the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of what they know.
Ānanda, just as one well produces one space within it, so too is it with the empty space of the ten directions. Filling the ten directions, how could it have a specific location? It follows karma."

I have discovered that the world is ignorant, deludedly taking causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature to be real; these are all merely conceptual calculations of the discriminating consciousness.
They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no actual substance.

Moreover, the more you speak, the more confused you become. You do not understand at all that the inherently endowed awakening within the Tathāgatagarbha is true emptiness, and that the inherently endowed emptiness is the essence of true awakening. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It conforms to the mind and responds to its measure; it is perfect and without fixed direction.

It appears solely because phenomena manifest according to karma, yet those ignorant ones deludedly regard it as being caused by external conditions or arising spontaneously. These are all merely the activities of the six consciousnesses;
how could their words possess any real meaning? This is the Dharma-door realized by the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha. ○ The nature of awakening is true.
The two phrases concerning "emptiness" (śūnyatā) have altered their phrasing from the preceding section and furthermore inverted the order of the sentences.
Previously, the fundamental Great [Perfection] (ben-da) was employed in conjunction with emptiness to form a fusion; thus, the fundamental Great is itself the character for emptiness.

Following the previous precedent, it should have been stated as "intrinsic emptiness" (xing-kong) or "true emptiness" (zhen-kong), as the wording could not differ. Now, the "emptiness" that previously referred to intrinsic nature has been replaced by the character for "awakening" (jue).
Thus, the "emptiness" (kōng) in this context refers to the character for "empty space" (ākāśa). If one were to follow the previous [passage] without inversion, it should have read:

"the true awakening of the emptiness of nature" (xìngkōng zhēnjué) and "the true emptiness of the awakened nature" (xìngjué zhēnkōng). In the present text, the two phrases are transposed; however, the meaning remains unimpeded.

Ānanda, seeing and awareness are devoid of cognition; they exist because of form and emptiness. It is just as it is for you now in the Jeta Grove: in the morning there is clarity, and in the evening there is darkness.

Even if it were the middle of the night, there would be light during the bright fortnight and darkness during the dark fortnight. Thus, clarity and darkness are distinguished by the faculty of seeing.
Is this seeing then the same substance as the clarity and darkness, or is it one with the great empty space? Or is it not?

Of one substance. Or identical yet not identical; or different yet not different. Ānanda, if this seeing were fundamentally of one substance with light, darkness, and empty space, then light and darkness—these two substances—would mutually negate each other; when it is dark, there would be no light.

When there is light, there is no darkness. If light were identical to darkness, then when light appears, vision would vanish. If they were necessarily one with light, then darkness should be extinguished;
if it were extinguished, how could one see either light or darkness? If light and darkness are distinct, then seeing is without arising or ceasing. How then can they be one?

If this essence of seeing were not of one substance with darkness, light, and empty space, then when you are separated from light, darkness, and empty space, what form or appearance would you discern as the source of seeing?
Separated from light, separated from darkness, and separated from empty space, this source of seeing would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.
Since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct (the character "distinct" [異] is used here in the sense of "separated" [離]), from what could seeing be established? Light.

Darkness and light are mutually opposed. How could they be the same? Apart from these three [elements], there is nothing; how could they be different? Yet, as space and vision are divided, they originally have no boundaries;
how could they not be the same? When seeing darkness and seeing light, their nature does not change; how could they not be different?

You should examine this further, examining it more and more minutely, scrutinizing it with precision and observing it with clarity: light comes from the sun, and darkness follows the dark moon; they pervade...
The clouds belong to the void; they condense and return to the great earth. In this same way, from what source does this essence of vision arise? Vision is cognizant while the void is inert;
they are neither a composite nor a union. It cannot be that the essence of vision arises of its own accord without a cause.
This direct pointing to "seeing" integrates with the preceding five great elements as returning to the Tathāgata-garbha.
"Seeing" is precisely the "greatness of the sense-faculties" (*indriya-mahābhūta*). It encompasses all six faculties; however, it merely cites the visual faculty as an illustration.

Yet, it takes only the nature within the faculty and does not take the superficial, physical organ (*bu-chén*). Therefore, although it speaks of "seeing" and so forth, it does not speak of "the eye" and so forth. This section—
Previously, by examining whether the visual consciousness and its objects are identical or different, and so forth, the false attachment to their "conjunction" (*saṃghāta*) was refuted.

Within this context, the characteristics of the objects are indeterminate, opening and closing between two or three categories. For instance, to speak generally of "form and emptiness" (*rūpa-śūnyatā*) is to combine light and darkness in contrast to emptiness.
To speak only of "light and darkness" is to open up form as encompassing emptiness. To speak of "light, darkness, and emptiness" together is... [the combination of all three].
"Opening up form to correspond with emptiness": this refers to seeing emptiness. "Only speaking of seeing emptiness" means citing emptiness to encompass form in order to correspond with seeing;
they alternate between concealment and manifestation, which is the subtle artistry of textual composition. "The awakening of seeing" is synonymous with the nature of seeing (seeing-nature).
Ānanda, the nature of seeing is detached from external objects and has no other object of knowledge; it exists only because of the two appearances of form and emptiness.
I shall now enumerate the present objects before us: the brightness of morning and the darkness of evening are the light and dark of the day;
the bright moon and the dark moon are the light and dark of the night. It is through these appearances of light and dark that the faculty of seeing can be analyzed. This...
Is this seeing identical in essence to light and darkness, or is it the great void that is neither light nor darkness?
Is it one with them, or not one? Is it both the same and different, or neither the same nor different?
Ānanda, if this seeing were originally one essence with light, darkness, and space, then light and darkness would mutually...
Opposing and usurping one another: when it is dark, there is no light; when it is bright, there is no darkness. If they were to merge as one, they would necessarily conflict with one another.

When they merge, seeing arises; when they conflict, seeing ceases. How then can one speak of "seeing light" and "seeing darkness"? Therefore, we know that light and darkness differ according to their conditions.
Yet you see that the substance [of vision] is ever-present; this demonstrates that it is not a single entity.

If this essence of vision is not a single entity with light, darkness, and so forth, then when you are separated from light, darkness, and empty space, what form or appearance would this fundamental analyzed vision have?
If you insist on seeking its characteristics, they would be no different from the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. This is because light, darkness, and empty space—...
Emptiness. Since all three are devoid [of self-nature], this seeing originally has no inherent substance; furthermore, from what could seeing be established?
Speaking from the former perspective, it would seem they are different; speaking from the latter perspective, it would seem they are the same.
However, light and darkness are ultimately opposed to one another, unlike the one who sees light and the one who sees darkness. How could they be the same? Apart from light, darkness, and emptiness—
Third: Since from the beginning there is no self-substance, how could there be difference? If it were so, would it not be neither identical nor different?
Yet, seeing and appearance are fundamentally one substance; one wishes to divide them into emptiness and seeing, yet fundamentally there are no boundaries to be divided.

How can they not be identical? Seeing darkness and seeing light, the nature of seeing does not shift; though objects differ, seeing remains one. It is manifest that they are not the same. How [can they be]?
How can they not be different? [They may be considered] as: (1) identical; (2) different; (3) either identical or different; or (4) neither identical nor different.

When one investigates through successive stages, none of these can be established. You must examine this more minutely—not merely minutely, but increasingly minute; not merely examining, but with thorough scrutiny.
Having already observed it with earnest investigation, you must now scrutinize that very observation with even greater precision. Scrutinize! Scrutinize!
In your contemplation, you must exhaustively investigate its source before ceasing. Thus, you will see that light follows from the sun and darkness follows the dark moon;
by extension, you will find that what is open belongs to empty space and what is obstructed returns to the great earth—all have their own origins.
Yet, from where does this essence of seeing arise? If you claim it does not arise from light or darkness, but definitely arises from empty space, then [consider] seeing...
Then there is awareness; emptiness is merely inertness. Awareness and inertness are not a composite in their essence. Knowing does not emerge from emptiness;
whether [the eyes] are open or closed, both are exhausted [in their nature]. Thus, the visual essence should not be able to emerge of its own accord from nowhere.

If this is so, then ultimately from what does it emerge? "Visual awareness" refers to the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). It constantly abides in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and does not give rise to discrimination. Therefore, it is said:
It is devoid of cognition; yet it must manifest through the emptiness of form. This is what is meant by "remaining unchanging while following conditions.
If one perceives that the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, then one should know that this is the boundless, immovable void.
Together with the movements of earth, water, fire, and wind, these are collectively called the six great elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*). Their nature is truly perfect and interfused;

they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing. Ānanda, your nature is submerged in saṃsāra because you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should observe this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they born or do they perish? Are they the same or different? Are they neither?

Arising and ceasing are neither identical nor different; you have never known this. Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing is luminous awareness, and the essence of awareness is luminous seeing.
It is pure and fundamental by nature, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of what is known.

Just as a single faculty of sight perceives throughout the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognition of tactile sensation—all these wondrous virtues are brilliantly clear and universally pervasive.
The Dharma-realm is all-pervasive throughout the ten directions; how could it have a specific location? It manifests according to karma.

The world is ignorant and deludedly conceives of it as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind. They are nothing but words and have no actual reality.

This assembly returns to the nature of phenomena. If this essence of seeing, together with hearing and cognition, is by nature perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that it is like the unmoving empty space compared to the moving earth, water, fire, and wind.
All are equally named the six great elements. Their nature is truly perfect and interfused; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing, and nothing more.

Ānanda, because you have sunk into delusion and are mired in provisional views, you lack the wisdom for transcendence and fail to realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—where "knowing" includes the nose, tongue, and body—the six faculties are all the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate this seeing and hearing.
Regarding this awareness: as for its own substance, it is neither arising nor ceasing; in relation to external objects, it is neither identical nor different;

it is neither subject to arising and ceasing, nor is it neither identical nor different. If you can awaken to the fact that seeing and so forth are neither arising and ceasing nor identical and different, yet also not non-arising and non-ceasing nor non-identical and non-different, then you will know that the nature of the store-consciousness is perfectly constant—neither a combination of elements, nor something that is not a combination. You...

One has never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the vision within the nature is precisely the clarity atop awakening; the essence of true awakening is precisely the vision of the luminosity of the nature.
(This follows the same principle as "the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form," all being expressions of the nature subsuming and fusing with phenomena.

When the nature and vision are mutually identical, this is the state within the Tathāgatagarbha where the true substance has not yet emerged, wherein seeing is entirely awakening; it is not the root of fetters belonging to ordinary beings.
This seeing is a vision of total awakening; it is not the silent, quiescent awakening of the two vehicles. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings and responding to the measure of their cognition, its wondrous function is manifested.

Speaking of it in terms of a single faculty, this faculty of seeing itself pervades the Dharma-realm, such that hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the perception of touch are likewise present within it.
One awakens to the realization that these are all the virtuous functions of the wondrous nature. Luminous and unobscured, they are pervasive and perfect;
how could there be any fixed location to grasp? This is for no other reason than that they manifest according to karma.
Depending on pure karma, they may even further manifest immeasurable sense-faculties and bodies; depending on defiled karma, they may even manifest as solitary, narrow, and inferior faculties.

The body—whether it be the immeasurable root-body (such as the Thousand Hands and Thousand Eyes) or the limited and inferior root-body (such as crawling insects)—which of these is not the great function of responding to conditions according to the mind?
Yet the world remains ignorant, deludedly regarding them as [the result of] causes and conditions (and so forth). How could there be any real substance in this?

This is the place where Mahāsthāmaprāpta realized perfect penetration. Question: Since this already takes only the nature within the sense-faculties, and it was previously revealed that these faculties are entirely the substance of the nature (*dharmatā*), why is it necessary now to laboriously integrate them again into the "Great"?
Answer: According to the specific intent of this sutra, both awakening and realization depend upon the six sense-faculties; therefore, [the previous section] specifically...

To reveal the entire substance of the nature: according to the general purport of the various sutras, it is only the *tathāgatagarbha* that constitutes the comprehensive characteristic of this nature.
Therefore, we now once again integrate the six sense faculties into the *tathāgatagarbha*. (Zhong says:)
"Nature-seeing, awakening-clarity, awakening-clarity-spirit, spirit-seeing": this refers to the seeing within nature, which is the clarity of original awakening;
