the clarity of original awakening is precisely the seeing of the clarity of nature. How could you have previously taken the eye to be seeing? ○ He said:
Because Ānanda identified with the combination of the four great elements, the preceding section rebuked him for his failure to awaken to those four elements. Therefore...
Ānanda mistakes the nature of seeing for the eye; therefore, this section rebukes him for his failure to realize the greatness of seeing.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and objects.
As you now survey the assembly of holy ones here, your eyes move through them one by one. As those eyes look around, they are like a mirror—there is no separate analysis. Your consciousness...
Within this, he pointed them out in succession: "This is Mañjuśrī; this is Pūrṇa; this is Maudgalyāyana; this is Subhūti;

this is Śāriputra. [He asked: "Does this consciousness that cognizes arise from seeing, or does it arise from forms, or does it arise from empty space, or does it emerge suddenly without any cause? "Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were to arise within seeing..."
Just as with ignorance, darkness, form, and space—these four are necessarily absent; fundamentally, your seeing does not exist.

Since the nature of seeing itself is non-existent, from what could consciousness arise? If the nature of your consciousness were produced within the objective phenomena and did not arise from seeing, then since you do not see light, [how could it perceive darkness?]
Nor does one see darkness. Since light and darkness do not impinge upon it, there is neither form nor emptiness. If even those characteristics do not exist, from what could consciousness arise?
If it were to arise from emptiness, it would be neither characteristic nor seeing. Without seeing, there is no discernment; thus, it cannot by itself know light, darkness, form, or emptiness.

It is not that the conditions for its extinction are absent; yet seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place in which to be established. Since it abides in neither of these two states, emptiness is the same as non-existence.
Existence is not the same as an object. Even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what would you distinguish? If there is no cause, how could it suddenly emerge?
"Why do you not distinguish the bright moon at midday? You should examine this more closely; examine it with subtle scrutiny.

When the seeing relies upon your pupils and projects toward external objects, it can be characterized as 'existent' and cannot be characterized as 'non-existent. Given that such consciousness arises in dependence [on these conditions], from what source does it emerge?"

The movement of consciousness makes seeing clear; they are neither blended nor conjoined. Hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognition are likewise so (it should not be that consciousness arises from no cause or source).
This direct pointing to the element of consciousness (vijñāna-mahābhūta) integrates it with the preceding six elements to show that they all ultimately return to the Tathāgatagarbha.

As for the sense organs (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya), these are categorized as only six; the reason there are no seventh or eighth is that the eighth [consciousness] is identical to the aforementioned element of the sense organs, and the seventh is likewise identical to the mental faculty (manas-indriya).
The word "nature" (xing) here refers to its essential form or characteristic (tǐxiàng), not to the ultimate true nature (zhēnxìng). Ānanda, the nature of consciousness...
It has no source; it arises and ceases in an instant, resembling a wild fire. It arises only by falsely relying upon the six kinds of sense organs and their objects.
For now, let us take as an illustration the case of the present visual consciousness, which arises delusively due to its organ and object, and discuss it by way of analogy.
"You should now survey this assembly of sages. Let your eyes range over them: the act of observing is the faculty (*indriya*); the assembly of sages is the object (*viṣaya*);
and the ranging of the gaze is consciousness (*vijñāna*). As your eyes look around, let it be just like a mirror—without further analysis, as the myriad phenomena are reflected therein.
When not a single thought arises, this is precisely the characteristic of the faculty. Your consciousness within this [is the eye-consciousness, together with its attendants]."

The eye-consciousness and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) are termed "recollection-based conceptualization" (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). This occurs only with respect to the primary object (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) and arises as the first moment of thought, not yet associated with names or designations. Following the eye-consciousness, it is termed "discriminative conceptualization" (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*).

This also arises with respect to the primary object, but in the second moment, it involves the conceptual grasping of names and designations, such as labeling [an object] as "Mañjuśrī" and so forth. However, this applies to the eye-faculty; by extension, the same holds true for the other four [sensory faculties]. As for the mental faculty (*manas*), when it operates independently of the five consciousnesses, it takes "solitary images" (*kevala-pratibimba*) as its objects;
these are also included within this category. Successively pointing them out: "This is Mañjuśrī," and so on until "This is Śāriputra. This consciousness—
First, as for that which cognizes: does it arise from seeing? Does it arise from forms? Does it arise from empty space?

Or does it emerge suddenly without any cause? Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were to arise within seeing, then it should be able to produce seeing itself independently of the four kinds of objective phenomena—namely, darkness, light, form, and emptiness.
I understand. However, if the dust has no root when it is removed, and the seeing-nature itself does not exist, from what could consciousness arise?

This would mean that consciousness is not produced by the sense organ alone. If your nature of consciousness were born from within the objects of perception, then it should not depend upon the seeing-organ.
It does not require seeing light, nor does it require seeing darkness; yet the characteristics spontaneously give rise to consciousness.

However, if the sense organs are removed and there are no objects, one neither gazes upon light or darkness, nor beholds form or emptiness. Since those characteristics do not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?

In that case, consciousness would not arise from a solitary object. If you claim that this consciousness arises from emptiness, being neither the mark (*nimitta*) nor the seeing (*darśana*), then if it were not seeing, color and emptiness could not be distinguished;
it would be the same as the previous case where the sense organs are absent and there are no objects. If it were not the mark, then the sense organs would have no basis to stand upon;
it would be the same as the previous case where the objects are removed and the organs do not exist. Situated between this state of being neither mark nor seeing, consciousness—
If its substance were like space, it would be identical to a tortoise’s hair. If the substance of consciousness existed, it would not be the same as material objects.
Since it lacks an intrinsic nature, how could it have function? Even if it were to give rise to your consciousness, what would it distinguish?
Thus, to claim that consciousness arises from emptiness apart from the sense organs and their objects is even more untenable. If you say this consciousness has no cause and arises suddenly—
As for that which "emerges," there is no moon within the eye; yet suddenly the consciousness that discriminates the bright moon arises—how truly abrupt this is!
And how could consciousness be such a thing? Thus, to say that it arises without cause is even more untenable. You should examine this further with great subtlety and scrutiny:
you see that [the visual faculty] relies upon your pupils and projects toward external objects; the sense organ (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*) are distinct and can be clearly described.
Existence is established; non-existence is not established. Form and emptiness are clearly distinct; these four are each unmixed with one another. Yet, from whence does such consciousness arise?
If one insists that it arises solely from seeing, then consciousness has discrimination and is called "movement," while seeing lacks discrimination and is called "clarity.
Since the movement of consciousness and the clarity of seeing are not of a unified substance, how could they be in harmony? As for hearing... [he] heard.
All that is perceived is merely a state of clarity and attachment. Since none of these are produced through a combination of conditions, none are born from consciousness.
When one investigates this through successive analysis, it cannot be that consciousness serves as their condition; could they possibly emerge spontaneously without any source?

If this consciousness-mind fundamentally has no origin, one should know that its capacity for discernment—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—is perfect, tranquil, and its nature does not arise from any source.
Together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are collectively termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their natures are truly interfused and perfectly harmonious.
All are the Tathāgatagarbha; fundamentally, they are without arising or ceasing. Ānanda, your mind is coarse and flighty;

you do not realize that seeing, hearing, discerning, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate these six consciousnesses of the sense bases: are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent?
Are they neither the same nor different? Are they neither empty nor existent? Fundamentally, you do not know the nature of consciousness within the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is luminous and harmonious. The true consciousness of enlightened clarity is wondrously aware and profoundly still, pervading and encompassing the entire dharma-realm;

it contains and exhales the ten voids—how could it have any fixed location? It manifests according to karma. Those in the world lack understanding and are deluded into thinking it is caused by conditions or arises spontaneously;
these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating mind. They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no actual reality.

If this consciousness-mind originally does not arise from the conditions of the sense organs and their objects, you should know that this discerning consciousness, together with the faculties of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, is perfect, tranquil, and not confined to any location.

Together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are collectively termed the "Seven Great Elements. When their characteristics are integrated, they return to the faculties; when the characteristics and faculties are integrated, they return to consciousness.
Yet what are these marks, views, and consciousnesses? They are all the true nature, perfectly interfused; they are simply the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing.
Ānanda, your mind is coarse and flighty; you are deluded by shallow talk concerning attachment to marks and lack the profound wisdom that is precise and penetrating.
You have not realized the awareness that arises from the six sense faculties, such as seeing and hearing.
Consciousness is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should observe the consciousness-mind of the six sense bases:

whether they are the same or different, empty or existent, neither the same nor different, and neither empty nor existent. If they were the same, then the characteristics of the internal and external would not be distinct.
If they were different, they would not mutually recognize one another within their own nature. If they were empty, there would be no manifest discernment.
If they were existent, there would be no trace of them to be perceived. The same applies to the case where both are negated.

When both "is" and "is not" have vanished together, the single truth naturally remains alone and serene. Furthermore, all people in the world know cognition as cognition and awareness as awareness; you, too, [do so].

It is the same here. Although I have repeatedly revealed this, even now you do not know that the truly real consciousness within the *tathāgatagarbha* is precisely this wondrously luminous cognition, the luminosity of original enlightenment; that this wondrously luminous cognition is precisely the truly real consciousness.
They are mutually fused and mutually identical. If this is so, why must it be called "consciousness"? One might as well call it directly "wondrous awakening. This wondrous...
The essence of awakened nature is profoundly still and ever-luminous, pervading throughout the entire dharma-realm.

It manifests as great function, encompassing and containing the empty space of the ten directions, interpenetrating all without interval; how could it have any fixed location? (Regarding the phrase "it does not follow the mind or correspond to objects": "mind" here refers to the consciousness-mind, and "objects" refers to the objects of consciousness.
It does not follow itself, just as the eye cannot see itself. That it suddenly appears as consciousness is solely because it manifests in accordance with karma; for all such cognitions...
Each arises only by means of seeds, and these seeds must depend on past karma; therefore, one must follow karma.

Nevertheless, their manifestation does not depart from the true essence. This meaning is not understood, and the world remains ignorant, deludedly regarding them as causes and conditions arising spontaneously.

All these are due to recognizing this consciousness-mind and giving rise to pervasive conceptual grasping (*parikalpa*). Even the various discussions regarding the transformation of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) into awakening belong to expedient discourse;
how could they possess any ultimate reality? This is the gateway to perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-prativedha*) realized by Maitreya.
Zhong said: "The generation and completion of the myriad dharmas do not depart from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), yet they are established upon emptiness.
Because of the sense organs (*indriya*) there is sensation; because of consciousness (*vijñāna*) there is cognition. Thus, there are seven. That which exists everywhere is called 'great.

These seven greatnesses encompass the aggregates (*skandha*), bases of cognition (*āyatana*), and realms (*dhātu*). They are revealed layer after layer. Previously, it was discussed how each and every one of these is the true nature (*tathatā*). Subsequently...

He then explains that each and every one of these pervades the entire Dharma-realm. The former [section] reveals that the essence of each phenomenon is inherently true and eternal; the latter reveals that each phenomenon is perfectly interfused and all-pervasive.

This proceeds from the shallow to the deep. The preceding passage stated that earth, water, fire, wind, and space are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, which is perfectly interfused and all-pervasive.
Up to the point of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), it merely says:
Its fundamental nature is the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet it has not yet reached the state of perfect fusion and universal pervasiveness.

Therefore, at this point, the two great categories of "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are brought forth to supplement the preceding meaning. "Seeing" refers to the sense organs; earth, water, fire, wind, and space refer to the objects (*viṣaya*); and "consciousness" refers to...

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the twelve spheres (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) do not go beyond the triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness.

Therefore, it is said that [the Master] brought forth "seeing" and "consciousness" to supplement the preceding meaning. It appears redundant yet is not redundant; it appears concise yet is not concise.

This is also a place where the text is interwoven with a grand and imposing structure. While those who interpret the scriptures certainly do not prioritize the literal words, they nevertheless cannot ignore them if they do not understand [the underlying principle].
Regarding the method of composing essays, one cannot avoid encountering obstacles at every turn when following the thematic principles and logical structures of the scriptures.
In the texts of the Four Sections, each paragraph concludes by stating that there is no fixed location; in the texts of the Seven Sections, every paragraph likewise states this.
How could there be any location? All these are merely the single phrase "the locus of mind and consciousness," from which many branches and leaves have grown forth.
Because Ānanda identified every object as having a location, the World-Honored One refuted them one by one according to the Dharma.

Later, when the World-Honored One spoke of "establishing a basis through causal logic," only then did [Ānanda] know the place where that basis was established. It was only upon entering the stream and losing all objective referents that he finally understood.
Know that the method for removing what is grasped lies in the single character "what" (suǒ). This one word is truly the great pivot between delusion and enlightenment. Question:
This sutra first directly refutes the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*), searching it through seven locations until it is found to have no essence whatsoever.
Even in the passage on the manifestation of seeing, it refutes it by way of collateral arguments, never showing the slightest leniency. Why, then, does it later [allow for] the eighteen [dhātus]?

The realm (*dhātu*) is already admitted to be the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*, the wondrous nature of *tathatā*. Reaching this point, it is even more described as pervading the entire *dharmadhātu* and encompassing the ten voids;
this is the complete embodiment of that nature. How is it that what preceded was the height of delusion, while what follows is the pinnacle of truth?
Answer: The former refers to the awakening and cultivation of the initial mind, which must proceed by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*).
To discern the true from the false, abandon the root of birth and death, and grasp the wondrous mind of nirvana, one must exhaustively shatter and resolutely discard consciousness.
Subsequently, through the universal integration of perfect understanding, there is no phenomenon that is not true and no phenomenon that is not as it is;

even down to the atoms of lands and the thoughts of kalpas, everything is nothing other than the single true Dharma-realm—how much more so the conscious mind, which cannot fail to be integrated with the Dharma-realm.
Ah. The old commentaries claim that the preceding sections may correspond to the "Contemplation on the Non-obstruction of Form and Emptiness" within the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.
This is not understood; rather, all of the above are responses to Ānanda’s deluded attachments, wherein each instance of delusion is reconciled so as to return to the True.

This is precisely a matter of subsuming phenomena into principle (*li*) and fusing appearances (*xiang*) into nature (*xing*). It has not yet reached the stage of arising appearances from nature or...

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their bodies and minds completely cleared away, attaining freedom from all obstructions.
Each member of this great assembly individually realized that their own mind pervaded the ten directions and perceived the emptiness of the ten directions.
Just as one observes the objects held in the palm of one's hand, so too all things that exist within the entire world are none other than the wondrous, luminous, and primordial mind of Bodhi.
This essence of mind is pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions. Turning back to observe the body born of one’s parents, one sees it as such.
It is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions—whether it remains or vanishes, it is indistinguishable;

or like a single bubble floating on a vast, tranquil ocean—its arising and ceasing leave no trace. Thus, with clear self-knowledge, you have attained your original, wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible.
Prostrating before the Buddha with palms joined, he experienced what he had never known before. In the presence of the Tathāgata, he spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha;

this section describes his awakening. At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, understood that there are three ways to shatter the deluded mind:
first, by seven refutations to secretly demonstrate its lack of location; second, by repeated interrogation...
The first three [verses] refute the non-mind by alternating between concession and refutation to determine its lack of substantiality;

this may be called the most subtle and exhaustive of the exquisite methods for destroying the deluded mind. The manifestation of the true mind also has three parts: first, the demonstration of seeing and so forth.

Furthermore, it precisely accords with their faculties and natures to point directly to its essential substance; second, it demonstrates the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth, extensively dissolving all phenomena to clarify their single essence;
third, it demonstrates the stages (*bhūmis*) and so forth, most thoroughly manifesting their perfect interfusion to reveal their complete totality.
Thus, that which reveals the true mind is also extremely subtle and utterly exquisite. Having received such [instruction]...
He revealed this. Thereupon, those whose bodies and minds had previously been at ease became instead utterly open and expansive;
they attained great mastery and great enjoyment, no longer bound by fetters or hindered by obstructions. Moreover, it was not only Ānanda;
each member of this great assembly came to know for themselves that this mind pervades the worlds of the ten directions, its measure being boundless. Previously, it was merely...

This was known by relying on the Buddha’s words; it was not self-knowledge. Now, for the first time, you have personally accepted and gained confidence in yourself, no longer turning according to the verbal instructions of others.

Previously, your capacity for vision reached only as far as the First Dhyāna. Now, you see the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as observing items such as palm leaves held in the palm of your hand.
Previously, you were turned by external objects, or you viewed objects as being other than the mind.
Some may say that material objects are illusory; yet now we see that all things existing within the world are none other than the wondrously luminous, primordial mind of Bodhi.
Previously, amidst a state of confusion and turmoil, we took this to be the nature of the mind, and were certain that it was deludedly situated within the physical body.
Now, however, we know that the essence of the mind is pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions and covering the entire world.
Ordinary people all say that space envelops the world, the world envelops the body, and the body envelops the mind; thus, they are bound layer upon layer, never transcending them.
Now, the mind envelops the ten directions and the body encompasses the exterior of space; inner and outer have been exchanged, and large and small have been transformed.
This is truly what is meant by "wondrously being able to turn things over. Yet, when one looks back at this physical body born of one's parents, it is as if it were empty space.
A single speck of dust within the center is uncertain whether it exists or perishes; a single bubble on the ocean has no trace of its arising or ceasing.
One should no longer abandon the ocean to recognize the bubble, nor mistake the bubble for the ocean. Previously, one did not know where the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) leads;

one did not know the nature of the mind that is quiescent and eternal; one did not know the locus of the inversion of body and mind; one did not know that the seeing-nature is the mind; and one did not know the [five] aggregates...
The sense bases and elements are the Tathāgatagarbha. Previously, I did not know that the seven great elements pervade the entire Dharma-realm;

now, I clearly know this for myself, and all doubt has vanished. Formerly, when the World-Honored One revealed the wondrous nature of precious luminosity—the originally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the mind—I was unable to recognize it despite having attained this mind. Now, I have attained it...
This fundamental wondrous mind is eternally abiding and indestructible; it does not depend upon recognition.

This is precisely the moment when Ānanda let out a cry at the "mouth of power," the point where one lets go of hand on a precipice. It is what is called: "The scale-weight has been moved to the very tip of the beam;
suddenly forced down, it performs a somersault. Thereupon, Ānanda prostrated to the Buddha with palms joined, having attained what he had never experienced before. And so, Ānanda...

At the place where he had seen and realized [the truth], he spoke a verse before the Tathāgata to praise the Buddha. ○ He-he said: "In the 'shattering of the false,' the seeing-essence is also shattered;
this is shattering it down to the subtle and wondrous point. In the 'revealing the true,' all myriad phenomena are revealed as true;
this is revealing them down to the subtle and wondrous point. Therefore, it is called the 'subtle and wondrous revelation. " ○ Zhong said: "[He] knew for himself."
The phrase "the mind pervades" is the primary point. Below this, from the great to the small, each layer is illuminated and shattered; all of this proceeds from the character *zhī* (to know).

Furthermore, the two lines "clearly knowing for oneself" serve as a summary. At the beginning of the first fascicle, the World-Honored One first states that [sentient beings] do not know the eternally abiding true mind.
Thus, it is evident that the single character *zhī* is the gate to all wonders. It should be understood thus.
To know the timing: it was merely said that within empty space there are the myriad things; within the myriad things there is the body; and within the body there is the mind.

My minor delusions no longer confuse my mind regarding the presence [of the mind] within the physical body. Previously, the World-Honored One reproached me for not knowing the eternally abiding true mind;

It is like a destitute beggar who suddenly obtains a precious jewel—how could I not rejoice and offer praise, and vow to repay this kindness?
The two know their own names; above and below they correspond.
Wondrously profound, all-holding, the Honored One of Immovability—the King of Śūraṅgama, rare in the world!

The first phrase praises the Buddha. "Wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*) praises the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the quality of *prajñā*.
"Dhāraṇī" praises the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is the quality of *vimukti*. "Immovable" praises the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*), which is the quality of *dharmakāya*.

"World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) is one of the ten titles. The four characters "Śūraṅgama-rāja" praise the Dharma. The three characters "rare in the world" offer a dual eulogy for both the Buddha and the Dharma.
All are difficult to encounter. "Perverted conceptions" refers to the discriminative grasping at the two notions of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
Just as one grasps at the discrimination of objects as the characteristic of the mind, and reckons the five aggregates and four elements as the characteristic of the body;

being deluded, one locates the mind within the physical body, identifying external objects as oneself and mistaking oneself for external objects. Thus, regarding the myriad phenomena of body and mind, one claims each has its own [independent existence].

Regarding the essential nature: the fact that the four great elements are entirely the result of the harmonious combination of causes and conditions, and so forth—matters that have been a source of delusion for billions of kalpas—are now all simultaneously dissolved.
As for the *saṃghī*: according to the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school, one passes through one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* (incalculable eon) prior to the stages;

from the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the eighth stage, one passes through another *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; and from the ninth stage to the Buddha-stage, one passes through yet another *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. Only after this does one attain [enlightenment].
Regarding the ultimate Dharmakāya: whereas [the gradual path] does not now require the arduous passage through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas to attain the Dharmakāya, this refers to sudden enlightenment.

Speaking in terms of gradual cultivation, one proceeds from the minute to the manifest, moving through the stages of confidence, abiding, practice, and penetration, up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), before finally realizing the ultimate fruit. Speaking in terms of sudden enlightenment, however, it occurs in a single thought-moment.

Non-arising, with the severance of the prior and subsequent limits, is what is called Buddhahood. Since it does not even involve the gradations of stages and positions, how could it involve passing through kalpas?
Long ago, the butcher Wide-Face came before the Buddha’s seat; his ignorance was suddenly extinguished, and he set down his knife.
He said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am counted among the number of the thousand Buddhas. The Buddha immediately confirmed this.

Indeed, by merely laying down his butcher's knife, he was already included in the number of the Buddhas; now that Ānanda’s Dharma-eye is clear and bright, it is only fitting that his words be granted.
May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges.
Bringing this profound resolve to serve every land within the dust motes, this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

This is the vow made after awakening. When I had not yet seen the Dharmakāya, I thought to myself that only the Buddha alone had attained the nature of enlightenment, while all sentient beings were entirely without such a share; therefore, I did not seek the path of Buddhahood above.
Previously, I did not save sentient beings. Only today do I realize that the Buddha and sentient beings are equal and non-dual.

Therefore, I vow to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and also vow to save sentient beings. Since the World-Honored One has, through various skillful means, explained this in detail and at length, enabling me to perceive this Dharma of equality, such profound kindness is truly difficult to repay. Now, I—
To distinguish these two kinds of profound resolve: above, one serves the Buddhas of countless eons; below, one delivers sentient beings across countless lands.

This is precisely what enables one to repay the profound kindness that is so difficult to repay—what is called a true dragon obtaining water, which immediately allows it to surge forth with waves and billows.
I prostrate and entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: I vow to enter first into this world of the five turbidities;
as long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall not pass away into *nirvāṇa* here.

This clarifies the vow to save sentient beings. In the past, during the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, I feared this Sahā world of the five turbidities, where all evils were rampant and beings were stubborn and difficult to transform; therefore, I made a vow to uphold this sūtra in a foreign land.

Now, beholding the equal Dharma-body, he has once again aroused great vows; thus, in this world of the five turbidities, he has vowed to enter it first, intending to deliver all sentient beings before entering parinirvāṇa.
As it is said: "As long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall likewise not take up nirvāṇa.
This is what Kṣitigarbha meant when he said that only after all sentient beings have been delivered will he realize Bodhi; this is precisely what is meant by "extensive."
This is the Great Mind.

Great Hero, Great Power, Great Compassion! I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions, so that I may quickly ascend to Unsurpassed Enlightenment and sit at the site of the Way throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Even if the nature of Śunyatā (empty space) were to perish, this diamond-like mind would never cease.
It moves and turns.
Yet such is my wish; how can I guarantee that it will surely be fulfilled?

For although my coarse delusions have been eliminated, the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies accumulated within the roots, along with their various unnamed categories and enumerations, have not yet been exhausted.

thoroughly eliminating my subtle delusions so that my four abodes may be instantly exhausted and the two deaths forever extinguished, enabling me to quickly achieve perfect enlightenment and universally establish a site of practice.
Only then can it be truly realized. As for my vow to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below, how firm is its resolve?

That emptiness is without substance and cannot be extinguished; yet, even if it were possible to extinguish it, this adamantine and steadfast mind of mine shall never regress. As it is said: "Even if space should come to an end, my vow shall not."
This is the ultimate state. World-Honored One, may You take this into Your compassionate consideration. ○ *Śūnyatā* (Śunyata) means emptiness; *Sakala* means solidity.

Upon receiving this single instruction, he suddenly attained his original mind. Subsequently, when he applied the principles, he attained sudden enlightenment; riding upon that awakening, all [delusions] were simultaneously eliminated.
It is so. I further pray that you may attain the fruit and ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment, wherein the perfect fusion does not obstruct the sequential unfolding.

Thus, although the Dharma-body is fully realized, it does not preclude the further removal of subtle delusions or the progressive passage through the various fruits; for subsequent matters must necessarily be eliminated gradually.
This refers to the sequential exhaustion [of the afflictions]. One who can shatter the solid core of sentient beings' delusions is called Mahāvīra (the Great Hero).

One who can uproot the deep roots of sentient beings' delusions is called Mahābala (the Great Powerful One). One who can bestow upon sentient beings the bliss of the two provisions (*saṃbhāra*) is called Mahāmaitrī (Great Loving-kindness).

One who can extract from sentient beings the suffering of the two deaths is called Mahākaruṇā (Great Compassion). The four abodes are: the ground of abiding in desire-attachment, the ground of abiding in form... [and so forth].

The dwelling-place of craving (*tṛṣṇā-vāsabhūmi*); the dwelling-place of craving for the formless (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā-vāsabhūmi*); and the dwelling-place of views in all places (*sarvatra-dṛṣṭi-vāsabhūmi*). There are two types of death:

death by segmentation (*paricchinna-maraṇa*) and death by transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*). From the entry into the main teaching (*samyak-artha-praveśa*) up to this point, the first cycle of the Dharma discourse—named "The Cycle of Destroying Delusion to Reveal Reality" (*mṛṣā-bhañjana-tattva-prakāśana-parivarta*)—is concluded. This completes the major section on the "Empty Tathāgatagarbha" (*śūnya-tathāgatagarbha*).

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, being among the great assembly, rose from his seat and bared one shoulder.

yet now, hearing the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s voice, it is as if a deaf person were trying to listen from beyond a hundred paces."
As for mosquitoes, they were originally not even seen by us, let alone heard of.

The sound of the Dharma you have preached has already dispelled my lingering doubts and regrets.

World-Honored One, if all the world’s faculties, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements are the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamental by nature, how is it that mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise, flowing and changing in succession, ending only to begin again? Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has said, earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally...
Their natures are perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, serene and eternally abiding. World-Honored One, if the nature of earth is pervasive, how can it accommodate water?

If the nature of water is all-pervasive, fire cannot arise. Furthermore, how can you explain that the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space without one subduing or extinguishing the other?
World-Honored One, the nature of earth is obstructive, while the nature of space is open and penetrating. How can these two both be pervasive?

"It pervades the entire dharma-realm, yet I do not know where this meaning leads. I only pray that the Tathāgata will let forth his great compassion and dispel the clouds of delusion for me and the great assembly.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata.

Because Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra had heard that the four aggregates and the seven elements are all the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, he clung to the nature as being difficult to reconcile with its manifestations, thereby raising two questions.

Although Pūrṇa’s rank had reached that of an Arhat—having already severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), having already destroyed the attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), and having already realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*)—he had not yet destroyed ignorance (*avidyā*), and his attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persisted; thus, he did not yet comprehend that all manifestations are [the Tathāgatagarbha].
[The World-Honored One] did not know the source from which the myriad dharmas arise; he had not yet clarified that the entire nature is itself form;
and he did not understand why the seven elements pervade everywhere. Therefore, he raised these questions according to his capacity.

Yet, it was specifically Subhūti who was chosen [to answer], because Ānanda is foremost among those of great learning, while Subhūti is preeminent in preaching the Dharma; both are renowned as "tigers of meaning" (masters of doctrine).

It accords with the ultimate principle above and accords with the capacities of inferior beings below; therefore, it is said to be "skillfully elaborated. When discussing the Single Truth, the Three Truths are fully present;
moreover, in every truth and every phrase, all fall beyond the views and understandings of the Lesser Vehicle. Hence, it is titled the "Ultimate Truth" (Paramārtha-satya).
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, from within the great assembly, rose from his seat (and so forth), and with reverence addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, regarding the four aggregates and the seven elements, the nature of the treasury is all-pervasive.

Sentient beings manifest this in every instance; they are skillfully able to expound upon the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) for the sake of living beings.
Yet, this primary truth is of an extremely profound and subtle principle, making it exceedingly difficult to grasp or correspond with.

Even though the World-Honored One ranked me as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, now that I hear the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous sound of the Dharma, I am like a deaf person standing more than a hundred paces away.

Thus, how profound and subtle is the Dharma-sound! Therefore, although the Buddha has proclaimed this Dharma to enable me to eliminate my delusions, I have still not yet fully understood its meaning;

“World-Honored One, although Ānanda and the others have attained awakening, the accumulated, beginningless, empty habitual tendencies within their faculties remain entirely intact.

"O Teacher, those who have already attained the state beyond outflows (anāsrava), though their taints are exhausted, still feel a lingering sense of doubt and regret upon hearing the sound of the Dharma now.

If this is so for us, how much more so for those who have not yet attained the state beyond outflows? Therefore, I have two doubts; I pray that the Tathāgata will resolve them."
Regarding this, there are two points of doubt concerning the continuity of the arising of all phenomena.
World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, all things in the world—the sense organs, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements—are the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamentally such.
Since it is said to be "pure," it cannot further admit defilement; since it is said to be "fundamentally such," it cannot further involve conditioned activity. I ask: how is this so?

If it is fundamentally pure and quiescent, for what reason did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise at the beginning, along with the sense organs, bodies, karmic fruits, and all conditioned phenomena?
Furthermore, if they were to arise suddenly despite being fundamentally pure and quiescent, they ought likewise to perish suddenly.
Finally, by what cause do they undergo sequential flux, ending only to begin again, continuing without interruption? Second: Five.

Great Perfect Interfusion Doubt: Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has taught that earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth are perfectly interfused, all-pervasive, tranquil, and eternally abiding—World-Honored One, if the nature of earth were all-pervasive, it should be purely earth;

since earth can overcome water, how could there also be room for water? If the nature of water were all-pervasive, it should be purely water; since water can overcome fire, [how could there be fire?]...
It should not arise. Why, then, do you say that the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space without one subduing or extinguishing the other?
World-Honored One, furthermore, the nature of earth is obstructive, whereas the nature of space is open and pervasive. Where there is obstruction, there is no pervasion;
where there is pervasion, there is no obstruction. How can both be said to be all-pervasive? [The same applies to] earth and water. It is difficult...
"Space, water, fire, earth, and emptiness are difficult to accommodate one another; yet the Tathāgata describes them all as perfectly interfused and omnipresent.

"I only pray that the Tathāgata will spread forth great compassion and explain the origins of the birth-continuum and the reason for its perfect integration.
By this, may the clouds of delusion be suddenly shattered and the sun of wisdom shine through with clarity, so that we may finally reach the ultimate stage where there is no doubt.

This is the position of the proponents [of this system]. Regarding the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) within the ultimate perspective, the Dharmalakṣaṇa school asserts that there are four types of ultimate truth:
first, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) as the conventional ultimate; the Four Noble Truths as the logical ultimate;

second, the emptiness of true suchness (*tathatā*) as the ultimate of realization; and the single true *dharmadhātu* as the ultimate of ultimates. This is based on the period following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

To answer that the myriad phenomena arise and continue, they originate from the two types of awakening inherent in the fundamental nature. To answer that the five great elements are perfectly interfused, they ultimately converge in the One Mind and the Threefold Treasury (Tripitaka).
These are clearly and entirely the Single True Dharma-realm; therefore, they belong to the ultimate, supreme meaning.

Those who have exhausted outflows and attained the stage of no-more-learning represent the middle capacity. Those śrāvakas of fixed nature represent the lower capacity. They have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness.

"Dedication toward the Supreme Vehicle" refers to those of superior faculties. "The two emptinesses" are the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

To attain the emptiness of persons is to know that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature; to attain the emptiness of phenomena is to know that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature. "The One Vehicle" is the Buddha Vehicle.
"The site of the field of quiescent extinction" is the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction (*mahā-nirvāṇa-samudra*). "Araṇya" is translated here as "secluded from clamor and contention."
It is also called a secluded and tranquil place. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly who were free from outflows and beyond training, saying:

"Today, for the sake of this entire assembly, the Tathāgata shall proclaim the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the ultimate meaning, so that those of inferior faculties among you—the Śrāvakas of fixed nature—may [attain realization]."

Those of the highest faculties who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness but turn toward the Supreme Vehicle—such multitudes as these—all obtain the One Vehicle, which is not the vehicle of the sheep or the deer.
This is the ground of the field of tranquil extinction; it is not the extinction of the Four Noble Truths. It is true *araṇya*;
it is the natural stillness of the fundamental mind, not the stillness of external objects. It is the place of correct practice, the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood, and not a peripheral one.

A "by-path" (xi) is a winding track. This refers to those śrāvakas of fixed nature and icchantikas devoid of the Buddha-nature, who cannot attain Buddhahood—like the sprout of a plantain tree or a rotten seed.
Now, however, all are brought back to the One Vehicle; they shall ultimately enter nirvana and all shall become Buddhas.
Only then is the discourse on the ultimate pinnacle of the Mahāyāna fully exhausted. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. Thereupon, Pūrṇa...
Those [beings], revering the Buddha’s Dharma-voice, listened silently and respectfully.

○ From here below, the "Non-empty Treasury" (*Asūnyagarbha*) is explained to demonstrate the cause for the continuity of birth. In contrast to the "Empty Treasury" (*Śūnyagarbha*), the latter concerns the gate of the True Suchness of the Mind (*citta-tathatā-mukha*);
it brings delusions back to the True to reveal the unchanging essence of the Treasury-Mind (*garbha-citta*). This [present section], however, concerns the Mind...
The Door of Arising and Ceasing: from the True, the delusive arises, thereby manifesting the function of the hidden mind as it accords with conditions.

Now, this function is twofold: first, according with defiled conditions, it gives rise to the functions of the six ordinary realms; second, according with pure conditions, it gives rise to the functions of the four noble stages.
Since the present aim is to open up delusion and bring about awakening, we shall for now speak solely of the defiled function; yet this entire function ultimately resides within the void below.
[This occurs] within the *Amoghasiddhi-garbha* [Sūtra].
The Buddha said: "Pūrṇa, it is as you have said: 'It is fundamentally pure; how could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Have you not always heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous? Pūrṇa, [have you not?]
He replied, "Indeed, World-Honored One. I have often heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.

The Buddha said, "What you call 'awakened clarity'—is it that the nature is inherently clear and thus called 'awakening,' or is it that awakening is not inherently clear and thus called 'clear awakening'?

Pūrṇa said, "If this lack of clarity were what is called 'awakening,' then there would be nothing to be made clear. The Buddha said, "If there is nothing to be made clear, then there is no ignorance."
Awakening is not something that can be awakened to; non-awakening is not something that can be illuminated. Furthermore, ignorance is not the nature of the profound clarity of awakening.
This section below answers the question: "How did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
The Venerable One has placed this point of inquiry as if one were reaching into a thicket of brambles to pull out a sticky lacquer pot, leaving people unable to move or turn. The world...
The World-Honored One is omniscient; he knew that the Venerable Pūrṇa was clinging to causes and conditions and had not yet forgotten his attachment to dharmas.
He therefore took the teachings previously expounded by Pūrṇa as a "test-probe" and a "shadow-grass," and questioned him, saying:
"Pūrṇa, regarding what you have said concerning purity... the great earth, excellent indeed is your question! Do you remember my former presence at the Dharma assembly?"

Within [the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*], it is said that "the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous" and "original awareness is luminously wondrous. Have you not heard this constantly? "Wondrous" (*miao*) is quiescence;
"luminous" (*ming*) is illumination. Wondrous luminosity is thus illumination within quiescence; luminous wondrousness is thus quiescence within illumination.
Quiescence and illumination are mutually fused, existing prior to the myriad phenomena of ignorance—a single segment of true reality that is naturally so.

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was hooked by the World-Honored One with a single cast and hauled up. He replied, "I have often heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning, yet I did not realize my nostrils were already in the World-Honored One’s hand.
Therefore, the Buddha again opened both gates simultaneously to examine him, asking:
"Since you have heard that this nature is wondrously luminous in its awakening and fundamentally luminous and wondrous in its awareness, how do you understand this in your mind? Is it..."
If the nature is inherently luminous and is simply termed "awakening" (*jue*), does this already include the meaning of "luminosity"?
Or is it that awakening is fundamentally not luminous, and one must apply luminosity to it, thereby using the dual term "luminous-awakening" (*mingjue*)?

Generally speaking, to be termed simply "awakening" without relying on false luminosity constitutes true awakening; whereas to use the dual term "luminous-awakening" while depending on false luminosity constitutes false awakening.

The two [Ananda and Mahakasyapa] raised their questions together, wishing for Purna Maitrayaniputra to resolve the matter for himself by choosing between them. Yet, the Venerable One’s habitual patterns were difficult to forget;
as before, his entire being fell into the pit of causal conditions and intellectual views. Unaware, he identified with clarity as a place to fall into.
Therefore it is said: "If one does not employ this clarity yet still calls it awakening, then the name 'awakening' is empty while the reality..."

"It is dark and without illumination. This is likely because, within the words, one is rejecting the true awakening that has nothing to illuminate, while in the underlying intent, one is deeply grasping at the deluded awareness that has something to illuminate.
How could one know that the moment one establishes "that which is illuminated," one immediately falls into the views of birth-and-death and causes-and-conditions;
it is no longer the inherently pure nature of awakening. Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
He told him: "Inferring from your intention, you seem to think that if there were nothing to be illuminated, then there would be no enlightened awareness;

you are almost afraid of the absence of enlightened awareness and thus insist on adding illumination to that which is already aware. Yet you do not realize that once you add illumination, [the problem remains]."
Thus, both meanings of "awakening" (*jue*) and "clarity" (*ming*) are simultaneously lost. This is because external clarity added to the essence is not inherently possessed by that essence;

it has arising and ceasing, and at times it exists while at other times it does not. Consequently, when one focuses on the moment the mind arises and there is clarity, that clarity is not awakening, for it is an external clarity added to awakening rather than being inherently present within the essence of awakening. When one focuses on the state where the mind is forgotten and...

Regarding the time when there is illumination: if one perceives it as such, it is not true illumination. This is because one has never previously awakened to the fundamental luminosity of the essence of awareness (*bodhi*).
This is precisely what is meant by the statement that both "having thought" and "not having thought" equally lead to confusion and delusion.

Since it is neither awareness nor illumination, both meanings are lost, and one falls entirely into ignorance (*avidyā*). How could you take this ignorance to be the profound stillness of your own awareness?
The nature of luminosity is indeed such! Yet, ignorance (*avidyā*) is not the same as the profoundly lucid and luminous nature.
For ignorance is precisely non-awakening (*a-bodhi*); it is turbid and dark. How, then, could it possess the meaning of profound lucidity?

Thus, although at first you feared only losing your luminous awakening, in the end you have come to entirely lose your true nature and fall completely into ignorance. [End of] "Awakening" (Jue Shang).

Furthermore, it is like a person staring fixedly with wide-open eyes, wishing to see their own eyes; they never expected to see "flowers in the sky" (empty blossoms), yet because the eye itself cannot be seen, they merely perceive the flowers reflected within it.
This passage from the *Zhengming Mingde* (The Rectification of Brightness and Virtue) falls entirely under this principle.
Zhong says: "The nature-awareness is wondrously bright; the original awareness is bright and wondrous. This refers to the awareness within the nature, which is wondrous.
As for "and yet it is luminous": this awakening is the primordial awakening; its luminosity is inherently subtle.

The character "original" (ben) refers to the character "primordial" (yuan) in the phrase "primordially luminous" from the first fascicle, meaning that nothing can be added to it—what is called "pure and primordially so.
It is linked with the character "nature" (xing) and does not stand in opposition to it. Now that this luminosity has reached such subtlety, what more could there be?

Furthermore, let us clarify this. The traditional interpretation holds that "wondrous clarity" (*miaoming*) refers to illumination within stillness, while "clarity-wondrous" (*mingmiao*) refers to stillness within illumination.

Master Tiantai said: "Clarity" (*ming*) may indeed be called "illumination," but "wondrous" (*miao*) carries the meaning of perfect fusion and unfathomability; it does not belong exclusively to stillness.

Thus, it is acceptable to say that the two characters "wondrous-clarity" (*miaoming*) inherently contain the meanings of both stillness and illumination. However, to say that [the two characters] refer to stillness and illumination...
To say that the character itself is the wondrous clarity is incorrect. The boundary between the real and the delusory lies precisely in this single character "one" (一).
If there is something [to which it refers], then clarity is not awakening; if there is nothing [to which it refers], then awakening is not clarity. Thus, the two characters "clarity" and "awakening"—
This is a deceptive evasion and will not suffice. True awakening is simply the absence of anything [to grasp]; it is not ignorance.
If there were no fundamental luminosity, it would also not be the nature of the profound clarity of awakening.

The nature of awareness is inherently luminous, yet delusion creates the notion of "luminous awareness. Awareness itself is not an object of illumination; it is because of this luminosity that an object is established. Once the object is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.

Within the state where there is neither identity nor difference, a blazing diversity comes into being. Based on that which is different from the objects of difference, identity is established through that very difference.
The manifestation of identity and difference leads, in turn, to the establishment of neither-identity-nor-difference;
this arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) and constitutes the three subtle states. Since the preceding section has already refuted [the self] as being entirely ignorance, it follows from that context:
the reason you have transformed your inherently endowed true awakening into ignorance is fundamentally due to nothing else.
It is precisely because the awakening of one's original nature must inherently possess innate luminosity—what is called "the nature-awakening is necessarily luminous.
You, however, have groundlessly and falsely added luminosity onto this awakening—what is called "falsely creating luminous awakening.
From this, fundamental ignorance is consequently established, upon which all delusions rely to take their initial footing. Therefore, know that the two characters "luminosity" and "awakening"—
This is precisely the root of the karmic fruits of sentient beings in the world of birth. Now, this nature of awakened wondrous clarity is the essence that is pure and original by nature;
it fundamentally does not belong to the "object" (the perceived), because it is neither localized nor non-localized.
Nor does it belong to "clarity," because it is neither ignorant nor non-ignorant. Therefore it is said: "Awakening is not something that can be illumined. Now, you—
Within the awareness of pure nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha*), one recognizes this awareness as necessarily luminous.

This single thought-moment of necessary luminosity then transforms the locationless awareness of nature into the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), whereby it falls into spatial location. Therefore, it is said:
"Because of luminosity, a location is established. Once fallen into location, one further transforms this great light of wisdom into the subject.
Because one perceives the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), it is said: "Since the object has already been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.

Once there is a seeing-aspect, one further takes the true reality of the realm—which is neither identical nor different—and transforms it into the appearance-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). Consequently, various distinctions come into being. Thus it is said:
"Within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing diversity is formed. This diversity, thus formed in a blazing manner, corresponds to that cause.

The establishment of what is distinct and yet further distinct is clarified: this distinction of what is established is based on a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), whereas this distinction of "blazing intensity" is discussed in very broad terms.
Thus, there is the establishment of sameness based on difference; that which is the same is also different.
There is the establishment of neither sameness nor difference based on both sameness and difference; that which is neither the same nor different is also different.

Furthermore, the world, empty space, and sentient beings—all these phenomena of indistinct and unsettled appearance—are all reflected here, serving as the embryo for the three dharmas within that coarse realm.
○ There is neither identity nor difference; this belongs to the characteristic of sentient beings.
It is because space is the same; this [the mind] resembles it in having no distinct form or appearance, yet it is not the same as space, and thus is said to have "no sameness.
The vessel-world is different; this [the mind] resembles it in having movement and spiritual awareness, yet it is not the same as the vessel-world.
Therefore, it is said that there is no difference. Yet, the necessity of clarifying both identity and difference arises because identity and difference manifest by being contrasted with one another;
this realm of sentient beings is not the same as the two preceding realms. Question:

Since this [realm] is identical to the world, space, and sentient beings, what is its distinction from the coarse realm below? Answer: This [realm] still resides within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
The darkness of the bonds suddenly manifests. Although all objective realms appear, they are merely the seeds of the sense organs, the body, and the physical world.

This is like the term *chiran*, which describes the intense blazing of fire; although it signifies something clearly manifest, the light of fire illuminates only the night, thereby signifying clarity within the midst of darkness.
Thus, although these realms appear, they still reside within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and have not yet [emerged].
It is greatly manifest; it is like the light of a fire in the midst of a dark night. ○ Zhong said:

"One does not realize that awakening is inherently luminous, yet one falsely adds an additional 'luminosity' upon top of that awakening. It is precisely this word 'luminosity' that gives rise to so many complications.
Within this, there is much debate among commentators regarding subject and object, or priority and sequence; they do not realize they are merely acting out of delusion."
"Clear awareness" is already the deluded capacity. Since the preceding section established the "object" (所) based on the "capacity" (能), this section further derives the "capacity" from the "object";

this is the sense of their arising from one another in succession, not that the object exists first and the capacity follows later. The passage beginning with "There is neither sameness nor difference" all proceeds from the arising of your deluded capacity;
the awakening of the fundamental nature is devoid of sameness and difference. Since the capacity and the object [are thus established]...

When establishing [the category of] "sameness," there is neither sameness nor difference; yet, within this state, they blaze forth as difference. This difference is different from that which is differentiated;
thus, based on difference, one further establishes sameness. Sameness and difference mutually negate one another, and one then establishes "neither sameness nor difference.
Within this context, both "sameness and difference" and "neither sameness nor difference" refer to the various deluded luminosities within the *ālaya-vijñāna*. (The following text is missing.)
The empty world and its sentient beings are merely appearances manifested by deluded clarity.
To interpret this passage regarding their differences and similarities by immediately citing "the empty world and its sentient beings" from the old commentary is far too premature.
Thus, through such disturbances, they interact and give rise to weariness; when this weariness persists for a long time, it gives rise to dust, which becomes turbid within itself.

From this, the afflictions of dust and toil are incited. When these arise, they form the world; when they are stilled, they become empty space. Empty space constitutes sameness, while the world constitutes difference.
That [state] has neither identity nor difference; it is truly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
This explains how the six coarse states arise from the three subtle ones, providing a definitive answer to the question of how they "suddenly" arise.
Thus far, these realms have come from non-existence to existence, whereby existence and non-existence mutually overturn one another; because difference establishes identity, identity...

Difference and identity manifest one another. Subsequently, by means of the characteristics of the boundaries of identity and difference, they reveal sentient beings who are neither identical nor different.
Thus, within the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*, the winds of objects stir in disorder, like flowers blooming in the void;
how profoundly turbulent this is! Such turbulence constitutes the conditions for mutual confrontation, giving rise in turn to wearying anxieties.
This refers to taking the appearances manifested by the preceding manifesting consciousness as objects; failing to realize they are manifestations of the mind, one grasps them as external realms.

One then initiates the calculation of numbers and discriminates between defilement and purity—this is what is called the *vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna* (consciousness that discriminates phenomena). It gives rise to the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), which is the first level of coarseness.
Having been fatigued for a long time, this continuity remains uninterrupted, further giving rise to the sensations of suffering and pleasure, and the distinction between self and other.
Continued: When the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) becomes coarse, it constitutes the characteristic of continuity; this is the second level of coarseness.

Due to long-standing weariness, the characteristic of defiled attachment arises, whereby grasping and clinging deepen, leading to the reckoning of "self" and "what belongs to self" (*ātman* and *ātmīya*);

this is the characteristic of clinging-grasping (*upādāna*), which is the third level of coarseness. Based on false attachment and discrimination, there are the characteristics of provisional names and words; all of these are [of the nature of] the self-...

The appearances become turbid; this turbidity is not caused by external objects muddying or defiling them. This is precisely the reckoning of the characteristic of names and words (*nāma-pada-lakṣaṇa*), which constitutes the fourth grossness.
Based upon these names and words, one follows after them and grasps at them, thereby creating various karmas and giving rise to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is the characteristic of initiating karma (*karma-utthāna-lakṣaṇa*), which constitutes the fifth grossness. Thereupon...
The sixth coarse characteristic of suffering bound by karma arises in succession:
through the movement of ignorance based on the awakening of nature, the mental object arises from ignorance; conditioned by the mental object, afflictions such as *rajas* arise.

Driven by the power of karma, they give rise to the locus of existence (*bhava-lakṣaṇa*), whereby mountains, rivers, and the great earth become firm and established as fixed forms. [Thus it is] still.
In the state where there is no characteristic of form, all is empty, vast, and expansive; the stubborn void becomes manifest.

This void is the aforementioned "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), which is now finally established. This world is the aforementioned "distinctive characteristic" (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa), which is now finally brought to completion.
Your question as to how mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise is truly due to this.
...and thus they arise. Furthermore, within those subtle objects, there was no characteristic of identity or difference;
it is only upon reaching this point that they become manifest and determinate, thereby constituting the karmic fruits of sentient beings as truly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

As for your question regarding how the various conditioned characteristics suddenly arise, they indeed arise in this manner. ○ Zhong said: "When the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) become turbid..."
In the subsequent passage, from beginning to end, the five aggregates are turbid.
Because sentient beings in the world possess karmic fruits, it is said that "from this, the dust of worldly toil and afflictions are aroused. Thus, one arrives at the midst of the clear sky.
One perceives various appearances of flowers; yet, when one examines their root source, they are all produced by a single thought-moment of deluded luminosity.
Within that single thought-moment, that which arises in profusion becomes the world, while that which is obscured and darkened within it becomes empty space.
Empty space is the common characteristic manifested within deluded luminosity, whereas the world is the particular characteristic manifested within it.
Various distinct characteristics appear: the karmic fruits of sentient beings and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

These are, in fact, the characteristics of neither identity nor difference manifested within deluded clarity. That which is called "neither identical nor different" is itself the true conditioned phenomenon.
How could it be considered a conditioned phenomenon only when the karmic fruits of sentient beings suddenly arise in full intensity? [The] Old...
To say that sentient beings are neither identical nor different is difficult to reconcile with the principles of the text.

Now, if one explains that the marks manifested by deluded thought are like shadows—empty yet active—then it can be logically sustained. ○ The Buddha said that the false visions of karmic consciousness arise from ignorance;
this must be understood as coming from the perspective of the wondrous clarity of fundamental nature-awareness and the luminous subtlety of original enlightenment. (2)
"Speech" refers to what is called *tathatā* (suchness). One sees that ignorance arises dependent upon *tathatā*;
there is no ignorance apart from *tathatā*. This kind of ignorance is what is known as the "ignorance of the aspect of arising.
Even Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, who have attained partial awakening, cannot know it; therefore, it is called a subtle affliction. Only a Buddha can exhaustively [penetrate] it.

Upon reaching ultimate awakening, through subtle and profound contemplation, one is able to penetrate and directly point it out; this is called "seeing the seeing," which means awakening to the eye-disease.

The *Sūtra* proceeds from ignorance to the coarse objects of perception, frequently employing the relationship between subject and object to link them together, so that one may know that subject and object are the very source from which all phenomena arise. Thus, the practitioner distinguishes between the true and the false.
After illumination, in a single thought-moment, subject and object are suddenly severed; one can then grasp and stabilize all phenomena, sitting back into the state of pure, original suchness.
This is what is meant by: "If one merely leaves behind delusive conditions, one is immediately a Buddha of Suchness. Formerly, a monk asked Master Langye Jue:
"If it is pure and originally so, how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Jue replied with a stern voice:
He asked, "If all things are fundamentally pure and serene, how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment.
Thus we know that when a single thought arises, the myriad dharmas are all complete; likewise, we know that when a single thought is non-arising, the myriad practices are fully perfected.
○ He said: Various schools have attempted to correlate the three subtleties and six coarsenesses of the *Awakening of Faith* with this section of the sutra, thereby...

There are various conflicting interpretations regarding this point. It is acceptable to correlate the first section with the three subtle states; however, it is not acceptable to correlate the subsequent section with the six coarse states.
This is because the six coarse states in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* are described from the perspective of a single individual’s transmigration through the cycle of birth and death.
The scriptural passage here speaks of the causes for the arising and continuity of all phenomena—mountains, rivers, and the great earth—and cannot be forcibly applied [to other contexts].
The character "láo" (fatigue) in "giving rise to fatigue through mutual dependence" is the same as the "láo" in "staring until fatigue arises."

Furthermore, the eyes and labor are mentioned together; these two instances of the word "labor" correspond to one another. That one can perceive empty space and the world, as well as the karmic fruits of sentient beings, is entirely a phenomenon manifested by the labor of the eyes.

Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation; thus there is the wind-circle that upholds the world. From emptiness arises agitation, and from the firmness of clarity arises obstruction;
as for those precious metals, it is the firmness established by awakened clarity that constitutes the gold-circle which sustains the lands.

The solid essence of awareness is perfected as a jewel; the shaking radiance gives rise to wind. As the wind and the gold rub against each other, fire arises, which serves as the nature of transformation.
The brilliance of the jewel produces moisture, and the fire above steams it; thus, a water-wheel forms, encompassing the worlds of the ten directions.
The following answers the question of how things successively migrate, ending and beginning again.
This first clarifies the cause for the continuity of the world-system. It is because, upon the essence of awakening (*bodhi*), deluded luminosity has already arisen;
this deluded luminosity necessarily gives rise to the bubble of space. The substance of this stubborn void is entirely obscured darkness, and this obscured darkness is in opposition to luminosity.
Brightness and obscurity oppose one another; unaware, the mind is stirred. One should know that all the winds of the world are entirely induced by the agitation of the deluded mind.
Therefore, above the wheel of space, there is a wind-wheel that sustains the world.
That the vessel-world (the physical universe) coalesces and remains without dispersal is entirely due to the sustaining power of the wind of ignorance. This element of wind is manifest and intimate.
It arises based on the deluded mind. Furthermore, both earth and gold possess the nature of solidity and both belong to the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*);
yet nothing is more solid than gold, and thus gold is the essential, substantial body of the earth element.

Because the mind moves due to the obscuration of space, it is said that "due to space, agitation arises. It is like a person who, while lying down in sleep, experiences confusion and distress; [this is] the awakening of clarity.

Through stubborn attachment, one falsely creates obstructions. It is like a person who, while lying prostrate, stubbornly seeks to pass through a narrow space and falsely perceives that some object is pressing down upon them;

from this, they immediately experience all manner of solid and obstructive phenomena. One should know that the gold and jewels of the world are all manifestations produced by a portion of stubborn attachment within the essence of luminous awareness.
It is as if one were to concentrate the mind and fixate on an image until it is transformed [into reality].
Stone is likewise a minor manifestation. For this reason, above the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala), there is a gold-circle (kāñcana-maṇḍala) that sustains the land.
This earth-element also clearly arises in direct dependence upon the deluded mind.

Through the deluded perception of rigid attachment, obstruction is established and stimulated to produce gold, which then becomes precious minerals. Through the deluded luminosity of movement, motion takes on the form of wind, and thus wind emerges.
When wind and metal rub against each other—the one solid and the other moving—there arises the light of fire. It transforms the raw into the cooked and changes existence into non-existence.
Although it lacks the function of a sustaining wheel, it possesses the capacity for transformation, and thus the fire-element arises.
These three aforementioned elements, though they arise in mutual dependence upon one another, are all accompanied by deluded awareness and deluded luminosity.
This refers to the characteristic of the mind. Below this, it does not carry the characteristic of the mind; rather, it employs only the two great elements of gold and water, from which water arises.
The radiance upon that jewel inherently contains moisture, just as the luster of a pearl emerges from water.
Fire possesses a vaporous and humid quality, which is capable of producing water; for instance, during times of intense heat, myriad things are often steamed and emit water.
Furthermore, because the jewel is luminous and further reflected by the light of fire, there is a water-circle that contains the moisture of the worlds of the ten directions.
These worlds of the ten directions are all enveloped by the waters of craving; thus it is from this that the element of water arises.

Because of the movement of deluded vision, the wind-circle is induced. Because of the hardness of the grasping mind, the gold-circle is induced. Because of the friction of parching, [the earth-circle is induced].
Thus, the fire-circle is produced by the power of aversion; because the love for existence is deep, the water-circle is produced.

Therefore, we know that the seeds of the four great elements do not exist externally, but are the two kinds of ignorance that produce moisture. A separate sutra states regarding the establishment of the world:
the earth-circle rests upon the gold-circle, and both constitute the element of earth. The gold-circle rests upon the water-circle, and the water-circle rests upon the wind-circle.
The wind-circle depends upon space, yet space has no dependence. Now, regarding the arising from the mind, the sequence is not entirely the same;
furthermore, to reveal the ultimate truth, it is said that space depends on ignorance (*avidyā*), while ignorance depends on fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
This is because one perceives that all phenomena originate from the mind where truth and falsehood are conjoined, and that apart from this mind, they possess no inherent substance of their own.
Fire ascends and water descends; through their mutual interaction, solidity is established. Moisture becomes the vast ocean, and dryness becomes the islands and sandbanks. It is for this reason.

Within that great ocean, flames constantly arise; within those sandbanks and islets, rivers and streams constantly flow. Because the force of the water is weaker than the fire, it solidifies into high mountains.

Therefore, when the rocks of these mountains are struck, they burst into flame; when melted, they turn back into water. Because the force of the earth is weaker than the water, [it likewise solidifies].
