They are extracted as grasses and trees; thus, forests and thickets, when encountered by fire, become earth, and through condensation, they become water.
Delusive thoughts arise in conjunction, serving as seeds for one another in succession. By these causes and conditions, the world continues in an unbroken stream.
This cause can establish the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and further produce the four abodes (*catur-āvāsa*) that are derived from them.

For the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is fundamentally the dwelling place of sentient beings; now, within these four, the specific abodes of sentient beings are clearly manifested, hence they are called the "four abodes.
Although those four great elements all equally accomplish transformative functions, among the four abodes, the three great elements of water, fire, and earth [predominate].
The traces [of their activity] are especially manifest. The nature of fire is to blaze upward; it presides over ascending. The nature of water is to moisten downward; it presides over descending.
When water and fire are in equilibrium (ji-ji), they interact and give rise to the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*). It is like a ceramic vessel, whose production depends entirely upon fire and water.
Once they have interacted and established solidity, moisture becomes the vast ocean, namely the Sweet Water Ocean (*Kṣīroda-samudra*).
The salt-water ocean becomes the dwelling place for aquatic beings, while the dry land becomes the continents—namely the four great continents—which become the realm for terrestrial beings.

The ocean is also established by means of solidity (*sthira*), for the great hollows that hold the water are entirely composed of solid substance. Thus, it is because of this principle of the co-arising of water and fire.
That great ocean is originally a place of moisture; fire should not exist there. Because it does not forget the vital energy (*dhātu*) of its mother, the flames of fire constantly arise.
The islands and sandbanks are originally places of dryness; water should not exist there.
Because they do not forget the vital energy of their father, rivers and streams constantly flow. Indeed, water regards fire as its "wife who overcomes me" (*ātman-kṣaya-patnī*).
Therefore, fire is the mother of the two abodes. Fire regards water as its "husband who overcomes me" (*kēwǒzhīfū*); thus, water is the father of the two abodes.
Now, the great ocean resembles its father yet does not forget the constituent essence of its mother; therefore, fire arises within the sea.
The islands and sandbanks resemble their mother yet do not forget the constituent essence of their father; therefore, [fire arises on] the islands...
There are rivers and streams. Furthermore, water is capable of overcoming fire;
if the nature of water did not descend to accord with fire, it would inevitably extinguish the fire—how then could it produce things? Now, however, water descends its own nature to accord with fire;
thus, the husband-water is subordinate to the wife-fire, and consequently high mountains are formed. Within these mountains, the realms where sentient beings dwell are established. Therefore:
As for mountain rocks that burst into flames when struck, this is because they have received a portion of the fire-element.

As for those that melt into water, this is because they have received a portion of the water-element. Earth is able to overcome water; yet if the nature of earth does not descend to conform to the water, [it cannot prevail].
In that case, its momentum would necessarily extinguish the water; how could it then produce living things? Now, however, the nature of earth descends to conform to water.
Since earth is inferior to water, it is drawn forth as grasses and trees, and thus the realm of sentient beings dwelling in forests is formed.

Therefore, when forests and thickets encounter fire and become earth, they receive a portion of the pneuma of earth; when they are squeezed and become water, they receive a portion of the pneuma of water.
This is the portion of the water-element’s qi. Through the seeds of ignorance, false delusions arise in conjunction;
first, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are produced from the deluded mind; next, through successive transformation, the four great elements are fully generated;

finally, by means of these various great elements, the four abodes are accomplished. Because these serve as the causal conditions for one another in succession, such is the nature of the world’s appearance.
Continuing: formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness proceed from end to beginning in an uninterrupted succession.
Every single cycle of formation occurs in this very manner of successive arising; thus, once they have suddenly arisen, there will never be a time of purification.
Although the principle herein resembles the concept of the mutual generation of the five elements found in non-Buddhist treatises, it is in fact...

They do not entirely coincide. If one were to align them point by point, there would be two inconveniences: first, the Five Elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) would be misrepresented, and the meaning of the Sūtra would become obscured;
second, it would lead those outside our teaching to believe that [the Buddhist view] does not transcend their own ideas.
This is because those outside our teaching correctly maintain only that the Five Elements can form the world, yet they truly do not understand its ultimate source. Even if...

They highly extol the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) and primordial chaos (*hùn dùn*), yet ultimately fail to recognize these as the deluded perceptions of their own minds—the universal ignorance (*avidyā*).
Now, I shall clearly point this out, precisely because it differs from the intent of those teachings.

Yet the old commentaries have instead taken "awakened clarity" (*jué míng*) and explained it as water, conflating it with the calculation that "Heaven produces water as the first transformation. Furthermore, they cite...
Beneath the Limitless (Wuji) and the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji), how can one cause them to eliminate old views and give rise to new awakening?
Now, while external teachings mostly direct the mechanism of transformation toward yin and yang, our school points directly to the fundamental source of transformation within the mind and nature.
Furthermore, it demonstrates that the origin of heaven and earth arises from the ignorance within our own minds; this is truly a great difference.

This is an external explanation that represents an extreme and erroneous attachment. Those who propagate the teachings are unable to draw the followers of external schools toward a clear understanding of the internal doctrine;
instead, they push back against the internal teachings and indiscriminately conflate them with external schools—a most grievous failure of judgment.

As for the terminology employed within the internal teachings, they frequently utilize the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*) rather than naming the "five phases" (*wuxing*). This was because later generations adapted and transformed [the system].

Their arising is merely similar in outline to the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). Therefore, in explaining the preceding four dharmas, I have followed the *Four Great Elements* (*catur-mahābhūta*) of Mount Gushan as the primary standard.
As for the first three great elements, it is evident that they arise in dependence upon the mind.
Regarding the subsequent four dharmas, I establish distinct names and terms, briefly adopting the theory of the "parental constituent of qi" from the Wēnlíng [Commentary] to assist in clarification.
...and that is all. ○ Master Konggu stated that the learning of Zhou Lianxi originated from Shouya;
he was evidently referring to the *Tàijí tú* (Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate). Who was this Shouya, that he could establish such a baseless conjecture?
Is he not indeed a sinner against the Inner Teaching? Or perhaps Konggu’s statement was merely hearsay and is certainly not to be trusted? ○ Zhong...

It is said: The vast oceans, islands, sandbanks, lofty mountains, forests, and marshes combine to form the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). These arise through the transformations of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), yet these four great elements are themselves the manifestations of the awakened mind.
This is what is meant by "all phenomena are but mind" (*sarva-dharmāḥ cittamātram*).

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, this delusion of clarity does not come from another; it is the fault of the awakening-clarity itself. Once that which is delusory has been established, the principle of clarity cannot transcend it.
For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not surpass form. Thus, the six delusions of form, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth are accomplished.

From this, the functions of seeing, sensing, hearing, and knowing are divided. Through the mutual entanglement of similar karma, combinations and separations bring about transformation. One perceives the clarity of forms.

When consciousness arises, the perception of clarity is formed; divergent perceptions form aversion, while identical perceptions form attraction. The flow of attraction becomes the seed, and the reception of perception becomes the womb.
Through their union, birth occurs, drawing together those of similar karma. Thus, through causes and conditions, there arise the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.

Whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation, each occurs according to its appropriate condition. Those born from eggs arise solely from perception; those from a womb depend on emotional attachment; and those from moisture arise through physical contact.

Sentient beings respond through transformation and separation; their emotions and perceptions unite and part, constantly changing and shifting one another. All karmic retributions follow their ascent or descent.

By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession. (This clarifies that principle cannot be transgressed. "Principle" is like the essence; "transgress" means to exceed. The essence of awakened clarity is obstructed and cannot be exceeded.)
This clarifies the cause for the continuity of sentient beings. For the Dharma-nature body is fundamentally all-pervasive and truly possesses no physical body;
yet even this physical body, when its origin is traced back, is likewise formed by the delusion of clarity.

This "delusion of clarity" is not some other entity, but arises from the wondrously luminous awakened mind itself, which initially gives rise to a single thought that then transforms into [the state of ignorance].
Awakened clarity becomes that which is falsely conceived. Once the falsely conceived has been established, the essence of profound, perfect, wondrous clarity is divided into six locations.
At the eye it is called "seeing"; at the ear it is called "hearing," and so on through the nose, tongue, body, and mind, each giving rise to localized obstructions.
They can no longer transcend these limits; they are no longer all-pervasive and universally penetrating. For this reason, hearing does not [perceive].

When a sound emerges, one sees it but does not transcend form; the same applies to the other four. Thus, by means of these six delusions—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch (with shadow, sound, and phenomena abbreviated)—one achieves their manifestation.
They defile the six sense organs and thereby become objects. From this, the six modes of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are differentiated.

It gathers the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) to form the sense-faculties (*indriya*). This is what is meant by the statement that the original single luminous intelligence is divided into the six harmonious combinations.

Once the faculties and objects are established, the signs of physical form manifest subtly; yet, as one has not yet entered a new birth, one must necessarily abide in the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*, also known as *antarā-bhava*).

[The intermediate existence] is situated between death-existence and birth-existence, hence it is called "intermediate existence. As the Sūtras state: "The six faculties of the intermediate existence are sharp and keen, surpassing those of the birth-body. The *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "Intermediate..."

The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) possesses a physical form and appearance corresponding to that which is to be born; for example, the intermediate state of a human resembles a human, and that of an animal resembles an animal, and so it is for the other realms of existence. Its body is the size of a child of five or six years;
though its physical dimensions are small, it is capable of performing various karmic actions and gives rise to perverted perceptions toward its parents.

It proceeds to birth by means of this intermediate state. If the karma of the three—the father, the mother, and oneself—is concordant, they become mutually entangled and one is born; these are the classes of womb-born and egg-born beings. Alternatively, there are those who do not depend on parents.
It is solely due to one's own karma that, when coming together, a form is formed, and when separating, a transformation occurs; this refers to the category of moisture-born beings (*saṃsvedaja*).

(All crawling insects are moisture-born; those in the heavens and hells are all transformation-born. When the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) of the two types—womb-born and egg-born—is about to enter the womb, in all places where there is no affinity, the great earth appears as if black ink;
only at the place where there is an affinity with the parents does a single point of bright color appear. This...
The intermediate state being (*antarābhava*), having seen the bright forms, immediately hastens toward that place, and its perception thus becomes fully realized.
If it is a male intermediate state being, he regards the father as an enemy; the father is an object of aversion, while he regards the mother with the perception of a companion;

the mother is an object of affection. For a female being, it is the reverse. (In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which clarifies the twelve links of dependent origination, there are two types of ignorance: first, the ignorance that moistens karma, which refers to the afflictions of the past.)
Second is the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana-avidyā*), which refers to the arising of attachment and aversion toward one's parents at the moment of entering the womb.
In this intermediate state (*antarābhava*), having perceived an attractive object, one directs craving toward the two drops of red and white [semen and blood] of the parents to serve as the seed.

These two drops of red and white then receive this conceptualizing mind (*saṃjñā-citta*) and form the embryo. Although this occurs through the union of the parents, it is actually brought about by the characteristics of one’s own karma.
It is the same. Thus, one is drawn in and enters the womb, just as a magnet attracts iron.

Because these three—the father, the mother, and oneself—act as causes and conditions, one consequently enters the womb and forms a body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Therefore, there arise the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.

As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Within the womb, there are five stages: during the first seven days it is called *kalala* (translated here as 'coagulated mucus'); during the second seven days it is called *arbuda* (translated here as 'blister'); and during the third seven days it is called *peśī*."

The fourth week is called *peśī*, which here means "soft flesh. The fifth week is called *ghanā*, which here means "firm flesh. The seventh week is called *praśākhā*, which here means "the stage of formation. Here, two [of these stages] are cited; hence the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

As for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of those born from moisture or by transformation, through the power of prior karma, regardless of proximity or distance, they become attached according to their inclinations;

at the very place where attachment occurs, they immediately undergo birth. Indeed, among the four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—each is evoked by its own determinate karma (*niyata-karma*); therefore, following...

It responds to these stimuli through the fixed retributions of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). That which is like distracted thought and lacks stability is *saṃjñā* (perception); thus, those born from eggs arise solely from perception.
That which is characterized by concentrated attachment and cannot be relinquished is *vedanā* (feeling); thus, those born from a womb exist because of feeling.
That which involves close affinity and does not change is *saṃskāra* (volitional formation); thus, those born from moisture are moved by such affinity. Having abandoned these, one moves toward...

"That" refers to separation; thus, transformation responds through separation. By means of these four minds, one invokes and responds to the various categories of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
This is where there is fixed order. As for the union and separation of emotion and thought, they undergo mutual transformation:
sometimes emotion changes into thought, sometimes thought changes into emotion; sometimes union changes into separation, or separation [changes into union].
Change is easily brought about through conjunction. Therefore, when receiving retribution, some that were flying and transformed become submerged, like a sparrow transforming into a clam;
others that were submerged and transformed become flying, like a fish transforming into a dragon. These strange and wondrous occurrences are likewise unstable.
For these reasons, as they pass through long periods of time, they mutually undergo transformation; the continuity of sentient beings thus has no end. ○
Hei said: "To annotate that the four phrases of form, fragrance, taste, and touch constitute the intermediate state (antarābhava) body is truly laughable.

It fails to recognize that when the World-Honored One spoke of the continuity of sentient beings, he did so by revealing it within the present moment itself—meaning that this very instant when a single thought flickers up is the root of birth and death for eternal kalpas. He was not speaking from the perspective of the distant past. Only in this way..."
The statement that Pangu was born from the Great Chaos [is merely a metaphor].
Pūrṇa, when conceptualization and craving bind together and craving cannot be severed, then throughout all worlds, parents and children continue in succession without end.
These things take desire and greed as their root. When craving and affection nourish one another and greed cannot be halted, then...
Among all beings in the world—those born from eggs, from transformation, from moisture, or from wombs—they devour one another according to the strength or weakness of their power.
These acts are rooted in the greed for killing. As humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human; when the human dies they become a sheep.
Thus it continues through ten types of births, dying and being reborn, mutually preying upon one another. Such evil karma arises together with them, persisting until the end of the future. This is...
In these cases, [the retribution] is rooted in theft and greed. You have taken my life; I shall repay your debt.
By reason of this cause and condition, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you will constantly remain in birth and death. You loved my heart; I cherished your form.

By reason of this cause and condition, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you will constantly remain in bondage. Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these three are the roots. By reason of these causes and conditions, karma...
"Continuity of the fruit.

This clarifies the cause for the continuity of karmic fruits. Pūrṇa, when all sentient beings were in the world in the past, their thoughts of affection and love were like glue or lacquer; they were firmly bound and could not be untied, and thus they underwent rebirth.
At that time, the flow of affection becomes the seed, and the reception of thought becomes the womb; thus, parents, children, and grandchildren continue in succession without end.
All such beings establish their very nature and destiny through lustful desire; therefore it is said that desire and greed are the root. (This desire and greed pervades all four modes of birth.)

For now, we shall speak only in terms of birth from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*). Furthermore, womb-birth extends to both humans and animals; for now, we shall distinguish it specifically regarding human beings, as this is easier to perceive.
Because there is craving and attachment (*tṛṣṇā*), there must be body and life. Because there is body and life, one must rely on nourishment.
They crave my sustenance, and I love their flesh and blood. Thus, craving cannot be ceased; consequently, among the four modes of birth in the world, the weak become the meat of the strong.
They eat one another, devouring each other in succession. These beings take the greed for killing as their foundation.
Because the karma of killing flourishes, humans eat sheep; when the sheep dies, it is reborn as a human, and when the human dies, they are reborn as a sheep.
From one life to ten lives, through death after death and birth after birth, they revolve in cycles of retribution, coming to devour one another. Such is the case.
Because of these evil karmas, they are born together in the same place from lifetime to lifetime, meeting one another to repay their debts until the very end of the future, with no cessation.
These cases have greed for theft as their root; it refers to taking what is not given.

Both taking [the victim] by force and taking [them] stealthily constitute theft. When humans eat sheep, it is "taking what is not given. When the sheep dies and becomes a human, they come to devour one another;
this is "stealthy taking. Therefore, these are called the greed of theft. To speak in terms of the greed of killing: "You owe me my life; you must return my life to me.
I owe you your life; I must return your life to you. To speak in terms of the greed of theft: then...
"I owe you a debt; I shall repay your debt. You owe me a debt; you shall repay my debt.
Because the debts of life are not settled, birth and death become mutually entangled. For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one remains constantly within birth and death, unable to escape.
Speaking in terms of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*): you love my mind, and I love your mind; I cherish your form, and you cherish my form.
By reason of these causes and conditions of love and cherishing, we meet and assemble in birth after birth.

Even after passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we remain constantly bound and unable to attain liberation (as was said at the Changsheng Hall on the seventh day of the seventh month). There are only three kinds of craving: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
It is the root. By these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession; thus one knows that the wandering through the three realms is caused solely by craving.

If craving is severed, one immediately emerges from the three realms. Question: In secular teachings, when discussing killing, it is considered most serious only when one kills another in the heat of anger or strife.
When discussing theft, it is considered most serious only when one robs or steals another's wealth or life. Yet, regarding the eating of meat—

[The opponent says: "To not permit [the killing of animals] seems appropriate for weighing the relative gravity of offenses. Why then does this scripture discuss only what is light while conversely omitting what is heavy?
[The author] replies: "There are two meanings to this. First, it is the principle of severing the light to illustrate the heavy.

That is to say, the worldly teachings of this land prioritize the prevention of disorder and seek to nourish the people; therefore, they merely sever present disorder without prohibiting [certain acts]."

Regarding the eating of meat: now, one who wishes to sever birth and death must cut off the conditions for birth; therefore, even the extreme case of eating meat is included among those things to be abandoned.
If one realizes that even minor [foods] still serve as conditions for birth and death, then it goes without saying that the same applies to major ones.
This is not because one wishes to neglect what is weighty. Second, it is the principle of severing the root and stopping the branches.

Generally speaking, when investigating the deep roots of all acts of killing and stealing, they mostly arise from the consumption of meat. For example, the eighty thousand Śākyas met their deaths at the hands of Virūḍhaka precisely because of this.
They know only to revile based on immediate circumstances, yet they do not realize that the distant cause originates from the grievance of eating fish.
For this reason, peace does not endure in this region. During times of peace, people indulge their appetites;

after three or five hundred years, for those who have enjoyed blessings, the blessings end and calamity arises, while for those animals whose retribution has been exhausted, they are reborn as humans—yet all still carry the karmic burden of killing.
This leads to resentment, which in turn brings about an age of chaos, resulting in the killing of immeasurable beings. Therefore, the Buddha prohibited the eating of meat;
this is the profound and far-reaching wisdom of the Sage, a statement that uproots the foundation and blocks the source. As the Sūtra says:

"If the world wishes to escape the kalpa of weapons, sentient beings must refrain from eating meat. Those gentlemen of external teachings who have not yet attained faith and understanding must by no means treat this lightly or disparage it.
"Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of the luminous clarity of awareness that clearly knows.
Because this knowing gives rise to appearances, they are born from deluded vision. The various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth flow on in succession."
This is false and illusory; it ends only to begin again.
This summarizes the response to the question regarding the sudden arising of beginning and end.
Pūrṇa, these three types—the world, sentient beings, and karmic fruits—are crazed and deluded, continuing in succession without interruption; though each is distinct, they are all thus.
If one traces its origin, it all arises from the wondrously luminous fundamental substance of the awakened nature. Initially, due to non-awakening, a single thought suddenly arises;
thus, it transforms into the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), which is termed "awakened luminosity" (*jue-ming*).

Because there is this awakened luminosity, it next further transforms into the nature of clear and knowing, thereby forming the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). Because there is this clear knowing, it next further brings forth the objective appearances of the environment, thereby forming...

Regarding the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*): the three subtle stages of ignorance are all present therein. It is by taking these objective aspects as its condition that one gives rise to the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), which completely encompass those six coarse stages;
in sum, they are all false perceptions. As for your question regarding how these three types [of ignorance] suddenly arise:
they all stem from the luminosity of awareness (*bodhi-prakāśa*), arising suddenly through false perception. Indeed, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—[and so forth].
The karmic fruits of sentient beings and all conditioned phenomena undergo successive transformation and flow;
this is not due to the existence of some separate entity, but arises solely from this illusory continuity of inverted perceptions. Therefore, they end and begin again.
As to your question regarding how these three types end and begin again, it is for this reason. One can see that what suddenly arises continues as a seamless whole.

Delusive phenomena are utterly devoid of any obtainable substantial reality; yet all manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment—is this not so?

Having concluded the answer to the first question, Pūrṇa subsequently raises further doubts and objections based on that response, to which the Buddha replies with four parables. Thus, the first question is finally resolved.
This is the meaning.

Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous awakening is fundamentally wondrously luminous and is neither increased nor diminished from the Tathāgata’s mind, then how did the various conditioned phenomena—the mountains, rivers, and great earth—suddenly arise without cause? Now that the Tathāgata has attained wondrous, empty, and luminous awakening..."
"When will the mountains, rivers, the great earth, conditioned phenomena, habitual tendencies, and outflows ever arise again?
This is Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra grasping at the nature of the cause to challenge the nature of the fruit. Pūrṇa said:
"If these sentient beings currently possess within their bonds the essence of wondrous awakening—which is fundamentally not non-wondrous and free from all defiled dharmas—then awakening is not..."
It is luminous and free from all obstructions. It is no different from the mind of the Tathāgata—neither increasing nor decreasing. In the Buddha it does not increase;
in sentient beings it does not decrease. It is equal and non-dual. Yet, from within this fundamentally pure essence, mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arose without apparent cause.
As for these various conditioned phenomena, it is now that the Tathāgata has attained the wondrous, empty, luminous awareness.
It restores the fundamental substance that is devoid of things and returns the fundamental luminosity of perfect illumination;

it is identical to the fundamentally wondrous and enlightened luminosity of sentient beings prior to the arising of phenomena such as mountains and rivers—the true awakening to which the Tathāgata has returned.
Originally, there was no difference between this and the true awakening of sentient beings before they gave rise to delusion.
Yet, since sentient beings have already arisen from the truth into delusion, should the Tathāgata alone not likewise arise from the truth into delusion? I venture to ask:

within the Tathāgata’s wondrous, empty, and luminous awakening, how can there exist the worlds of mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as conditioned sentient beings and the karmic fruits of their habitual outflows?
"When will there ever again be such a state where [defilements] suddenly arise?
This question assumes that the causal nature of sentient beings has a beginning, and thus suspects that the resultant virtue of the Tathāgata has an end. Master Zhong’s commentary states:
"Since the Tathāgata has attained the awakening to emptiness, how could conditioned existence ever arise again? This question seems rather shallow. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, a person...
Among the five types of views held by me, there is one which claims that the nirvāṇa attained ultimately comes to an end, and one returns to become a sentient being again.

This is what is called "after awakening to emptiness, one is reborn in the various realms of existence" (kūnyo-kaku-go fuku-shō-shoyū). It closely resembles that [view]. This was likely the position of the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Lesser Vehicle at that time.

There has always existed this kind of attachment. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, riding upon this [opportunity], requested the Buddha to once and for all eliminate it—namely, the total eradication of delusion.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "For example, it is like a person lost in a village who mistakes south for north. This delusion..."
Furthermore, they exist because of delusion and emerge because of awakening. Pūrṇa said: "Such deluded people do not arise because of delusion, nor do they arise because of awakening.
Why is this? Delusion has no fundamental root; how, then, could it arise because of delusion? Awakening does not give rise to delusion."
"How does awakening occur? The Buddha said, "When that deluded person is in the midst of delusion, suddenly there appears one who awakens them by providing instruction.
Pūrṇa, what do you think? Even though this person was previously deluded, would they become deluded again regarding this village?
No, World-Honored One. Pūrṇa, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise thus. This delusion has no fundamental basis."
The nature is ultimately empty. Originally, there was no delusion; it is only because of the awakening to delusion that delusion is extinguished.
Once awakening does not give rise to delusion, this serves as a metaphor for the fact that ignorance is fundamentally empty.

Since all phenomena arise from ignorance, and ignorance itself has no inherent substance, we shall not yet discuss the myriad phenomena produced by it. First, we take the mind that has lost its way as a metaphor. The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
Pūrṇa, it is like a person who is lost and, in a certain village, mistakes the south for the north.
Now, if one is deluded regarding this direction, then awakening must occur in relation to that other direction.
One does not know whether this single delusion arises because of the delusion regarding this direction, or whether it emerges because of the awakening regarding that other direction. Pūrṇa.
The Buddha said: "Such a deluded person does not arise because of delusion, nor do they arise because of awakening. Why is this? Delusion does not produce itself as the root of delusion;
how, then, could it arise because of delusion? Awakening and delusion are opposites; how could they produce one another?
How, then, could it arise because of awakening? The Buddha further said: "While that deluded person is in the midst of delusion, suddenly there is an awakened person who points it out."
He causes them to awaken, and the four directions become radiant. "Pūrṇa, what do you think?
After this person has been long deluded and deeply confused from the past, once they have awakened, would they ever again become deluded regarding this village? He replied, "No, World-Honored One."
Once awakened, one no longer falls into delusion. The Buddha then addressed him directly, saying: "Pūrṇa, it is likewise with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;

after their awakening, they do not fall into delusion. This is because this delusion of ignorance does not take its own substance as its basis, nor does it take the nature of enlightenment as its basis. It comes from nowhere; it is fundamentally and utterly empty. It is also...
It is like the confusion of one who has lost their way; there is no further cause for it. Moreover, from the very beginning when one was in a state of delusion, there was no delusion to be found.
It arose suddenly from a single thought, appearing as if one were deluded regarding the essence of pure awakening;
yet, this is not true delusion. If it were true delusion, then that delusion would already have a root, and how could one ever awaken again? For delusion is fundamentally...
It has no root; therefore, it is said to be "as if existent. It is just like mistaking south for north:

while the directions themselves do not actually change, once one realizes that this was a delusion, the delusion is immediately extinguished. Once extinguished, how could it ever arise again? It is also like one who is disoriented regarding the directions.
If one simply realizes that the "south" of delusion fundamentally has no "north," then the appearance of the north is instantly extinguished, and it should not arise again as a "south.
Thus, it can be seen that within the true nature of awakening, ignorance fundamentally does not exist;
even the source from which the myriad dharmas arise is originally empty.
It is also like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky; when the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky.
Suppose there were a foolish person who, in that empty space where the flowers had vanished, waited for the flowers to reappear. Do you consider such a person to be foolish or wise?

Pūrṇa said: "In emptiness, there was originally no flower; it was only through deluded vision that arising and ceasing occurred. To perceive the cessation of the flower as the emptiness itself is already a perversion.
To then command it to appear once more is truly the act of one who is mad and deluded. How can such a mad person be called wise rather than foolish?"

The Buddha said, "It is as you understand it. Why do you ask how the mountains, rivers, and the great earth could ever emerge again from the wondrous, enlightened, luminous void of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas?
This metaphor illustrates that the myriad dharmas are currently non-existent. If even ignorance itself is empty, how much more so the myriad dharmas produced by it?"
To clarify this by means of an analogy: it is like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky; these flowers are fundamentally not real.
If the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky, yet they are also not truly non-existent.

Suppose there were a foolish person who, at the spot where the flowers had vanished from the sky, waited for them to appear once more. Pūrṇa, do you consider such a person to be foolish or wise? Pūrṇa.
He said: "Space is fundamentally without flowers; it is through deluded vision that one perceives their arising and ceasing.
Since they do not truly cease, to perceive the cessation of flowers within space is already a perversion. How much more so to command them to emerge again? This is truly called madness and folly;
even the character 'foolish' (yu) is insufficient to fully describe it. How can such madmen be further designated as either foolish or wise?"
"Yes," the Buddha said, "this person who awaits flowers in the sky is truly as you understand them: one who is decidedly ignorant and not wise.

Since you already know that one who waits for flowers in a clear sky is utterly foolish, how can you wait for phenomena such as mountains and rivers to arise within the Tathāgata’s wondrously luminous essence?
To hold that all phenomena cease with the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is already a perverse delusion."
Furthermore, if one hopes that the Buddha gives rise to the myriad dharmas, how does this differ from those deluded people?
In this way, false thoughts will no longer arise; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, it is like gold ore mixed with refined gold; once that gold is pure, it can no longer become mixed again.
Just as wood becomes ash and cannot once more become wood, so too are the bodhi and nirvāṇa of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, it is not only that delusion no longer arises again, but even reality no longer undergoes change. It is like ore containing gold:
while the gold is within the ore, the two substances are mixed together, and the ore is intermingled with the refined gold.
Once the ore has been extracted, the gold is entirely pure and can never again become adulterated; thus, one who seeks ore within the gold is a fool. It is also like this...
When wood encounters fire, it becomes ash. Once it has become ash, it cannot again become wood; thus, to seek wood within the ashes is likewise foolish.
By this analogy, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas may be understood. Those Buddhas and Tathāgatas have realized unsurpassed wisdom and virtue beneath the trees;
they have shattered ignorance, exhausted the five stages of dwelling, and overturned all afflictions.
The restoration to completion is the essence of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*), which is called *bodhi*.

Because the cause is exhausted and the fruit is fulfilled, the merit of perfect purity and cessation is realized; the wandering of transmigration ceases, the two deaths are forever forgotten, and all saṃsāra is overturned.
Thus, one restores the original nature of suchness, which is called *nirvāṇa*. The light of *bodhi*-wisdom is like the brilliance of refined gold.
Once purity has attained *bodhi*, afflictions (*kleśa*) will never arise again, just as refined gold can never again become ore.

*Nirvāṇa* is quiescent extinction, comparable to wood ash; once one has entered *nirvāṇa*, one will never again sink back into birth and death (*saṃsāra*), just as wood ash can never again become wood. Therefore it is said, "it is also like this. This is then...
Delusion is fundamentally non-arising; it is not only upon becoming a Buddha that it ceases. Reality is fundamentally unchanging; why then do you expect a Buddha to arise anew?
Therefore, know that even within the realm of sentient beings there is neither arising nor change, let alone for one who has attained Buddhahood—how could such a one possess arising or change?
You asked about the cause by which the myriad dharmas arise and continue; I have explained arising for you.
The continuation concludes here. ○ The explanation of the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is finished.
○ Below this, the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is explained in order to demonstrate their perfect interfusion.

Now, within the empty *garbha*, characteristics are destroyed to reveal the nature; since characteristics do not exist, what could be said to be unimpeded? Within the non-empty *garbha*, from the nature...

The characteristic of arising is already manifest; how then could there be non-obstruction? Therefore, within the first two *piṭakas*, the principle of perfect interfusion was briefly introduced, yet the discourse on non-obstruction remained incomplete. How could the doubts of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra be avoided?

Now, wishing to fully elucidate the reasons for non-obstruction in order to dissolve questions regarding the attachment to characteristics, one must discuss the *piṭaka* of Emptiness and Non-emptiness. For indeed...
When emptiness is itself non-emptiness, then essence is entirely identical to appearance; yet essence is inherently unimpeded.
When non-emptiness is itself emptiness, then appearance is entirely identical to essence; how then could appearance be obstructed?

Pūrṇa, furthermore, regarding your question that the natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally interfused and pervade the entire dharma-realm, you wonder how the natures of water and fire do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another;
and you further inquire how empty space and the great earth, both pervading the dharma-realm, can coexist without contradiction.
Pūrṇa, it is like this: for example, the substance of empty space is not itself any of these manifold forms, yet it does not obstruct those various forms.
To elaborate. Why is this so? Pūrṇa, when the sun shines upon that great void, it becomes bright; when clouds gather, it becomes dark; when the wind stirs, it moves;
when the sky clears, it becomes pure; when vapors condense, it becomes turbid; when earth accumulates, it becomes a haze; and when water settles, it becomes reflective. What do you think?
Are these various conditioned phenomena in different directions produced because of those [conditions], or are they produced by the void itself?
There is. If it were produced by that [sun], Pūrṇa, then when the sun shines, since it is the light of the sun, the worlds of the ten directions would all be of the same solar color;
how then could one see the round sun again within the sky? If it were the light of the sky, the sky should illuminate itself.

"How is it that during the time of clouds and mist at midnight, one does not see its radiance? One should know that this luminosity is neither the sun nor space, yet it is not different from space and the sun.
This answers the subsequent question regarding how the five great elements can be perfectly interfused. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra relies upon the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
They cling to their old views, stubbornly asserting that the various great elements (*mahābhūta*) are inherently obstructive by nature.

They argue that while it might be said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is unobstructed because it is empty, now that you claim it is fully endowed with all the great elements, it must necessarily be obstructive; how could there be any principle of non-obstruction?
Thus, they not only fail to understand that the manifested characteristics are non-obstructive, but they also continue to harbor doubts regarding the unmanifested nature itself.

It appears to be obstructed; yet the Tathāgata dispels this doubt not only by explaining that the nature which has not yet manifested is unobstructed, but also by providing a detailed explanation that even the characteristics already manifested are themselves unobstructed.

If even the manifested characteristics are unobstructed, how much more so the unmanifested nature—how could it possibly have any obstruction? Therefore, in this section, the unobstructed nature is discussed, and the phrasing is most [precise].
[This section is] brief, as it explains the non-obstruction of characteristics; its text is the most extensive. The Buddha said:

"Pūrṇa, furthermore, you asked why earth, water, fire, and wind are perfectly interfused and all-pervasive, yet you doubt how the natures of water and fire do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another.
You also questioned that since both space and earth are all-pervasive, they ought not to be able to coexist within one another. I shall now [explain this for you]."
"You, Pūrṇa, should clarify this through an analogy. The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally not the seven elements, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those seven elements.
It is like space: its essence is not the various phenomena, yet it does not obstruct the unfolding of all those phenomena.
Why is this so? Pūrṇa, that great void space—its so-called essence is not the various phenomena."
This [nature] is utterly empty and vast, fundamentally devoid of a single thing. Nevertheless, when the sun shines, it is bright; when clouds gather, it is dark; when the wind stirs, it moves;
when the sky clears and becomes limpid, it is pure. When the vapors of smoke and mist coalesce, it becomes turbid.
When earth, wind, rain, and sleet accumulate and obscure the sky, it forms a haze. When water is clear, profound, and motionless—
Thus, it intermingles and reflects with empty space. This is what is meant by "not refusing to manifest.

(Although the seven characteristics do not correspond one-to-one with the seven elements, they nevertheless roughly accord with their number. What do you think? Such various phenomena occur simultaneously in each respective place.
Regarding all conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*): are they produced by causes and conditions such as the sun and so forth, or do they exist of their own accord within empty space?
If you say they are produced by those causes, Pūrṇa, let me briefly illustrate this by taking the single characteristic of the sun as an example;
the remaining six may be understood accordingly. Now, when the sun shines, since it is the light of the sun, it should then—
The entire world shares in the substance of a single day; one ought not to see a separate, round sun.

How could there be another round sun like a basin or a bowl seen within the sky? Since a round sun is already seen, why is it that everything outside of that sun is not itself the luminosity of the substance of space?
Why, then, do you claim that this luminosity belongs exclusively to the sun? If you say it does not...
"This is the brightness of the sun; this is the brightness of space. Space is eternal and brightness is ever-present; space ought to illuminate itself.
Why, then, would it be without radiance during the time of clouds and mist at midnight? One should know that this brightness is neither the sun nor space;
it is not identical to space and the sun, yet it is not different from space and not different from the sun; it does not exist apart from space and the sun. Since—
It is neither identical nor separate; thus one knows that it is pure by nature, yet manifests according to karma. Question:

Space is used as a metaphor for the nature (dharmatā), and the seven characteristics such as brightness are metaphors for the seven elements (mahābhūta). To what phenomena do the seven conditions, such as the sun, correspond? Answer:
The seven great elements arise according to karma; thus, "the sun and so forth" serve as metaphors for the respective karmas followed by each of the seven great elements.

Question: In the general heading, only emptiness and form were mentioned; emptiness was used as a metaphor for the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha), and form as a metaphor for the seven great elements. However, in the section providing the inquiry and explanation:
It would suffice merely to clarify that [the nature] is not empty and is not different from emptiness. Why then add seven conditions to say it is "not the sun" and "not different from the sun"?
Answer: If one does not add [the qualification of] the sun and so forth, two things will be incomplete.

First, it fails to fully reveal the falsity [of the mind]. This is because one must state that both [mind and emptiness] are not [the reality], and that they are not different, only then can it be revealed that they are entirely and circuitously false, beyond any possibility of being pointed out or described.

If one were to speak only of "emptiness" in isolation, there would still be something that could be pointed out and described. Second, it fails to fully reveal the subtlety [of the mind]. If one merely says it is not empty, without saying it is not...
If one speaks only of the sun, then one merely manifests the unimpeded nature, without simultaneously manifesting the unimpeded characteristics.

If one says only that it is not different from space, but does not say it is not different from the sun, then one merely manifests non-contradiction with the nature, without simultaneously manifesting the non-destruction of characteristics.

The following section follows the scriptural text. The passage from "Observing that the characteristics are fundamentally false" to "they cannot coexist" appears earlier, while the passage from "The true, wondrous, enlightened clarity" to "there is nothing to rely upon" appears later.
Since the words and meanings do not connect, it is clearly a misplaced interpolation (*cuojian*). Here, I have corrected it according to the lecture text.
The true, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this. When you clarify it through space, then space appears;
when you clarify earth, water, fire, and wind individually, then each appears individually; if you clarify them all together, then they all appear together. How do they appear together?

Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a body of water. When two people look together at the sun in the water and walk off in opposite directions—one to the east and one to the west—each person perceives a sun that follows them. Since there was originally no fixed standard [of a single sun], one should not raise the objection:
"This sun is one; how can it go in different directions? If each person has their own sun, how is it that only one appears? It is exactly so.
It turns into delusion; there is nothing upon which to rely. (This section originally appeared later; it is now moved forward.

This is the application of the Dharma to the analogy. That original, true, wondrously enlightened, luminous mind does not cling to a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), nor does it reject various characteristics;
it is likewise so. If you follow the karma that gives rise to emptiness and take emptiness as your clarity, then [the great...]
On a large scale, it is like the void of the kalpa at the beginning of a great trichiliocosm; on a small scale, it is like digging a well until earth is removed and space immediately appears.
If one seeks to manifest each of the elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—it is like holding up a mirror to seek fire or holding a water-crystal to seek water.
Then they each manifest individually, just as fire emerges when one seeks fire, or water emerges when one seeks water.

If earth, water, fire, and wind manifest their brilliance simultaneously—such as when a blower manifests wind from his mouth or fire manifests from within firewood—then they also present themselves to one another and appear together, just as the strength of fire follows the wind, and the intensity of the wind follows the fire. Truly.

"Wondrously enlightened clarity manifests in accordance with karma in this way. How does this differ from the fact that the essence of empty space is not identical to its various attributes, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those seven attributes?
As for the individual appearance of these attributes, there is no need to discuss them; how is it that they appear together?
Now, I shall further employ a metaphor to illustrate the metaphor: Pūrṇa, it is like a single body of water in which [reflections appear]..."

Regarding the reflection of the sun: suppose two people look together at the sun reflected in this water. If these two people walk in opposite directions, east and west, then each person perceives a separate sun following them.
Originally there was but one reflection; yet now one follows toward the east and the other follows toward the west.
Of these two reflections, which is the fixed reality? (The term "zhǔndìng" means to determine or ascertain the true reality. Thus, while they are in one place...
When the two great elements of water and fire appear, what can be established as their definitive reality? Since there is no prior standard of certainty, one should not raise the objection:
"If they are one, how can they function separately? nor the objection: "Since they are dual, how can they appear as one?

Even if objects possessed a fixed reality, such debate and refutation might still be permissible; however, since they now lack both fixity and reality, one must instead attend to this very lack of fixity.
Regarding the realm of reality, if one proceeds through circuitous debate and refutation, the difficulties will only increase, leading further into the realm of the false and illusory.
It is like observing that "one" is real and knowing that "two" is false; yet once both "one" and "two" are established as distinct, it is proven that "one" is likewise illusory.

Thus, between "one" and "two," which can be relied upon as a basis? Consequently, the simultaneous manifestation of the various great elements is also merely a circuitous and illusory phenomenon; there is no [ultimate reality].
This can serve as a reliable basis for understanding. How does this differ from the case where light arises from emptiness, which neither is identical to nor separate from existence?
The water is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha* nature; the reflections are metaphors for the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*).

The two people walking in opposite directions is a metaphor for karma that follows along with both [subject and object]. The two shadows appearing in the east and west are metaphors for the characteristics that manifest together. Zhong says: "In various commentaries..."
To claim that the "sunlight" mentioned here is as false as the "moonlight" in the second fascicle, and furthermore,
to treat the wondrous manifestation of both [the sun and moon] as a falsehood based on the subsequent passage’s circuitous and empty rhetoric,

is to let the words subvert the meaning— a fault of using metaphors to burden the Dharma. This is because one fails to recognize that the second fascicle reveals the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, and thus [misinterprets it].
The true moon is used as a metaphor for the Real (the True), while the moon’s reflection is taken as the illusory.

This reveals that the Tathāgatagarbha is unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging; thus, the reflection of the sun in water is borrowed to describe and illustrate this wondrous state of simultaneous manifestation.
One need only observe that the single Tathāgatagarbha manifests simultaneously with the seven elements, just as a single reflection of the sun appears wherever one goes, whether east or west. Its...
It is clearly seen by oneself. If one must insist that the shadows of the sun are one, how can they move separately?
Since each shadow already corresponds to a separate sun, how could they manifest as one? Thus, such arguments are merely circular and false, providing no reliable basis for understanding.

When one contemplates the fundamental falsity of appearances, there is nothing that can be pointed out or described; it is like seeking to tie empty flowers together to form an empty fruit—how can one then interrogate them regarding the principle of their mutual subversion and extinction?
When one contemplates the fundamental reality of the nature, it is solely the wondrously enlightened clarity. This mind of wondrously enlightened clarity was originally neither water nor fire.
"Why do you again ask about those things that are mutually incompatible? (This section originally appeared earlier; it is now moved to later.
This passage cites the aforementioned unreality to answer the previous question. Simply observe closely the characteristics of the seven elements.
If a fruit were real, it could be pointed out, just like the reflection of the sun in water. Since it is fundamentally illusory, there is nothing that can be pointed out.
To falsely claim that something can be pointed out is already a delusion, like grasping at a flower in the sky as being truly existent.
If one further interrogates its characteristics regarding their mutual suppression and extinction, it is like once again seeking a flower in the sky and expecting it to...
To further posit the fruit of emptiness is truly the delusion of delusions and the falsehood of falsehoods. How can one then interrogate it regarding mutual subjugation or extinction?
Because this empty space is vast and open, utterly devoid of all characteristics, when one contemplates the nature of the seven elements, they are found to be fundamentally pure and true;
they were not water or fire from the start. Since even water and fire do not exist, who can be said to be incompatible with one another?
If you understand water and fire, then you will understand earth and space. As for your question regarding why the great earth and empty space cannot coexist—why indeed do you ask such a thing?
When one contemplates that the fundamental nature of appearances is false, then all appearances are the very nature itself; what is not empty is itself empty.

Thus, appearance and nature are without obstruction. When one contemplates that the fundamental nature is originally true, then the entire nature is appearance; emptiness is itself non-emptiness, and thus nature is without obstruction.
You asked about the reason for the perfect fusion of the five great elements; I have now finished explaining for you the reason for this perfect fusion. Question:
Since both nature and appearance are mutually unobstructed, and since they do not suppress or extinguish one another but rather accommodate each other, [how is this so]?
Why is it that now, as they blaze forth, they are utterly extinguished and find no place to abide? What is the reason for this? The answer is given below:

"You take form and emptiness to oppose and seize one another. Thus, the two characters "oppose" (*qīng*) and "seize" (*duó*) are precisely the reason. It is known, therefore, that this violent extinction is not empty;
the root of the affliction lies in the beginningless false habituation of sentient beings to oppose and seize, and not in that [emptiness] itself.

The appearance of reality is indeed like this. It is like the moon moving and the shore shifting; the delusion lies in the false perception that the clouds are racing or the boat is moving, yet it is not as if the moon or the shore truly possess such motion.
Again, it is like seeing water or fire in a dream and grasping at them as real, only to be scorched or extinguished by them;
the moment one realizes it is a dream, one can simply pass straight through with an upright body, for there is no longer any burning.
As for "submergence," how could there be any suppression or extinction? Thus we know that what is now blazing and manifest is truly due to long-standing firm attachment;
it is simply that the merit of transcending such attachment has not yet been realized. Examining the doubts of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra in detail:

he maintains that if something is called "perfectly interfused and all-pervasive," it must necessarily include suppression and exclusion; if, on the other hand, it allows for non-extinction and mutual containment, he fears it cannot be considered perfectly interfused.
Pervasive. The Buddha’s non-extinction of appearances is precisely this perfect interfusion and pervasiveness.
Yet, he does not analyze with them how they are compatible or how they are non-extinguished. He merely traces the origin of the seven elements;
they are all the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting according to karma. Their nature is entirely true, while their appearances are entirely delusory.
Since these are all false and illusory—like flowers in the sky or the reflection of the sun in water—who is there to be extinguished by whom? Who is there to be contained by whom?
Thus, one should not even inquire whether they are extinguished or not extinguished; why then must one distinguish that they do not mutually suppress or extinguish one another?
One should not even inquire whether they are compatible or incompatible; why then must one distinguish that such-and-such is compatible?
Ah! This means tracing back to the root and exhausting the source, searching out the provenance; without waiting for further debate or refutation, the knot of doubt is shattered.
The explanation of the empty and non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is now complete.

From here below, the three collections (Tripitaka) are perfectly manifested to encourage practice. Because the preceding sequential three collections were urgent in their aim to shatter delusion and achieve awakening, they all proceeded by demonstrating the deluded realms of sentient beings;
they had not yet had the leisure to universally encompass both the holy and the ordinary, or the defiled and the pure conditions.
[They did not yet fully reveal] that the ten realms are of one suchness and non-dual, thereby manifesting the entire substance and great function of the *cittaprakṛti* (the mind-as-such). Now...
Since the two types of delusions, coarse and subtle, have been successively shattered and exhausted, the wondrous clarity is revealed and the eye of the Way is perfected.
It is therefore appropriate that the spiritual treasury of all Buddhas be thoroughly emptied and displayed to the very bottom;

thus, this comprehensive synthesis is fully manifested to reveal the perfect fusion of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka). At this point, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra must harbor a latent doubt, arising from the preceding extreme discourse.
Sentient beings currently dwell within deluded realms; yet, as for their essential nature and phenomenal characteristics, both are entirely unobstructed.
If this is so, then there should be no distinction between the noble and the ordinary, and all should equally perceive them without obstruction.

Why is it that we, though equal [to the Tathāgata], constantly encounter obstructions, while only the Tathāgata alone attains non-obstruction? Thereupon, the Tathāgata, in response to their thoughts, pointed out the reason for this. Therefore, there follows the subsequent section.

Regarding the circular demonstration of this passage: since the old commentaries neither distinguish the errors nor infer the underlying intent, they cause the scriptural text at this point to lack a concluding summary before it and a subsequent introduction after it. Furthermore, how could any coherent connection be established here?
Pūrṇa, you have used the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose and supplant one another within the Tathāgatagarbha;

thus, the Tathāgatagarbha conforms to form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, there is the movement of wind, the clarity of space, the brightness of the sun, and the darkness of clouds.

Sentient beings become bewildered and distressed, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses; thus they give rise to worldly toil and the appearances of the mundane world.
This subtly resolves our latent doubt as to how movement could result in obstruction.
As for those present who were questioning why sentient beings possess such obstructions, the Buddha pointed out the cause of their becoming obstructed, saying:
"Pūrṇa, that you all possess all manner of obstructions—what other reason could there be? It is truly because of you."

The karmic consciousness is not empty; as the characteristics of subject and object have not yet been shattered, it follows the karma of form and emptiness, mutually usurping one another within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This is like ordinary worldlings who turn their backs on emptiness and rush toward existence; thus, by means of form, they usurp emptiness.
The provisional [nature] has a semblance of existence yet tends toward emptiness; thus, through emptiness, it is overturned and usurped by form.
As they overturn and usurp one another, the Tathāgatagarbha follows your karma to manifest as either emptiness or form; this is because True Suchness (Tathatā) accords with conditions.
Because it is associated with the deluded mind, one perceives that form and emptiness pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

Therefore, within this Dharma-realm of form and emptiness, when opening one's eyes, one sees only the myriad phenomena arrayed before them: wind moves while space is still, yet movement and stillness obstruct one another;
the sun is bright while clouds are dark, yet light and darkness exclude each other. This continues until even earth and space find no room to contain one another.

Water and fire clash and extinguish one another; worldly afflictions fill the foreground, completely forming a defiled land. One does not realize that appearances are fundamentally empty and have no basis for reliance.
This is solely because sentient beings are internally obscured by ignorance and driven by the power of karma, becoming deluded and distressed.

As in the lower realms and the three miserable paths, having thought constitutes delusion; whereas in the higher realms, the two vehicles [of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] are characterized by non-thought.
This leads to bewilderment; that is to say, whether with mindfulness or without mindfulness, they all equally return to delusive bewilderment.

Because of this bewilderment, one does not know oneself, turns one's back on pure awakening, and unites with delusory objects; thus, worldly toil arises, and the appearances of the world come into being.
The entirety of nature manifests as phenomena; that movement results in obstruction is due solely to this self-delusion and self-contradiction.
How could it be the fault of nature and phenomena?

I unite my wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—with the Tathāgata-garbha; and this Tathāgata-garbha is nothing other than wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one; the small manifests the large.
The large manifests within the small; without moving from the site of enlightenment, one pervades the worlds of the ten directions. The body contains the infinite space of the ten directions;
upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests jeweled royal lands, sitting within a mote of dust to turn the Great Dharma Wheel. Thus, the dust is extinguished and one merges with awakening.
Therefore, he brings forth the wondrously enlightened nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This secretly resolves the latent doubt that the Tathāgata alone has attained unimpededness.

Since the one who is the proper recipient of the teaching had already doubted why the Tathāgata alone attained such unimpededness, the Buddha, on that account, personally explained the cause of his own unimpededness, saying: "As for me..."

As for attaining all-encompassing non-obstruction, how could there be any other method? It is simply by employing that perfectly湛 (zhan) and unarisen, undying nature within the six sense faculties to dissolve that pervasive *tathāgatagarbha* which manifests as both form and emptiness, arising and ceasing.
As for the Tathāgatagarbha, although during delusion it may manifest as form, emptiness, arising, and ceasing, its delusive essence is fundamentally and eternally empty;
its appearances are not substantially real. Now, by fusing with the wondrously luminous and eternally abiding nature, these delusive marks of arising and ceasing are found to be utterly non-existent.
There remains only the wondrously pure, fundamental awakening—the nature of profound clarity—which is perfectly interfused, illuminating, and all-pervasive.
The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) refers to abiding in the Great Treasury of Radiance by means of suchness-wisdom (tathatā-jñāna) in accord with suchness-principle (tathatā-tattva).

Now, when sentient beings turn their backs on awakening, even True Suchness (bhūtatathatā) follows along with defiled conditions and accords with the principle of delusion, thereby forming the phenomena of the mundane world.
How much more so when one practices the wondrous cultivation that accords with the nature—how could there not be the manifestation of wondrous functions? Therefore:
From essence arises function. Within this principle-dharmadhātu, there is unimpeded dependent origination.
Speaking in terms of the dharmadhātu of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena: because the principle is indivisible, the principle is one;
because phenomena have no limit, phenomena are immeasurable. Because the principle has no boundaries, the principle is great; because phenomena have boundaries, phenomena are small.
One becomes infinite, and the infinite becomes one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears.
Thus, principle and phenomena are without obstruction. Speaking in terms of the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena:
a single atom, a single hair, a single body, and a single world are all "one. Many atoms, many hairs, many bodies, and many worlds are all "infinite. Even a minute speck of dust...
The tip of a hair is small; boundless lands and boundless bodies are large. One becomes infinite, and the infinite becomes one.
Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears. Thus, all phenomena are mutually unimpeded. To verify this through the apprehension of signs:
for instance, the Immovable Bodhimanda pervades the worlds of the ten directions—is this not the transformation of the one into the infinite? As for the body...
It encompasses the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions; is it not that the immeasurable is made one? Within a single hair-tip, a jewel-king land is manifested;
within the center of this, the support is manifested, and one sits amidst motes of dust, turning the Great Dharma Wheel.

Within the support, the center is manifested—is this not the manifestation of the great within the small? Though it be a jewel-king land, it remains but a hair-tip; though it be the Great Dharma Wheel, it remains...

Yet it is but a subtle atom. Is this not the manifestation of the small within the great? All of these are the manifestation of objects of measure (*yathā-vastu*) within the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*).
This is truly because those Buddhas who turned their backs on awakening to unite with the sensory dust have extinguished the dust to unite with awakening;

thus, those who reversed the manifestation of the marks of the worldly realm of affliction have brought forth the wondrously awakened luminous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The entire mark becomes the nature. What is there to doubt?

That one alone attains unimpededness is due solely to being neither deluded nor averse [to reality]. How could it be a matter of a difference between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)?
From here below, the *cittaprakṛti* (store-nature) is perfectly revealed. Not only is the single mind (*ekacitta*) fully endowed with the three stores (*trikosa*), but furthermore, within each...
Within a single treasury, the ten dharma realms are perfectly complete. If they are "not," then all ten realms are "not";
if they are "immediate" (i.e., identical), then all ten realms are "immediate"; if they are "fused," then all ten realms are "fused.

Because it is not all, yet is all, and furthermore fuses and sweeps away all, those whose minds are coarse and floating rather than sinking into contemplation of the three truths and three modes of observation will find this difficult to grasp.

I immediately established a clear contemplation. I did not understand the Buddha’s profound intent in detail; it was simply this: directly pointing out that sentient beings inherently possess the original mind from the very beginning.
It is thus. Perfectly interfused and supremely wondrous. Whether sentient beings are deluded or the Buddhas have realized it, it remains as such.

It is always just like this; there is simply no increase or decrease. Furthermore, you should know that it does not depart from the perfectly wonderful, luminous mind pointed out within the preceding faculties.

However, following the ten manifestations and one destruction, it was only then that the four aggregates and seven elements were clarified, and subsequently, their permanence and pervasiveness were advanced.
Now, reaching this point, they are ultimately and perfectly interfused, leaving nothing further to be said.
Furthermore, [this teaching] adds more; from beginning to end, it reveals only the nature of mind. When has it ever spoken of the gates of contemplation?
If the gates of contemplation were already established here, one should simply practice according to them. What use would there be for Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration? Master Zhong said:

The textual meaning here is difficult to disentangle. Although it is said that by extinguishing dust one unites with awakening, such that the one and the many, the small and the large, mutually encompass and enter one another to give rise to great spiritual efficacy, within the Tathāgatagarbha not even a speck of dust is established; thus, it is "not all.
Yet, although it is not all, it fully contains the myriad dharmas; thus, it is "all. Furthermore, they mutually dissolve and...
It exists. It is inconceivable. Why do you doubt that the Great [Reality] pervades the Dharma-realm without encroaching upon or displacing one another?

Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind (the character "wondrous" is repeated; "wondrous" here means quiescence). It is not mind (it encompasses both the sense organs and consciousness), nor is it emptiness. It is not...
It is not earth; it is not water, not wind, not fire. It is not the eye, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. It is not form, nor sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomena.

It is not the element of eye-consciousness, and so on, up to the element of mind-consciousness. (In this place there are no five aggregates, for the five sense organs and the six objects of perception subsume the aggregate of form.)

The mind-faculty (*manas*) and the six consciousnesses subsume the latter four aggregates (*skandha*). As for the sense bases (*āyatana*), when they are expanded, they are: "neither illumination nor non-illumination" (this closely resembles the phrasing of the *Heart Sūtra*, except that it initially includes the word "illumination" [*ming*].

The meaning is that non-illumination has no substance; its substance is primordial illumination. Therefore, it is spoken of in conjunction with it. Illumination is the true mind, so it would seem inappropriate to negate it. However, illumination is established in opposition to non-illumination and is thus a dependent phenomenon;

since this perfect mind is free from all dependence, it is also negated). "Illumination and non-illumination are exhausted. (Where the word "exhausted" [*jin*] is not included, it refers to the causes and conditions of saṃsāra. Where the word "exhausted" is added beneath each branch, it refers to the causes and conditions of nirvāṇa). And finally, "neither..."

Aging is not death; it is not the exhaustion of aging and death. (The phrase "and so forth" indicates omissions in between: second, formations; third, consciousness; fourth, name-and-form; fifth, the six sense bases; sixth, contact; seventh, sensation;

eighth, craving; ninth, grasping; tenth, becoming; eleventh, birth. It is not suffering, not its origin, not its cessation, and not the path. (These are the Four Noble Truths practiced by the śrāvakas. It is not knowledge, nor attainment.

(These are the wisdom and principles realized by those of the Lesser Vehicle. It is not dāna (generosity), nor śīla (ethical discipline). (Holding the precepts. It is not vīrya (diligence). It is not...

Kṣānti (patience/forbearance). Not dhyāna (meditative concentration; at the initial stage, "concentration" is stillness or śamatha, and "dhyāna" is contemplation or vipaśyanā; when practice is perfected, "concentration" is samādhi, and "dhyāna" is prajñā).
Not prajñā (wisdom). These six perfections are the practices by which one approaches [the goal]. Not pāramitā (reaching the other shore; this is the principle toward which one proceeds).
Thus, it extends even to not being tathāgata (Tathāgata), not being arhat (Worthy One), and not being samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfectly Enlightened One). Not Mahā...
Nirvana (the totality of the four virtues of perfect quiescence). It is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure (the specific characteristics of Nirvana).
Because it is neither worldly nor supramundane (where "worldly" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings and "supramundane" refers to the four types of noble ones), [it is beyond both].
This first clarifies that by departing from the myriad phenomena, one reveals the empty Tathāgatagarbha.

Although the wondrous nature gives rise to two aspects—active and quiescent—in accordance with the two conditions of defilement and purity, the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally the wondrous, perfect, and round mind, originally void and tranquil.
There is not a single thing that does not belong indifferently to all phenomena; therefore, it is not the seven elements, nor the six sense organs, nor the six sense objects, nor the eighteen realms.
This is not a worldly dharma; it is not the dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, nor the dharma of the Śrāvakas.
