This is not the Dharma of Bodhisattvas; it is not a supramundane Dharma. It is not the three titles of the Tathāgata, nor the four virtues of Nirvāṇa.
This is not even the supreme-supreme supramundane Dharma. For it concerns only the essence of mind, and thus is neither ordinary nor sagely;
it points directly to the human mind, which is why it does not maintain the views of sagehood or ordinariness, even regarding the mind itself.
The Buddha transcends both [existence and non-existence].

This is the Tathāgatagarbha, the primordial luminosity of the wondrous mind. (By adding the character "luminous" (*míng*) once more to the previously mentioned "fundamental wondrousness" (*běnmíào*), and further qualifying it as "wondrous mind," it is shown that while function is present, it is contained within the essence; thus, one does not become stuck in the functioning of existence.
It is the mind itself and emptiness; it is earth, water, wind, and fire; it is the eye, and likewise the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The mind is itself form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects; it is itself the eye-consciousness element, and so on, up to the mind-consciousness element (the dharmas of the six ordinary beings).
It is itself ignorance and the extinction of ignorance; and so on, up to itself old age and death, and the extinction of old age and death (the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas).
It is itself suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; it is itself knowledge and attainment (the dharmas of the śrāvakas). It is itself...
Dāna is itself śīla, itself vīrya, itself kṣānti, itself dhyāna, itself prajñā, itself pāramitā (the Bodhisattva-dharma).

In this way, it extends even to: it is itself tathāgata, itself arhat samyaksaṃbuddha, itself mahāparinirvāṇa, itself permanence, itself bliss, itself self, and itself purity (the Tathāgata-dharma). Because they are all thus.
This is because they are both mundane and supramundane.
This clarifies that by means of the myriad dharmas, the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is revealed.
Since not a single thing among the dharmas of the ten realms can be found apart from this mind, one relies solely upon the essence of the *garbha*-mind, which is itself the ten realms.
This is its very substance. Whatever is grasped by the hand is without exception it; even mind and Buddha are both identical to it.

This is the wondrously luminous source of the mind, the Tathāgatagarbha, which is detached from identity and detachment from non-identity—it is identity, yet not identity (the two characters "not identity" should be read as "is identity").
This pair of negations and illuminations reveals the *tathāgatagarbha* as both empty and non-empty.
Now, since all phenomena are simultaneously "not this," they are also simultaneously "identical to" the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is wondrous and luminous; it is primordially and inherently possessed.
It is not something to be produced through cultivation. Its fundamental essence is a perfect spirituality that does not stagnate, and it certainly cannot be fixedly categorized.
It is neither identical to nor distinct from that which is not; yet, transcending both identity and non-identity, it functions with sovereign freedom as circumstances require.
It is entirely non-identical yet identical, entirely identical yet non-identical; it is identity itself and non-identity itself.
When one reaches this point, the state of perfect interfusion is consummated, manifesting the wondrous nature of the mind beyond further addition. Originally, when the Buddha responded to Ānanda:
In response to Miaoding’s request, [the Buddha] set aside the provisional and limited practices cultivated by those of the Two Vehicles and revealed the fundamental samādhi of all Buddhas.
The reason this samādhi is so exceptionally distinct is that it fully manifests the inherently wondrous, perfect, and circular samādhi of one's own nature;

therefore, commentators should not employ the notion of "cultivation" extensively, as it would still conflate it with conventional paths. Furthermore, within this śamatha, there is discussed exclusively...
This fundamental samādhi (ben-ding) primarily reveals the reality of the nature (xing-zhen), yet the intent to explain its cultivation is extremely sparse.

From the third fascicle onward, it directly points to the essence of the fundamental samādhi of the *tathāgatagarbha* (zang-xin), manifesting the sequential emptiness of the treasury (*krama-śūnyatā-garbha*).

Thereupon, the great assembly each realizes for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions, eternally abiding and indestructible; thus, the sudden teaching (don-yi) is fulfilled. However, the perfect teaching (yuan-yi) remains unmanifested.
This is to manifest it. Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra suddenly raises two difficulties, which serve as the introduction to the latter two *piṭakas*.

Thereupon, in answering how the myriad dharmas arise and continue, he briefly manifests the function of the *cittadhātu* (store-mind) in accordance with defiled conditions, thereby revealing the sequential "non-empty *garbha*.
This thus briefly provides for both essence and function, and the intent of the Perfect [Teaching] is already revealed; yet, it is still not yet complete.

This clarifies [the matter]. Furthermore, it answers the objection that the five great elements cannot coexist, while demonstrating the principle of the non-obstruction between nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), thereby revealing the treasury of sequential emptiness and non-emptiness. This, then, merely clarifies non-obstruction to resolve doubts regarding obstruction;

as for the characteristics that are identical to nature and the immeasurable, inconceivable karmic functions, as well as the nature that is identical to characteristics—[these remain to be explained].
The inconceivable and wondrous essence of their interpenetration has not yet been fully revealed.

Furthermore, by means of the latent doubts of those present according to their capacities, he exhaustively discusses with them the conditions of defilement and purity, as well as the four meanings and four aspects; only then will all perfect functions be completely manifested.
Moreover, by opening the two and merging the two, while simultaneously brushing away and fusing both pairs, the wondrous essence of the three-in-one is finally [revealed].
It is most manifest. However, its function must be realized before it can be manifested; therefore, it is briefly described as being accomplished through cultivation.

Its essence, however, is primordially and spontaneously present; thus, its unchanging nature is still clearly revealed. Even though it is manifested through cultivation, it is not produced by cultivation.

Thus, the subsequent threefold treasury of perfect interfusion subsumes the preceding threefold treasury of successive stages, all collectively manifesting the perfectness of one's own mind that is inherently possessed.
It is meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and not a gate of insight (*vipaśyanā*) that can be established.
How then do the sentient beings of the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have transcended the world, employ their minds of cognitive objects?
To fathom the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata using worldly language and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is like a lute, a harp, a *konghou*, or a *pipa*:
though they possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce music. You and all sentient beings—

It is likewise so. The true mind of precious awakening is perfectly complete in each and every one; yet, just as when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal manifests its radiance, when you briefly raise your mind, the afflictions of worldly toil arise first.
This is because you do not diligently seek the path of supreme enlightenment, but instead cherish and cling to the Lesser Vehicle.
"To be satisfied with a small attainment"—this reproaches Pūrṇa for failing to seek diligently and instead merely engaging in verbal disputation; it is intended to urge him toward further progress.
Now, the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind, is thus. How can there be the world of desire, the world of form, or the formless world?
There are sentient beings and those of the two vehicles who transcend the world; each takes their own fundamental wisdom as the knower and each relies upon their realized object as the known.
Taking this very mind-object of what is known as a point of comparison, they infer and speculate that the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Tathāgata is likewise the same.
How could they know that unsurpassed *bodhi* is the most subtle and supreme, being fundamentally not [the same]?

This should be reflected upon. Furthermore, you employ worldly language—such as "overwhelming," "extinguishing," "not tolerating," and "the convergence of causes and conditions"—and thus intermingle these with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
How could you know that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the perfectly integrated Threefold Canon (*tripiṭaka*)?
This is fundamentally inconceivable. It is beyond thought. Yet, you suddenly attempt to conceive of it with a deluded mind and through deluded words;

how far removed this is from the truth! Now, the wondrous nature resides within humans; it contains wondrous function by virtue of its wondrous essence, yet it must still be brought forth by means of wondrous wisdom.
It is like the lute, the zither, the *konghou*, or the *pipa*: though they possess wondrous sounds, if there is no [skillful] hand...
The finger, however, ultimately cannot produce it. You and all sentient beings are also like this.

This precious, awakened true mind—(which truly possesses the three meanings of being free from defilement, luminosity, and functional utility)—is fully present and perfectly complete in every person, just as lutes, harps, and other instruments all possess wondrous sounds.
Yet, the reason some can produce sound while others cannot is simply due to the presence or absence of a skillful finger.

As I have attained this within my mind, it is manifested through my hands; thus, with a single press of a finger, radiant light bursts forth, illuminating heaven and earth, all of which constitutes wondrous function. Is it not because there is a wondrous finger that one can produce wondrous sounds?
(The "Ocean Seal" is the Buddha-mind, the Samādhi of Constant Abiding. You, however, for a mere moment raise your mind, and worldly afflictions fill your eyes, while objects and forms proliferate.

Luo, if you do not manifest wondrous function, is it not because you lack the wondrous finger that fails to produce the wondrous sound? There is no other reason for the non-manifestation of wondrous function:
it is because there is the unsurpassed path of awakening, which is the fruit of Buddha-wisdom—namely, the wondrous wisdom that manifests wondrous function.
This is what the Buddha initially used to unite with the *tathāgatagarbha*. It is because you are unwilling to be diligent [in this].
While seeking the path to unsurpassed enlightenment, they cherish the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), taking its merits to be easy and its benefits immediate.
Content with what is meager, they regard the illusory treasures of the "Transformation City"—such as the six supernormal powers and eighteen transformations—as sufficient.
No longer knowing where the true treasure lies, they fail to set forth. If they were willing to seek diligently, they would walk hand-in-hand with the Tathāgata.

Proceed! I shall certainly not deceive you; will you not exert yourself? ○ The *Zongjing* says: "When music of extraordinary tones is enjoyed, if one presses the fingers, the *gong* and *shang* notes accord with the rhythm.
When a person possesses the nature of awakening, if they employ their wisdom and skill, that skillful application is in profound harmony with reality.

Success or failure rests with the person; refinement or coarseness depends on oneself. Therefore, when the Sugata pressed his finger, he manifested the light of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi for all sentient beings."
Raising the mind manifests the signs of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). ○ Zhong’s Commentary states:

"In the preceding text, it was said that by extinguishing the dust and merging with awakening, one gives rise to the wondrous awakening of True Suchness (*tathatā*), as well as 'one becoming immeasurable' and so forth. This is what is meant by: 'When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light.

The second instance of the character 'give rise to' (*fa*) corresponds precisely to this; whereas previously it was said that by turning one's back on awakening and merging with the dust, one gives rise to worldly afflictions."
There is a worldly characteristic, namely: "As soon as you raise your mind, the dust of affliction first arises. The preceding passage is the Dharma; this present passage is the analogy.

These do not constitute two separate layers of meaning. At this point, one understands that what was spoken in the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision possesses only its name, but has not yet reached its full realization; it is only in this sūtra that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are clearly explained.
The threefold treasury is perfectly integrated; it is the single mind of tranquil extinction.
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata share the same precious awakening, perfect luminosity, and truly wondrous, pure mind; we are non-dual and complete."
Yet I, having encountered beginningless delusive thoughts in the past, have long remained in saṃsāra; though I have now attained the Holy Vehicle, I am not yet ultimate.

World-Honored One, all your delusions are completely extinguished, and you alone possess the wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata: regarding all sentient beings, [how can they attain this state?]"
"For what reason does delusion exist? Why do we obscure our own wondrous clarity and undergo this drowning in samsara?
Thus, Pūrṇa sought out the cause of delusion and prepared himself for spiritual cultivation. Pūrṇa said:
"As the Buddha has taught, the precious, awakened true mind is perfectly complete in each and every being; therefore, my precious, awakened true mind is one with that of the Tathāgata."
The wondrous, pure mind is uniformly perfect; it ought to be without dualistic characteristics.
Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusive thoughts, which obscured my own wondrous, pure, and perfectly luminous jewel-like awareness, giving rise to this succession of birth and death.
Having long remained in saṃsāra, although I have now attained the Holy Vehicle, I am not yet ultimate. While the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted, ignorance still remains. Its...

It is indeed appropriate that they do not know how delusion arises from its cause. As for the World-Honored One, having exhausted the five abodes and extinguished the two deaths, all delusions are completely and perfectly eradicated; he alone is wondrous, true, and eternal, and is thus called the Great Awakened One.
He must certainly know the cause of delusion. I venture to ask the Tathāgata: by what cause do all sentient beings give rise to delusion? Please look back and consider this yourself.
This obscures the wondrous clarity, leading one to undergo this drowning and submersion. Previously, you asked how that which is fundamentally pure and serene could suddenly arise;
the World-Honored One answered that it arises due to ignorance (*avidyā*). Now you ask: by what cause does this ignorance itself arise?
This is what is meant by "directly tracing it back to its ultimate source."
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unexhausted. I shall now question you again by means of matters currently manifest in the world.

Have you not heard that in the city of Śrāvastī, a man named Yaśodharāta (meaning 'Gift from the Sacrifice,' so called because he obtained [the child] by petitioning a deity), suddenly one morning looked at his face in a mirror?
He took pleasure in the head with its visible eyebrows and eyes within the mirror, and grew angry and reproached himself."
Not seeing his own face, he mistook it for a malevolent spirit (chimei) and ran about wildly and uncontrollably. What do you think?
For what reason does this man run about wildly without cause? Pūrṇa replied, "This man’s mind is deranged; there is no other reason."
From here below, the text uses illustrative examples to clarify that the root of delusion is itself causeless. The Buddha told Pūrṇa:

"Based on your deduction that there is no duality, you have already believed in your own original truthfulness and accorded with the Buddha’s perfect permanence. Furthermore, you have believed in the Buddha’s eternal realization;

thus, even doubts regarding the arising and continuity of the myriad dharmas and delusions concerning the difficulty of reconciling essence and characteristics have all been shattered. Nevertheless, although you..."
Doubts have been removed, yet other delusions remain unexhausted; they still do not realize that this ignorance has no cause, and thus they seek it out by force.
Right now, there happens to be a matter before us, and I shall use this to clarify it for you.
Have you not heard of the case of Yan-luo-da-duo (Śaṇmukha) in the city of Śrāvastī, who suddenly one morning looked into a mirror and became obsessed with his reflection?

The eyebrows and eyes within a mirror can be seen, yet one who cannot see the face and features of their own head and, thinking "this [face] is not visible," considers themselves to be a *chimei* (a mountain demon) and then runs about wildly and without restraint—what do you think?
They are not actually a *chimei*, yet they consider themselves to be one. From what cause does this person’s madness arise? It should not be so.
"To run about frantically for no reason. When Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was questioned by the World-Honored One, he immediately understood clearly and replied:
"This person merely has his mind become deranged and runs; there is no other cause. 'For no reason' means there is no cause."

The Buddha said: "Wondrous awakening is perfectly luminous; its fundamental nature is perfect, luminous, and wondrous. Since it is designated as 'delusion,' how could it have a cause? If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion?
From these various delusions, they arise one from another in succession; through accumulating delusion upon delusion, they have passed through dust-like kalpas.
Even though a Buddha may explain and reveal it, one still cannot turn back from such a cause of delusion. Because delusion exists of itself due to confusion, one recognizes this confusion."

Without cause, delusion has nothing upon which to rely; since there is not even arising, what is there to be extinguished? One who attains Bodhi is like a person awake recounting the events of a dream.
Even if the mind were sharp and lucid, by what causes or conditions could one grasp at things within a dream?
How much more so when they are without cause and fundamentally non-existent? It is like that Daṇḍa in the city; how could he have had any cause or condition for his own fear?
He ran about with his head spinning. Suddenly, the madness ceased. The spinning was not something obtained from outside; even if the madness had not ceased, what would have been lost?
Pūrṇa, such is the nature of delusion. For what reason does it exist? (One should say: "For what reason is it so?")
This is the application of the analogy to the Dharma. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra understood the matter but was confused regarding the principle;
therefore, the Buddha guided him by means of what he clearly understood. He said that this awakening is furthermore subtle, furthermore luminous, and furthermore perfect.
A single awakening possesses these three meanings; it is inherently and originally perfect, inherently and originally luminous, and inherently and originally subtle. It is not...
It is a provisional cultivation and realization, yet it has never been anything other than delusion. Since it is already designated as "delusion," it must have arisen abruptly;
how, then, could it have a cause? If it had a cause, it would be called "true. How, then, could it be called "delusion"?
One who seeks a cause within delusion fails to understand the principle of delusion. Furthermore, both ignorance and delusive thought—

This is the most fundamental subtle affliction. From its initial characteristic of delusion, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*); from its characteristic of movement within that delusion, it is called discursive thought (*vikalpa*).
Subsequently, wherever ordinary beings are deluded regarding the Reality, that is ignorance; wherever they cling to the semblance, that is discursive thought.
These mutually incite one another; how many layers are there? They revolve and depend upon each other, proceeding from delusion.
Accumulated delusion has persisted for as long as atoms and kalpas, yet one can never find the initial characteristic of its cause.
Even with the Buddha’s eightfold voice and four kinds of analytical eloquence, he could not retroactively deduce and explain its primal causal origin.

This is truly because the substance of delusion is fundamentally empty and thus cannot be described. It is like a person at the beginning who suddenly speaks falsely, and this is passed down in succession from one to another.
False speech is false; when one investigates its causes, they are successively all empty. Thus, the cause of delusion is itself the very cause of confusion.

Failing to realize that there is no cause, it perpetually manifests as existing of its own accord. If one recognizes that delusion has no cause for its arising, one will see for oneself that all falsehoods are fundamentally empty and have nothing upon which to rely.
Not only does one realize the emptiness of falsehood, but one also realizes the ultimate...
If it has never arisen from the very beginning, what will there be to extinguish at the end of the kalpa?

Thus, your claim that the World-Honored One has completely extinguished all delusions is itself a delusion. Although I have now attained Bodhi, I can only say that these delusions originally have no cause;
how could I possibly extract a "causeless delusion" to show it to others? Therefore, [I have] attained...
Enlightenment is like a person who has awakened and speaks of events from a dream.

Although the mind may be sharp and clear, there is no other method by which one could pick up an object from within the dream to show it to others. Furthermore, objects in a dream are but shadows and echoes;
they seem to have causes and seem as if they could be picked up, yet even these cannot be grasped. How much less so, then, can the deluded thoughts that are fundamentally without cause?
Since there is nothing at all, one seeks its cause of arising, wishing to seize and sever it; how could this possibly be achieved?
This delusion is without cause, just like the case of Devadatta’s madness: it was not because someone taught him to be mad.
Nor is it that madness originally existed upon one's head; it was simply that one was deluded regarding one's own head and mistook it for a reflection.
One ran about in madness out of self-terror. Suddenly, when this madness ceases, one realizes that this head was never obtained from without.
Even if the madness has not yet ceased, the eyebrows are still above the eyes and the nostrils continue to hang downward, never having moved.
If not even a single thread of it remains attached, how could there be anything lost? Pūrṇa, your deluded nature is no different from the madness of Śaśaviṣāṇa;
how could its cause have a fixed location that you might seek from the Tathāgata?
If you simply do not follow after the three kinds of continuity—the world, karma and its fruits, and sentient beings—then because these three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise.
Thus, the madness of your own *yantradada* within the mind will naturally subside. This subsiding is itself *bodhi*.
The supremely pure and luminous mind is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm; it is not obtained from others. Why, then, rely on arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization?
It is like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within their own garment, yet remains unaware of it while wandering in poverty and exposure elsewhere.
He wandered about begging for food; though he was truly impoverished, the jewel had never been lost.

Suddenly, a wise person pointed out the jewel to him, whereupon his wishes were fulfilled according to his heart and he attained great abundance. Only then did he realize that the divine jewel was not obtained from without.
This is the teaching on the method for ceasing madness. You investigated the cause of delusion, intending to find its fundamental cause and sever it through arduous cultivation.
Now that you have realized it is causeless and fundamentally empty, why must you still act thus?
You need only refrain from following the three kinds of conceptualization—the continuity of manifesting karma, its fruits, and sentient beings—in accordance with worldly conditions.
As for the mind: because the three conditions are severed, coarse afflictions and coarse objects have already been exhausted.
Consequently, the subtle flow of thoughts within the three subtleties—which serve as the deep cause for coarse afflictions and objects—naturally ceases to arise.

This is truly because coarse thoughts have been eliminated through matured practice, and thus subtle thoughts also follow in being exhausted. Since both the coarse and the subtle are delusions, how could fundamental ignorance [not be extinguished]?
If you can exist alone, then the nature of madness within your mind—the *Yajñadatta*—will naturally dissolve and come to rest.
Once this madness ceases, you are immediately *bodhi*. This is what is meant by: "To know illusion is to leave it; to leave illusion is to awaken.

Upon reaching this point, you will know the supreme, pure, and luminous mind (*vijñāna*). ("Supreme" means transcending all else; even the provisional vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas refer to it as pure and luminous.)

It is not that which is merely "supremely pure and luminous. It is primordially pure and inherently pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; it is originally one's own possession, not something obtained from others.
Why, then, rely on skin and bones, undergoing toil and hardship for kalpas on end, to achieve cultivation and realization?
To clarify this further by means of an analogy: suppose there is a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within his own garment, yet he is unaware of it.
Consequently, he wanders through foreign lands, impoverished and exposed to the elements, running about begging for food. Although he is destitute, the jewel has never been lost.

Suddenly, a wise person points out the jewel to him; his every wish is then fulfilled according to his heart’s desire, bringing him great wealth and prosperity, whereupon he finally realizes [the truth].
The divine jewel was originally an object within one's own clothing; it was not obtained from without. Thus, "resting is itself bodhi," which is not obtained from others.
There is no need for laborious cultivation or realization—it is simply like this. This does not merely clarify for Pūrṇa how delusion can exist;
it also resolves Ānanda’s doubts regarding his seeing forms to arouse his resolve and his request for me to bestow the samādhi.
Both are now clearly explained. Question: Is this sudden cessation the same as the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, or is it different?

Answer: The intent of "cessation" is the same, but they differ in terms of their respective stages. For an ordinary person at the stage of common ground or within the stage of names, [the cessation is merely conceptual].

Upon hearing this Dharma-gate, one awakens thoroughly to the reality that the false is empty. Entering through the gateway of the ear and forgetting the object of perception is precisely not following worldly discrimination;
it is the sudden severance of the three conditions. From this point, by means of forgetting, non-arising occurs;
from non-arising, exhaustion occurs; from exhaustion, emptiness occurs; and from emptiness, cessation occurs. This is a single path of rest, proceeding from the shallow toward the deep.
Profound! It continues until the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), which is precisely the manifestation of the supreme, pure, and luminous mind of *bodhi*.

This is entirely identical [to the previous teaching]. If Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra had already exhausted the knots of the faculties following the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), why would he need to reverse his previous practice and again enter through the gateway of the ear?
He merely proceeds from the emptiness of the perceiver and the perceived, suddenly bringing to rest both the grasping at dharmas and conceptual discrimination.
When birth reaches the point where quiescent extinction manifests before one, then the supremely pure and luminous mind also manifests before one.

This is because in the preceding stage, both the dualistic attachments to persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi* and *dharma-dṛṣṭi*) were simultaneously extinguished, whereas in this stage, only the attachment to phenomena is extinguished; thus, it is said that there is a difference in terms of their respective stages.
Zhong says: "Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise. Regarding the three conditions: they are, for example, the mutual dependence of light and darkness, and so forth.
The "conditions of the world" refers to such things as being entangled by common karma. The "conditions of sentient beings" refers to [the afflictions of] killing, stealing, and greed.
The "conditions of karmic results" refers to falsely taking these to be clear awareness. These three together constitute the general causes.

○ From here below begins Ānanda’s third set of doubts and their causes and conditions. First, within the section "The Manifested Vision Transcends Sentiment," he doubted that the nature of vision does not arise from causes and conditions.
Second, prior to the section "The Perfect Revelation of the Seven Great Elements,"...

One might doubt that the myriad dharmas do not arise from causes and conditions. Now, this third point concerns the doubt that the realization of the fruit and the attainment of the Way likewise do not belong to causes and conditions—that there is a fruit without a cause.

This is indeed highly questionable. The underlying intention is likely this: one has heard that the Buddha long ago rejected causes and conditions, yet within his words he also speaks of causes and conditions;
having spoken of causes and conditions, he then asks why one must rely on cultivation and realization. Therefore...
He raised this question. Previously, he had doubted the nature and characteristics [of phenomena]; now, he doubts cause and effect.
At that moment, Ānanda, amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rose, and addressed the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, you have just spoken of the three conditions for severing the karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—[briefly citing the fruits of karma, though the intent encompasses all sentient beings in the world; the character ‘ye’ (karma) should likely be an error for the character ‘děng’ (equal)]—thereby severing the three causes.”
When non-arising is realized within the mind, the madness of Cūḍapanthaka naturally subsides. This subsiding is itself bodhi; it is not obtained from others.
Thus, the nature of causes and conditions is clear and evident. How could the Tathāgata suddenly discard causes and conditions? I attained awakening through causes and conditions.
World-Honored One, why should this principle apply only to us young śrāvakas in training? Within this assembly now...

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others, having heard from the aged brahmin the causes and conditions regarding the Buddha, gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, attained awakening, and achieved the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Now, if you say that bodhi does not arise from causes and conditions, then the doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) taught by Kauṣṭhila and others in Rājagṛha would become the primary truth (*paramārtha*). We pray that you will bestow great compassion upon us and dispel our confusion and distress.
This refers back to the Buddha’s words to maintain the doctrine of causes and conditions. At that moment, Ānanda (and so forth) addressed the Buddha.
His intention was that since the Tathāgata had already rejected causes and conditions, yet within his speech he also stated that when conditions are severed, causes do not arise.
When madness ceases, bodhi manifests; this is the teaching of causes and conditions, which is so clear and evident that it seems impossible to discard.
Why, then, do you wish to abandon it all at once? Furthermore, these causes and conditions are the gateway for us to enter the Way and the ground upon which we awaken;
for those such as ourselves, they truly possess great benefit. Moreover, it is not only our age [that stands to gain].
Few have studied under it to receive its benefits; even the venerable elders of former times, such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana and others, all attained realization through this very means.

To say now that one does not rely on causes and conditions is to contradict the claims of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who assert that after eighty thousand kalpas, one spontaneously attains the Way—stopping at the ultimate point like a ball of thread unwinding until it reaches its end. This [latter view] instead becomes the first [refutation].
Is it the ultimate truth? Even if the Tathāgata does not fall into the category of causes and conditions, would he not surely fall into the category of spontaneity?
This is yet another point where we are bewildered and lack understanding; we further hope that you will lift the veil and resolve our doubts.
Pūrṇa’s inquiry having been fully resolved, he again yielded the floor to Ānanda to pose a question, thereby returning to the primary interlocutor.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "It is just like the case of the city dweller, Yaśoda, whose state of madness, through its causes and conditions, might be extinguished."

Then the nature of non-insanity emerges spontaneously; causes and conditions are spontaneous, and the principle reaches its ultimate limit here. (This merely explains it by way of analogy; if one applies it to the Dharma, however...)

One must say that it is through the cessation of the causal conditions of ignorance that Bodhi naturally emerges. Ānanda, the head of Śaṇḍha was originally natural; it was inherently so from the beginning. There is no "not-being-so" that is not itself.
For what reason did he fear his head and run about in a frenzy? (The following section uses the head as a double refutation. First, regarding the refutation within the context of "naturalness":

if the fundamental nature belonged to the category of the natural, sentient beings would always spontaneously perceive their own nature and would never again fall into delusion or transmigration. Why, then, do there still exist those who are deluded and turn away from it? It is evident, therefore, that Bodhi does not belong to the category of the natural.)
If one’s head is naturally present, yet becomes crazed due to causes and conditions, why would it not remain naturally present even when lost due to causes and conditions?

The original head is never lost; it is merely that through madness and fear, delusions arise, while the head itself undergoes no change whatsoever. Why, then, rely upon causes and conditions [to lose it]? (In this teaching on the refutation of causes and conditions, it is said:

"If the nature of Bodhi originally exists naturally and later, through the false conditions of ignorance, turns away from it so as to become invisible, one then claims that this nature entirely belongs to causes and conditions. This would mean the true nature has actually been lost, and only then could one believe that causes and conditions are not false. Now, why would it be lost without relying on causes and conditions? Indeed... )

The nature is fundamentally never lost; it is only through groundless delusion and turning away that it seems as though it has been lost. Yet, even at the very moment of this deluded turning away when it appears lost, the original nature truly undergoes no change. Once one has seen the nature and shattered delusion, why would this nature depend upon causes and conditions?

Madness is originally natural; there is inherently a state of madness and fear. Before one was mad, where did this madness lie hidden? (From here below, he uses "madness" to negate both [naturalness and causality]; first, he negates naturalness.

If non-madness were natural, then since the head is fundamentally without delusion, why would one run about in madness? (This negates causality. If non-madness were natural, then "madness" should be non-existent.)

"Spontaneity" is merely a reversal of "causes and conditions. If one awakens to the original head (this follows the previous discussion regarding the head to simultaneously sweep away both [notions], awakening to the fact that the head is neither spontaneous nor caused by conditions), and recognizes the frantic running (this follows the previous discussion regarding the madness to simultaneously sweep away both, knowing that the madness is neither spontaneous nor caused by conditions), then both "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity" are mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, I say that because the three conditions are severed, it is the Bodhicitta. When the Bodhicitta arises, the mind of arising and ceasing ceases. This is merely...
Arising and ceasing; when both ceasing and arising are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*).

If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), then it would be clear that the spontaneous mind arises and the arising-and-ceasing mind ceases—yet this too is arising and ceasing. That which is without arising or ceasing is called "spontaneous.

It is like how various phenomena in the world, when blended and unified into a single entity, are called the nature of combination (*saṃghāta-svabhāva*); that which is not a combination is termed the "original" (*mūla*).
Yet this nature is fundamentally not "thus"; it is a harmony that is not a union. It is detached from both union and suchness; it is neither union nor detachment.

Only this phrase may be called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*). Awakening (*bodhi*) and Nirvana remain far distant; they are not to be realized through your diligent cultivation over kalpas.

Though you may memorize and uphold the pure and wondrous principles of the twelve divisions of the Tathāgatas’ scriptures throughout the ten directions, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Like the sands of the Ganges, these merely increase frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
These two—causality (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*)—are both to be discarded as naturally void. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As for what you call causality and spontaneity, let us now examine them by means of the previous analogy of madness. It is just like Yajñadatta; the nature of his madness..."
When conditions are extinguished and eliminated, the nature of non-insanity naturally emerges.
Thus, the causal conditions you cling to as the natural principle of both the mundane and supramundane realms are entirely contained herein; there is nothing further remaining.
This is why you hold fast with parsimony and refuse to relinquish them, failing to realize that this is not yet the ultimate truth. If you claim that the head is fundamentally natural, then...
It must have been thus from the very beginning; there is not a single moment or a single place where it is not spontaneous.
One should not be startled by what is a *chimei* (a mountain spirit) and fall into madness. That you are now suddenly startled by the absence of a head and run about in a frenzy surely has a cause;
it is certainly not spontaneous. Not knowing for what reason you fear the lack of a head and run madly, it is clear that this head is not spontaneous.

Now, if you claim that the head is originally natural and that one suddenly becomes startled by the absence of a head and runs madly because of looking into a mirror, why does one not likewise lose the head at the very moment of looking into the mirror?

Furthermore, at the precise moment when one is deluded by panic and running wild, the head has never been lost and has undergone no change; thus, it is clear that this head certainly does not depend upon causes and conditions.

In general, it is said that if this head were natural (*svabhāva*), there would be no madness or fear; if this head were produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there ought to be a true master [of it].
Now, because there is fear, it is not natural; and because there is no loss [of the head], it is not produced by causes and conditions.
If one were to say that madness originally arises from nature, then it should have always existed from the very beginning.
In one's state of madness and terror, one does not know where this madness was hidden prior to its onset, nor why it did not arise then.
If you claim that madness does not emerge spontaneously but arises from causes and conditions, then the head itself would originally have been free from madness.
Why do you suddenly run about in such a frantic manner? Therefore, know that it is not only that the head does not belong to causes and conditions or to spontaneity;

even madness does not belong to causes and conditions or to spontaneity. Since you know that both the head and madness do not belong to causes and conditions or to spontaneity, you should know that both wondrous enlightenment and ignorance likewise do not belong to causes and conditions or to spontaneity. You...
Alas, you have been solely deluded regarding the treasure of your own home, rushing outward in pursuit of it; thus, clinging to conditions and clinging to a self are things you cannot avoid.
If you were to awaken to the fact that your original head is neither conditioned nor self, and recognize that your frantic running is likewise neither conditioned nor self, [you would be liberated].

Thus one knows that causes and conditions, as well as spontaneity, are all merely the muttering of sleep-talking within a dream; they are all equally frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*) and possess no real meaning.

Therefore, when I say that the Bodhicitta arises from the severance of the three conditions, I mean that once the three conditions of discursive conceptualization and frivolous proliferation are eliminated, that itself is the true Bodhicitta. This is because attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been removed.
Regarding this: within the three types of continuity, the non-forgetting of conceptualization is precisely *prapañca* (proliferation).

What was stated previously—that one does not follow after conceptualization—is precisely for the purpose of bringing *prapañca* to rest. When *prapañca* ceases, ignorance has no basis; awakening (*bodhi*) is free from obstructions.
What need is there to wait for anything that is not true? Nevertheless, although it is identical to awakening, one must not further attempt to produce awakening.
Conceptualization. Why is this? If the thought of bodhicitta arises, then the arising mind is born and the ceasing mind is extinguished;
this is still merely a mind of arising and ceasing, not the true bodhicitta.

Not only is this a mind of arising and ceasing, but even if both arising and ceasing were exhausted within the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*), one could not give rise to a mark of spontaneity. Why is this?

If the mind arises naturally, then as arising occurs, cessation occurs; this too is entirely a mind of arising and cessation, and is not the true path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*). Why is it that "natural" is still considered arising and cessation?
It is because those who reckon non-arising and non-cessation to be "natural" are like worldly phenomena where various characteristics blend together to form a single entity; this is called...
Regarding the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), that which is in contrast to this conjunction is termed "original suchness" (*prakṛti*).
Original suchness is spontaneity (*svabhāva*); conjunction is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This very original suchness is a relative phenomenon.
It is not truly primordial; thus it is also a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). As it is said:
"A hair’s breadth of lingering thought is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion results in ten thousand kalpas of bondage.

Until one reaches the state where the primordial is not primordial, and where union is not union—where both the primordial and union are utterly transcended—and where both transcendence and non-transcendence are simultaneously negated; having reached this point...
This alone is the correct phrase. This alone is the living phrase. This alone is the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*).
It is by repeatedly discarding [all views] until there is nothing left to discard that one accords with the true path of non-effort—the true *bodhicitta*.

Having reached this point, fearing that the Venerable One might mistake intellectual understanding for realization, he strikes him right on the head once more, saying: "Even so, you have attained it."
Reaching such a state, even Bodhi and Nirvana remain far distant. It is precisely at the moment one attains the phrase that true aspiration is born;

it is exactly then that one should cultivate practice and advance toward Bodhi. How could this be like you, who take mere erudition and memorization as well as lifelong toil to be the means of cultivation and realization?
Even if you were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, you would ultimately never succeed.
This is indeed a realization. The reason for this is simply that they are unwilling to relinquish the dharmas of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, it is not merely that they memorize the teachings I have spoken—like a vessel receiving water without spilling a single drop—but do so in vain as mere conceptual proliferation.

Even if one were able to memorize the twelve divisions of the sutras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—including their pure and wondrous principles—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it would merely increase frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). This has no connection whatsoever with the fundamental matter;
as the saying goes, "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure. Regarding the study of words and letters, in sum—
This is called the habit-energy of names and words; it obstructs the gate of self-awakening because one cannot penetrate the nature of the person within.
If one can distance oneself from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then rest is itself *bodhi*.

Since this does not even rely upon arduous effort, how could there be any difficulty in accomplishing it over the course of kalpas? ○ Panshan said: "The path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages. To study [it]...

This is to weary the body, like a monkey grasping at reflections. One must arouse great courage and ferocity, severing speech, stilling thought, forgetting subject and object, and cutting off all images.
Transcending directly in a single leap, one does not traverse the gradual path; only then, through this great matter of causal conditions, will one know the definitive point.
○ He said: From "If you awaken to your original head" onwards, he elucidates the correct principle. The single word "awaken" (悟) [is the key].

First is the single character for "knowing. This is the wondrous secret for ceasing madness. It is through realizing that one's original head is neither spontaneous nor produced by causes and conditions, that one subsequently comes to know the frantic running about is likewise neither spontaneous nor produced by causes and conditions.

By awakening to the original head, one finally perceives that the fundamental face is what is truly real; by knowing the frantic running about, one only then awakens to the fact that seeking outward is delusion. Furthermore, one awakens...
By realizing the fundamental head, one knows that it is inherently pure; by recognizing the wild running of consciousness, one knows that phenomena manifest according to karma.
You have long been deluded regarding your own family treasure, rushing outward in pursuit, clinging to conditions and clinging to the self—this was indeed inevitable.
However, were you to personally see the original source, your wild mind would suddenly cease, and you would know that causes, conditions, and spontaneity are all but dreams.
Dreaming and speaking in one's sleep both constitute frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); they are not the true meaning.

Therefore, when I say that the bodhicitta arises from the severance of the three conditions, this is the method for ceasing madness and awakening to the fundamental source. How could it be comparable to causes, conditions, or spontaneity?

Although you have discoursed with certainty and clarity upon the principles of causality and spontaneity, and are renowned among men as foremost in erudition, yet because of this habituation to extensive learning over many kalpas, you could not escape the peril posed by the Mātanga woman.

Why, then, did you need to wait for my Buddha-peak divine mantra? Now, the fire of lust in the Mātanga woman’s heart has been instantly extinguished; she has attained the stage of Anāgāmin within my Dharma.
The Forest of Diligence is perfected and the River of Craving is dried up, bringing you liberation.

Therefore, Ānanda, though you have for kalpas memorized and upheld the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments, it is not equal to practicing untainted karma for a single day and remaining far removed from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.
As with Mātangī, who was formerly a courtesan, yet by the power of the divine mantra, her lustful desires were dissolved.
Among the Dharma, she is now known as the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlā. Together with Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, they simultaneously awakened to their past causes.

They realized that throughout successive lifetimes, craving had been the source of suffering; because they had cultivated untainted goodness for even a single thought-moment, they were able to transcend the bonds of existence.

Or perhaps you have received a prediction of enlightenment; how then can you deceive yourself? You still linger here merely to observe and listen—“observe and listen” (觀聽) being synonymous with “see and hear” (見聞).
This is an extreme statement regarding the弊 (dangers/defects) of mere erudition, intended to urge you toward further cultivation.

Although you discuss causes and conditions and spontaneity with such certainty and clarity that there is not the slightest error, people in the world praise you as one of great learning, ranking you as...
First: Even with this extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas, he was still unable to escape the peril of Matanga’s amorous arts.

If such vast learning were truly capable of liberating one from suffering and averting calamity, why would it have been necessary to wait for the power of my secret mantras and spiritual assistance to suddenly extinguish Matanga’s lust-fire and enable him to realize the third fruit and achieve diligence?
"Ānanda, the river of craving has dried up; have you also escaped the peril of lust? Believe me, it was not by the power of mantras that you were freed;

you certainly could not have attained liberation on your own. Therefore, Ānanda, though you have throughout kalpas memorized and maintained the Tathāgata’s secret, inconceivable, and wondrously adorned teachings that he never previously revealed, it is not equal to practicing for a single day [the path of non-attachment]."
Regarding the karma of outflows (*āsrava*): one abandons the provisional and returns to the real, remaining far removed from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Practice arises while understanding is severed; one enters the non-discriminative state where both body and mind are simultaneously cut off. First, by severing attachment, even the nature of things is found to be non-existent.

Subsequently, by severing aversion—one who raises up these two sufferings of love and hate, which arise together with birth and are most difficult to eliminate—one distances oneself from them. The decisive pivot lies solely in this single moment.
Furthermore, consider the case of Mātaṅgī. Having been a courtesan in her past lives, she was able to dissolve her lustful desires through the power of a divine mantra.
Within the Dharma, she is now known as the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī. Together with Yaśodharā, they both awakened to their past causes;

they realized that the retribution of their female bodies was entirely due to the depth of their past craving for desire, and thus their past karmic conditions were opened and transformed, leading them to repentance and awakening.
It is profoundly significant. Now, Yaśodharā’s body was already of a delicate constitution, and the courtesan Puṇḍravardhanī (Daṅga) was an even more inferior vessel;

yet, through cultivation for but a single thought-moment, both attained great benefit, with some even emerging from the bonds of existence, as in the case of Mādrī attaining the third fruit of the path.
Some have received predictions of enlightenment, such as Yaśodharā upon her attainment of Buddhahood; they have all realized high levels of realization.
Yet you, a magnificent man known by the multitudes among devas and humans, instead remain self-deluded and self-obscured, bound and entangled by yourself.
You linger in what you have seen and heard, unable to relinquish them; you see before your eyes that cultivation brings benefit yet do not practice it, clearly knowing [the futility of] worldly play.
To debate without merit and remain attached to it, merely guarding one's extensive learning while stagnating in a low position—is this not a cause for extreme shame?
These words of bitter urgency are meant to reproach [the opponent] and to encourage [the practitioner]. They are meant to encourage.
One should know that this particular debate by Ānanda is of the utmost importance; for, as previously stated, he has already exhausted all arguments regarding causes and conditions.
Later, there is further discussion regarding cultivation and realization. If there were cultivation and realization in a straightforward sense, it would contradict what was previously stated.

If, on the other hand, they were entirely neither cause nor condition, then subsequent cultivation and realization would be rendered void. Thus, these sacred words truly appear to be mutually contradictory.
Yet this must be distinguished. Now, to clarify that the Truth is fundamentally without location is like saying that the head is fundamentally without loss;
how then could there be actual cultivation or actual realization? It is certainly not the case that one falls exclusively into [the realm of] causes and conditions.

Furthermore, to clarify that the manifestation of delusion is like the onset of madness, does it mean that there is ultimately no cultivation and no realization? Nor is it the case that one falls exclusively [into the realm of non-causality].
It falls naturally into place. From this, one knows that this sutra involves neither cultivation nor realization;
yet it certainly does not obstruct the existence of cultivation and realization, and while there is cultivation and realization, it still does not obstruct the absence of cultivation and realization.
Thus, the preceding and following passages are no longer contradictory. How profoundly subtle and wondrous is its purport! [Then Subhūti] asked a question out of his own fullness.
At this point, it completes another cycle, called the Cycle of Non-arising and Non-obstruction.

This is because at the end of the third fascicle, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction on shattering the false to reveal the true, had merely awakened to the falsity of what he clung to and first perceived the truth that had been overlooked.
Thus, he only then thanked the Buddha for dissolving his inverted thoughts and subsequently requested that further subtle delusions be eliminated. Up to this point...
At the beginning of the fourth fascicle, Pūrṇa raises two questions on behalf of others concerning the continuity of birth and the perfect interfusion [of principle and phenomena].
The Buddha answers the first question by profoundly investigating how the myriad dharmas originate from ignorance, yet are fundamentally empty and unarisen.

He answers the second question by perfectly manifesting that nature and characteristics are the Buddha’s bodhi-knowledge and vision, which are thoroughly interfused and unimpeded. This, together with the three rounds...
This is even more difficult. Thus, by thoroughly eliminating subtle afflictions without remainder, the principle of non-arising and non-obstruction becomes ever clearer.

Furthermore, one should know that in the previous section, the two types of grasping (*dvividha-grāha*) were primarily explained in terms of their conceptual nature (*vikalpita*), which pertains exclusively to the realm of awakening.

In this section, the investigation extends to the innate (*sahaja*) forms of the two graspings, simultaneously opening the way for the intention of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This is because subtle afflictions must be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, if one returns to the nature of concentration (*samādhi*), then within the first cycle, the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness is discussed to directly point to the essence of the wondrous concentration inherently possessed by one's own mind,
thereby fully manifesting its permanence and omnipresence. Within this [subsequent] cycle, the latter two *tathāgatagarbhas*,
up to the perfectly integrated three *garbhas*, are discussed to provide a detailed exposition of the wondrous [concentration] inherently possessed by one's own mind.
The function of samādhi fully manifests its unimpeded and perfect interfusion.
This is precisely the wondrous, perfectly round true mind by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi; it is the fundamental samādhi of suchness, not requiring further cultivation.
Among the three names, this is "wondrous śamatha," and to penetrate and awaken to this is "subtle and secret contemplation. Furthermore, this mind and this samādhi are one.
All sentient beings, including those of provisional and limited capacities, are entirely unable to fathom this; therefore, they practice in confusion and ultimately achieve no real fruit.
Thus, among the four aspects of the true Dharma in the title of this sutra, this precisely belongs to the Tathāgata’s secret cause.
Having finished explaining *śamatha* to lead them to realize that the wondrous mind is inherently endowed with perfect concentration.
The section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) within the first division is concluded.
From this point onward, the text provides answers to Ānanda’s request for the "wondrous samādhi" by means of entering deeply through the single gate of the wondrous mind.

Although the old commentary categorizes this as the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is not logically incorrect, Tiantai judges that the stage of the Perfect Teaching’s *zhù* (abiding) is identical to this.
A separate stage is what is called "true cultivation. However, prior to this stage, it is not yet fully permitted to be considered cultivation;
one should know that this section of the treatise discusses cultivation while it is still at the initial gateway of cultivation.

Regarding realization, there is indeed an initial stage of realization, for only when the merit of perfect penetration is accomplished does one’s faith become full, allowing entry and abiding. Furthermore, the reason this sutra differs from the provisional and Hinayana teachings lies solely in...
One employs the faculties (*indriya*) rather than consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore, the preceding section revealed the truth by beginning with the nature of the faculties;
now, in discussing cultivation and realization, one selects the fundamental faculty to enter into perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-samyaktva*).

Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, had their doubts and delusions eliminated; their minds awakened to the true reality (*dharmatā*), and their bodies and minds became light and tranquil, attaining what they had never experienced before.
Weeping again with grief, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Unsurpassed One of Great Compassion, Pure Jewel King! You have skillfully opened my mind, being able to employ such various [teachings]...”
Through causes and conditions and skillful means, he exhorts and guides those submerged in darkness, leading them out of the ocean of suffering. World-Honored One,
although I have now received such sounds of the Dharma and know that the Tathāgatagarbha— the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind— pervades the worlds of the ten directions,

containing and nurturing the pure, jewel-adorned lands of the Tathāgatas, the Sovereign Lands of Wondrous Enlightenment throughout the ten directions, the World-Honored One has nevertheless rebuked me for my lack of merit despite my extensive learning.
I have not yet attained through cultivation. I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King;

though I have obtained this great residence, I must enter it through its gates. I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion, but will show the way for those of us in this assembly who are still shrouded in darkness—how to cast aside the Lesser Vehicle and ultimately attain the path of the Tathāgata’s nirvana without remainder, as originally resolved upon at the start of our aspiration.
"May those in training be able to subdue their past objects of attachment, attain dhāraṇī, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; remaining in the assembly with a single mind, he awaited the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
This passage describes how the great assembly attained realization and benefit, and further requested the method of cultivation.

Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha discourse on the arising and continuity of the myriad dharmas up to the sudden abandonment of causes and conditions, were instructed through five successive expositions;

thus, their five layers of deep delusion were all eliminated, and they realized the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) in their hearts. (The true mark refers to the aforementioned True Ultimate Nature, the locus of quiescence, and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.)
Their bodies and minds became light and serene; they attained what they had never experienced before and reached the ultimate stage free from doubt.
They no longer harbored any suspicion regarding the nature of causes and conditions. Although they had shed many tears of grief previously, their realization was still shallow.
Thereupon, once again shedding tears of sorrow, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "Our delusions and falsehoods have sealed us tightly; our provisional doctrines remain stubbornly entrenched."

I close [this discourse]. Relying upon the Great Compassion of the Unsurpassed One, the Pure Jewel King (Pure Wisdom; called the "Jewel King" because his benefit and joy are inexhaustible), you have skillfully opened and clarified my mind.
You were able to thus push aside the false and bring forth the true, using various subtle causes and conditions and skillful means to exhort and encourage me.
You led those people who were mired in afflictions and obscured by ignorance out of their attachment and aversion.

...the ocean of suffering. What kind of grace is this? World-Honored One, although I have now received such a sound of the Dharma through the power of its full exposition, I have come to know the Tathāgatagarbha—the wondrous, awakened, and luminous mind—which is all-pervading and all-encompassing.
Compared to my former state, I feel as though I have changed my head and face; my joy is already immense, and I consider myself to have attained knowledge.

This one matter is completely resolved; there is nothing further to be done. Yet the Tathāgata further rebukes those whose learning is fruitless, saying it is not as good as practicing untainted karma for a single day.
However, this nature of the treasury has no walls in the ten directions and no doors on the four sides; there is no way to enter it. Today I am like a traveler who has lost his way and is adrift.
It has been a long time since we have been here. Suddenly, we have received from the Heavenly King the gift of a magnificent mansion.
Although we have obtained this great residence, we must enter through its gates; without finding the gate, the house cannot be inhabited.

We only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion and show the way to all of us who are shrouded in darkness within this assembly, so that we may all cast aside the *śrāvaka* vehicle and the *nirvāṇa* with remainder.

Thus, they ultimately attain the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa without remainder. The path of their original aspiration was based on the Small Vehicle, which merely severs the four abodes of views and afflictions;

yet five abodes still remain, like a conjured city. Now, wishing to advance toward the precious destination where the five abodes are fully exhausted, it is impossible for anyone other than a true guide to point out the original route. However, this...

In the assembly, there were many who were still in training (śaikṣa). Since the World-Honored One had not permitted the use of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) for observation and subduing, he now asked these practitioners:

"By what skillful means shall you restrain and subdue the habitual攀缘 (pān-yuan—clinging/objects of perception) and the dualistic conceptualizations of self and dharmas that have persisted since beginningless time?
Only then can you attain the Great Dhāraṇī and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as one enters through a gate."
"Are you dwelling in a magnificent mansion? Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground;
all those present in the assembly focused their minds single-pointedly, awaiting the Buddha’s compassionate instruction. Muzhou said: "Have you all yet found a point of entry?
If you have not yet found a point of entry, you must seek one. Once you have found a point of entry, thereafter..."
"You must not fail the old monk; therefore it is said that one has 'attained the gate. In a single morning, one is equal to all Buddhas.
If one does not attain the gate, one will not see the excellence of the inner chamber. Thus, after awakening to the hidden mind, one again requests to enter the gate.
Zhong said: "The true mark is markless; the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha pervades the ten directions."

That which is intrinsically pure, transcending names and free from signs, is this very nature. To lose sight of this nature is like being a transient traveler; to perceive this nature is like finding a magnificent mansion.

To perceive the nature yet fail to cultivate it is like finding a house but not entering it. Therefore, I request the Tathāgata to explain the path by which he originally resolved upon his aspiration for enlightenment.

This is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Regarding the "original" in the phrase "the original arousal of the mind," this "original" refers to what is called in the first fascicle the "true mind free from all devious characteristics.
"Nirvana without remainder" is the perfect fruit; "the path of the original arousal of the mind" is the perfect cause.
Having already seen one's nature, those who further seek to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision must first have it revealed through seeing, and then awaken to it through cultivation.
This necessarily requires entry through a gateway; this correctly introduces the subsequent passage concerning "entering deeply through a single gateway."

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those among the assembly—both pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who had not yet attained mastery over the bodhicitta, and for the sake of sentient beings in the future age of the Dharma’s decline who have resolved to attain bodhicitta, proclaimed to Ānanda and the great multitude:
"You all must resolutely resolve upon the bodhicitta. He then revealed the path of wondrous cultivation of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Regarding the wondrous samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata, one should not give rise to weariness; rather, one ought first to clarify the two definitive meanings of the initial resolve for awakening.
This first section briefly indicates these two meanings. Although the Buddha’s compassion is shown as being universal, the followers of the Two Vehicles still require specific guidance.

[The Buddha] said: "At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas within the assembly who had turned from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great, and who, though they had already resolved upon the bodhicitta, were not yet autonomous and had not found the gate through which to enter;

and furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings of the final dharma period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—including ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or inferior capacities—who are able to resolve upon the bodhicitta—"

For the sake of this assembly, I shall open for them the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle and provide the path of wondrous practice, so that by means of this path they may proceed directly to the Buddha-vehicle. Thereupon, he first showed Ānanda and the great multitude:
"You all have become weary along the middle path and clung to resting in the conjured city. Now that you have resolutely resolved to generate the bodhicitta, you must certainly..."

Advancing toward the place of treasure, regarding the wondrous samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata as the path by which one proceeds to that place of treasure, one will no longer experience further weariness. However, how should one apply this effort?

One should first clarify the initial awakening (ādikṣaṇika-bodhi) arising from fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi); there are two resolutions for the correct mindfulness that first initiates cultivation.
This establishes the meaning that it must not be altered. ○ In the section on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the Buddha spoke of "wondrous *śamatha*" and "subtle, secret contemplation.
Now, in discussing the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), he first speaks of "wondrous *samādhi*. This is a self-determined distinction made by the Buddha himself;
it has long been impossible to force an artificial interpretation upon it. Yet, the old commentaries take the three types of *śamatha* and entirely subsume them within the Path of Seeing.
Since this section is judged to be the initial expedient for the first part of the Way, how could the Buddha’s intent possibly be insufficient to follow? How, then,
are the two meanings of the "initial mind" determined?
This inquiry raises two meanings.
First, it establishes the definitive sense that the cause is identical to the fruit, such that one enters *nirvāṇa* suddenly by clearing away turbidity.
The four characters "the cause is identical to the fruit" constitute the first definitive thesis; "clearing away turbidity" and so forth constitute the direction of this thesis.
This refers to the reason why one must necessarily ensure that cause and effect correspond.
If cause and effect were not identical, one could not clarify the turbid and attain *nirvāṇa*. This single principle is concise in wording but profound in meaning;

its profundity lies in reaching all the way to the ultimate realization of the Tathāgata’s fruit of cessation. Furthermore, although this passage mentions both cause and effect together, the underlying intent is...

To briefly clarify the distance between this realization of the fruit and those others: it is not comparable to the fruit of the Small Vehicle’s transformation of the city, which merely corresponds to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching;
nor is it comparable to the fruit of the Initial Teaching’s "gill-fish" [fish-gills], which merely stops at the second stage of practice (*caryā*).

This is because those [lower vehicles] take the mind of birth-and-death consciousness as their fundamental cause for cultivation, whereas here the cause and fruit are fundamentally different; therefore, they cannot be compared.
One must distance oneself from the ordinary fruits of Buddhahood; therefore, one must first explain this primary determination.
Second is the determination concerning the meaning of attaining sudden entry into perfect penetration by resolving the knots through the sense-faculties and liberating oneself from entanglements.

Resolving the knots through the sense-faculties constitutes the core tenet of this second determination, while liberation from entanglements and so forth constitutes its ultimate aim. This refers to what is...
Since one must necessarily resolve the knots from their roots, if one does not do so from the roots, one cannot escape entanglement and enter directly into perfect penetration.

This single point involves a brief meaning expressed in extensive text. It is "brief in meaning" because the perfect penetration described seems to pertain only to the initial stages of entering and abiding [in the path], and thus is shorter than the previous meaning of *nirvāṇa*. It is "extensive in text" because...
The essential meaning of this entire scripture and the practical application of its practice are both contained entirely within this section.

Therefore, not only is this section longer than the preceding ones, but the subsequent explanations of the two doubts, the demonstration of the sequence, and the selection of the fundamental source all serve to fulfill the meaning of this section.

Question: How does one begin the process of entering and abiding in the stages [of cultivation] through the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate? Answer: In the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate, the practice consists solely of...

Prior to abiding and after abiding, one then directly transcends and enters [the state of non-abiding]. Furthermore, comparing this section to the preceding one: the former reveals that the fruit is distant yet ultimate;
this [latter] reveals that the cause is skillful and realization is swift. For even among those who have passed through the six sense faculties, one must still select those with perfect faculties.
As the text says: "Between those with perfect faculties and those without, the difference is as vast as a day compared to an eon; how much more so [in other cases]?"
Compared to those who enter through consciousness and sense-objects, how could this method be merely a matter of doubling days into kalpas?
Thus we know that this Dharma-gate is most skillful and swift. Master Zhong said: "The meaning of 'decisive' (jué-dìng) refers to that which is fixed and unchangeable.
The first meaning is to cause one to examine the mind generated at the causal stage, establishing it as the foundation for further cultivation."
It points to the five turbidities as the root of birth and death—that which causes the void to arise and perish.
It instructs one to select and revolve [the faculties] so that one may achieve accomplishment by relying on the perfect, profound, and unarising-unperishing nature.

Next, it instructs one to examine the root of afflictions so that one knows what must be subdued, thereby attaining the rank of the Tathāgata; it further identifies the six sense-faculties as the intermediaries and thieves who plunder the household.

This is followed by the principle of the mutual interpenetration of worlds, which fully reveals the numerical quantities and relative superiority or inferiority of the six sense faculties, so that one may know how to choose among them.
Having attained the nature that is free from arising and ceasing as the mind for the causal stage, one further examines the root of afflictions to select the perfect faculty (*yuan-gen*).
By entering deeply through a single gateway, all six faculties will be simultaneously subdued, and one can thus perfectly realize the fruition of the ground.
"I have awakened, Ānanda.

As for the primary truth: if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvakas, cultivate the bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the resultant ground, Ānanda."

If, while on the ground of practice, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible.
For this reason, you should clearly illuminate all the conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world.
All undergo transformation and extinction. Ānanda, observe the phenomena of the world that can be produced:

which among them is indestructible? Yet, one never hears of empty space decaying or perishing. Why is this? Because space is not something produced; therefore, from beginning to end, it is without destruction or extinction.
Thus, within your own body, that which is solid is earth; that which is moist is water; that which is warm to the touch is fire; and that which moves and vibrates is wind.
Wind. By means of these four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), your profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind is divided into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
From beginning to end, it becomes turbid through five layers. What constitutes this turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water, which is pure by its very nature;
yet when dust, soil, ash, or sand—substances that are inherently obstructive—are introduced, the two natures [of clarity and obstruction] are thus established as their inherent properties.
They do not follow one another. Suppose there were a person in the world who took dust from that soil and threw it into pure water;
the soil loses its solidity, the water loses its clarity, and its appearance becomes turbid—this is what is called "turbidity. Your five layers of turbidity are likewise thus.
