This elucidates the first determination: that by means of the cause being identical to the fruit, one may suddenly enter nirvana from within turbidity.
Ānanda, what is called the "primary meaning" (paramārtha) is that all merits reside entirely within the initial mind.
If one departs from the first arising of thought, then the unsurpassed path will not be accomplished. If you wish to cast aside the Lesser Vehicle and cultivate the Bodhisattva path...

Those who enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is the same as or different from the state of awakening at the stage of the resultant fruit. Ānanda, if, at the causal ground,
one still takes as the fundamental cause of cultivation the mind of birth-and-death— arisen from the seeds of karma and perfumed by conventional names and words— with which one seeks [awakening],...
The Buddha Vehicle is the fruit of true permanence, neither arising nor ceasing. To seek it like striking ice for fire or digging the earth for heaven is impossible.
This is because the mind of arising and ceasing is characterized by conditioned activity and impermanence, whereas the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing is unconditioned and indestructible.
Since cause and effect must correspond in this manner, you should first observe all phenomena throughout.
Regarding the receptacle world and the categories of the permanent and impermanent: all phenomena that can be produced are ultimately impermanent;

they all undergo transformation and extinction, being like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows. Even if one were to say they do not perish, Ānanda, you should further examine the conditioned phenomena of the world that can be produced:
which among them is indestructible? Although there may be things that are well-preserved, in the end they will not...
One hears of the decay and destruction of empty space. Why is this? Space is not something that can be produced; since it cannot be produced, it likewise cannot be destroyed.
Thus, if one seeks the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing, one must take as a cause that which is unproduced and indestructible;
one should no longer employ a mind characterized by arising and ceasing. The reason one must necessarily take non-arising and non-ceasing as the causal mind is that [the fruit]...
Why is this so? It is because the ocean of the sentient beings' minds is currently turbid and disturbed by the five corruptions, never being clear and bright.
Now, if one wishes to clarify it in order to attain the wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*, it cannot be accomplished unless one takes the profound, perfect, unborn, and undying nature as the causal mind.
Indeed, this profound, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind is fundamentally free from turbidity; how [could it otherwise be so]?
From these there arises turbidity. Thus, within your body, that which has the characteristic of solidity is earth, such as the flesh and bones;
that which is moist is water, such as mucus and saliva; that which is the sensation of warmth is fire, such as feverish heat; and that which is movement is wind.
Breathing and such [functions] are thus entangled by these four great elements. Consequently, your profound and perfect fundamental essence is divided and split into the six sense organs:
as vision in the eye, as hearing in the ear, as sensation in the nose, tongue, and body, and as cognition in the mind.
What was originally a single, luminous intelligence becomes the sixfold combination; within that which is fundamentally without partition, it spontaneously forms itself [into these divisions].
Separated thus, from beginning to end, there are in total five layers of turbidity.
Yet, why are they called "turbid"? Ānanda, it is like clear water: its inherent nature is purity.
If there are such things as dust, soil, ash, or sand, their substance is obstructive and possesses physical form and mass. These two entities are, by their very nature, [distinct].
They are certainly distinct in nature and do not interfere with one another. Suppose someone were to take some dust from that [dry land] and cast it into this pure water;
then that which was obstructive would lose its obstruction, and that which was clean would lose its cleanliness, and their appearance would become turbid.
Because it is turbid, disturbed, and unsettled, it is called "turbidity. I say that your five layers of turbidity are likewise so.
The pure and awakened mind fundamentally has no interaction with the four elements or the six sense organs;

yet, due to the sudden arising of an initial thought, the subject-object distinction was created, whereby the pure and awakened mind became clouded and invisible, just like water [stirred by sediment].
How does this differ from turbidity caused by the dust of the earth?
Ānanda, you see the empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions; yet space and seeing are not distinct. Space exists but has no substance; seeing exists but has no awareness.
These are interwoven to form a delusion. This is the first layer, called the *kalpa-turbidity*. Your body now manifests as a composite of the four great elements.

It constitutes the substance [of this turbidity]. Sight, hearing, awareness, and cognition become congested and obstructed; water, fire, wind, and earth revolve and cause cognition to arise. These interweave and falsely form [this state];

this is the second layer, called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Furthermore, within your mind, the nature of recollection, cognition, and study gives rise to knowing and seeing, and appearances manifest within the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Apart from the objects there are no marks; apart from cognition there is no nature. These interweave and falsely form [this state]; this is the third... [layer].

The three layers are called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Furthermore, as you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing, your perceptions and insights constantly desire to remain in this world, while the movement of karma perpetually shifts the lands.
These weave together to form delusion; this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Your seeing and hearing originally possess no distinct natures; yet, separated by various sensory objects, they give rise to unaccountable differences. Within their nature, they know one another; within their functioning...
They turn away from one another; their similarities and differences lose their standard. Interwoven, they falsely come into being. This fifth layer is called the turbidity of life.
This specifically clarifies the characteristics of the five turbidities. Ānanda, what are the five layers of turbidity? The first layer is as follows:
Relying upon the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), when you raise your head and look at space, it appears as four boundless directions.
One does not know who is the seer and what is the emptiness; emptiness and seeing are blended into a single mass, without any distinction.
As stated previously, even though empty space has a name, this emptiness is fundamentally the essence of purity. Now, with...
When seeing and form are intermingled, emptiness becomes a state of chaotic emptiness, and the essence of emptiness is lost.
As stated previously, when one perceives emptiness, that which is perceived is not [merely] emptiness; it is the fundamentally inherent, lucid awareness.
Now, when this is intermingled with emptiness, seeing becomes a state of muddled seeing, and the awareness of seeing is lost. This is "stolid emptiness."
Delusory views are continuous and dense, like warp and woof woven tightly together, whereby delusory appearances are formed.

This first layer is called the *kalpa-turbidity* (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Because these views encompass the four natures (hearing, smelling, tasting, and knowing), and emptiness encompasses the four great elements, there arise the *kalpas* of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness for mountains, rivers, and so forth.
The second layer, based upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), is profoundly full and perfect.

Within [this state], there was originally no physical form composed of the four great elements. When you entered the womb, you absorbed the father’s essence and the mother’s blood, thereby forming a body of the four great elements.
Consequently, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—which are fundamentally one refined spirit—were originally without obstruction or hindrance.
Because your four great elements became congested and could not flow freely, that which was without obstruction became obstructed.
Earth, water, fire, and wind are originally a single substance; fundamentally, they possess no sentience.
Yet, being led by this brilliant essence (*jīngmíng*), they are taken as objects, causing the arising of sensation and perception. Thus, that which was without sentience comes to have awareness.
One rotation and one congestion—like a warp and a woof—interweave so densely that they cannot be divided. Therefore, the four great elements, though originally insentient things, arise from causes.
It is like weaving illusions: though it be but the prick of a needle’s point or a blade of grass, there is always a sensation of pain.

For this reason, sentient beings firmly give rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which serves as the king of all views; the sixty-two views are all subsumed under it. This second layer is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
As for the third layer, it relies upon the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); furthermore, within your mind, you recollect past objects through consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Perceiving present objects while reciting those of future realms—such empty practices are all the activities of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This nature of the mental consciousness gives rise to deluded awareness. This characteristic of the mental consciousness can manifest the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); yet when awareness is separated from the six sense-objects, awareness has no self-characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of its own.
When sense-objects are separated from deluded awareness, the sense-objects have no self-nature (*svabhāva*). These two phenomena are mutually dependent upon one another.
It is also like warp and woof woven tightly together; as objects of perception fill the mind, there is no moment that is not disturbed and troubled.

This is the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). (Affliction means to disturb; turbidity means weariness. The fourth layer depends upon the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); within its profound and perfect midst—

Fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death. It is only that you, from morning until evening, undergo the constant flux of every thought-moment, with arising and ceasing never ceasing. Birth follows from habitual tendencies;
among ordinary people, there is none who does not crave life. Thus, one knows that the physical form (the term *jiàn* here refers to the corporeal substance) always desires to remain in this world.
Death follows the flow of transformation, yet ordinary beings possess no share of autonomy;
thus, the movement of karma (what is also called the "karmic consciousness") constantly migrates through lands (entering all realms of the three worlds and four modes of birth).

Each flow and each migration is like a single warp and a single woof, woven so densely that they cannot be separated, resulting in boundless birth and death. Because of this, one wanders through the seven destinies.
The transformation of all the characteristics of sentient beings constitutes the fourth layer, called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

As for the fifth layer, it relies upon the *vijñāna-skandha* (referring specifically to the eighth consciousness and not the first six). Your seeing and hearing through the six faculties are originally one and the same substance.

Yet there is no difference in their nature. It is merely because the various objects such as form and sound create obstructions that the faculties are split apart by these objects, though they do not actually give rise to distinct entities. Fundamentally, they are one refined spirit, sharing the same household;
thus, within their nature, they know one another—such as the eye being able to hear and the ear being able to see. Once the six functions have formed, each opens its own gateway; therefore...
In their functioning, they oppose one another, like the eye’s inability to hear or the ear’s inability to see; yet in their nature, they know one another, appearing as the same rather than different.
In their functioning, they oppose one another, being different rather than the same. Whether they are the same or different, these two cannot be fixed;
thus, both lose their standard of reference. This identity and difference are also like warp and woof woven together in close density.
These six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are congealed and obstructed, and life is entrusted within them; both essence and function lack sovereignty.

This is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*). (The reason it relies upon the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is that the non-discriminative seeing and hearing within the faculties are precisely the eighth [aspect], the subjective perceiving division.

These five turbidities have been unable to attain clarity since the single thought-moment when the luminous stillness became obscured and turned into emptiness; they desire to return to profound stillness.
Regarding the essence of the Perfect [Mind], you must urgently seek the means to clarify its turbidity.

Ānanda, if you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death, and rely upon the accomplishment of the non-arising, non-ceasing, perfectly profound nature. By means of this profound stillness, you should revolve that which is false and illusory.
The cessation of birth. Subduing [the delusions] to return to the original enlightenment, one attains the nature of the original, luminous awareness that is free from arising and ceasing;

this serves as the mind for the stage of the causal ground. Only then does one fully perfect the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition. It is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel:

when the vessel is deep and motionless, the sand and soil naturally sink, and the clear water appears before one; this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions. When the mud is removed and only pure water remains, it is called...
The fundamental ignorance is forever severed; the characteristics of clarity are pure and refined.

All manifestations do not become afflictions, for they all accord with the pure and wondrous virtues of Nirvana (the nature inherent within the six sense faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing possessed by sentient beings is precisely Original Enlightenment; the Tathāgata’s Nirvana without remainder, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, is Ultimate Enlightenment).
This teaching provides the method for clarifying turbidity and hastening toward the fruit. Ānanda, the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) of ordinary beings is profound and perfect;
though it is identical to that of the Buddhas, because of the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), they wander through birth and death and thus lose true permanence.

Because of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), they are disturbed by the dust of dharmas and thus lose true bliss. Because of the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the realm of space...
Because they are insentient, they lose the true self; because they possess the turbidity of views and the turbidity of life, their faculties and bodies are impure, and thus they lose true purity.
Now, one desires to immediately take these four natures, which possess the five turbidities, and thereby remotely accord with the four virtues of the Tathāgata.

As for those who realize the ultimate fruit through sudden enlightenment, where does their path lie? That which is the root of birth and death is precisely the consciousness-mind of the six sense bases.
All ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited vehicles take this as their basis and practice in a confused manner; thus, their causes do not accord with their fruits.
Now, one must decisively select and discard it so as not to employ it. This is the accomplishment of the perfectly湛 (zhàn) and tranquil nature, which is neither born nor extinguished.
This is precisely what is inherent within the faculties, as I have demonstrated in my previous ten chapters. To clarify these two views:

that which is proximately present within the six faculties and distantly pervasive throughout the myriad dharmas is something that ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or Lesser Vehicles obscure through their delusion, remaining unaware of it even as they use it daily.
Now, having decisively grasped it, one relies upon it; once relying on this profound nature, one employs this very profound nature to revolve back from its false constructions.

The five turbidities of arising and ceasing—(the character "swirl" [xuan] is most wondrous: to clarify turbid water, one gathers it to swirl, and the sediment naturally settles)—are thus suppressed, and the essence of original awakening is restored.
From this, one attains the nature of perfect, luminous awareness that is free from arising and ceasing. When this serves as the mind for the causal ground, the cause becomes identical to the fruit.

This is the stage of the fulfillment of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). From here, passing through the first abode (*prathamā-bhūmi*) and onward until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhatva*), it serves as...

The cultivation of the stage of fruition takes wondrous enlightenment as its realization of that stage. Once one has thus fully accomplished the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition, the fruition becomes identical to the cause.
To apply this again to the previous analogy: it is like one who clarifies turbid water by storing it in a still vessel.
When it is still, deep, and unmoving, the sand and soil naturally settle, and the clear water appears before one. The sand and soil represent the fivefold turbidity;
the still vessel represents the nature within the faculties; and the clear water represents the profound, perfect, original substance (*tattva*).

Reaching this stage is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), at which point one finally severs the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-vicikitsā*) within the realms. However...
The sand and soil that previously settled have not yet fully subsided, and the mud remains; this is a metaphor for ignorance (avidyā) being latent but not yet severed.

If the mud is removed and only pure water remains, it can then be called the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance, at which point the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) beyond the realms are entirely eliminated.
Once these two types of ignorance are exhausted, the manifestation of clarity becomes pure and refined, without even the slightest [impurity].
When the obscuration is cleared away, one freely manifests the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world, even manifesting residence within birth and death.
The six sense organs are mutually fused, moving with ease in all directions as one pleases, free from affliction;

all these become wondrous functions that perfectly accord with the Tathāgata’s eternal bliss, selfhood, and purity, and the wondrous virtues of Nirvāṇa. It is like when the mud has been exhausted and only pure water remains: no matter how much it is stirred, it does not become turbid.

This is further confusion. Now, regarding the distant fruit of *nirvāṇa*, it is only attained by being in accord with the initial resolve made at the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) in this manner.
How can you not apply your attention to careful observation? Question: Why must one necessarily rely on seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to examine the causal mind?
Answer: It is because of these four entanglements that your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous enlightenment is divided.
The mind functions as seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing are entirely the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind.

This means that since turbidity is formed through seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, it must likewise be clarified through seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—what is called "falling from the ground, one must likewise rise from the ground. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "For example, like pure [water]..."
In a pond, when a mad elephant enters, it makes the water turbid; yet if a bright pearl enters, the water immediately becomes clear.
One cannot say that there are no elephants or pearls outside the water. The mind is likewise: when afflictions enter the mind, they can make the mind turbid;
when various wholesome dharmas such as compassion enter the mind, they can make the mind pure. Nevertheless, defilement and purity are not fixed. True...
Delusion arises from conditions. If one is ignorant of this, then thought after thought one transmigrates in saṃsāra, losing the true nature.
If one illuminates it, then mind after mind is quiescent, perfectly realizing nirvāṇa. Therefore, as when using one wedge to extract another, one uses the coarse to meet the coarse.
If one does not cling to delusion, one need not even speak of emptiness; illusory shadows will subtly vanish, and the flames of wisdom-light will subside. ○ First Decision.
Having definitively established that because the cause is identical to the fruit, one enters nirvana immediately by clearing away turbidity;
as for the second meaning: you must all resolve to generate the bodhicitta and give rise to great courage and vigor toward the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
One must resolutely abandon all conditioned marks (*saṃskṛta-nimitta*). One should carefully examine the root of afflictions (*kleśa-mūla*).
Since beginningless time, these have given rise to karma and moistened rebirth; who is it that acts, and who is it that receives [the results]?

Ānanda, if you cultivate bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, you will not be able to know where the false roots and objects (*viṣaya*) are inverted. If you do not even know their location, how can you...?
Subduing [the afflictions] to attain the stage of a Tathāgata. Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what was knotted, how could they know it has been untied?
You have never heard of empty space being torn asunder by you. Why is this? Because space has no form or characteristics, and thus possesses neither knots nor untying.
Therefore, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six serve as the intermediaries for thieves. From yourself...

It is the treasure of the kalpa-household. Because sentient beings in this beginningless world (the "world" being synonymous with the "mundane") give rise to entanglements, they are unable to transcend the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*).
This clarifies the second definitive method for resolving the knots at the sense-faculties to liberate oneself from entanglements and enter directly into perfect penetration.

As for what is called the "second meaning": although the Buddha’s compassion in benefiting sentient beings is urgent, the bestowing of the teaching must await the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment.
You all must certainly arouse the bodhicitta and give rise to great courage and vigor toward the One Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, desiring directly to attain perfection.

Having fulfilled the six perfections and the myriad practices, one resolutely abandons the provisional and inferior methods of former cultivation that take the mind of arising and ceasing as their cause.
As for those various conditioned phenomena, where does the actual point of application lie? That birth-and-death is the root of the fruit of suffering;
it is the six consciousnesses. Afflictions are the root of the cause of suffering; they are the six sense organs. Afflictions...
Since the six sense organs are present, these six consciousnesses constitute the root of birth and death;
yet the six sense organs, in turn, serve as the root of the six consciousnesses. You all should carefully examine this root of affliction:

from time immemorial, the karma produced by the manifest aggregates and the births moistened by the intermediate state (namely, the ignorance of aversion and attachment when seeking parents) are precisely what constitutes affliction.
However, if one asks who creates [suffering] and who receives it, the fundamental basis can then be inferred. That basis is precisely the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
The eight consciousnesses give rise to the six consciousnesses, which are entirely afflictions and serve as the cause of suffering.

The six consciousnesses attract birth and death, serving as the fruit of suffering. While a coarse analysis suggests that only the six consciousnesses create [it], a subtle investigation reveals that—
These are created by the eight consciousnesses themselves; although they appear to be experienced by the six consciousnesses, their destruction is experienced solely by the eight consciousnesses.
Therefore, it is said that one creates and experiences for oneself. It can be seen, then, that the six sense organs are the root of afflictions.
Ānanda, if you cultivate bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, then internally—
The root of delusion is like the physical body composed of the four great elements and the six sense organs;
the external objects of delusion are like the insentient vessel-world of empty space. Neither can know where this inversion resides.
If one does not even know its location, how can one subdue these delusive inversions and attain the ultimate fruit of the Tathāgata?
It is thus. Although the body of the faculties and the vessel-world are extremely vast, the actual points where they are bound are exceedingly simple and not complex;
one must certainly know this before one can understand it. Ānanda, observe how a rope is used to form knots in the world:
although all the strands together constitute the substance of the knot, the actual place where it is knotted lies in only one.
As for the "thighs": if one knows them without seeing them truly, one will ultimately be unable to understand them. If one can see them, then one will know and understand them.
To clarify this through analogy: except for empty space, which cannot be torn or split and is fundamentally devoid of form or shape, [nothing else is like it].
There are no knots to be untied. As for all other things that possess form and shape, where there is a knot, there must be an untying.

Thus one knows that within these faculties, apart from form, nature, and substance, there are no knots to be untied. If the six essences descend into the two superior faculties, the organ of hearing and the organ of sight, [the same applies].
The sense-faculties have forms and characteristics; where there is bondage, there must be liberation. If this is so, what constitutes the essential substance of the locus of true bondage?
It is your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as body and mind (the mind being the faculty of intellect)—these six faculties act as intermediaries for the thieves of the six consciousnesses.
The faculties draw forth the consciousnesses, which engage in inverted discrimination, and thus... [as before]... take hold of suchness.
Within the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness), all the great treasures of the household are entirely plundered by the six external sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
This is like how, in the world, external bandits must rely on an internal traitor to provide guidance and instigation before they can successfully carry out a plunder.

Once the household treasures have been plundered, that which is perfectly penetrating departs while that which is obstructive remains; though one wishes not to form [karmic bonds], it becomes impossible to avoid doing so.
Now, the sentient root-body refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), while the insentient vessel-world refers to the container-world (*bhājana-loka*).
These two phenomena encompass all dharmas; within these two, sentient beings are universally bound and fettered.

All lack self-mastery; collectively, they constitute the substance of bondage. However, the actual locus of this knotting does not reside in the vessel-world (the external environment), but solely within the root-body (the sentient being).
Because of this, from time immemorial, the world of sentient beings has been enmeshed in entanglement.
Once the roots are knotted, how could one transcend the vessel-world and attain unimpeded freedom? Thus, if even a single root were untied, not only—

One attains mastery over the body and likewise transcends the vessel-world (the physical environment), thereby achieving great sovereignty. (The thirty-two manifestations of Avalokiteśvara described in the subsequent text are precisely the signs of this transcendence.
Therefore, those who are deluded seek to escape the three realms, whereas those who have awakened need only understand the six sense faculties.
People know only that the six consciousnesses are internal thieves that plunder the family’s treasures; they do not realize that these consciousnesses invite the internal thieves to plunder the home.

"Treasures" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Therefore, one should know that the arising of delusions is these six faculties; the creation of karma is these six faculties; and the experiencing of retribution is these six faculties.
Even the "treasures plundered from the house" are these six faculties. These six faculties are, in truth, the fundamental source of the knots of birth and death.
Thus, what was previously asked—"Who acts? Who receives?"—and what follows—"One plunders oneself"—are the points of mutual response.

Ānanda, what are called the world of sentient beings (referring only to the physical bodies of the faculties and not the material environment)? "World" (*loka*) refers to temporal flux; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation.
You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms.
The past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten directions and three periods of time. All [sentient beings] are thus encompassed.
Sentient beings weave their delusions into mutual formation; within their bodies they trade and shift, and worlds intersect one another.

Yet the nature of these realms, even if extending throughout the ten directions, has its fixed positions clearly defined. In the mundane world, we only designate east, west, south, and north; there is no fixed position for above or below, and no fixed direction for the center.
Nevertheless, the four numbers are necessarily distinct. As these arise and interact with the world, three times four and four times three result in twelve permutations, which flow and transform.

Three repetitions: one, ten, a hundred, and a thousand. These encompass the beginning and the end. Within each of the six sense faculties, there are twelve hundred merits (this character "de" [merit] should be understood flexibly as having the meaning of "neng" [capable]).
This is based on the world of sentient beings to reveal the number of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*).

The practitioner already knows that the untying of the knots must proceed from the sense organs; however, since there are six organs, yet the untying occurs through only one, it is necessary to make a selection.
To select the organ, one must thoroughly comprehend the number of the six sense organs. Without knowing their number, upon what basis could one choose? This...
The *kośa* (sections) serve to clarify numerical quantity. Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? The term "world" (*loka*) pertains to time;
its meaning is that which flows on and does not remain still. The term "realm" (*dhātu*) pertains to place; its meaning is that which is fixed in its spatial orientation.
You should now know that the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and above and below constitute the realm; thus, there are spatial orientations.
Ten. The past, future, and present constitute the world (*loka*); thus, there are three temporal divisions of the world.
This world is, in fact, the world within one's own body. For all sentient beings, this body is formed through the interweaving of various delusions;
therefore, the arising of worlds and realms exists right within the body. They trade and flow, mutually transforming one another.

It traverses without ever stopping; it is simply that people do not realize it. Although the realms extend throughout the ten directions, within these ten directions, only the four cardinal points are taken as primary, while the zenith and nadir are not.
This is because the zenith and nadir are merely the "above" and "below" of the four cardinal points and lack a fixed location of their own.
Furthermore, the four intermediate corners (intercardinal directions) are not taken, because within those four corners, two cardinal directions meet.
It is thus named. Because there is no fixed direction, once the number four is clarified, it intersects with the three periods of time (*adhvan*).
Either the periods intersect with the directions to form three times four, which is certainly twelve; or the directions intersect with the periods to form four times three, which is likewise twelve.
In every turn, they are all twelve. Thus, through shifting and changing, from one they become three.
Multiplying by ten, a hundred, and a thousand, the numbers increase in succession. Now, let us clarify this by applying it to the engagement with the world.
First, considering each of the four directions in terms of the three periods of time, they together form twelve.

Second, within the three periods of time of the eastern direction, one is transformed into ten, thus forming thirty; the same applies to the southern, western, and northern directions. Thus, there are four sets of [thirty].
Each [direction] has thirty, totaling one hundred and twenty. In the third stage, the thirty in the eastern direction transform ten into a hundred, thereby becoming three hundred.
The same applies to the other three directions. Thus, with each of the four directions having three hundred, they total one thousand two hundred.
Applying this analogy to the world’s engagement with the directions is likewise so; this is what is called the "threefold transformation of flux. This is the natural order of this world.
This is the fixed number. Now, the world within the body consists precisely of these six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Since their number is fixed at one thousand two hundred, then beginning with the eye and ending with the mind, the total of the six organs—each with its respective merit—is likewise exactly one thousand two hundred.
This so-called quantity is fully established: it does not increase in sages, nor does it decrease in ordinary beings. It is the comprehensive numerical measure.
It is indeed so. Question: Regarding the world within the body, while the "world" (loka) aspect is beyond dispute, the "realm" (dhātu) appears to be inconsistent.

Why? Because a realm has a fixed location, whereas the body is constantly shifting and changing. Answer: While that which is outside the body can be seen to shift and change, how could one perceive such shifting within the body?
Just as the world is not truly immobile, it must also be moving at all times. [This is from the] *Za* (Miscellaneous).

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that when one travels and comes and goes through hundreds of thousands of myriads of worlds, the people within those worlds perceive [the traveler] as neither moving nor shifting;
how could they possibly be aware [of it]? One should know that within the body there is likewise a fixed locus.
Since movement and change are also observed outside the realms, what is the use of emotional speculation?
Furthermore, these numbers of one thousand and two hundred merely refer collectively to what ordinary beings possess; they do not constitute the sublime functioning of true nature.

As in the following text, the three faculties of ear, tongue, and mind being "perfectly complete" (one thousand and two hundred) means they are simply more fully developed than the other faculties; how could they possibly pervade the entire Dharma-realm?
This is what is meant. Thus we know that when referring to the true sage, the merits of the six faculties are all immeasurable in number.
Now, the intent of this section is merely to facilitate the selection of a faculty; it is necessary to clarify these quantities, yet they do not constitute the primary locus of practice.
The true purpose of cultivation lies solely in the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty. Changshui [Zhuan] applied himself with profound intent to this.
Zhe drew a diagram to show people, claiming that the intent of cultivation lies solely therein.
Although this has its own separate logical basis, it fails to recognize that it obscures the original, correct intent of cultivation. The wise should not be deluded by it. ○ Zhong said:
The three and four interpenetrate: by multiplying the three by the four and the four by the three, both result in twelve;
this is the first multiplication. These twelve then each transform into ten, resulting in one hundred and twenty; this is the second multiplication.
These one hundred and twenty then each transform into ten, resulting in one thousand two hundred; this is the third multiplication.
Ānanda, you should further distinguish the relative superiority and inferiority among these faculties. For instance, when the eye looks out, it sees what is bright behind and what is dark before;

it sees clearly what is in front, but what is behind is entirely dark. Looking to the left and right, it perceives only two-thirds of the field. When considering its overall function, its merit is incomplete:
three parts constitute its functional merit, while one part lacks such merit. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the ear—
Listening is all-encompassing; nothing is left out in the ten directions. When active, it reaches both near and far; when still, it is without boundary.
You should know that the faculty of hearing is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits. As for the nose smelling odors, it functions through the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

Yet, while there is inhalation and exhalation, it lacks the interval between them. Examining the faculty of the nose, it is deficient by one-third; you should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the tongue...
To proclaim and disseminate all mundane and supramundane wisdom, the words are methodical and the principles are inexhaustible.

One should know that the faculty of the tongue is complete with twelve hundred merits. Just as the body perceives touch and recognizes the disagreeable or agreeable—it can perceive when there is contact, but does not know when separated;
it requires separation to be one and contact to be dual—this is verified by the faculty of the body. Since three parts are lacking one, one should know [the same applies here].

The body possesses only eight hundred merits; yet its willful receptivity silently accommodates all mundane and supramundane dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether saintly or ordinary—embracing them all without exception to their very limits.
You should know that the faculty of the mind possesses one thousand two hundred merits in full.

This distinguishes the relative quality of the six sense-faculties according to their respective directions. While the various directions possess mutual variations of superiority and inferiority, within the Sahā world there are three superior and three inferior faculties;
yet, one particular faculty can still be singled out as the most superior. Therefore, such a distinction must be made.

Now, regarding the number of the six faculties, if one were to argue from the perspective of the interpenetration of worlds, there would indeed be no superiority or inferiority. However, since they are called "faculties" (*indriya*), how could they not [differ]?
There is both completeness and deficiency. Since there is both completeness and deficiency, how could there not be superiority and inferiority?
Ānanda, among these six faculties, you must determine which is superior and which is inferior. For example, the eye has the function of seeing.
Because it does not see what is behind, it is dark; because it sees what is before, it is bright. [By comparing] the brightness of what is in front with what is behind...

The darkness, as well as what is observed to the left and right, constitutes the four directions. According to the *Guṇaparyāya-śāstra*, there are two hundred [units] for each of the four directions and one hundred for each of the four corners.
Now, that which is seen by the eye in front, along with the left and right—these three directions already constitute six hundred.
Together with the two previous corners totaling two hundred, they form eight hundred; only the one side behind totaling two hundred and the two corners behind totaling two hundred are not seen.
Dividing these one thousand two hundred into three parts, what is now seen—eight hundred—is two-thirds.
Dividing the four sides into four parts, what is now seen consists of three sides; this is three-quarters.
This refers to its functional efficacy. To not perceive in all directions is for it to lack a portion of its merit.
You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits, and thus it does not achieve perfection. Take the ear, for instance: its function is hearing.
Yet its hearing is most comprehensive, leaving nothing out across the ten directions. When there is movement and sound, it immediately knows whether it is near or far; when it is still...
There is no sound, yet it penetrates further into the boundless and limitless. It is like striking a drum in the ten directions: it is heard simultaneously in all ten places;
the myriad pipes are silent, and the myriad objects do not obstruct it. You should know that the faculty of hearing is complete with one thousand two hundred merits.
Among the sense faculties, it is the most excellent. For example, the nose has smelling as its function. Smelling involves both inhalation and exhalation;
yet while there is exhalation and inhalation, the intermediate junction is lacking. As in the case of regulated breath:

once the exhalation is complete, there is a brief pause before one subsequently inhales. At that moment of brief pause, what is called the "lacking of the intermediate junction" occurs. Since the breath already...
The merit is incomplete; thus, it amounts to only eight hundred [years]. (Changshui says: "The entry and exit phases together constitute three parts. One part is four hundred years.

Because it is missing during the middle phase, it is only eight hundred. As for the function of the tongue, it does not matter whether it tastes flavors, but rather how it proclaims and spreads [the Dharma].

All mundane wisdom and supramundane wisdom can be extolled by it. Although its expressions may have spatial divisions and its phrasing may be limited, its principle is inexhaustible and its meaning is universally pervasive.
Therefore, even the most coarse and shallow worldly speech all penetrates the ultimate truth.
One should know that the faculty of the tongue is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits.

It may also be said that this is excellent. (For instance, when the Patriarch attained enlightenment upon hearing lewd words, it was supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*). When Confucius was alerted by the song of a child, it was mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*). If this is so, then even the words of a fool possess both types of wisdom.
It is like the body, which takes the perception of touch as its function. When touched, there are both adverse and favorable sensations;
yet, while one can perceive them when in contact, one does not know them when separated. Not knowing them when separated is a deficiency of one part. When in contact, one can...

Awakening involves both opposition and conformity; thus it possesses two aspects. When examined through the three divisions of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it lacks one of the "separation-in-the-middle" [divisions].
One should know that the body possesses only eight hundred merits and does not achieve perfection.
As for the mind, its function is to receive perfuming and maintain seeds; therefore, it can silently contain the ten directions and the three periods of time, even unto the world.
The supramundane dharmas—whether mundane or sacred—are all encompassed within it to their very limits.
Thus, the faculty of the mind is complete with one thousand two hundred merits; it may also be called excellent.
Regarding the merits of the six faculties, there are degrees of superiority and inferiority, which you must determine for yourself as follows. Question: How does one penetrate all dharmas?
As for this, it is that which can encompass all limits; yet those who have not attained thorough penetration do not possess this capacity. Why, then, are they both equally called "perfect"? Answer:
The faculty of mind (*manas*) inherently possesses this capacity, yet the ignorant are unable to bring it forth. This is not the fault of the faculty of mind.
It is, for example, like a sharp blade that is inherently capable of cutting, yet cannot be honed by an unskilled craftsman. This is not [the fault of the blade].
This is the offense of a sharp blade.

Ānanda, if you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death and trace it back to its root until you reach that which is neither born nor extinguished, you must examine these six faculties of reception and function (where "reception" refers to the experiencing of sensory objects and "function" refers to the exertion of their capacities): which are joined and which are separated; which are deep and which are shallow?
Who possesses perfect penetration? Who lacks it? If one can, within this context, awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration—(the phrase "awaken to perfection" is an abbreviation;

for in selecting a faculty, one seeks that which is detached, profound, and perfect, while discarding that which is conjoined, shallow, or deficient—it is evident through examination by these six criteria that only the ear-faculty fully meets the selection. This is because although the eye is likewise a detached cognition, it does not reach the level of profundity and perfection;

although the tongue is likewise perfect, it does not reach the level of detachment and profundity; and although the mind is likewise profound and perfect, it does not reach the level of pure detachment. Thus, the only faculty in which all three qualities are complete is the ear-faculty alone. To oppose that non-... [text ends]

From the initial weaving of deluded karma, one may attain the circulation of perfect penetration; compared to those with non-perfect faculties, their progress differs by factors of ten million times a kalpa.
I shall now fully reveal the fundamental merits of the six kinds of profound, perfect luminosity; their quantities are as such.

According to your detailed discernment, choose that which you can enter, and I shall clarify it for you so that you may advance. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have each cultivated [this] within the eighteen realms.
They all attained the perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi; during that interval, there was no difference in their excellence or inferiority.

It is only because you are of inferior capacity and have not yet achieved perfect mastery of wisdom therein that I proclaim this method for you, so that by entering deeply through a single gate, you may enter the one without delusion, whereby those six faculties of cognition will become pure simultaneously.
Having already revealed above that the merits of the six faculties are either complete or deficient, this [section] now requires you to select which among the six faculties is the "perfect faculty.
Ānanda, since the six faculties are the very root of afflictions, they are the deep source of birth and death.
Thus, to follow them is to initiate birth and death; to oppose them is to bring the cycle of saṃsāra to rest. You now wish to oppose them...
The flow of desire within birth and death—desire being the five sensory objects, also known as the five desires—proceeds from the shallow to the deep.
One must trace back to the very root of this flow, striving to exhaust the source of birth and death until one reaches the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
There is no other method for applying oneself to this task than to examine these six sense organs through which experience occurs: which perceive by contact, and which perceive at a distance?
Who is deep and difficult to fathom? Who is shallow and easy to know? Which is complete and universally penetrating as a faculty for use?

Which is deficient and not universal? If you can examine and investigate within these six faculties of sensory reception, you will realize which is the faculty of universal penetration that may be employed to counteract those beginningless entanglements of sensory dust and desire.

For those wandering in birth and death, once they have attained this perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), if one compares its merit and virtue with that of faculties which are neither detached nor profound, nor perfect and round, it is as if the former exceeds the latter by a factor of a thousand eons.

Now, I have fully revealed the nature of profound stillness, perfection, and luminosity within the six sense-faculties; this is what sentient beings inherently possess, identical in every single one, and is not produced through cultivation or effort.
It is so. Its merits may be complete or deficient; their measure is thus. However, according to your own inclination, examine them carefully within.

That which can be entered is called "awakening" (meaning clarity free from doubt); that which is definitively adopted is called "discernment" (meaning choosing). Awakening must be awakened to by oneself; discernment must be discerned by oneself.
Why do you not speak to resolve this? I shall now clarify the stages of gradual cultivation so that you may advance directly forward without falling back.
However, my heart desires to let you choose for yourself rather than choosing for you.

It also exists inherently. This is truly because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, in accordance with the capacities of beings in their respective regions, allow for a thousand variations and myriad distinctions.
Whether one practices through any of the eighteen realms or even the seven great elements, every single gateway is accessible;

all may enter and attain the perfect, unsurpassed *bodhi* without any difference in quality or inferiority that would allow for human selection. As it is said: "The nature of the sages is such that there is nothing [it does not encompass]."
Penetration—whether following or reversing—is in every case a skillful means. However, because your faculties are inferior, you have not yet attained the perfect, penetrating, and sovereign wisdom;
thus, at the gates of the six sense organs, you cannot yet avoid obstruction. Therefore, I proclaim this so that you may, from among these six gates, select one alone and enter deeply into it.
If you enter deeply into one gate and attain the non-delusiveness of a single faculty, then...
To understand one is to understand all. Those six organs of cognition are simultaneously purified, and one attains liberation without expending further effort.

Thus, having already subtly demonstrated the examination of the ear-organ through the six preceding meanings, and having proceeded from awakening to cultivation and from cultivation to realization, the essential points of the practice for untying the knots are, for the most part, fully covered. [The Knots Untied] Opening.
The first character, "ni" (逆), is the wondrous function of turning from the mundane toward the sacred. When the flow runs outward toward form, it is "following" (順);

when the flow returns and revolves back to the One, it is "reversing" (逆). It is also like the *I Ching*: the trigram of Earth over Heaven forms Tai (Peace), while Heaven over Earth forms Pi (Obstruction);

Earth over Mountain forms Qian (Humility), while Mountain over Earth forms Bo (Stripping Away)—all of which carry the meaning of reversal. Therefore, it is said: "When the five elements proceed in their natural order, the great earth..."

The fire pit. The five inverted elements (*pañca-viparyāsa*). The great earth and its precious treasures. "Easy" refers to counting in reverse. One must know that in the practice of cultivation there is no other special skill or subtlety;

this single character "reverse" (*ni*) encompasses everything without exception. According to the later section on Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration, "entering the stream and forgetting the object" and so forth refers to reversing the flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
"The hearing and the heard being exhausted" and so forth refers to returning to and exhausting the root of the flow.

...Thus, when quiescent extinction manifests, one immediately reaches the state of non-arising and non-ceasing. ○ Zhong says: The two terms "shallow" and "deep" are largely inappropriate in this commentary.

In my view, "conjunction" and "separation" distinguish among the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body; "perfection" and "imperfection" distinguish among the three faculties of eye, nose, and body.
This [term] specifically distinguishes the mental faculty (*manas*), which should be understood as following from the discourse on the flow of desire, because mental thoughts are so turbulent.
To be "connected" means that the deep current of desire arises from discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).

When it is deep, it is difficult to satisfy; when it is shallow, it easily dries up. Furthermore, it is said: "When there is movement, there is distance and proximity; in stillness, there is no boundary.
Following that movement, it seems as though there is distance and proximity; yet within my own stillness, listening all around is boundless.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how can one flow against the current, enter deeply through a single gate, and cause the six sense faculties to become pure simultaneously?
This question was posed because his understanding had not yet reached full clarity; thus, building upon the two previous points, he requested further instruction. Ānanda addressed the Buddha.
He said, "World-Honored One, the Buddha has taught that one should turn back the flow of desire within birth and death to reach the state of non-arising and non-extinction.
Yet I do not know what this 'flow of desire within birth and death' is, which I am to turn back.

Furthermore, since the merits of the six faculties possess degrees of superiority and inferiority, such that each faculty differs from the others, how can one enter deeply through a single gate so that all six faculties are transformed simultaneously?"
"Purity! I expect the World-Honored One must have a teaching to address this. ○ This question differs from the subsequent doubt.
Doubt arises when faith is insufficient and one seeks to determine right from wrong; a question arises when understanding is not yet thorough and one requests further instruction and clarification.
Therefore, when the Buddha provides his answer below, he merely supplements what was previously shown, making it even more detailed and clear. And...
This serves to increase understanding; it does not involve the severing of doubts for them. Only by clarifying the intent of this question can one fully comprehend the subsequent answer.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. You have already extinguished the world of sentient beings within the three realms."

The afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*). (These are the afflictions abandoned by seeing the truths; namely, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). They are also called the "flood of views" (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*). This refers to the arising of discriminative views when the mental faculty (*manas*) encounters mental objects (*dharmas*). Because of these afflictions of view, one wanders through the three realms and cannot achieve liberation.

Therefore, by abandoning these afflictions of view, one realizes the first fruit [of the path] and enters the stage of the Path of Seeing. However, one still does not yet know the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated within the faculties throughout successive births.

Those tendencies must be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in order to be eliminated. (The afflictions abandoned through cultivation are the ninety-one grades of afflictions of thought. They are also called the "flood of desire" (*kāma-ogha*) and the "flood of existence" (*bhava-ogha*)).

The flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*). Regarding the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*): it refers to the craving of the five faculties for the five sense objects; this is termed the "affliction of volition" (*cetanā-kleśa*). Because of this affliction of volition, one transmigrates within the desire realm and is unable to escape from it; therefore, it is called the flood of desire. Regarding the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*):

not forgetting cause and effect is termed "existence. This refers to the afflictions of volition within the form and formless realms. Because of these afflictions of volition, one transmigrates within the form and formless realms; therefore, it is called the flood of existence. Regarding the flood of ignorance: it is the lack of clear understanding, which is precisely the delusion (*moha*) among the afflictions of volition within the three realms. Because of this ignorance...

They circulate through birth and death; therefore, they are called the "outflows of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*). By severing these three outflows, one realizes the four fruits. From the second fruit up to Arhatship, all are termed the "path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*); thus, they are called the "afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation. Regarding the "sentient beings of the world of the three realms":

This is because the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the four abodes are all abandoned within the realm (*dhātu*), and are not abandoned by those who have already transcended the world. The above clarifies that their attachment to self (*ātma-grāha*) is not yet exhausted.

How much more so regarding the distinctions and numerical categories of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*jāti-sthiti-anyathātva-nirodha*)? (Arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing refers precisely to the delusions abandoned by Bodhisattvas; Tiantai identifies these as the views and afflictions outside the realm. They are also called "identical-in-essence ignorance" [*tongti wuming*].)

Within the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), the subtle delusions that are both conceptual and innate—namely, the *sands-of-the-Ganges* of ignorance—are subsumed together as the "state of abiding" (*sthiti*). According to the *Awakening of Faith*, among the three subtleties, the second is the "phase of production" (*utpattilakṣaṇa*).

The latter two of the three subtleties and the first three of the six gross states constitute the "phase of abiding. The fourth and fifth of the six gross states constitute the "phase of differentiation" (*nānātvalakṣaṇa*), while the fifth is the "phase of cessation" (*nirodhalakṣaṇa*); the sixth does not participate in this. Regarding the numerical divisions: from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), there are forty-two categories.
While these are roughly divided into forty-two categories, if subdivided, they would be immeasurable. Thus, it is shown that the grasping at phenomena remains entirely present [in these stages].
This was the prior response concerning the characteristics of the stream that one must oppose. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Although you have already passed from the state of an ordinary person into the state of a sage, having realized the first fruit and entered the stream of the sages, you have only severed the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*).

As for the active seeds within the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* and the beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), these must necessarily be eliminated through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)."
As for "severing," it refers to the afflictions of thought (*sahakleśa*). You still do not understand this. Such is the case even for the views and thoughts within the realms;
how much more so for the ignorance that is of the same essence as arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within this *ālayavijñāna*. This is what is called the views and thoughts outside the realms.
Their number is exceedingly vast; how could they be within the scope of measurement for you followers of the Two Vehicles?

Your question regarding what constitutes the "outflows" (āsrava) refers precisely to the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) that you have not yet severed, as well as the distinct delusions of the "dust-like sands" of ignorance (*avidyā*).
These are the locations where the outflows of desire reside, and it is these that you must oppose and thoroughly investigate. [This concludes] the section from the fifth fascicle onwards.
The three voids and the six knots are all established on this basis; that which is severed by the stage of the Path of Realization is likewise this.
Now, you should observe for yourself: are these six faculties before you one, or are they six? Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see?
Why does the eye not hear? Why does the head not tread? Why do the feet not speak? If these six faculties were definitively...
"Thus they form six. Just as I have now proclaimed this subtle and wondrous Dharma-door to you in this assembly, which of your six sense faculties comes to receive it?

Ānanda replied, "I hear it with my ears. The Buddha said, "It is your ears that hear; what concern is there for your body or mouth? Your mouth asks about the meaning, and your body rises to show reverence.
Therefore, you should know that they are not one, yet they ultimately constitute six; they are not six, yet they ultimately constitute one. Ultimately..."
"It is not that your faculties are fundamentally one or six. Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six.

Because of the inverted and fluctuating delusions since beginningless time, the meanings of 'one' and 'six' have arisen within the perfect and湛 (zhan—profoundly still) nature. You, as a Srotāpanna, although you have attained the dissolution of the six, have not yet eliminated the 'one.
It is like the great void of space which combines with various vessels; because the shapes of the vessels differ, they are given different names."
Regarding emptiness: when one contemplates emptiness by removing the vessel, that emptiness is said to be one. How could that great void space be either the same as or different from you?
How much less could it be called "one" or "not one"? Thus, your awareness of the six faculties of reception is also like this.
Below this, in order to answer the meaning of "one entrance and six purities," he first distinguishes that fundamentally there is neither one nor six. The Buddha said:
"Since you do not understand the reason for 'one entrance and six purities,' you should carefully observe these six faculties present before you:
are they ultimately one, or are they ultimately six? Ānanda, if you say they are one, then the ear ought to be able to see."
The eyes can hear; the head can be stepped upon while the feet speak. Yet now, why is it not so?
If one were to say these are six [distinct organs], then the body, mouth, and ears should each be unrelated to one another.

Why is it that at the time of inquiring about the Dharma, one uses the ears to hear, the mouth to inquire about the meaning, and the body to respectfully receive [the teaching]? Therefore, one should know that this is not [the case].
Either it must be six, because they are mutually opposed in their functions; or it must be one, because they are mutually cognizant in their nature.
It is certainly not your sense-organ that originally possesses a fixed oneness, nor does it originally possess a fixed sixfoldness.
Ānanda, you should know that since this organ is neither a fixed one nor a fixed six, and yet...

Now, there currently exists that which is both "one" and "six. This arises entirely from a single moment of inversion since beginningless time, whereby [the mind] becomes firmly bound with the six external sense-objects in one place, revolving and alternating with them.
Within the originally perfect and湛 (zhan—serene) state, the meanings of "one" and "six" emerge.
Ordinary people at the level of the mundane ground grasp this as "six," while those of shallow understanding among students grasp it as "one," yet neither has ever realized its perfection.
It is neither one, nor is it the fundamental reality of the six; how, then, could "one" or "six" be obtained?
Although you have now realized the first fruit and do not enter the six sense-objects, you have already attained the dissolution of the six and certainly do not cling to them.

Yet, the empty habitual tendencies within the faculties have not yet been eliminated; your clinging to the existence of *nirvāṇa* shows that you have not yet transcended "one. This is precisely what is meant by:
Shallow interpreters cling to this as being "one. As long as that "one" has not yet been extinguished, the seeds of the six sense faculties remain individually present;
thus, it is no wonder they do not understand the meaning of "the one entering the purity of the six.

Furthermore, the descent of the profound, perfect, and wondrous nature into the six sense faculties is just like the vast empty space merging with various vessels; it is due to the shapes of those vessels [that the space appears divided].
The differences between square, round, long, and short arise because of their combination with various objects; thus, one comes to say that space itself has distinctions.
Even if one were to remove the vessels and observe the space, one could still say that space is one. Yet, one fails to realize whether it is one or different.
The vessel-like form of space is, after all, the great void; how could it be established by your verbal explanations as being either identical or different?
Since it cannot be established by you as being either identical or different, how much less can it be renamed as "this great void is one" or "not one"?
Thus, to speak of space as being either distinct or identical is truly false. Since space is...
Thus, your understanding of the six faculties of sensory reception is likewise so: because the faculties are conjoined, you speak of their nature as six;
because the faculties are dissolved, you speak of their nature as one. This too is merely empty speech;

for how could the perfect and profound stillness be subject to your verbal descriptions, truly becoming distinguished as "one" or "six"? Therefore, the nature of these faculties is fundamentally neither one nor six.
Therefore, with one single understanding, the six are simultaneously dissolved. Zhong said: "Though the six have been dissolved, 'one' has still not been abandoned.
Various interpretations are thus in confusion. Master Lián (Zhiyi) said: "It is sufficient simply to use the original language [of the scripture]. The Sūtra says:

'Originally relying on one brilliant clarity, it is divided into six harmonious combinations. Now that the six harmonious combinations have been dissolved, one merely maintains the one brilliant clarity."

Furthermore, it is said that one contemplates emptiness by removing the vessel; how could one possibly wish to remove emptiness itself? It is not that one is ill at ease with emptiness, but rather that one is ill at ease with the attachment to there being a "single emptiness.
Attachment to a single, refined spirit is just like this. Only when both "oneness" and "multiplicity" are simultaneously discarded does one realize that the substance of the mind is empty space.
To be the same is oneness; to be different is multiplicity. When both oneness and multiplicity are eliminated, they are further eliminated.

It is not one. To know the sameness and difference, the right and wrong of empty space, and to realize that nothing is established, then even "one" perishes along with it, and the perfect stillness remains undivided.

Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adhered to and gives rise to seeing (initially forming the essence of seeing).

This essence of seeing reflects forms, and by binding with forms, it constitutes the sense organ. The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements" (forming the *paramārtha-indriya*). For this reason, it is called the "substance of the eye."

It is like a cluster of grapes. (The subtle atoms of the eye-faculty rest upon the pupil, spreading out horizontally, like crystal, without obstructing one another. The four coarse elements of the floating root—(the "four elements" refer to form, odor, taste, and touch;

though sound and mental objects are omitted by ellipsis, according to the meaning of the text, it simply means "among these various objects")—rush forth as turbulent escape toward forms, thereby forming the floating coarse root.

Through the mutual impact of the two aspects of movement and stillness, [the energy] surges within the wondrously perfect [mind]. Adhering to the profound clarity, hearing is activated. The essence of hearing reflects sounds, and by coiling back the sounds, it forms [the faculty].
The faculties. The fundamental source of the faculties is designated as the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

because of this, it is called the substance of the ear, resembling a newly curled leaf (the atoms of the auditory faculty reside within the ear cavity, coiled and dwelling there like curled birch bark). The four objects of the floating faculties flow outward and rush toward sounds; through the two conditions of openness and obstruction, they are manifested.

Within the wondrously perfect [state], the clarity is adhered to and the sense of smell is produced. The essence of smelling reflects fragrance, and by receiving fragrance, the faculty is formed. This is the fundamental source of the faculty.

The eyes are the pure four great elements; because of them, the substance of the nose is named. It is like a pair of hanging claws (situated within the nostrils, with the back above and the surface below, like a pair of fingernails).

The four sensory objects flow as floating roots, rushing toward fragrances. Through the blending of the two types—*tian* (which is the taste of flavorlessness) and *bian* (which is the totality of the five tastes, the taste of having flavor)—they intermingle.
Within this wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes sticky and gives rise to tasting. The essence of tasting reflects upon flavors, and they are twisted together.

The sense-faculty is formed by taste. Its fundamental source is designated as the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Because it takes taste as its object, it is named the "tongue-body. It is shaped like a new crescent moon.

This floating faculty consists of the four sensory objects; it flows and rushes toward tastes. Through the two modes of contact—conjunction and separation (the meeting of boundaries)—within that wondrous perfection, the clarity of stillness gives rise to awareness.
The essence of awareness reflects upon contact, and by grasping that contact, the faculty is formed. Its fundamental source is designated as the pure...

The purified four great elements are called the "body," like the body of a waist-drum (the colloquial name for a *janggu*; "body" refers to the hollow cavity; it has a narrow waist with leather stretched over both ends).

The staff resembles a human body; the four sensory faculties float and flow, rushing toward their objects of touch. Through the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrously perfect [state], the clarity of stillness becomes "knowing.

This essence of knowing reflects the dharmas, and by grasping these dharmas, it forms the faculties. The fundamental source of the faculties is termed the "pure four great elements" (*mahābhūta*); for this reason, they are called the "mental faculties" (*manas-indriya*).

These mental faculties are the physical sense organs (the "flesh-balls of the heart"), shaped like opening and closing lotus flowers, with a single aperture at their center. This was formed from the initial absorption of the parents' vital essence and blood.

At that time, the mind immediately attaches itself to this [object], rushing toward the realm of dharmas—what is called the "shell of ignorance. Yet, because it cannot be seen by people within the body, the character *si* (to think) is used to clarify that its location is wherever there is the faculty of deliberation.

It is like seeing in a dark chamber: one who dwells in the light cannot see a single thing in the darkness, whereas one who dwells in the darkness can see all the forms within the light. Thus, the mental faculty (*manas*) resides in this place of profound obscurity and silent stillness, acting as the strategist for the operations of the five preceding faculties;
it is by means of this state that its cognitive essence is characterized. The four sense-objects flow forth from the floating roots and rush toward the realm of dharmas.
This clarifies that the fetters of the sense organs arise from sensory objects. Now, the profoundly still, perfect, and wondrous mind is fundamentally free of any clinging or attachment.

Why, then, did the faculty of sight first come to be? It was because of the two kinds of color-objects—light and darkness—which, by their mutual contrast and manifestation, caused the nature of stillness within the wondrous perfection to become "sticky," much like glue adhering to an object. Once this nature of stillness was soiled by this stickiness, it gave rise to delusion.
It is seen; yet it has not yet formed a root or a knot. Subsequently, the essence of seeing again reflects upon these two colors of light and darkness, blending them into a single mass.
It then gathers and knots the objects of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) to form the dominant sense-faculty (*indriya*).

This faculty is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that were originally pure; therefore, it is said that the source of the faculties is termed "pure four great elements. However, it is subtle.
It is difficult to manifest; only the divine eye of a sage can perceive it, while ordinary beings cannot behold it. It is not something that the coarse sense organs (*bāhyendriya*) can compare with.
Because the supreme sense organ (*paramārthendriya*) serves as its fundamental basis, the substance of the eye is then established, just like the flower-bud of a *pu-tiao*.
Its coarse characteristics are prominent and are commonly perceived by ordinary beings; this is what constitutes the "floating dust" sense-organ (*bu chen zhi gen*).
Among the various sensory objects, it flows outward and rushes toward forms, taking form alone as its objective condition (*ālambana*), and thus revolves following after form without end;

the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is thereby bound. To investigate this further: it arises from the mutual impact of two types of characteristics, namely movement and stillness, and so forth. (And so on.)
The flowing and wandering toward sounds is that by which the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) is bound; it arises from two kinds of characteristics, namely penetration and obstruction, and so forth.

The flowing and wandering toward fragrances is that by which the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇa-indriya*) is bound; it arises from the intermingling of two kinds of characteristics, namely tranquility and transformation.
(As stated above... It flows out and rushes toward flavors; this is how the tongue-faculty becomes bound. Through the two kinds of mutual friction—separation and conjunction, etc.
(as stated above)... it flows out and rushes toward tangibles; this is how the body-faculty becomes bound. Through the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing, etc.
(as stated above)... it flows out and rushes toward mental objects (*dharma*); this is how the mind-faculty becomes bound. This flow is like water rushing downward.
It descends as swiftly as a beast breaking free from its tether and rushes like a horse galloping down a slope; such is the force of its natural momentum that nothing can restrain it.

If one wishes to attain the state where dust-like defilements are forgotten and fetters are exhausted, how could this be achieved without employing the counteractive method? What else could possibly control it?
The commentary says: Since the preceding text stated that [the nature] is neither one nor six, how then can there be the distinction of the six sense organs?
Therefore, this passage sets forth their origin, showing that within the wondrously perfect nature, there are fundamentally not six;

it is only because of the clinging of delusion that light is emitted, leading eventually to outward wandering. "Adhesion" (*nian*), "knotting" (*jie*), "coiling" (*juan*), and "twisting" (*jiao*) all refer to forms of binding.
Another name [for this state] is consistent with what was explained previously.
Ānanda, it is because these six faculties, through that awakened clarity, possess a clarity that is itself awakened; yet they lose that essential lucidity and, adhering to delusion, emit light.
Therefore, at present, when you are free from darkness and free from light, there is no essence of seeing; when free from movement and free from stillness, it fundamentally does not exist.

Listen to this inquiry: Hearing has no penetration and no obstruction; the nature of smelling does not arise; it is neither changing nor tranquil; tasting has nothing from which it issues; it neither departs nor joins;
the perception of touch is fundamentally non-existent; it has neither extinction nor birth. Thus one understands where [the senses] find their resting place.
