This restates the preceding reason that because there are knots due to external objects, they have no substance apart from those objects.

Ānanda, these six faculties all arise from the essence of the nature of awareness, which is profoundly still and luminous; through a single movement, it transforms into the "luminous awareness" that is capable of illumination.

Consequently, you have lost the essence of awakened clarity and discernment. From this, vision arises by clinging to light and darkness; hearing arises by clinging to motion and stillness, and so forth.
All the refined radiance of the six sense organs is produced by clinging to delusion. Therefore, your current seeing does not transcend form;
if you were removed from both darkness and light, the substance of seeing would cease to exist. Hearing does not transcend sound; if you were removed from...
When movement departs from stillness, there is no substance for hearing. This extends to the point that when openness and obstruction depart, the nature of smelling ceases;

when tranquility and change depart, the nature of tasting ceases; when separation and union are abandoned, the perception of touch ceases; and when external arising and ceasing are transcended, cognitive awareness ceases.
Such is the inability of the sense organs to be detached from their objects. However, what is called the "absence of a visual essence" refers merely to the absence of...
The accumulation of views resides in the eye; it is the deluded substance that becomes obstructed as the root-faculty.
It is not the case that its constant substance—the sovereign function of illumination—is also simultaneously annihilated. The same applies to the other five [faculties].

How is it, Ānanda, that you mistakenly recognize this, and further harbor doubts regarding annihilation in the subsequent text? ○ Gushan says: "That 'awakened clarity' (jue-ming) refers to true clarity (zhen-ming). There is..."

This is indeed a case where that which is already difficult to determine becomes even more indeterminate. Now that this has been understood.
One should no longer maintain the view that there is an absence of intrinsic nature apart from external objects.
It is like a person in deep sleep, lying soundly upon a bed and pillow while members of his household are pounding silk or husking rice during his slumber.
While dreaming, this person hears the sound of pounding and threshing, yet perceives it as something else—either the beating of a drum or the striking of a bell.
During the dream, he wonders at the bell, thinking it is merely the resonance of wood or stone. Suddenly waking, he immediately recognizes the sound of the pestle and informs his family:
"While I was dreaming, I was confused by this sound of pounding and mistook it for the resonance of a drum. (He wondered about the bell in the dream, but upon waking, spoke of the drum.)

[This is a brief illustration of mutual reflection. Ānanda, when this person is in a dream, how could they fail to remember stillness and movement (where "movement" implies motion), or opening and closing, or penetration and obstruction (including the physical ear)?
Although their form is asleep, the nature of hearing is not obscured. Even if your form were to dissolve and the light of life were to pass away, how could this nature be extinguished by you?

This is cited to verify the permanence [of the auditory faculty] through dreams. Previously, Ānanda had grasped the Buddha’s teaching that, apart from movement and stillness, there is fundamentally no substance of hearing;

yet he gave rise to the doubt that the nature of the sense-organ is subject to annihilation. Now, by the demonstration of striking the bell, the presence of sound is verified in movement and the absence of sound is verified in stillness;
however, this has not yet reached the point of verifying it by departing from both movement and stillness simultaneously.
Therefore, this is cited once more to verify the state where both movement and stillness are simultaneously transcended during sleep.

Furthermore, there is another proof that the nature of hearing does not perish: for instance, when a person is in a deep sleep upon their bed and pillow, and someone in the house pounds silk or husks rice, with the sounds of the block and the pestle resounding in chaotic harmony, that person hears the sound of the husking within their dream.
The sound of pounding [grain]. His consciousness was clouded and his perception inverted; he took it to be the beating of a drum or the striking of a bell.
Furthermore, within his dream, he marveled at its clarity, thinking, "Why is this the resonance of wood and stone?
At that moment, he suddenly awoke and realized, "This is the sound of a pestle. He then told his family members, "While I was dreaming, I heard this sound of pounding. He was about to—

This refers to the resonance of a drum reaching the ear. Regardless of whether the pestle striking the mortar is real or the bell and drum are false, one perceives them all distinctly within the locus of the auditory faculty.
Ānanda, when this person is in the midst of a dream, they have forgotten their entire body;
how then could there still be the two objects of motion and stillness, or the physical ears characterized by opening, closing, penetration, and obstruction, for them to remember? Nevertheless—

Furthermore, although the physical form is asleep, the nature of hearing does not become darkened; thus, there is yet another clear verification that this nature is not extinguished when separated from its objects.
Moreover, it is not only that one does not sleep within a dream, but even after death, one does not sleep. To discuss this to its ultimate conclusion:
"Even if your physical form dissolves and your life departs, when your eyesight falls to the ground, this nature remains constant.
How could it be extinguished along with your physical form? At this point, Ānanda, becoming even more insistent, asked another question:
"If this faculty of the root-nature is unrelated to motion and stillness, and unimpeded by birth and death, why did the Tathāgata say—"
"Free from movement and free from stillness, how could there originally be a substance for hearing? The Buddha should have replied:
"When I said that apart from objects there is no substance for hearing, I meant that there is no accumulated hearing in the ear that coagulates to form the substance of the faculty of hearing.
If this substance were forgotten, then the nature of hearing, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm, would manifest in its fullness; how could it ever result in annihilation?"

It is thus that it is clearly shown the reason why, from the beginning, there was no substance of hearing; this demonstrates that it was Ānanda’s own erroneous interpretation, and not a contradiction within the Buddha’s own words.

Otherwise, if the Buddha had previously stated that [hearing] has no substance apart from its objects, and later stated that it has a substance apart from its objects, there would ultimately be no way to resolve the difficulty of this internal contradiction in his own speech. Wuxing said:

Ānanda’s doubt extended to the lack of substance in the six sense organs. The reason the Tathāgata singled out the hearing-nature (*śrotra-dhātu*) as being permanent was to awaken the capacity for the perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-abhijñā*) of the ear-organ.
Regarding the line "mistaking the sound of pounding for a drum or bell," this merely takes up the fact that the hearing-nature is not obscured.
The four lines beginning with "Even if your physical form were to dissolve" represent a further step, meaning that it is not only during dreams [that this nature persists].
It is not obscure; even after death, it is not obscure.
Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed sounds and forms and drifted with every thought, they have never awakened to the purity, subtlety, and permanence of their own nature.
Failing to follow that which is constant, they pursue birth and extinction; thus, life after life, they wander through defilement.

If you abandon arising and ceasing and maintain the true and constant, the light of constancy will manifest before you. At that moment, the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will all dissolve away.
Conceptualization and appearances act as dust; the consciousness and emotions act as grime. When both are left far behind, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright.
"How is it that one does not achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?
This section shows that because delusion constantly pursues cessation, there is saṃsāra; by abandoning cessation and maintaining constancy, one immediately achieves perfect enlightenment.
Now, if the nature of hearing does not follow birth and death in this way, then how could the sensory objects be pursued? And how could the nature...

How could one not guard it? For all sentient beings, since beginningless time, have pursued the delusive and been confused about the true, following these sensory objects of form and sound, and flowing with every thought, never having awakened to the nature within the faculties—which is pure and unstained.
Subtle yet unbound, eternally abiding and devoid of arising or ceasing—such is the manner in which delusion arises.

Failing to follow the constant nature inherent within the sense faculties, one instead flows outward and rushes toward sensory objects, thereby committing various karmic acts associated with those objects.

Consequently, one migrates through the six realms, wandering from birth to birth with inexhaustible fruits of suffering; thus, the triad of delusion, karma, and suffering is fully present and lacking nothing.

If one can abandon this cycle of birth and death and no longer rush toward the sensory dusts, maintaining the true and eternal while turning the faculties inward to reflect back, this is what is meant by "detaching from黏 [sticking] and subduing within.
One will then attain the manifestation of the constant light, which is what is meant by "subduing and returning to the original truth, giving rise to the radiance of the fundamental luminosity.
At that moment, the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will dissolve away; this is what is meant by the "radiant nature."
This is the clarification. As for the remaining five types of attachment, they should be uprooted through complete liberation. Furthermore, it does not end here.

Once the faculties, objects, consciousness, and the mind have been entirely dissolved, after this dissolution has occurred, the essence of the pure, tranquil, and unified state within the mind—that very aspect of the tranquil unity being contemplated—is yet another most subtle and difficult-to-remove dust. And as for this...
Not relinquishing the mind of profound stillness is likewise a state of cognitive attachment; it is called "attachment to dharmas" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

This is yet another kind of defilement that clings closely to the body and is difficult to scrape away. If you can distance yourself from both of these, then coarse and subtle dusts and impurities will be purified until nothing remains.
At that moment, your Dharma-eye will be clear and bright; this is precisely the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. How could it be otherwise?

Does one thereby achieve unsurpassed enlightenment? For the Dharma-eye is clear and bright; although one may have only recently reached the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), because the causal ground is authentic and true, the fruition will not be circuitous.
Thus, from the very first arousal of the mind, one is certain to achieve perfect awakening.

Upon reaching this state, even the profound unity is forgotten—how then could the six sense-faculties remain bound? This is a metaphorical explanation for the severance of the nature of the faculties.
The section on Doubt concludes. A student asked Master Gaocheng, "Master, what is it like when there is no lamp after nightfall?
The Master said, "For one who has realized the Way, the constant light is ever-present; what dawn or dusk could there be? The student said, "Why do I not see the Master's light?
The Master said, "With what kind of eyes would you attempt to see it? The student said, "Ordinary people..."
"Now, look with your own eyes. The Master snapped his fingers and said, "Excellent!

All sentient beings, through the mutual entanglement of sense organs and objects, have from time immemorial mistaken the thief for their own son. To this very day, they remain constantly bound by shackles and fetters.
If you, using your eyes to see and your consciousness to discriminate, seek the Buddha-way, you are turning your back on your original mind and following after the flow of thoughts."
Transformation. Regarding such a person, whether face-to-face or separated by distance—*Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Volume Four;
*Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Volume Five.
Compiled and edited by the lay practitioner Liaʼan Liu Daokai of Baxian;
presented for verification by the śramaṇa Lizhi of Chengdu.

The following provides a corroborative commentary to resolve the doubt regarding the separate establishment of the source. The old commentary states that this section restates what was not seen previously.
Regarding the "knots" [of the sense-faculties], how can it be that you understand them yet ask again? If this were the case, it would be most unreasonable.

For the preceding text clearly explained that the six [faculties] act as mediators for thieves who plunder the family’s treasures, providing a detailed demonstration of the origin of the knots of the faculties and the method for resolving those faculties.
Why, then, Ānanda, did you suddenly act as if you did not know that the six faculties are the knots, thereby troubling the Buddha with a redundant question?
You should know, Ānanda, that you have already identified the six sense faculties as being the knots. Yet now you further inquire about the origin of these knots;

this is precisely co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*), the root of the knot of birth and death. You do not realize that the very substance of the six faculties is itself [the origin], for apart from this there is nothing else.
Therefore, the Buddha replies below: "If you wish to recognize and know co-nascent ignorance, the root of the knot of birth and death, it is only you..."
"The six sense organs; there is nothing else.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained this second gateway of meaning, when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie the knots, if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe such people will ultimately be unable to untie it."

“World-Honored One, it is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training. Since beginningless time, we have been born and extinguished together with all forms of ignorance.
Although we have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called ‘those who have left the home life,’ we are like those suffering from quotidian malaria.

We only pray that the Great Compassionate One will take pity on us who are submerged in the depths. Regarding our present bodies and minds today, what constitutes these fetters, and by what name are they designated?”
"Understand this! May you also cause sentient beings suffering in the future to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the entire assembly; shedding tears and lifting his heart in sincerity, he waited expectantly for the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha Tathāgata.
This is a separate inquiry into the root-source of the bonds of birth and death. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the second gateway of meaning, providing a detailed demonstration of the origins of the sense-faculties' knots and the method for untying them, I already know that the six faculties are these knots.
However, I do not yet know whether, apart from these six faculties, there exists elsewhere a deeper root above them which serves as [the source of bondage]."

"Is there not a fundamental source for the formation of knots? As I observe those in the world who untie knots, if they do not know the origin of what was knotted, they will ultimately be unable to untie them.
This is true not only for worldly people; it is likewise for me and the śrāvakas here in this assembly who are still in training.
Why is this so? Because from the beginningless past, we have coexisted with various forms of ignorance, arising and ceasing together."

Upon birth—emerging from the mother’s womb—one either cries or laughs; this capacity exists spontaneously without waiting for instruction, which is called "beginningless habitual conditioning" (*anādikāla-vāsanā*) and is also termed "co-emergent ignorance" (*sahaja-avidyā*).
From birth until death, and from death back to birth, one wanders through successive waves of existence, perpetually sinking into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Although I have attained these roots of merit from extensive learning and am thus called a renunciant (*pravrajita*), yet I have attained...
At the moment of awakening, it briefly resembles liberation; yet when entering the realm of worldly toil, one remains bound as before.
This is what is meant by "seeming enlightened while speaking, but returning to delusion when facing objects. Like a double-day malaria, one experiences alternating chills and fevers.

All of this is driven by the power of innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*). I pray only that, out of great compassion, you will take pity on those drowning in suffering and provide me with a definitive instruction for today.
"Equalizing body and mind—what is the root source of these fetters? By what method can they be resolved?
This will not only bring benefit to the great assembly gathered here now, but shall also enable future sentient beings to escape the suffering of saṃsāra within the three realms of existence.
Having spoken these words (and so forth), he offered this unsurpassed instruction. Ānanda’s intention was likely one of doubt.
Co-nascent ignorance alone is the root of the fetters of birth and death, serving as the primary source of bondage. How could one know that it is precisely these six sense faculties?
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training, and also for the sake of future generations—

To serve as the cause for the transcendence of all sentient beings and to act as their eyes for the future, [the Buddha] used his hand, which possessed the purple-gold light of Jambūnada, to stroke Ānanda’s crown.
Immediately, the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways.
From the crowns of each of the Tathāgatas dwelling in those worlds, precious lights emerged; at that same moment, within those worlds, these lights...
They came to the Jeta Grove and sprinkled water upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. The great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the entire assembly heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice and in unison to Ānanda:
Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and know the innate ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death—the very root of bondage—it is none other than your six faculties;

there is no other thing. Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that enables you to swiftly realize peace, bliss, liberation, and the wondrous permanence of tranquility, it is likewise your six faculties and nothing else.

These Buddhas have collectively testified that the six sense organs are the source from which the knots are untied. At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly,
and for the sake of future sentient beings as a cause for their transcendence of the world— so that they may rely upon this for cultivation and realization,
and so that they may serve as eyes for the future, enabling them to believe, understand, and remain undeluded— he then rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head with his hand.
The "Crown" (uṣṇīṣa) dharma is manifested as an opening. At that moment, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways, signifying that the six sense faculties were about to be liberated.
From each of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, there issued a precious light from their uṣṇīṣas;
these lights came from those worlds and descended to anoint the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, signifying that the wondrous nature within these faculties is the supreme uṣṇīṣa-dharma.
"The Bhagavāns of the ten directions share a single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa.
When the great assembly had obtained this rare omen, they further heard the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, speaking with one voice to Ānanda, saying:
Excellent! Ānanda, do you wish to recognize and know that co-nascent ignorance which causes you to revolve in birth and death and serves as the root of bondage?
It is none other than these six faculties of yours right now; there is no other thing.
For this nature of the faculties is the very head of co-nascent ignorance and the deeply entrenched root of birth and death. Apart from—
These six sense organs have no further source of bondage. Moreover, they are not merely false sources; they are, in fact, true sources.

For they are the foremost of offenses and yet the primary of merits. If you further wish to know of unsurpassed Bodhi—attesting to the principle of Suchness with the wisdom of Suchness so that you may swiftly realize the fruit of severing the four virtues—is it not also for you to do so?
It is none other than these six sense faculties; it is not some external thing. As the saying goes, "The one who unties the bell is the very same person who tied it.
All Buddhas proclaim this in common; thus, it is evident that this is not the private teaching of a single Buddha, and it should be especially believed and accepted.
Although Ānanda had heard such sounds of the Dharma, his mind was still not yet clear.

He bowed his head to the Buddha and said, "How can you say that my cycle of birth and death and the state of wondrous, eternal peace and bliss are identical to these six sense faculties and nothing else? The Buddha told Ānanda:
The sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share a common source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky.

Ānanda, knowledge arises from objects, and characteristics exist because of the sense organs. These characteristics and the faculty of seeing lack inherent nature, being like two reeds leaning against each other.

(Just as reeds grow in pairs, embracing one another so that they stand upright—falling if alone—and as their substance is solid on the outside while hollow within, this prose passage takes up only their mutual leaning to illustrate their inability to stand independently, while the verse retains the image of the solid exterior and hollow interior to metaphorically represent the sense organs and their objects, which are neither empty nor existent. This is so.

Therefore, you now know that "knowing" (which refers to the internal faculty of mind) and "seeing" (which refers to the external five faculties), when established as knowing, are fundamentally ignorance (*avidyā*).
When knowing and seeing are themselves without seeing, this is *nirvāṇa*, untainted and truly pure. How could any other thing be admitted within this?
This detailed explanation shows that both bondage and liberation arise from the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Although Ānanda had heard such Dharma-sounds, his mind was still not clear;
therefore, he asked again about transmigrating through birth and death and realizing the wondrous permanence—how it is that all of these are solely the six sense-faculties and nothing else.
He harbored doubts, thinking that although the Tathāgata has often spoken of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), even the most essential and concise summary consists of ten items.
Regarding the eight elements and so forth, why now speak only of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), while the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are not mentioned?
The World-Honored One, drawing out the branches and extending the vines, further provides an explanation and says:
"The reason I mention only the faculties and not the objects is not that I have omitted the six objects. It is simply because when one clings to the characteristics of both faculties and objects..."

Upon contemplation, the sense organs (*indriya*) constitute the internal body and belong to sentient beings, while the sense objects (*viṣaya*) constitute the external vessel-world and belong to the insentient;
thus they appear to be eternally distinct. Nevertheless, both the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*) arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).

Fundamentally, there is but a single mind that delusively divides into the realms of sentient beings and the vessel-world. Tracing back to the source and exhausting its origin, they remain a single entity. Since the roots and objects share the same source, when one is bound...
They are bound together; when liberated, they are liberated together. Thus, bondage and liberation are non-dual.

Because they are solely non-dual, by grasping the faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*) is included therein. As for why consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not mentioned: the nature of consciousness has no source;
it is merely the false conceptualization of external objects, like flowers in the sky, which utterly lack substantial reality. Since it is neither the root of bondage nor—
This is the essential point of liberation; thus, by taking up the faculties (*indriya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also included therein.
Since the six objects (*viṣaya*) have no separate substance and the six consciousnesses are utterly void, all Buddhas alike declare that bondage and liberation depend solely upon the six faculties.

Furthermore, by what means do the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) come to be established? Ānanda, it is through the six external objects that the cognitions of the six faculties subsequently arise;
thus, the faculties are established in dependence upon the objects. It is because of the six internal faculties that the characteristics of the six objects subsequently exist;
thus, the objects are established in dependence upon the faculties. When the object is separated from the faculty, it certainly lacks an independent self-nature (*svabhāva*); so too with the faculty.

The object (dust) is devoid of an independent self-nature; thus, the two dharmas of the characteristic (object) and the seer (faculty) arise in mutual dependence, like two stalks of reeds leaning against one another. If they were solitary, they would fall to the ground and could not stand.

Moreover, the *śālukā* plant—being solid on the outside yet hollow within—can also serve as a metaphor for how both the emptiness and existence of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are neither one nor the other.
Since the sense organs and their objects possess no dual substance, bondage and liberation depend solely upon the sense organs.

Therefore, if you now fail to comprehend the principle that both emptiness and existence are neither, regarding the nature of the six sense organs which possess cognition and vision, [you will remain deluded].

They falsely establish two types of cognition: that of emptiness and that of existence. Just as ordinary beings are deluded regarding the nature of the six sense organs and take them to be existent, and the followers of the Two Vehicles obscure the nature of the six sense organs and take them to be empty—both are establishing [dualistic] cognition.

Ordinary beings are fully possessed of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsa*) and remain long submerged in the realm of segmented birth (*paricchinna-bhava*), all because they are deluded by taking existence as their fundamental basis.
The followers of the Two Vehicles still retain the fifth abode and have not yet transcended the realm of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
It is easy. All [schools] take the obscuration of emptiness as their fundamental basis; establishing cognition upon this—does this not arise from the root of ignorance?

If, within the nature of the faculty of knowing and seeing, one is free from the dualistic views of existence and emptiness—just as ordinary beings eliminate the view of grasping at existence and the two vehicles eliminate the view of biased emptiness—then there is no view at all. Ordinary beings eliminate the first four abodes of attachment.
First, one attains the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder). For the two vehicles, excluding the fifth stage, one attains the ultimate *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).

This very "non-seeing" (*adarśana*)—is it not precisely the untainted, true purity of nirvana? To establish knowing and seeing upon [the duality of] knowledge and vision is bondage by means of the root-bondage.
To detach knowing and seeing from vision is liberation by means of the root-liberation. Bondage consists solely of the root-bondage; yet furthermore...
There is no other thing that can serve as the root of bondage; liberation occurs only through the liberation of the faculties.
Yet, there is likewise no other thing that can serve as the root of liberation. How, then, within this bondage and this liberation, could another thing be admitted as their fundamental source?
Thus, your separate request for a "root of bondage" is truly an error. Question: This knowledge and vision—[is it... with...?

Are the "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the "knowledge and vision" taught after the complete manifestation of the Three Baskets (*tri-piṭaka*) in this present sūtra the same or different?
Answer: There is no separate dharma; they differ only in their general scope. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the names are designated but the meanings have not yet been explained;

thus, it is extremely broad in its application. This sūtra, however, is explained by the Buddha’s own golden mouth, wherein the Three Baskets are completely manifested; this is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge.
It is seen that this also refers to what sentient beings inherently possess, rather than what is achieved through cultivation and realization.
However, regarding sentient beings in their present state, it has never been pointed out exactly where this is possessed; thus, it was not yet precise.

Now, in this context, by pointing directly to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision within the nature of the six sense organs as they currently exist in sentient beings, it is finally rendered truly precise.
This is not a mere generality. It is because "knowledge" refers to the internal faculty of the mind (*manas*), while "vision" refers to the external five faculties (*indriya*).

Since the nature of these faculties is all-pervasive and eternally abiding, it constitutes the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa, wherein the three collections [of precepts, concentration, and wisdom] are perfectly complete.
How could this be anything other than the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision? The "single transmission" and "direct pointing" also secretly refer to this very point.

[End of section. ○ Previously it was said, "By means of causes and conditions, one establishes objects. Here it is said, "By means of knowledge and views, one establishes knowing. The harm of such establishment is as described above.
Therefore, the way of the Way-realized is to see without anything seen and to know without anything known. When not a single dharma is established, then every place of establishment is the Truth.
○ The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) says: "Worldly birth-and-death and world-transcending nirvana both arise from knowing."
One perceives that which is established by means of words and letters. If one lacks the knowledge and vision of words and letters, then names and essences are fundamentally empty.

Within this wondrously luminous mind, what further thing could there be to act as a condition or an obstruction? [The monk] Rui-lu met Chan Master Dao-an and received the Dharma from National Teacher Yao.
Once, while reading the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, he arrived at this passage and read it with a broken syntax, saying: "Knowledge and vision are established... (sentence).
"Knowing is itself the root of ignorance; when one knows that seeing is non-existent, this very seeing is nirvana.

Upon hearing these words, someone remarked to the Master, "You have broken the syntax! The Master replied, "This is the place where I attained awakening; I shall never change it for the rest of my life."
The commentary states: The two characters "knowledge" (zhī) and "vision" (jiàn) refer to what was previously termed "seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing," which point to the six sense faculties.
Within the sphere of knowledge and vision, false forms of light and darkness arise; they adhere to the profound stillness to give rise to seeing, and flow outward in pursuit of visible objects.

This very faculty of knowing and seeing is itself the root of ignorance. If, within this faculty of knowing and seeing, one does not follow after external objects, but detaches from their clinging and turns inward to rest, such that an inner clarity radiates light, then this very faculty of knowing and seeing is itself the root of nirvana. To establish the knowing is the basis of ignorance;
therefore it is said that one revolves through birth and death. Yet, it is solely through your six sense-faculties that [ignorance arises]; when there is no [clinging] seeing, that is nirvana.
Therefore, it is called peace, bliss, wondrous permanence, and also your six sense faculties. Ānanda asked: "What is this bondage?
From what is it called liberation? To establish knowledge within knowledge and vision is precisely bondage; when knowledge and vision are free from [the notion of] seeing, that is called liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse.
The verses are divided into two categories: first, *geya* (translated as "corresponding verse"), which refers to verses that summarize the preceding prose;
second, *gāthā* (translated as "recited verse"), which does not depend on prose but consists of verses recited in praise.
The true nature is empty of the conditioned; because it arises from conditions, it is like an illusion. The unconditioned has no arising or ceasing; it is unreal, like a flower in the sky.

(That is, while there is arising and ceasing, fundamentally there is no arising or ceasing. Thus, both meanings are simultaneously dissolved, which is the sense of perfect reality. To posit "no arising or ceasing" in opposition to "arising and ceasing" means that both are unreal;
this is the provisional teaching of the Lesser Vehicle.)

This verse states that the nature of consciousness is empty and illusory, like flowers in the sky. According to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiang zong), there are five categories of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only):
the first four are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and the fifth is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The intent of this verse may be expressed thus: "How profound!
Great indeed is the function of the sensory faculties (*indriya*). Yet, when we speak of consciousness, conditioned consciousness lacks true self-nature and is entirely illusory."
Because it arises by relying on causes and depending on conditions, it is likened to a magical illusion.
As for unconditioned consciousness, its "non-arising and non-ceasing" is established in contrast to arising and ceasing; both are unreal and are likened to flowers in the sky.

"The causes for bondage and liberation are identical; there are no two paths for the noble and the ordinary.

This verse means that bondage and liberation are non-dual. Since the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) have no dual substance, bondage and liberation consist solely of the six sense organs.
Therefore, when bound, they are bound together; when liberated, they are liberated together. Both bondage and liberation belong to these very organs; they share the same basis.
This is the cause. When bound, one is an ordinary person; when liberated, one is a sage. Both sages and ordinary persons are this very faculty;
there is no second path. Thus, apart from the six faculties, how could there be any other bondage or liberation? Therefore, I say that bondage and liberation are non-dual.
Observe the nature of their intersection: it is neither empty nor existent.
This verse reiterates that the faculties and objects share a common source. Furthermore, the two phenomena of faculty and object are like intertwined reeds;
they do not merely rely upon one another for support. Observe the essential nature of these intertwined reeds: while the exterior is solid, the interior is empty. Thus it was said.
That which exists within is fundamentally empty; as soon as one speaks of its emptiness, that which is outside is fundamentally real. This serves as an analogy for the faculties and their objects.
When one speaks of existence, its essence is empty and vast, sovereign and unconditioned. When one speaks of emptiness, its function is perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Thus, both emptiness and existence are neither; one must ultimately reach the state where both emptiness and existence are transcended.
No; it is only then that the meaning of their sharing a single source is fully realized.
Delusion and obscurity are themselves ignorance (*avidyā*); illumination and clarity are liberation.
This verse emphasizes that bondage and liberation are non-dual. Thus, the two dharmas of faculty and object are neither empty nor existent.
Therefore, when ordinary beings are deluded regarding the six sense faculties as being existent, they lose their essence of sovereign non-attachment.

When those of the Two Vehicles obscure the six sense faculties as being empty, they lose their function of universal manifestation and mutual fusion. Consequently, both fall into the five abodes and two deaths;
thus, this delusion and obscuration is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). As it is said: "To establish cognition within cognition and vision is itself ignorance."
This is the fundamental principle. If one overturns delusion to give rise to awakening, yet does not again cling to existence;

if one transforms obscurity into clarity, yet does not again sink into emptiness—then one remains far removed from the five abodes and two deaths. Thus, the manifestation of enlightenment is itself liberation. This is what is meant by "knowing and seeing without seeing";
it is precisely the nirvana that is untainted, truly pure, and free from outflows. At this point, bondage and liberation are non-dual.

Cao further named them "knots. Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, these precious layered flowers were woven together to form a headcloth;

though they were originally of one substance, as I contemplate it, when the Tathāgata tied one knot, it received the name 'one knot,' and if he were to tie a hundred, they would become a hundred knots."
In the end, it is called "a hundred knots. How much more so in this case, where there are only six knots; they never reach seven, nor do they remain at five.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata allow that only the first, second, and third instances are not called knots?

The single cloth is a metaphor for the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). The six knots are metaphors for the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). A single cloth ought to form only one knot; why then are there six?
Therefore, the Buddha again asked in return: "This folded silk cloth was originally but a single strand.
I first tied it into one knot, and you named it a 'knot. As for the second and third, how could they also [be called knots]?"
"It is called a knot. Is it that this cloth is one while the knots are many?
Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, this precious cloth of layered flowers is produced by weaving; although it is a single strip, it originally has no multiple substance.
Yet, as I reflect upon it, by one twist one obtains one knot, and if there are a hundred twists, they are called a hundred knots. Now, this cloth..."
There are six knots; they rarely reach seven, nor do they ever remain at five. These six knots are clearly manifest and are not merely products of arbitrary naming.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata permit only the first knot to be called a "knot," while the second and third are not so named?
This critical inquiry is intended to lead Ānanda to realize that the substance of the cloth is one, which, due to the knots, becomes six.
This is to demonstrate that the six knots are entirely formed from a single piece of cloth.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Regarding this precious flower-cloth, you know that this cloth originally consists of only one strand; it was when I tied it six times..."
"There are six knots in this name. Observe this carefully: the substance of the cloth is the same, yet it differs because of the knots.

What do you think? When the first knot was tied, it was called the 'first. In this way, up until the sixth knot was produced. Now, I wish to take the name of the sixth knot and establish it as the 'first.
Would that be possible? "No, World-Honored One. As long as the six knots exist, this name of the sixth [remains]."
"In the end, this is not the primary [solution]. Even if I were to exhaust my discernment throughout successive lifetimes, how could I cause these six knots to have their names confused?

The Buddha said: 'It is so. Although the six knots are different, if one traces them back to their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth; it is only by causing them to be jumbled together that they appear as such.'"
In the end, it cannot be accomplished. Thus, your six sense faculties are also like this: within ultimate sameness, there arises ultimate difference.
Is it not appropriate that I ask this question in order to provoke you into discerning this for yourself? The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As for this precious flowered cloth, you already know that its origin is a single strand; yet because of my tying six knots, it has come to have six knots."

You should further examine this in detail: before they were tied, the substance of the cloth was the same; since not even a single characteristic could be established, how could there be six characteristics?
Once they have been tied, differences arise because of the tying; the six characteristics are definitively distinct, so where does the single characteristic remain?
What do you think? It is because of the first knot that it is called the "first," and up to the sixth knot that it is called the "sixth.
I now wish to take the sixth and treat it as the first, just as one might use the faculty of the mind as the faculty of the eye.
"Is it possible to obtain such a thing? The World-Honored One, because they know one another within their own natures, made it difficult for them to achieve the unification of the six into one.
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. These six knots still exist; this is called the sixth, and it can never become the first.
Even if I were to exhaust the cleverness and eloquence acquired throughout my successive lives, I could not cause these six knots—"

They are designated by names due to confusion; because the Venerable One uses these names in a way that contradicts their middle state, he replied that the six knots cannot be confused in their naming.
The Buddha welcomed this and granted his approval, saying: "What you say is so.

Although the six knots are indeed different, if one looks back to their original cause, they were originally fashioned from a single piece of cloth. Yet, once the one has become six, the one can no longer be seen within the six."
It must not be confused; if it were allowed to become disordered, it would ultimately fail to achieve its function.
Thus, your six faculties present before you are also like this: prior to their being bound together, they were originally one body, fundamentally without distinction or difference.
Once they have been bound, each has its own boundaries and divisions; thus, the mind cannot serve as the function of the eye, and the eye cannot serve as the function of the mind. From...
Within ultimate identity, there arises ultimate difference. For within the fundamental substance of the true mind, even a single characteristic cannot be apprehended;
how then could the six knots be apprehended? This is what is meant by "ultimate identity. Yet, when delusion arises from the truth...
Now that the six knots have already been formed, their sequence cannot yet be disordered; how then could those six ever be momentarily forgotten?
This is what is meant by "the completion of an ultimate difference. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) commentary states that the six knots are a metaphor for the six layers of vertical emergence.
Regarding the two terms "same" and "different," they are ultimately not applicable here. This is because [the sequence consists of]: first, movement; second, stillness; third, hearing;
fourth, cognition; fifth, emptiness; and sixth, cessation. One may only speak of these as a "succession," but one cannot speak of them as "same" or "different."
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "If you find these six knots unsatisfactory and wish for them to become one, how can that be achieved?
Ānanda replied, "As long as these knots exist, disputes will arise; within them, the notion will spontaneously emerge that 'this knot is not that,' or 'that knot is not this.
If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and the knots no longer arose, then there would be neither 'this' nor 'that. (The Six Sense Organs)

Only then can one speak of "this" and "that. If one uses the analogy of pushing vertically through six layers, how could one possibly distinguish between this and that? Since they cannot even be called "one," how could the six be established?
The Buddha said: "When the six are resolved, the one perishes; it is exactly like this."
This further examines and clarifies that the six are resolved and the one is extinguished. The Buddha told Ānanda: "I have tied this flowered cloth into knots;
you must surely find them disagreeable and do not wish for them to remain as six knots. I only wish for them to return to being a single cloth.
What strategy would you employ so that this could be accomplished? Ānanda replied: "If the six knots persist, then they are distinct from one another."
Each has its own fixed position and each has its own name. If one were to treat these six as a single unit, then sharp disputes would arise, for it is absolutely impossible;
this is because the knot of this is not the knot of that, and the knot of that is not the knot of this.

If the Tathāgata were today to untie all six knots together as one, then since there would be no knots, there would be neither "this" nor "that. This being so, [the distinctions between them] would vanish.

Since they do not exist, even "one" cannot be found; how much less so "six"? The Buddha then used a metaphor to confirm this, saying: "When the six are dissolved, the one perishes. It is exactly like this. For the entirety of the six sense-faculties is but the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because it arises from clinging to delusion and emits light, it is called "seeing" when in the eye, "hearing" when in the ear, and so forth. Thus, the six faculties—*rūpa*, *śabda*, *gandha*, *rasa*, *spraṣṭavya*, and *dharma*—are all but the radiance of the One Mind. They are like the six windows of a house; though the windows differ, the space within is one. Therefore, the six gates are distinct, yet their essence is identical. This is what is meant by "the six dissolve and the one perishes. Once the six are dissolved, the one also vanishes. When the six are dissolved, there is no longer any place for the one to abide. When the one perishes, there is no longer any basis for the six to arise. This is why it is said that the six dissolve and the one perishes. This is the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching. Furthermore, the six gates are the gates of the mind; the mind is the master of the gates. If the gates are opened, the mind flows out; if the gates are closed, the mind returns. When the knots are untied, the essence of the "one" becomes empty; it is like the six knots being untied and the single cloth becoming empty.
Yet, when the "one" perishes, its true substance is not lost along with it; rather, it simply no longer establishes itself as a "one" in contrast to the six knots.
[This concludes the answer to the question: "When the six are untied, does the one perish?"]

Because your mind-nature has been deranged since beginningless time, false perceptions have arisen; as these delusions arise without ceasing, the laboring faculty of sight gives rise to the dust of phenomena.

It is like having blurred vision when the eyes are fatigued, resulting in the appearance of floating flowers. Within the profound clarity of the essential spirit, all the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the world, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana, arise causelessly through disorder;
they are all merely the deluded labor of madness—the inverted appearances of floating flowers.
This answers the question regarding the sequence for loosening the knots while first demonstrating the order in which they are tied.
Although the six sense organs are like the six knots, within each of these six organs there are further six layers of karmic manifestations.

From time immemorial, your wondrously luminous fundamental awakening—the nature of the mind—has horizontally given rise to ignorance and become deluded; from this ignorance, the three [poisons] have been produced.
Subtlety constitutes the first knot; this corresponds to the "knot of extinction" within the Perfect Penetration.
Thereupon, deluded views arise, and one perceives phenomena as truly existent; this is the stage of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), which constitutes the second and third knots;

this corresponds to the "knot of emptiness" and the "knot of awakening" within the Perfect Penetration. Thereupon, the arising of delusion does not cease, and wearying vision gives rise to the dust of objects; thus one perceives...
"I" and "mine" constitute the stage of the person-grasping (pudgala-grāha); the remaining three fetters complete it.

Within the context of perfect penetration, the "fatigued vision" corresponds to the root-fetter, while the "arising of dust" corresponds to the two fetters of movement and stillness. What is meant by "fatigued vision arising as dust" is like this:
when the eye's pupil is fatigued, one sees wild flowers; these arise from confusion within the clear, brilliant, and pure essence, without any external cause. Can this not be understood?

One sees that all the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the world, as well as all conditioned phenomena—birth and death, nirvana, and all other conditioned dharmas—are merely illusory floral appearances arising from the deluded agitation and inversion within the nature of mind;
how could they possess any true reality? Because each of the six sense faculties possesses these six layers, delusion arises from the truth. From [the nature of mind]...
From the subtle toward the coarse, the sequence of their arrangement is clearly visible. This *nirvāṇa* is established in contrast to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
It refers to those of the Two Vehicles who cling to appearances and views, regarding [phenomena] as non-existent and thereby falling into the view of dharmas (*dharmadṛṣṭi*).
Zhang Zhuo’s statement that “*nirvāṇa* and birth-and-death are equal to empty flowers” precisely refers to this.

Ānanda said, “This entanglement is identical to a knot; how can it be untied? The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth in his hand and pulled its left side taut, then asked Ānanda, “Is it untied like this? “No, World-Honored One.
He then turned the cloth over and pulled its right side taut, asking Ānanda again, “Is it untied like this? “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, “I…”
"Now, pull it from both the left and right with your hands; you are ultimately unable to untie it. By what skillful means (*upāya*) can it be untied?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "If one unties it at the center of the knot, it will immediately fall apart. The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is."
If one wishes to untie it, one must do so at the center of the knot.
This further asks for the method of untying the knot and secretly reveals its essential point. Ānanda asked:
"This labor of the seeing-faculty arising from the dust of toil is a knot formed from a single cloth; I do not know what kind of skillful means should be employed."
Only then can it be untied. The Tathāgata took the tied cloth with his hand and pulled its left side, asking, "Is it untied like this?
He replied, "No, World-Honored One. This is an analogy for how ordinary beings are obstructed by the six sense faculties, clinging to them as being real.

Thus, one remains submerged in birth and death for a long time; how could this be a method for liberating the faculties? He then turned his hand and pulled again on the right side, asking once more, "Is it liberated in this way?
[Aniruddha] replied, "No, World-Honored One. This analogy refers to the contemplation of the Two Vehicles, which views the six faculties as empty.
Yet they remain forever obscured from Nirvana; how could they attain perfect penetration? This is because both the attachment to emptiness and the attachment to existence are..."
When one attempts to untie a knot by pulling at its ends, it remains entirely biased and crooked; neither end can be loosened.
Thereupon, the Buddha said to Ānanda, "If I now pull from both sides, left and right, and it still cannot be untied, what skillful means do you have that might allow it to be released?

Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, one must apply effort to the very center of the knot; once untied there, it will disperse. This is what is called following the principle of "following the command" (from the mandate).
One stroke at the root—this is what it means to bring a thousand matters to completion and a hundred tasks to their proper conclusion.

From the twenty-five sages hereafter, there were none who did not begin by binding the mind to break through the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate); thus, they all realized perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). The Buddha certified this, saying: [as recorded in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*].
So it is; so it is. If you wish to untie the knot, you must certainly not believe that the mind itself is the knot.

Now, although the "knotted mind" is used as a metaphor for the Middle Way, this Middle Way is not formed by combining that emptiness and existence, nor is it established separately from emptiness and existence.
Rather, it is the realization that this root-nature is inherently free and unconditioned, fundamentally not belonging to existence.
It is simply a matter of not being deluded by existence; there is no further need for the laborious contemplation of emptiness to destroy existence.
When one realizes this fundamental nature, its pervasive manifestation is mutually integrated; it fundamentally does not belong to emptiness, but is simply a matter of not obscuring it as emptiness;

there is no further need for the laborious contemplation of existence to destroy emptiness. As in the subsequent "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ," one neither clings to existence nor contemplates [emptiness].

Emptiness. By simply reversing the hearing and returning to the source, one forgets sensory objects and enters [the truth] instantaneously. From this, the two kinds of emptiness are gradually realized and the wondrous essence manifests, whereby the self is naturally dissolved.
When both [subject and object] are empty and non-arising, the Great Function arises, and emptiness itself is transcended.

Thus, reversing the hearing to return to one's own nature is precisely the binding of the mind; it is the Middle Way that simultaneously transcends both emptiness and existence. As the ancients said: [text fragment].
Dà (Dacheng) forcibly distinguishes three contemplations; his explanation is fragmented and redundant—truly like adding legs to a snake.

Regarding the various schools that take "annihilation" and "permanence" as the left and right [sides] and "the Middle Way" as the knot of the heart: a detailed examination of the preceding and following texts reveals that there is no such intention at all.
Master Tiantai said: "The left and right" refers to the ends of the knot; therefore, one exerts effort in vain and achieves no merit. "The knot of the heart" refers to...

This is because one must understand the root of bondage. Thus, even in leisure, success is achieved; this is truly due to the fact that the deluded and frantic mind, being confused, grasps at objects, thereby forming a knot.

This is the "knot of the mind. If one does not resolve it within this knotted mind, then all other methods of resolution—whether shifting left or right, abandoning one thing or grasping another—will be unable to achieve anything. This refers to what are called the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
All various phenomena, such as emptiness and existence, are likewise fully encompassed.
Ānanda, I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse, composite characteristics of the mundane world.

When the Tathāgata elucidates mundane and supramundane dharmas, he knows their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their respective conditions. This continues in this manner, even unto the sands of the Ganges.

Even a single drop of rain outside the boundaries of the world, you know its number; all the various things before you—the straightness of pines and the curvature of thorns, the whiteness of cranes and the blackness of crows—you fully comprehend their fundamental origins.
Therefore, Ānanda, choose whichever of the six faculties you prefer from within your own mind.
If the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of sense-objects will naturally vanish. When all delusions have been eliminated, what need is there to wait for anything that is not true?
This is to stimulate his desire [for practice] so that his mind may be resolved; one must select those of "perfect faculties" (*indriya*) as the conditions for their awakening.
Ānanda, although I have previously sternly rejected [the notion of] causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), nevertheless, the Buddha-dharma has never failed to arise from causes and conditions.

However, the causal conditions I speak of do not mean that consciousness arises from the combination of the four worldly conditions, that a person arises from the combination of three conditions, or that the various classes of beings arise from the combination of two conditions. What I am now explaining is the principle of causal conditions.
This is intended to select those with complete faculties so that they may enter through a single gate and clarify the great matter of the causal conditions.

Thus, I have observed the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones, as well as all mundane and supramundane dharmas; I know the fundamental causes of each one, for they all arise from conditions.
For example, the six classes of ordinary beings take good, evil, and immovable karma as their cause, and at the time of entering a rebirth...

Taking the two objects of aversion and attraction as conditions, the four types of noble beings take the causes accumulated through repeated cultivation of the teachings and principles of the various vehicles over many lifetimes as their cause, and the guidance provided by the spiritual friends they encounter as their condition; this continues in this manner even for that which is most difficult to know.

One could know the number of raindrops falling beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; one would clearly understand the causes and conditions for the straightness of a pine tree, the curvature of a thorn bush, the whiteness of a crane, and the blackness of a crow.
Since the Buddha’s wisdom is such, the explanations of the Dharma he provides are certainly free from error or deviation.
What is permitted for realization will never lead to error. Therefore, Ānanda, you should have firm conviction in selecting a faculty from among the six;
choose one perfect faculty and enter deeply through that single gate. Once the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of sensory objects will naturally cease.
Then the five faculties should be uprooted and completely liberated. When all illusory fetters have vanished, what need is there for anything that is not true?
How then could one fail to achieve supreme enlightenment? To abandon the selection of the faculties and instead seek to bind the mind—I do not understand this.
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *karpāsa* cloth, when these six knots appear before you, could they be untied simultaneously?
Could they all be removed at once? "No, World-Honored One. "These knots were originally tied in succession; today they must be untied in succession.
Although the six knots share the same substance, the knots themselves were not tied at the same time. Therefore, when they are untied, how could they be removed simultaneously? The Buddha said:
He said: "The untying of the six faculties is likewise so;
this clarifies that there is a sequential order to their liberation. "Ānanda, I now ask you: these six knots in the cloth appear before you."
"I shall untie its entanglements all at once; can they be removed simultaneously as my hand touches them, rather than requiring a sequential process?
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. These knots were originally formed by tying one through six, arising sequentially."
I now wish to explain this. It must also proceed from one to six, resolving them in successive order. Why?

Although the six knots share the same substance as the cloth, the tying of the knots did not originally occur simultaneously; therefore, the Buddha’s statement that they may be removed all at once is impossible.

The Buddha said: "The liberation of the six sense faculties is likewise so. Although the knots of the six faculties do not necessarily follow the sequence of eyes first, ears second, nose third, tongue fourth, and so on, within each of the six faculties there exists, individually, the characteristic of sixfold knots."
Thus, there has never been a lack of sequential order. Since there is indeed a sequence, would it be possible to seek simultaneous liberation from all knots?
Master Lien said: "The sequence of binding and untying does not mean that after the eye-knot is untied, one next unties the ear-knot, and then the nose-knot.
The six knots cannot be untied all at once; one must necessarily untie them starting with a single sense organ."
Next, the five faculties are liberated spontaneously. The liberation of the six faculties is likewise so. This should be understood as belonging to the preceding section.
From "When this faculty is first liberated" onwards constitutes a distinct point. The above clarifies the sequence of liberating the knots;
the following clarifies the functional capacities obtained through such liberation.

This root is first understood; one first attains the emptiness of persons. When the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, it constitutes liberation from phenomena. Once liberated from phenomena, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise.
This is called a Bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from within samādhi.
To explain this according to its sequence: regarding the binding of the faculties, it proceeds from the derangement of the mind-nature to the arousal of dust through wearying vision;

moving from the subtle toward the coarse, it is established through conformity. As for the liberation of the faculties, one traces back from the arousal of dust through wearying vision to the derangement of the mind-nature;
returning from the coarse to the subtle, it is dissolved through inversion. Therefore, this—

The first stage of understanding the faculties: one first attains the emptiness of persons. This involves forgetting the dust of movement (entering the stream while forgetting the object), which serves to eliminate the sixth knot;

next, one forgets the dust of stillness (neither movement nor stillness arises), which eliminates the fifth knot. This corresponds to the fruit of Srotāpanna. By severing the conceptualization of self-attachment, this is the elimination of the delusions of view.
Next, the faculty of hearing is exhausted (the hearing and that which is heard are both exhausted), which eliminates the fourth knot. This corresponds to...

The latter three fruits involve the severance of innate self-grasping, which refers to the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*). Once the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is realized, personal grasping is eliminated;
thus, the so-called "dusty views" that stir up defilement and all worldly birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are completely exhausted.

From this, emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, resulting in the liberation of phenomena. First, one abandons attachment to wisdom (*jñāna-āsakti*)—that is, realizing that the subject of cognition is empty of the object of cognition—and thereby severs the conceptual grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*), which serves to eliminate the third knot.

Next, one abandons attachment to principle (*tattva-āsakti*)—that is, the extinction of both the emptiness and that which is emptied—and thereby severs the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha-sahaja*), which serves to eliminate the second knot.
This is because, while one may empty the person but not empty phenomena, one has attained only a partial realization of emptiness.
It is not yet perfectly luminous; therefore, it is only at the stage of liberation through dharmas (*dharmavimukti*) that one attains perfect luminosity.
Once attachment to dharmas has been eliminated, what is called the false manifestation of knowledge and vision—both supramundane and mundane *nirvāṇa*—is completely exhausted.

Having thus liberated oneself from dharmas, both are empty and do not arise. By realizing the emptiness of the person (*pudgalanairātmya*), the two types of self-view—the conceptual and the innate—are [eliminated].
Arising. By realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), both the two types of views regarding phenomena—the conceptual and the innate—are extinguished.
Nevertheless, although one realizes the two kinds of emptiness, the marks of those two emptinesses still remain; these are further emptied by means of that very emptiness. Hence it is said:

"Both being empty, they do not arise" (when arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one). This serves to eliminate the first knot. As for what is called the "wild confusion of the mind-nature," both [the subject and object]...
All mountains, rivers, and the great earth, at the mere thought of it, are transformed into supreme awakening; this is precisely the time for that.
When the knots are thus untied, it is called the Bodhisattva’s wondrous cause arising from samādhi, attaining the wondrous fruit of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Abiding within this patience, the Bodhisattva perceives not the arising of even the slightest phenomenon, nor the cessation of even the slightest phenomenon.

Therefore, it is called the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and one enters the stage of "Abiding in the Initial Resolve. As for your question regarding the sequence of loosening the knots, the order is as follows;
yet when the six are untied, the one vanishes, leaving no further residue. Zhong said: "One who attains the emptiness of persons has no attachment to the self;
this breaks the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). When the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation through the Dharma; thus,"

One destroys the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and attains the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). As for "both being empty," it means that both person and phenomena are empty, and even that emptiness itself is empty.

From this state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). This is like clearing turbid water: the sand and silt settle of their own accord. This is what is meant.
Regarding the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena: the six sense faculties constitute the persons and phenomena; within each faculty, there are both the person and the phenomenon.
Grasping is likewise both root and basis; within it lie the two emptinesses of person and phenomena. Although there is a sequence of before and after, such is the natural law (*dharmatā*).
There is no "before and after" within that which is beyond before and after. This is precisely the conclusion regarding the actual resolution of the mind.
It is like a person whose fundamental vital energy (*yuanqi*) was originally injured, manifesting the two symptoms of cold and heat. A fool might then take hot medicine.
Some may take cold-natured medicines, yet none can bring healing. The wise do not use hot-natured medicines, nor do they use cold-natured medicines;

they simply employ medicines that directly support the fundamental vital energy (*mūla-prāṇa*). Then this illness is first healed: the symptoms of heat recede first, and once the heat symptoms are restored to normalcy, the symptoms of cold are also eliminated.
Once both heat and cold have been removed, even the regimen for their regulation is forgotten. This is the nature of the method.
Bondage is like the vital energy being injured. The dual attachments to emptiness and existence are both bound together, like manifesting the two symptoms of cold and heat simultaneously.
The emptiness and existence of the Hīnayāna and Pratyekabuddhas cannot resolve this; it is like a fool taking both cold and hot medicines, neither of which can cure the ailment.
This sutra now causes one not to cling to either emptiness or existence, just as one does not employ either cold or hot [remedies].
These are the two medicines. "Only" means causing the root to revolve and detach from the dust, which is like using only direct medicine to support the primal qi.
When this root is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons; this is like a disease first recovering, where the feverish symptoms are first eliminated.
When the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation from phenomena; this is like the feverish illness being settled, and the cold ailment is also removed. This is liberation.

The Dharma has been concluded. Both are empty and do not arise; it is like when cold and heat have been dispelled, even the remedy is forgotten. [This concludes] the answer regarding the sequence for relaxing the knots.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, attained the perfect penetration of wisdom (i.e., *shijiao*) and awakening (i.e., *benjiao*) through the six sense faculties.
Thus, they attained freedom from doubt. At once, they joined their palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:

“Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have swiftly attained unimpeded understanding. Although we have realized the meaning of the ‘one’ and the ‘six’ being lost, we have yet to reach the fundamental root of perfect penetration.
World-Honored One, we have been adrift and wandering through accumulated kalpas, solitary and exposed. With what heart or what concern could we have anticipated this?”
“O Buddha, our elder brother! We are like infants who have lost their mother’s milk and suddenly encounter a compassionate mother.
If, through this meeting, we achieve the Way, the secret mantras we obtain will be identical to our original realization; they will be no different from what we had not yet heard.

We pray that you will deign to show great compassion and bestow upon us the secret majesty, fulfilling the Tathāgata’s final instruction. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and withdrew.
This is the secret transmission of the Tibetan Esoteric School;
may the Buddha grant his silent empowerment. This is precisely the request for the fundamental root of perfect penetration as the gateway for entering the Flowered Hall.

Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, although they have not yet attained a sudden and complete realization of the principle of wisdom and the perfect penetration of awareness, are in truth...
It was also decisively clear; there was no longer any doubt. Thereupon, they joined their palms, prostrated themselves, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today, because we have awakened to and understood the six liberations, our bodies are unimpeded. Because we have abandoned the one [delusion], our minds are unimpeded."

Although we have realized that the six [senses] are resolved and the one is extinguished, we truly have not yet reached the point of knowing which among the six faculties is the fundamental faculty of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong ben-gen*) that we ought to select and employ.
World-Honored One, we have been adrift and wandering through the various realms of existence since time immemorial;
for countless kalpas, we have been solitary without a teacher to guide us, and exposed without virtue to protect us. What heart could we have?
What need for further deliberation? As the younger brother of the Buddha, sharing the same celestial lineage as him, I suddenly partook of the milk of the Dharma during a time of saṃsāra.

It was like a child who had lost its mother’s milk suddenly encountering a compassionate mother; I rejoiced that this had occurred beyond all expectation. If, moreover, by virtue of this fortunate encounter...
I have attained the fruit of sainthood and do not fail the title of being the Tathāgata’s younger brother.

Although I have now received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the secret words, these remain merely matters of extensive learning and memorization; they are not yet the domain of my own wisdom. I am like one who counts another's treasures;
there has not been even a hair’s breadth of new realization, and in truth, I am no different from when I had not heard them. I only pray that you will bestow upon me your great [compassion].
"O Compassionate One! Bestow upon me the secret and wondrous adornment; fulfill the Tathāgata’s final instruction and his ultimate, complete teaching of compassion.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, then rose and listened in silence, withdrawing into seclusion in the hope of receiving the Buddha’s hidden transmission.
This was because he hoped for the Buddha’s direct pointing to a single gate, so that he might attain profound entry. Thus it is called "the hidden" (*miṅ*).
Regarding the term "bestower" (the one who confers), its meaning implies that it need not necessarily be spoken by the Buddha himself.
This fully reveals the appropriateness of such a great expedient manifestation and the intent behind the mutual encouragement between teacher and disciple.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the Arhats free from outflows within the assembly:
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats, having been born into my Dharma, have attained the state of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa). [Note: Bodhisattvas are also termed 'those beyond learning. Master Zhi said:

'Without giving rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation or study, one is eternally sovereign within the light of formlessness'—this is the clear proof of a Bodhisattva who has reached the stage of no-more-learning. I now ask you: regarding your initial generation of the [Bodhi]mind..."

The mind has awakened to the eighteen realms (the reason the seven elements are not mentioned is that the six objects subsume the first five elements, while the sense organs and consciousnesses subsume the latter two). Which among these constitutes perfect penetration?
By what skillful means does one enter samādhi?
This passage records how the twenty-five sages each recounted their methods of perfect penetration (yuantong) in response to Ānanda’s request.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not speak further himself, but addressed the great Bodhisattvas and great Arhats in the assembly, saying:
"You have all been born within my Dharma and have diligently practiced with arduous effort until you reached the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Now I ask you: from which primary dharma did you first give rise to the bodhicitta?

Among these eighteen realms (*dhātu*), which one did you realize as the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-prativedha*)? By what skillful means did you enter samādhi? You should speak fully and without concealment."
"I shall select and adopt from among them. Question: From this point on, each presents their own method of perfect penetration (*yuantong*).

Are these the same as, or different from, those in the Chan school who enter the Way through seeing forms or hearing sounds? Answer: They are not entirely the same, yet they are also not entirely different.
For those of the Zen school, the point of realization attained in this present life is not necessarily a dharma-gate resulting from gradual cultivation.

For instance, did Lingyun take the peach blossoms as his gate of practice? It was simply that through the intense pressure of investigating the doubt until its power reached its limit, there was a sudden, fleeting breakthrough at the very moment of seeing form.
As for the current methods of contemplating the Four Noble Truths, impurity, or the analogy of tasting medicine, [they are likewise not the ultimate path].
For the most part, these are the dharma-gates practiced through long-term cultivation until realization is attained. If this were the case, I would not dare say they are identical.
Nevertheless, those in the Chan school also have distinct causes and conditions; a master with true insight can foresee them in advance.

For instance, if one’s affinity lies in the realm of sound, one will certainly not attain awakening through the realm of form—and this applies even to persons, scriptures, staffs, shouts, and spoken words.
And so forth; each is fixed and must not be confused. If one traces it back to the past, it is perhaps due to the force of long-standing habituation.
Otherwise, how could the master have known this in advance? If this is so, then [the master] is no different from the various sages.
