I also do not yet dare to say there is any difference. Only those such as Xiangyan and Upasanta, who attained awakening through scent and touch respectively, seem to have experienced a sudden, instantaneous event;
thus, it is similar to the "awakening in this very life" found in the Chan school. Let the wise examine this.
○ Zhong’s Commentary states: "Regarding the places where the twenty-five sages realized perfect penetration, every single instance they brought forth was [the Way]."
All of them are so. As for the point where one applies the eye and hand, one does not know from where to awaken and enter, nor from where to break through.

Without waiting until after the realization of the fruit, one has already attained the ultimate perfect penetration at the very stage of the cause. This single school of the Chan Gate is clearly what the various elders have brought forth.
Furthermore, it is said: "By merely mentioning the eighteen [dhātus], the seven are already subsumed. Therefore, it was previously stated: "Ten..."
When the Tathāgata practices each of the eighteen realms one by one, he attains the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi.
Furthermore, these eighteen are merely the six faculties; when each faculty is divided into the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness, they are simply referred to as the six.

The meaning of this is also comprehensive. Therefore, the preceding text states: "That which causes you to revolve in the wheel of birth and death, and that which brings about blissful, wondrous permanence—these are equally the six sense faculties; they are not other things."
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya (which means "Fire-Weapon" in this context), immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"While we were at the Deer Park and at the Cock Garden (both of which were formerly sites where ancient emperors raised livestock), we witnessed the Tathāgata first attain the Way."
Through the Buddha’s voice, I awakened to and clearly realized the Four Noble Truths.

When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "I am the first to declare understanding," the Tathāgata certified me, naming me Ājñāta (which means "understood"). The wondrous sound is subtle and perfect; through this sound, I attained arhatship.
When the Buddha asks about the most perfect penetration, according to my realization, the sense of sound is supreme.

This was the realization through the sensory object of sound. At that time, the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, we abandoned the Buddha and practiced our respective paths in the Deer Park and the Cock’s Garden.
Yet, as soon as the Buddha attained enlightenment, he came first to deliver us. Therefore, we perceive that the Tathāgata was our very first [disciple]."
Upon attaining enlightenment, the Buddha turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for us three times, relying entirely upon vocal sound.

That we ourselves realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths was likewise dependent upon vocal sound. When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Who has attained realization? I alone was the first to understand and awaken.

Therefore, the Tathāgata has used the name "Understanding" to certify me. Furthermore, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.
When the Four Noble Truths were being taught, those Śrāvakas of true practice only grasped the principle of arising and ceasing;
yet that wondrous sound was secretly perfect, penetrating through to the Unconditioned Four Noble Truths. Only I secretly developed a profound understanding and realized it.
The perfect and true principle is to awaken to and enter the soundless samādhi through sound itself, thereby attaining the Mahāyāna arhatship.
Now, as the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is supreme. This is the true essence of the teaching in this land:
its purity lies in hearing sounds. Therefore, the compilers of the sutras take Dignāga as the beginning and Avalokiteśvara as the end.
The "wondrous sound of the Tathāgatagarbha" refers to the esoteric and perfect reality of sound; "esoteric awakening" means the realization of the perfect principle.
The "Four Truths" are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Upānanda (which is translated here as "near-little" or "the nature of form," meaning that atoms are a minute portion of form) immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I too, when observing the Buddha’s initial attainment of enlightenment, contemplated the signs of impurity and gave rise to great revulsion.
I realized the nature of all forms, seeing how they proceed from impure white bones and subtle atoms back to empty space; thus, both emptiness and form..."
The two absences constitute the path of no-more-learning. The Tathāgata has certified me, naming me Vimalacitra. Since the dust of form was purified, wondrous form became subtle and perfect.
Through these characteristics of form, I attained arhatship. When the Buddha asks about the most perfect penetration, according to my realization, the causal factor of form is supreme.
This is the entry into awakening by means of the sense-object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*). Upānanda (and so forth) said to the Buddha:
"I too observed that when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he was afflicted by much desire; the Buddha then instructed him to practice the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) to remedy it."
Contemplate this body: within it are thirty-six impurities; externally, there are nine orifices from which foul secretions constantly flow.
From birth until death, not a single part is pure. As the wholesome mind turns into an unwholesome mind, one gives rise to great weary detachment and awakens to the nature of all forms.
Beginning with impurity, they return to white bones and subtle dust; ultimately, they are empty. Taking form as...
Illness. Taking emptiness as the medicine, once one returns to emptiness, the illness is cured and the medicine is discarded.

When both emptiness and form are non-existent, one suddenly realizes entry [into the truth] and achieves the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). The Tathāgata seals me, saying that this is precisely the nature of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Thereupon, characteristics are exhausted and the nature manifests;
I universally observe that all forms are the Buddha’s form, and that they are all the Tathāgatagarbha mind, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The *dhātu* (element) is subtle and perfectly round; therefore, through the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), I attained Arhatship.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the cause of form is supreme. For while all Buddhist teachings arise from causes and conditions, I have used form as the cause for entering into perfection.
As for the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*): first, the notion of bloatedness (*vyādhmātaka-saṃjñā*); second, the notion of the livid (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*); third...
1. The perception of decay; 2. The perception of being smeared with blood; 3. The perception of festering pus; 4. The perception of being devoured by worms; 5. The perception of scattering;
6. The perception of bones; 7. The perception of burning.
The youth Fragrance-Veneration (Gandhabhūti) immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to contemplate thoroughly the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion and pure fasting.
I saw bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was serene as it entered my nostrils. I contemplated this scent: it is neither wood nor empty space.”
It was neither smoke nor fire; it departed without attachment and arrived from nowhere. Thereby my conceptual mind dissolved, and I realized the outflow-free state.

The Tathāgata certified me and I received the name "Aromatic Purity. Mundane odors suddenly vanished, and a wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive. From this, I attained the stage of Aromatic Purity.

I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied: "As I have realized it, the sense of fragrance is supreme" (he was named Xiangyan because he adorned the Dharma-body with wondrous fragrances).
This is the entry into awakening through the sense-object of fragrance. The youth Aromatic Rigidity (Gandharvaśrī) said to the Buddha:

"In the past, I received instruction from the Tathāgata to carefully contemplate, in all places, the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena, such as the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses."
At that time, I took my leave of the Buddha and sat in quiet seclusion. Within my pure chamber, I perceived only the bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense;
its fragrance was serene as it entered my nostrils. Now, fragrance is but one phenomenon among conditioned things. I then observed this scent closely:
it was not the wood itself, yet it did not emerge from the wood alone; nor was it the smoke or the fire.
It does not emerge from another; it is not a combination. It does not emerge from a collection; it is not emptiness. It does not emerge from no cause; all four natures are absent.
Gathering and dispersing in an instant, it departs without attachment. Interrupted or continuous, it comes from nowhere.
Through this, the mind dissolves, one enters non-discrimination, and the untainted (anāsrava) is revealed. One penetrates the blazing [of reality].
The substance of incense is, in itself, the Tathāgata-garbha mind; therefore, the Tathāgata sealed me with the name "Incense-Veneration" (Gandhavimala).
From this point on, appearances were exhausted and the fundamental nature manifested; the sensory breaths of dust suddenly vanished, and the wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive.

All fragrances are, in truth, the fragrance of the Dharma-body. Through Incense-Veneration, I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the senses], this is what I have realized: Incense-Veneration.
This is the highest. This closely resembles the point of awakening in the Chan (Zongmen) tradition, yet it still relies heavily on conceptual discrimination;

the Chan school would likely not be like this. However, after awakening, although the vision of the Truth (Dharma-realm) is the same for those in the Chan school, the depth of their realization varies according to their past roots and cannot be fixed. These various sages likewise see through to the hidden mind (cittaprakṛti).
There is no difference. However, the stage of realization for those at the initial resolve is certainly fixed at the seventh stage of faith or above, extending through the first dwelling (*āśraya*).

In this respect, their realization is also the same. Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of them as being identical in the stage of perfect penetration (*pariṇata*). Hereafter, all cases shall follow this principle.

The two Dharma-Prince sons, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, together with five hundred Brahmās in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Throughout kalpas beginningless, we have served as skilled physicians for the world. We have tasted the plants, trees, grasses, metals, and stones of this Sahā world with our own mouths;
there are a total of one hundred and eight thousand names and species, all of which we know thoroughly."
Whether bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, or pungent; whether combined with other substances, innate, or transformed; whether cold or hot;

and whether toxic or non-toxic—all such tastes he fully knows. Serving the Tathāgata, he thoroughly understands that the nature of taste is neither empty nor existent, neither identical to the body and mind nor separate from the body and mind.
By discerning the causes of taste, he attains awakening through the grace of the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
I seal the names of my brothers, the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. They are now Dharma Princes within this assembly;

through the awakening to clarity via flavor, they have attained the rank of Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, that which I have realized is that the cause of flavor is supreme.
This is the entry into awakening through the sense-object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*). The two Dharma-Princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, (and so forth), addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since beginningless kalpas, we have served as skilled physicians for the world. We have tasted all the flavors of this world with our own mouths;
their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand. We fully know the flavor of the five fundamental tastes, as well as that which is flavorless."
Whether it be the blandness that forms a harmonious blend with various flavors, or the innate properties of ingredients used as they are,
or the transformations resulting from processing such as refining, roasting, or steaming— whether they are cold or hot, toxic or non-toxic— he is able to know them all thoroughly.
Serving the Tathāgata, he did not forget his past cultivation. He immediately observed from the locus of taste and thoroughly understood the nature of flavor.
When the tongue and the medicine touch, the flavor manifests intensely; therefore, it is not empty. Although it manifests upon contact with the tongue, it actually lacks any form or characteristic;
therefore, it is not existent. The tongue is the body, and the tongue-consciousness is the mind. If the various medicines do not come, then the tongue and the consciousness—

Since bitterness and the other flavors do not manifest of themselves, they are not identical to the body and mind. Yet, since the gustatory consciousness does not taste them, how could the various medicines manifest bitterness and the rest on their own?

Therefore, they are not separate from the body and mind. When one investigates the causes of flavor one by one, tracing back where these flavors originate, one suddenly awakens to the realization that all intense flavors have never, from the very beginning, arisen from the medicines nor from the body.
The mind is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness.

Having been blessed by the Buddha-Tathāgata, who bestowed upon my brothers the names of the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, it is because the Tathāgata has served as our guide throughout kalpas of dust-like eons that he thus seals us.
Therefore, we are now Dharma Princes within this assembly; yet, regarding the time of our initial awakening, it was solely due to the flavor [of the teaching].
Awakened clarity: the storehouse mind opens to enlightenment, leading to the attainment of the rank of Bodhisattva. Although this is a high realization, its original name is not changed.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the cause of flavor is supreme.
Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, we heard the Dharma and left the household life. At the time when the monks were bathing,"

Following the custom, he entered the room. Suddenly, he awakened to the cause of water: since it neither washes away dust nor washes the body itself, there is peace and security in the interval, and one attains the state of non-possession.
Without forgetting his former training, this has continued until the present day; he left the household life under the Buddha and attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
That Buddha was named Bhadrapāla (also translated as Xiànshǒu or Xiànhù). Through the manifestation of clarity via wondrous touch, he attained the station of a Buddha’s son.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I testified that, according to my realization, the sense-base of touch is supreme.
This is the entry into awakening through the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). Bhadrapāla and his companions (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the past, during the time of the Buddha Majestic Sound King (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja*), we heard the Dharma and left the household life. We encountered a situation while accompanying the monks for a bath;
suddenly, we awakened to the cause of water. At the moment of bathing, as our bodies touched the water and the water touched our bodies, there was a blazing intensity between them."
The sensations of cold and warmth manifest. Thus, one must investigate from what cause these sensations arise.

If you say they exist because of washing away dust and impurities, then since dust is fundamentally insentient, how could it manifest sensation? Therefore, the manifestation of sensation does not depend on washing away dust.
If you say they exist because of washing the conscious essence of the *indriya* (the sensory faculty), then as for that consciousness...
The substance of this body cannot be defiled by washing; nor does it manifest through contact merely because the body has been washed.
When one investigates the dust and investigates the substance, they find themselves at ease and autonomous in the space between the two pillars, attaining a state of non-existence.

Upon realizing that this sense-object of touch has no place from which it comes, one awakens to and enters the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā). Thus, even during the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, one had already attained the vision of the Truths.
Now, following the Buddha’s transformation, I have attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). What was formerly my initial resolve is now realized as a profound station.
That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla. From this single touch, every place of contact becomes a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and everything seen is *bodhi*.

Through the clarity proclaimed by wondrous touch, I have realized the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the faculties, according to what I have realized, the faculty of touch is the cause.

Above. ○ Regarding "the cause of water": this means that water serves as the cause for awakening through guidance. In this section, one must not become confused regarding the discussion of "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*).

For contact is an object (*viṣaya*); it is the characteristic mark when the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) comes into conjunction with the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), and one perceives therein cold, warmth, roughness, or smoothness.
○ Master [Fazhao] said: "The two characters 'object' (*viṣaya*) and 'substance' (*bhāva*) have been explained in various ways by many scholars..."
First: there is no need for deep analysis; it is simply a matter of emphasizing the cause of awakening to water. Does this water wash away dust? Dust has no inherent substance of its own;

what dust could possibly be washed away? Does this water wash away the physical body? The body belongs to the four great elements, and these four great elements are fundamentally empty. What body could possibly be washed?
Since external dust and the internal body are both non-existent, how can there be anything in between? Thus, who is there to be washed by the water?
Now, as for the meaning of "contact" (*sparśa*): it is named through the interaction between water and the self.
Since both are now absent, where can the fruit of contact reside? Without contact yet called "contact," contact is in truth no-contact. It is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous.
This is the wondrous true suchness-nature of the original Tathāgatagarbha; hence it is said that "wondrous contact proclaims clarity.
Nevertheless, this is still an intellectual interpretation. To take this as awakening is not yet sufficient; it is not yet sufficient.
Mahākāśyapa (the Great Kāśyapa of Radiant Light), the Bhikṣuṇī Suvarṇaprabhāsā, and others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.
I had the opportunity to draw near to him, hear his Dharma, and practice its teachings. After that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics and lit lamps."

Continuing with brightness, she applied purple-gold light to the forms and images of the Buddhas. From that time forth, in life after life and birth after birth, her body has always been perfectly full as a mass of purple-gold light.
These bhikṣuṇīs of purple-gold light and the others were my own kinsmen; they resolved their minds for enlightenment at the same time as I.

I observe that the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) in the world undergo transformation and decay (the object of the Dharma being the general category and the preceding five being the specific ones; this is because one observes the shadows left by the falling away of the first five objects, encompassing both the general and the specific).

Yet it is called "six" because it is solely through emptiness and stillness that one cultivates cessation; thus, body and mind can traverse hundreds of thousands of kalpas as if in the snap of a finger.

(This is evidenced by the fact that he now wears the golden-threaded *kaṣāya* and has entered meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda, awaiting the descent of Maitreya. Through the dharma of emptiness, I have attained the state of an Arhat;

the World-Honored One declared me the foremost among those who practice *dhūta*. (*Dhūta* means "shaking off," for it is able to shake off the dust of dharmas. Thus, the wondrous Dharma was opened and clarified.

I have extinguished all outflows (*āsrava*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied that, according to what I have realized, the faculty of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is supreme;
this is because I attained awakening through the sense-object of phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*). Mahākāśyapa [and so forth] addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In a past kalpa, I encountered the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa. I heard his Dharma and practiced it accordingly. After that Buddha had passed into extinction, I..."
They made offerings to the śarīra and lit lamps to perpetuate the light; they constantly used purple-gold to coat the images of the Buddha.
Because of these two kinds of superior causes, they have attained bodies of purple-gold radiance throughout successive kalpas, baring their shoulders and swallowing the sun.
These Bhikṣuṇīs of Purple-Gold Light and others are my kinsmen; they have made the vow to attain enlightenment at the same time as I.
Since the mind is thus, the radiance of the body is likewise. I observe that the six sense objects, both general and specific, appear momentarily based upon the mental consciousness;

they arise and perish from moment to moment and thought to thought. Loathing this transformation and decay, I further cultivate the contemplation of emptiness and enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This absorption can extinguish the faculty of the mind and the objects of dharmas. When the concentration is profound, body and mind remain unmoving.
I forgot both place and time; what was exceedingly long seemed as brief as a moment. Passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas felt like the snap of a finger.

By means of the dharma of emptiness, I contemplated and shattered the dust of dharmas (*dharmarajas*). When appearances were exhausted and nature manifested, I awakened to and entered the *garbha-citta*, attaining the state of an Arhat.
Because I was able to shake off the dust of dharmas, the World-Honored One declared me the foremost among those who practice *dhūta*. It is simply because I am not bound by the dust.
Therefore, the six sense objects are all wondrous and pervade all places; every single thing is a path of entry. Every movement and action is nothing other than Buddha-work.
Whether flowers fly or bracelets jingle, these are all occasions for settling the spirit. When the Dharma-melting merges with the hidden mind, the wondrous clarity unfolds.
Once the hidden mind has entered, there is forever no further falling away; thus, all outflows are extinguished—this is the fruition of the fruit.

The Buddha asked about perfect penetration. According to what I have realized, the *dharmadhātu* (the causal nature of phenomena) is supreme. [End of the section on the perfect penetration of the six sense objects.
From here below, the perfect penetration of the five sense faculties is presented. As for those who lack one of the six faculties, the faculty of hearing is retained as the final stronghold.

Therefore, in accordance with the capacities of those in this region, I have examined the five faculties in detail. Among the four [faculties], each contains the characters "revolve" (xuán) and "return" (fǎn).

This is because the dharma-gate of the faculties is fundamentally the principle of revolving the faculties to detach from sense objects; this is not the case for sense objects or consciousnesses, which can be seen by careful examination.

Aniruddha (which means "Free from Poverty" or "As One Wishes"; he was the son of King Śuklodana and the Buddha’s cousin), having in the past offered a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha, was moved by that merit to experience wish-fulfilling bliss for ninety-one kalpas.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep.

The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying I was of the same class as animals: 'Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster; you may sleep for a thousand years, yet you shall not hear the Buddha's teaching.'"
[Name: Having heard the Buddha’s reproach, I wept and reproached myself. For seven days I did not sleep, and I lost both my eyes.

The World-Honored One showed me the Samādhi of the Vajra of Delightful Vision (i.e., turning vision back to see and forgetting objects), the Illumination (i.e., manifesting the original luminous brilliance). This is the Vajra Samādhi (the celestial eye appears before one like a vajra;

it is firm and indestructible, unlike the physical eye which is easily destroyed). It is not by means of the eyes that I perceive the ten directions; the essential reality is transparently clear (i.e., the Tathāgatagarbha).

The mind gives rise to its fundamental luminosity, and the eye of the mind opens wide; it is as if observing fruit in the palm of one's hand. The Tathāgata has sealed me, and I have attained Arhatship.

Since the Buddha has revealed the source, all that is cultivated and realized is perfectly complete. When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, to revolve the seeing and return to the source—this is the foremost method.
This is the entry into realization through the faculty of the eye. Aniruddha (and so forth) lost both his eyes;
fortunately, the World-Honored One showed me the Samādhi of Illumination for Joyful Vision and the Vajra Samādhi. This is entirely the practice of turning back the vision to see one's own nature.
By cultivating this samādhi, one attains the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), exchanging [the physical eye] for a cluster of grapes.
The celestial eye: herein, this clarity does not follow the sense organs; though it relies upon the organs to manifest, it does not depend on the physical eye.

One perceives a single Buddha-world with such refined truth and penetrating lucidity that it is as if looking at a fruit in the palm of one's hand. This stage is equal to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

As one gradually increases [in realization] until all that can be seen is fully perceived, the stage is equal to the seventh level of faith (*śraddhā*) and the four fruits. Therefore, the Tathāgata has certified me, and I have attained [this realization].
The Arhat said: "When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the Way, according to what I have realized: I reverse the function of seeing to perceive the nature of seeing;

this is called 'revolving the seeing. I do not follow after sensory objects but follow the sense-organ; this is called 'following the source. Revolving the seeing and following the source—this is simply the foremost expedient means.
"Delighting in the Illumination of Seeing" is roughly similar to the practice of the "Sun Contemplation" in the cultivation of the Pure Land. It involves the eyes...
Although it is not seen, one desires to see it with the mind and eyes; through the culmination of this desire to see, one suddenly attains illuminating clarity.
Because it is neither lost nor destroyed, it is named "Vajra."

Cūḍapanthaka (translated here as "Successor of the Path," also known as "Snake-Slave," and who was the bhikṣu who recited the broom) immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and paid homage.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "I lack the capacity for recitation and retention, and do not possess the nature of great learning. Having first encountered the Buddha, I heard the Dharma and went forth into homelessness;

yet, though I sought to remember and uphold a single verse of the Tathāgata, for a hundred days I was unable to retain what came before while forgetting what followed, or to retain what came after while forgetting what preceded it."
The Buddha took pity on my folly and instructed me to dwell in *anāgārika* (the rainy season retreat) and to regulate the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

At that time, as I observed the breath—its subtlety (subtle when concentration is attained), its exhaustion (exhausted when concentration is deep), its arising (*jāti*), its abiding (*sthiti*), its alteration (*anyathātva*), and its cessation (*nirodha*)—I perceived these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
My mind suddenly opened wide, attaining great unimpededness, until finally, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I achieved [Arhatship].
The Arhat, dwelling beneath the Buddha’s seat, was certified as one beyond training. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, he replied:
"According to what I have realized, by reversing the flow of breath and following emptiness, this is the foremost."
This was the entry through the faculty of the nose. Cūḍapanthaka (and so forth) said to the Buddha:

"In the past, I was a great Dharma teacher who was secretive and stingy regarding the Buddha-dharma; I refused to teach others and thus received the retribution of being dull-witted and lacking the capacity for retention.
Yet, due to my past roots of goodness, I first encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and went forth as a monk."
The Tathāgata took the two characters for "broom" (*tiáo* and *zhǒu*) and made them into a single verse-line for me to memorize.
For one hundred days, I managed to remember "tiáo" but forgot "zhǒu," and remembered "zhǒu" but forgot "tiáo. The Buddha then took pity on me and said, "This person is foolish.
Although the distant cause lies in fundamental dullness, the proximate condition also stems from mental confusion. He then established a skillful means for me.
He instructed me in *śamatha* (tranquil abiding): "Sit upright and count your breaths. Initially, as the counting gradually harmonized, the mind and the breath became mutually dependent.

As the mind grew increasingly subtle, the breath likewise became increasingly fine. I then silently turned my gaze inward; within that state of subtle breathing, I further investigated its arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
I even pushed my inquiry to the point where I realized that a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) is further composed of ninety *kṣaṇas*. One...
In each instant, there are further nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing. When such focused effort has continued for a long time, it is like a single bean exploding within cold ashes;
one then attains the simultaneous forgetting of mind and breath, suddenly becoming vast and unimpeded.
This is what is called "when a single breath does not remain, the Way comes to meet you. From this point on, outflows are exhausted and one becomes an Arhat, dwelling in the state of a Buddha.

Seated beneath him, I attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), according to what I have realized, it was simply by tracing back the movement of the breath to its most subtle point until it also returned to emptiness. What I call "perfect penetration" is this; it is the foremost.
There is simply nothing further to be added. In the past, the Minister Mo Jiang went to visit Chan Master Nantang Jing to inquire about the essentials for resolving his mind.

The Master instructed him to maintain a state of intense mindfulness (*tisi*) at all times. Once, while entering the latrine, Mo Jiang smelled a foul odor and hurriedly covered his nose with his hand;
at that moment, he attained realization. He then presented this verse: "From the beginning, my natural grace has always loved elegance; I have often laughed at the passing moments..."
People seek outwardly; though there are myriad distinctions and a thousand differences, there is no place to find it. What is attained is originally at the tip of one's own nose.
This, too, is from the side of the breath, yet it strikes away even the nostrils. ○ Regulating the breath (*ānāpāna*) and counting the breath (*gaṇanā*) are different.
In the Tiantai *Zhi Guan*, "regulating the breath" means to be free from wind, gasping, and so forth, remaining subtle, continuous, and sovereign. Counting is not [the same].
"Counting the breaths; when the counting becomes dualistic, it leads to illness.
Then Kauṇḍinya (translated here as "Ox-chewer") rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have a karmic affliction of the mouth. In past kalpas, I habitually mocked śramaṇas, and consequently, in life after life, I have suffered from this ox-chewing ailment. O Tathāgata..."

"Show me the Dharma-gate of the single-flavor pure mind-ground. (He was given a rosary and instructed to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. I attained the cessation of the mind and entered *samādhi*.

I contemplated that the awareness of flavor is neither a substance nor a thing. Instantly, I transcended all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally, I was liberated from body and mind; externally, I cast off the world.
I distanced myself from the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) like a bird escaping its cage. Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, my Dharma-eye opened.

"Purity" (where conceptualization and signs are the dust and the conscious mind is the defilement; when both are distanced, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright—this is precisely that meaning).

You shall become an Arhat, personally certified by the Tathāgata as having entered the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, that which I have realized is this: returning to the flavor and revolving the faculty of cognition—this is the foremost.
This is the entry through the faculty of the tongue. Ghoṣila (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, because I saw an old monk who had no teeth while eating and laughed at him for resembling an ox, I have been reborn with an ox's tongue in life after life.
My experience has been like that of an ox's empty chewing; such is the retribution for frivolous mockery. Fortunately, I have now encountered the Tathāgata."
Please prevent me from falling into slander. Grant me a rosary so that I may recite the Buddha’s name, severing all miscellaneous conditions and maintaining a single-minded, pure mindfulness.

This is the Dharma-gate of the one-flavored, pure mind-ground. Having instructed me to cease distraction and enter stillness, I was thus able to extinguish the mind and first enter the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, having instructed me to arise from stillness and bring forth illumination, I was thus able to perform observation.
In tasting flavor, one knows its nature; it does not arise from the substance of the sense organ, nor does it arise from the substance of the object.

This is because external flavor does not come to the organ, and the organ does not taste by itself; therefore, it is not the substance. The tongue does not perceive through contact, and the object does not taste itself; therefore, it is not the object.
Being neither substance nor object, in the space of a single thought, one suddenly awakens and enters [realization]: that this is fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, transcending all at once.
All outflows [āsrava] vanish like frost at sunrise. Thereupon, one is inwardly liberated from body and mind; the faculties are released and fetters untied.
Outwardly, one leaves behind the world and transcends the vessel-world [bhājana-loka]. Realizing that the three realms of existence are fundamentally empty, one distances oneself from them.

No longer are there any dependencies or afflictive entanglements. Like a bird escaping its cage, there is no obstruction wherever one goes. Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, the Dharma-eye is pure and clear. Thus it is.

Nevertheless, having perfected faith and entered the stage of abiding, one becomes an Arhat. Sealed personally by the Tathāgata, one ascends to the path of no-more-learning; this is not the same as the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized: I returned the flavor and turned back the faculty of cognition. While flavors are manifold, the cognition is of but one kind.
By reflecting inwardly upon the nature of tasting, I awakened to and entered the storehouse mind (*ālaya-citta*). This is the foremost method.

Pilingavatsa (which means "residual habit"; it refers to one who possesses the habitual tendencies of former nobility, such as when he insulted a river deity by calling her a slave) immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I followed the Buddha to enter the Path. I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the various things in the world that are not to be relished.
While begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gate (the Dharma-gate being the Truth of Suffering), and I did not notice the road."
Poisoned, he pierced his foot, and his entire body was in pain. I remained mindful and aware, cognizing this deep agony;

though I perceived the perception of pain, I perceived the pure mind, which is free from the perception of pain. I further reflected: "How could there be two simultaneous perceptions within this single body?
Before long, having restrained my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty. Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted, and I attained the state of an Arhat.

Han: Having obtained the seal of personal certification and realized the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), when the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I testified that "pure awakening leaving the body behind" is the foremost.
This is the realization through the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Pindola Bharadvāja said to the Buddha (as related at length):

"When I first resolved my mind and left home under the Buddha, I frequently heard the Tathāgata preach the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) among the Four Noble Truths—such as the three sufferings, the four sufferings, the eight sufferings, and so forth.
Shortly thereafter, while begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating this Dharma-gate of the Truth of Suffering. It did not [cease].
On the path to awakening, I was wounded in the foot by a poisonous thorn. The poison spread through my body, and my entire frame was racked with pain.
As I reflected upon this unpleasant occurrence, I encountered an unpleasant object; it was at that very moment that the thorn was crushed and pecked out.
I reflect that there must first have been a cognition capable of perceiving pain before one could cognize this deep agony. At the precise moment of cognizing this deep agony, I was not pained by it.
He then turned his attention and observed this knower of pain; it was simply the body’s sensation.

He perceived that while there was deep pain, his own fundamental awareness—the essence of the pure mind—was beyond the reach of pain; in reality, there was no pain capable of afflicting this aware mind.
Thus he reflected in detail: at the very moment of actual pain, there is the awareness that knows the pain, yet there is that which the pain cannot reach.
Regarding this awakening: how could there be two awakenings within this single body? Since the body is one, how could there be two awakenings?

It is said that "one" is the true, while "two" is the deluded. Having investigated in this manner, one should collect the mind in a single point, following only the true awakening that is painless and pure, and no longer following the deluded awakening that perceives pain. Thus, one collects the mind.

This is the ultimate state. When truth is pure and delusion is severed, before long, both body and perception are forgotten. Within twenty-one days, the outflowing mind is entirely exhausted, and the nature of the storehouse consciousness manifests before one.
Thus, desire and ignorance become utterly unattainable. One’s rank equals that of the four fruits and the seven stages of faith;
one becomes an Arhat, receives the seal of personal certification, and realizes the stage of No-More-Learning, being perfectly like one whose faith is fulfilled.

I have entered and taken up residence. When the Buddha asked about the penetration of perfect enlightenment (*yuan-tong*), as I have realized it, there is only the single, perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening;
there is no further bodily form. This is the foremost. In the Zen school, one such as Linji was struck with the staff three times after being questioned three times.
Only those who can cast off the body through pure awakening may enter from the point of pain. Zhong said: "Wood and stone."
Because there is no cognition, whether one is cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, one perceives nothing at all. Because I possess cognition, I am aware of this pain.
Since the body is empty, there is no one who experiences pain; since the mind is empty, there is no one who perceives the pain.
"Pure awareness remains while the body is discarded"—when both body and mind are discarded, the mention of "mind" alone is for the sake of brevity.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind has been free from obstruction.
I recall my births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; from the very moment I was first in my mother’s womb, I knew emptiness and stillness.
Thus it continued until the ten directions became empty, and I also enabled sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness, having received the illumination of the Tathāgata.”

The nature of awareness is true emptiness; the emptiness of nature is perfectly luminous. Having attained arhatship, one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like clarity and emptiness, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and is sealed as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Liberated into the emptiness of nature, I am supreme. Thus, when the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, [I spoke thus].
"As I have realized it: all marks enter into non-being; where there is no 'non-being,' even that is exhausted. Turning back from phenomena to return to nothingness—this is the foremost.
This is the entry through awakening by means of the mental faculty. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since the distant kalpas of the past, I have already realized the nature of emptiness and attained unimpeded mind. I am free from the obscurity of the intermediate state between deaths and the delusion upon emerging from the womb. Since [then]... [he said].

Recalling his births, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he realized from the very moment he was in his mother’s womb that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all empty and that the substance of birth is utterly unattainable;
this is the emptiness of the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*). Beyond his mother’s body, extending to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, all are equally empty and quiescent;
this is the emptiness of the environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*). This still belongs to the category of self-emptiness (*ātmaśūnyatā*).
Upon emerging from the womb, you will extensively transform sentient beings so that they together realize the principle of emptiness and each attains the nature of emptiness;

thus, you will be fully endowed with the two benefits. Such was your past cause. Furthermore, you have been graced by the Tathāgata’s revelation of the principle that the nature of awakening is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awakening. You now know that this nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous and pure by nature.

Nevertheless, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. By realizing this awakening, one attains arhatship and suddenly enters the precious, luminous ocean of emptiness of the Tathāgata, walking hand-in-hand with the Tathāgata;
this is precisely what it means to be quiescently identical to the Buddha.
Furthermore, one attains the same knowledge and vision as the Buddha, as previously fully manifested in the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), namely, the "Great Light of Wisdom. This then—
My illumination is identical to that of the Buddha. Thereupon, the Tathāgata conferred his seal of approval upon me, establishing me in this state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Both person and phenomena are empty; all is liberated. The principle of emptiness thus realized is the one true, primordially existing nature-body of true emptiness that is not empty.

Having exhausted the principle of emptiness, there is nothing further to be added. When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], as for what I have realized, it is from myself...
The mark of the person, the mark of a sentient being, the mark of a life-span, as well as the mark of dharmas—all enter into the non-marked.
Thus, both the negation and that which is negated are exhausted. First, by means of emptiness, one empties all marks; thus, both the person and dharmas are empty.

Next, by means of emptiness, one empties the mark of emptiness itself; thus, both the medicine and the disease are removed. One merely turns this mind-dharma (that is, the cognitive nature within the faculty of thought).
It is not an object of sensory perception; it returns to ultimate emptiness. This is the foremost:

that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and entirely empty—this is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. [In another sutra] it clarifies that Subhūti was, in the past, the Tathāgata Blue Dragon.
Observing this, he spoke of his own profound mind without further concealment, even before the great beings of the Ten Stages. Furthermore...

What is there to regret? Yet, the traditional commentaries all treat this as a classification of the Hīnayāna; thus they suppress the profound and elevate the shallow, thereby defying the Buddha’s words and misrepresenting the Sage in many ways.
[This concludes the section on] the five faculties and the realm of perfect penetration.
The following section sets forth the perfect penetration of the six consciousnesses. Now, at the beginning of the Sutra, the mind of consciousness was interrogated and refuted;

it was condemned as the root of birth and death, and it was stated that sentient beings mistakenly identify with it, thereby needlessly entering the cycle of saṃsāra. Even those of the provisional and lesser vehicles rely upon its cultivation yet ultimately achieve no real fruit.
How, then, can it now be said to enter perfect penetration? This has already been clarified in the previous discussion on the pervasiveness of the element of consciousness.

Now I shall restate this: although consciousness is a reflection of the sensory objects and is the height of delusion, it has no separate self-nature apart from the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the One True Mind.
It is like a reflection in water; though utterly illusory, it has no separate self-nature apart from the water.

Only those who are deluded and attached perceive the reflection as real and forget the source, thereby creating the cycle of transmigration through arbitrary clinging—just as a foolish person mistakes a reflection for reality.
Forgetting the water, one may mistakenly suffer drowning; the stakes are no small matter, and thus one cannot help but issue this warning.

If you awaken, then consciousness itself is the truth, and since consciousness is not apart from the truth, why doubt its perfect penetration? It is like a wise person who observes a reflection and knows it is water;
yet the reflection is not separate from the water, and one can still obtain the utility of water—how could one then suffer drowning? Therefore:

These six sages, along with Maitreya who follows them, were all able to perceive reality immediately upon recognizing it; thus, they all realized the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) without obstruction. Question:
Why do you not cause people to perceive reality immediately upon recognition, but instead necessarily teach them to enter through the sense faculties?
Answer: A verse states: "The nature of the sages is such that there is nothing they do not penetrate; whether following the natural order or acting in reverse, both are skillful means. First...

The mind enters right concentration; their speed differs according to their kind. This is precisely because sense objects and consciousness are all slow, whereas the faculties alone are the most rapid.

It is like the disparagement of the two vehicles: it is not that they will ultimately fail to become Buddhas, but rather that the kalpas required pass through points as numerous as dust motes, making them the ultimate in slowness.
Therefore, beginners are cautioned not to give rise to such [limited] minds. Furthermore, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body...
The five consciousnesses somewhat resemble the nature of non-conceptual faculties; thus, they are conflated with the first five sense-faculties.

Furthermore, their subsequent conceptualization somewhat resembles the deliberative function of the mental consciousness; thus, they are conflated with the subsequent mental consciousness. Such is the case for the Śrāvakas who are ignorant of the Dharma.
There are none who do not become deluded by this; it must be discerned. Now, I shall briefly clarify the characteristics of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*);
the other four may be understood by analogy. For example, when the eye reflects in a mirror, there is not a single moment of movement. It is simply as within the mirror, without further analysis.

This is the seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*) of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Within that, the eyes range over [the image], observing black and white, large and small, much and little, good and—

The natures of the unwholesome and so forth are distinct and unmixed; when they are not associated with verbal designations (*nāma-pada*) and are roughly discriminated in accordance with recollection, this is visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
From this point, by means of sequential indication and analytical investigation, there arise immeasurable distinctions;

this pervasive grasping of verbal designations and conceptual construction is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) concomitant with the eye. Now, we shall take only the second, visual consciousness.
However, one must not allow the faculties (*indriya*) and the nature of the mind (*citta*) to become confused or conflated.
Thus, students of the Nature School (*xìngzōng*) should not neglect the Dharma Characteristics (*fǎxiàng*).
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since the beginningless kalpas, my mental vision (i.e., visual consciousness) has been pure. I have taken birth in this manner as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Regarding the various transformations of both the mundane and supramundane realms, I have attained unimpeded penetration upon a single sight. On the road, I encountered the brothers Kāśyapa."

He followed [his brothers—whose names appear in the *Maudgalyāyana-āgama*] to proclaim the causes and conditions. As the Buddha’s verse says: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions / I declare to be emptiness; / They are also called provisional designations, / And are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

These four lines constitute the Four Teachings—Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect—and through them, Śāriputra attained a thorough understanding of the perfect principle. Having realized that the mind is boundless, he left the household life to follow the Buddha.

Seeing that the clarity of awareness was perfect and full, he attained great fearlessness and became an Arhat. He became the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma (these two phrases distinguish him from Rāhula).
When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, [Ānanda] said: "According to what I have realized, it is the mind and the faculty of sight that emit light."
"Radiant insight and vision—this is the foremost.
This is the entry through the awakening of eye-consciousness. Śāriputra (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since the vast and remote kalpas of the past, my eye-consciousness has been clear and sharp. I have undergone such births as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River throughout the world."
Regarding the supramundane, the various differentiations of illusory delusions and manifold transformations pass over the eye-consciousness in a single glance;
they are transparently clear and unobstructed, requiring no laborious investigation or deep analysis by the mental consciousness to be known. For many lifetimes it has been thus.
Even in this present life, he had never known the Buddha, until he happened to encounter the Kāśyapa brothers on the road. They...
He followed him and requested that he preach for him the causal conditions of the four lines [of verse].

Upon hearing this stanza but once, he immediately attained realization of the storehouse mind (ālayavijñāna), which pervades the entire Dharma-realm and encompasses the ten voids, being without limit or boundary. Thereupon, he left the household life to become a monk under the Buddha.
Although his prior realization of the ground was thorough, he had not yet been able to exhaust its depths or reach its furthest reaches to ascend to the peak and achieve the ultimate.
Now that he has reached this state, his visual consciousness is bright and perfect; every matter is clearly understood, and there is nothing that does not penetrate through.
Thus, he preaches the Dharma endowed with the four fearlessnesses. For fear arises from a sense of insufficiency; because his vision is thorough, his preaching is free from any deficiency. From...
He attained the state of Arhat and was foremost in wisdom; his physical virtue and spiritual merit both flourished, making him the eldest son of the Buddha.
By inquiring of the Buddha’s teachings, he awakened to the Dharma-body; thus, he was "born from the mouth of the Buddha.

Within the teaching, he nurtured the holy embryo until the Dharma-body manifested from its subtle beginnings; thus, he was "transformatively born from the Dharma. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, [he replied as follows]:
That which I have realized issues forth as radiant light from the thorough penetration of visual consciousness.
This light and the visual consciousness both reach the ultimate limit of the boundless; this alone is the foremost. According to another sutra, Śāriputra was the Tathāgata Golden Dragon in the past;
thus we know that his attainment of the Dharma in seven days and his realization of the fruit in half a month were all skillful manifestations.

[End. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (whose practice pervades the Dharma-realm is called "Universal," and whose rank adjoins that of the Ultimate Sage is called "Worthy"; this one is not a bodhisattva prior to the stages [bhūmi], but rather an echo and shadow of the Ancient Buddha alongside Mañjuśrī;

therefore, in the narrative, he is also slightly different from the other sages. It merely states that he has long attained realization, and only at the very end does it reveal his original cause as having originally arisen from the auditory consciousness. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and...
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have already served as a Dharma Prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct their disciples who possess the roots of bodhisattvas to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra, they derive their names from me.

World-Honored One, I employ mental hearing (which is the ear-consciousness) to discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings. Even if there were [beings] beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions..."

If there is a single sentient being who, within their own mind, gives rise to the practice of Samantabhadra, at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, all arriving at that person's location.
Even if their obstacles are so profound that they do not yet perceive me, I will secretly stroke their crown, protect and comfort them, and cause them to achieve success.
When the Buddha asked about the perfection of penetration, I spoke of this fundamental cause: the mind.
To hear and achieve clear, penetrating, and sovereign understanding—this is the foremost.
This is entry through awakening by means of the auditory consciousness. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have already served as a Dharma Prince to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, inheriting the family legacy of the Buddhas."

To assist in propagating the Buddha’s transformation: whenever Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct their disciples who possess the perfect and sudden roots of a Bodhisattva to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra—such as the Ten Great Vows, wherein every single color and fragrance completely pervades the Dharma-realm—it is for this reason.
Whenever one cultivates my practice, one derives one's name from me; thus, one is also named Samantabhadra. The breadth of the model he provides is as follows:
"World-Honored One, at that time, I used only my auditory consciousness to discern the knowledge and views of sentient beings and to select and perfect the practices of Samantabhadra.
If there were even a single sentient being beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions who manifested the practice of Samantabhadra within their hearts,
I would immediately mount my six-tusked elephant and, according to the extent of their resolve, divide myself into immeasurable [forms]..."

I shall manifest my physical body before them; those with light obscurations who are able to see me will receive my manifest protection, while those with deep obscurations who have not yet seen me will have their heads stroked by me in secret, thereby being shielded and protected so that they remain free from demonic hindrances.

I comforted them, ensuring that none would fall back or regress, so that those at both shallow and deep stages achieved success without exception. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I replied:
"Although I have long attained realization through many kalpas, if one traces it back to its original cause, there was also an initial expedient means.

It was simply by employing the faculty of auditory consciousness to engage in conceptual discernment according to thoughts, universally illuminating the capacities of all beings, thereby attaining great mastery. By this means—"

This is merely the first step toward entering the Perfect [State]. According to the texts, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and Śrīkṣetra—all these great Bodhisattvas—were not disciples of Kāśyapa;
therefore, the matter of their receiving the seal and attaining fruition is not mentioned.
To trace back how he assisted in proclaiming the Great Teaching, it was no more than what Puhua did for Linji.
Yet, once a single Buddha has raised the banner of the true command, all Buddhas must bow before him; how can one be constrained by such things as chronological order or formal rank?
Sundarananda (translated here as "Glorious Joy," the Buddha’s own younger brother) immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first left the household life and entered the Path under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated regarding *samādhi*, and I had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The World-Honored One instructed me and Kauṣṭhila to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose. When I first applied myself to this..."

He practiced contemplation for twenty-one days and beheld the breath within his nostrils entering and exiting like smoke. His body and mind became internally luminous, and the world appeared as a vast, hollow void, universally pure and transparent like lapis lazuli.
As the appearance of smoke gradually vanished, the breath from his nose became white. His mind opened and his outflows were exhausted;

all his inhalations and exhalations transformed into radiant light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions. He attained the state of an Arhat, and the World-Honored One bestowed a prediction upon him.

"I shall attain Bodhi. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied: "By means of the cessation of breath, I long ago attained illumination; through the perfection of this illumination, I extinguished all outflows. This is the foremost."

This is the entry into realization through nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*). Although nose-consciousness is mentioned, one does not grasp at the discrimination of nose-consciousness at the moment of smelling an odor;
rather, one grasps only the intention of observing the breath. Sundarananda (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I first left the household life, I studied the Way under the Buddha. Although I upheld the Buddha’s precepts and discipline, regarding *samādhi*..."

My mind was constantly distracted; I had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). My heart was agitated by craving, my concentrated mind failed to achieve stability, and it was difficult to shatter delusions;

thus, I had not yet realized the fruit. The World-Honored One instructed me and Kauṣṭhila that we should together receive the Dharma-gate of the nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) to collect this scattered mind and contemplate the white mark at the tip of the nose. When I first contemplated with focused attention, after twenty-one days, I saw—
The breath within the nostrils enters and exits like smoke. This is because respiration arises from wind and fire, which stir up the turbidity of afflictions;
thus its appearance is like black smoke. Those who are deluded do not perceive it, but only through diligent contemplation can one see it.

When pure observation becomes manifest, the signs of meditative concentration gradually form and afflictions gradually dissipate. Internally, it penetrates the five viscera; externally, it pervades the great trichiliocosm.

The interior was luminous while the exterior appeared empty; as the smoke vanished, it turned white. Thereupon, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) manifested, and afflictions were extinguished without remainder.

As for the black smoke of the inhalations and exhalations that had turned white, it further transformed into light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, merging mind and object into a single unity.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One prophesied that I would attain Buddhahood in the future and realize the fruit of perfect enlightenment.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "I reverse the process of breathing through the nose. From black it becomes white; from white it becomes light.

As the breath is sustained for a long time, clarity is revealed; the characteristics vanish and the nature manifests. When the radiance is complete and perfect, all outflows are extinguished. This is the foremost method. Zhong said:
"In the previous method, one regulates the breath based on the sense organs (roots) in order to collect the mind. In this method, one contemplates the breath based on consciousness."
To settle his mind, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For many kalpas past, my eloquence has been unimpeded; I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness and have deeply penetrated the true mark of reality. Thus it continues, even unto...”
Regarding the secret Dharma gates of the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have provided subtle and wondrous elucidations among the assembly, attaining fearlessness.
Knowing that I possess great eloquence, the World-Honored One has used the wheel of his voice to instruct me to proclaim them forth. Thus, before the Buddha—
Assisting the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma, I attained Arhatship through the lion’s roar. The World-Honored One has certified that my preaching of the Dharma is unsurpassed.
When the Buddha inquired about perfect penetration, I replied that by means of the sound of the Dharma, I have subdued demonic adversaries and extinguished all outflows; this is the foremost method.
"This is the entry through the awakening of tongue-consciousness. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges, I have possessed unimpeded eloquence to proclaim the provisional meanings of the Two Vehicles—suffering and emptiness—and I have deeply penetrated the true meaning of the One Vehicle’s reality-mark (*dharmatā*).
Thus, even regarding the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which were long kept silent and not spoken..."

Whether it be the Dharma, or teachings that are half-luminous and half-obscure, or teachings spoken from the perspective of the East or the West, I am able to reveal them with subtle and wondrous clarity, fully exhausting their intended meaning and bringing them forth. Having attained the utmost skillful means, I have also acquired the four fearlessnesses.
Now, within this assembly of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One knows that I possess great eloquence. At this—
Among the three wheels of body, speech, and mind, I shall exclusively employ the single wheel of vocal sound to assist in propagating the Buddha’s transformation of the world.

Therefore, before the Buddha, I shall assist the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma; above, I shall support the Buddha’s teaching through the lion’s roar, and below, I shall transform sentient beings.
Beginning with the benefit of others and concluding with my own benefit, I have attained the state of an Arhat. While the World-Honored One was in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,...

At that assembly, Mañjuśrī designated me as foremost in preaching the Dharma. Now, when the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), I rely on the consciousness of the tongue and the sounds of the Dharma.
Internally, I subdue the demons and grievances of the mind; through analytical exposition, they are destroyed.
Externally, I subdue the demonic harms of the celestial Māras; through manifest revelation, they are eliminated. Thus, all outflows (*āsrava*) are extinguished, and I enter into perfect penetration.
This is the first. Question: Why is it that one does not take other tastes [as the object], but takes only the preaching of the Dharma?
Answer: Both are functions of the gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*), yet the preaching of the Dharma is superior; therefore, it is singled out for selection.

However, since the preaching of the Dharma seems to require the subtle and detailed discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the fact that it now employs only the gustatory consciousness also reveals the inherent nature of the preaching of the Dharma itself.
It is simply a matter of employing mindfulness (*anusmṛti*); there is no need for strenuous deliberation, yet the arising [of wisdom] will be inexhaustible.

In the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the World-Honored One stated that all the great disciples were those who "secretly concealed their inner realization while manifesting outwardly" to assist the Buddha in propagating the teachings.
Therefore, it was only in the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* that the great disciples dared to speak freely, recounting their own distant causes.
None of these have planted roots of goodness for only one or two kalpas; they are all those who have planted roots of goodness throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Those designated as "Anāgāmin, Arhat, and Aśaikṣa" are likewise not of the common sort who merely realize the emptiness of persons;

their attainments are by no means comparable. ○ Zhong says: Speaking the Dharma is the function of the tongue-organ, yet it is through this tongue that one chews upon the flavor of the Dharma. Thus, the tongue—
"Śrī Upāli—(herein 'Upāli' means 'Foremost,' and is also translated as 'Close Attendant')—immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world; I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue..."*

He subdues all māras and restrains all non-Buddhists. He liberates himself from the worldly outflows of greed (greed being one of the "outflows of desire," while the "outflows" include those of existence and ignorance).
He receives the Buddha’s teachings and precepts (initially receiving the two hundred and fifty rules for śrāvakas), and so on, up to the three thousand points of dignified conduct.

Eighty thousand subtle [transgressions]. (This refers to the Bodhisattva precepts. The restraints for walking, standing, sitting, and lying down each number two hundred and fifty. When these are paired with the three clusters [of pure conduct], they become three thousand. When assigned to the seven branches of body and speech, they become twenty-one thousand.

Furthermore, when assigned to the four categories of afflictions—greed, anger, delusion, and their equal combination—they become eighty-four thousand. Nature-offenses (refers to those prohibited dharmas whose essential nature is evil, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth.

Prohibitory offenses (refers to those prohibited dharmas whose essential nature is not evil, but which open the door to various evils by serving as preliminary conditions; thus, they are forbidden to block and prevent all evils, such as alcohol and the like. All are completely purified.
Purified, with body and mind stilled and extinguished, I became an Arhat. Among the assembly of the Tathāgata, I am the leader;
my heart was personally sealed by the Buddha. Upholding the precepts and cultivating the person, I was esteemed the foremost by the multitude.

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I began by taking hold of the body until the body attained mastery, then sequentially took hold of the mind until the mind attained thorough penetration. Thereafter, both body and mind were entirely fluent and sharp. This is the first [method].
1. This is the entry through body-consciousness. Upāli said to the Buddha (as follows):
"I was a minister who attended upon the Tathāgata when he was a prince. From the very beginning, I followed the Buddha as he left the city to renounce the world. Left.
The above is not a departure from the truth. He personally witnessed when the Tathāgata’s path was not yet accomplished and he underwent six years of diligent austerity;
he personally saw when the Tathāgata’s path was perfected, subduing all Māras and overcoming all non-Buddhists, and attaining liberation from the outflows of worldly greed and desire.
Thereupon, following the Buddha’s instruction, he taught me the two hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus, up to the three thousand eight hundred [rules].
The myriad bodhisattvas possess the precepts; both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed transgressions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*) are entirely pure.

Through the bhikṣu precepts, they pacify their bodies; through the bodhisattva precepts, they extinguish their minds. From the precepts, concentration arises, whereby body and mind are brought to stillness and extinction.
Thus, through concentration, wisdom arose, and I attained Arhatship. Among the assembly of the Tathāgata, I am the foremost leader; the Tathāgata personally certified my mind.
Upholding the precepts and cultivating the body, I am esteemed by the assembly as unsurpassed. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, [I spoke thus].
At first, I took the Bhikṣu precepts to restrain my body; thus the body attained mastery and was free from transgression.
Next, I took the Bodhisattva precepts to restrain my mind; thus the mind attained penetration and gave rise to samādhi and wisdom.
Thereafter, both body and mind became entirely proficient and sharp, and through the consciousness of the body, I entered into perfect penetration. This was the foremost. [I did not choose this.]

While the function of awakening to contact is indeed present, one merely takes up the efficacy of maintaining the precepts, because the function of awakening to contact is inferior to that of maintaining the precepts.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "At first, on the road..."

While begging for alms, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvā (which means "papaya-tumor," so called because there was a tumor on his chest like a papaya), Gayā, and Nadī—who proclaimed the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions (examining that it is not a worldly, composite, coarse phenomenon).
I immediately resolved my mind and attained great penetration. The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe, which I donned, and my beard and hair fell away of their own accord.
As I travel through the ten directions, I encounter no obstruction. My supernormal powers are so manifest that they are ranked as unsurpassed.
Having attained arhatship, it is not only the World-Honored One who does so; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also praise my spiritual power as perfect, clear, pure, sovereign, and fearless.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. I replied: "By turning back the turbid flow of the mind, the light of the heart was manifested and proclaimed, becoming as clear and crystalline as a muddy stream that has been settled for a long time.
This is the foremost [method].
This is entry through awakening by means of the mental consciousness. Mahāmaudgalyāyana (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying: "At first, I..."

While begging for food along the road, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers, including Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who expounded for me the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions—a teaching far surpassing the shallow dharmas of causes and conditions realized by the Hīnayāna.

Thereupon, from my mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), I suddenly gave rise to the bodhicitta; immediately through that mental consciousness, I entered sudden universal penetration and attained great penetration.

I attained realization. When the Tathāgata bestowed his *kāṣāya* robe upon me, my hair and beard fell away of their own accord; all this was through the Buddha’s spiritual power, accomplished the very moment he spoke.
As I traveled throughout the ten directions, I encountered no obstacles. My supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) were so brilliant that they were deemed unsurpassed.

Having realized the essence of the perfect penetration of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), I further developed its function of perfect penetration. From this, I have realized the fruit of enlightenment.
Having attained Arhatship, not only the World-Honored One, but all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, praise my spiritual power:
it is fully developed from the true nature and is perfectly luminous; it is far removed from reliance on karma and is pure;
it is such that nothing is contrary to one's will and it is sovereign; it cannot be obstructed or suppressed and is fearless—all of this is obtained through the mental consciousness.

Furthermore, when the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied that by reversing the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and returning to the wondrous stillness, I caused the light of the mind to manifest its wondrousness and its wondrous functions to appear.
Reversing the consciousness is like settling a turbid stream; bringing it forth is like making it clear and crystalline.
By transforming the mental consciousness, one realizes the *tathāgatagarbha* mind; this is the foremost method. Question: You previously spoke of the arising and ceasing of the mental consciousness.

[Objection: There is no reason for this. Now you speak of "perfect penetration" (yuantong). How can this be so? [Response: It is because one clearly perceives that the mental consciousness arises from the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and that apart from the storehouse-consciousness there is no separate mental consciousness.
By means of this, one immediately enters the storehouse-consciousness and attains perfect realization. The section on the perfect penetration of the six consciousnesses is concluded.
Ucchuṣma, before the Tathāgata, joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I constantly recall that in the distant past, many kalpas ago, my nature was characterized by much lust. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śūnyarāja."

It was taught that excessive lust enters and becomes a mass of fierce fire. I was instructed to contemplate throughout my entire frame—the four limbs and all the warm breaths (the character "cold" is a mistranslation;
