it should read "all the sensations of warmth"). As the divine light coalesced within, it transformed my lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.
From this point on, all Buddhas called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I became an Arhat.
Han: "I made a great vow in my heart: 'When all Buddhas attain the Way, may I become a powerful Malla warrior and personally subdue their demonic adversaries.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied that by clearly observing the sensations of warmth within my body and mind, they flowed through me without obstruction;
once all outflows were extinguished, a great jewel-flame arose, and I ascended to supreme enlightenment. This is the foremost."
This is the entry through awakening by means of the fire element. Vajra Fire-Head, before the Tathāgata, joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha.
He did not mention rising from his seat because a vajra does not sit.
"I constantly recall that in the distant past, during my time as an ordinary being, my nature was characterized by much lust. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world, named..."
The Tathāgata Śūnyarāja said that those who indulge excessively in lustfulness do so because they are fundamentally driven by the sensation of warmth. While alive, this becomes the fire of desire;
at death, it becomes the fire of karma. When the power of karma intensifies, it becomes a mass of fierce flames.

He taught me to contemplate everywhere within the hundred bones and four limbs the element of fire (*tejas*), desiring that they might recognize their fear and suddenly cease their lustful minds. Thereafter, he followed the error with a correction.
One may achieve wondrous contemplation. Within my meditative observation, a divine light coalesces within; I see throughout my entire body nothing but a single mass of fire.
Filled with both fear and revulsion, I distance myself from lustful thoughts. Although the fire is hot and distressing, its essence possesses radiance.
Now that the mind of lust has ceased, there is no longer any heat or distress; seeing only radiance is itself the transformation.
By transforming a mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom, my entire body dwells within the *ābhāsvara-samādhi* (Fire-Light Samādhi).
For this reason, all the Buddhas address me by the name "Fire-Head" (*Agnimukha*). Although this expresses my name, it is also equivalent to their formal authorization and seal of approval.
By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is only a single mass of fire-light. Through this right reception (*samāpatti*), one becomes an Arhat;
one gives rise to the fire of the true emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature and the true fire of the emptiness of nature, thereby forming the mind of the causal ground.
Having realized the stages from the seventh faith onward, one enters the positions of abiding. Furthermore, although this Fire-Light Samādhi is...
The internal realm can manifest external appearances. When fire blazes fiercely, even Māra gazes upon it with fear. Thus I resolved my mind:
whenever I encounter a Buddha attaining enlightenment, I vow to become a powerful warrior to subdue the demonic adversaries. Such was my aspiration upon realizing the fruit of the path.
Now that the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I have observed with clarity that the fires of desire within the body all arise from lust.

The mind. The warmth and tactile sensation of body and mind collectively designate the fire element (*tejas-mahābhūta*). Since the lustful mind has already been extinguished, it does not constitute the fire of karma;
therefore, there is no obstruction. The divine light and the fire of wisdom melt into the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), pervading the entire Dharma-realm;

therefore, it circulates freely. With the fire of wisdom, one burns the fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*); what could remain unexhausted? Thus, all outflows (*āsrava*) are dissolved. By means of the perfect fire element...
The subtle function of this penetration is to crush demons and protect the Dharma; its immeasurable power gives rise to great jewel-flames.
From this, one ascends to unsurpassed enlightenment, whereby one’s fundamental nature becomes equal to that of a Buddha, yet one manifests in a position of auxiliary transformation.

Is it your intention that this alone is the foremost among the methods of perfect penetration? [Note: According to the examination of the virtues and ranks of the various sages, they are mutually comparable. However—

The traces [of the teaching] have both provisional and ultimate aspects; the words have both hidden and manifest meanings. Students should briefly set aside the traces to grasp the fundamental, and having attained the meaning, forget the words;
they must not recklessly distinguish between the Great and the Small [vehicles]. Master Lien said: "Of the three great calamities, water arises from greed and fire is produced by anger.
That lust is now likened to a fierce fire is because the Dharma has no fixed metaphors; it is simply that the mind of lust itself is soaked [in suffering]."
Gradually moistening the roots of birth and death is likened to water; the flourishing and blazing of lustful desire that withers the seeds of purity is likened to fire.

Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (who first leveled the external earth and thereby realized the mind-ground, subsequently maintaining his original awakening and perfectly realizing the treasury-mind, and is thus named Earth-Holder) immediately rose from his seat and prostrated himself at [the Buddha’s] feet.
Bowing at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying: “I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabha appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.
I constantly went to all major roads, ferry crossings, and narrow, treacherous stretches of land where conditions were improper and caused damage to carts and horses;
I leveled and filled them all, or built bridges, or carried sand and earth. Through such diligent toil, I passed many years.”
During the time when the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, there were sentient beings who, at the city gates and marketplaces, would have others carry their goods for them.
I would first carry them for them to wherever they were going; once the goods were set down, I would depart without taking any payment.

During the time of the present Buddha Viśvabhū (which means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All"), when the world was plagued by widespread famine, I served as a porter, carrying loads regardless of the distance.
I approached him and took only a single coin. Or, when oxen drawing carts were mired in the mud, I used my supernatural powers to push their wheels for them and relieve them of their suffering.
At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast. I leveled the ground at that moment to await the Buddha.
Viśvabhū Tathāgata rubbed the crown of my head and said to me: "You must level the ground of the mind; then the ground of the world will all become level."
"Peace! My mind was immediately opened. I saw that the minute particles of my own body were equal and indistinguishable from all the minute particles that constitute the world.

These particles, by their very nature, do not touch one another; even weapons cannot touch them. Thus, regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), I realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and became an Arhat.
Having turned my mind back, I now enter the stage of a Bodhisattva. I have heard [the teachings] of the Tathāgatas..."
I have come to proclaim the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the Wondrous Lotus. I was previously a witness to this and served as the leader.

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I observed that the two objects—the body and the realm—are equal and without distinction; they are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, from which dust arises through delusion.

When the dust is extinguished, wisdom becomes perfect, and one achieves the Unsurpassed Way. This is the foremost [method]. (This may also lead to awakening to the production of the world through false thought, as well as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s bestowal [of the prophecy]).
[This is] the meaning of recording the purity of the Buddha-land.
This is the great awakening and entry based on the ground. The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during the time of the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa, I was a bhikṣu who exclusively practiced the ascetic discipline of leveling the earth. At that time...

whether high and deep and perilous, or narrow and constricted— that are improper and cause harm to carriages and horses, I shall level them all.
I filled them in. At times I built bridges to facilitate crossings; at other times I carried sand and earth to repair vital roads.
Thus, through diligent toil, I passed through the presence of immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world without ever succumbing to even a moment’s indolence.
Furthermore, I cultivated the practice of the power of renunciation: whenever there were sentient beings in the marketplace who required someone to carry their goods, I would carry them for them.
When he reached his destination, he would set down his goods and depart immediately, taking no payment for his services. He practiced such complete renunciation during times of plenty.
During the era of Vipaśyin Buddha, when the world was plagued by widespread famine, I carried hungry people on my back to find food, regardless of the distance;
I accepted only a single coin. Such was my moderation even during years of scarcity. Thus did I accumulate [merit].
Through the practice of vows throughout kalpas, he has thus elicited meritorious retributions and possesses supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Sometimes, when oxen drawing carts become mired in the mud, I use my supernormal powers to push their wheels and relieve them from their suffering. Such is the manner in which he extracts suffering through supernormal power.

My mind has also become equanimous. Yet, this is merely an equanimity of mind that still pertains to phenomenal appearances.
At that time, the Great King of the land prepared a vegetarian feast and invited the Buddha. I then repaired the path by which the Buddha would pass to await him.
Vipaśyin Tathāgata, pitying me for my long-standing toil in these activities, took me under his compassionate protection and empowerment, causing me to return to the principle. He then stroked my—
The Peak addressed me, saying: "The world is uneven and heaven and earth harbor grievances.
Why labor so diligently over this? You need only level your own mind; then the ground of the world will all become level."
Thus we know that because the mind in this Sahā world is treacherous, it gives rise to the heights and depths of mountains and valleys;
whereas because the mind in Sukhāvatī is level, it results in a ground as flat as the palm of a hand—this is the proof thereof.

When I heard these words, my mind immediately opened, and I realized that the minute particles of the body constitute the internal earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), while the minute particles of the world constitute the external earth element. These two earth elements—
They are equal and without distinction. Since there is no distinction, the body is the elements, and the elements are the body;
their self-nature is fundamentally empty, and they do not touch or rub one another. Even weapons such as blades and spears are merely external categories of the earth element.

When these touch the body, which is the internal earth element, it is like cutting through light or slicing shadows—there is absolutely no injury. This is what is meant by "placing one's head before a white blade. One...

It is as if one were cutting through the spring breeze. Having practiced the bodhisattva path for kalpas since time immemorial, it was only at the end of the *Vyuṣita-kalpa* that he severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāva-āsrava*), awakened to the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), and became an arhat. Moreover, he attained only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). This is like forging iron.
The coarse defilements fell away first; then, at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, they immediately turned toward the True Vehicle and entered the ranks of the Bodhisattvas.
There, they heard the four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa and the present Tathāgatas of the ten directions preaching the Buddha’s knowledge and vision during the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra.
This accords with my own element of earth; therefore, I previously served as a witness for it and became a leader in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Now that the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, I have observed with clarity that the two objects—the body and the realm—namely, the two aspects of the earth element, internal and external, are equal and without distinction.
They are nothing other than the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which, following karma, falsely manifests and gives rise to these appearances of objects.

When the dust of defilement is eliminated, wisdom becomes perfect; when appearances are exhausted, the true nature manifests. Having accomplished the Unsurpassed Way, one has already entered the knowledge and vision of the Supreme Vehicle.
Since proceeding from the mundane to the sacred involves valuing the ultimate over the provisional, all take the element of earth as the gateway for initiating practice and entering into principle.
This constitutes the foremost means of perfect penetration. It is simply the first.

The Youth Candraprabha—(the term "youth" [kumāra] is an epithet for a bodhisattva, signifying the virtue of perpetual innocence. When Confucian scholars hear the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta Sūtra* state that Confucius was the youth Dīpaṃkara, they are indignant at such a trivialization.

They fail to realize that Mañjuśrī, the ancestral teacher of Śākyamuni through nine generations, is also called a "youth. How could there be any sense of trivialization here? immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Bodhisattvas cultivate the contemplation of water and enter samādhi. They contemplate that the watery element within their bodies is inseparable;

beginning with mucus and saliva, they exhaustively examine all such things—saliva, lymph, marrow, blood, feces, and urine—and find that these substances circulating within the body are identical in nature to water.
Thus, they perceive the water within their bodies as equal to the fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King Buddha-land beyond the world.
There was no distinction. At that time, I had first accomplished this contemplation; I saw only the water and had not yet attained the state of being bodiless.
While I was practicing dhyāna within my room as a bhikṣu, a disciple of mine peered through the window to observe the room.
He saw only clear water filling the entire room and could see nothing else. Being ignorant and childlike, he took a piece of tile or gravel and threw it into the water, causing a splash.

The water made a sound; he looked back and departed. After I emerged from meditative absorption, I suddenly felt a pain in my heart, like that experienced by Śāriputra when he was afflicted by the "Harmful Ghost.
I reflected to myself: "I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions for illness.

(To know whether an Arhat has illness or not, one must clarify the two bonds of cause and fruit. That which is summoned by past seeds but has not yet received a body in the present is called the 'bond of cause' [yoni-bandhana]. That which is summoned by past seeds and has already received a body in the present, such that the body itself must undergo [the experience], is the 'bond of fruit' [phala-bandhana])."

This is called the "bondage of the fruit. If a śrāvaka of true practice has newly realized the four fruits and has severed the "bondage of the seeds" such that they will not undergo further existence, yet their present body has not yet been extinguished, then the bondage of the fruit still remains.

Consequently, all illness and suffering must be experienced by the body; thus, Śāriputra’s headache and Pindola’s eye pain were both of this nature. Once they have entered parinirvāṇa and return again through compassionate vows, then both bondages are absent, and there will be no more actual physical suffering.
Why, then, does he suddenly experience heartache today? Could it be that he has regressed? At that time, the youth came quickly before me and spoke as above.
When this matter occurred, I told him: "If you see water again, you may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris.
The youth followed my instructions; later, when he entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he again saw the water, and the tiles and debris were exactly as before.

He opened the door and removed them. When I subsequently emerged from concentration, my physical body was restored as it was originally. I encountered immeasurable Buddhas, and in this manner, [the process] continued until the mountains and seas returned to their natural state.

It was only upon attaining the state of Universal Pervasion under Tathāgata King of Penetration that I was able to transcend the body. My nature became one with the empty truth of the fragrant water-oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions, without duality or distinction.
Now, under this Tathāgata, I have received the name "Childlike Truth" and am included in the assembly of Bodhisattvas. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied:
"By means of the single flavor of the flowing nature of water, I attained the patience of non-arising and fulfilled Bodhi. This is the first.
1. This is the entry into awakening through the water element (*āpas-mahābhūta*). The youth Candraprabha said to the Buddha:

What is this contemplation of water like? First, one contemplates the watery nature within the body as being non-contradictory and inseparable.

One begins with the nasal mucus and saliva, proceeding through the lymph, essence, blood, and the excretions of both large and small intestines, leaving nothing unexamined. As for the mucus, saliva, and excretions, they are close to the exterior.

The characteristic of water consists of the bodily fluids, essence, and blood. Regarding the internal characteristic of water, it flows from the exterior to the interior and from the interior to the exterior, circulating repeatedly within the body.
Furthermore, mucus, saliva, and fluids are the clear aspects of water; essence, blood, excrement, and urine are the turbid aspects of water.
Although the clear and turbid differ, the nature of water is one and the same. Contemplating in this manner, once the observation of the internal is matured, [one proceeds to the external].

Extending outward and expanding, one perceives the water within this body as being identical to the great lotus flower in the Flower Treasury Ocean (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) outside the world-system. Within that lotus flower, there are immeasurable seas of fragrant water;

in each of these seas, there is a single flower, which supports twenty tiers of world-systems (kṣetradhātu) stacked high like a banner. This is called the Floating Banner King World-System (Pūṇḍarīka-rāja-kṣetra). Its...
Among the various seas of fragrant water therein, there is no further limit; they are equal and without distinction.
Because they are fused by the contemplation of the mind, the body is not small and the seawater is not large. At that time, I first accomplished this contemplation;

as the power of contemplation was still shallow, I saw only the water, yet the characteristics of water had not yet vanished. The entirety of the water was the body, yet the characteristics of the body still remained. [End of excerpt]
"Even without a physical body, [the distance] is still far. I recall another matter:

once, when I was a bhikṣu sitting in meditation in my room, a disciple peered through the window and saw only clear water filling the room. He playfully threw tiles and gravel inside before departing. After I emerged from samādhi,"
Suddenly I felt a pain in my heart, much like the headache Śāriputra experienced when he was seized by a ghost while emerging from meditative absorption.
I thought to myself: "I have now realized the path of Arhatship; the fetters of the sons of affliction (*putra-bandhana*) have been severed.

Moreover, as one who has long since attained realization and returned, even the fetters of the fruits (*phala-bandhana*) are absent. Having long been free from the conditions of illness, why does this sudden disease of heart-pain arise?"
"Could it be that you have lost your resolve for the Way that has led to this? At that time, the youth recounted the matter of throwing the tile as he had previously described it.
I then told him, "If you see such a thing again, you should open the door and remove it."
The youth followed the instructions. Indeed, he saw the water again; indeed, he cleared away the rubble and debris. Thereafter, he emerged from meditative absorption as before and was no longer ill.
Now, the appearance of water is a dependent reflection of a solitary image that can only be seen by oneself, yet he was able to cause others to see it as well.
Is this not the extraordinary power of contemplation, an inconceivable realm? From this point onward, furthermore...

After many kalpas, he encountered immeasurable Buddhas. Thus, it was only upon the appearance in the world of the Tathāgata Sovereign King of Mountains and Seas Pervasive Penetration that his profound contemplation was finally perfected.
Grasping is shattered and the aggregates are seen as empty; once this body is empty, the visualization of water is also empty.
Only then does one attain what is called the true emptiness of the nature-water and the true water of the nature-emptiness—pure, pervasive, and all-encompassing.

They are fused into a single whole, being neither two nor distinct. Now that I have encountered the Tathāgata and joined this assembly, I have fully realized the true virtues of a youth and attained the dharma-emptiness of a bodhisattva.

Although this was brought about by the accumulation of causes from past lives, how could I dare forget the grace of the Buddha’s Dharma-milk? When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:
"Within my body, the nature of water flows as a single taste, no different from the oceans of lands beyond the world-spheres. Nature...
Merging with true emptiness, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), realizes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) through to its depths, and brings Bodhi to perfection;
this alone is the foremost. Question: When Moonlight entered meditative absorption, the youth threw a tile at him.
As for this single piece of rubble, does it ultimately exist within the mind or outside the mind? If it were outside the mind, it should not cause pain. If it were inside the mind, then...
"From where do these shards and rubble enter? He replied: "Setting aside the shards and rubble for a moment, consider this water within the room.
Does it ultimately exist outside the body or inside the body? If it is outside the body, from where does this water emerge after one has entered meditative concentration?
If it is inside the body, from where does this water enter after one has emerged from concentration? If you know [the nature of] the water..."

By observing its entry and exit, one immediately knows the interior and exterior of the rubble. Question: From where does the water within the room come? Answer: It is produced by the concentrated mind;
it is the "form born of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). In the past, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) turned stone into stone through their resolute minds;
thus, what is so extraordinary about the concentrated mind producing water? This was the case with Master Shui Guan of Mianzhu County in Hanzhou.
The traces are entirely of this nature. Master Padmasambhava said: "It is fortunate that these are merely tiles and rubble; they cause only heartache.

But if one were instead thrown into swords and blades, what would happen? The Sūtra says: "When first establishing this visualization, one has not yet attained the bodiless state; because the body still remains, there is slight suffering."
When this contemplation is perfected, there is ultimately no great harm; even if one were cast into swords and blades, it would merely cause pain in the heart but could not inflict injury.
For those who have not yet lost their sense of self, the body and water are two distinct things, and they still perceive their own body as being identical to that water.
For those who have lost their sense of self, the body and water are one; if one seeks for a "self-body," it cannot be found. Since the body no longer exists, who is there to suffer?
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitaghoṣa (Immeasurable Sound)—this sound being produced by the wind arising from and vibrating within the navel-cakra, which is also called the 'conjoined wind-element'—who revealed to Bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (fundamental enlightenment is the Dharmakāya; 'wondrous' is liberation; and 'clarity' is Prajñā). Observing this world..."
The elements and the bodies of sentient beings are all driven by the power of illusory conditions and wind.

At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the elements, the movement of the world, the motion and stillness of the body, and the stirring thoughts of the mind. All these movements were non-dual and without distinction.
I then realized the nature of this multitude of movements: they come from nowhere and go nowhere; throughout the ten directions, they are subtle...
Sentient beings, deluded by the dust of the world, are all equally false and illusory.

Thus, throughout the entire trichiliocosm, all sentient beings are like hundreds of mosquitoes and gnats contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring together, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.
Not long after encountering the Buddha, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At that time, through the hearing of the mind, they beheld the East.
I was a Dharma Prince in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, serving the Buddhas of the ten directions. My body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things without obstruction.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], I said: "By observing that the power of wind has no dependence, I awakened the Bodhicitta and entered samādhi.
I have united with the Buddhas of the ten directions to transmit this one wondrous mind; this is the foremost."
This is the entry into awakening through the wind-element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*). The Dharma Prince Vairocanaprabha said to the Buddha:
"I recall that in the past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitaghoṣa.
This, too, was realized through the howling of ten thousand apertures. Thus, the Tathāgata Amitaghoṣa revealed the wondrous original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) of the Bodhisattvas."
The clarity [of the mind] inherently possesses the three virtues, which serve as the source of illumination. This is the very substance of the capacity for contemplation.
One should then contemplate this world and the bodies of sentient beings as both the support and the object of observation; all are driven by the power of wind.

They are induced by the movement of the deluded mind’s conditions, causing the wind of clarity to emerge. Furthermore, this power of wind can also transform this vessel-world and the sense-faculties of the body.

These are, in general, the delusive objects of observation. At that time, I practiced meditation according to the Dharma, observing the establishment of this realm as being sustained by the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), and observing the transformation of the world as resulting from the subtle shifting of the winds.
I observed that every movement and stillness of this body is impelled by the winds, and I observed this mind.

Moment by moment they shift and flow; ever-new, they do not abide, all being stirred by the wind. Observing the world, the body, and the mind in this way, one sees that their various movements differ;
yet upon investigating their cause, one finds they all arise from the movement of the single thought of ignorance-wind, without any distinction between them.
At that time, I clearly understood that the nature of these manifold movements comes from nowhere.
When departing, there is nowhere to which one goes; it is the very nature of wind. If there were truly something that came from existence to existence, it would not be illusory.

Since there is nothing that comes from non-existence to existence, one can see that the sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all deludedly inverted within the wind, being nothing more than a single shared illusion.
When this is pursued to its ultimate limit, it extends even to the three thousand great [thousandfold worlds].
A thousand [worlds]. Within the entire realm governed by a single Buddha, all sentient beings are like a hundred mosquitoes contained within a single vessel;
their chirping and clamor resound in confusion, yet they do not exceed the dimensions of that vessel as they stir up a frantic noise.
How tranquil this is! Observing the shattering of such collective movement, one encounters immeasurable sounds as if—
Not long after arriving, he realized that coming has no point of origin and departing has no destination; that all phenomena, in their very essence, are devoid of arising and ceasing.
He swiftly entered the stage of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. Having awakened to non-arising, his fundamental enlightened mind opened, and within movement, he perceived the unmoving.
Thus, he personally reached the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the East and became a Dharma-heir to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.

Prince, you have served all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions without exception, emulating each one perfectly. Furthermore, you have not merely succeeded to and flourished under a single Buddha alone.
By this means, you have realized that the deluded body and mind both belong to the power of wind, and you have beheld the true mind of the Dharmakāya.
It emits great radiance, penetrating all things without obstruction, like pure lapis lazuli; from this comes the name "Lapis Lazuli Light.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the senses], I observed that the power of wind has no basis and thereby understood its falsity;
I awakened to the Bodhicitta and attained the Truth. Entering samādhi, I realized the true wind of the nature-emptiness—the true wind of the nature.
Emptiness. It unites with the Buddhas of the ten directions above, attaining equality with the Buddha-fruit; it transmits the single wondrous mind below, transforming sentient beings.
This constitutes perfect penetration and is the foremost. Zhong said: "The east is the head of all movement, yet the name of the Buddha is 'Immovable'—this is stillness within movement.
To transmit the single wondrous mind is to realize the fundamentally awakened state that is without movement."
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I and the Tathāgata both attained the Boundless Body (the *ākāśakāya* among the ten bodies) under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Although it is not a different substance from the Dharmakāya, while the Dharmakāya is all-pervasively interfused with everything...”

This is the partial integration of the great element of space. At that time, he held four great precious jewels in his hands. (The old commentary is erroneous because it takes the subsequent phrase "the four great elements have no support" as a reference to earth, water, fire, and wind as the four jewels;

They illuminated the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space. Furthermore, within his own mind, he manifested a great circular mirror, from which ten kinds [of light] were emitted.

Subtle and wondrous jewel-light flows and permeates throughout the ten directions, reaching to the very limits of empty space; all the lands of the various banner-kings come within a single mirror, entering my body.
My body becomes identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction; my body is able to skillfully enter the lands within every mote of dust.

Extensively performing Buddha-works, he attained great conformity. This great supernormal power arose because I contemplated that the four elements have no basis and are born and perish through delusive thought;
that empty space is non-dual and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical. By illuminating this identity, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "I attained samādhi by contemplating that space is boundless; my wondrous power is perfectly luminous, and this is the foremost [method].
This is the awakening through entry via the great element of space. Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja (and so forth), saying to the Buddha: "I recall in the past..."
I and the Tathāgata were together in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, where we attained the body of boundless space and great supernormal powers.
This is not the same as the dull, severed, sunken, and obscure state of no utility grasped by ordinary, inferior beings.

At that time, having attained the four wisdoms, I held these four great precious jewels in my hand, which illuminated the Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into...
"Empty space" refers to the convergence of form back into emptiness within one's own mind. Furthermore, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifests from within the self-mind;

from this single Mirror Wisdom, the ten wisdoms manifest as identical with the Truth. Thus, these ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light flow and permeate the ten directions, reaching to the very limits of empty space, entirely forming a magnificent adornment. This is the fusion of emptiness into form. One simply beholds these various banners.

The oceans of royal lands enter into the mirror of the Dharma-body; because they are subsumed by principle, they penetrate the pores of the form-body, and the body being identical to empty space, there is no mutual obstruction.
Because they are subsumed by phenomena, these lands are gathered into the body, such that there is no body that is not a land.
Furthermore, one sees the body skillfully enter lands as numerous as motes of dust, responding universally according to the capacities of beings, and extensively practicing [the path].

Buddha-activity consists of benefiting oneself and others, thereby attaining great accordance. This is the manifestation of the divided body entering into lands; there is no land that is not the body.
As explained above, when form is fused with emptiness, all lands are subsumed within the divided body. By what means, then, are such great spiritual powers attained?

It is because those of the common world, non-Buddhists, and followers of the Small Vehicle cling to the four great elements as being substantially existent outside the mind, thereby creating great obstacles. By virtue of this—
I observed with clarity that these four great elements are fundamentally without support; they originally arise from the birth and extinction of deluded thoughts and ultimately return to emptiness.
Furthermore, I contemplated that empty space is non-dual and that the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical.

Thus, emptiness is not different from the land, and the land is not different from emptiness. Then, within the very locus where form and emptiness coincide, there was a sudden illumination, and I attained the realization of non-arising.
"Endurance. With quiescence manifesting before me, I entered the realm of perfect penetration. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:

'By contemplating the boundlessness of space, I entered samādhi; thus I attained unimpededness between emptiness and form, such that body and land interpenetrate, and my wondrous power is perfectly luminous.

Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after the passing of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I went forth into homelessness;

I have observed with clarity that the ten directions are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). My conscious mind is perfectly luminous, entering the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the grasping of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

(The perfected nature is like hemp; the dependent nature is like a rope; the imagined nature is like a snake. Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this is the foremost.
This is the great awakening through consciousness. Maitreya Bodhisattva (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. I went forth from the household life under that Buddha;
yet, although my body had left the home life, my mind still longed for wealth and nobility, and I delighted in visiting noble families and associating with kings."

"Great Minister, at that time, the Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa instructed me to practice the samādhi of 'mind-only consciousness,' causing me to penetrate the realization that the myriad objects of experience are merely manifestations of my own mind-consciousness— just like dreams or illusions, arising and ceasing without reality."
How could one fail to investigate and clarify the mind and consciousness, while instead placing weight on the objects transformed by them?
Therefore, by observing *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) for oneself, one ceases external longing and mental distraction, thereby accomplishing mental stability and entering *samādhi*.
Throughout kalpas past, one has served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges through this samādhi; when the concentration of consciousness-only is profound, the myriad objects—
It is like lightning: light on the outside but heavy within; there is no further running or seeking. Thus, the mind that seeks worldly fame ceases and vanishes.
Upon reaching the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I then attained the unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the cognitive mind (*vijñāna-citta*).

This is because what was previously practiced did not depart from the five stages of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and still belonged to the provisional teachings; only upon reaching this point does one exhaustively penetrate the principle of consciousness.
What is called the nature-consciousness’s clear knowing is the awakened clarity of true consciousness.
This wondrous awakening is profound and still, pervading the entire dharma-realm, merging into the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. First, worlds are consciousness-only.

Even throughout the entirety of space, including the lands of the Tathāgatas—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—all arise from the transforming consciousness and do not come from without. Second, all Buddhas are consciousness-only.

"World-Honored One, since I have realized that this is but mind-only and consciousness, from within the nature of the dharmakāya-consciousness flow forth the saṃbhogakāya and nirmāṇakāya, the infinite Tathāgatas.
If even the Tathāgatas flow forth from the nature of consciousness, how much more so can it be known that sentient beings of the other nine realms flow forth from it?
Thus, having reached the ultimate limit of *vijñapti-mātra* and perfectly realized the *dharmadhātu*, one beholds all Buddhas."
The environment and its inhabitants are both one's own mind; how could this very mind not attain Buddhahood?

Therefore, I received the prediction of becoming a successor (upapadya), immediately succeeding Śākyamuni Buddha in his position and destined to become a Buddha myself. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the Way], I replied:

"I have observed with clarity that the ten directions are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). This conscious mind is perfectly luminous, fully accomplishing the true nature of all phenomena. Having entered the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)," [I attained this realization].
Truly, one awakens to and realizes the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), no longer being deluded by names and signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).

One becomes detached from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—which possesses marks yet lacks intrinsic substance—and from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—which has a name but no essence—thereby attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and entering into perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*).
This is the foremost [stage]. The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is precisely the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and that which is produced by the karmic consciousness...

The appearance-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) constitute the two parts. From these two parts of appearance and seeing, there further arises pervasive conceptualization, namely the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
To be far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Master Lián said: "Because one does not awaken to consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), the mind turns away and pursues external objects. If one realizes consciousness-only, then..."
Gathering all objects back into the mind, one views worldly fame, reputation, profit, and sustenance as being like a dream or an illusion; how could one still be deluded by or attached to them?
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, immediately rose from their seats and [bowed] with their heads...

He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).

Twelve Tathāgatas appeared in succession during that single eon—namely: Immeasurable Light, Boundless Light, Unattached Light, Majestic Light, Light of Affection, Light of Joy, Wondrous Light, Inconceivable Light, Peerless Light, Incomparable Light, Light Outshining the Sun, Light Outshining the Moon, and Light Surpassing the Sun and Moon. These were the twelve Tathāgatas. Of these, the final Buddha..."
His name surpasses that of the sun and moon. That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like two people:
one is single-mindedly intent on remembering, while the other is single-mindedly intent on forgetting. Between these two, they may meet and yet not meet, or see and yet not see.
Because the two remember each other and their mutual mindfulness is deep, this continues from birth to birth, such that they are like a form and its shadow, never separated.
It is different. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If a child runs away and flees, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish?
But if the child remembers the mother as much as the mother remembers the child, then throughout successive lives, mother and child will not be separated or far apart.

If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha’s name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future; they will not be far from the Buddha, without needing to travel by way of the various directions.
Immediately, my own mind opened. It was like a person who has been perfumed with incense; their body carries a fragrance. This is what is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.

On my original ground, I entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. Now, in this world, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.
When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I have no preference; I simply gather all six sense faculties into a state of pure mindfulness.

Subsequently, one attains *samādhi*; this is the foremost [of all attainments]. (Zhong says: It is like a person with debts who flees to a royal household; the creditors dare not challenge him. This is because that upon which he relies is superior.

When sentient beings cultivate the *nienfo samādhi* and take refuge in the Buddha, the various māras of birth and death dare not invade or afflict them. For within the ocean of birth and death, only the Buddha is worthy of reliance.)
This is because [the Buddha] has attained great awakening through seeing. He mentions "seeing" alone because seeing encompasses all six sense faculties.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his kind, (and so forth) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are sands in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitābha. The twelve Tathāgatas..."
Subsequently, one kalpa was completed. The last Buddha of that period was named Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū. That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha (Buddhānusmṛti).
If we consider this from the perspective of principle (li), "mindfulness" (nian) refers to initial enlightenment (shijue), and "Buddha" refers to original enlightenment (benjue).

If we consider it from the perspective of phenomena (shi), "mindfulness" means to maintain a clear record without forgetting, and "Buddha" means to emit light to guide and receive [sentient beings]. As for the mindfulness of the Buddha...
For example, suppose there are two people here: one who is exclusively mindful and one who is exclusively forgetful.
Because he is exclusively mindful, whenever he encounters or sees [something], it remains with him; because he is exclusively forgetful, he neither encounters nor sees it.
If both persons are mindful and both possess deep mindfulness, they will certainly encounter and see one another, following each other from birth to birth like a form and its shadow. And so it is.
They are not at variance with one another. Now, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child;
this is the case when one person is exclusively mindful. Yet, if the child flees and wanders away, what is the use of such remembrance? This is the case when one person is exclusively forgetful.
If the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, then both are deeply mindful. Thus, the mother and child pass through...

Birth is not separated from birth; it proceeds directly from one birth to the next, like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing. Thus, through the mindfulness of the Buddha, [the truth] may be known.

If sentient beings bring the Buddha to mind, they should practice the mindfulness of the Buddha by combining both the gate of contemplation on phenomena (*sāṃketika*) and the gate of contemplation on ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).
Furthermore, they should practice the mindfulness of the Buddha by combining both the samādhi of single-mindedness in phenomena and the samādhi of single-mindedness in principle.
Then one will certainly see the Buddha in the present—either seeing him within meditative concentration or seeing him in a dream. In the future, one will certainly see the Buddha;

when the retribution for this life ends and the aggregates dissolve, one will see the Buddha come to receive and lead one away, attaining rebirth in an instant, and upon the opening of the lotus flower, beholding the Buddha.
Yet, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss exists right here; it is not truly ten trillion lands away.
Because the earth is vast and far-reaching, one is not distant from the Buddha. There is no need for any further expedient means to achieve the opening of the mind.

By being near the Buddha and being permeated by the Buddha, the mind likewise becomes the Buddha. It is like being near a fragrance and being permeated by that fragrance; thus, the body also becomes fragrant.
Therefore, know that the opening of the mind is not something superficial; it must be the manifestation of the Buddha from original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

By means of the fragrant light of mindfulness of the Buddha, one adorns the Dharma-nature, the primordial Buddha. This is what is called "Adornment with Fragrant Light. This was my own state at the stage of the causal ground.

By means of the mind that recollects the Buddha, not a single thought arises; the six sense faculties become profoundly tranquil. Thus, one reaches the fulfillment of faith, enters the stage of abiding, and realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Now, within this Sahā world, through the empowerment of majestic power, I gather those who recollect the Buddha and lead them back to the Pure Land.
Being thus fully endowed with the two benefits, when the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I found nothing [to choose] among the sense organs.

If you choose to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, then all six sense faculties will be gathered and restrained. When the eyes do not grasp at forms, this is the eyes reciting the Buddha’s name;

even when the mind does not engage with dharmas, this is the mind reciting the Buddha’s name. Because all six faculties are thus gathered and restrained, pure mindfulness can continue uninterrupted, leading to the attainment of *samādhi* and the realization of the state of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Although his present rank is that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), [he has already realized this].
The beginner’s faith, identical to that of the multitude, enters and abides in the fulfillment [of the path], thereby attaining perfect penetration; this is the foremost method.

○ Single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name is fundamentally no different from those who resolve to practice Chan meditation. Therefore, following the practice of nianfo (recitation of the Buddha’s name),...
This is followed by the practice of Zen meditation. Thus, one knows that in this land there are only two gates, which serve as the essential paths for entering the Way.
For it is understood that both Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are ministers who assist Amitābha; one welcomes beings through the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
First, regarding my instruction of the assembly through Zen meditation (*chán*), I have opened various doors and windows according to the capacities and dispositions of those within this realm.
Consequently, people of the world generally regard Zen meditation as superior while looking down upon those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*niàn fó*).

I know that such people not only fail to understand the profound secret of the Buddha-recitation method, but they also do not comprehend the subtle essence of Zen meditation. If one does not [understand] this...
If you approach Zen meditation with a distracted mind, you will certainly not attain enlightenment.

Likewise, if you do not approach the recitation of the Buddha's name with the intensity of a cat stalking a mouse, you will certainly not be born in the Pure Land. Do not say that reciting the Buddha’s name is easy while Zen meditation is difficult;
you should know that if it is difficult, both are difficult, and if it is easy, both are easy. This depends on the individual. If one’s power of faith is shallow, [both practices will be difficult].
It is deep; it is merely a matter of the intensity or mildness of habitual tendencies. ○ The Seven Great Perfect Penetrations are concluded.
Generally speaking, among the twenty-five gates, the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) usually begin with form (*rūpa*).

Here, however, they begin with sound (*śabda*), and yet the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is reserved for the very end. This is precisely because the true essence of the teaching in this land is pure within sound.
It begins with sound and concludes with hearing; thus, it serves as the fundamental framework for the essence of the teaching and uniquely accords with the spiritual capacities of those in this land.
Furthermore, while the seven elements begin with the element of earth, within this context the element of fire takes precedence.
Since excessive lust summons fire, this scripture—by addressing the falling into lust—arises as a teaching to warn those who are overly preoccupied with learning.

First, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is eliminated. Furthermore, while the seven great elements originally culminate in the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), they now conclude with the element of the faculties (*indriya-dhātu*).
This is because the *Amitābha* (Śrī-śikhin) method of mindfulness of the Buddha follows closely after that of Avalokiteśvara.

The practice cultivated by Avalokiteśvara is the singular path to Nirvāṇa for all Buddhas—the ultimate fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Now, as for those who are unable to cultivate the *nirvāṇa* of their own minds...
Next, there is nothing better than reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land].

This is because of the profound meaning of the scriptural passage which does not conclude with Maitreya, but rather concludes with Śrī-Ābhāsvara (Śākyamuni).
