At that time, the Śramaṇa Līzhīfāng of Chengdu showed the proof.
Then, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, countless *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named...”
"O Avalokiteśvara, under that Buddha I gave rise to the bodhicitta. That Buddha taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
This is a detailed exposition of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, intended for the capacities of those in this land, so that people may single-mindedly practice it."
Thus, the twenty-four sages were presented in succession. At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Avalokiteśvara.
His lineage was profound and his influence far-reaching; his name was bestowed in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.”
This is the correspondence with the teaching. At that time, before that Buddha, I then gave rise to the bodhicitta:
first, the wholesome mind, which is the vow to exhaustively sever all afflictions and the vow to study the immeasurable dharma-gates;
second, the compassionate mind, which is the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings; third, the straightforward mind, which is the [vow to realize] the Buddha-way...

The above refers to the fulfillment of one's vows. Having already resolved upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta), one must uphold the holy teachings. That Avalokiteśvara Buddha taught me the Three Wisdoms (*prajñā*):
first, the nature of hearing within the faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*), which is not the same as the hearing of mere erudition.

The hearing of sutras and the understanding of their meaning rely entirely upon the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with it. Second, the correct [state] of non-conceptualization.
It is not the same as the universal mental factor of volition (*cetanā*), nor is it the perverse volition that thinks of good or evil.
First, it arises from the correct cultivation of non-action, which is not the same as all virtuous deeds or various types of meritorious practices.
From these three kinds of wisdom, one immediately attains the integration of body and mind to enter this great *dhāraṇī* gate, never again falling back.
One has already deviated from the direct path by taking a circuitous route. Those practitioners do not uphold the sacred teachings but merely indulge their own whims;
perhaps they even follow false teachers—how can they avoid laboring in vain without merit? Question: In the first fascicle, you have already rejected contemplation as delusory.
Why, then, do you employ contemplation here again? Answer: The reason it was rejected previously was because Ānanda...
To single-mindedly identify this discursive thought as real and refuse to let it go is to mistake a thief for one’s own son;
therefore, it must be refuted and shattered so that one may recognize the thief and seek out the true son.
The present use of this thinking is like knowing it to be a thief yet borrowing the thief to kill the thief—turning misfortune into merit. Furthermore, regarding the twenty-four sages...
Although the gates through which one practices differ, when it comes to the essential application of the mind for observation, all employ this very contemplation.
Without this contemplation, there is no place to begin. Therefore, the foundational efforts of the twenty-four sages are all manifested within the single gate of Avalokiteśvara.
It is like making a lamp or candle from oil and wax; without being lit by fire, it will never shine. If...
This means that without relying on deliberation, one directly investigates by transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Thus, this single gate appears to be taught specifically for those of the highest faculties. Should one’s faculties be somewhat dull, it is unavoidable to enter by means of conceptual thought.
For those of inferior faculties, once they have attained hearing and reflection, they must further exert themselves in cultivation before they can gain entry. This being so—

It is clearly evident that the teachings on hearing, contemplation, and cultivation are presented according to their respective levels of depth. However, one must not employ distracted or deviant thoughts;
if one employs distracted or deviant thoughts, one will ultimately be unable to enter [the path]. Therefore it is said: "Know that the faculties are confused by distracted thoughts."
"In profound clarity, there is ultimately no seeing. It is further said: "Even though Ānanda possesses a powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts.

From this point onward, from the passage beginning with "starting from within the faculty of hearing" until "the state of quiescent extinction manifests before one," the text provides a detailed exposition of the sequential process of untangling the knots and the stages of cultivation and realization.
This constitutes the primary practice for entering the Perfect [Teaching] and is the most essential core of the entire sutra. Indeed, as mentioned above—
The arousal of the mind is the vow; this constitutes practice based upon that vow, ensuring that the vow is not in vain.
The superior’s upholding and receiving of these teachings constitutes cultivation based upon those teachings, ensuring that the teachings are not betrayed.
"At the very beginning, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object.
I have already given rise to this mind and received these teachings; however, what is the method for the initial application of cultivation?"
That which is called the nature of hearing arising from learning, reflection, and cultivation is fundamentally the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* mind;
it is a single entity possessing six functions. When present in the eye, it is seeing; when in the ear, it is hearing; and so on, up to being cognition when in the mind.
Now, we take the second [function], hence the term "within hearing. At this initial stage within hearing, if one does not give rise to a single thought, one turns the light back upon itself.
"Shine. To focus intently on the nature of hearing is called "entering the stream. For when one follows hearing and rushes toward external sounds, it is called "flowing out";
when one turns back to hear and shines upon the nature within, it is called "entering the stream. "Wang" (亡) means liberation.
"Object" (*suǒ*) refers to the sense-object of sound. Since the nature of hearing now turns inward exclusively, it no longer conditions any of the various sense-objects of sound;
this is what is meant by "the object is lost. For the knots of the faculties arise entirely from the objects; thus, when the objects are lost, the knots can be exhausted.
This "object" includes both the objects of movement and stillness, and here one first becomes detached from the object of movement. [Section on] Hearing.
The two characters "zhong" (middle) distinguish this from the middle of the physical ear, nor from the middle of the auditory consciousness;
rather, it is the middle that swallows all phenomena whole, wherein the entire dharma-realm is exhausted. It is also the site of the quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle, the true *araṇya*.
This is the locus of correct practice. If you have not yet attained clear understanding through the sūtras, you may recognize it directly within the midst of quiet sitting.

When the practitioner rises at the fifth watch, when the night air is clear and bright and the first sounds of nature begin to stir, if not a single thought arises, one perceives this nature of hearing. It is vast and perfect, luminous and illuminating, [pervading] mountains and walls.
There is no obstruction. The ocean’s darkness does not obscure it; sounds, whether great or small, distant or near, are reflected with perfect clarity, leaving nothing out.
Even the slightest breeze stirring the trees or the sound of footsteps ringing on the steps is not missed. This holds true even for things several li beyond the eastern horizon.
When a great bell tolls, its sound is indeed distinct and clear; yet simultaneously, several li away to the west, the clamor of many drums is likewise resonant and unmistakable.
Thus it extends even to the wailing on the southern streets and the laughter on the northern lanes.

The wheels of the carriage and the hooves of the horses each appear distinctly within the midst of perfect hearing, like reflections appearing in a great round mirror where not even a hair’s breadth is hidden.
When one reaches the state of profound stillness and silence, the hearing of that tranquility becomes even more boundless.

Only upon reaching this point does one realize that the wondrous nature is inherently possessed and is not something produced through cultivation; it has merely been obscured by the habitual conditions of a distracted mind during ordinary times.

[This is] a matter of concern. One merely fails to realize that [the mind] is obstructed and betrayed by itself. As for "entering the stream," it means to turn back the hearing that hears sounds in order to hear one's own nature.
"The locus where there is no locus" refers precisely to the two sensory objects of movement and stillness; "movement" refers to the presence of sound.
"Quiet" means the absence of sound. Now, first, there is the cessation of moving dust. However, there are two kinds:
first, convoluted sounds, which refers to those possessing meaning, such as the category of convoluted speech; second, direct sounds.
That which is called "meaningless" refers, for example, to the sounds of wind, water, birds, beasts, bells, drums, and so forth.
These distorted sounds (*kuṭila-śabda*) are further divided into two types: first, worldly distortion; second, logical distortion. Worldly distortion is again of two types:
first, the powerless; second, the powerful. Regarding the powerless, there is that which is termed "criticism of the past."
Now, as for the writings and affairs of others from the past, they do not concern one's own self; they merely indulge in distraction and lack the power to increase afflictions.
Therefore, it is said that they are "powerless. To be "powerful" means that by describing various sensual objects, they cause the mind to give rise to greed;
by describing various injustices, they cause the mind to give rise to anger; and by slandering behind one's back or praising while face-to-face, they provoke the mind. First.
All words concerning benefit and harm cause people to remain unaware; anger and joy suddenly erupt, and right mindfulness is lost.
These are all instances of worldly deviousness (*saṃvṛti-kuṭilatā*). As for the deviousness of principle (*tattva-kuṭilatā*):

it is as when one explains the principles of the internal and external, the heterodox and the orthodox, even down to the fundamental tenets and the profound, wondrous intent of the Dharma gates—causing people to remain unaware and instead give rise to understanding based on mere words, or to engage in deliberation and speculation.
Discursive thought is likewise a wandering following the flow of sound; it is the greatest obstacle to the fundamental hearing.
Therefore, in the Gate of the Patriarchs, the teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs are treated like enemies.

A practitioner must first refrain from engaging with all these various crooked sounds, but instead abide immovably in the inwardly directed nature of hearing—serene and luminous—and thus the coarse and manifest [delusions] will be eliminated.

Discrimination will forever cease and no longer arise. As for the sounds of flowing water, the movement of wind, the ringing of bells, the beating of drums, and all other straightforward sounds, these are even more difficult to eliminate;
one must apply the practice of "entering the stream" with meticulous care and earnest dedication.

They have long since perished and vanished of their own accord. Question: If the practice of "listening inwardly" has reached completion, does it mean that all sounds are as if in a state of drunken sleep—obscure and unperceived?

Answer: No. Regardless of what sounds may exist, the practitioner merely maintains the nature of hearing through perfect illumination, ensuring it does not leak out or flow toward the sounds. To clarify this further by means of an analogy: suppose there is a person...

It is like being dazed by water; unable to cross by oneself, one relies on another to pull one across. That person instructs one to look up at the sky and not look at the water for even a single breath.
If one forgets this instruction and looks at the water for even a single breath, one immediately drifts away and sinks.
This is also like that: turning the hearing back toward one's own nature is like looking at the sky, while no longer following after sounds is like not looking at the water.

There will be no further affliction of transmigration, just as there is no longer the affliction of drowning. Thus one knows that sounds cannot be eliminated; rather, one should simply practice "returning the hearing" with constant diligence.
This is also like how water cannot be eliminated; rather, one should simply look toward the heavens with single-minded devotion. Question:
Since all sounds are unreal, being like dreams and illusions, what remains after they have completely subsided? After all, it is nothing at all.

"Is it then that all who have heard and attained the Way are like those who are deaf? He replied, "Not so. This is not true cessation. It is merely that the faculty of hearing accumulated through sensory objects has dissolved;
for a time, the mind sinks into a state of withered stillness. However, before long, the mental faculty of hearing will open wide, pervading all of space.
This is what is called the manifestation of the fundamental luminosity. One will surely hear upward as far as the Peak of Existence and downward as far as the Avīci Hell."
When one reaches the point of extreme proximity, even sounds such as the crawling of insects or the fighting of ants—things one has never before been able to hear—one will surely hear them;
how much more so other sounds? Such a state of doubt, like that of a deaf person, is truly base and inferior. Question:

This "entry into the stream where the object of perception perishes"—is this practiced only during periods of quiet sitting, or is it also practiced while engaged in worldly affairs? Answer: If one takes only...
In seated meditation, what is the use of carefully distinguishing between distorted and curved sounds? One must simply maintain the same state in both movement and stillness;
only then will one achieve great samādhi. Question: It is easy to forget during seated meditation, so I shall not ask about that now.

Suppose there is someone engaged in worldly affairs who visits an old friend and practices on the road, merely practicing "hearing back toward one's own nature" (*pratyāśravaṇa*) while not grasping at any other sounds. How should this be understood?
Precisely while the nature of hearing is serene and still, suddenly midway through, one hears the speech of an acquaintance across a wall.
If this sound does not follow [the hearing], then the task of inquiry is abandoned. If it does follow it, would that not constitute a state of transmigration?

Answer: This sound is admitted to involve discursive thought (*vitarka*), yet it does not constitute the process of transmigration. As the verse says: "Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they pursue sound, they transmigrate.
If, at the time of pursuing sound, one is not deluded regarding fundamental hearing, this is merely the pursuit of sound—how could it lead to transmigration?
Question: Please explain the characteristics of transmigration and non-transmigration. Answer: You have conversely inverted the nature of hearing itself.
At that time, when a sound to be sought appears before you, if you single-mindedly seek it and the nature of hearing becomes entirely obscured and confused, this is the state of saṃsāra.
However, if at the very moment you seek the sound, the nature of hearing remains distinct and clearly unobscured, this is the state of nirvāṇa.

This is merely a temporary search that returns [to its source] immediately; it is also called "attaining function and then resting. How can this be said to be the same as "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*)?
Taking this as an example, whenever one engages in various matters, one should always reflect according to this principle.

Generally speaking, when a beginner practices in stillness, they gain the most power. Once stillness and concentration (*samādhi*) are established, one will gradually be able to engage in affairs without becoming deluded. If...
For a beginner whose practice of stillness and concentration has not yet been perfected, it is truly difficult to suddenly hope to engage with worldly affairs without confusion. Question:

Since engaging with worldly affairs without confusion is said to be truly difficult, it seems that for a beginner practicing "listening to the return," it will be hard to fully integrate both principle and phenomena. Answer:
Those who abide by worldly truth would rather abandon principle to ensure the success of affairs; those who practice the Way would rather abandon affairs to ensure the perfection of principle.
Now, for one beginning their cultivation and progress, who would require you to continue as before, meticulously investigating worldly affairs and striving to achieve both?
You should know that for one who has entered the path through "listening inwardly," though they remain in the world, they seek only to simplify their affairs.
Economize your speech. In the daily affairs of life, proceed with a carefree spontaneity. When you attain stillness, remain still.

Unless it is absolutely unavoidable, let every action and every word cease as soon as they are employed. Furthermore, while in the midst of such activity, do not allow even a hair’s breadth of delusion.
Even if words or deeds go astray, pay them no heed and feel no regret; strive only for uninterrupted "hearing back" (reversion), and the mind will naturally become serene. Question: The Patriarch...
"What do you mean by 'this side' and 'that side'? [The Master replied: 'In neither case is there any lack of function. Question: This has long been considered a great loss;
it is only after passing away and reviving, or being resurrected from death, that one can attain the subtlety of each. It does not mean that the beginner can achieve this immediately. Question:
"Regarding this section, many past commentaries supplement it with Tiantai’s Threefold Stop-and-Contemplation (*san zhiguan*). Why do you not do so now? Answer: "..."

The initial mind of the three contemplations enters by not departing from the deliberation of the six consciousnesses. Now, at the beginning of this sutra, the six consciousnesses are discarded and not employed;
by what means, then, does one enter the three contemplations? The perfect and subtle principle of this sutra is entirely the fundamental endowment of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
This is explained in detail within the *Śamatha* [section]. However, before a practitioner has yet begun cultivation, they must first achieve a perfect understanding (*yuanjie*).

When it comes to the time of actual practice, the practice arises while the conceptual understanding ceases. It is simply a matter of turning back to listen once; this is extremely simple and convenient, requiring no laborious establishment of extensive *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This is what the Chan school refers to as "entering directly with a single blade."
Once that which enters has become tranquil, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly do not arise.
Above, one departs from the knot of motion; thus, the knots of both motion and stillness are simultaneously removed. This is because when motion is eliminated, stillness manifests.
This is the principle of spontaneity. Effort is doubly discarded through this natural momentum.

Now, although one has entered the stream and lost all objective referents, though at first there were no referents, how easily could those referents have been lost? Though at first one entered the stream, how easily could that stream have been entered?

Although it is said that one must strive so that not a single thought arises, one cannot avoid the emergence of movement amidst stillness. To constantly withdraw and gather the mind is not true quiescence.
Upon reaching this state, the object of focus vanishes and there is nothing that does not vanish; one enters the stream and there is no stream into which one does not enter.
All movement is simultaneously stilled; the emotions are withdrawn and extinguished. With nothing remaining to enter the stream, both states achieve stillness.

From this one knows that while the previous "extinguishing of objects" merely involved the extinguishing of movement, the present state of "already stilled" signifies that the knots of movement have been completely severed.

Only after stillness is achieved does the [true] knot become manifest. Once one has attained such tranquility, one applies further effort and exerts power in the practice of "listening inwardly" (*fanwen*).
As this practice becomes increasingly profound and penetrating, even "stillness" itself vanishes; thus, the two sensory objects of movement and stillness are completely and simultaneously liberated.
Question: The cessation of movement is indeed the cessation of sound. However, the object of sound and the nature of hearing are as opposed as black and white; how can they be easily [unified]?

Because they involve discrimination, it is easy to eliminate them. As for the dust of stillness, it accords with the nature of hearing; the nature of hearing is ultimate stillness, and the dust of stillness is likewise still.
Both are without boundaries and both are without discrimination; thus, I fear it may not be easy to eliminate them. [The Master] replied:
"I am concerned only that you have not yet clearly perceived the nature of hearing. If you could see it clearly for yourself, how could [it be difficult]?"
There is a principle of distinction. This is because the nature of hearing is the mind, while the stillness of the dust is the environment.
The mind is a luminous awareness that is never obscured; the environment is dark, stubborn, and devoid of cognition. The environment is simply the environment, and the mind is simply the mind.
As you are you, and I am I, how could they be difficult to distinguish? It is like an ordinary worldly person who, upon entering deep into the mountains, finds no further entry.
In all these places, one is able to discern the stillness of the mountains; yet, in reality, one’s own faculty of hearing does not perceive even a hair’s breadth of it.
When one reaches a bustling marketplace, that stillness is entirely lost. This is because the previous state of stillness was entirely the stillness of the mountains;

apart from the mountains, there is no longer any stillness—this is what is called "stillness as an object. If one can single-mindedly reverse the hearing to listen inward, then the stillness of the nature will be ever-present.

Whether dwelling in the mountains or in the marketplace, if one’s stillness does not waver, that is the true nature of hearing. Thus, the nature of hearing is fundamentally unrelated to the dust of stillness;
yet when the sounds are urgent and intense, it is very easy to lose it. What difficulty could there be in this?
Generally speaking, after losing [the focus on] movement, there is no other skill or method; it is simply that through the maturation of one's practice, progress occurs naturally.

Reaching this point, one’s stage corresponds to the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), while in relation to the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it is equivalent to the first fruit (*phala*).
Thus, through gradual increase, that which is heard and that by which one hears are both exhausted.
The former [method] entirely eliminates the objects (*viṣaya*), while this method liberates the faculties (*indriya*).

Because the preceding diagram established the expedient means for eliminating objects, it posited the duality of the "capable" (the subject) and the "object" (the sound) of hearing, thereby causing the faculty of hearing to eliminate its objects.

In this way, as one gradually increases one's efforts and advances in practice, once the characteristics of the objects are exhausted and there is nothing external to confront them, then the faculties themselves no longer persist; even the "hearing" that is capable of hearing ceases to exist.
The faculty and the nature of hearing that hears—both are extinguished; therefore, it is said that "hearing and what is heard are exhausted.
This constitutes the initial resolution of the three fetters and the prior attainment of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Question:

Since you have already fully clarified the nature of the faculties and now cause both motion and stillness to vanish, if you further cause the nature of the faculties itself to vanish as well, does this not result in total annihilation?

"Yes. [The Master] replied, "It is simply because the roots are exhausted; why do you speak of the extinction of their nature? [The Questioner] asked, "Are the roots and the nature two different things?

[The Master] replied, "The root is like ice, and the nature is like water. Ice and water originally have no separate substance; therefore, they are not two. However, when ice freezes, it becomes separated."

Water melts and flows; thus, it is not one. Now, when you say the faculties are exhausted, it is merely like ice melting; how could it be like water drying up? Question: Previously, after the two objects had vanished, it was said that only the nature of hearing remained, which was extremely tranquil, profound, and boundless. Now that the internal faculties are exhausted, what further appearance arises to distinguish this from the former state? Answer: The previous stage served as a preparatory means (*upāya*). Now, having first used the ears to investigate the ears, the ears themselves have been exhausted. Having first used the eyes to investigate the eyes, the eyes themselves have been exhausted. Having first used the nose to investigate the nose, the nose itself has been exhausted. Having first used the tongue to investigate the tongue, the tongue itself has been exhausted. Having first used the body to investigate the body, the body itself has been exhausted. Having first used the mind to investigate the mind, the mind itself has been exhausted. Freed from those two objects, one temporarily grasps the nature of hearing as internal and the two objects as external.

Turning away from the external and facing inward, the internal faculty remains ever-present; thus, hearing is called "middle" and the flow of sound is called "entry," both of which are internal characteristics.

When the two objects are finally washed away and forgotten, the external characteristic no longer exists. Since there is nothing more to face externally, the internal characteristic gradually dissolves until it reaches total extinction.
Yet, there is a sudden enlightenment; there is no longer anything internal or external—this is the mark of the total exhaustion of the sense faculties (*indriya*).

If one examines this in light of the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), reaching this point constitutes the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Previously, the faculties were contrasted with their objects (*viṣaya*); the objects were regarded as "other" and the faculties as "self.

By excluding the other to establish the self, and by turning away from the other toward the self, the notion of a self (*ātman*) remained distinct and clear. Now, however, both faculties and objects [are seen to be empty].
"Extinction" (*miǎn*): both subject and object have perished, and there is no longer self or other; there is only the single *dharmatā*. Therefore, it is called "emptiness of persons.

As for the stage of realization, one should reach the seventh level of faith, which corresponds to the seventh *vihāra* of the *Pratyekabuddha* vehicle and the rank of an Arhat among the four fruits of the Small Vehicle.
Furthermore, one should know that these are the seven stages of faith (*śraddhā*) representing the high realization of a Bodhisattva.

This is merely based on the severance of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is said to be equal to the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; it does not mean they are truly identical to Arhats.
It is like a worldly Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate) of the lowest rank who temporarily matches the highest rank of a government official—how could their true name and status be entirely the same?
When hearing is exhausted and does not abide, that which perceives and that which is perceived are both empty;

this is liberation from contemplation and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*). After hearing is exhausted, the sense faculties and their objects are utterly detached, and a profound, singular, and boundless realm manifests before one.
This is what is "perceived," while the wisdom that illuminates this realm is the "perceiver. If [hearing] is thus exhausted...

If one abides [in this state], then the realm of wisdom will constantly confront [the subject], and the duality of subject and object will persist, ultimately becoming an obstacle to further progress.
Only by exerting effort and advancing further can one transcend this realm and not remain dull or stagnant therein;

thus, both the awakening wisdom and the awakened realm become equally empty and quiescent, merging into a state where no further opposition exists. This is regarded as the "severance of dharmas" (dharmoccheda) in comparison to what follows.
This refers to the grasping of subtle, continuous discursive thought.
When the awareness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bodhi*) is perfectly perfected, that which is empty and the act of emptying both cease;

this is liberation from the "repeated emptiness. The emptiness of the emptiness of the object of awareness—that is called the awareness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bodhi*), which is itself the repeated emptiness.
This is wisdom. This wisdom of the "repeated emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā), when first arising and not yet perfected, has both the subject that empties and the object that is emptied clearly present.
Now, when the realization of emptiness is perfectly complete, not only does the wisdom-object that was to be emptied cease, but the wisdom of repeated emptiness itself also perishes accordingly.
It is like drilling wood with wood: once the fire emerges, both pieces of wood are consumed. This...

The period prior to the "waning moon" (the fifteenth day) is designated as the stage of severing the innate attachment to dharmas; it corresponds to the tenth faith of the Perfect Teaching and is equal to the ten abidings of the Separate Teaching.
According to the three emptinesses, one subsequently resolves the two fetters and achieves the liberation through dharma.
When arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one.

Thereafter, the understanding that even a single knot is entirely empty and non-arising occurs. Indeed, when movement and stillness, the faculties and their objects, and emptiness and cessation—the six knots—are all extinguished.
In brief, all of these are the mind of arising and ceasing. First, one understands that movement ceases and stillness arises. Second, one understands that objects cease and the faculties arise.

Third, one understands that the faculties cease and awareness arises. Fourth, one understands that awareness ceases and emptiness arises. Fifth, one understands that emptiness ceases and cessation arises.
Upon reaching this point, if one dwells in the final mark of cessation, one will be shrouded by that mark of cessation and will remain perpetually in a state of universal voidness. One should...
This is a subtle obstacle that causes one to fall from the summit; therefore, even at the top of a hundred-foot pole, one must advance further.
However, this need not be laboriously eliminated through further exertion; it is sufficient simply to maintain a mind free of dwelling attachment and wait for a single kṣaṇa.

When this fundamental principle manifests before one, then this characteristic of cessation is utterly transcended. What is called "quiescence" is not a quiescence that exists in opposition to movement;
rather, from the beginningless past, it is the quiescence of being inherently unmoving. As for what is called "cessation":
It is not a cessation through counteraction; rather, it is a cessation of that which has been fundamentally non-arising since beginningless time.

This is the essential body of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*), the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, the reality-limit of *tathatā*. It is pure and self-sovereign, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
It is also called the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction and the Great Treasury of Radiance. It is truly the entire substance of the true mind, and from it all phenomena...

All functions are fully contained within this; when this principle manifests before one, then the mountains, rivers, and the great earth shall, by a mere thought, transform into supreme enlightened awareness.

The barriers between the sense organs will dissolve and open, such that the six faculties will function interchangeably for one another, and all the superior capacities below them will issue forth from this.
According to the stage reached, it should correspond to the first bhūmi, where one is free from fragmented attachments.
With one portion of ignorance, one partially realizes one portion of True Reality; yet, through this single severance, all is severed, and through this single realization, all is realized.

Thus, the merits of the forty-four stages are implicitly and fully possessed. Although its stage is said to be equal to that of the first bhūmi in the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), there is in truth a vast difference between the gradual and sequential approach and the perfect and integrated approach, as wide as the distance between heaven and earth. [The Section on] Gradual Succession (Cidi).

The section on "Resolving Knots" concerns the stages of cultivation and realization. Below this, the extraordinary excellence of what has been attained is explained in detail. The preceding section concerns the causal practice of perfect penetration;

this, however, concerns the resultant function of perfect penetration. Question: Causal practice is the essential requirement for cultivating the Way and ought to be explained in detail; why then is the text so extremely brief?
The fruition and its function manifest spontaneously once their merit is perfected; one might think they should be treated briefly, yet why is the text so detailed? Answer:
This scripture is identical for both the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas. From the latter half of the fourth fascicle to the first half of the fifth fascicle, it concerns the Tathāgata himself.
There is, in total, one fascicle of this scripture. It provides a detailed and exhaustive explanation of the faculties (*indriya*) and the cultivation of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-saṃbodhi*).

As for the reason why it speaks of the "fruition-function" (*phala-vṛtti*), it merely states that mountains, rivers, and the great earth may, at the mere thought [of the practitioner], transform into supreme enlightened awareness (*anuttara-jñāna*).
It further states: "From this, the six faculties function interchangeably. The phrasing is extremely concise. Now, the Bodhisattva speaks...
If the practice is detailed, one should respect what the Tathāgata has shown; if the application of the teaching is abbreviated, it does not supplement the Tathāgata’s essential text.

Both extremes are not sublime. Therefore, the practice should be concise while the application of the fruit should be extensive; thus, both the extensive and the concise are appropriate to their respective purposes.
Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains universal clarity throughout the ten directions and achieves two kinds of excellence:
first, above, one harmonizes with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power (*karuṇā*) as the Buddha-Tathāgatas;

second, below, one harmonizes with the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful yearning as all those beings. (The sentient beings of the six realms should also...)

Some versions include the four characters "Original Sublime Awakening Mind" (yǒu běn miào jué xīn), which are not repeated here. The following thirty-two manifestations (sānshí'èr yìng) correspond to the power of loving-kindness (cílì), while the fourteen fearlessnesses (shísì wúwèi) correspond to the reliance on compassion (bēiyǎng).

When the causal practices are fulfilled, the fruit arises accordingly. Precisely at the moment when ignorance is suddenly severed and true reality is suddenly realized, in a single kṣaṇa, one suddenly transcends the mundane world without being bound by the realms within it;

and one transcends the supramundane without being bound by the emptiness beyond the realms. One perceives only quiescent illumination encompassing all space, perfectly pervasive throughout the ten directions.

Upon attaining clarity, one immediately gains two kinds of sublime merit. First, above, one harmonizes with the fundamental, wondrous mind of enlightenment of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same essence as the Buddhas;
furthermore, one shares the same compassionate power as the Tathāgatas, functioning identically to the Buddhas.
This is because the fundamental, wondrous mind of enlightenment is inherently possessed by every person; therefore, as soon as it is realized, one harmonizes with those above. Second, below...
The sentient beings of the ten directions and the six realms share in his sorrowful longing. For that which the Bodhisattva realizes is what all sentient beings equally receive;
therefore, one who realizes this principle is able to share in the sorrows and afflictions of sentient beings, accomplishing their welfare through every means without omission.
Such is the nature of the two kinds of excellence. Regarding "compassion" (*karuṇā*): it refers to seeking out [beings] with pity and drawing them forth.

Suffering and yearning—this means that the aspiration to emulate the Sage and the pursuit of bliss share the same sorrowful yearning; it is the intent of the *I Ching* regarding "sharing the calamities of the people.
Previously, by establishing an objective through causal cognition (*hetuvidyā*), three kinds of continuity arose.

Now, by entering the stream and losing the objective, two kinds of excellence are attained. Establishing an objective is the root of delusion; losing the objective is the source of awakening. Establishing an objective...

This refers to the root of delusion in the very first thought-moment, which is the most subtle; it refers to the loss of the object, which is the coarsest aspect of the initial application of the practice.
This is because at the time of delusion, one proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, whereas at the time of awakening, one enters from the coarse to the subtle.

The pivotal mechanism for the transition between delusion and awakening does not go beyond the two characters "establishing" (li) and "losing" (wang). However, this character "object" (so)—the object that is lost—is particularly difficult to eliminate.
From the first fascicle, the text begins with the inquiry into "where the mind resides. Subsequently, what is successively refuted is merely the single character *suǒ* (所, "object" or "place").
It is called the "established object," the "perishing object," the "heard object," the "awakened object," and the "empty object.
By emerging from one such object, one immediately enters another. This single character *suǒ* is truly a stain that clings to the very body and is difficult to scrape away; it is indeed subtle.

It is the root of the two subtle attachments to self and dharmas. Only when one reaches the perfection of Bodhi and returns to the state of non-attainment will these objects of perception be completely exhausted.

World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, that Tathāgata bestowed upon me the [teaching of] "illusory-like" [wisdom] (the first being provisional and the second being heard...).

Therefore, it is like an illusion. "Hearing-perfuming" (the character *wen* here refers to the essence of the fundamental awakening of the nature of hearing; "perfuming" refers to what is called the internal perfuming of fundamental awakening). "Hearing-cultivation" (this character *wen* refers to the hearing that reverses the mechanism of auditory perception; it is the wisdom of initial awakening.

"Cultivation" means advancing in practice through this "turning back of the hearing" to achieve perfect penetration). The Vajra Samādhi (is ultimately perfected as a single nature, and thus is like a vajra).
Because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, my body manifests thirty-two transformations to enter all lands.
This title indicates the transmission and reception of the name of this samādhi to manifest its wondrous response.
World-Honored One, because in a past kalpa I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I was granted by that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of Illusory Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation.
Thus I attained the essence of a Buddha; for I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgata, and am equal to the Buddha.
This is its function. With both essence and function fully integrated, my body manifests as the thirty-two transformations, responding to conditions and meeting sentient needs as they arise.

I enter all lands, appearing in every realm without exception. Regarding these thirty-two transformations: they manifest as bodies within the ten dharma realms, perfectly responding to the various capacities of beings.
When expanded, there are thirty-two; when condensed, they comprise only the four classes of sages and the six paths of ordinary beings.
It encompasses all categories of beings. The Bodhisattva responds to their conditions and meets their needs, like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers.

However, those sentient beings who hope for a response must exert wondrous resonance; if there is no wondrous resonance, one certainly cannot falsely claim that the compassionate response is not all-pervasive.
○ Zhong said: "The object of sound is fundamentally empty, yet the nature of hearing is eternally abiding. Within this eternal abiding, everything..."
The sensory object of sound, as well as all phenomena, are entirely like an illusion.
By means of this illusory dharma-gate, one begins with cultivation through hearing and culminates in realization through hearing. Acting without action, yet action is truly non-action;
responding to conditions through application, the fundamental essence remains as it is (tathatā). This samādhi is named the Vajra of Illusory Hearing-Cultivation and Hearing-Practice.
Samādhi is the very foundation of the thirty-two manifestations. ○ He said: The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
First, the mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi; this corresponds to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Second, the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas;

this corresponds to the ninth stage through the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Third, the mind-made body that is spontaneously born in all its aspects and is free from deliberate effort.

The birth-body (*janma-kāya*). This refers to entering the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*) by means of equal enlightenment (*sambodhi*). The noble lineage-body (*ārya-gotra-kāya*) manifests simultaneously;
Avalokiteśvara’s thirty-two responses are precisely this lineage-born, co-emergent, non-active mind-made body (*anabhisamskāra-manomaya-kāya*).

"World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi and advance in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), such that their resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) becomes manifest and perfected—(resolute understanding being the wisdom of realization arising when the practice has reached its ultimate limit;

'manifest and perfected' meaning the wisdom of realization is about to be thorough yet not yet thorough, about to be complete yet not yet complete; the character 'perfect' is explained here as 'full')—if they enter a semblance samādhi and advance in the cultivation of the Middle Way's untainted state, then their partially true resolute understanding becomes manifest and perfected;

and so on, until if they cultivate the diamond-like untainted state, their ultimate resolute understanding becomes manifest and perfected. For them, I shall manifest the body of a Buddha and preach for them."

The Dharma causes them to attain liberation. (Question: How can a Bodhisattva manifest the body of a Buddha? Answer: It is like a mirror that has already become clear; when a form is confronted with it, the image appears. If the King were to visit the mirror of a subject’s house, how could there not be the King’s image? Question:

Does an Equal-Enlightenment Bodhisattva need to rely on the stage of the First Abode to manifest a body and preach the Dharma? Answer: Even when a celestial Māra manifested as a Buddha-image, Guṇaprabha still paid him homage; how much more so for the manifestation of the Wondrous Principle by a Bodhisattva of the First Abode? Though Equal-Enlightenment is honored, who would dare not look up to it?

As for those in training (from the three fruits prior to this, both the rank of the Wise and the rank of the Sages belong to those in training), they are tranquil, wondrously bright, delighting in solitary and sublime stillness, seeking spontaneous wisdom, and superior.

“Miaoxianyuan (Wondrous Manifestation of Perfection). Before him, I manifested the body of a Pratyekabuddha (appearing in a world without a Buddha; observing the transformation of phenomena and realizing for oneself that they are unborn, thus named ‘Solitary Realizer’) and preached the Dharma to bring about his liberation.

If there are those in training who sever the twelve links of dependent origination—whereby the excellence of the nature manifests when conditions are severed (observing conditions to awaken to the Way, knowing that delusion regarding the excellent nature arises from the twelve links, and thus severing them;

when conditions are severed, the excellent nature manifests)—and if the excellent and wondrous [nature] manifests in perfection (the ‘excellent and wondrous’ is precisely the excellent nature), then before me...”
Before those [beings], I manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation. If there are those in training (śaikṣa)—

who have attained the emptiness of the Four Truths (the sixteen moments of mind of the Path of Seeing, wherein they sever the afflictions belonging to the Four Truths and realize the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings), and who enter Nirvana through the Path of Cultivation (from the stage after the first fruit,

they progressively sever the eighty-one categories of innate afflictions of the three realms, realizing a portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation in each category)— and whose supreme nature is fully manifested, I appear before them in the body of a Śrāvaka and [preach the Dharma].
I preach the Dharma to cause them to attain liberation. (Having concluded the inquiry regarding the four noble vehicles:

If there are sentient beings who desire to awaken their minds clearly, deeply penetrating that sensual desire is the root of suffering, who refrain from violating the dust of desire—refraining not only from coarse and debased forms among humans, but finding no pleasure even in the delights of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations—and who seek purity of body, I manifest before them in the form of a Brahma King and preach the Dharma for them.
(The Brahma King is the Lord of the Realm of Form. Regarding the preaching of the Dharma, as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "The Great Brahma Heavenly King spoke the...")

This refers to the desire for discourse; it causes them to attain liberation (causing them to leave behind the dust of desire and be born in the Brahma-world). Although they have abandoned seeking yet possess everything, their further intense longing is equivalent to the "lower accomplishment" mentioned below.
If there are sentient beings who wish to be lords of devas, ruling over the celestial realms, I manifest before them in the form of Śakra.
I preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment. (As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "Śakra Devendra’s various skillful discourses" refers to this.

If there are sentient beings who wish to have mastery over their bodies as they travel throughout the ten directions (the ten directions comprising the six heavens of desire and the four continents), I appear before them in the form of a Paranirmita-vaśavartin deity (translated here as "Mastery over Others' Creations";

the Sanskrit is *Vaśavartin*. This means "accomplishing one's own pleasure by means of what others have created. This refers to the Lord of Māra, the sovereign of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations at the summit of the Desire Realm) and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to...

Regarding their accomplishment: if there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery, such as flying through the void (and being able to reach other realms), I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara (that is, Mahesvara at the peak of the Form Realm, with three eyes and eight arms, riding a white ox and holding a white fly-whisk), and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

(In general discussions of the various devas, one is cited to represent the rest. While Brahma-kings seem restricted to the First Dhyāna, they actually encompass all four; Śakra seems restricted to the two [lower] Desire Realms, yet he likewise represents the others.)

In reality, this includes all six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). As for the separate mention of the Heaven of Māra (*māradeva*), it is because the two types of Māras do not belong to the category of the "legitimate" devas; therefore, they are mentioned additionally. However, the four formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) are omitted, as this treatise concerns manifesting one's body, and beings in the four formless heavens do not delight in bodily forms;

thus, [the Buddha] does not manifest there. If there are sentient beings who love to preside over ghosts and spirits (the eight classes of beings), protecting the land (subduing Māras and safeguarding living beings), I appear before them in the form of a Great General of the Devas (referring to the eight generals under each of the Four Heavenly Kings, with Vemacitra as their chief) and preach the Dharma to them, causing them...

As for their accomplishment: if there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect its inhabitants, I appear before them in the form of one of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma to them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
(The Four Kings should properly be categorized among the Celestial Rulers; their inclusion here after the Generals is likely an error by the translator.

"World" refers here to all the lands on each side of Mount Sumeru. If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces and command spirits and deities, [I appear before them in the form of Śakra Devendra and preach the Dharma to them, enabling them to achieve their goal.]
Before them, I manifest in the body of a crown prince of the Four Heavenly Kings (such as Nanda and others) and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

(This concludes the section on seeking [fulfillment] from the various devas. If there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings (ranging from the Golden Wheel-turning Kings down to the minor kings of scattered states—these "scattered" kings are like the many grains of millet), before them I manifest in the body of a human king and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

(Question: Among the common people of the world, there are those who harbor deluded ambitions for the imperial throne. Does the Bodhisattva manifest in the body of an emperor to teach them the Dharma that fulfills their desires? Answer: This must be because [the Bodhisattva] possesses virtue and embraces benevolence, yet cannot bear the chaos of the age. He makes a vow to be the sovereign of the Way in every lifetime to govern the state through principle.

The Bodhisattva manifests as the very form they aspire to, teaching them the causes for being born into nobility and the virtuous deeds of an emperor, merely to perfume the seeds of a future life. How could he teach them the arts of usurpation? Hereafter, this shall be applied analogously.
If there are sentient beings who love their clan and lineage, and are esteemed and deferred to by the world (meaning they are deferred to by others), toward them I—

First, I manifest in the body of an elder (an elder is endowed with ten virtues: noble lineage, high rank, great wealth, majestic authority, profound wisdom, advanced age, pure conduct, perfect etiquette, praised by those above, and revered by those below;
thus he is the leader of his clan) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve perfection.

If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and terminology, dwelling in purity (broadly learned and possessing strong memory, finding joy in the Way, such as the kings of the various regions or figures like Shao Yong), I manifest before them in the body of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) and...

I preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success. If there are sentient beings who love governing territories (such as the Three Ducal Ministers and Chancellor), adjudicating states and districts (such as Governors, Prefects, and Magistrates), I appear before them in the form of an official and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

(The three preceding categories seem to be subsumed under the Confucianism of this land. If there are sentient beings who love various arts of calculation and divination to protect and sustain themselves (such as Guo Pu of this land...)
...such as those of the *ḍomba* class, or those categorized among medical practitioners, diviners, and various artisans—I shall appear before them in the form of a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*;

here translated as "Pure Conduct," one of the four castes) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success. If there are men who delight in study and leave the household life, upholding the various precepts and codes of discipline...

(From the ten precepts up to the full ordination of two hundred and fifty precepts: Before them, I manifest in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

If there are women who delight in learning and renunciation, upholding all the prohibitive precepts (from the five precepts up to the full ordination of five hundred precepts), before them I manifest in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment. If there are men...

Son, if there are those who delight in upholding the five precepts, I manifest before them in the form of an *upāsaka* (here translated as "attendant male") and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

If there are women who abide by the five precepts, I manifest before them in the form of an *upāsikā* (here translated as "attendant female," meaning one capable of serving as an attendant to a *bhikṣuṇī*) and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment. If there are women...

As for the person: internal governance establishes the self (the woman holds her proper position within; hence it is called "internal governance. Being noble yet capable of diligence, and being wealthy yet capable of frugality—hence it is called "establishing the self") to cultivate the family and the state.
(The domestic sphere is the source of all transformations; thus, it pertains to the order or disorder of the family and the state.

Before such individuals, I manifest the body of a female ruler (the consort of a Son of Heaven), a noble lady (the wife of a lord of a state), a titled lady (a wife whose rank is derived from her husband’s glory), or a great matron (such as Ban Zhao, the wife of Cao Shu-shu), and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve perfection.
If there are sentient beings who do not damage their male organ (those who throughout their lives do not violate the precepts regarding women), before them I manifest the body of a youth.
I shall appear in a male body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

If there are virgins who delight in remaining in their state (never marrying), who do not seek out aggression, and who would not comply even if subjected to forceful violence, I will manifest before them in the form of a young maiden and preach the Dharma for them.

Now, this is their accomplishment. (The search for rebirth in the human realm is concluded. These are all Bodhisattvas who adapt to circumstances, meeting them as they arise; like one carrying a bamboo pole and a wooden puppet, they perform upon whatever stage they encounter. This is what is called "gathering through commonality.
If there are devas who wish to leave their celestial status—(from here on, the eight classes of beings are mentioned; the *garuḍa* is omitted due to a brevity in the translation;

thus there are now seven classes)—although these seven realms of existence all possess supernatural powers, merit, and authority, they are collectively termed "evil destinies" because each has its own suffering and affliction. Therefore, many desire to escape them to become humans, hoping thereby to advance in their cultivation. To them, I manifest a celestial body and preach the Dharma.

The Dharma causes them to achieve accomplishment. (Because they enter into bliss, they are caused to achieve accomplishment; because this bliss emerges, they are likewise caused to achieve accomplishment.

If there are nāgas who wish to emerge from their nāga class, I manifest in a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment. (This is like the case of Nāgārjuna transforming five hundred nāgas so that they all received full ordination.

If there are yakṣas (translated here as "light-footed" [keng-chieh], which refers to yakṣas; there are three types: those on the earth, those in the void, and those in heaven) who wish to cross over to their own kind, [I manifest accordingly].

Before them, I manifest in the body of a yakṣa (the Bodhisattva also manifests his own form, for there is not so much as a single thread’s breadth of separation between the Bodhisattva’s countenance and the yakṣa’s mind) and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

If there are gandharvas (translated here as "fragrance-aggregates"; they are the musical deities of Śakra), who desire to be liberated from their class, I manifest before them in the body of a gandharva and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to achieve accomplishment. If there are asuras (translated here as...)

They are not handsome, for while the women are beautiful, the men are ugly. To those who desire liberation from their own kind, I manifest before them in the form of an asura and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.

If there are kinnaras (beings with human forms and horns on their heads, the celestial musicians of Indra), who desire liberation from their own kind, I manifest before them in the form of a kinnara and preach the Dharma.

I cause them to achieve success. If a mahoraga (a great serpent that moves on its belly) desires to be liberated from its kind, I manifest before it in the body of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for it, causing it to achieve success—just as when the Venerable Kapi was a serpent and received the Three Refuges;

having finished listening, [the Buddha] manifested as an old man in plain white robes and departed. This clearly demonstrates that Bodhisattvas are mixed among dragons and snakes, possessing neither fixed names nor fixed forms. (The manifestation of the bodies of the eight classes of beings is concluded. If there are multitudes of people who desire...

Those who cultivate themselves as humans— those who, while currently among humans, seek to attain a human body again after casting off this one, and who progress in their cultivation from lifetime to lifetime— I manifest in human form and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success. As for those non-humans,

whether they have form (such as those possessing auspicious or calamitous spiritual brilliance), or are formless (such as those who are ethereal, dispersed, or dissolved), or possess thought (such as ghosts, spirits, and numinous entities),
or lack thought (such as those whose spirits have been transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone)— if they wish to deliver their own kind, I appear before them in all such forms.

He manifests his body and preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment. (Question: Since those in the state of non-conception belong to earth, wood, metal, and stone, what Dharma does he preach so that they may attain liberation?)

Answer: The spiritual transformations of the Bodhisattva are subtle and wondrous, unfathomable. There is a distinct skillful means: this teaching is not spoken with the mouth, nor is it heard with the ears. (According to the thirty-two manifestations, none exceed the ten realms of existence. Within these ten realms, there is no manifestation as a Bodhisattva nor as a hell-being.

Some say: "Avalokiteśvara is already a Bodhisattva; why must he further manifest as such? Furthermore, the suffering of hell is too heavy to be delivered. This is called the "Pure and Wondrous Thirty-two Manifestations Entering the Realms.
All are achieved through the effortless, wondrous power of samādhi, cultivated through the熏 (xūn—perfuming) and 修 (xiū—cultivation) of hearing. They are sovereign and free.
This is the name of this realization. As explained above, such manifestations are indeed not non-existent, yet they do not involve defilement;
this is called the "Exquisite Purity" of the thirty-two manifestations. These are the bodies that enter into various lands. The reason for this is that they all arise through samādhi.

Through the cultivation of hearing and the practice of hearing, it is like the morning sun scattering its brilliance and a bright mirror manifesting forms; no effort of physical energy is required, nor is any expenditure of mental thought needed.
Conditions and objects appear spontaneously, originally devoid of deliberate action; hence it is called the "wondrous power of non-action.

Following the surging waves and drifting with the currents, it responds universally and appropriately to every situation; hence it is called "spontaneous accomplishment. There is nowhere it cannot manifest.
This concludes the explanation establishing that [the Bodhisattva] shares the same power of compassion as all Buddhas.

Regarding the thirty-two manifestations, there are slight differences compared to those in the "Universal Gate" (Pumen) chapter; however, their fundamental essence is identical, and it is permissible for some to be present in one place while absent in another.

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he fully manifests a body within the realm of bodhisattvas; according to the *Vyākhyāna* (Śikṣānanda’s commentary), he also transforms into beings in the hells.
World-Honored One, by means of this power of the effortless and wondrous Vajra Samādhi— perfumed by hearing and cultivated through hearing—
I share in the same compassionate longing as all sentient beings of the ten directions, the three periods of time, and the six realms. Thus,
I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of merit of fearlessness within my body and mind.
This title indicates that the name of the Samādhi, as well as compassion and reliance [upon the Buddha], constitute the foundation of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
"Fearlessness" refers to sentient beings; for one who has encountered calamity is in the midst of terror, yet by receiving rescue and attaining liberation, they achieve fearlessness.
"Merit" (*guṇa*) refers to the Bodhisattva; saving living beings and delivering them from fear is truly the most wondrous merit of a Bodhisattva.
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One. By now, through this superior power of universal compassion, I have attained the thirty-two marks of response.

Furthermore, by means of this power of the unconditioned wondrous Vajra-samādhi—perfumed by hearing and cultivated through hearing—and because I share in the same sorrowful longing with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, I have realized the Great Compassion of the same essence as all sentient beings."
Therefore, sentient beings look up to me in their sorrowful suffering and longing for joy; I immediately extract their suffering and bestow joy upon them.

If there are those who encounter hardships or dwell in fear, and they but once invoke my name, they shall immediately receive rescue and liberation, and no fear shall arise. I cause all sentient beings [to attain this].
Within my own body and mind, I have attained fourteen kinds of fearless merit; this is what is meant in our region by the saying:
"When one person is blessed, ten million people depend upon them."
First, by not observing the self through the observer, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions who contemplate my voice to immediately attain liberation.
(This is the first of the eight hardships; it serves as the general category, while the following seven are the specific ones.

Second, through the revolving of knowledge and vision, I cause all sentient beings, even if they enter a great fire, to remain unburned by the flames. Third, through the revolving of observation and hearing...
Furthermore, it causes all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters not to be drowned by the water.
Fourth, by severing and extinguishing delusive thoughts so that the mind harbors no intent to kill, it causes all sentient beings who enter the realms of ghosts not to be harmed by them.

Fifth, by perfuming the faculty of hearing until it becomes perfected hearing, the six sense-faculties are dissolved and restored, becoming identical to the auditory faculty; this can cause sentient beings who are about to be victimized by weapons to have those weapons break into pieces.
It destroys them, making their weapons like slicing through water or blowing upon light; their nature is without movement or agitation.
Sixth, when the cultivation of hearing becomes brilliant and penetrating, its clarity pervades the Dharma-realm, such that the nature of all dark obscurations cannot remain whole.
It can cause sentient beings—yakṣas (previously explained), rākṣasas (the terrifying), kumbhāṇḍa ghosts (those who bewitch), piśācas (ghosts that devour vital energy), and pūrṇas... [to be subdued].
(Heat-disease demons) and the like, though they draw near, cannot see him with their eyes (just as the local deity could not see Dongshan, or the ghost messenger could not see the presiding monk).

Seventh, when the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back inward, one becomes detached from all sensory dust and delusions; this enables one such that the shackles and fetters used to bind sentient beings cannot take hold.
Eighth, when sounds are extinguished and perfect hearing prevails, one universally generates the power of compassion, enabling one to cause sentient beings to pass through... [the sutras].
When traversing perilous roads, one cannot be plundered by bandits;
this enables sentient beings to attain fearlessness regarding the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). What are these fourteen? First:
because I do not follow the cognitions and views arising from the dust of sound, but instead turn back the mechanism of inverted hearing to reflect upon my own nature, this is [the first].

Avalokiteśvara: By means of contemplation, one contemplates the contemplator. Since I am of the same substance as all sentient beings, when I contemplate in this manner, I simultaneously encompass all sentient beings within that same contemplation.

Therefore, whenever sentient beings throughout the ten directions whose bodies are tormented by suffering and whose minds are agitated call my name with single-minded devotion, each shall attain liberation according to their respective voices.
This is because, though I observe their sounds, it is as if one were to observe sentient beings through sentient beings;
for sentient beings and the self are one. Thus, the general hardships of suffering and affliction become fearlessness.
Second, seeing that fire is the cause, one sees karma as the father; thus, one sees the fierce fire. When the sound is heard and one is liberated, the vision likewise turns away.
Being detached from form is called the turning back of knowledge and vision; one no longer summons fire.

Therefore, those who single-mindedly invoke the Name, even if they enter a great conflagration, cannot be burned by the fire; they are fearless regarding the perils of fire. Third, hearing is taken as the cause of water;
thus, when the karma of hearing intersects, one sees a great body of water. Now, taking contemplation as hearing, the faculty of hearing—
It returns and no longer summons water; therefore, one who can single-mindedly recite the name will not be drowned even if swept away by water.
There is no fear in the peril of drowning. Fourth, killing is the cause for this ghost to appear.

Now, when one turns the hearing inward, internal delusive thoughts are extinguished and external karmic deeds of killing are eliminated. When the mind is free from killing, it no longer summons the ghost. Therefore, it is said:
Sentient beings who invoke [the Buddha’s] name shall enter the realm of ghosts without being harmed by them; thus, they have no fear regarding the perils posed by ghosts.

Fifth, when practicing "hearing back" (*pratyāśravaṇa*), one employs the true hearing of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) in its entirety to internally permeate the deluded hearing, thereby perfecting the nature of true hearing.
Consequently, the six sense faculties are dissolved and restored, all becoming identical to the faculty of hearing. This is what is meant by "one faculty returning to the source."

This is the liberation of the six sense faculties. Since the six faculties are identical to the hearing of sound, and sound-hearing has no form, it means that the entire body is dissolved into formlessness.
How could that which is formless have any place where a blade might strike?

Therefore, it can cause the sentient beings whose names are invoked, when they are about to be executed, to find that the swords of their executioners break into pieces one by one, even as they brandish their weapons.
It is also like cutting water or blowing upon light; within my own nature, which does not receive the blades of weapons, there is not the slightest movement.
As it is said: "To bring one's head before a white blade is just like cutting the spring breeze. How, then, could one fear the calamity of weapons?
Sixth, when the power of hearing and perfuming reaches its ultimate limit, the inner luminosity radiates forth, and this light pervades the entire Dharma-realm; then, as for the various ghosts...
Deities are beings of subtle, hidden, and obscure nature; since their very character is to turn toward darkness and away from light, how could they possibly endure such radiance and remain whole?

Therefore, even when yakṣas up to pūtanas—beings who respond to the mere mention of their names—approach his side, they are unable to look upon him, being eclipsed by the light emanating from the Bodhisattva’s body. It is as follows:
The owl sees at night but is blind by day; the rākṣasa cannot see toward the sun, yet the ghost finds it difficult to see.

What, then, is there to fear? Seventh: when you practice "hearing back," the nature of sound is completely dissolved and sensory objects vanish. As seeing and hearing turn inward, they enter back into the source.
The faculties are extinguished. When both faculties and objects are eliminated, there is nothing within to which one is attached and nothing without to which one is bound.
One departs from all sensory dusts and delusions. By means of this wondrous power, one bestows grace upon sentient beings, enabling them so that shackles and fetters cannot bind them;

thus, even the difficulty of these shackles and fetters is no longer a cause for fear. Eighth: when practicing the practice of "hearing inwardly," sounds are extinguished and one attains liberation from the sensory dust of sound.
When one hears perfectly and realizes the ultimate nature of the faculties, sensory objects cease; thus, there are no longer external adversaries.
When the nature is perfected, all things return to internal fusion. Therefore, in every place, the power of compassion arises universally.

By means of this compassionate power, one bestows grace upon sentient beings, enabling those with cruel hearts and poisonous minds to be transformed into compassionate kin and relatives, so that they no longer harbor malicious intentions toward one another. Thus, although...
When traveling on perilous roads, bandits cannot plunder one; thus, what need is there to fear the hardships of thieves?
Such is the nature of the fearlessness regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) attained by sentient beings. Question:

How does the Bodhisattva’s immediate reversal of what is seen and heard concern sentient beings, such that those who invoke his name are instantly liberated from water and fire? Answer: Long ago, Cai Shun—
When a mother bites her finger, she feels a corresponding pain in her heart; is this not because mother and child share the same substance and are thus interconnected?
If even ordinary people can experience this, how much more so those who have realized the great compassion of the same substance—how could one doubt that they cannot act in such a way?
If one’s mind is free from the intent to kill, one may enter even the realm of ghosts. Those who can be seen by ghosts and ridden by them are all those who habitually take life.
When people of this world are possessed by ghosts, they often place blind faith in the false doctrines of shamans and sorcerers, slaughtering many animals in hopes of averting calamity;
how could such people possibly escape harm? ○ He said: "One does not [rely on] Guanyin oneself."
"Not harboring even a hair's breadth of the view of self" refers to the aforementioned passages such as "that which is heard is exhausted and that which perceives is empty.
"Observing with observation" means observing by means of the contemplation of perfect penetration;
this refers to the aforementioned "illusory Vajra Samādhi" and the subsequent "perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening."
Ninth, the fragrance of hearing is free from sensory dust; it cannot be plundered by forms and can cause all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greed and desire.

Tenth, pure sound is free from dust. (Sound merely designates the objects perceived by the ear; it does not yet designate the faults. "Dust" (*rajas*) designates the two faults of defilement and obscuration.

Thus, "pure sound is free from dust" means that although the sound itself is not destroyed, it is already free from the faults of defilement and obscuration; this is the oneness of mind and object. Alternatively, the character "sound" (*yin*) may be an error for the character "hearing" [*wen*]. When the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, there is no...
Facing whatever is confronted, they enable all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to be free from all hatred.
Eleventh is "Dissolving Dust and Revolving Radiance": their dharma-realm body and mind are like lapis lazuli, transparent, penetrating, and unobstructed;
they enable all those of dull nature and obstructive hindrances, including the icchantikas (here translated as "those without a virtuous mind"), to forever leave behind the darkness of ignorance.
This enables sentient beings to attain fearlessness regarding the three poisons. Ninth: by hearing inwardly and detaching from sensory objects, one becomes utterly liberated from form;
thus, one can manifest forms according to conditions while form cannot plunder [the mind]. It is like water reflecting an image or a mirror manifesting a likeness;
how could the image or the reflection ever plunder the water or the mirror? By means of this wondrous power of non-attachment, one bestows protection upon sentient beings.
It can cause sentient beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire; yet, the poison of greed remains fearless. Tenth:
the purely singular, perfect sound is entirely free from the characteristics of defilement and obscuration. The sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) merge into a single dharma.

Since there is no longer a sense organ that acts as the subject, there is likewise no object that acts as the counterpart. For hatred arises from opposition; when there is neither subject nor counterpart, then—

Hatred has no cause from which to arise. By means of this wondrous power of non-hatred, one bestows grace upon sentient beings, enabling all those who harbor anger and resentment to leave behind all hatred; thus, the poison of hatred becomes nothing to fear. Eleventh:
to dissolve the delusory dust of obscuring darkness and to revolve the wondrous awakening of brilliant clarity; therefore, outwardly regarding the dharma-realm and inwardly regarding the body...
The mind is like pure lapis lazuli, brilliant and penetrating without obstruction. By means of this wondrous power of non-delusion, it bestows its grace upon sentient beings,
enabling all those who possess the darkness of view-afflictions, the dullness of thought-afflictions, the innate obstructions of ignorance,
