and even those of the *icchantika*— the most extreme in their delusion— to forever depart from the gloom of ignorance.
Yet they are fearless toward the poison of delusion.
Twelfth: Their forms are fused and they further hear [the Dharma] while remaining unmoved at the site of enlightenment;

they enter into the mundane world without destroying it, and are able to pervade the ten directions to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, serving as Dharma princes at the side of each and every Buddha. They are able to...
To cause those beings within the Dharma-realm who are childless and desire a son to give birth to a son of merit and wisdom. Thirteenth:
the six sense-faculties are perfectly penetrating; their clarity and illumination are non-dual, encompassing the worlds of the ten directions.

This establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the Empty Tathāgata-garbha, which receives and upholds the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions without error, and is able to...

For those sentient beings who seek a daughter within the Dharma-realm—which has no children—this [Dharani] gives birth to a girl of upright appearance, endowed with merit, gentleness, and compliance, whom all people love and respect, and who possesses auspicious marks.
This enables sentient beings to obtain the fearlessness of fulfilling two kinds of requests. Now, for one who seeks sons or daughters, what could there be to fear?
They fear that they will ultimately fail to attain it. When a Bodhisattva fulfills their quest, they immediately cast off this fear of non-attainment.
Eleventh: when the physical form is dissolved, one hears again that the entire body becomes a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.
If the characteristics of the body were not fused, then this body would not be that, and that body would not be this; how then could it arise and be omnipresent?

Is it not like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers? Because their physical forms have already merged, they are able to remain unmoved from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) while pervading all places to make offerings to the Tathāgatas.
At the side of each Buddha, they serve as Dharma Princes (*dharmarājaputra*), succeeding the Dharma Kings and possessing the way of a son.
Furthermore, being fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, they possess the virtue of a man; thus, they are able to cause those sentient beings who are childless to obtain offspring.
For those who seek a son from me, a son endowed with merit and wisdom shall be born; and for those who seek a son, there is no fear that they will not obtain one.
Thirteenth: when the practice of "hearing inwardly" reaches its ultimate, the six sense-faculties become perfectly interfused, such that the eye is like the ear.

The ears are like the nose; both may be used interchangeably, yet their luminous illumination is non-dual. They encompass and nurture the wondrous Jewel-King lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions.
Because this luminous illumination is non-dual, the Great Perfect Mirror is established to manifest that there is no image that does not appear within it.
Because it encompasses the realms of the ten directions, it is established as the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness; this clarifies that there is nothing it cannot contain.
Because it only contains, it is able to accord with and follow the Dharma-gate; because it only illuminates clearly, it is able to receive and accept without error.
To accord with and follow is the仪 (yi) of Kun (the Earth); to receive and accept is the virtue of a woman. Therefore, it enables sentient beings who are childless to seek a daughter from me.
She was born with a handsome appearance, endowed with merit and gentle character; she was a woman beloved and respected by all, possessing auspicious marks.
As for those who sought her hand in marriage, none feared they would not obtain her.
Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm of ten billion suns and moons, there are six hundred and twenty billion *Ganges-sand* numbers of Dharma Princes currently dwelling in the world.
They cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings;
their skillful means and wisdom, which accord with the capacities of sentient beings, each differ. From the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, [I have developed...]
The Gate of the Sublime Ear. Thereafter, my body and mind become subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

I am able to cause sentient beings to hold my name, such that the merit of those two—myself and those sixty-two billion *Ganges*-sands of Dharma-princes who hold it together—is exactly equal and without difference. World-Honored One, my single name is no different from those many names.
Through my cultivation, I have attained true and perfect penetration;
this enables sentient beings to obtain the fearlessness of being called by name. What is there for those who hold the name to fear, such that you speak of "fearlessness"?
It is likely because those who hold the name may harbor hesitation, fearing that their merit will not be sufficient, or perhaps they encounter [obstacles].
Those who possess many names fear they may not measure up; this is the mark of one who is fearful.
Now, those who uphold the name of a Bodhisattva are utterly liberated from these two fears; therefore, they are also called "Fearless. Fourteenth:
Within this trichiliocosm, there are a total of ten billion suns and moons. Now, the various Dharma-Princes currently dwelling within this world-system together—

There are as many as sixty-two billion *Ganges* sands in number. Their practices according to their own realization, their cultivation of the Dharma and establishment of models, and their teaching and transformation of sentient beings through expedient means according to others—acting in accordance with the skillful wisdom of those beings—are each different.
Should there be anyone capable of fully upholding these names, their merit shall be unsurpassed. However, by me...
The attained root of perfect penetration lies solely in the single gateway of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), wherein the subtle is manifested.

This enables a single body to respond to infinite bodies and a single mind to respond to infinite minds; it is subtly wondrous and all-encompassing, pervading the entire Dharma-realm with sovereign non-obstruction, fully possessing the dharma-gates of the myriad sages.
Thus one knows that [this is the path] of the sixty-two billion bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
[They] realize that all [are] not apart from my Dharma-realm ocean of wisdom.

Therefore, between these two individuals—one who holds my single name, Avalokiteśvara, and one who holds the names of those many Dharma-princes—if their merits are weighed, they are equal and without difference.
World-Honored One, my single name and their many names differ in number; why is this so?
The merit of those who uphold [this practice] is truly equal and without distinction.
Because I have cultivated the single gateway of the ear-faculty and attained true perfect penetration, although there are many other sages, they can together match only my one person.

This is because the sentient beings of this region possess sharp faculties of hearing and thus mostly love the Way; therefore, Avalokiteśvara’s transformation is supreme, while the other faculties are dull.

Those who love the Way are few; this is why the transformations of the various sages are inferior. Thus, although their stages of practice may be equal, they differ according to the capacity of the beings they encounter.
Yet, as for the merit of holding the Name, it is established as perfectly equal on this basis. That sentient beings find fearlessness through calling the Name is likewise so.
○ It is evident that the Bodhisattva took responsibility for himself, saying, "Only I have attained true and perfect penetration. It can be seen from this that [the attainments of] the other sages...
It is not that [the previous statement] was not true; Mañjuśrī’s discernment merely serves to clarify this point once more.
This is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness, which provides all beings with merit.
This is the name of these fetters. As described above in various ways, these are called the fourteen powers of bestowing fearlessness.
They not only liberate one from dread, but also preserve one's merit; thus, my own merit is entirely contained within sentient beings.
Having thus completed the explanation of how he shares the same compassion and yearning as all sentient beings,

[Aniruddha] said: "World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully obtain the four inconceivable and unconditioned wondrous virtues."

This explains the four inconceivables. Although the preceding sections clearly demonstrated how [the Buddha] conforms above and harmonizes below, these were all according to the capacities of beings and thus still possessed limitations;
they could still be conceived by the mind and discussed in words. This [section], however, fulfills the measure of ultimate perfection, such that it admits no further conjecture or deliberation.
Furthermore, while the preceding sections all indicated "arising from samādhi" and thus still relied on the causal mind, this [section] proceeds directly...
Because I have inherited the perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I have already entered the stage of fruition; this must be the realm of Samantabhadra (the Equal Enlightenment).
World-Honored One, I have further attained this perfect penetration of the non-differentiation among mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, whereby I have cultivated and realized the unsurpassed Way.
Thus, my cultivation is perfect and my realization is perfect; furthermore, I have skillfully attained the four inconceivable, effortless [powers].
Because its wondrous virtue is ultimate, it is inconceivable; because it is supremely divine, it is beyond deliberation.
It is spontaneously sovereign and not produced through conditioned volitional effort; therefore, it is called "the wondrous virtue of non-action."

First, because I initially attained the wondrously wondrous faculty of hearing (the "hearing" that turns back to hear itself is *ādi-bodhi*; the nature of the self-nature is *mūla-bodhi*. When the initial and fundamental awakenings merge as one, both become wondrous;
thus it is called the "wondrously wondrous nature of hearing"). The essence of the mind abandons [external] hearing, such that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing can no longer be partitioned;
they form a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening. Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and preach boundless secret spiritual powers.

Mantra. Within it, there may appear one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, or eighty-four thousand śakaras (translated here as "firm and indestructible") heads.
[There may also appear] two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, or eighteen arms.
From twenty to twenty-four arms, and so on, up to all eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms,
or eighty-four thousand *mudrā* (translated here as "seals") arms; with two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes, and so on,
up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes— whether manifesting compassion or majesty.
Whether through meditative concentration or wisdom, they rescue and protect sentient beings and attain great sovereign mastery.
This clarifies that a single body can manifest many inconceivable forms. Indeed, these are the perfect penetrations realized by the twenty-four sages.
Each and every one is wondrous. Yet that which I have realized—the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing—is the root of all perfect penetrations;
it is the most wondrous among the wondrous. First: because from the moment I first attained this most wondrous mind of hearing, I focused my spirit with single-minded concentration.

Having completely shed the characteristics of the sense organs, one causes seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition not to be restricted to their respective original organs, yet without being able to separate them;
they instead return to the essence of the single True Dharma-realm, becoming a single, perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening.
They penetrate one another and function interchangeably, without obstruction or hindrance; whether as one or as many, there is nothing that is not possible. Therefore, I am able to...
Within a single body, he manifests numerous wondrous countenances; within these numerous wondrous countenances, he proclaims boundless secret mantras.
This is truly inconceivable. What are these "wondrous countenances"? They are like the head, which serves as the center for the six sensory functions.
The arms represent the compassion that receives and embraces; the eyes represent the wisdom that illuminates and understands. These are all the wondrous countenance.
Yet sentient beings take their own bodies and faculties for granted, remaining deluded and unaware, so that they function entirely as karmic activities.

Since I have attained them, they are like spring entering its proper season, or like the moon moving through the sky. Whatever is grasped by the hand becomes a wondrous function. Speaking first of the head, it manifests of itself.
From one head up to eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads;
speaking of arms, from manifesting two arms up to eighty-four thousand *mudrā* arms; speaking of eyes, from manifesting two eyes...
Up to eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes, which correspond both to the number of afflictions (*kleśa*) and serve as their antidote;
they are fully endowed with eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates. Among these, some bestow compassion to gather the hearts of virtuous people, which is the aspect of joy;
others manifest majesty to break the courage of malevolent spirits and demons.
This is the aspect of wrath. Alternatively, through concentration (*samādhi*), it employs the gate of quelling and dispersing agitation; this is the aspect of clarity and withdrawal.
Alternatively, through wisdom (*prajñā*), it destroys the cavern of ignorance; this is the aspect of opening and illuminating. The heads, arms, and eyes all possess fourfold distinctions;
therefore, they can respond universally to the afflictions of the world, providing skillful guidance and instruction, responding to every stimulus without fail.
The mind rescues and protects sentient beings, thereby attaining great mastery. If the physical form can be thus, one may know by analogy that the mantra should likewise possess these four qualities.
Regarding the wondrous countenance, it should be able to manifest from the very first stage (Prathamā-bhūmi);
there may simply be differences in the number [of heads or eyes]. The Sūtra states that even Śakra is able to manifest a thousand heads and eyes, yet when we evaluate his...
The fundamental position corresponds precisely to the third stage (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching; the meaning can be inferred by analogy. Master Zhong said:

"Sentient beings are deluded regarding this enlightened nature, and thus the six sense organs manifest eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). Bodhisattvas awaken to this enlightened nature, and its entirety manifests as eighty thousand virtuous functions.
If you do not believe in these bodhisattva virtues and functions, simply observe the afflictions of your own six sense organs."
Thoughts fly about in every moment; is there any limit to them?

Second, through my hearing (hearing being the nature of hearing) and reflection (reflection being the practice of entering oblivion), I have escaped the six sense-objects (meaning that both the phenomena of movement and stillness are clearly non-arising).
Thus, just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, I am able to manifest each and every form and recite each and every mantra with wondrous skill.

With this form and these mantras, I am able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings; therefore, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, they all call me "The Bestower of Fearlessness."
This clarifies the inconceivability of each individual body and form. Second, by means of the merit of my hearing and contemplation, I have emerged from the six sense-objects;

like a sound passing through a thick wall without any obstruction, I am thus able to manifest each individual form with marvelous skill, appearing as various bodies in accordance with various capacities, and reciting each mantra while speaking [the Dharma] from each respective body.
Mantra. Each of his individual bodies and each of his mantras bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings and liberate them from their terrors;
thus, he causes the sentient beings of lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions to all call him the "Bestower of Fearlessness.
This is because his merit in universally rescuing suffering across all dust-like realms is exceptionally superior. Question: How does this differ from the fourteen [vows]?
What is the distinction between [the Buddha's] fearlessnesses? Answer: The fourteen fearlessnesses merely cause sentient beings to liberate themselves by invoking his name;
they do not yet involve manifesting a physical form or reciting mantras. How could these two possibly be conflated?

Third, by virtue of my cultivation of the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and pure root, may all worlds where I travel cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.

This clarifies the inconceivable nature of his transformative influence. Thirdly, because he cultivated the single gateway of the ear-faculty—the fundamental, wondrous, and perfect penetration—he has already attained the pure original root.
Consequently, regarding the objects of the six sense-fields, he is entirely free from attachment and is able to relinquish them all.
Through this relinquishment, he invokes further relinquishment; thus, in all the worlds he traverses, his transformative influence remains and his spirit persists, likewise enabling all beings...
He gave up the precious treasures of his body and offered them all to me, seeking my compassion to accept them and perform the work of a Buddha through this gift.
Indeed, the stingy mind of sentient beings is the most difficult to break, and the mind of renunciation is the most difficult to arouse.
That he was moved to break his stinginess and delight in renunciation upon merely passing by is truly due to the inconceivable power of majestic spiritual authority.

It is indeed so. Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized ultimate fruition, one is able to use various precious jewels to make offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm.
If one seeks a wife, one obtains a wife; if one seeks a son, one obtains a son; if one seeks the three...
One attains samādhi by seeking samādhi; one attains long life by seeking long life; and so on, up to attaining great nirvāṇa by seeking great nirvāṇa.
This clarifies the inconceivable nature of making offerings. Fourth, since I have already first attained the *tathāgatagarbha* mind, I ascend...
Having ultimately entered the ocean of wondrous adornment, the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma has been opened;
possessing immeasurable merit and wisdom, they can produce infinite treasures from their hands.

With these various treasures—namely, robes, garlands, incense, and lamps—they offer them to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, equaling those who are as sublime as the four seas, extending even to...
Toward all sentient beings of the six realms within the dharma-realm, one should offer equal and sincere worship with a mind of universal equality.
One's kingdom, cities, wife, and children are called external wealth; one’s long life and physical existence are called internal wealth.

By means of this giving of material wealth, one enables sentient beings to obtain wives when seeking wives, obtain children when seeking children, and even obtain long life when seeking long life. This is therefore the gift of material wealth.
Furthermore, samādhi and nirvāṇa belong to the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

Seeking samādhi and attaining samādhi—whether it be the stage of the one fruit, the two fruits, or up to the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood—and likewise seeking great nirvāṇa and attaining great nirvāṇa:
even though the Tathāgata is the most supreme and ultimate fruit, he still bestows it upon those who achieve it; this is why it is called the gift of Dharma. Indeed, I...
Observing sentient beings, they possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata; therefore, they offer the same offerings as a Buddha.
Through the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—they perform such inconceivable true worship.

Among these four inconceivables, the first three still pertain to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), while the fourth declares the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddha-mind, which closely approximates the supreme realization of Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue).

Question: Why does the first stage of perfect penetration overlap with the profound stages? Answer: For a person of perfect capacity, the first stage encompasses the merits of all forty-two stages without omission.
Since this is the case for the first stage, it is likewise for every subsequent stage; there is no need for doubt.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "I have attained the Samādhi of Universal Illumination through the gateway of the ears. By means of the mind’s mastery over its objects, I entered the phase of 'flowing-in' and thereby attained Samāpatti.
This has led me to the fulfillment of Bodhi; it is the foremost method. World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well-attained this Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration.
In the midst of that great assembly, he bestowed upon me the prophecy of my name as Avalokiteśvara. It was because of me...
Because my observation and hearing of the ten directions are perfectly luminous, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions;
this concludes the perfection of penetration. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I entered deeply through the single gateway of the ear-faculty.

Through the accomplishment of the practice of "reversing the hearing," the six faculties were spontaneously uprooted, and quiescent extinction manifested before me. By means of the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination, I attained the supreme state of being equal to all Buddhas.
The Buddha, descending to transform sentient beings, establishes teachings according to conditions; there is nothing he does not master.
Tracing back to its original cause, it is simply the entry into the stream and the forgetting of objects that serves as the foundational practice.

By means of this, one attains samādhi, accomplishes bodhi, and perfectly realizes the cultivation and verification of the stage of fruition. This so-called "perfect penetration" is the foremost. World-Honored One, that...

The Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata, praised me for having skillfully attained the Dharma-door of perfect penetration. Within that great assembly, he bestowed upon me the prophecy of the name Avalokiteśvara.
This was at the time of my initial realization during the first stage of the Bodhisattva path (*prathamabhūmi*). Thus, we have already seen the harmonious union between teacher and disciple.
Because my perception of the ten directions is perfectly luminous—like sound passing through a wall, or like the moon reflected in water—I accordingly [respond to all].

Responses accord with conditions; thus, the name of Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Having realized this, I further see the mutual resonance between the response and the invocation.
Name and reality correspond perfectly, and its renown spreads everywhere. Through this, I have attained perfect penetration.

How could this be a mere coincidence? According to the *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi Sūtra* and the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*, both state that this Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood long ago in the past, with the title Tathāgata *Saddharmaprabhāsa*.

Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* explains that in the past, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha bestowed a prediction upon Prince Animiṣa, naming him Avalokiteśvara. Thus, regarding the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka*:

These are all merely names for the concealed fundamental essence and the manifested traces of the present sutra. Now that he has attained perfect penetration, he is indeed the latter incarnation of the Prince.
When the assembly had each finished speaking, [The text continues: ...the assembly had each finished speaking.
At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light from his lion throne (symbolizing the manifestation of his entire body).

This light reached far to drench the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas, as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions (signifying the penetration of one’s own fruition into the fruition of others), as well as the crowns of the Dharma-Prince Bodhisattvas (signifying the penetration of one’s own cause into the cause of others).

That the light specifically drenched their crowns signifies that this principle of perfect penetration is the most extraordinary and unsurpassed teaching. Those Tathāgatas likewise [emitted light] from their five...

Their bodies simultaneously emitted jewel-like radiance from every minute particle of dust, which came to drench the crowns of the Buddhas' heads, as well as those of all the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats in the assembly.
The forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all resounded with the sounds of the Dharma; these lights interlaced and entwined like a net of precious threads.

(This symbolizes that the manifestation of perfect penetration means that all sounds are the voice of the Buddha and all forms are the form of the Buddha. This entire great assembly attained what they had never experienced before. (This indicates their mutual illumination.)

In the height of joy, they attained thorough enlightenment. All universally obtained the Vajra-samādhi (revealing that the King of Śūraṅgama is the adamantine precious awakening, the impartial Dharma-realm).

Immediately, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingled and variegated (the differentiation of the flowers into distinct colors serves to symbolize conduct).

The empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures (the treasures possess radiance, which serves to symbolize wisdom). This great earth and its mountains within the Sahā world...

The rivers simultaneously vanished (symbolizing that the myriad phenomena have merged into one), and only the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, appeared, merging into a single realm (symbolizing the ultimate realization of the single nature).

Chanting and hymns were spontaneously performed (symbolizing that the Dharma-music of perfect penetration is omnipresent). [This corresponds to the passage in Volume Four concerning Pūrṇa’s inquiry into how the mountains, rivers, and great earth suddenly arise from the fundamentally pure state;
it was precisely to enable him to behold this境 *jingjie* so that it might now manifest before his eyes.]

This is the Buddha manifesting a portentous response. For when the various sages each describe their perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), it is as if all the doors of a magnificent mansion have been opened;
thus, the Buddha again manifests a portent to respond to them. These sages reveal the truth through words, while the Tathāgata reveals it through physical signs;
together they desire that sentient beings, by receiving the words and contemplating the signs, may achieve awakening.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince: "Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and the Arhats, each of whom has spoken of the skillful means by which they first attained the Way, all claiming to have cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In their respective practices, there is in reality no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence. I now wish..."
To cause Ānanda to attain awakening, [the Buddha spoke] in twenty-five sections. "Who shall correspond to this capacity?

Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for those sentient beings in this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the Unsurpassed Way, by what gate of skillful means can they achieve success with ease?"
This edict was for Mañjuśrī to select the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*).

The reason he alone was commanded is that he is the Great Wisdom of the Site of Quiescence (*śānta-maṇḍala*) and the Dharma-eye of all the assemblies. Thereupon, after the Tathāgata had manifested these auspicious omens, he addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta, saying:
"You should now observe these twenty-five great Arhats who are beyond training..."
Whether it be a Bodhisattva or an Arhat, what each person cultivates and realizes is equally termed "expedient means" and "reality.

Yet, in their respective practices, there is truly no distinction of superior or inferior, nor of priority or sequence. For while there may be a thousand paths and nine crossroads, the royal city remains one;
whether one travels slowly or swiftly, with skill or clumsiness, the destination reached is the same. I now wish to cause Ānanda to open [his understanding].
He attained great enlightenment. He wondered among these twenty-five lines, who might possess the capacity to respond to Ānanda’s faculties?

Furthermore, he considered not only the capacity of this one person in the present, but also, after his parinirvāṇa, what means must the sentient beings of this world rely upon as the true cause for entering the Bodhisattva vehicle and seeking the ultimate fruit of the unsurpassed path.

"Only by facing the specific capacity of the individual can one achieve realization easily. Since one must always practice according to that capacity, yet can only take up a single gate, it is essential to make a selection.
Mañjuśrī, you possess the eye that discerns dharmas; therefore, please examine this for me with meticulous care."
It would be well to bring forth this wondrous gate to bestow grace upon future students.
Then Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and,
sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha.
Rising from his seat, he prostrated himself. This was in accordance with the command of his venerable teacher and to receive the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power for his empowerment.

Although this was a great being who had already attained the fruit of enlightenment, he followed such formal protocols to manifest the proper conduct; this may serve as a warning to those who harbor arrogance.

The nature of the ocean of awakening is tranquil and perfect; this perfect tranquility of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous. When primordial luminosity shines forth, the "object" arises; once the object is established, the nature of the shining light perishes.
This explains the origin of the selection [of the path]. The verse says: If you wish to seek the return from delusion to truth, you must understand how delusion arises from truth.
Furthermore, by what cause do all these delusions arise? To examine the nature of human beings: it takes cognitive awareness as its basis.
Because its substance is awakening, it takes "awakening" as its reference; because its measure is profound and vast, it takes the "ocean" as its reference.

This nature of the ocean of awakening is tranquil and still, yet limpid; it is free from all arising and ceasing. It is penetratingly clear and perfect, free from all partiality or obscuration. Being both perfect and limpid, it is thus.
Collectively, this is termed the nature of awakening (*bodhi*). This nature of awakening is fundamentally and inherently wondrous; it does not depend on artificial effort and has no spatial location.
This is because, upon that originally luminous nature, a false illumination and function arise, thereby establishing spatial locations.

Once the locations are falsely established, the original nature of that illumination and function is consequently lost. It is like clouds arising that must necessarily obscure the sun. This is precisely...
Based on fundamental enlightenment (*benjue*), the karma-consciousness (*ye-shi*) is formed. "The ocean of awakening" refers to the essence (*ti*); this indicates the Greatness of Essence.

"Serene and perfect" refers to the characteristic (*xiang*); this indicates the Greatness of Characteristic. "Primordially wondrous" refers to the function (*yong*); this indicates the Greatness of Function.
These three greatnesses serve as the basis for all delusions.

"From delusion comes space; based on space, worlds are established. When thought becomes clarified, it forms a land; when perception arises, it becomes sentient beings. This clarifies the arising of all phenomena.
Having become deluded regarding the nature of awareness, one forms the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*);

consequently, becoming deluded regarding the nature of emptiness, one forms "stubborn emptiness. Therefore, it is said: "From delusion comes space. From within this darkness where emptiness is obscured, [the seeds] congeal...
Darkness constitutes form. Furthermore, two kinds of worlds are established: the insentient and the sentient. Therefore, it is said that "the world is established based on space.
Because a portion of the floating vacuity of chaotic thought is taken up and coagulates into something insentient, the physical realm (the *bhājana-loka*) is formed;
hence it is said that "when thought clarifies, the land is formed. Because a portion of the floating vacuity of delusive thought is taken up and coagulates...
There is that which knows; because it constitutes the body of faculties, it is said that cognition and awareness constitute sentient beings.
This is precisely the arising of the two divisions of appearance and perception based upon the ignorance of the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The minute dust-motes of worlds with outflows are all born dependent upon emptiness.
When the bubble ceases, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so, then, the various realms of the threefold existence?
This clarifies the cessation and return of all phenomena. Now, this empty space of delusion is vast and has no exterior;
it is not inherently minute or inferior. Yet, when compared to Great Enlightenment, it is immeasurably greater.
This space arises within Great Enlightenment like a single bubble in the ocean, and thus becomes exceedingly minute and inferior. If even space is such, how much more so are the outflows?
As for these lands as numerous as motes of dust, all of which are established within space—how infinitesimal must they be?
Thus, if this bubble were to perish, even the space that encompasses the external realms would return to its original non-existence;
how much more so could the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—which arise from space—possibly exist independently? They originally derive from the ultimate void.
Therefore, it can be swiftly extinguished. This means that when one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all be dissolved and vanish.
Question: Since you have just clarified the process of arising, why do you suddenly speak of returning to extinction? Answer: Returning to extinction is precisely returning to the source.
Now, as we select those with superior faculties to enter deeply, we are specifically planning the path for returning to the source; therefore, I have fully elucidated the process of arising.
"Empty. This is merely to initiate the ease of returning to cessation. ○ Zhong says:
"The nature of the ocean of awakening is tranquil and perfect" refers to the "nature-awakening is wondrously luminous" and the "fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous" in Volume Two.

"Perfect luminosity shines forth, giving rise to objects" refers to "based on luminosity, objects are established; since objects are falsely established, they give rise to your false subjectivity. This is delusive confusion.

"There is empty space" up to "all things arise depending on space" constitutes eight propositions; these refer to the arousal of worldly dust (*rajas*), whereby arising forms the world and stillness constitutes empty space.
The two lines "When the bubble perishes, space is fundamentally non-dual" refer to the severance of the three conditions.

The three causes do not give rise [to delusion]; the nature of madness naturally subsides. This "subsiding" is precisely Bodhi. Throughout this entire *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the truth is revealed both horizontally and vertically;
every point converges upon it like mirrors reflecting one another's light. One must urgently fix one’s gaze upon this.
The nature of returning to the source is non-dual; yet there are many gates of expedient means. The sagely nature is all-pervasive; both following and reversing are expedient means.
For those of initial resolve entering samādhi, their progress—whether slow or swift—is not of the same order.

This clearly explains the selection of the appropriate faculties. Now, while all phenomena can be brought to cessation, once one has recognized the path back to the source, if one attains that return to the source, the principle is singular; the awakened nature is certainly not dual.
However, for those who wish to enter this non-dual awakened nature, there are indeed many expedient doors, just as the capital region is one, yet the entryways are many.
There are many divergent paths. If one is a sage who has fully realized this nature, then all phenomena are perfectly interfused and every matter is without obstruction.
Thus, whether it be hatred or love, suffering or joy, there is nothing that is not a gateway for entering into principle; one must not make discriminations between them.
If a person who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment wishes to enter samādhi, they may possess either perfect faculties or imperfect ones.
As for the roots [of capacity], days and kalpas differ by multiples; thus, there are certainly differences in the speed of realization.
To accord with the faculties of this region is "accordant," while to oppose the faculties of this region is "adverse. Being accordant leads to speed, whereas being adverse leads to slowness.
How could one not exercise careful discernment? It is like the roads leading to the capital: they vary a thousandfold in being circuitous or direct; how could all of them be shortcuts? Furthermore—
One must not fail to choose the path before rushing forward.
When the perceptions of form coalesce into dust, the refined clarity cannot penetrate through. How can one fail to achieve clear penetration? It is therein that one attains perfect penetration.
Sounds are mixed with speech; they consist merely of phonemes, names, phrases, and meanings. One does not contain all others—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Its perception is not constant—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The nature of taste is not inherent; it exists only when there is tasting. Since its perception is not constant or uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration through it?

Tactile sensation is clarified by that which is touched; there is nothing it does not clearly perceive. Yet, the nature of contact and separation is not fixed; how can one attain perfect penetration through it?

"Phenomena (dharmas) are called internal objects. Relying on an object necessarily entails a subject; since subject and object do not universally pervade one another, how can one attain perfect penetration?

This passage selects the six sense-objects as not being the path of perfect penetration. As stated previously, "their practices are in reality neither superior nor inferior," yet for the sake of those with capacities in this region, there are differences in slowness and speed.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, at a point where there is truly no superiority or inferiority, forcibly makes a distinction.

Regarding their relative superiority or inferiority, there is no place where they differ; yet you have forcibly distinguished them, weighing and evaluating twenty-four sages one by one to provide their titles, none of which are truly appropriate for this fundamental, universal method of penetration (*samantamukha-prativedha*).

In the end, you alone selected the single gateway of the ear-faculty as the most excellent. Although Śāṭa contemplated the emptiness of the nature of form and thereby attained awakening, [he did not reach the ultimate].
However, this nature of form originally relies upon deluded thoughts to form the dust of obstructions and veils.

If one attempts to comprehend it through the essence of the mind, it will ultimately not be thoroughly penetrated. How could there be such an object—neither clear nor penetrating, murky and turbulent—that the initial resolve could rely upon to realize perfect penetration?
Although Cunda heard the sound of the Dharma and attained awakening, [he did so by relying on the faculty of smell].
"Voice" (*svara*) refers to direct sound; "speech" (*vāc*) refers to indirect sound. Cunda entered [the path] through the Four Truths, yet he took up only the indirect;
thus, this voice is mixed with speech. Having fallen into speech, he merely grasps the flavor of those names and phrases.
A single syllable that directly designates its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is called a "name" (*nāman*); two syllables that involve representation are called a "phrase" (*pada*).
The definition of distinctions constitutes a "phrase" (*pada*); "flavor" (*rasa*) refers to the meaning and flavor contained therein. Now, this principle is perfect while words are partial;
how could a beginner, at the outset, comprehend a single word as encompassing all principles of meaning? How then can one rely upon such [words] to realize perfect penetration?
Although Xiangyan entered awakening by smelling the dust of fragrance, that fragrance-dust necessarily depends upon the meeting with smoke.
It is only when at the nose that one perceives fragrance; once separated from it, the characteristic of fragrance no longer exists.

Thus, this fragrance is not permanently abiding. It cannot cause the awareness to be eternal. Since the awareness is not eternal, the fragrance likewise is not eternal. How, then, could one attain perfect penetration through fragrance?
Although King Bhaiṣajyarāja attained awakening by means of the sensory object of taste, the nature of this taste is also not permanent.
The substance of fire exists only when it combines with flavor at the appropriate time; it cannot cause this nature of flavor to remain constant whether combined or separated.

Since it is not constant, how could it achieve perfect penetration through flavor? Although Bhadrapāla attained awakening by means of the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), touch lacks its own independent characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and depends dualistically upon both subject and object—specifically, internally upon the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
It is capable of contact. It relies on external form-objects (*rūpa-viṣaya*) as its objects of contact; it is only in the interval between them that the characteristic of contact manifests.
If there were no objects, the characteristic of contact would not manifest. This characteristic of contact—whether in conjunction or separation—is by nature indeterminate.
It is difficult to rely upon this to attain perfect penetration. Although Kāśyapa attained entry through the dharma-object (*dharma-viṣaya*), the dharma-object is not... [the text continues].
The substantiality of the five external sense-objects is merely their shadow; they are perceived solely by the mind as "solitary-shadow" objects. Therefore, they are called "internal objects.
When the mind arises to perceive them, it focuses exclusively on a single object, abandoning one thing while attending to another.

They necessarily possess spatial location, and both subject and object are restricted; how could they possibly be universally pervasive? It is difficult to rely upon them to attain perfect penetration.

Master Zhong said: "To distinguish is not to distinguish between the sages, but to distinguish the dharmas; yet even this is not to distinguish the dharmas, but to distinguish the capacities [of the practitioners].
Whenever it is asked, 'How does one attain perfect penetration? this refers specifically to the capacities of Ānanda and the great assembly.

As for the various sages, they have each already attained perfect penetration by relying on their respective dharmas, and the Buddha has already granted that there is no superiority or inferiority among them."

Daokai said: "It is not that the sages did not attain perfect penetration; rather, it means that if practitioners were to cultivate in the same manner as the sages, they would find it difficult to attain perfect penetration, because such an approach does not accord with the capacities of those in this region."

Although the seeing-nature is brilliantly clear, it illuminates what is before but not what is behind; thus, one half of the four quarters is deficient. (The "four quarters" refers to the four intermediate directions;

the intent includes all four cardinal directions. It possesses twelve hundred merits: eight hundred for the four cardinal directions and four hundred for the four intermediate corners. Now, only the rear direction and two corners—totaling four hundred—are missing, which is but a deficiency of one-third. To say it is "deficient by half" is merely a loose way of speaking. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? The breath of the nose flows in and out;
yet there is no mingling of these gases before one's eyes, and they remain fragmented, never truly interpenetrating. How...

Which [sense] attained perfect penetration? The tongue is not a sense-field without a source (Wuxing says: it must be that the tongue-faculty is not without a source). Through flavors, awareness and cognition arise.

When taste has perished and is utterly non-existent, how can one attain perfect penetration? The body and its objects of touch (the term "objects of touch" directly refers to the preceding sense-field of tangibility) are each distinct from the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (the character "perfect" honors both "enlightenment" and "contemplation";
Perfect Enlightenment is the independent, absolute whole; Perfect Contemplation is the all-encompassing, non-dual wisdom).

Since their limits do not meet in dark harmony (limit means boundary; "dark" means profound, and "meeting" means knowing), how can one attain perfect penetration? The faculty of cognition is a confused mass of thoughts; it is turbid...

Upon final realization, there is no longer any seeing; yet thoughts and perceptions cannot be escaped. How, then, can this be called perfect penetration? (The tongue has two functions: speaking the Dharma and tasting flavors.

If we discuss speaking the Dharma, it involves unimpeded eloquence—what is called "having no end"—and thus it is somewhat close to perfect penetration. However, if we consider only the single aspect of tasting flavors, one perceives only when an object meets the sense organ, and perception vanishes as soon as the object ceases; it does not have the capacity to enter into that which is "without end. How, then, can it be called perfect penetration?)
This distinguishes the five sense organs as not being the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Although Śrotas (Śrotāpanna) attained awakening through the faculty of sight, although this faculty of sight is indeed clear and penetrating, it can only see three directions and two corners;
regarding the direction behind and the other two corners, it cannot see. How, then, can one rely on such an imperfect faculty to seek to realize perfect penetration?
Panthaka attained awakening through the faculty of the nose. However, when the nose-faculty goes out, it grasps fragrance; when it comes in, it perceives fragrance.

Yet, there is a lack of mutual exchange between these two moments. Since this intermediate exchange is lacking, the process becomes fragmented and interrupted, with the two states failing to interpenetrate.
How can one hope to realize perfect penetration based on such a fragmented thing? Pāṭaliputra [Ānanda] relied upon the faculty of the tongue...
To enter into awakening. However, it would be groundless to claim that the tongue can perceive and understand independently of flavors.
This is not the case here; rather, perception arises because of flavor, and when flavor ceases, perception ceases. How can you rely on this to seek realization of perfect penetration?
Pilinda attained entry through the body-faculty. Yet, as for the preceding sense-object of touch, I have already rejected it.

It is not perfect. Now, this body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is entirely identical to that touch-object (*spraṣṭavya*). The cognition within their conjunction is manifested through the mutual dependence of faculty and object;
neither is it the perfect enlightenment nor the perfect contemplation. Therefore, the boundary of the body and the boundary of touch—
When separated, it cannot perceive in the darkness; it exists when conjoined and is absent when disjoined.

How can you rely on this to seek realization of perfect penetration? Subhūti attained awakening through the faculty of the mind (*manas*), yet this faculty of mental cognition is intermingled with the discursive thoughts of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among all the consciousnesses, the mental consciousness is the most chaotic and the most stubborn.
It is difficult to subdue. That which is "tranquil and lucid" refers to the nature that is completely detached from the functioning consciousness (*manovijñāna*), being tranquil and clearly aware.

If the faculty of cognition is entangled with discursive thought, then this tranquil lucidity will ultimately have nothing to perceive, like those in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*).

They enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), investigating and seeking its profound clarity, yet even this cannot be attained; when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back down.
This is precisely why those who have practiced for a long time are still unable to escape conceptual thought;
how much less can those with a beginner’s mind hope to realize perfect penetration by relying upon this? For perfect penetration is, by nature, the supreme fruit of non-discriminative concentration.
If one’s thoughts and perceptions have not yet been liberated, how could one possibly attain this fruit? Regarding "seeing" and "smelling": these select out the faculties that are incomplete.

Regarding "tasting" and "touching": these select out the faculties that are shallow despite their capacity for cognition. Regarding "mental cognition": this selects out the faculty that is not purely detached. Question:
If the faculties are capable of revolving back toward their source, such that turning them reveals the true nature (*prakṛti*), why are they also selected out?

Answer: Although all faculties are generally proximate to their respective natures and thus superior to the objects and consciousnesses, among the six, they are not uniform in their completeness or deficiency.
As the preceding text states, "Complete faculties and incomplete faculties differ by a factor of ten million times.
Here, we specifically exclude those that are combined and those that are shallow, intending thereby to select only the ear-faculty.

"Consciousness arises from the mingling of the three harmonies. (The phrase "consciousness-seeing" should be read as "seeing-consciousness," which refers to visual consciousness. The treatise states: "From the harmony of two, consciousness arises," meaning that when the sense faculty and the object are in conjunction, consciousness arises therein. Here, however, it speaks of "the harmony of three.")

Because it includes the body as the support, along with the sense organs and their objects, it is called "three. To question the root is to call it "non-characteristic. Since the self-body has no prior fixed nature, how can one attain perfect penetration?
When the mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions, it arises from the power of great causes; yet the beginner cannot enter this—how then can one attain perfect penetration?

The contemplation of the nose is originally a provisional device (the contemplation of the nose refers to forming the visualization of white at the tip of the nose). Now, by concentrating the mind and abiding [therein], once this abiding is established...

As for the mental factors (*caitta*) that abide within the mind: how does one attain perfect penetration? By expounding the Dharma and playing with sounds and texts, one awakens those who have already achieved success;

yet names and phrases are not themselves untainted (*anāsrava*). How does one attain perfect penetration? Upholding precepts or violating them merely restrains the body (restraining the consciousness of the body, not the body-faculty itself).

If there is no body, there is nothing to be restrained. Originally, this does not pervade all things. How does one attain perfect penetration? Spiritual powers are based on past causes; what connection do they have to the Dharma?

Discrimination—(the three characters "discrimination of dharmas" [fǎ fēnbié] are alternative names for the mental consciousness, as the mental consciousness is precisely the nature of discrimination regarding the objects of dharma)—its thoughts take conditions as their object and do not depart from things.
How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
This distinguishes the six consciousnesses as not being the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Śāriputra attained awakening through the eye-consciousness.

Although this visual consciousness externally confronts the insentient objects of form and internally relies upon the non-discriminative eye-faculty—where the one which depends and the two upon which it depends combine to produce the three—if one interrogates their source, they have no fixed nature.
As for these characteristics, since their substance has no fixed nature, how can one rely upon them to realize perfect penetration?

Although Puxian attained awakening and entry through the auditory consciousness, and although this mental hearing penetrates the ten directions, it was entirely due to his cultivation of the practices of Samantabhadra.
Through the power of the Great Cause, the ear-consciousness comes to hear through the entire dharma-realm;

it is not that the ear-consciousness itself is inherently subtle, but rather that it can accord with the initial mind to achieve this sublime fruit. Since this is not something that can be entered by the limited faculties of the initial mind, how could one hope to realize perfect penetration through it?
Sundara attained awakening and entry by means of the nose-consciousness; however, as for this tip of the nose—
The perception of whiteness was originally established as an antidote, yet it is merely a provisional designation; this perception does not inherently exist within the nose-consciousness.
It serves only to restrain and collect scattered thoughts. Once the mind is fixed, it is biased and localized toward a single point—how, then, could it be perfected?
For the true mind has no abiding place; to have an abiding place is delusion. How can you rely upon this and seek to realize perfect penetration? Pūrṇa...

One enters into awakening through that tongue-consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*). However, although the Dharma-preacher employs language and script through the tongue-consciousness, it is because the long-accumulated causes of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra have matured over kalpas, and he possesses the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), that he is able to attain awakening;
this is not something achievable by the tongue-consciousness alone at a single moment. Furthermore, names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) are formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Originally belonging to the conditioned, it is not an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharma. How, then, can one seek to realize perfect penetration through this?
Upāli attained awakening by means of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). However, this observance of precepts can only restrain body-consciousness;
beyond body-consciousness, there is nothing further to be restrained. If it were the realm of perfect penetration, it should universally dissolve the myriad dharmas of the body-element. Now...
If you bind this [faculty] but cannot bind that, then much remains left out. How can you rely on this to seek to realize perfect penetration?

Maudgalyāyana attained awakening through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). However, the mental consciousness is the nature of the discrimination of dharma-objects (*dharmaviṣaya*), whereas supernatural powers are the result of the force of causes from kalpas past;
there is no connection between them. Even if it were by way of the mental consciousness, [it would still not lead to perfect penetration].

These moments of thought involve clinging to objects; one cannot remain detached from them. Since this is not a state that transcends sensory objects and is universally pervasive, it will be difficult to attain perfect penetration.

This sutra begins by refuting the six consciousnesses of the sense-bases as the root of birth and death, warning that one must not rely upon them for confused practice; yet the various sages, in their own accounts, still describe these six gates in detail.

This means that one sees that the nature of the sages is all-pervasive. Mañjuśrī further selected [this method] to exclude others, in accordance with this sutra’s prohibition against erroneous application.
If those of initial resolve employ this to seek perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), they will not achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*;
indeed, there are many who instead become *śrāvakas*, *māras*, or heretics. This is as in the case of the six sages who attained correct perfect penetration.
Those [who succeed] are extremely few; this is why they must be weeded out.

If one contemplates the nature of the earth element, it is characterized by solidity and obstruction rather than penetration; being conditioned, it is not the nature of the Sage. How, then, could one attain perfect penetration through it?

If one contemplates through the nature of water, thoughts and perceptions are not real; suchness is beyond both conceptualization and observation. (Suchness refers to the essence of perfect penetration and ultimate reality.)

This is the dharma of being free from thought and immovable. Any arising of the mind through discrimination, reflection, or observation is entirely inconsistent with it; conversely, this clearly demonstrates that the revolving of hearing does not belong to reflection or observation. How then could those who insist on applying the three contemplations have failed to see this? How does one attain perfect penetration?

If one contemplates by way of the nature of fire, one merely loathes existence and fails to achieve true detachment; this is not a skillful means for a beginner. How does one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates by way of the nature of wind, movement and stillness are not without opposition; since opposition is not the supreme awakening, how can this be so?

"How does one attain perfect penetration? (Question: "The dharma-gate of 'listening inwardly' also enters through movement and stillness; how does it differ from this? Answer: "That [method] gradually sheds the two objects of movement and stillness in order to grasp the hearing-nature that is neither moving nor still.")

This serves as a skillful means for beginners; it takes the nature of wind—characterized by movement and stillness—as the gateway to entry. This is why it is so vastly different [from other methods]. If one contemplates through the nature of emptiness:

the state of dullness was not originally awakening; the absence of awakening differs from Bodhi. (Those in the world who revere the great void as their fundamental nature should realize this. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? If one contemplates through the nature of consciousness:
to contemplate consciousness is to see it is not permanent; to harbor a mind is a delusion. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? All...

These practices are impermanent; the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Cause and effect now yield different results; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration? (Changshui says:

The Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha is the most essential in this land. Although it is said to involve arising and ceasing, it must rely on the power of mindful recollection. By focusing single-mindedly within the heart, combined with the power of the Buddha’s vow, one is born directly into the Pure Land. Once arrived in that realm, progress becomes even more rapid. Now, to manifest the perfect faculties, Avalokiteśvara is supreme.
This is the method of alternation between suppression and exaltation; therefore, a selection must be made.)
This distinguishes the seven great elements as not being the perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*). Śīlaskandha entered awakening based on the greatness of the earth element;

however, this nature of earth is a solid, obstructive substance that cannot penetrate freely in all directions. Furthermore, it is a necessary material for leveling and filling, and thus largely belongs to conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) practices.
Only upon encountering the Buddha and attaining equanimity does one finally realize the holy nature; yet for a beginner, this is entirely...

You involve yourself with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). How can you rely upon this conditioned state and seek to realize perfect penetration? Candraprabha attained awakening through the greatness of water;
yet this contemplation of water is precisely accomplished by binding one's thoughts. As long as one has not transcended conceptualization, it is not the true nature.
For the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) cannot be brought into correspondence with the methods of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Why is this so?

Do you wish to realize perfect penetration by relying on this discrimination of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought)? Ucchuṣma attained awakening through the greatness of fire; yet even he was one who universally contemplated the nature of fire out of a sense of revulsion and sought liberation from it.

This is not the method where body and mind are both severed, nor is there even the nature of severance—this is the truly fundamental dharma of detachment. Furthermore, among sentient beings at the initial stage of the path, do they not all possess much desire? Moreover, [it is not the case that...]* *Note:

The source text appears to be an excerpt from a Buddhist commentary (likely the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra Commentary* by Master Ci'en). The final sentence fragment suggests a rhetorical question regarding the commonality of desire among practitioners.*
Those who possess few desires or are free from desire do not represent a fixed, definitive method for the initial stage of practice.
How, then, can one seek to realize perfect penetration through this? Vairocana attained awakening and entry by means of the wind-element;
he observed that the four elements, as well as body and mind, are all driven by the power of wind. Wind is characterized by both movement and stillness, and is thus a relative phenomenon.
Phenomena (*dharma*), by virtue of existing as opposites, belong to the cycle of arising and ceasing and are impermanent; they are not the essence of supreme awakening.
How, then, could one seek to realize perfect penetration through them? As for Ākāśagarbha’s realization through the greatness of space:
this nature of emptiness is produced by obscurity and darkness; it is dull, inert, and insentient, lacking any cognitive awareness. If...
The nature of bodhi is characterized by clarity and intelligence, which is precisely the opposite of dullness and obscurity.

To seek the fruit of clarity and intelligence through the cause of dullness and obscurity is like attempting to produce fire by drilling ice; how can one hope to realize perfect penetration through such means?

Maitreya attained awakening through the vastness of consciousness (*vijñāna*). He cultivated only the contemplation of consciousness; yet the consciousness he contemplated arises and ceases from moment to moment, lacking the nature of permanence.
Even if one exhausts the limits of investigation, should there remain a mind that seeks to dwell [upon it], this is still merely the realm of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
It is like a tranquil flow of water: from a distance it appears calm and still, yet in reality it does not abide, being entirely empty and void.

[The Master said: "This is delusion! How can you seek to realize perfect penetration through this? Mahāsthāmaprāpta attained awakening by means of mindfulness of the Buddha through the six sense faculties.
However, whatever involves movement and flux belongs to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and falls within the realm of impermanence.
Now, although Mahāsthāmaprāpta is said to 'completely gather the six sense faculties,' he primarily emphasizes the succession of pure mindfulness. Since it is called 'pure mindfulness'—"
In the end, they result in states of thought. Since these are said to be successive, they cannot avoid arising and ceasing.
If one takes this as the cause for being reborn to see the Buddha, then cause and effect correspond, and there is nothing that is not possible.

However, if one takes this as the cause while seeking the realization of the perfect penetration of non-arising and non-ceasing in the present life, then cause and effect are dissimilar, and it will certainly be difficult to attain. And why is this so?
Based on this, one might falsely hope that perfect penetration can likewise be attained. Examining these together, the reason why various gateways must be selected is fourfold:

first, they do not accord with the specific suitability of the practitioner; second, they are not convenient for those at the initial stage; third, they require separate auxiliary supports; and fourth, they are not the constant practice of cultivation.
It is evident that [the chosen gateway] accords with the specific suitability, is convenient for the beginner, and does not laboriously require external supports.

Generally, only one gateway is suitable for cultivation: that of the ear-faculty. Among the seven elements, the first five correspond to objects, the sixth corresponds to consciousness, and the seventh corresponds to the faculties;
compared to the preceding [five aggregates], they merely add the characteristic of vastness, yet their essential discernment remains the same.
I now address the World-Honored One: Since the Buddha has appeared in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this direction lies in purity within hearing and sound.
If one wishes to attain samādhi, it must truly be entered through the midst of hearing.
From here below, the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) alone is selected as the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).

This serves to demonstrate what is specifically appropriate for this particular direction, thereby contrasting it with what was previously deemed inappropriate for that direction. For the Sage’s establishment of the teachings varies according to circumstances;

there are some Buddha-lands where the Buddha performs his buddha-work through the radiance of his light, while there are some Buddha-lands where he performs his buddha-work through the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Matters such as these— even using gardens, groves, and pavilions, or even empty space, or through silence and non-explanation,
as in the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa, where there is no verbal teaching and beings are led to enter the practice of discipline solely by means of various fragrances—
I now inform the World-Honored One that although a Buddha has appeared in this Sahā world, in this region...
Sentient beings of this region possess particularly sharp faculties of hearing; they are able to penetrate immeasurable distinctions of principle and phenomena through the nature of hearing itself.
Therefore, the Buddha, in accordance with the specific capacities of those in this direction, performs buddha-work by means of sound.
Thus, to accommodate the sharpness of their auditory faculties, the union of sound and hearing constitutes the true, pure, and clear teaching-body for this region.
Since the substance of the teaching resides in sound and hearing, how could one who wishes to enter right concentration abandon the substance of the teaching to seek it elsewhere?
Therefore, one should enter solely through the nature of hearing within the faculty of the ear.

This is because the sounds of the teaching serve merely as a preliminary lead-in, whereas the nature of hearing is truly the wondrous mind; thus, although the realization relies simultaneously upon both sound and hearing, [the essence remains the latter].
In the cultivation of meditative concentration, one should simply select the faculty of hearing alone. Thus, from the initial selection of faculties up to this point,
it is only with this single phrase that the ear-faculty is definitively and clearly identified as the fundamental faculty of perfect penetration— the most wondrous dharma-gate.

Free from suffering, they attain liberation. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust, attaining the power of great mastery and bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings.
O Wondrous-Voiced Avalokiteśvara, your voice is like the Brahma-voice and the sound of the ocean tide.
The Savior brings universal peace; by transcending the world, one attains eternal abiding.
This praise extols the virtues of self-benefit and benefiting others that can be realized.

Now, if one seeks the excellent and perfect gateway of penetration (*pariṣuddha-dvāra*) such that the essence of the teaching is uniquely identified as the nature of hearing (*śrutatva*), and thereby uniquely transcends all other gateways, it is none other than Avalokiteśvara.
O Guanyin! Those two kinds of suffering—segmented birth-and-death and the birth-and-death of transformation—are difficult for people to escape, yet you are able to leave them behind.
Those two kinds of bliss of liberation—liberation from fetters and sovereign mastery—are difficult for people to attain, yet you are able to achieve them.
To leave suffering and find bliss—how excellent is Guanyin! How she is able to benefit herself through the nature of hearing!

Furthermore, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters everywhere into Buddha-lands as many as motes of dust; thus, the time is exceedingly long and the space is exceedingly vast.
Having attained the power of great mastery, he manifests thirty-two transformations to preach the Dharma according to conditions.
He bestows the gift of fearlessness upon sentient beings. Because he seeks out voices to rescue them from suffering, he is called "Seeker of Sound" (Qingsheng).
Because his preaching of the Dharma is unhindered, he is called "Wondrous Sound" (Miaoyin); because he seeks out voices to rescue them from suffering, he is also called "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanyin).

Because the nature of his sound is unattached, he is called "Brahmic Sound" (Fanyin); because his responses do not miss the proper time, he is also called "Tidal Sound" (Chaoyin). Because he possesses these four sounds, [he is so named].
Its grace extends to ordinary beings, so that it rescues the world from suffering and all attain peace; thus the world receives benefit.
Its grace extends to the sages, so that they obtain the ultimate fruit of eternal abiding; thus those beyond the world receive benefit.
Such is the way the faculty of hearing benefits others. ○ To examine this in detail, the Bodhisattva forgets the sounds and dust [of sensory objects].
Yet, when practicing the nature of hearing, and even when calling upon names or praising virtues, one perceives only the sound while not perceiving the hearing itself. Why is this?

It precisely demonstrates that a person of perfect realization does not destroy the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), whereas those at the initial stage of the Way eliminate sensory objects merely to seek the liberation of their faculties.
After attaining perfect penetration, all wondrous functions reside entirely within sound. How could this be like the state of "extinguishing like ashes" [the Hinayana cessation]?
Is it that the fruit is eternally destroyed and rendered useless?
I now address the Tathāgata: as Avalokiteśvara has said, it is like a person dwelling in stillness when drums are struck simultaneously from the ten directions.
The ten locations hear at once; this is the perfection of reality. The eyes do not see beyond obstructions; the mouth and nose are likewise so.
The body knows only through contact (these two lines appear inverted; they should read: "The body knows only through contact, and the mouth and nose are likewise so").
Mental thoughts are chaotic and disordered. Hearing sounds across a wall, one can hear both near and far; this is not uniform for the five faculties. This is the penetration of reality. Sound.

The nature of sound consists of movement and stillness; within hearing, it may be present or absent. When there is no sound, it is called "no-hearing," yet this is not a case where the nature of hearing itself is non-existent.
Since sound is absent, there is no cessation; since sound is present, there is no arising. Being perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the eternal reality.

(This sentence concludes the meaning and should properly appear at the end of the subsequent section to form a final summary; however, for the sake of textual convenience, it is placed here as a transitional conclusion. Even if one were in a dream, it would not be [non-existent] due to a lack of thought.
There is none. It transcends discursive thought and deliberation; body and mind cannot reach it.
This reveals that the faculty of hearing is fundamentally real and definitive, allowing one to swiftly attain perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*) without the need for external aids or other causes.
This directly reverses the previous [faculties] which required auxiliary conditions. Yet, this is why the gateway of the ear is uniquely sublime.
Why is this so? I now address the Tathāgata: regarding the faculty of hearing as taught by Avalokiteśvara, there are three kinds of reality.
First, for example, when a person is dwelling in quietude and drums are struck simultaneously from all ten directions, they hear them all at once in those ten locations.
At first, one cannot distinguish where the hearing occurs and where it does not, nor where...
First, as for hearing: where does it hear after? This seeing and the nature of hearing in the ear-faculty are fundamentally perfect and complete within every person;
therefore, they pervade the ten directions without the slightest obscuration. This is what constitutes the true perfection of the Perfect [Vehicle].
Second, although the eyes can see, they cannot see beyond obstructions; it is like being unable to see outside when separated by a window screen.
This is like the fact that when things are separated by skin, one cannot see the internal organs. The body only knows there is touch when it comes into contact with an object;

the same applies to the mouth and nose regarding flavors and fragrances. If they are separated by even a few inches, there is no longer any perception. Although the faculty of the mind (manas) is pervasive, [it functions in this way].
Yet it constantly entangles the mental consciousness; thoughts fly about in confusion, utterly lacking any coherent thread.

Thus, while the other five faculties lack present spiritual penetration, the faculty of hearing is otherwise: it hears through walls, unlike the faculty of sight which cannot see through paper or skin;
it hears both near and far, unlike the other three faculties which do not perceive beyond a certain distance.
It is without thought and eternally still; it is not like the faculty of the mind, which is constantly thinking and agitated.
This is something that the other five faculties cannot equal—is this not what is called "penetrating reality"?

Third, the nature of sound is subject to movement and stillness, yet within the essence of the hearing-nature, which is profound and serene, these qualities circulate and alternate; when there is movement, it is clearly perceived.
When it exists, it appears; when still, it is silent and non-existent. Worldly people are deluded and inverted;

thus, during moments of silence and the absence of sound, they are confused into thinking there is "no hearing. According to the principle, this is merely the absence of sound, not the actual absence of the nature of hearing.
Therefore, since the nature of hearing does not perish along with the absence of sound, how could it possibly arise along with the presence of sound? [It is beyond] arising and ceasing.
Free from both extremes, it abides serenely and eternally; can this not be called the true reality?
Furthermore, even within a dream, at the very moment when the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is active, it seems as though the nature of hearing is temporarily severed.

Yet, when one still hears the sound of pounding and mistakenly takes it for the beat of a drum, one knows that this nature of hearing does not cease to exist simply because there is no conscious thought;

it does not thereby become non-existent. Thus, the awakening that is the essential body of the nature of hearing and the contemplation that is its illuminating function are always one, whether awake or asleep, requiring no deliberate thought. As previously stated, the moonlight is *tathatā* (suchness).
