Regarding "not [subject to] vitarka and vicāra": this is precisely because those [states] are themselves the conceptualization of vitarka and vicāra.

This emerging conceptualization of vitarka and vicāra is, in fact, the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), yet it is distinct from the body of the four external sense organs and the mind of the internal mental faculty (manas).
That which others cannot reach is all the more sufficient to demonstrate that this is ever-true. These three kinds of reality are all already fully possessed by ordinary beings;

they do not come into existence only after realization. If one cultivates them further on this basis, it is like sailing a boat with the wind or fanning a fire with the breeze—what difficulty could there be?

Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonetics may be proclaimed and clarified. Yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow sounds, they wander in saṃsāra.

Even though Ānanda possesses powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts. Is this not because he follows what he has sunk into? By reversing the flow, one attains freedom from delusion.
This clarifies that the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is most suitable for beginners, thereby reversing the previous point regarding its unsuitability for beginners.
Furthermore, in this Sahā world, the faculty of hearing is clear and sharp; one must rely on verbal expression to achieve full understanding.

Therefore, the Buddha, in accordance with these faculties that are expediently sharp, extensively proclaimed all the sūtras and śāstras. Yet, as for the śāstras that expound the meaning of the sūtras, they are none other than—
This reveals the perfectly湛 (zhan) and wondrous nature; yet this perfectly湛 and wondrous nature is not separate from the faculty of hearing.
One ought to rely upon sound to turn the hearing back toward one's own nature, just as one might use a finger to see the moon.

Alas, how regrettable that those of wild wisdom fail to understand the Tathāgata’s original intent, and instead remain deluded regarding their own inherently existing faculty of hearing, pursuing it in a single-minded [but misguided] way.
To follow sounds and pursue echoes is merely to drift along with words and phrases; how is this different from grasping at the finger while mistaking it for the moon?

Furthermore, it is not only sentient beings who drift along with sounds; even you, Ānanda, despite your powerful memory, would still inevitably fall into error regarding the pure and wondrous principles of the twelve divisions of the Tathāgatas’ scriptures, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Consider this: when thought pursues false objects, it is dragged away by external things and can no longer act with autonomy.
Is this not precisely following after the dust of sound, failing to recognize the inward-turning flow, and thereby becoming submerged?

If you know that following sound and going with the current inevitably leads to drowning, then you will know that by reversing the hearing and turning the flow back, you will surely attain the true, eternally abiding, and non-delusory nature.
It can be seen that this single method of the "Whirling Stream" accords with the medicinal and pathological needs of the faculties and capacities of those in this land;
for all beginners, what could be more suitable? What, then, is there that cannot be used?
Ānanda, listen attentively! Upholding the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra King, the inconceivable, illusion-like True Samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas.
Although you have heard all the secret gateways of countless buddhas, if you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, [you will not attain realization].
"Accumulating learning leads to error; one should instead hold fast to the Buddha through hearing. Why not hear that which hears itself?
This is a specific entrustment to those who are ready for the teaching, mandating that they must practice according to this gateway. Ānanda, you should listen attentively.

On this day, as I select the faculties, I do not dare to act on my own authority or self-will; thus, whether I lower or raise [the standard], it is entirely in reliance upon the Buddha’s majestic power.

Therefore, that which has been explained here is precisely the aforementioned Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi, and the single path to Nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.

Although you have retained much of the Buddha-dharma, you merely delight in extensive learning and do not cultivate the supreme karma of the outflows-free (anāsrava). Consequently, your outflows of desire are deep and heavy, and your habitual tendencies remain.
It is not exhausted; the more one accumulates, the less effective it becomes, ultimately resulting in the error of falling into lustful attachments.

(The former masters said: "The words and phrases of the Patriarchs are like a pair of worn-out straw sandals; it is better to go barefoot than to wear them. Now, if even the accumulation of learning can become an obstacle, how can this learning be considered precious?
Furthermore, the very nature of hearing is the wondrous essence itself; there is no need for external seeking, yet it is present in our daily lives.)
They do not realize this; instead, they take that which was originally heard to go forth and uphold the Buddha-dharma of all Buddhas.
It is like using a golden bowl to beg for food—it would be better if the bowl itself were filled with food.

Why, then, do they fail to recognize and grasp what was originally heard, but instead invert the faculty of hearing to listen to the nature of hearing? This is truly because the Tathāgata’s establishment of teachings is nothing other than a desire for people to...

One awakens to one’s own original nature; yet now, you abandon that original nature to labor over the pursuit of spoken teachings. How could this be the intention behind the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings?
For when there is much hearing, the mind becomes distracted and difficult to gather; when one turns back to hear, the spirit coalesces and it is easy to enter.
Therefore, he instructs them to turn back and listen once more, whereby they immediately attain non-delusion. ○ He said: "From hearing, one hears."
This is merely reflecting back upon one's own nature; it is not truly focused on the faculty of hearing.

To hear—that "hearing" specifically refers to the faculty being bound—is not something that arises spontaneously; it exists by virtue of sound and receives its name from it. When you revolve this hearing, you become detached from sound.

One who can thus escape desire—what name shall we give them? Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. Seeing and hearing (referring to the faculties) are like illusory cataracts;

the three realms (referring to the objects) are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the faculties are removed, the dust of the senses vanishes and awakened awareness becomes perfectly clear.
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination, it encompasses the void. Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream. Mā...
"Gaṅgā is in a dream; who can retain your form?
This passage cites the supreme name of the Wondrous Gate from above to describe the great error of non-cultivation, thereby warning that one must cultivate "return-hearing" alone.
Yet, it has not yet explained how to cultivate or how to realize it. Therefore, it says again: "If..."
Now, as for cultivation and realization, what is it like? That which is the knotting of the faculties: when it occurs in the ear, it is called "hearing.
This hearing does not arise without cause; rather, because the dust of sound strikes [the faculty], the essence of listening reflects the sound, and by coiling back the sound, it forms the faculty.
From beginningless time, there has thus been the name of the "ear-faculty," a gathering of hearing.
It is bound and obstructed; there is no further liberation. Since it is bound by grasping at sound, it must wait for the release from sound to be liberated.
Therefore, one must first reverse the faculty of hearing and turn it back toward one’s own nature in order to seek liberation from sound.

Once the sensory object (the dust) that is to be released has been dissolved, the faculty (the root) that releases it is also exhausted. There remains only the single wondrous nature; how could there be an ear-faculty again?
This is what is meant by that name. It is like water which originally freezes into ice due to cold; therefore, the ice must shed its coldness to become water again.
Yet, this does not merely resolve one faculty, for the remaining faculties still remain bound. Although the characteristics of the faculties are six, their essential nature is one.
Originally, from this single nature, the six faculties were suddenly formed; as it is said, "When one is bound, all are bound."

Therefore, by understanding a single faculty, the remaining faculties are liberated accordingly; this is what is meant by "understanding one is to understand all. It is like a piece of brocade with six flowers:
although the flowers are distinct, they are connected by a common base thread; thus, if one flower is torn, the others are all destroyed.

(This is an analogy based on horizontal connection, showing that the six faculties share a single process of formation and destruction, unlike the vertical analogy of the cloth. This is how, when a single faculty returns to its source, [all are liberated].
Is this not exceedingly simple? That the six sense-faculties are simultaneously liberated—is this not exceedingly essential?
Once the six sense-faculties are liberated, the world of sentient beings can no longer bind one; how much more so, then, can one transcend the physical world (*bhājana-loka*)?
For the physical world entirely depends upon the body of the sense-faculties for its establishment; thus, seeing and hearing are as [empty as]—
The illusory cataract: the three realms are like flowers in the sky. From the cataract arise the flowers; when they exist, both exist together, and when they cease, both cease together.
Now that you have once again turned back from the six [sense objects] and attained liberation, hearing and the others have already returned to non-existence.

This is just as when the cataract-afflicted organ has been removed, the sensory realms naturally dissolve along with it, like the total extinction of flowers in the sky. Thus, the essence of original enlightenment is perfectly complete.
It is completely pure and clean. This means that it is utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects, and the numinous light shines alone.
Now, when the physical body is liberated, the material world immediately dissolves; is this not exceedingly easy and extremely swift?

To speak at the ultimate level, when the sense organs and their objects have dissolved to the point of supreme purity, this is precisely the time when the luminous aspect is refined and pure. This is the Constant, Quiescent Light, which penetrates all.
To penetrate the Dharma-realm is to realize that it is as boundless as empty space, its silent illumination and radiant light pervading and encompassing all—
far more than the great ocean containing a single bubble, let alone the vessel-worlds and the physical bodies established within that space.
Having already reached this state, you look back upon the various affairs of the world;
they are truly like a dream. Because while in delusion you were unable to realize this illusion-like state, you took them to be real;
only after awakening do you know they were a dream. Thus, the reason you are constrained by malevolent arts and lack freedom is as follows:

As for this "division," it arises precisely from mistakenly identifying the reflected images of perceived objects as the mind, while failing to recognize the perfect, profound, and wondrous mind within the sense-roots— a mind that is still and luminous,
encompassing emptiness, and beyond all constraints. If you had earlier recognized this wondrous mind within the roots and understood how the roots transcend their realms,
even to the point of being still and luminous while encompassing emptiness, thereby attaining great liberation, then Dāngakī would have been within you.
Within the ocean of awakening, dreams are like bubbles or dust. Furthermore, how could the events of a dream cause your physical form to linger?
Why, then, do you not exert yourself? In the preceding passage, "seeing is not seeing" pointed to the ultimate reality of the fundamental substance;
thus, the name "seeing" no longer applies. Here, it points to the ultimate reality reached through practice; thus, hearing— [is likewise not hearing].
Even the names for them would not be established.
It is like a skilled worldly illusionist who conjures various men and women; although one sees their various faculties move, they are all pulled by a single mechanism.
When the workings of the mind cease and one returns to profound stillness, all illusions lose their inherent nature. The six sense organs are likewise:

originally they depend on a single brilliant essence, which divides into six harmonious combinations. When one faculty comes to rest, the functions of all six cease to operate; defilements vanish the moment they are recognized.
It becomes perfectly bright, pure, and wondrous; while residual dust remains for those still in training, when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.
This uses metaphors to illustrate the principle of the single return of the faculty of light and the sixfold liberation from attachment.

How is it seen that by returning a single sense-faculty to its source, both the subjective world of emotions and the objective world of the vessel are simultaneously transcended? It is like a skilled worldly illusionist who conjures all manner of things through illusion.
The male and female forms, with all their faculties complete, appear as if truly alive and moving. This is because they are moved by the strings held in the hands of the illusionist;
thus, the mouth and eyes of the illusory person also move. If the strings do not move, then the mouth and eyes likewise do not move.

Thus, movement occurs only when the mechanism is pulled, and stillness occurs only when the mechanism ceases. When the mechanism ceases and returns to stillness, both [the forms and the consciousness]...
Relying on the locus of illusion, even that which is "non-existent" is extinguished, and thus all illusions are established as being without intrinsic nature.
To know this is to know the six sense faculties. The presence of those six faculties within a person is likewise so:

it arises solely because True Suchness (tathatā) does not maintain its own nature and becomes conjoined with ignorance (avidyā), thereby forming the essence of the clarity of consciousness, which serves as the collective substance of the six essences. This is precisely—
This is the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*, which is also the subtle *ādāna-vijñāna*. It is metaphorically termed "one refined spirit.

It is like a magician’s single mechanical device. The six sense organs fundamentally rely upon this one refined spirit to separately grasp the six sense objects, each forming its own sensory characteristic.
Thus, when it is in the eye, it is called "seeing"; when in the ear, it is called "hearing," and so forth.
Because it is formed through the conjunction of the faculties and their objects, it is called the "sixfold conjunction. It is like men and women created by illusion.

Thus, although the six functions appear distinct, they are merely the transformation of a single brilliant essence; likewise, although the various faculties appear to move, they are ultimately drawn by a single mechanism.
If one reverses the hearing and turns the faculties back, then in a single place, restorative stillness is achieved.
Then one should have extracted the round and attained liberation; yet the six functions all fail to be established, becoming like the cessation of activity and returning to stillness.
Even the vessel-world—the world of defilement composed of the six sense-objects—should dissolve at the mere thought of it, suddenly becoming perfectly bright, pure, and wondrous.
Thus, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth would, at the mere thought of it, be transformed into supreme enlightened awareness.

Is this not precisely what is meant by "all illusions being devoid of self-nature" within the metaphor? Reaching this point, both the subjective mind and the objective vessel are transcended, and there is no defilement that is not exhausted.
If there remains anything further that is not yet exhausted, one still dwells within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

The task is not yet finished. If ignorance is exhausted and fundamental luminosity is fully realized, this is precisely the perfectly accomplished ultimate fruit realized by the Tathāgata—unsurpassed bodhi.

Since the dharma-gate is thus wondrous and the method of cultivation and realization is so skillful, such that even attaining Buddhahood is without difficulty, why not select this one faculty as the gateway for those at the beginning stage?
It is the essential path. Regarding "remaining dust": it is called "with remainder" because ignorance has not been completely severed.

To speak in the ultimate sense, even the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is likewise so. Therefore, when various texts refer to those in training (*śaikṣa*), they mean the bodhisattvas who are still in training prior to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment.
Question: In the preceding text, you referred to bodhisattvas as being uniformly "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*); why do you now speak of them as being "in training"? Answer: The preceding [text]...

His status is distant from that of a Buddha, yet it manifests his transcendence of the two vehicles; therefore, he is called "One Beyond Training" (aśaikṣa). Now, being adjacent to the Tathāgata, he is contrasted with the Buddha’s ultimate state of being beyond training;

thus, even the Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) is still considered "with training" (śaikṣa). This is like one who, though adjacent to the Most Honored One, does not adopt the title of "Most Honored One" for himself.
The great assembly and Ānanda: turn back the inverted faculty of hearing; by hearing inwardly, you shall hear your own nature. When this nature is perfected, it becomes the unsurpassed Way.
Such is the reality of perfect penetration. This is the single path to Nirvāṇa for countless Buddhas. All Tathāgatas of the past—
This gateway has already been accomplished. All present Bodhisattvas now each enter into perfect clarity.
Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma; I, too, have realized it through this, not only Avalokiteśvara.
This further elaborates upon what has been realized in order to inspire a spirit of admiration and to universally exhort you to diligent practice.
Such is the swiftness of the efficacy of the practice of "turning the hearing inward. Now, for the great assembly here and for you, Ānanda:
You should immediately turn back your inverted faculty of hearing; do not follow after external objects, but follow within.

If you can truly reverse your hearing so that it becomes the hearing of the Tathāgata’s secret Dharma-gate, and hear the nature of hearing that is inherently present within yourself, and take this nature as the mind for the stage of practice (*yinyuǎn dìxīn*), you will be able to establish the path to unsurpassed enlightenment. For although the gates to perfect penetration (*yuántōng*) are many—

There are many methods; however, if one seeks true and perfect penetration that accords with the capacities of those in this land to cure the disease of excessive learning, there is only this single gate.

This single gate is the one great highway by which countless Buddhas have reached the home of Bodhi, and the primary gateway for entering the ocean of Nirvana. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the past [have followed it].
The present bodhisattvas also enter by means of this. Thus, there are already many precedents before us;
therefore, future practitioners must certainly enter through this dharma-gate. Furthermore, it is not only the Buddhas and bodhisattvas who enter through this gate;
even I have realized [enlightenment] through this very gate. How could it be otherwise?
It is especially so for Avalokiteśvara. Now, if one does not practice oneself but only exhorts others to practice, people may not follow;
yet, if one enters first and leads others to enter together, who would not join?
Mañjuśrī’s intention is profoundly deep and earnest. Kai said: "If this gate is expanded, even the two masters, Confucius and Laozi, entered through it. Therefore—
Confucius said, "At sixty, one's hearing becomes attuned. Zhuangzi said, "What I call 'hearing' does not mean hearing that [external object];

it is simply hearing itself. Thus, we know that the two characters "returning to hearing" (fǎn wén) are truly an excellent medicine for treating the specific ailment of this [spiritual] realm, a practice shared by all three teachings; it is only that the realizations attained differ in their depth.

Truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught: when seeking expedient means to rescue those of the final age who seek to transcend the world and achieve the mind of nirvana, Avalokiteśvara is supreme.
All other expedient means are, in truth, the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
To immediately renounce worldly toil through actual practice, rather than merely engaging in constant study;
to preach the Dharma equally to those at shallow and deep levels—this is my response to Your Majesty’s command.

Truly, as the Buddha has ordained, I shall inquire into various skillful means, such as the twenty-five practices, to determine who possesses the appropriate capacity to save all beings during the final kalpa after my parinirvāṇa in this realm.
Sentient beings who seek to transcend the world and enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle must achieve the mind of *nirvāṇa* as they seek the Unsurpassed Way.
Among the four types of inquiries you have posed, that which most perfectly accords with the Buddha’s intent is solely the single gateway of Avalokiteśvara’s ear-faculty;
it is the foremost of all. As for the expedient means entered by the remaining twenty-four sages, they are all...
It is through the empowerment of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that one may, upon encountering a single circumstance, abandon worldly toil (*saṃsāra*).
This is not a practice universally applicable to all times, nor is it a teaching spoken for those of superior, middling, or inferior faculties, or for those of shallow or deep capacities alike.

It is like the case of Nanda who lost his sight, or Pindola who was pricked by thorns; people do not all experience this in the same way. How could such a state be entered through ordinary, uniform means? It is like [the case of] Puhua...
The great causes of the Venerable Śāriputra, the innate eloquence of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti’s realization of emptiness, and Śāriputra’s pure vision—all belong to the profound mind;

how could they be accessible to those of a beginner's stage? The lustful nature of Śuddhipanthaka and the lack of recitation in Cūḍapanthaka were merely confined to shallow minds; how could they be the domain of the great mind? Since each is thus limited, it is certain that...
Since there are partialities [in other methods], how could they universally enable practice for all? How can one enter both the shallow and the deep, as in the "ear-door" of Avalokiteśvara?
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, the untainted and inconceivable. I pray that you will bestow your grace upon future generations, so that they may have no delusions regarding this door.
This expedient means is easily accomplished and is fit to be taught to Ānanda, as well as to those submerged in the final age of decadence.
If one cultivates by means of this faculty alone, its perfect penetration will surpass all others; such is the true nature of the mind.
This is the request for empowerment through further progress. Now, this single gateway of the ear-faculty is precisely the three Tathāgatagarbhas previously described;
it is the untainted karma previously described; it is the inconceivable, illusion-like Mother of Buddhas, the True Samādhi, previously described.
I now prostrate myself before it. I pray that all Buddhas, by their spiritual power, will empower those who advance in the future.
Practitioners all enter directly with a single blade from this gate, without even a hair’s breadth of doubt.
If one takes this dharma-gate as the primary expedient means, then accomplishment is easily achieved; therefore, it is fit to teach this dharma to Ānanda.
Furthermore, this Dharma may also be used to deliver those sinking and mired in the final kalpa.

However, the reason for employing only this single gate and not others is that by practicing and advancing through this one gate alone, one can transcend the perfect penetration of the twenty-four sages;
it is simply this that constitutes the true and essential core. ○ In this sutra, Mañjuśrī appears four times, and in each instance...

The profound purport is as follows: First, regarding the imperial decree that Mañjuśrī should take the mantra to provide protection—this was because those who were not persons of great wisdom were incapable of upholding this dhāraṇī-heart.

Second, regarding the inquiry into the two meanings of form and emptiness as being non-dual—this was because those who were not persons of great wisdom were unable to dispel difficulties and resolve entanglements for others.
Third, regarding the decree to select one who had attained perfect penetration—this was because those who were not persons of great wisdom did not possess [such realization].
The Right Eye. One who lacks the Right Eye cannot discern faculties; it is only the King of Geese that can select milk from within the water.
Fourth, regarding the inquiry into the name of the sutra: because the Dharma taught in this single assembly begins and ends by returning to fundamental wisdom.
○ The section on the Tathāgata’s instruction to enter deeply through a single gate is concluded. ○ Second, the Determination of Meaning.
At this point, the discourse was concluded.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly attained clarity of body and mind, receiving a profound and great instruction.
They contemplated the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa as being like a person who has traveled far away on business and, though not yet returned, clearly understands his own home.

On the road where they were returning, there was a vast assembly of the eight classes of beings (the assembly of devas and humans), those of the two vehicles still in training (the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Hīnayāna), and all the newly resolved Bodhisattvas (those at the initial stage of the Mahāyāna). Their number was as many as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers.

They had all recovered their original mind (this is the same mental state as that described at the end of the third fascicle regarding "attaining the original wondrous mind"; however, while in the former case they had awakened to it, here they have realized it through direct proof). They were far removed from dust and free from defilement (this refers to the characteristics of conceptualization).

Dust refers to sensory objects; defilement refers to the conscious mind. Both are to be abandoned. When that which perceives realizes the emptiness of what is perceived, dust is distanced; when emptiness extinguishes [the grasping], defilement is left behind. Thus one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye (this is the Path of Seeing at the first stage;

according to the Perfect Teaching, it is the initial mind of the Ten Abidings). Upon hearing these verses, the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlā attained Arhatship (which corresponds to the seventh level of faith in the Perfect Teaching).
Immeasurable sentient beings all resolved their minds upon the peerless Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This passage describes the awakening and realization of the great assembly. Once Mañjuśrī had finished speaking these verses, Ānanda and the entire assembly attained clear and lucid understanding of their own bodies and minds.
Previously, although their bodies and minds were bright and clear, they had only known the sequence of the knots being untied;
they did not yet know through which gate one enters. Now, they have definitively understood that it is through the ear.
Entering through the gate, there is no further doubt; thus, both body and mind are completely clear and lucid.
This is because the twenty-five sages, together with Mañjuśrī, have explained everything in exhaustive detail; hence it is called "receiving the great revelation.
This refers to the ultimate and supreme fruit of contemplating the Buddha, Bodhi, and Great Nirvāṇa. It is like a destitute son who has long since fled to another land.
They immediately wished to return home, yet did not know the way. Today, I have pointed out for them a single path back home.
Although they have not yet reached their destination, if they proceed straight ahead from here, they will certainly never again encounter a forked road.
Thereupon, the entire assembly gathered—from the eight classes of celestial beings and dragons down to bodhisattvas at the initial stage—numbering three hundred and... [the text continues].
Their number was as great as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. All had attained their original mind; there was truly nothing they did not realize.
They were far removed from dust and free from defilement; there was no delusion they did not sever. They obtained the purity of the Dharma-eye; there was no realization they did not perfect.

Thus the great assembly obtained benefit. As for the Mātaṅga girl, who is now ordained as the bhikṣuṇī named Śailā, she attained arhatship immediately upon hearing these verses and fully realized the seventh stage of faith;
thus she was the one who obtained the least benefit. Now, ten Ganges-sands are still finite, and this extends even to immeasurable sentient beings.
All those present at the Dharma assembly gave rise to the peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind.
Among the vast multitude who had first entered the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), none could be fully described; all obtained benefit. Question:

The fruit of the first stage realized by Ānanda should correspond to the initial "faith" (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Yet, among the assembly who heard this sutra today, there were those who had not previously realized it. How is this so?
Yet, there are still those who attain new realization. Why, then, is Ānanda—who had already attained realization previously—not included in this rank? Answer:
When the treatise discusses the severance of the delusions of views (*darśana-heya-kleśa*), what was previously realized is no longer considered "new"; thus, why would it need to be listed here?

However, if one discusses the arousal of the bodhicitta as well, since Ānanda has already demonstrated his realization of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and spoke of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the three [bodhi] minds have not yet been manifested; therefore, he too has not [yet attained this].
He is listed among those in the central position. ○ Zhong says: "Previously it was called a 'path' and a 'gate'; here it is called a 'household.
This means that realizing the faculty of hearing is the path to the household of Bodhi and the gate for entering the household of Bodhi."

From this point downward, three specific matters—observing the precepts, the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), and the recitation of mantras—are added for those of the lowest faculties who are at the very beginning of their practice;

therefore, the major section designates this as the "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). As for the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arising from these precepts, they are still the wondrous concentration that eliminates sensory objects and exhausts the root [of affliction], as well as the wisdom of the three emptinesses obtained through that concentration. Observe that the text of the *Sūtra* merely...
It is evident that his nature was detailed regarding precepts, yet concise regarding concentration and wisdom. Question: Why were these [precepts] not employed in the preceding section? Answer:
Because those of medium capacity have light and subtle afflictions, they do not spontaneously give rise to the four mindfulnesses such as lust.

Furthermore, since they possess the power to provide protection at the time of the extinction of sensory objects, and worldly deviousness cannot find entry, how could there be the spontaneous arising of the four mindfulnesses? Up to this point...
Regarding Ānanda’s first fruit of realization, he was already able not to enter the six sense-objects such as forms and sounds;

yet, by merely adding the practice of "turning the hearing inward," he no longer expended much effort to forget these objects. How much less could he have given rise to thoughts of lust and the like on his own?

Therefore, one should know that this gate is specifically for those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) are habitually heavy—those who do not wait for external sounds to provoke them, but who repeatedly give rise to lust and other passions spontaneously.

Regarding the "four mindfulnesses": the addition of the four precepts serves as the preliminary expedient for "returning the hearing," while the addition of the practice of maintaining mantras at the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*) serves as the auxiliary practice during the actual process of returning the hearing. The old commentaries were entirely ignorant of this;
how could it be that from this point onward there is a separate dharma-gate? Generally, people have habitually and superficially pointed to the ear-door alone as being supreme.
Regarding the initial expedient means: examining this section now, it appears that even the "Gate of the Ear" is still an expedient path for those at the beginning of their practice;
only [the subsequent stages] constitute the most fundamental expedient means for the very first stage of the mind.

Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet. His mind and its traces were perfectly clear and bright; he was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy.

Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed his head and addressed the Buddha: "O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood.
In practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion. I have often heard the Tathāgata speak thus..."

He said: "To first deliver others before one has delivered oneself is the aspiration of a Bodhisattva. To have awakened oneself to perfection and then be able to awaken others is the manifestation of a Tathāgata in the world.
Although I am not yet delivered myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age. World-Honored One, these sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha;
teachers of false doctrines are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. I wish to gather their minds and lead them into [the Way]."
Samādhi. How can one cause them to be established in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far removed from all demonic activities, and attain non-retrogression regarding the bodhicitta?
This request for the establishment of the site of enlightenment serves as the rule for concentrating the mind during the final age. Once the great assembly has obtained [this],...
Having attained enlightenment, Ānanda adjusted his robes amidst the assembly, rose from his seat, and faced the Buddha with palms joined in prostration.
At that moment, he first realized the mind that is neither born nor extinguished—this is precisely the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King;
his mind was perfectly luminous. Furthermore, he realized that the faculty of hearing is the gateway for entering this state of non-arising and non-extinction.

The traces [of his realization] were perfectly clear and luminous. He felt sorrow for the delusions of kalpas past and rejoiced in the sudden awakening of this day; thus, grief and joy mingled within him.
Once his own ailment was removed, he took pity on the ailments of others. Desiring to benefit future sentient beings, he then prostrated himself before the Buddha and said:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood and am certain..."
Entering deeply through the single gateway of the ear-organ, one practices from within this door; it is direct, straightforward, and secure, leaving no further room for doubt.
Indeed, I have often heard the Tathāgata speak these words: "To seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself is the aspiration of a Bodhisattva.
To awaken oneself fully and thereby be able to awaken others is the way of a Tathāgata."
Regarding his response to the world: "Although I have not yet attained self-liberation, I vow to study as a Bodhisattva and vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age.
Since I encountered the Buddha and heard his teaching, I already know the path of practice; I enter through hearing.

Yet, I fear that in the final age, sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha, while heterodox thoughts and divergent paths of teaching will become increasingly numerous. Thus it was said.
When the heterodox and the orthodox are intermingled, those who strive in cultivation find their minds at a loss as to where to turn.

If one wishes to gather the mind and enter *samādhi*, how can one cause them to be established in the ground for entering the Way, so that heterodox teachings and demonic activities cannot disturb or shake them, and they may finally attain non-retrogression from the *bodhicitta*? Question: Before a Bodhisattva has...
"To attain deliverance oneself before delivering others; the Buddha first awakened himself and only thereafter awakened others. What is the sequence of their limits? Zhong replied:

"In the case of a Bodhisattva, it begins with the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). That which can be seen still involves the expenditure of profound resolve (*gambhīra-citta*); these are matters prior to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)."
This refers to taking the fruit as the cause. In the case of the Buddha, it is called "responding to the world. Since his karma was already complete, he did not exert further effort;
this is what occurs after the attainment of wondrous enlightenment. This refers to taking the cause as the fruit. The scriptural words themselves are clear on this point.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, praised Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent!
Just as you have asked concerning the establishment of the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings sinking in the final age, listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."

"Ānanda and the great assembly replied, 'So be it; we respectfully accept your instruction. The Buddha told Ānanda, 'You have often heard me, within the *Vinaya* (the Basket of Discipline), proclaim the three principles of certainty for the practice of cultivation:
namely, that the gathering of the mind constitutes the precepts (*śīla*), and from the precepts arises meditative concentration (*samādhi*')."
Wisdom arises from concentration; these are what are called the three untainted trainings (*trīṇy aśaikṣāṇi*).
Although the three untainted trainings were previously indicated, the precepts (*śīla*) are especially fundamental.

For in the preceding text, the forgetting of objects and the liberation from the sense bases were all explications of concentration and wisdom, yet the precepts had not been mentioned. Therefore, they are specifically clarified here. At that time...
“World-Honored One, in the midst of the great assembly, you praised Ānanda, saying: ‘Excellent! Excellent!

Just as you, with a mind intent on delivering sentient beings, have asked about the establishment of the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect those who are submerged and sinking. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, ‘So be it,’ and respectfully received the instruction. The Buddha then addressed him, saying: ‘You have not...’”
Have you not often heard it proclaimed within our Vinaya Piṭaka that there are three definitive principles for the practice of cultivation? What are these three principles?
Precepts constitute one of them. As for what is called precepts: they do not merely restrain the body;

rather, every subtle movement of thought is censured and forbidden until not even a single thought arises—this is what is designated as "precepts. This is because, by focusing the mind, the movement of the thoughts becomes minimal.
One gradually approaches meditative concentration (*samādhi*), just as when the wind ceases and the waves gradually subside; this is how concentration arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*).

As the mind’s stillness reaches its ultimate limit, the original luminosity gradually manifests, simultaneously illuminating all phenomena (*dharmas*), like the water in a lake becoming clear and still while the waves cease, and its own essence radiates light.

Illumination encompasses even the finest thread and hair; this is wisdom arising from concentration. When these three are fully perfected without the slightest leakage, they are called the "Threefold Training in the Outflows-Free" (trīṇi śikṣāṇy anāsravāṇi).
Not only does this ensure one does not fall into the three realms of existence, but it also ensures one does not fall into the two extremes of emptiness and existence;
this is true outflows-freedom, and is not comparable to that of the Lesser Vehicle. Furthermore, ethical discipline is truly the foundation for concentration and wisdom.
The vanguard. If the root of precepts is impure, then concentration and wisdom have no means by which they can arise.
It is like constructing a house: one first secures its foundation. Without a foundation, merely erecting a structure in empty space will surely not result in completion.
Therefore, among the three principles of determination, the precepts are primary; and within the precepts, there are furthermore four determinations of pure and clear instructions.
The Preface states: This sutra takes the precepts as its foundation from beginning to end.

The World-Honored One foresaw that during the age of the Dharma’s decay, false teachers would proliferate, and those who disregard the Vinaya and distort proper conduct would mislead and confuse sentient beings.

Therefore, in this sutra, he begins by using Ānanda’s demonstration of his own downfall as the opening theme; now that Ānanda has attained awakening, [the Buddha] specifically acts for the sake of future multitudes.

Śāṇavāsa requested on his behalf that a site for the *bodhimaṇḍa* be established. The World-Honored One spoke with earnest and repeated exhortation, first proclaiming the precepts as a definitive and clear instruction.
He stated once: "After my parinirvāṇa, there will be many followers of Māra. He stated it again: "After my parinirvāṇa... and so forth.
Furthermore, he repeatedly concluded by binding them with this: "If it is not spoken thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān," just as an elder [warns a child].
The testament is both profoundly sorrowful and utterly decisive; it causes people’s tears to fall and makes their hearts grow cold.
Upon reading this point, if one does not know how to apply oneself to its critical examination and elucidation, one truly fails the Venerable Ka (Kāśyapa) and his single-minded, compassionate heart.
Ānanda, what is it that I call "disciplining the mind"? It is called precept-keeping.

If the beings of the six realms throughout all worlds do not harbor lustful thoughts, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death. You cultivate samādhi in order to emerge from worldly toil;

if the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall.
The Path of Māra consists of three grades: those of the superior grade are Māra kings; those of the middle grade are the subjects of Māra; and those of the inferior grade are Māra women.
These various Māras also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have realized the Unsurpassed Way.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Final Dharma, many such subjects of Māra will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), causing sentient beings to fall into attachment.
They see a pitfall and lose the path to Bodhi. You should teach the people of the world that when practicing *samādhi*, they must first sever the lust of the mind;
this is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever lust while practicing dhyāna-concentration, it is like steaming sand and grit in the hope of producing rice; even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it will still only be called by that name.

Hot sand. Why is this? Because this is not rice, but is composed of gravel and sand. If you seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a lustful body, even if you should attain wondrous awakening, it will all be rooted in lust.
With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape.
By what path can you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata? You must cause the mechanism of lust to be severed in both body and mind; even the nature of severance must be...
There is none. Regarding the Buddha’s bodhi, such [a hope] may be aspired to. What I have spoken thus is called the word of the Buddha;
what is not spoken thus is the word of Pāpīyān.
This first explains the precept against sexual misconduct. In various sutras, the precept against killing is placed at the head, because when establishing transformation, compassion is primary.

In this sutra, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed at the head, because for true cultivation, the departure from desire is fundamental. This is because the energy of desire is coarse and turbid, defiling the wondrous clarity;
the habituation to desire leads to madness and delusion, easily causing one to lose right concentration (*samādhi*), continuing the cycle of birth and death, and losing true permanence.
Nothing is more severe than this; therefore, it must be the foremost precept. Ānanda, what is meant by "restraining the mind"? I call this "precept.
Within the Vinaya, offenses are categorized by their gravity, yet sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying are the most serious.
To speak specifically of the precept against sexual misconduct: if the beings of the six realms throughout all worlds do not harbor lustful thoughts, then not only...
The body does not transgress, nor does it give rise to even a single thought of conceptualization. Indeed, all sentient beings rely upon lustful desire to sustain their life-destinies;
thus, they are bound within birth and death. If the thirst of desire were to wither away, then this wretched physical form would no longer continue.
Furthermore, you have cultivated the samādhi of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, originally intending to transcend the two delusions of views and thoughts.

Regarding worldly afflictions (*kleśa*): if the lustful mind is not eliminated, then the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃjñā*) can never be severed, and one will certainly be unable to transcend worldly afflictions.

Even if one possesses great wisdom, possesses penetrating eloquence and discernment, and brings forth meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), giving rise to wondrous states—so long as one does not sever lust, and does not abandon lustful thoughts during the time of meditative concentration, then whenever there is mental activity, the realm of desire will manifest accordingly.
Since one's thoughts are already fixed upon the realm of desire, and no realm of desire surpasses that of Māra, one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra, just as water flows toward moisture.

According to the thickness or thinness of one’s merit, one is divided into the superior, middling, or inferior grades: if not a king of Māra, then a subject of Māra; if not a subject of Māra, then a daughter of Māra.
This is like those who practice the dhyāna of emptiness within the realm of the *skandha*-māras, yet retain their worldly afflictions and extensively transform them into jewels.

This refers to the *yuan* (the female spirit). This is likely because when the mind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) comes into contact with sensory objects, it flows forth and thus falls into this state. If one lacks meditative concentration and wisdom, and possesses only the habit of lust, then one falls directly into hell;
how could there be the retribution of a demonic palace? Those various demons also have followers who initially do not consider themselves demons.

Through the development of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), they mistake what is not the fruit for the fruit. Each of them claims to have achieved the path of the supreme, ultimate fruit. Such is their delusion.

How can one fully describe this? Therefore, after my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Dharma’s decay, there will be many such demonic followers—specifically those who practiced meditation while harboring lust in previous lives—who will come to act as teachers.

Possessing supernatural powers and wisdom, they will secretly teach the practice of sexual intercourse as a Buddhist rite, transmitting it to one another and causing all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views.
Seeking to transcend desire and views, you instead fell into attachment and dogmatic views. Once ensnared by these deviant paths, you have forever lost the true path to Bodhi.

This is just like Udraka Rāmaputra, who attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; yet upon merely being touched by a woman’s hand, he gave rise to lustful thoughts and immediately lost his supernormal powers.
If you wish to deliver sentient beings, from this day forward, you must teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi.
One must first cause them to sever the lust of the mind. This is called the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;

it is not a transmission from no teacher. Therefore, Ānanda, if one claims that one can cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without severing lust, it is like steaming sand, hoping for it to become rice—even if one were to pass through a hundred [eons].
For a thousand kalpas, it shall be called only "hot sand" and not "rice. Why? Because rice has grain as its basis, whereas this is not the basis of rice, being composed of sand and stone.
For you to seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a lustful body—how is this any different from steaming sand to make rice?
Even if you were to attain wondrous enlightenment, it would all stem from the root of lust. With lust at its foundation, one revolves through the three realms.
There is simply no way out; how is this different from the appearance of heat-phenomena in sand?
If so, by what path can the ultimate fruit of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa be cultivated and realized? One must cause the mechanism that triggers lust to be severed in both body and mind.
For the lust-mechanism of the body is set in motion by the mind, and the lust-mechanism of the mind is set in motion by—
When mindfulness runs wild and is released, only when not a single thought arises can one achieve the simultaneous severance of both body and mind.

Yet, if the nature of severance persists, it will ultimately stand in opposition to desire. As long as the residual traces of the conditions of desire have not been forgotten, there is no thorough exhaustion.

Therefore, one must ensure that even the nature of severance is absent; only when both the illness and the medicine are removed is one truly a person free from illness. In this way, one may hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
This is to be hoped for. This, then, is the true path to the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa. If, in the final age, one preaches the Dharma as I have taught it, that is the Tathāgata’s correct teaching.
If one does not speak in this way, but instead claims that sexual conduct does not constitute an obstacle, that is the teaching of Māra Pāpīyān.
There is but a hair’s breadth of difference between the Tathāgata and Pāpīyān. Can you [discern this]?
"It is not that they fail to discern. Master Zhong said: 'The "trigger" (ji) is that from which the lustful mind spontaneously arises.
If the nature of cessation were not present, then the round reflection of desire would still remain, and upon encountering the trigger, it would immediately manifest.'"
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
You practice samādhi to fundamentally escape from worldly toil; if the mind of killing is not eliminated, you cannot escape the world.

Even if one possesses great wisdom and dhyāna-concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever killing, they will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. Those of the highest grade become great [spirits].
The powerful ones shall become *yakṣas* and various ghost generals who fly through the air; those of middle capacity shall become earth-walking *rākṣasas*;
and those of inferior capacity shall likewise become such beings. These ghosts and spirits will each have their own followers, and every one of them will claim to have realized the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, declaring that they attain Bodhi by eating meat.
"Ti lu, Ānanda, I have permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat. These meats were all produced through my supernatural power; they originally possessed no life-force.
You, O brāhmaṇa, live in a land that is largely humid and damp, further compounded by sand and gravel, such that grasses and vegetables do not grow there."
"By the empowerment of my great compassion and supernatural power, and through the influence of great kindness and pity, I have provisionally designated this as 'flesh. You have obtained its flavor;
how can you, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, eat the flesh of sentient beings and yet still call yourselves sons of the Śākya? You all should know this."

These meat-eaters, even if they attain an opening of the mind that resembles samādhi, are all great rākṣasas; when their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death.
They are not disciples of the Buddha. Such people kill one another, devour one another, and eat one another without ceasing.
"How does such a person emerge from the three realms? You must teach the people of the world to practice *samādhi* and, next, to cease taking life;
this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddha of the past. Therefore, Ānanda..."
If one does not cease killing yet practices meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, seeking not to be heard by others;
such people are said to be "the more they seek to hide, the more they reveal themselves. This applies to pure bhikṣus and all bodhisattvas.

When traveling on a forked path, one does not tread upon living grass, much less pluck it with one's hands. How can those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to satisfy their hunger?

If sentient beings do not consume the silks, cottons, and brocades of the East, nor the boots, furs, woolens, milk, curds, and clarified butter of this land, then such bhikṣus are truly liberated from the world and have repaid their karmic debts from past lives.

He does not wander through the three realms. (This is a reversal in the translator’s phrasing; it should rather say: "He does not wander through the three realms to repay his karmic debts from past lives.
Why is this? Because he has taken on their physical forms, he is bound by those conditions. It is like a person who eats the hundred grains grown in the earth; his feet never leave the ground.

One must ensure that, regarding all sentient beings, neither the body nor the mind—through either the physical form or the mental aspect—is "taken on" or "consumed. I declare such a person to be truly [liberated].
Regarding liberation, as I have spoken here, it is called the teaching of the Buddha; if it were not spoken thus, it would be the teaching of Pāpīyān.

This clarifies the precept against killing. The killing prohibited herein refers not only to humans and animals, but extends downward to even flies, lice, snakes, scorpions, and the like—all must not be killed.
Furthermore, this applies not only to direct killing; even consuming meat for one's own body is likewise forbidden.
This is not permitted. Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of restraining body and speech; even mental thoughts must be brought to cessation.
Ānanda, moreover, in all worlds, if the beings within the six realms do not harbor thoughts of killing, they will not follow along with the continuous succession of birth and death.
To carry a life-debt is to create the conditions for birth and death; by not killing, one does not continue this cycle.
You practice samādhi with the original intention of escaping the dust and toil of the world. If the mind of killing is not eliminated, then you cannot escape the dust.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the habit of killing, you will certainly fall into the realm of spirits. For although ghosts and gods...
Although they are distinguished by superiority and inferiority, they are all equally states of miserable rebirth; therefore, those who enter from the human realm are said to have "fallen.
If such a person was a practitioner of superior dhyāna, they shall become a powerful ghost, just as those honored and titled "Emperor" or "Heavenly One" among humans.
If they were of middling capacity, they shall become flying yakṣas or various ghost generals, like the mountains and rivers [of the world].
Regarding those such as village tutelary deities (*shajin*), if they are of inferior grade, they shall become terrestrial *rākṣasas*, such as those who dwell along the seashores.

These various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers; they recognize themselves as being correct and do not know their error, each claiming for themselves that they have realized the Unsurpassed Way.
Therefore, after my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (*mappō*), this class of beings will flourish.
It flourishes in the world; they proclaim that eating meat does not hinder one from attaining Buddhahood, and thus my teaching has declined.

Yet, within the Vinaya of the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) teachings, I also permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat—those not seen, not heard, and not suspected [of being killed for oneself], as well as meat from birds that died naturally. How could this have been without reason? It is because these meats were all [the remains of] my own spirit...

They are produced through the power of transformation, like mountains of fish meat in the ocean; these are all manifestations of great compassion and skillful means, and do not possess actual life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, because the land where you Brahmins dwell is largely humid and damp, compounded by sand and stones, various vegetables do not grow there.
If there were no meat to eat, who would sustain their bodies and lives? Therefore, through the supernatural power of my great compassion, I have transformed [the meat].
It is made of meat, intended for you to taste and eat for a time; it is not real meat.

You should see that whenever the Buddha permits the eating of meat, it is all a skillful means (*upāya*) used by the Buddha to gradually lead beings toward compassionate transformation. After my parinirvāṇa...
This is, in truth, meat that takes life. How can one eat such life-taking meat and yet still be called a son of the Buddha?

You should know that for a meat-eater, even if they should happen to attain the opening of the mind within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and experience the manifestation of objective realms—which may resemble *samādhi*—it is not true *samādhi*, because of their consumption of meat.
Their obstructions are profound; their active manifestations are all those of great rākṣasas, and when their retribution ends, they will surely sink into the sea of suffering.

It is certain that such people are not disciples of the Buddha. If one considers oneself a disciple of the Buddha and seeks to escape the three realms, yet such a person kills and devours others so that the debt of life remains unpaid, there will be no time for liberation. How, then, could they escape the three realms? Thus, you—
To teach the people of the world how to cultivate *samādhi*, it is necessary to first sever the taking of life.
This is the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One of former Buddhas.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one were to claim that one can cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without severing the karma of killing, it would be like a person who plugs their ears and shouts loudly, seeking someone to hear them.
I have heard that these are called "those who wish to conceal but reveal all the more. For they practice meditation to avoid transgressions, yet instead commit acts of killing;
they plug their ears to avoid others, yet instead raise their voices loudly. Hence, they are said to "wish to conceal but reveal all the more.
Furthermore, pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not intentionally trample or intentionally pull up the living grass by the roadside, out of their benevolence and compassion.
It extends even to plants and trees. How could Great Compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food?

Not only is their flesh and blood unfit for consumption; even silk, floss, and woven silks produced by silkworms, as well as boots, furs, and wool derived from beasts, and milk, curd, and clarified butter—all these, though not the flesh and blood of their own bodies, are likewise [unfit].

These are also but parts of that body. If bhikṣus do not wear the silk, cotton, or fine fabrics of the East, nor the boots, furs, or woolens of my Western land, such bhikṣus will truly be liberated from the world;
they shall no longer wander through the three realms, having repaid their karmic debts from former lives. Why is this? Because by wearing those...
Every part of the body serves as a condition for that [impurity]. For example, the people at the beginning of the eon possessed bodies that emitted light and could tread upon the clouds;
this was because they consumed the "earth-fat" and ate fragrant rice. Consequently, their bodies became solid and heavy, and their feet no longer left the ground.
Thus, even the parts of the body are unfit for consumption, let alone the flesh and blood themselves. This being so—

One who cultivates samādhi must ensure that both their own body and mind, toward all sentient beings—whether regarding their bodies of flesh and blood or their parts such as hides and fur—neither consume them with the body nor crave them with the mind.
I declare that such a person is one of true liberation. Since they possess no evil karma, they naturally have no enemies; what need is there to speak of not being liberated? Hereafter...
"O World, as I have spoken this, it is called the Buddha’s teaching; if it were not spoken thus, it would be the teaching of Pāpīyan.
How could a person discard the Buddha’s teaching to follow the teaching of Māra?"
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms in the world: if their minds do not steal, they will not follow along with the continuous succession of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; if the mind that steals is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the habit of stealing, you will inevitably fall into deviant paths—becoming either a high-grade spirit or a medium-grade one.

Spirits and demons; base and depraved persons possessed by various demons. These various evil ones also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such spirits and deceivers will flourish in the world.

Concealing their wickedness and fraudulence, they will call themselves "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*), each claiming for themselves that they have attained the dharmas of a superior person, thereby deluding and confusing others.
Ignorant one! Fearing that you will cause them to lose their minds, wherever you pass, their households will suffer depletion.
I have instructed the bhikṣus to wander for alms according to the directions, so as to cause them to abandon greed and achieve the path to Bodhi. These bhikṣus do not cook food for themselves;

they rely on the remnants of their remaining lives, lodging as travelers within the three realms, demonstrating a single coming and going. Once gone, there is no returning. How can you, a thief, falsely claim to be me?
Wearing the robes [of a monk] while peddling like a merchant for the Tathāgata, they perform all manner of karmic deeds while claiming them all to be the Buddha-dharma;

yet they instead disparage the bhikṣus who have left home and are endowed with the precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna path. Because of this, they mislead immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind and cultivates samādhi, and is able [to do so] before an image of the Tathāgata...
In the past, such a person has lit a single lamp upon their body, burned a finger-joint, or incinerated a single stick of incense upon their flesh.
I declare that this person has, at once, repaid all karmic debts from beginningless time; they bid a final farewell to the world and are forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).

Although they have not yet clearly illuminated the path to supreme enlightenment, this person’s mind is already resolved regarding the Dharma. If one does not perform such acts of self-sacrifice, [one cannot attain this].
Even if one were to achieve the unconditioned through subtle causes, one would inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay past debts, just as it was with my own meal of horse fodder;
these cases are exactly equal and no different. You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* and only thereafter renounce theft;

this is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One of former Buddhas. Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not renounce theft while practicing dhyāna...

Regarding meditative concentration: it is like a person pouring water into a leaking chalice, seeking to fill it; even if they were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would never be restored.

If, however, there are bhikṣus who do not store so much as a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls, who give whatever remains from their begged food to hungry sentient beings, who join their palms in salutation to the assembly at great gatherings, and who treat being struck or reviled by others as if it were praise—then they shall surely...
He renounces both body and mind, sharing his flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings.

He does not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) and twist them into his own interpretations to mislead beginners. The Buddha seals such a person as having attained true samādhi;
what he speaks is called the word of the Buddha. To speak otherwise is to "assist" (or "peddle")—that is, to assist the thieving mind and to peddle [false views].
This is the Buddha-Dharma).
This clarifies the precept against stealing. This act of theft does not consist merely of pilfering another's property;

rather, it includes all instances of practicing deception through speech, using guile to entice or intimidate, and even harboring a single thought of seeking gain or offerings—these are all [forms of theft]. Ānanda!

Furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms within the world, if their minds do not steal and not a single thought of covetous desire for profit arises, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death. You practice samādhi fundamentally to escape from worldly toil;
if the mind that steals is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world. Only by detesting the dust can one leave it; how could one who craves the world ever be able to leave it?

How far removed from the world they are! Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) manifests before them, if they do not cease their thievery and continue to seek profit through underhanded means, their minds will turn toward the perverse, and they will inevitably fall into deviant paths.

As for those of superior grade—mountain spirits and water monsters who possess various supernatural powers, appearing like immortals yet not truly immortals, like gods yet not truly gods—and those of middle grade—vicious demons who manifest demonic powers—...
Those who bewitch others are base and depraved individuals possessed by various demons; their words and actions are strange and aberrant, and they delude and confuse people.

These various malevolent spirits also have their own followers. Having entered their hearts and bellies, these people do not recognize their own transgressions, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, there will be many such demonic and perverse beings who remain hidden.

They conceal their wickedness and deceit, falsely claiming to be realized masters (*jñānin*). They further terrify people with demonic speech, seeking to cause them to change their hearts and alter their wills so that they revere [the deceiver] as if he were a divine spirit.
Consequently, wherever they go, the households waste away and their wealth is dissipated.
Such is the harm wrought by the flourishing of these demonic and heterodox influences. If it were my teaching, it would be quite different from this.

It is quite the opposite. When I instruct my bhikṣus to go wherever they may be and beg for food with their alms bowls, it is precisely because I wish to cause them to abandon greed and realize the Path of Awakening. By begging according to the directions, they do not cook for themselves.
The reason for this is that they regard this remaining life as a mere sojourn, dwelling as travelers or guests in the inn of the triple world.
Within this, I have briefly shown you this one instance of coming and going. From now on, I shall not return again.
How could I allow such a person to remain lingeringly attached to the human world, becoming dregs of the hells?

Why do these demonic and heterodox thieves steal my robes, assume my monastic appearance, and use the Tathāgata as a broker for profit, engaging extensively in trade and commerce to create the three [evil paths]?
They perform worldly deeds while all claiming, "This is the Buddha-dharma. This is preaching what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma.
Conversely, they slander those who have left the household life and uphold the complete precepts, calling them followers of the Hīnayāna path. This is preaching the Dharma as being non-Dharma.
Taking the right as wrong and the wrong as right, they thereby mislead and delude immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell. Who would not [condemn] this?
How great is the harm wrought by demons and malevolent spirits! Furthermore, among all things that people cherish as their most precious treasure, none surpasses this very body.
Therefore, when a bhikṣu of my teaching resolves to cultivate the Great Samādhi, he first performs a minor act of self-sacrifice before an image of the Tathāgata.

Whether by offering one's own body as a lamp, a finger-joint, or an incense stick, one causes that person to repay the debts of past lives, depart from the world, and be liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
One who can practice such deeds, though unable to immediately ascend the path to Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), is certainly able to have faith in the Dharma of Great Enlightenment.
If one does not practice such deeds, even if one were to attain enlightenment, [it would be of no avail].
They return to the human realm to repay their past debts; such was the case when I once ate horse barley for three months in the royal stables of the city of Vairaṇyā.
Indeed, even the body may be abandoned, let alone external objects—how then could one not sever the habit of stealing? Thus, in teaching the world to cultivate samādhi, you must...
This causes them to subsequently sever the practice of stealing. This is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddha of former times.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one practices meditative concentration without severing stealing, it is like pouring water into a leaking cup;
even over kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be filled. For this reason, the Vinaya prescribes that for bhikṣus, apart from their robes and alms bowls, [all else] must be shared.
Not storing even an inch [of food] is to cease greed. Giving away the remnants of one's alms to hungry sentient beings is to cease stinginess.
Joining palms to pay homage to the assembly is to avoid arrogance. Praising others equally when they strike or revile one is to be free from the mark of self.
Abandoning both body and mind is to be free from attachment. Sharing one’s own flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings is to leave nothing behind. Such is the conduct of a bhikṣu.
All of these are for the purpose of achieving a mind free from theft. Furthermore, how could one be willing to resort to crooked means to provide for oneself?
As for the permission to keep the "one hundred and one" necessary items, this merely prohibits the other two [categories].

Or, regarding the allowance that one may not enter a great assembly to avoid humiliation and refuse offerings, as well as the rule that alms should not exceed one's own body’s requirements and so forth—these all belong to the *neyārtha* (provisional meaning), such as in the Sarvāstivāda [Vinaya].

As stated in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: "If one can rely solely upon the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and does not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*) to perversely interpret them for one's own sake or to mislead future learners, the Buddha will seal such a person as having attained true samādhi.
What I have spoken in this manner is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not spoken in this manner is the teaching of Pāpīyān. Is this not so?
"Discerning Bhikṣu, Ānanda, it is thus with the sentient beings of the six realms in this world:

even if their physical and mental conduct regarding killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct has been fully perfected, if they engage in great falsehood, then their *samādhi* will not attain purity; they will become demons of craving and views, losing [the Way]."

They come as those who sow seeds of falsehood—namely, those who claim to have attained what they have not attained, or declare they have realized what they have not realized; or those who, seeking worldly preeminence and supremacy, say to others:

"I have now already attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna, the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an Anāgāmin, the path of an Arhat, the vehicle of a Pratyekabuddha, or the various stages of a Bodhisattva from the ten bhūmis down to the stages prior to the bhūmis. They seek from such people worship and repentance.

Coveting their offerings, these icchantikas (i.e., *icchantikas*) extinguish the seed of the Buddha. It is like a person cutting down a tāla tree with a sword (once a peṭala tree is cut by a sword, it does not revive).
The Buddha says that such people have forever destroyed their roots of goodness and possess no further knowledge or vision.
Sunk in the three seas of suffering, they fail to achieve samādhi. After my parinirvāṇa,
I shall command all bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest bodies within that age of the Dharma’s decline, assuming various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra—
whether as śramaṇas, laypeople, householders, kings, officials, boys, girls, or even courtesans and widows.

Those who engage in deceit, theft, slaughter, or trade may be associated with them as colleagues (one of the four methods of attraction). One praises the Buddha Vehicle to cause their bodies and minds to enter *samādhi*.
Yet, one never says of oneself, "I am truly a Bodhisattva" or "I am truly an Arhat," lest the secret causes of the Buddha be leaked or the junior practitioners be disparaged.

This is done except when, at the end of life, there is something entrusted to them in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). How could such a person delude and confuse sentient beings, thereby becoming a great [hindrance]?
False speech. You have taught the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, yet later you yourself have severed the great false speech [of your own teaching].
This is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One of the former Buddhas.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great false speech, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood in hopes of obtaining its fragrance—it will never exist.
In this regard, I instruct the bhikṣus that in the dojo of the straightforward mind, even amidst all actions within the four modes of deportment, there must be no pretense whatsoever.
How then can one claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior man? It would be like a destitute person falsely styling himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution;
how much more so for one who would falsely usurp the title of Dharma King! If the ground is not true, the fruit will be distorted. To seek Buddhahood...
