"Bodhi! It is like a person trying to bite their own navel; whom could one possibly bring to accomplishment?

If bhikṣus have minds as straight as bowstrings and are entirely truthful, entering samādhi, they will forever be free from demonic interference. I certify that such people shall accomplish bodhi, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
What I have spoken in this way is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not spoken in this way is the teaching of Pāpīyas."

This clarifies the precept against false speech. Ānanda, in such a world, although the sentient beings of the six realms may be free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—thus fully possessing the three precepts and perfecting the three practices—if their words do not accord with their conduct, [they have failed].
One who commits a great falsehood will fail to achieve samādhi; they will become a demon of craving and views and lose the lineage of the Tathāgata.
What is meant by a "great falsehood"? It refers to claiming to have attained the Way when one has not, or claiming to have realized the fruit when one has not.

Taking what does not exist to be existent, they seek only to be the most honored and supreme in the world, always placing themselves at the forefront and saying, "I have already attained the [third]..."

As for the fruits—ranging from Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas to Bodhisattvas at the stages prior to the bhūmis—if one causes others to seek repentance for their essence while coveting their ritual arrangements and offerings, such a person is an icchantika who extinguishes the seeds of the Buddha.

Like wood severed by a blade, they shall never again revive. The Buddha has prophesied that such a person’s roots of goodness are forever severed, and they shall possess no further knowledge or insight.

Sunk in the three miserable realms, they shall not achieve samādhi. Now, after my parinirvāṇa, I command all the bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest forms in accordance with the needs of beings, appearing within that age of the final dharma to assume various guises and deliver sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra.
They may manifest compliant appearances as śramaṇas, lay devotees, kings, officials, or even young boys.

They may manifest as women, or even as courtesans, widows, adulterers, thieves, butchers, or merchants—whether pure or defiled—blending their light with the dust of those beings to gather them through the practice of *samānārthatā* (common purpose). They extol the Buddha Vehicle to lead them into the Way;
yet they do not permit themselves to claim to be true Bodhisattvas or true Arhats, nor do they leak out secret mechanisms to others.
Before those who are beginners, one should only briefly reveal the essential message at the time of death, leaving behind words to entrust the Dharma so as to inspire faith in others.
For generally, if one remains [in the world], one does not leak [the secret]; if one leaks it, one does not remain. This is a fixed rule.
How can it be that a heterodox person, having leaked [the secret], still remains? It is clear that such a person is deluding and confusing sentient beings, seeking only respect and material gain.
Thus this false speech is established; you must be careful not to believe it.
Therefore, when you teach the world to cultivate *samādhi*, you must subsequently cause them to sever all such great falsehoods.
This is the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past. For this reason, Ānanda, if one does not sever false speech—
Those who practice meditative concentration may have words that seem correct, yet their conduct proves them wrong; it is like carving fragrant wood from excrement—such a thing is impossible.

Therefore, in my teaching, I instruct bhikṣus that every movement and every stillness must rely on a straightforward mind and straightforward speech, not tolerating even a single thought of falsehood.
How can they falsely claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person? How is this any different from [the former example]?
Those who, being mere individuals, falsely assume the titles of Emperor or King, do nothing more than bring about their own ruin and loss of life.

Furthermore, even a petty king of a small state would not tolerate the unauthorized usurpation of such honorable titles; how much less so for one who is majestic and sublime, the supreme venerable one beyond the mundane world?
Do you wish to steal their name and position? Seeking such a fruit through such causes—since the cause is not true, the fruit will likewise be circuitous.
It is like a person trying to bite their own navel; it is simply impossible to reach. If you truly desire to achieve Bodhi, you must make your mind as straight as a bowstring.
With a straight mind and straight speech, all things shall be real, and by entering samādhi, [enlightenment] will come naturally.
One does not become a Māra of craving and views, but rather achieves unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. As the Sūtra says: "The study of the Way begins with refraining from false speech.
This is what that means. What I have spoken in this way is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not spoken in this way is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
You should discern this for yourself. As for "biting one's navel": to seek perfect enlightenment through false speech is like [trying to reach one's navel by biting it].
From the mouth to the navel, one cannot reach it.
*Lengyan Shuotong*, Fascicle Six;
*Lengyan Shuotong*, Fascicle Seven.
Compiled by the lay devotee Liaoyuan Liu Daokai of Baxian;
verified by the śramaṇa Lizhi of Chengdu.
I now first explain the sublime gateway for entering samādhi and practicing cultivation, as you, Ānanda, asked about the method for gathering the mind and seeking bodhi.
The path of the Bodhisattva must first maintain these four kinds of restraint as clearly as ice and frost;
[with such purity], the "three of mind and four of body" cannot arise of their own accord, for their arising would have no cause. Ānanda, if these four matters are not lost or neglected...

If the mind does not even take as its objects form, sound, smell, taste, or touch (the six sense-objects; only four are mentioned here as a linguistic abbreviation), how can any demonic activities arise?
This is the concluding response to the question. Ānanda, when you first asked about the site of enlightenment, you immediately inquired how to collect the mind.
I shall now first explain the wondrous gate of practice for entering *samādhi*, which lies solely within the single gateway of the ear-faculty.

However, those who seek the path to Bodhi must first maintain these four types of discipline—abstaining from sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying—so that they are pure and stainless, as bright as ice and frost. This is because these four constitute the root, while the others are the branches and leaves.
Once the root is severed, how can the branches and leaves grow? Furthermore, the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, along with false speech and frivolous talk...
Regarding the fourth of the four types of speech—slander and harsh words—it will certainly have no cause for arising.

Ānanda, if one maintains these four matters in this way, keeping them in mind without forgetting and not transgressing even in the slightest degree, then the mind will no longer be conditioned by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*);
how then could there be any demonic activities whatsoever? For the objects depend on thought for their persistence; when thought ceases, the objects [cease].
Upon what does it rely? Māra relies on the sensory dust (*rajas*) to enter; if the dust is forgotten, upon what can Māra rely? This is the purity of the root of precepts (*śīla-mūla*);
thereafter, one may contravene present karma and develop meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

If there are residual habits that cannot be extinguished or eliminated, you should instruct this person to single-mindedly recite my unsurpassed divine mantra, the *Mahā-sattva-vaipulya-praṇidhāna* from the Radiant Light of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa.

This is the heart-mantra spoken by the Tathāgata’s Unseen Crown-Mark (*anavalokitamūrdha-lakṣaṇa*), the unconditioned mind-Buddha, who emits radiance from his crown and sits upon a precious lotus flower. Furthermore, regarding your own past lives:
Regarding Mātanga, their karmic conditions spanning kalpas and the habitual tendencies of affectionate attachment were not formed in a single lifetime or a single kalpa.

Yet, as soon as I proclaimed [the Dharma], her love was forever severed and she became an Arhat. She was but a courtesan with no intention to practice; [how much more so for those who have long cultivated the path].
Supported by my spiritual power in secret, you shall swiftly realize the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

How could it be difficult for you, the śrāvakas gathered here, to seek the Supreme Vehicle and be certain to attain Buddhahood? It would be like raising a handful of dust in a favorable wind; what difficulty could there be? (How much more so!)
This is intended to instruct the mantra-practitioner on how to eliminate past karma. Generally, present karma is easy to regulate; one can personally contravene it.

However, habitual tendencies from the past are difficult to eradicate and necessarily rely upon spiritual power. Now, when a practitioner is inclined toward the correct yet remains stubbornly attached to the heterodox, or desires purity yet is biased toward defilement—such that they seem to be secretly driven by forces beyond their own control—all of these are summoned by past habitual tendencies.

Even those whose own fruition is not yet realized will likewise receive the prediction from Buddhas throughout the ten directions and themselves attain Buddhahood.
This is truly because the Buddhas hand over the transmission to one another, and the patriarchs pass it down in succession; there is only this one [path].
There is nothing else; for there is no other thing. Thus, both self and others rely upon this mantra for their predictions of enlightenment.
If the Tathāgatas of the ten directions rely upon this Mantra-heart, it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel—there is nothing it cannot accomplish.

Therefore, they are able to rescue and deliver all beings from suffering throughout the ten directions, simultaneously liberating them from all calamities, from the hells up to the various great and small misfortunes.
It delivers one from all manner of calamities—from the peril of bandits to hunger, thirst, and poverty—causing them to dissolve at the mere thought [of this mantra].
Thus, those who seek relief from suffering and rescue from danger all rely upon this dhāraṇī.

If the Tathāgatas of the ten directions accord with the mind of this mantra, they can cause the four requisites to be fully provided and enable one to attain knowledge of others' minds; therefore, one is able to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions.
Throughout the four modes of deportment, his offerings were never unsatisfactory. Furthermore, he was able to open his mind and penetrate the essential points of the Dharma;
thus, within assemblies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all recognized him as a Prince of the Great Dharma. In this way, he served his teacher and succeeded to the Dharma.

Is there anyone who can transcend this mantra? If the Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this Heart-Mantra, whether applying it to material things or responding to daily activities, they cause people’s hearts to find joy and sincere submission.

Therefore, all those from past kalpas who have had an affinity with or a karmic connection to this mantra shall be gathered and received [into its protection]. As for those of small roots and inferior capacities:
For those who lack affinity with this mantra and are startled or terrified upon hearing it, may they be freed from such terror;
rather, may they be gathered in and transformed by its subtle power. Is there anyone capable of standing outside this mantra?

Furthermore, from their initial attainment of enlightenment until their entry into *nirvāṇa*, all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have relied upon the recitation of this Heart Mantra. All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions...
After his parinirvāṇa, the Dharma was entrusted through the transmission of mind-to-mind seals, with lamp lighting lamp in succession.

From the Age of True Dharma (*saddharma*) to the Age of Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), all have transmitted this mantra-heart; can it not be said that this is what is employed from beginning to end?
Thus, when I speak of this *Bhadrārī* (Pañca-rakṣā) mantra of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa-Raśmi-sañcaya, it is truly the essential application of all Buddhas, and yet it is the most essential.

Because it is originally inexhaustible, even if one were to recite it continuously from dawn until dusk for a single day—without repeating a word or phrase—and continue in this manner for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one would still never reach the end. This is what is called the "Dharma-gate of a Single Syllable."
Even if one were to write it with ink from the oceans, it could never be exhausted. Furthermore, this mantra is none other than the Great Uṣṇīṣa described within the sūtras;
it is most honored and unsurpassed—how could one not pay it the highest respect and uphold it?

This is especially true for you who are still in the stage of training, prior to the third fruit, and have not yet escaped the realm of segmented existence nor ended the cycle of saṃsāra. If you resolve your minds with utmost sincerity, desiring to attain...
If one who has attained the fruit of arhatship does not maintain this mantra while sitting empty-handed in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they will certainly attract māras;
they will often become insane or deranged, frequently encountering visions of terrifying or seductive beings.

To claim that one can distance oneself from demonic affairs through body and mind alone without maintaining the mantra is impossible. You are practicing right concentration and desire to sit in the site of enlightenment.
It is sufficient to maintain this dhāraṇī exclusively.

Ānanda, if in any world, in whatever land there are sentient beings born in that country, using birch bark, palm leaves, paper, silk, or white woolen cloth, they write out this dhāraṇī during the day and store it in a fragrant pouch; even if such a person’s mind is clouded and has not yet attained [realization], [they shall be protected].
If one recites and remembers it, wears it on the body, or writes it within one's home, it should be known that throughout their entire life,
this person cannot be harmed by any poisons whatsoever.
This permits writing it down and carrying it without reciting it.

Ānanda, if in any world, according to the lands therein, sentient beings take whatever materials are produced in their own country—whether birch bark, palm leaves, paper, or white cotton cloth—and write this dhāraṇī upon them, and store them within incense sachets; such is the intention of human hearts.
I am dull-witted and not quick of mind; I have not yet been able to recite it from memory. Therefore, I shall merely have you transcribe it.
Whether you carry it upon your person or write it within your home, you should know that for as long as such a person lives, no poisons whatsoever shall be able to harm them.
Because this mantra-heart is like the *ātharvaṇa* medicine, when any poison touches it, there is none that is not dissolved and dispersed.
The benefits of copying and wearing [this mantra] are as described above. ○ Regarding *pata* (white cotton cloth): it is a type of paper produced in India;
there are those whose value is immeasurable.
Ānanda, I shall now further recite this mantra for you, to protect the world and enable one to attain great fearlessness and achieve [all goals].
Sentient beings give rise to supramundane wisdom.
This is a detailed exposition of the divine efficacy of protecting life and assisting the Path.

Since the previous exhortation to uphold [the precepts] briefly explained assisting the Path and protecting life, this is now explained in detail. Ānanda, I shall now further recite this mantra for you. There is...
There are two functions. First, to rescue and protect the sentient beings of the world so that they attain great fearlessness; this means saving the world and obtaining peace and security.
Second, to bring sentient beings to the fulfillment of supramundane wisdom; this means transcending the world and attaining eternal abiding.

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite this themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such sentient beings who uphold and recite it cannot be burned by fire or water, nor can they be drowned by water; neither great poisons nor minor poisons can harm them.
In this way, even up to the point that devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, terrestrial deities, māras, and enchantments—all their evil incantations—cannot take hold.
Their minds attain right concentration (*samādhi*). All curses, sorcery, poison, gold-poison, silver-poison, and [the harms of] plants, trees, insects, and snakes [are likewise neutralized].
The poisonous vapors of the myriad things, upon entering the mouth of this person, become the flavor of nectar (amṛta).

All malevolent stars, as well as various ghosts and spirits and those with cruel hearts and poisonous minds, cannot give rise to evil toward such a person. Even the Piṇāyakas and all the evil kings of ghosts [are unable to do so].
Together with their retinues, they shall all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.
This is how the Śākya rescues and protects the world, enabling it to attain great fearlessness. What is meant by his ability to rescue and protect the world?
If, after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings in the final age are able to recite this mantra themselves or teach it to others...

Those who recite this mantra should know that such a person who upholds the mantra cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and all poisons, whether great or small, cannot cause them harm. Such adverse conditions will be unable to inflict injury.
Likewise, even gods, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, *bhūtas*, and malevolent demons—all their evil spells—will be unable to take hold. These evils...

No living being can inflict harm upon them. Even if there should be those who forcibly seek to administer poison, they are powerless against this person, for they are sustained by the power of their mantras and have attained samādhi, with their minds entering into right concentration (*samāpatti*).

Should any curses, malevolent spells, poisons, or even the toxic vapors of all manner of things enter this person’s mouth, not only will they be unable to cause injury, but they will moreover be transformed into something sweet.
It reveals the supreme flavor: namely, churning the great rivers into cream and curd, and transforming the vast earth into gold.
Moreover, not only can evil not be inflicted upon such a person, but even the arising of evil within them is impossible.
All malevolent stars, ghosts, spirits, and cruel, venomous people—when before such a person—will find that evil does not arise of its own accord; this is what is meant by "beholding virtue."
This is what is meant by "the appearance being transformed while the intent dissolves," and "the heart being transformed upon beholding the breeze of compassion.
Furthermore, it is not merely that they are unable to give rise to evil; rather, their evil turns into kindness and their calamities transform into auspiciousness.

From Pinnayaka onwards, all the evil ghost kings and their retinues have benefited others through the recitation of mantras; they all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.
One can see that good and bad fortune, calamity and blessing, are transferred according to oneself; thus, the protection of the world through the power of this mantra is also said to be ultimate.
Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is constantly accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-koṭis*.
The family of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbharāja consists of individual members, each having hosts of vajras as their retinue, who attend upon them day and night.
Should there be sentient beings who, even with a distracted mind and not in samādhi, remember this in their hearts and maintain it in their speech, [they shall attain the fruit].
These are the Vajra Kings who constantly follow those sons of good family; how much more so for those who have resolved upon the bodhicitta.
These Vajra Bodhisattvas, the Kings of the Treasury, with their refined essence, swiftly and urgently stimulate the divine consciousness of such a person.
At that moment, this person’s mind will be able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons, knowing them thoroughly and universally, attaining non-retrogression.
Doubt. From this point downward, up until the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), all explain the accomplishment of the supramundane wisdom of sentient beings.
What is meant by being able to accomplish the supramundane? Ānanda, it is to protect the world from calamities, [and] spirits and ghosts...
One may lend strength to assist the supramundane path; this is not possible for those who have not attained the deep stages of a bodhisattva.

You should know that this mantra is itself the adamantine precious awakening (*vajra-ratna-bodhi*). Therefore, like voices responding to one another and essences seeking their kin, there are always countless Vajragarbha Kings Bodhisattvas and their retinues who attend upon it day and night. Even if... [the assembly] should...

Those who have been born into this world and practice the path for a long time, yet whose minds are distracted and who have not yet attained certainty in abiding constantly in *samādhi*, need only remember this mantra in their hearts and recite it with their mouths.

This Vajra King will also constantly follow them, because they are not among those who are negligent or defiled, and because the mantra dwells within their hearts; how much more so, then, for those who have attained certainty?
As for one who has resolved to attain Bodhicitta and further maintains mantras, how should their attendant conduct themselves? Moreover, it is not merely a matter of attendance;
the essential spirit of the Bodhisattva and the essential spirit of the practitioner have been fundamentally and inherently one and the same.
Moreover, when combined with the power of mantras, I know that this Vajragarbha King will surely use his refined mind to secretly impel the practitioner and awaken their spiritual consciousness,
causing the person’s mind to open at the appropriate time so they can remember events from eighty-four thousand Ganges-sands of kalpas,
penetrating the three periods of time with certainty and understanding them without doubt, [revealing] their past lives.
They must penetrate these. If one does not first develop penetrating clarity, then one will mostly be obscured by the "shading of the corpse" (the transition between lives) and fall into darkness;
how then could one escape the evil realms for long kalpas, be born into superior states, and ultimately realize the fruits of the path?
From the first kalpa until their final body, in every successive birth, they will not be born in such evil states as yakṣas,
rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and various hungry ghosts— whether with form or without form,
with perception or without perception.

This clarifies that one does not fall into the evil realms. By the power of this mantra, once this person has attained the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), from the time they first resolved upon *bodhicitta* at the beginning of the first eon, until the day they descend to be born as a Buddha upon the fulfillment of the causes for their final body—in the interval between these, their practice is forever free from all deviousness or complications. In every birth, they shall not be born as a yakṣa.
From the rākṣasas up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception— such evil places as these— by means of this mantra-heart,
which is a pure and white dharma and the supreme good, the various realms of existence cannot defile it.
If these sons of good family read, recite, copy, transcribe, wear, or preserve it, and offer various forms of worship,
they will not be born in states of poverty, lowliness, or unpleasantness throughout kalpa after kalpa.
This clarifies that one will not be born into lowly or base circumstances. Such a son of good family, regarding this mantra-heart,
whether reading it face-to-face with the original text, or reciting it from memory without the original, or drawing its seal or copying or transcribing it,
or wearing it secretly as a talisman or carrying or concealing it— by making offerings in these various ways, they shall not be born into poverty or lowliness throughout kalpa after kalpa.
This is a source of joy. By means of this mantra-heart, it is the most supreme and most noble of dharmas. It is like a crown prince dwelling in the womb, whose nobility surpasses all ministers.
Although these sentient beings may neglect their own persons and fail to perform meritorious deeds, [they partake in] all the merits and virtues of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

He gives all of this to such a person. By virtue of this, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), unspeakable, and beyond description—they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas.
Their immeasurable merits will be like clusters of *akṣa* berries, cultivated together in one place, never to be dispersed.
Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of morality, and for those who have not yet attained the precepts, [to attain them].
It causes those who have not yet received the precepts to obtain them; it causes those who are not diligent to attain diligence; it causes those who lack wisdom to attain wisdom;
it causes those who are not pure to quickly attain purity; and it causes those who do not observe the fast and precepts to spontaneously fulfill them.

This clarifies the merits obtained in the present life. Even if these sentient beings who uphold the mantra do not personally perform meritorious deeds themselves, the Tathāgata bestows all his merits upon them.
By means of this *dhāraṇī*-heart, they become fully endowed with the ten thousand practices (*sāhasrika-caryā*).
All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous qualities of all Tathāgatas manifest therein. Furthermore, due to the merits bestowed by the Buddhas mentioned previously, and...

One feels that throughout future kalpas, one will always be born in the same place as all Buddhas. This is because one’s vital energy (*qi-fen*) has interfused with that of the Buddhas, and their minds have attained perfect union.
The Buddha does not depart from the mind, nor does the mind depart from the Buddha. Since one constantly follows the Buddha, [this state is realized].
Every single aspect of the Buddha’s merits has its share; that which the practitioner cultivates is precisely what the Buddhas have realized.
These are forged into a single whole, like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits, through intimate cultivation and permeation, remaining inseparable throughout long kalpas.
Not only this, but it can also cause those who have broken the precepts to have their roots of discipline purified, for the power of the mantra is as efficacious as a spiritual mind.
A single grain of cinnabar can transform iron into gold. For those who have not yet attained the precepts, it causes them to attain the precepts;

the mantra-mind possesses the faculty of morality (*śīla-indriya*). For those who have not yet achieved diligence, it causes them to achieve diligence; the mantra-mind possesses the faculty of energy (*vīrya-indriya*). For those who lack wisdom, it causes them to attain wisdom;
the mantra-mind possesses the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*). For those who are not pure, it swiftly brings about purity.

Purity: This refers to the mantra-heart possessing pure faculties. Even if a person has karmic obstructions from past lives such that they repeatedly desire to observe the fast and precepts (*upavāsa*) but cannot achieve success, the mantra can bring it to fruition.

Or, if one is hindered by karma or by physical obstacles, or lacks a teacher or a ritual altar and thus cannot observe the fast and precepts, it is permitted to simply maintain the mantra, which is equivalent to observing the fast and precepts.
Ānanda, when these sons of good family maintain this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them—(receiving meaning to maintain;

"prior to receiving" means prior to maintaining the mantra)—all their offenses of breaking the precepts, regardless of whether they are light or heavy, shall be extinguished at once after they have maintained the mantra.

Even if one has consumed alcohol or the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*), or engaged in various forms of impurity, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, spirits, and deities will not regard this as a transgression.
Even if one wears impure or tattered clothing, whether walking or staying still, [they remain unperturbed].

All shall be equally pure. Even if one does not construct a ritual altar, does not enter a *maṇḍala*, and does not practice the Way, yet recites and upholds this mantra, it is no different from the merit of entering an altar and practicing the Way;

there is no distinction between them. Should one commit the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) or the four offenses involving expulsion (*pārājika*) or the eight offenses involving suspension (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—the four offenses being the four root grave sins of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, by committing which one is forever cast out from the Buddha—[this mantra shall purify them].
Beyond the Dharma—this is what is called a *pārājika* offense in the Sanskrit language. For a bhikṣuṇī, there are likewise four such offenses, namely: touching, the eighth, concealing, and following.
Once this mantra has been recited, even such grave offenses will be completely eliminated, like a mound of sand scattered by a fierce wind, leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.

This clarifies the manifestation of the eradication of karmic offenses. Ānanda, if these sons of good family can merely maintain this mantra, even if they have violated prohibitive precepts prior to maintaining it, once they have maintained it, all violations—regardless of whether the transgressions of the precepts were light or heavy—are instantly extinguished.
However, once the offenses have been extinguished, one must not create them again. Furthermore, regarding those [offenses] committed prior to maintaining [the mantra]:

Furthermore, even if one has previously consumed alcohol, pungent foods, or various other impure substances, by once holding this mantra, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will not regard it as a transgression;
or, out of true compassion, they may grant permission. Thus, those who are unable to fully observe the fast and precepts [are absolved].
I also permit you to maintain [these practices]. Nevertheless, you must truly and earnestly embrace them with all your heart, never forgetting or losing them;
only then can it be said that wine and meat do not obstruct the path to Bodhi.

Not only this, but even if a practitioner is pure and poor and lacks resources, though they may wear unclean and tattered garments, in every action and every station, they are entirely equal to those who are pure.
Regarding the merits sustained by those in pure places, even those who are wealthy do not fall under this category.

Furthermore, the aforementioned altar rituals are extremely difficult to fully prepare. Even if one does not construct an altar, nor enter a *dōjō* to practice the Way, simply upholding this mantra constitutes abiding in the Great Samādhi;
it is a true ground of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), which is superior to merely possessing [the ritual implements].
For those who do not possess a concentrated mind while observing the characteristics of the altar, it is therefore no different from the merit of entering the altar and performing the rites;

there is no distinction between them. Furthermore, even if a layperson has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, or if an ordained bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has violated the four parājikas or eight parājikas—crimes which are otherwise considered irredeemable through repentance—nevertheless, by reciting...
Having recited this mantra, such heavy karma will be extinguished almost entirely, like sand blown away by a fierce wind, leaving not even a hair’s breadth remaining.
However, what was transgressed prior to holding the mantra may be eliminated by relying on the power of the mantra;
it does not mean that one may commit these evils with impunity, thinking there is no fear because of the mantra.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas,

have accumulated all manner of light and heavy karmic obstacles from previous lives that they have not yet had the opportunity to repent— if they can read, recite, copy, or transcribe this mantra, and wear it upon their person,
or place it within their dwellings, houses, gardens, or pavilions— then such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in boiling water.
This extinguishes past karma. Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, since immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago,
have committed all manner of light and heavy transgressions and obstacles, which they were unable to repent for in previous lives— if they can now either read,
recite, or copy this mantra, wear it upon their bodies, or place it within the dwellings, houses, or estates where they reside— [then these karmic hindrances shall be eliminated].
Within these gardens and pavilions, such accumulated karma from successive lifetimes is like snow melting in boiling water; how could it not be extinguished?
As it is said: "A single lamp can dispel the darkness of a thousand-year-old chamber."
Before long, all shall attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
This concludes the preceding section on the accomplishment of the supramundane wisdom of sentient beings.

By the power of upholding this mantra, one can both generate goodness in people and counteract and eliminate evil; therefore, practitioners shall before long all attain the realization of non-arising.
Patience. After attaining this patience, both sin and merit are empty; the distinctions between the holy and the ordinary are exhausted.

Thus, one may regard demons and Buddhas as identical, traversing all realms of suffering and evil without obstruction or discrimination. This constitutes the successful fulfillment of the aids to the Path.

To examine the previous manifestation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), it was produced by the accomplishment of the meditative mind (*samādhi-citta*); now, the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is produced by the accomplishment of the wisdom mind (*prajñā-citta*).
One should know that the latter stage is deeper than the former. If one follows the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), [the distinction is as follows].

One realizes this patience (*kṣānti*) upon entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). If one follows the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-vyākhyāna*), it should be at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) or above.
According to the six categories, the first four constitute the *siddhānta* for producing human and celestial goodness; the fifth is the *siddhānta* for remedying and destroying evil;
and this present category is the *siddhānta* for entering principle through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). As for the preceding "rescue from difficulties" and the subsequent...
This is the response to such requests; it is the *loka-anuvartana-siddhānta* (the world-pleasing teaching).
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet given birth to children and desires to conceive, if she can do so with a sincere heart—
Recall this mantra. Or, if one wears this *Sītātapatrā* upon one's person, sons and daughters endowed with merit and wisdom will be born.

Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life. Those who wish for their karmic rewards to be swiftly fulfilled shall quickly attain fulfillment (this refers to the fruits of merit and reward).
Physical vitality, strength, and complexion shall likewise be so. (This is further within the context of long life.)

Furthermore, this collectively clarifies that one will not decline, but rather that the hundred members of the body shall remain healthy and robust. After the end of life, one will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to one's vows;
one will certainly never be born in a remote region or among the lowly, much less in any mixed or inferior form.
This clarifies that what is sought shall be as one wishes. Furthermore, Ānanda, (and so forth). How much more so for miscellaneous forms?

Indeed, there are a thousand kinds of treasures in the ocean; first, one seeks that which accords with one's will. By means of this mantra-heart, it becomes a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*); one may take it without restriction.
It is inexhaustible when used. Therefore, during one's lifetime, one attains mastery according to one’s will; and at the time of death, one likewise succeeds in being reborn according to one’s vow.
Ānanda, if in various lands, prefectures, counties, or villages, there should be famine, pestilence, or the calamities of war and bandits—

In places of strife and contention, as well as all other lands of calamity and distress, one should transcribe this divine mantra and install it at the four gates of the city, as well as upon various caityas (i.e., *jātī*, here meaning places where offerings are made), or atop *dhvajas* (banners).

One should cause all sentient beings within that realm to welcome this mantra, prostrating with reverence and making offerings with a single-minded focus. Furthermore, one should cause the people to each wear it upon their own bodies.
Or, if placed individually in one's own dwelling or land, all calamities and misfortunes will be entirely extinguished.
This demonstrates the peace and security of the realm. Ānanda, if in all lands (and so forth), they are entirely extinguished.
By means of this mantra-heart, it is a treasure that stabilizes the nation; it cannot be rivaled by the Beryl of Huashi or the pearls that illuminate a carriage.
Ānanda, in whatever land or place sentient beings possess this mantra, the devas and nāgas will rejoice, and the winds and rains [will be harmonious].
The seasons proceed in harmony; the five grains flourish in abundance; and the myriad people enjoy peace and happiness.
This demonstrates that the people are concordant and the year is bountiful. Ānanda... [and so forth] ...peace and happiness.

By means of this mantra-heart, one becomes the sovereign of the four seasons and the master of the ten thousand phenomena. Therefore, rain and sunshine accord with the proper times, just as Zhuangzi said: "When the spirit is concentrated and still, it brings about..."
The people will suffer neither from diseases nor calamities, and the years' harvests will ripen. However, it is also necessary for the entire nation to maintain reverent faith;
only then will one obtain spiritual efficacy. This is like a practitioner of mantras: it takes a long time before they become efficacious; how could there be swift results in a mere moment?
If, despite possessing the mantras in their entirety, one keeps them high on a shelf and never offers them reverence, or even places them in a vulgar and defiled location, [they will yield no fruit].
To fail to sweep away dust and filth, yet to demand that there be no miraculous efficacy, is likewise a profound delusion.
Furthermore, it is able to suppress all malevolent stars and their transformations according to the directions; calamities and obstructions do not arise, and people suffer no untimely deaths.
Manacles, fetters, cangues, and shackles shall not touch their bodies; they shall sleep peacefully day and night, and never experience evil dreams.
Ānanda, in this Sahā world, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars (namely, the twenty-eight lunar mansions) as their leaders.
Furthermore, there are eight great malevolent stars that serve as their masters (the eight stars being those of the five elements, plus Rāhu, Ketu, and Bhauma). They act as...
Various forms appear in the world, capable of producing all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings; yet where this mantra-ground exists, they are all completely extinguished.
Within an area of twelve *yojanas*, it becomes a consecrated boundary (*sīmābandha*), such that no evil omens or disasters can ever enter.
This demonstrates the transformation of misfortune into good fortune. Furthermore, it can suppress [calamities] such that they can never enter.
For transformations, anomalies, disasters, and obstacles are all induced by the deluded karma of one's own *sabhāga* (homogeneous class).

Since the power of the mantra accords with a hundredfold auspiciousness, all evil transformations are extinguished in heaven; thus, neither disaster nor ill omen enters its domain. From among the rulers of this land, one emerges...
"Excellent words! Even the malevolent planet Mars withdraws and departs; how much more so, then, for the unsurpassed Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī-hṛdaya?
For this reason, the Tathāgata has proclaimed this mantra to protect beginners and all practitioners in future ages."
Entering samādhi, body and mind become serene, and one attains great peace and stability.
Furthermore, no demons, ghosts, spirits, or the karmic debts and calamities from beginningless time—whether old karma or lingering grievances—shall come to cause harm or affliction.
You, as well as all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, shall rely upon my maṇḍala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma.

If the preceptor from whom one received the precepts encounters pure monks and yet does not give rise to doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart, then these good sons shall attain mental penetration within this very body born of their parents; otherwise, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods.
This is the exhortation that you should uphold. Such is the greatness of the power of mantras.

This illusory nature originally arises from the ignorance of the initial phase of birth (*ādi-bhava-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*);
it has no real substance and no real locus of dependence. One can see that while the True is unchanging, the false is fundamentally empty.

What is called the "inversion of the world"? Originally there is no cause, yet it serves as the cause from which they are born; originally there is no place, yet it serves as the place where they dwell.

There are three periods of time and four directions in the world; as the three intersect with the four and the four intersect with the three, they harmoniously combine and interpenetrate, revolving to form twelve.

There are twelve categories. Therefore, the world arises entirely from the single thought-moment of deluded movement within sentient beings.
Thus, the internal sense-faculties and external objects are neither before nor after; they are fully present all at once. To speak of the six sense-objects by way of example:

Because these six types of deluded conceptualizations—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—constitute the nature that creates karma, therein...

Therefore, the worldly objects—sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and so forth—and the faculties—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth—exhaust the twelve transformations to form a single cycle of reciprocal rotation.

Furthermore, there are realms that revolve through the characteristics of inversion, which likewise comprise twelve categories. What are these twelve? They are:

The world is inverted; this is the common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*) of sentient beings, as it is shared by all.

If one shatters the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and severs birth-and-death through fragmentation (*bheda-saṃsāra*), then one realizes *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), and the inversions of sentient beings begin to cease.

If one shatters the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), severs birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-saṃsāra*), and realizes *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), [the inversions are completely extinguished].
When [the mind] is overturned, the world’s inversion first becomes empty. Therefore it is said: "Inversion does not arise.
This is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi. ○ This treatise discusses the inversion of the world solely by establishing it based on this realm and forming it based on this world;
it specifically points to the world. Although the term "world" appears frequently from here until the end of the scroll, [it refers only to this].

The twelve classes of beings all refer exclusively to sentient beings; they must not be conflated with the world-system. One should synthesize the meaning according to the respective passages, rather than forcing an artificial distinction between them.

Ānanda, because the world is characterized by the delusive cycle of saṃsāra and the inversion of movement, the combination of vital energies gives rise to eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Due to this, there are egg-born beings such as the kalala (here translated as "congealed mucus," which is the first stage within the womb), which circulate through various lands;
fish, birds, tortoises, and snakes—beings of these kinds fill the world.
Below this, the various types of birth are listed individually; here, the causes and effects of egg-birth (*aṇḍaja*) are clarified.
Ānanda, what is meant by egg-birth? That which is born from within a shell is called an egg. An egg arises solely from thought (*saṃjñā*). This delusion is precisely thought.
Due to the world’s delusion, beings transmigrate; they lose sight of the unmoving true essence and suddenly undergo false movement. Thereupon, they look downward...
Gazing at heaven and earth, they suddenly ascend and suddenly descend; suddenly arise and suddenly perish. They are arrogant and unruly, beyond restraint—is this not perversion?
Because this movement is fundamentally perverted, they interact through the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Through the harmonious blending of these breaths, eighty-four thousand chaotic thoughts of floating and sinking are formed, corresponding to the transformations induced by the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). This is that which creates [the world].

This is the cause. Because of this, there exist the stages of the egg and the *kalala*, through which one undergoes birth after birth and death after death, transmigrating within the realms of existence.
One becomes a fish, a bird, a tortoise, or a snake; such species fill the world. This is the fruit produced by those causes.
As for cases where a fish transforms into a bird or a snake transforms into a tortoise, one suddenly forgets the manner of swimming.
Thus they attain the form of flying and singing, suddenly forgetting their state of crouching and bending, and attain the substance of limping and staggering.
Even to the point where cranes cry out to one another and egrets gaze at one another— their varieties are beyond reckoning—
and who among them is not the result of such inversion?
Due to the causes of the world’s defiled cycle of rebirth and the inversion of desire,

eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts are combined and nurtured into existence. Consequently, there is the *arbuda* (herein called "blister," which is the second stage within the womb),
which flows through various lands, filling them with all classes of beings— humans, beasts, dragons, and immortals.
This clarifies the causes and effects of birth from a womb (*jarāyu-jā*). What is meant by "womb-birth"? That which emerges from being contained and stored is called a womb.

The womb exists because of emotion (*kleśa*); this defilement is precisely emotion. Due to the world as cause, one becomes deluded regarding this intrinsically pure and luminous essence, and suddenly falls into the dust of emotion, turbidifying the true nature and entering the cycle of defiled saṃsāra. When emotion gives rise to craving, it is termed the inversion of desire.
The womb is formed through the union of the vital essences; this is called "harmonious blending and growth. Sentient emotion has both biased and correct aspects:
bias leads to horizontal [birth], while correctness leads to vertical [birth]. These are termed the eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of horizontal and vertical birth;

these are the causal factors that create them. Because of this, there is the stage of *arbuda* within the womb, as one transmigrates through various lands, becoming human, animal, dragon, or immortal—such are the categories.
Pervasive. Human and celestial beings are vertical; dragons and beasts are horizontal. These are the fruits produced by such causes. In total, they are nothing but a single state of perversion.
This arises from the perversion of the world’s causal attachment to the realms of saṃsāra. Through the combination of warmth, eighty-four thousand [forms] are formed.

With these inverted and chaotic thoughts, there thus arises the stage of the *kleda-bhasa* (the "moisture-phase corpse," which refers here to soft flesh—the initial sign of moisture-born birth). Since they do not enter a womb, the two preceding stages do not exist.
Thus they transmigrate through the lands, teeming with crawling and wriggling creatures that fill every corner.

This clarifies the causes and effects of moisture-born beings (*saṃsvedaja*). What is meant by "moisture-born"? To be born through reliance on moisture is called "moisture. Moisture arises from union;

attachment is precisely this union. Due to the world of causes, they do not know the True Mind, which is without abiding—like a mani jewel that manifests colors according to its surroundings and has no fixed form of its own—yet they rush toward objects like a wind, pursuing the times and clinging to power.

One clings to saṃsāra because one’s course is inverted. Thereupon, through the conjunction [of conditions], warmth is formed. It is like people whose passions are exhausted who rush toward places of clamor;
their destination is not fixed. It is like turning the hand over to create clouds or turning it back to bring down rain—this is called the eighty-four thousand inverted and chaotic thoughts.
Thus, there arises the stage of the *kalala* (the moist phase), which is characterized by moisture and obscuration.
They include the wriggling and crawling, such as the *hēijī* (vinegar flies) and *mièměng* (gnats). These kinds fill the world;

yet because throughout their lives they did not accord with the Way and righteousness, being deficient in every matter and lacking the spirit of a man, they receive this retribution of being wriggling and devoid of consciousness.
Due to the false inversions caused by the transformation and saṃsāra of the world, eighty-four thousand new and old disordered thoughts are formed through the conjunction of contact.

Because of this, there is the flow and circulation within realms of existence of the *kalala* (the *kalala* is here translated as "hard flesh," for it immediately forms a body and lacks the characteristic of softness;

those below this that are called *kalala* refer to the fifth stage, *praśākhā*, which is termed "formation," as it follows specific features and is not a general designation), which undergoes transformation and flies away.
They act; their kind fills [the world].
This clarifies the cause and effect of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*). What is meant by transformation-birth? To suddenly exist where there was nothing is called "transformation" (*hua*).

Transformation implies being free from [fixed] response; change and transformation is precisely this freedom. It arises from the world of causes: suddenly reverent, suddenly negligent; suddenly joyful, suddenly angry.

"Three in the morning, four in the evening. This refers to the shifting and revolving of saṃsāra. One fails to realize that the true master remains unchanging while following conditions, and remains unchanged while following conditions;

yet one instead turns back upon this truth and acts contrary to it. With the mouth at rest but the mind in suffering, such a person—due to these false inversions—alters their principles at every turn.
Disenchanted with the old, they delight in the new; preferring red over white, they become attached through the process of synthesis.

Thus, eighty-four thousand new and old disordered thoughts are formed. Consequently, there are transformed appearances (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and *kalala* that circulate through the lands, shedding the old to enter the new, undergoing metamorphosis and flight.

It is like a sparrow transforming into a clam—changing from flying to sinking—or a dung beetle transforming into a cicada, or a silkworm transforming into a butterfly—changing from crawling to flying. Though their forms differ, they pass one into the other in succession.
Their kind fills the world; it is simply because throughout their lives they lacked any moral integrity and gave rise to disturbances at every turn that they have experienced this retribution.

Question: The sutras state that those in the hells and the various heavens are all born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Why does this refer specifically to the class of beings that undergoes metamorphosis? Answer:

Regarding the place of defilement for those born by transformation, it is called "accomplishment through the contact of harmony" (*saṃnipāta-sparśa*). As for the place of defilement for the heavens...

The denizens of hell perceive foul odors; these are all transformations based on karmic projections (*karma-vipāka-nirmāṇa*), rather than the wondrous transformations born of spontaneous intent (*manomaya-nirmāṇa*). Therefore, they may be subsumed within the category of "transformative flight" (*pariṇāmika-udbhijja*).
Due to the delusions of attachment and inversion that cause the obstruction of the world’s stagnation and cyclic existence, eighty-four thousand [afflictions] are formed through their conjunction.

Essential brilliance and chaotic thoughts—because of these, there are *kalala* (embryonic stages) with physical forms that circulate through lands; there are brilliant spirits of auspicious and inauspicious omens, their kinds filling every space.
This clarifies the cause and effect of the realm of form. What is meant by "possessing form"? It arises because, regarding the world, one does not know its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

One possesses the light of great wisdom that pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it is fundamentally without obstruction. Yet, you instead serve water, fire, the sun, and the moon in search of illumination.
By relying on light to establish a focal point, you have consequently created obstructions and failed to attain perfect penetration.
Is this not a state of inversion? You abandon your own inexhaustible radiance and instead identify with that which is merely bright and conscious.
This constitutes the ultimate state of affairs. Thereupon, through their harmonious conjunction, eighty-four thousand types of subtle and chaotic thoughts are formed;
these are what are called "playing with the spirit-soul. By means of such causes, there arise material forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands.
Among them, those in the heavens become the sun, moon, and stars; the auspicious become portents of rest, while the inauspicious become omens of calamity. By...
Reaching down to all spirits and numinous beings—down to the minute glow of fireflies and the luster of oysters—their kinds fill every space;

there is not one that is not merely the retribution received through obstructed and inverted [perceptions]. ○ All the devas of the Form Realm sit here, because all these devas possess bodily radiance.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the eighty spirits are all... due to... [the power of the Buddha].

The source of obstructive perceptions constitutes this refined radiance; therefore, although it is most refined and most spiritual, it has not yet escaped the state of being subject to that wheeling cycle of inverted appearances.
Due to the causes of the world’s dissolution and the delusions of samsaric inversion, the conjunction of darkness forms eighty-four thousand obscured and chaotic conceptions.
Consequently, there exists the formless *kalala*, which wanders through the realms, dispersing into emptiness and sinking away.
These types are so numerous as to fill [the realms].
This clarifies the cause and effect of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). What is meant by "formless"? It arises from the world’s cause: through weariness with existence, one clings to emptiness;

by extinguishing the body, one returns to non-existence, which is called the cycle of dissolution. Being deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (*sāsrava*), one takes this to be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); thus it becomes a source of confusion.
Inverted, they weary of existence and return to non-existence; thus, they rely upon the dark and obscure void.
Consequently, they combine with darkness to form eighty-four thousand subtle, hidden, and chaotic conceptions—namely, states of being dazed, silent, profound, and murky.
Due to such causes, there arise formless *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands, becoming empty, vacuous, and diffused. This is...

The heavens of the Formless Realm exist to grind away and eliminate sinking and stagnation; they are presided over by deities of space, whose kind fill [the realm] entirely, being none other than the fruits received from delusion and inversion.
Question: In the Formless Realm where there is perception, the substance of karma is not established.
On what basis is it also called *kalala*? Answer: Although there is no substantial entity of karma, it does not preclude the existence of birth bound by karma;
therefore, it is also called *kalala*. This is a designation based on its functional meaning.
Due to the world’s causes—the revolving shadows of delusive forms and inverted perceptions—there arise eighty-four thousand latent knots of confused thoughts through the combination of memories.
Consequently, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages characterized by conceptual signs, which circulate through various lands as gods, ghosts, and spirits.
These types fill the world;

this clarifies the cause and effect of existence-with-perception (*saṃjñā*). What is meant by "existence-with-perception"? It arises from the world’s causes: through a perverse longing for spiritual powers, one pursues shadows and indulges in recollective thoughts.
These are hazy and superficial, resembling the real yet lacking true authenticity; they are called the "transmigration of the phantom" (*wangxiang*), characterized by clinging to shadows.
Yet they neglect the Truth and become deluded by shadows. Morning and evening they grasp at their minds, suspending them in a single place;
thus, through the conjunction of recollections, eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts are formed. As it is said: "The Way, as a thing, is hazy and indistinct."
They all see their reflections, yet they have not truly seen their original face. It is also said: "Continuous as if it were present;
its use is without exertion. This means that the longer one uses it, the more it becomes entangled and fails to disperse.

Due to such causes, there arise the *kalala* (embryonic stage) characterized by conceptualization, which flows through various lands and becomes ghosts, spirits, or numinous beings, having no fixed end.
As for actual form, it possesses only the marks of conceptualization; all arise from practicing in confusion, whereby one attains its shadow but not its reality.

Thus, even though they possess the five supernormal powers, they have not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows. Such beings abound, and there is none among them who has not merely received the fruit of inverted perceptions based on shadows.
Due to the causes of worldly ignorance, dullness, cyclic existence, delusion, and perversion, they combine with stubbornness to form eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts.
Consequently, there are "unconscious kalala" beings who transmigrate through various lands;
their spirits transform into earth, wood, metal, and stone, and such types fill the world.
This clarifies the cause and effect of the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñin*). What is meant by "non-conceptualization"?
It arises because, within the world of causes, one does not know that one’s own nature is originally perfect and vibrant. When it is in the eye, it can see; when it is in the ear, it can hear.
It is like a jewel in the sunlight, whose colors have no fixed form; it is like a gourd on water, which cannot be pressed down. Yet, one forcibly suppresses it, as if pressing down a stone.
It is like a fish trapped in ice; this is what is called a corpse whose soul has not yet dispersed. Is this not the dullness of saṃsāra, resulting in deluded inversions?

Because of these deluded inversions, one combines with stubbornness to produce eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts—namely, the destruction of the physical frame and the casting aside of intelligence, resulting in cold ashes and withered wood.
It is like wood that is utterly devoid of warmth. For such reasons, there exist *asaṃjñika-kalala* (unconscious embryos) that transmigrate through the realms.
Because they do not understand the principles of the Truths (*satya*), they stubbornly cling to ignorance;

being the very pinnacle of dullness and stupidity, their spirits are transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone—such as the "essence" produced from a flower-pillar or the "Yellow-Headed One" who turned into stone. Their...
All things are filled with these; they are nothing other than the fruits received through delusion and inversion.
Above, those in the realms of form and formlessness, as well as those with and without perception, are all practitioners who have failed to attain the truth;
thus, they are divided into four categories. Master Lien asked: "If one is withered and parched, there would be no perception. Furthermore, what is meant by 'confused perception'?"
It is like withered grass that has just dried up; though its roots are not yet severed, it will grow again when the time comes.

Thus, earth, wood, metal, and stone, through the power of their stubborn nature, become stubborn objects. Consequently, when they encounter conditions and are touched by emotions, they continue to flow and revolve according to their former patterns.
Due to the false and inverted cycle of mutual dependence within the world, these combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts based on causes.
Consequently, there arise non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala*, circulating through various lands.
The various jellyfish and similar creatures take shrimp for their eyes; such species fill the world.
This clarifies that there is no causal relationship involving form. What is meant by "not having form"?

It is because, throughout the world, it does not know its own nature as being in opposition to the various sensory objects; rather, it takes all phenomena as companions and stands preeminent before all things. And...
On the contrary, they rely on others, taking them for their own strength; they await external things to achieve their utility, thus creating the cycle of mutual dependence.

They lose the true nature of heaven and cling persistently to the floating and false, becoming deluded by artificiality and inverted views. They become stained by power and influence, relying upon fame and reputation.
Through these harmonious combinations, they give rise to eighty-four thousand causes of dependency and chaotic thoughts, like a fox borrowing the tiger’s majesty—a mere guest on its journey.
This refers to the category of the "Lord's Command" and the like. Because of such causes, the resulting fruit is fundamentally without form, yet it acquires form by depending on external objects.
Because it lacks the characteristics of form, it becomes the *kalala* (embryo) in its form-aspect and transmigrates through the realms.
Just as the water scorpion takes bubbles of water for its body and uses shrimp for its eyes,
so too are all the various ghosts and spirits that rely on grass and wood, as well as the eighty-four thousand families of worms within the body, filling it to overflowing.
Yet the destinies of falsehood and perversion lead to suffering. Below this are the four modes of birth, which represent the height of delusion;
as Wenling said, "the more one's deluded emotions wander, the more one's transformation from the principle deviates."

Due to the nature of delusion that causes beings to revolve in samsara by drawing one another through the characteristics of the world, these combine with mantras to form eighty-four thousand confused thoughts of summoning.
Because of this, there exist non-material forms and non-material *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands.
Curses and incantations arise; their like fills the world.
This clarifies that it is not the case that there are no causes and effects in the formless realm. What is meant by "not being without form"?

It is because, throughout the world, people do not know that their own nature possesses meritorious virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges that accord with that nature. Unable to draw these forth to bring them into manifestation, they instead resort to heterodox [practices].
Regarding the karma of verbal misconduct: through the influence of habitual perfuming and inducement, one’s nature is altered.

Because these factors mutually induce one another within saṃsāra, and because one’s nature has become inverted, they combine with mantras to produce eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning.
This refers to such things as the present-day practices of drawing talismans, performing mudrās, and invoking spirits or ghosts. Due to such causes, that which is evoked—
The fruit was originally not formless, yet it further became a formless *kalala*. Because it exists when summoned, it is not non-form;
because it does not exist when not summoned, it is formless. Thus, the revolving lands arise through curses and incantations.
For example, in the case of a man made of *cāṇḍalī* wood, by the power of incantations, there are such things as predicting auspiciousness or reporting misfortune. Such is their kind.
They are everywhere. This occurs because one summoned spirits and ghosts during the causal stage; thus, they appear as humans during the resultant stage.
Consequently, their nature becomes perverse and they head toward suffering. ○ There is another kind of heterodox deity and ghost in the world that listens to and is employed by humans.
As for orthodox deities, unless one possesses utmost sincerity and supreme virtue, they cannot be moved; how could they respond to a deluded person?
How could they be summoned? These two aforementioned types are both transformations resulting from conjunction.

Because the world arises from the conjunction of delusions and revolves in inverted confusion, the harmonious blending gives rise to eighty-four thousand varieties of reciprocal and chaotic conceptualizations.

Thus, there exist the *kalala* (embryonic stage), the *arbuda* (tumor-like stage), and the *peśī* (flesh-like stage), which are neither existent nor non-existent, yet manifest as the perception of existence, as they circulate through various lands.
Those such as the *pulu* (parasites) transform one substance into another; their kind fills the world.
This clarifies that they do not possess the cause-and-effect relationship of "having thought" (*saṃjñin*). What is meant by "not having thought"?

It is because, within the world, they do not recognize the True Lord as their most intimate being, but instead turn their backs upon Him; thus, regarding what is not their own kin, they forcibly [impose their will].
To treat as one's kin those who are not one's own children, and to force upon oneself as one's own possessions things that are not one's own;
to forcibly unite what is actually separate—this is called the cycle of false conjunctions. When these two types of false conjunctions combine, one's nature and emotions become utterly obscured;
this is called the delusion of ignorance. Thus, through the blending of these differences, eighty-four thousand chaotic and mutually revolving thoughts are formed. This is called...

One appropriates what belongs to others as one's own. Because of such causes, the resulting fruit is not characterized by the perception [of the object], yet it constitutes a *kalala* through perception.
Since another’s property is fundamentally not intended for me, it is said to be "without perception";
yet because I forcibly take possession of it, the notion of "I" arises, and thus it is said to be [constituted] by perception.
The formation of perception is like the *pulu* (wasp larvae): originally they are silkworms and do not possess the perception of being bees, yet in the end they develop the perception of being bees.

Their distinct substances transform into one another, and their kind fills the world. This is truly because, while in the causal stage, they habitually practice deception—seizing the property of others and taking it as their own;
therefore, in the resultant stage, they are likewise seized by others and taken as their own. Thus, they are deluded and overturned.
In these inverted realms, is there not further suffering?

Due to the inversion of killing and mutual enmity within the world, which serves as the cause, they combine to form the eighty-four thousand "monsters" who harbor the notion that their parents are food.
Thus, there exist non-ideational and ideationless *kalala* beings who circulate through the lands.

For example, there are creatures such as the earth-owl that take clods of earth for their offspring, and the mirror-breaking bird that takes the fruit of poisonous trees and embraces them as its young;
once the offspring have matured, both the parents meet their end by being eaten by them. Such species abound.
This clarifies that it is not the case that there is no cause or effect for the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*). What is meant by "not being non-perception"?

It arises from the world of causes: because [beings] do not know that all sentient beings are of one body and were all their own parents, relatives, or kin in previous lives, they—due to their delusion and ignorance—devour one another and act as mutual enemies. This is called the cycle of enmity and harm, or vengeful killing.

They sought one another out to put an end to their delusions. Thereupon, each became filled with such extraordinary awe that they conceived the thought that there were eighty-four thousand beings who eat their own parents.
They said, "Parents love their children so much that there is no kindness they will not extend. The desire to repay their grace is as vast as heaven and has no limit.
Now, to instead forget this supreme kindness and supreme love, and to harm them and eat them—this is truly unbearable! We wish to hear from you, O Celestial One, why this is so."
This is an extremely extraordinary matter. For such reasons, the resulting fruit is not without the characteristic of perception; it is not a non-perceiving kalala.
Indeed, if one infers the origin of this birth, it was originally brought about by harboring resentment and seeking retribution;

therefore, it is said to be "not without perception. Yet, because the event transpired beyond the realm of conceptual thought, it is also called "without perception. Such is the flow [of these events].
Regarding the transformation of the land: it is like the earth-owl that takes a clod of earth as its offspring, or the *pāribhadra* tree that takes the fruit of a poisonous tree as its seed.
When these offspring grow up, both parents meet their end at their hands.

Such beings fill the world because, in a previous life, they received the utmost kindness and affection from others, yet in turn repaid that kindness with enmity and harm; thus, they are met with the requital of their grievances. Although they are one's own children...
Yet it is truly a grievance. To kill those who follow such perverted ways—is this not further suffering?

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Wu" in the *Shiji*, in the sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor, one *xiāo* bird and a "broken mirror" were used. Meng Kang stated that the *xiāo* is the name of a bird that eats its mother.
The beast called Pòjìng (Broken Mirror) is known as the "Eater of its Father. Because the Yellow Emperor wished to exterminate its kind, it was employed in all the hundred sacrifices.
The Pòjìng resembles a *chū* (a type of wild boar) but has the eyes of a tiger; that it is now described as a bird is likely an error by the translator.
These two aforementioned species are transformations of the *lí* (separation). ○ Zhōng says: "Resentment and harm" do not refer merely to ordinary resentment; rather—

Bestowing kindness and being ungrateful for it; resentment enters the very marrow of one's bones. To "kill the inverted" means that the causal conditions of previously bestowing kindness have, by this point, fully become the mechanism of killing.
"Monstrous" (*kai*) refers to strange or extraordinary states, such as the fruit of a poisonous tree.
Since their resentment was so deep, they encountered a strange realm and took it as the condition for their rebirth;

thus, they conceived the thought that their parents were edible, yet remained unaware that their bodies had entered the fruit. Because they inherently possessed the thought of eating their parents, it is said that this is not a state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*).
Furthermore, because they took birth within the fruit, it is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*). Alas! What is this?
Regarding such matters, there arises this perception. What kind of perception is this that is so numerous as eighty-four thousand?
If one traces its origin, it is simply caused by resentment and harm. How grave indeed is the malice of resentment toward human beings!
We must be careful not to cause others to resent us, and we must also be careful not to resent others.
*Lengyan Shuo Tong*, Scroll Seven;
*Lengyan Shuo Tong*, Scroll Eight.
Compiled by the layman of Baxian, Liu Daokai (pen-name Feiyuan), and edited by the śramaṇa Lizi of Chengdu.

The first section establishes that the ignorance-infused True Suchness (*tathatā*) produces defiled functions, which serve as the cause for the twelve classes of sentient beings. This has already been explained.
From here on, this section explains how the True Suchness (tathatā) perfumes ignorance to produce pure functions, thereby serving as the cause for the fifty-five stages of Bodhi.
Ānanda, among each and every class of such sentient beings, there likewise exists twelve types of inversion, just as...
By pressing upon the eyes, a chaotic profusion of flowers arises, distorting the wondrous, perfect, true, pure, and luminous mind. Thus, such empty and delusive discursive thoughts are fully present.
This [passage] connects what precedes with what follows. Ānanda, within each and every one of these twelve classes of sentient beings, there is also...
Each possesses twelve inversions (*viparyāsa*); one is currently manifest, while the others lie dormant. It is like the illusory flowers that appear when one presses upon the eyes.
Upon investigating their origin, they all exist within the wondrously perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind.
Because these manifest states are mutually inclusive as a whole, they constitute one hundred and forty-four births. Such are these disordered thoughts.
Ultimately, it is utterly false and unreal; yet the pure, luminous true essence remains steadfast as it was.
If one can overturn defilement to become pure and advance through the stages of sainthood, how could this be difficult? ○ He said:

"In the state of delusion, within each category, there are individually present twelve inversions. Therefore, during cultivation, within each stage, there are also individually present the merits of all stages. This...
The fifty-five stages of the Great Principles must not be overlooked.
As you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, I shall establish three gradual stages based on the original cause of your fundamental deluded thoughts.

Only then can it be eliminated. It is like removing poisonous honey from a clean vessel, washing and rinsing that vessel with various hot water, mixed ashes, and incense, before subsequently storing ambrosia within it.
This clarifies that purity is established by reversing defilement. Since the previous question asked at what stage of gradual progression one attains the "eye" of cultivation, it is said:

"Now, you who cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi and the ear-door samādhi have no other expedient means than to establish three gradual stages within the very causes of your original inversion and the deluded thoughts from which you were originally distracted; only then will false illusions be extinguished."
To transform defilement into purity, one must necessarily act upon the locus of defilement itself; this is what is meant by "arising right where it is" and "extinguishing right where it occurs.
For example, if one removes poisonous honey from a clean vessel, one washes that vessel with various hot waters mixed with ashes and incense, and subsequently stores nectar within it.
The "clean vessel" is a metaphor for the non-arising and non-ceasing nature inherent within the sense faculties.
"Nature" (*xing*) is the fundamentally pure essence from the beginning. "Removing the poison and honey" is a metaphor for eliminating auxiliary causes and hollowing out the [false] nature.
"Washing and cleansing with ash-water" is a metaphor for subduing manifest karma. "Later storing ambrosia" is a metaphor for establishing the stages of sagehood.
An ancient master said: "Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To dally with shadows is to weary the form; it is to fail to recognize [the source]."

Form is the source of the shadow; raising a sound stops the echo.
