Yet one who does not know that sound is the origin of the echo is like one who seeks the shadow by removing the form, or seeks the fruit of Buddhahood by distancing oneself from sentient beings—this is like seeking an echo by silencing the sound.
Therefore, know that delusion and awakening are one path, and that the wise and the foolish are not distinct. For this reason, one cultivates and realizes the Buddha-samādhi.
The ground must enter from its original cause through the fundamental state of deluded thought. ○ He said:

"Pure vessel" refers to the illusory and empty body, which is precisely the Dharma-body; this points directly to the six sense-faculties. If it were not a ground of neither-arising-nor-ceasing, how could it contain poison or honey?
And how could it ever be washed clean?
What are called the three stages of gradual progression? First, through cultivation, one eliminates their auxiliary causes. Second, through true cultivation, one hollows out their primary nature.
Third, through further advancement, one opposes their manifest karma.
This sets forth the names of the gradual stages. What are the three kinds of gradual stages? First is Cultivation (*xiūxí*):
when one is single-mindedly practicing through the single gateway of the ear-faculty, one must eliminate its auxiliary causes. Second is True Cultivation (*zhēnxiū*):
when the effort of "listening inward" has taken hold, one must hollow out its fundamental nature. Third is Advancement (*zēngjìn*): when [one practices] inwardly...
When you hear that your practice has progressed, you must further contravene your current karmic activities.
If these three conditions are removed, the nectar-like Dharma of quiescent extinction will manifest. In the past, when Qingyuan first visited the Sixth Patriarch, he immediately asked:
"What should I devote myself to so as not to fall into stages? The Patriarch said: "What have you been doing? He replied: "Even the Noble Truths I do not..."
Wuzu said, "In what rank do you fall? He replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths; how could there be any rank?
Thus one knows that the Dharma has no gradual progression; gradual progression arises from people.

Therefore, the Tathāgata observes capacities and establishes teachings, forcibly establishing gradual stages within the absence of gradual stages, and forcibly establishing rungs where there are no rungs. This is for those of the highest capacity.
If a person knows that it is an illusion, they immediately depart from it; once they have departed from illusion, they are enlightened. How could there be any gradual stages? Master Zhong said:
"The preceding discussion of precepts, concentration, and wisdom constitutes the three definitive meanings for cultivation. These first two gradual stages are precisely the precepts."
"Contrary to manifest karma" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Washing and storing nectar" refers to the arising of wisdom (*prajñā*) from concentration.
What are the auxiliary causes? Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves by their own power;
they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment—namely, edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food. Therefore, the Buddha said that all sentient beings..."
All abide by means of food. Ānanda, all sentient beings live because they consume what is sweet and die because they consume what is poisonous.
Therefore, when sentient beings seek *samādhi*, they should sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world. These five pungent things, when eaten cooked, arouse lust;
when eaten raw, they increase anger. Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent things, even if they are able to proclaim the twelve [dhātus],...
The various classes of sūtras state that the celestial immortals of the ten directions loathe their foul stench and all keep their distance.

When hungry ghosts encounter them while they are eating, they lick their lips and mouths. Because they constantly dwell with such ghosts, their merit and virtue daily diminish, and they receive no long-term benefit.

For those who eat pungent roots, when they cultivate *samādhi*, the Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and benevolent deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them; even those of great power...

The Mara King, finding an opportunity, manifested himself in the form of a Buddha and came to preach the Dharma to them. He reviled the prohibitions and precepts, and praised lust, anger, and ignorance.
At the end of their lives, they became members of the Mara King’s retinue; when their demonic blessings were exhausted, they fell into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda!
Those who cultivate bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots. This is called the first stage of progressive advancement in cultivation.
(Hiñgu root is like a radish; it emits a pungent and foul odor when exhaled. It is unknown here [in this land] and therefore not recognized).
This is a separate explanation for excluding auxiliary causes. What is meant by "auxiliary cause"?
Ānanda, in this world, among the twelve classes of beings, that which is most essential for daily use is food and drink. Without food and drink, life cannot be sustained;
therefore, they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment. These are: the solid food of humans, and the nutriment of contact enjoyed by ghosts and spirits.

They eat [this]. The deities of the dhyāna-heavens take the joy of meditative concentration as their food; the deities of consciousness take the continuity of life through the concentration of consciousness as their food.
Therefore, the Buddha said that all sentient beings abide in dependence upon food.

Since food is that upon which the life-faculty depends, one must not fail to discern between what is wholesome and what is poisonous. Ānanda, all sentient beings live when they consume what is wholesome.
If one eats poison, one dies. Yet there is that which is not poison, yet is in fact more severe than poison:
it is the five pungent vegetables. These are: leeks, garlic, chives, scallions, and asafoetida.
All of these must be abandoned by those sentient beings who seek samādhi. Why is this? Because when these five pungent vegetables are eaten cooked...
To stimulate the fire of lust by consuming raw meat is to agitate the liver qi and increase anger; thus, there is nothing acceptable about eating it either raw or cooked.
If a person eats pungent food, even if they can eloquently expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, their breath will remain impure.
The celestial immortals (*deva-rṣi*) of the ten directions loathe their foul stench and all distance themselves from them. Various hungry ghosts (*preta*), however, hear the stench and approach;
as they eat, these ghosts lick their lips and mouths. Thus, they dwell constantly with ghosts. Because the celestial immortals are far away, their merit and virtue (*puṇya*) diminish daily;
because the ghosts are near, they find no lasting benefit. Furthermore, it is not only that the celestial immortals will not listen to their recitations.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas and their benevolent deities will not come to protect his concentration; instead, he will merely invite hungry ghosts to lick at his belongings.

Moreover, he will draw in the Māra King, who will find an opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma to him, destroying the prohibitions and precepts while praising the three poisons.
Until the end of his life, he will become a member of Māra’s retinue; when his demonic blessings are exhausted, he will again fall into the Avīci Hell due to this single [transgression].
Foul and putrid odors lead to the extreme suffering of Avīci Hell; what difficulty is there in renouncing them that one would not courageously sever them?
Ānanda, those who cultivate Bodhi have already employed the practice of entering the stream within hearing and causing the objects of perception to vanish.
Furthermore, one must permanently sever the five pungent roots; this is what is called the first stage of progressive cultivation.

Although the text initially identifies the practitioner as one who cultivates Bodhi, it subsequently speaks of severing the pungent roots, which clearly demonstrates that the first stage of progression necessarily involves the concurrent practice of perfect penetration (*yuantong*).
If one were merely to sever the five pungent roots, on what basis could it be hastily termed "progressive cultivation"?
The people of the world all claim that pungent flavors can ward off pestilence. When they frequently witness the spread of natural calamities, they urge others to eat pungent foods to avoid them.
Judging from the sutras, this is actually the very source that invites pestilence.
Driven by the karmic forces of worldly beings, they thus perversely increase their own misfortune; one must not fail to take this as a warning.

"What is right nature? Ānanda, for such sentient beings to enter samādhi, they must first strictly maintain pure precepts, forever sever lustful thoughts, abstain from wine and meat, consume food purified by fire, and never eat raw, living things. Ānanda," [he said].
This is the practitioner: if one does not sever sexual desire and killing, it is impossible for them to transcend the three realms.
One should regard sexual desire as being like a venomous snake or as encountering an enemy thief; first, one must uphold the four parājikas and eight parājikas of the śrāvaka.
Holding the body motionless, one subsequently practices the pure discipline of a bodhisattva; holding the mind so that it does not arise, one achieves the fulfillment of the prohibitive precepts.
Thus, within the world, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing; theft and robbery will not occur, and there will be no mutual burdens or debts.
Furthermore, in this world, they do not fail to repay their past debts; such people are pure and cultivate samādhi.
Without needing the divine eye, their physical bodies naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions, behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and personally receive the holy instructions.
Attaining great supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), wandering through the worlds of the ten directions, possessing pure past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), and encountering no hardships—
this is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.
This is a specific explanation of "excising the primary nature" (*samyaktva*). It is called "primary" in contrast to the "auxiliary. For lust and killing are as if innate things;
they do not depend on instruction to manifest spontaneously. They arise together with the body and exist together with one's nature;
they are truly the primary nature of birth and death, and therefore they must be excised. Why are they called the "primary nature"? Ānanda, it is thus:
Sentient beings, when the practice of "hearing back" gains entry, they enter samādhi. Furthermore, one must first strictly maintain the pure precepts;

for it is only through the precepts that concentration can arise. Although the disciplinary rules are many, sexual misconduct and killing are the foremost among all evils—what is termed "the primary nature. One who upholds the precepts must forever sever the mind of lust.
I do not consume wine or meat. Generally, regarding all fresh and living things that have not passed through fire, I dare not eat them;

for if I cannot bear to harm even insentient beings, how much more so must I refrain from killing? This is the ultimate extent of my precept against taking life. (In this way, Gao Chai did not break off growing branches, and Mao Shu did not clear the grass from his courtyard—this was precisely with this intention in mind.
Ānanda, if a practitioner of the Way does not sever lust and killing, they will be unable to transcend [the world].
Within the three realms, there is no such place where this does not occur, for the cycle of birth and mutual destruction has not yet ceased.
Furthermore, lust is a profound source of both birth and death; as it is rooted in the mind and habitualized, it is most difficult to abandon suddenly.
A practitioner of the path should contemplate lustful desire as being like a venomous snake, never daring to become intimate with it, and like seeing an enemy thief, never daring to approach it.

Thereupon, he first upheld the four parājikas of the śrāvakas—lust, killing, stealing, and lying—as well as the eight *niḥsargika-pāyantikās* for nuns, including the [first] eight and the subsequent eight.
He maintained his physical body without movement and did not transgress the seven branches of conduct. Subsequently, he practiced the pure discipline of a bodhisattva;
regarding the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*), he ceased them from the mind and maintained his mind so that they would not arise, not for even a single thought-moment.
Birth occurs when one’s prohibitions and precepts are not fulfilled. Now, by severing lust, one does not give rise to further birth; by severing killing, one does not kill others.
When there are no causes for the karma of birth and killing, there will naturally be no retributive fruits of birth and killing.
Furthermore, by refraining from theft and robbery, one is free from the karmic burden of debt; thus, in this world, one does not have to repay past debts. These are the three karmas.
Once these have been removed, one is called a pure person. This pure person cultivates samādhi;
its primary practice is the observance of pure precepts, and its auxiliary practice is the perfection of both the primary and auxiliary paths.

Before long, they will behold with their own physical bodies born of parents—without needing the divine eye—the worlds of the ten directions. Their eyes having seen the Buddhas, their ears likewise hear them.

The Dharma. Having personally received the sacred decree, rather than seeing or hearing from afar, one attains great supernatural powers (*mahābhijñā*) and travels through the worlds of the ten directions with unimpeded coming and going.
Thereby, one penetrates past lives, clearly understanding the purity of the past; having attained freedom from hardship and peril, one shall not enter the evil realms in the future.
Now, as for observing and seeing the ten directions, the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*) is purified.
Purity: Hearing the Dharma and receiving it in person purifies the faculty of the ear; attaining the power to travel through realms purifies the faculties of the nose, tongue, and body;

having no obstacles regarding past lives purifies the faculty of the mind. Although these are obtained by excavating one's fundamental nature, which of them is not produced by the wondrous cultivation of the gateway of the ear? This is called the second stage of progressive advancement in practice.
Next, the ears. ○ He said: "When the three karmas have been eliminated, one is called a pure person. One who cultivates *samādhi* does so by means of precepts.
To perceive the worlds of the ten directions with the physical eye is the supernormal power of the divine eye; this is the sign that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been exhausted.
The two phrases beginning with 'beholding the Buddhas' refer to the supernormal power of the divine ear. The two phrases beginning with 'attaining great supernormal powers'..."

This is the supernormal power of the psychic faculties (ṛddhividhi-jñāna), which is the characteristic of the exhaustion of the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha). The two phrases concerning the purity of past lives (pūrvanivāsa) constitute the supernormal power of recollecting past existences (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna), which is the characteristic of the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha). All of these arise from meditative concentration (samādhi) and give rise to wisdom (prajñā).

"What is meant by 'present karma'? Ānanda, when a person thus purely maintains the prohibitive precepts, their mind is free from greedy lust and does not flow excessively toward the six external sense objects.
Because they do not flow outward, they revolve back to the source and return to themselves. When the sense objects are no longer grasped, the faculties have nothing with which to pair.
The flow is reversed and the six functions become one; the six modes of perception cease to operate. The lands of the ten directions appear brilliantly pure, like..."
A bright moon hangs within the lapis lazuli; the mind is joyful and serene. Wondrously perfect and impartial, one attains great peace and stability.

Within it, the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [wisdom] of all Tathāgatas is fully manifested. This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From this point on, they gradually cultivate, establishing themselves in the stages of sagehood according to their initial resolve. This is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.

[Zhongyun: In various sutras, one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) only upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*). That this [sutra] attains it prior to the stage of faith is because what is termed "fruit" in other sutras is here termed "cause.
Since the causal ground differs from that of other sutras, the title of this scripture is "The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata."]
This is a specific explanation regarding the contradiction with present karma. What is meant by "present karma"?

Ānanda, for such a person who maintains pure precepts, their mind is already free from lustful desire. Because there is no lustful desire within, they [remain unaffected] toward the six external sense objects.
It does not flow out excessively, yet it is not permitted to be entirely absent.

That it is said to "not flow excessively" is because the beginningless habitual tendencies within the faculties have not yet been completely purified; the objects they encounter still remain, and current karma has not yet ceased.
Since there is no further outward flowing, one does not follow the perceptions and views arising from external objects, but instead returns to the original source of truth.
Externally there is nothing entered; since the sense-objects are no longer conditioned, internally there is nothing issued forth;

since the faculties have no more counterparts, one finally succeeds in turning back from the flow of desire to perfect the single brilliant essence. Thus, when the six faculties encounter their objects, they give rise to no discrimination.
Like a mirror reflecting an image, the six faculties cease their activity.

Because the sense organs do not contact their objects, the lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a clear lapis lazuli with a bright moon suspended within; how can anything be as pure as this?
Because the objects do not intersect with the senses, body and mind are blissful; they are wondrously perfect, impartial, and unmoving in suchness, attaining great peace.

Stable! How joyful it is! Thus, the profound and far-reaching secrets of all Tathāgatas, the perfect interpenetration and inclusion of all things, the purity in which not even a speck of dust can be established, and the wondrousness of all transformations—these so-called four virtues of the fruition stage—all manifest within the scope of this person’s own mental capacity.
This person does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as existing.

He realizes that not even the slightest phenomenon arises, nor does he perceive the extinction of any phenomenon; he thereby attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Taking this non-arising and non-extinction as the mind of the causal stage, he then gradually and perfectly accomplishes the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage. Faith serves as the foundation for all of this.
Abiding serves to perfect virtue; practice serves to perfect the self; orientation serves to perfect others; and the stages serve to sever delusions and realize the Truth.

According to the practices initiated, one establishes the ranks of the sages. This is the process of withdrawing the faculties and forgetting sensory objects, precisely intended to counteract present karmic activities;
thus it is called the third stage: the Gradual Progression of Advanced Practice. *Ganhui* (Dry Wisdom) Stage.

Previously, the three stages of gradual progression were clearly set forth; yet the compiler of the sutra arbitrarily interpolated the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) therein, treating them as the ultimate stage of perfect penetration and the supreme fruit above the four fruits of arhatship. This is a forced and disjointed arrangement that is truly unintelligible. I shall now specifically rectify this.
Feng Guqu remarked: "To examine the explanations of various commentators at length is not as good as reading the sutra text thoroughly."
This is indeed for a good reason.
Ānanda, these sons of good family have dried up the craving of desire; their faculties and objects no longer meet. Their remaining physical forms before them will not continue to be reborn.
Their grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom. The nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, polishing the fruits of the ten directions and drying up existence.
That wisdom is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*). The habit-energy of desire is first dried up, yet it has not yet connected with the flow of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-water.
This clarifies the Stage of Dry Wisdom. Ānanda, because this good man was previously free from greed and lust in his mind, his craving for desire has now become parched and withered.
While in the preceding stage he merely attained the severance of both body and mind, here he [severs]...

Their nature is likewise non-existent; hence it is called "withered. Because the functions of the preceding six [senses] do not operate, one arrives at this state where the faculties and their objects do not meet.

In the previous stage, one merely attained the initial cessation of the six sense-objects; here, however, the mind and its objects are entirely beyond mutual dependence. Hence it is said they "do not meet.
Due to this withered non-meeting, the conditions for birth within the three realms are utterly out of reach. Manifesting—
The remnants of the former substrate remain as mere fruits of bondage; they will no longer continue into rebirth, for the bondage of the seeds is forever severed.

Because of the preceding state where body and mind were blissful and so forth, the mind becomes empty and luminous. Upon reaching this point, one clings to that emptiness and luminosity of the mind, which is purely a single mass of wisdom.
Because of the preceding state where the land was brilliant and so forth, one penetrates the nature of universal wisdom. Upon reaching this—

Thus, the nature of wisdom becomes luminous and perfect, its brilliance penetrating the worlds of the ten directions. Because the principles of the Buddhas previously realized are now fully manifested, the Buddha-wisdom resides within me.
Reaching this stage, one accomplishes the body of wisdom; possessing wisdom alone, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*).
Why is it called "Dry Wisdom"? It is because the water of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-flow has not yet reached its source.
Confused. These arise incessantly. Now, at the initial stage of manifest karma, the most subtle habit-energies of desire and attachment first begin to wither and dry up;
yet fundamental ignorance remains entirely intact. Having not yet connected with the water of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-flow, there is no water to moisten it.
Therefore, it is said that one possesses wisdom while it is "dry. Once one enters the First Abode (Prathamabhūmi), this ignorance is partially severed.
One has partially realized the Truth and is now connected to the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata. Such is what is called "Dry Wisdom" (śuklavidarśanā). Master Zhong said:
"Within the perfect clarity of the nature of wisdom, the essence of the vajra is already complete. It is like an extremely sturdy and sharp boat;
it can carry and ferry all things without exception. Yet, if the current is shallow or the banks are constricted, it cannot function as it should."
The mind attains mastery, giving rise to the functional activity of the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā). Thus it is said that "Heaven possesses its wisdom.

Although this function depends on conditions, the essence remains undiminished. After entering the stage of faith, it is like a boat moving upon water; one gradually enters and gradually becomes vitalized.

Gradually it becomes active, gradually it expands; gradually it expands, gradually it deepens; gradually it deepens, gradually it forgets; gradually it forgets, gradually it approaches; gradually it approaches, gradually it arrives.
Thus, there is the boat that enters the stream, the boat in midstream, the boat that reaches the shore, and the boat that turns back.
Although cause and effect correspond, from beginning to end one does not depart from *qianhui* (dry wisdom), until the attainment of perfect Bodhi.
Upon entering the ocean of adornments, even "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā) is insufficient to name it.
○ This section below concerns the stage of the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā). Guṣan considers that the ten minds are differentiated from the first abode (prathama-vihāra);

this is because, prior to dwelling in the Perfect Teaching (vaipulya), one does not yet attain realization, and thus no formal stages are established. Consequently, the ten [faiths] are subsumed within the three preceding gradual steps.

[The Master] Xìn agrees, and Zhengmò follows him; this seems plausible. However, the sutra text states prior to the four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*) that "these good sons are entirely the forty-one pure minds," and later, in the concluding summary, it further says they "skillfully accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
If the fruit of the ten faiths were included within the three gradual sequences (*anupūrva-krama*), then [the count would be inconsistent].
It should not be necessary to explicitly list their positions or provide a detailed enumeration of their numbers.

If you argue that those in the stage of "Round-Truth Abiding" (yuanjia) do not attain realization while in the preceding stages, then why would they ever attain realization in the subsequent stages either? Now, following the scriptural texts and specifically the *Yingluo jing*, we shall continue to list the ten stages as before;
although the "Stages of Faith" (xinwei) in the Round-Truth school differ in name from the "Ten Faiths" found in other sutras.
The same [term is used], yet its meaning is in fact vastly different.

That is, with this very mind, flowing into the center of the center, the perfect and wondrous blossoms; from true wondrous perfection, there again arises true wondrous and wondrous faith that is eternally abiding.
All delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder, and the Middle Way is purely true; this is called the Abode of Faith.
This clarifies that the initial faith is precisely the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

Once the practitioner possesses this mind of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), they employ this very mind to enter the current of the Dharma. Therein, they do not accept divergent branches nor any devious turns, but flow straight along in unison.
From this point on, they begin to meet the Tathāgata’s counter-flow; this is where it starts. Thus, they have entered the center of the center.

It flows inward. Thus, the perfection of the six faculties functioning interchangeably and the subtlety of simultaneously transcending both the sentient and the insentient unfold and flourish, like a flower beginning to bloom.
This wondrous perfection is not the same as the "semblance of the subtle" and "semblance of the perfect" in the preceding stages;
it is true subtlety and true perfection. Riding upon this opening of the mind, one further advances, causing that which is truly subtle to progress even more.

Regarding "wondrous" and "truly perfect": to further advance toward perfection is called "proceeding from the true wondrous perfection" to again manifest the true wondrousness, like a flower in full bloom.
From this, one’s wondrous faith becomes permanently established, personally seeing that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in their threefold nature;

this is not merely a faith based on inference or comparison. It is simply the awakening wherein the views of sage and ordinary person cease, and the sentiments regarding cause and effect are forgotten.
All notions of self, notions of dharmas, and notions of non-dharmas are simultaneously swept away, so that all discursive thoughts are extinguished without remainder.
There remains only the perfectly penetrating Middle Way, which is pure and true; all else is mixed and false.

To have attained firm and certain conviction is called "Abiding in Faith" (*śraddhā-vihāra*). This stage, according to the analogy of untangling the knots, corresponds to first attaining the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and severing the sixth and fifth knots.

According to the analogy of the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), it corresponds to the state where movement and stillness do not arise. According to the analogy of the four fruits of the śramaṇa, it corresponds to the stage of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
When one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the conceptualization of self-attachment is severed; this refers specifically to the delusions of view within the realm of desire.

With true faith and clear understanding, all things become perfectly penetrating; the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) can no longer act as obstructions. Thus it continues, even unto...
Throughout countless eons of the past and future, all habitual tendencies from abandoning one body and receiving another manifest before him.
This son of good family is able to recollect them all without any forgetfulness; this is called the dwelling of the mind in mindfulness.
This clarifies that these two forms of faith constitute the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). When the practitioner reaches the stage of faith, it is true faith rather than semblance faith;
it is clear and lucid because it arises from direct perception. Every sense faculty and every sensory object interpenetrates one another without exception, such that all are perfectly interfused.
Because all are perfectly interfused, the aggregates (*skandha*) cannot obscure, the sense bases (*āyatana*) cannot confine, and the realms (*dhātu*) cannot obstruct.

Separated by three [eons], all are unimpeded. Because of this, one is thus able to recollect from afar the relinquishing of bodies throughout countless past kalpas and the receiving of bodies throughout countless future kalpas.

Even down to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*) produced by the power of karma—such as the pride of Piṅgala and the anger of Śāriputra—these subtle habits manifest clearly before them. This person...
One is able to remember everything with profound clarity, without the slightest omission; because mindfulness leaves nothing behind, it is called the "Abiding in Mindfulness.

According to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), at the stage of the two levels of faith, perfect penetration is still far off. Yet here, this stage is described as "all-encompassing perfect penetration";
thus we know that it is equal to the second stage (the second abiding) of that teaching.

Wondrously perfect and purely true, the essence of truth undergoes transformation. The habitual tendencies from beginningless time merge into a single, brilliant lucidity. By means of this alone—this brilliant lucidity—one advances toward ultimate purity;
this is called the mind of diligent effort.

This clarifies that the three types of faith are precisely the faculty of progress (*vīryendriya*). Once the practitioner has attained abiding in the mind of faith, then that which is "wondrously perfect" is purely the One True Reality.

As this Truth endures, it becomes refined; as refinement reaches its peak, transformation is initiated. It is because of this refinement that transformation occurs, and through transformation, refinement is further enhanced.
Once the practitioner has attained abiding in the mind of mindfulness, they then recollect the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time. Thus, there is no...
The initial habitual tendencies are completely melted away without remainder, all becoming wisdom and penetrating into a single luminous clarity.
From this, one takes this true essence and true illumination as the basis and advances toward the ground of true purity. This luminous clarity is the very substance of Bodhi.
It is the wisdom of suchness (tathatā-jñāna). True purity is the essence of nirvana; it is the principle of suchness (tathatā-tattva).

To accord the wisdom of suchness with the principle of suchness—what else could this be called but the mind of diligence? At this stage, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exhausted, reaching parity with the second fruit of the Small Vehicle.
When the essence of mind manifests before one, consisting purely of wisdom, it is called the "abiding of the mind in wisdom.

This clarifies that the four types of faith are themselves the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). In the preceding stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*), it was said that the mind grasps at emptiness and luminosity;

thus, a sense of grasping still remained. Upon reaching this stage where the essence of mind manifests before one, that grasping is completely integrated and transformed. It is further said: "Purely..."
This is wisdom (*prajñā*). As long as one still retains the notion of "this," it remains so;

but when one reaches the stage where it is purely wisdom, then in daily life, everywhere is wisdom, and one simultaneously forgets that "it is. "Yi" (以) means "to employ"; it refers to recognizing the treasure and being able to use it.
To recognize the treasure and be able to use it—how could this not be called the mind of wisdom abiding? The previous section on Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) spoke of "purity."
This is "wisdom" (*jñāna*): it is the wisdom that severs delusions, like the night approaching dawn.
This [next term], "pure wisdom" (*prajñā*), refers to the wisdom that realizes the Truth, like the sun rising at dawn.
Maintaining the clarity of wisdom, it is pervasive, tranquil, and profound; this tranquility is wondrous and eternally凝 (concentrated). This is called the "abiding of the settled mind.
These five stages of faith constitute the root of concentration (*samādhi*). In the preceding stage, because the mind was seen to be luminously penetrating, wisdom was purely clear;
yet if this clarity of wisdom were not maintained by the power of concentration, deluded thoughts would arise and become biased.
The field is not pervasive; right mindfulness is lost; and because it is interrupted and not constant, it is what is called "illumination without stillness," like a lamp in the wind.
Now, by maintaining the clarity of wisdom, that which is tranquil and profound becomes all-pervasive, and that which is tranquil and wondrous remains eternally concentrated.
These are all the signs of Great Samādhi; how could they not be called the "abiding of the concentrated mind"? This stage is the stage of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception).
Exhausted, the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm have already been severed, which corresponds to the three fruits of the Small Vehicle.
When the light of Samantaprabha illuminates and the nature of clarity penetrates deeply, advancing only without retreating, it is called the "Non-retrogressive Mind."

This clarifies that the six faiths constitute the power of progress (*vīrya-bala*). The preceding section belongs to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); from this point onward, they belong to the five powers (*pañcabala*).

Just as when the roots of a fruit-bearing tree have been established for a long time, there is a functional power that cannot be uprooted, so too, once the practitioner has attained a concentrated mind and abides therein, wisdom is then generated from that concentration, and the light of concentration shines forth, yet it does not abide [in mere concentration].
It is luminous, yet the nature of this luminosity penetrates deeply. It is like one who polishes a mirror: the more it is polished, the clearer it becomes;

and as this clarity continues without end, there is progress and no regression. Generally, when samādhi and prajñā are one-sided, one often suffers loss and regression. Now, through samādhi, wisdom is brought forth;

the mind remains unmoving while the principle is fully revealed. Through wisdom, one enters samādhi; once the mirror has been thoroughly cleared, the mind remains eternally concentrated. Thus, samādhi and prajñā [are unified].
Mutually supporting and mutually stimulating one another without end—how could this not be called the "non-retrogressive mind"?

The previous diligence still belonged to the realm of the "mind with object," like a horse being spurred by a whip; this non-retrogression is the "mind without object," like unfurling sails with a following wind.
The mind advances with serenity; it is maintained without loss. The vital energy of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions interconnects with it; this is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.
This clarifies that the seventh stage of faith is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Although there was previously no regression, diligent effort and uninterrupted practice still involved deliberate exertion. Reaching this stage, although one is vigorous, no sign of toil is perceived; hence it is said to be "serene."
When the mind is maintained until it reaches a state of tranquility, one will then move with ease and spaciousness, forever remaining free from peril.
Yet, what is it that is being maintained? It is precisely the life-vein of the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas.

Because I maintain this life-vein of the Dharmakāya without losing it, I naturally come to share the same vital energy as all Buddhas; we intermingle and connect, becoming perfectly unified and seamless.
Combined, these constitute the protection of the internal mind-dharmas and the external Buddha-dharma; thus it is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.

In this stage, according to the *Jiejie* (Unraveling the Knots), one should eliminate the fourth knot. According to the *Yuantong* (Perfect Penetration), one should reach the point where "that which hears hearing is exhausted.

According to the four fruits, this corresponds to the fruit of Arhatship, wherein one severs the innate clinging to a self (*ātmagrāha*)—specifically, the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarāga-kleśa*) within each of the two upper realms.

Thus, with awakened clarity and stability, one is able to employ wondrous power to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha’s own abiding state. It is like two mirrors facing each other, their radiance intermingling;
within them, wondrous reflections penetrate one another in infinite layers. This is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).

This clarifies that the eight stages of faith are the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). Because the essence of awakening (*bodhi-tattva*) is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) mentioned previously, it is called "the maintenance of awakened clarity. Upon reaching this stage, it manifests as wondrous power (*miao-li*).

One then employs this own wondrous power to redirect the compassionate light of other Buddhas toward the Buddha within one's own mind, abiding therein with radiant clarity. It is like two mirrors facing each other, wherein reflections are contained within.

Reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers, radiating forth without end. This is what is meant by saying that the mind does not depart from the Buddha, and the Buddha does not depart from the mind.
Because one turns away from the Buddhas of others toward the Buddha within one's own mind, it is called "dedication of the mind" (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
The light of the mind secretly turns back, attaining the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, unsurpassed, wondrous purity. Abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one achieves non-forgetfulness;

this is called the "abiding of the mind in precepts" (*śīla-citta-vihāra*). This clarifies that the nine stages of faith are the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*); because the observance of precepts relies upon firm faith, the mind of the preceding stage [is thus established].
The light and the secret revolve; one’s own mind and the Buddha-light merge as one.

Thus, one immediately attains the self-nature of innate truth, the eternally concentrated and immovable Buddha-body, and the unsurpassed, wondrously pure ocean of great quiescence. "Eternally concentrated" pertains to the mind, while "wondrously pure" pertains to the object.
Having realized this principle of the Buddha, mind and object become one. From this point on, one dwells peacefully in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), even to the slightest degree.
It does not fall away into the realm of the conditioned and is attained without loss; because it is free from the fault of transgression or loss, it is called "abiding in the mind of precept.
In this stage, according to the *Unraveling of the Knots*, it corresponds to the perfect luminosity of emptiness, which removes the third knot.

According to the *Perfect Penetration*, it corresponds to the realization that the perceiver is empty of the perceived, in order to sever the conceptualization of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). This is the [realm of] the *dhātu*.

This refers to external delusions regarding appearances. "Constantly concentrated" (*cháng níng*) means the eternally abiding true mind; its constant concentration in wondrous purity is entirely the mark of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the precept-mind of all Buddhas.
If for even a single thought one engages in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and loses this state, it constitutes a breach of the precepts.

Abiding in the mastery of precepts, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, reaching wherever one wishes; this is called the abiding of the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).

This clarifies that the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*) is present even within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). While in the preceding stage, abiding in the precepts was still limited to the essence of immovability, upon reaching this stage, the function of mastery gradually emerges.
There is no request that is not fulfilled, and there is nothing to which one cannot go; thus, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions.
One is born in a buddha-land according to one's vows; this is called the dwelling of the vow-mind.
This stage, according to the "Unraveling of the Knots," corresponds to the attainment of dharma-liberation, wherein the second knot is removed.

According to the "Perfect Penetration," it corresponds to the extinction of both emptiness and that which is emptied, serving to sever the innate clinging to dharmas—namely, the afflictions of thought beyond the triple world. The Stage of the Ten Faiths concludes. Master Zhong said: "Cultivating practice..."

At the beginning, one must first wither and sever all craving and desire, so that the nature of the mind becomes empty and luminous; only then can one enter the wondrous, perfect true nature (*tathatā*).

When this true nature is luminous and perfect, subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) will manifest. Through their manifestation, they are subsequently transformed, such that pure wisdom remains free of habituation.

Furthermore, one maintains this through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), causing a profound stillness to emit radiance and entering deeply into the luminous nature, guarding it so as not to lose it. This is—

They turn back the Buddha’s compassionate light and protect the Buddha’s pure precepts; thus they traverse the world of dust without being defiled, proceeding wherever their vows lead—this is the sequence of the ten levels of faith.

Ānanda, these good sons, by means of true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds (namely, the aforementioned ten levels of faith). From the essence of these minds, [the power of] manifestation arises.

[The ten faiths] are manifested; the ten applications interpenetrate, perfectly accomplishing the one mind. (Because of this single phrase, Gushan subsequently judged that the ten faiths were opened out from this stage.
However, since it cannot be reconciled with the final explanations regarding the fifty-five stages and so forth, it is difficult to follow. This is named the Abiding of the Arising Mind.
The following clarifies the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*). There are two meanings to "abiding": first, the sense of firm and permanent abiding;
second, the sense of being born and dwelling within the Buddha-family. According to the subsequent text, the emphasis is specifically on being born and dwelling within the Buddha-family.

Ānanda, these sons of good family who cultivate perfect penetration, by means of true skillful means, give rise to the ten kinds of faith mentioned previously, allowing not even a hair’s breadth of [delusion] to enter between them.
Regarding defilement: when the mind is refined, its radiance becomes manifest. The five faculties and the five powers are all fully possessed;
thus, the one mind is the ten minds, and the ten minds are the one mind. They interpenetrate in successive layers, fundamentally lacking two distinct entities.
Thereupon, the ten functions are subsumed to perfectly accomplish the one mind. From this one mind, the mind is bound.

This is the initial understanding. Because the myriad practices are fully perfected, it is named the "Abiding in the Arising of the Bodhicitta. ○ According to the analogy of "untying the knots," this stage corresponds to having already attained liberation from the dharmas;

both [subject and object] are empty and do not arise. With the exception of the first knot, according to the analogy of "perfect penetration," this corresponds to the point where birth and death have been extinguished and quiescent extinction manifests before one.
This is what is meant by a Bodhisattva attaining the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from within *samādhi*. It is precisely this.
This is the entry into the "Abiding in the Arising of the Mind" (Cittotpāda-vihāra). Once the practitioner has entered and abides therein, there is no further effort required.
Although the subsequent stages are distinct, they are like a bird flying up a mountain: one sees the tiers of the mountain clearly, yet from the beginning, there is no laborious climbing.
○ He said: "The wondrous, perfect true mind is neither one nor ten; it is spoken of in terms of the distinctions of its functions."

Therefore, there are ten characteristics. If these ten characteristics are not manifest, it is not called the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). If the ten characteristics are not harmonized, it is likewise not called the arousal of the mind.
When illumination arises within the mind, it is like pure gold appearing within clear lapis lazuli; one treads upon this prior wondrous mind to form the ground.

This is called the stage of "Abiding in the Cultivation of the Ground" (*bhūmi-parikarma-vihāra*). Following the previous stage of "Abiding in the Initial Resolve," the mind acts as the wisdom that brings forth illumination, and principle acts as the object to be illuminated.
When wisdom accords with principle, it is like pure lapis lazuli in which refined gold appears within; this is accomplished through the ten applications mentioned previously.
Having accomplished the mind of the first stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one possesses the ground that serves as the foundation; only then is one fit to tread upon it.

From this point forward, at every step, one treads upon solid ground. At all times and in all places, one cultivates and refines the mind-ground, whereby all wholesome dharmas naturally arise and great compassion increases.
Therefore, it is named the Stage of Cultivating the Ground (*caryā-pratipatti-bhūmi*). The preceding stage is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Seizing upon prior karma, one first forms the aggregate-body (*skandha*). This is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) riding upon the power of that karma to bind together its objective sphere and falsely establish a locus of dependence.
Although it is said that "one's feet tread upon solid ground," such words from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*) are not to be clung to as definitive.
○ He said: "Observing the two characters 'ground-preparation' (*zhidi*), this stage corresponds to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)."
Indeed, the ten stages do not exceed the perfection of this position.

The mind-ground and its cognitive functions both become clearly manifest; as one traverses the ten directions, one attains freedom from obstruction. This is called the Stage of Cultivation and Practice (Pratipatti-vihāra).
Following the previous stage of abiding in the cultivation of the grounds (*bhūmi*), the mind is itself wisdom; this is initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). The ground is itself principle;

this is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Because the mind and the ground mutually interpenetrate and know one another, sharing a single essence of awakening, both are attained with perfect clarity.
Once one has clearly seen this, one will surely reach it through practice. Traveling in this manner throughout the ten directions, one moves with effortless spontaneity and without obstruction.
This is what is meant by "passing through a grove of a hundred flowers without a single leaf clinging to the body"; therefore, it is called the dwelling of cultivation (*xiūxíng zhù*).
It is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), where distant things are seen as if right before one's eyes; the destination is reached with great speed. The mountains...
The walls do not obstruct them.

Their practice is identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive his spiritual resonance. Like an intermediate state being seeking parents, their subtle faith communicates in the dark as they enter the lineage of the Tathāgata;
this is called the Stage of Noble Birth.
Having established oneself through practice, one initiates action based on principle, such that the action does not deviate from principle.

Because the primordial and the emergent are identical in perfect enlightenment, it is said that "action is the same as the Buddha. When one's action is thus, one is carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata and covered by the robe of the Tathāgata;
one receives the Buddha’s breath. This refers to what was previously called the "interconnection of breaths," which is like two [people breathing together].

This is what is meant by "receiving a portion of the Buddha's breath," whereby they merge into one. Now, provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna) is like a father and true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) is like a mother;
their spontaneous union is like that of an intermediate state being (antarābhava) seeking its own parents—a passage that is obstructed yet becomes permeable.
To enter without entering—this is to uphold the Buddha’s legacy. At the initial entrustment to the holy womb, it is just as when a prince dwells in the womb;
his nobility supersedes all ministers. This is called the "Abiding in Noble Birth. ○ This corresponds to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) uniting with the karma of the parents at one place.

Having already entered the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One—just as when the fetus has fully formed and its human features are complete—it is called the Stage of Abiding in the Perfection of Expedient Means.
It is also called the Stage of Noble Birth, for one has already entered the womb of the Way; grasping the Buddha’s two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate, one causes them to coalesce and solidify.
The "sacred embryo" is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) which, having taken up the two drops of red and white from the parents, forms the coagulated and viscous mass (*kalala*).

Therefore, it is said that one personally receives the lineage of the Awakened One. This constitutes the complete possession of all skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) for the liberation of sentient beings.

He is perfectly like the Buddha; there is nothing lacking. Just as the six sense organs are fully formed in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and human characteristics are complete, he is perfectly like his parents.
This is called "abiding in the perfection of skillful means. As for entering the womb, it is described as "wandering."
As Yongjia said: "Always walking alone, always stepping forth alone; those who have attained enlightenment travel together on the path to Nirvāṇa. This is precisely that journey.
His countenance is like that of a Buddha, and his mental state is likewise identical; this is called the Abiding in Right Mindfulness.

It is said that by being fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya*), one’s appearance becomes like that of a Buddha. Not only does the outward form resemble the Buddha, but the inner mind is likewise identical;
this is called the "Abiding in Rectitude of Mind" (*samyak-citta-vihāra*). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "When this Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings, his mind remains fixed and unmoved.
That is to say, whether hearing praise of the Buddha or slander of the Buddha, his mind remains fixed and unmoved. Whether hearing praise of the Dharma or slander of the Dharma..."
The mind remains steady and unmoving when praising or disparaging the Dharma; the mind remains steady and unmoving when praising or disparaging a bodhisattva;

the mind remains steady and unmoving when praising or disparaging the conduct of a bodhisattva; the mind remains steady and unmoving when speaking of sentient beings as being finite or infinite, easy to deliver or difficult to deliver;
the mind remains steady and unmoving when speaking of the Dharma as being finite or infinite, subject to formation or destruction, existent or...
There is no [movement]. When the mind is settled and unmoving, being solely and uniquely unmoving, it is called the "Abiding in the Right Mind.
Should there be even a hair’s breadth of mental movement, its correctness is lost. Thus, the verse of praise by Ratnakūṭa to the Buddha says: "Unmoved by blame or praise, like Mount Sumeru;
regarding the good and the bad with equal compassion. ○ He said: Regarding the characteristic of the mind, this refers to the Buddha-mind not...
This is the characteristic of movement. When the mind is settled, it does not move. A rectified mind is precisely a settled mind.
When body and mind are unified, they grow and increase day by day; this is called the stage of non-retrogression.
When the mind and appearance are in harmony, and the inner and outer are as one, then body and mind merge to become the Buddha-body and Buddha-mind.

Through this process of nurturing and cultivation, they gradually increase; this is called the "Stage of Non-retrogression. The aforementioned "mind of non-retrogression" refers to the non-retrogression of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);
this [stage], however, refers to the non-retrogression of both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The ten spiritual marks of the body are simultaneously perfected; this is called the Dwelling of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta).

When the outer body and the inner mind increase together and reach this stage, then the bodhi-body, the vow-body, the transformation-body, the power-body, the adornment-body, the majestic-body, the mind-born-body, the Buddha-body, the dharma-body, and the wisdom-body are all simultaneously perfected.

He is complete, possessing the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet it is on a small scale, and his power is not yet fully developed—this is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (kumārabhūmi).
When his form is fully realized and he emerges from the womb, becoming a true son of the Buddha, it is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince (dharmarājaputrabhūmi).
When the ten bodies are fully perfected, the form is established. Upon reaching this state of brilliant and blazing splendor, one emerges from the womb.
Capable of inheriting the family legacy of the Tathāgata and possessing a share in the Tathāgata’s precious treasury, this is what is meant by "born from the Buddha’s own mouth."
Born through transformation by means of the Dharma, they are truly the sons of the Buddha. How could it be otherwise for those who dwell as Dharma-princes?
Thus we know that all who are titled "Dharma-princes" belong to the stages from the ninth dwelling (*navama-vihāra*) and below.
This constitutes the manifestation of a full person. It is like a great king of a country who delegates all the affairs of the state to his crown prince;
when that son of a Kṣatriya king has reached maturity and the ceremonial anointing is performed for him, it is called "abiding in the consecration."
Upon emerging from the womb as a child, one gradually grows up and manifests the state of adulthood, becoming capable of performing the Buddha’s work.
Possessing the virtues of an adult, one is fit for great responsibility;

therefore, one is entrusted with governance so as to transform and guide the ten directions, just as a king delegates matters of state to his crown prince. The crown prince is, that is to say, the heir apparent.
Those Buddhas sprinkle the water of wisdom upon the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head.

This is just like a Kṣatriya king who, having arrayed his precious elephant and golden throne, takes the waters of the four great oceans and sprinkles them upon the crown of his heir apparent, thereby causing him to succeed and flourish the Buddha-dharma and inherit the royal lineage.
How is this any different? This is what is called the stage of Empowerment (Abhiṣeka), by which the Ten Abodes are perfected.
...it is so. ○ The tenth stage, the Dharma-Cloud Ground (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), is called the Bodhisattva of Empowerment (Abhiṣeka). Now, this tenth dwelling also partially attains [this state].
If one discusses the "partial truth" (bhūta-tattva) of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), within a single stage all the merits of the various stages are fully present.

Since it is thus for the ten dwellings, it is likewise for all that follows. Furthermore, in comparison with the Provisional Teachings (quan-jiao), this already equals their ten grounds; yet its subtlety—

Awakening (*bodhi*). This stage extends only to these two lines. It is only at the stage of Sublime Awakening (*miao-jue*) that it is first said that the light of the Buddhas' wisdom completely pours upon one's crown.

Now, this present stage is adjacent to that, and because the wisdom of those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-ren*) is powerful, they receive the empowerment immediately. From the initial arousal of the mind (*citta-utpāda*) up to the stage of Noble Birth (*sheng-gui*), it is called "entering the holy embryo" (*sheng-tai*).
From the stage of Fulfillment of Expedient Means (*fang-bian ju-zu*) up to the stage of Youthful Truth (*tong-zhen*), it is called... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
One nurtures the holy embryo until reaching the stage of the "Abiding Prince," which is called "Emerging from the Womb. Upon reaching this stage, one is designated a "Consecrated Prince.
The above ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute the foundation for accumulating merit; the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*) represent the gradual progression of that accumulation.

Reaching this position, the Way is perfected and virtue is complete. If one does not engage in the work of delivering sentient beings, one is merely a self-enlightened person. Therefore, [the following] is explained in detail.
Practicing the six perfections and performing great Buddha-works constitutes the subsequent ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), which is what is meant by "proceeding while relying on the source.

To further correlate this with the preceding analogy: the first six of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are like a person who has turned their mind [toward the Dharma] and is initially cultivating wholesome karma.
Regarding the latter four minds: it is like a person who, by adding the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, creates the karma for rebirth in the Pure Land.

The first dwelling is like completing ten kinds of virtuous and pure karmas throughout one’s life, thereby perfecting the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that leads to rebirth at the end of that life. The second and third dwellings are as follows.

Just as when passing into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one is neither bound nor fettered; in the fourth stage, like seeking the Buddha within the intermediate state, one is received and led into the lotus-womb.
From the fifth stage to the eighth stage, one grows and matures within the flower. In the ninth stage, like the flower opening, one beholds the Buddha.
The Ten Abodes. It is as if one has personally received the prediction of enlightenment. [End of] The Ten Abodes.

Ānanda, once these sons of good family have become children of the Buddha, they are fully endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas and act in accordance with the ten directions;
this is called the Practice of Joy.

This is the first practice of the perfection of giving. Ānanda, when these sons of good family emerge from the womb as princes and are established in the position of consecration, they have already become sons of the Buddha.
Having become sons of the Buddha, they are fully endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas, which permeate them within;
thus their countenances are serene and their backs are suffused with radiance, great joy pervading their entire bodies, as they further extensively practice and bestow [these virtues].
Whether it be material giving or the giving of the Dharma, he accords with the wishes and aspirations of the ten directions; there is nothing he does not give without seeking anything in return.
He causes all sentient beings to feel joy and delight, yet remains free from the notion of a self and the notion of sentient beings. He perceives neither giver nor receiver.
Thus, those nearby admire his virtue, while those far away cherish his kindness; this is called the Practice of Joyful Giving. It is not... [incomplete].
This is indeed appropriate.
Being well able to benefit all sentient beings is called the practice of "Beneficial Action" (Anugrahacaryā).
This is the second practice, the perfection of ethical discipline (Śīlapāramitā). For by being compliant and joyful, one is then able to benefit sentient beings.
However, if one lacks the root of virtue within, how can one benefit others? This Bodhisattva upholds the pure precepts;
regarding forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, his mind has no attachment, nor does he give rise to even a single thought of desire, even for the sake of sentient beings.
Thus he proclaimed, causing them all to abide in unsurpassed pure precepts, until they themselves attained liberation and caused others to attain liberation;
until they themselves found happiness and caused others to find happiness. This is called being truly able to benefit all sentient beings.
Is it not fitting, then, to call this "Beneficial Conduct"? ○ Zhong says: There are three types of precepts, among which the precept of benefiting sentient beings is supreme.
Having attained the mind of the Buddha’s precepts through the nine stages of faith, one reaches this point where one practices with the Buddha’s precepts as one's conduct.
To awaken oneself and awaken others, thereby attaining freedom from opposition and resistance, is called the practice of non-anger.
This is the third practice, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Through joy and the act of benefiting others, all people will hold one dear.

Yet, can one truly ensure that no reckless person will cause harm or injustice? It is for this reason that this Bodhisattva constantly cultivates the dharma of patience; having already attained the capacity to endure, he is thus [established].
To awaken oneself is [the perfection of wisdom]. To teach others how to practice patience is to awaken others.

To joyfully endure all forms of verbal abuse and physical assault without any resistance or opposition—not only without resistance, but even without the slightest thought of anger—is therefore called the practice of non-aversion. ○ Zhong says: Regarding the six perfections herein, they do not...
Compared to the conventional path, if there is even a single moment when one does not receive the joy of the Dharma, that is stinginess regarding giving;

if there is even a single thought that fails to protect sentient beings, that is the breaking of precepts; if there is even a single thought of discriminating among sentient beings, that is anger and resentment.
Therefore, it is called "perfect" (or "round").
Arising in all categories, extending to the limits of the future, equal throughout the three periods of time, and penetrating the ten directions—this is called inexhaustible conduct.
This is the fourth perfection of conduct. Through it, one benefits both self and others; whether in accordance with or contrary to conditions, all is as one. The Bodhisattva cultivates this.
On that day, one’s progress becomes boundless. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva cultivates various forms of diligence, from the first diligence up to universal diligence—these ten types of diligence.

Maintaining this diligence until the very end of the Avīci hell realms, he brings all births to completion and attains Buddhahood, continuing until the furthest limits of future kalpas, never once [failing].
One should reflect upon this with resolve. Why is this so? It is because one practices diligence in order to know the equality of the three periods of time.
One practices diligence in order to penetrate the ten directions and to know the entire dharma-realm. Now, the arising of the lineage is the foremost mind;
reaching the end of the future is the eternal mind; and the equality of the three periods of time is the non-erroneous mind.
The inverted mind is thoroughly penetrated throughout the ten directions; this is the vast mind. Since all four are inexhaustible, they are called the "Inexhaustible Practices. ○ He [Hé] says:
Responding to conditions according to their capacity, one manifests bodies of various kinds, extending to the limits of the future to benefit beings immeasurably.
Vertically penetrating the three periods of time and horizontally encompassing the ten directions—this is the perfection of effort (*vīrya-pāramitā*). The first two lines refer to sentient beings.
"Boundless vows to deliver [all beings]" refers to the second couplet: "Infinite Dharma gates I vow to learn.
To bring all things into harmony and attain freedom from error regarding the various Dharma gates is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.

This is the fifth practice, the perfection of dhyāna (meditative concentration). Now, when generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence have been cultivated, the characteristics of concentration will begin to manifest.
This bodhisattva, by means of a single moment of concentrated mind, upholds all dharmas and unifies various dharma-gates.
They know that all samādhis share the same essential nature, yet they also understand that there are various distinctions which cannot [be reduced to a single state].
The delusions are clarified in every detail, without failing by even a hair’s breadth.

Now, if a concentrated mind cannot sustain the various dharma-gates, this is called "deluded concentration" (*mohasamādhi*); regarding the dharma-gates, it has not yet escaped error and remains a distracted mind.

That now there is no error—how could this be anything other than having departed from the practice of delusion and distraction? *Dhyāna* in Sanskrit is translated here as "calm contemplation" (*jinglü*).

Now, freedom from delusion is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and freedom from distraction is tranquility (*śamatha*). Therefore, it undoubtedly belongs to the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Thus, within sameness, a multitude of differences is manifested; yet within each distinct characteristic, sameness is individually perceived. This is called the "skillful manifestation of practice."

All that follows is the *prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom). It is a single *prajñāpāramitā* that is expanded into five, just as the six root afflictions are expanded by dividing "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) into five types.

The reason for expanding these five kinds of profound *prajñā* is to harmonize the myriad practices within the first five perfections, causing them all to become the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*). This present single practice is both principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*).

This is unimpeded wisdom (*asanga-jñāna*). Since the Bodhisattva has already unified all various dharmas, within this unity they cannot manifest difference, and within difference they cannot perceive unity; how, then, could this be considered the wisdom of integration?
That which is called "unity" is precisely the supramundane dharma of equality; that which is called "difference" is precisely the mundane dharma of differentiation.
Now, within the identical, the diverse appears; within the dharma of equality, the dharma of differentiation appears.

Thus, principle does not obstruct phenomena, and the Real is fused with the conventional. Within the differentiated, the identical is seen; within the dharma of differentiation, the dharma of equality appears.
Thus, phenomena do not obstruct principle, and the conventional is fused with the Real. The Real and the conventional are mutually fused; phenomena and principle...

This is the simultaneous manifestation of both [wisdom and practice]. How could this be anything other than the non-virtuous conduct of Subhūti? At the tenth stage, one attains the Buddha’s mind of wisdom; reaching this point, one takes wisdom as one's practice.
In this manner, it continues until: within every single atom that fills the space of the voids of the ten directions, the worlds of the ten directions are manifested.
Manifesting the sense-objects and manifesting the sense-realms without mutual obstruction or hindrance is called the practice of non-attachment.

This is the seventh wisdom of the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighajñāna*). The Bodhisattva does not merely cause the identical and the different to mutually integrate;

rather, expanding and extending this principle, the large and small contain one another, and the one and the many are without obstruction. In this manner, it extends even to the empty space of the ten directions.
It satisfies every atom. Within each and every atom, the worlds of the ten directions appear;

that is to say, within every single atom of all the atoms in the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakuṭa-lokadhātu*), one perceives the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). When the realm enters the atom, the realm does not diminish;
thus, the small does not obstruct the large. When the atom contains the realm, the atom does not enlarge; thus, the large does not obstruct the small. This is what is called the ultimate...
The great is identical to the small; their boundaries and surfaces are not perceived. The extremely small is identical to the great;
all objective realms are forgotten and severed. This is possible only through non-attachment. If there were even a hair’s breadth of attachment, how could the great and small be mutually integrated?

Therefore, it is called the Practice of Non-Attachment, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom) ranks second. ○ Zhong says: "Attachment" means the sense of lingering obstruction. There is no...
If there is obstruction, then there is attachment. In the third stage of abiding (*trīya-vihāra*), one attains non-obstruction: this means that objects do not obstruct the mind;
this mutual non-obstruction means that objects do not obstruct objects.
Various manifestations appear before one; all are the foremost *pāramitā*, termed "the practice of reverence.
This is the eighth, the ultimate wisdom of the other shore (*pāra-gata-jñāna*). Within the identical, difference appears; within difference, identity appears. Within the small, the large appears;
within the large, the small appears. Thus, various things manifest before one. Indeed, these various transformations are entirely...
They belong to *prajñā*. All are integrated by the unobstructed wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*;
therefore, they all reach the other shore. There is nothing that is not the foremost *pāramitā*. Among the six perfections, *prajñā* alone is the most honored;

thus it is called the "honored practice. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* occupies the third position. Regarding the first five perfections: if they lack *prajñā*, [they cannot reach the other shore].
All [such practices] fall into the realm of phenomenal characteristics; they merely invite karmic retribution and fail to reach Nirvana.

Now, the five perfections and myriad practices all rely upon wisdom; therefore, every practice reaches the other shore. This is truly not easy to attain, which is why the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* calls it the "difficult-to-attain practice.
A former master said: "Vividly clear at the tips of the hundred grasses—vividly clear is the intent of the Patriarch. This is precisely [the meaning].
That which is called "manifesting before one" is entirely the foremost *pāramitā*. Master Zhong said: "This stage subsumes the seven preceding practices.
The former belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
Thus, through such perfect interfusion, one is able to fulfill the patterns of the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called "skillful practice of the Dharma.

This is the ninth wisdom of teaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. As described above, being perfectly interfused and unimpeded, one’s virtues are equal to those of the Tathāgata, and one’s conduct is likewise identical to that of all Buddhas.
Thus, every word and every action accords with the [teachings of] the Buddhas of the ten directions.

The Buddha’s discipline consists of the teachings established for the ultimate benefit of others. According to the faculties of sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma at the appropriate time, causing all to rejoice;
therefore, it is called the "Practice of Wholesome Dharmas" (*kuśaladharma-caryā*). Thus, the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) occupies the fourth position.
This, moreover, subsumes the aforementioned eight practices: the former constitutes self-perfection, while this constitutes the perfection of sentient beings. [This applies to] walking and sitting.
All have become established as rules and patterns; they resemble, in their subtle likeness, the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Each and every one is pure, untainted, the single true unconditioned, for such is the nature of reality itself; thus it is called "True Practice."
This is the tenth [perfection], the wisdom that does not contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

It subsumes the two aforementioned types of unimpeded practices for the benefit of oneself and others, and it also encompasses the preceding five perfections. Taken together, each and every one of them is pure and untainted (*anāsrava*).
From the beginning, there has been no defilement by the desires of ordinary people or outsiders, nor is there ignorance regarding existence or non-existence;
each and every thing is the single true unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Nor does it involve the arduous labor of the provisional and limited stages of cultivation and realization. Why is this so?

Because cultivation arises from the nature (*prakṛti*), it does not hinder the fact that the entirety of cultivation is itself the nature. The nature is primordial and spontaneous; it does not depend on provisional, gradual cultivation for its completion. Therefore...
Purity does not belong to the outflows (*āsrava*); the single truth does not fall into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Because it is without outflows, it is not a practice apart from delusion;
it ultimately becomes the true cause. Therefore, it is called "True Practice" (*bhūtacaryā*). Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not a practice of effortful action;
it possesses an ultimate, real fruit. Therefore, it is called "Real Practice" (*satyavṛtti*). Reaching this point, the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is fully accomplished. And...

What has been taught and what has been practiced are all entirely true. Generally speaking, regarding the five practices opened up by the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the first two constitute the essence of *prajñā*, for they are the profound *prajñā* that possesses the non-obstructive wisdom of the two dharma-realms.
The next two constitute the function of *prajñā*; that is to say, the *pāramitās* are the means of self-benefit in the pursuit of the fruit.
"Function. This refers to the function of the Buddha’s rules for teaching the Dharma to benefit others.

The final [character] "Mo" (末) subsumes the preceding essence and function, as well as the five perfections and myriad practices, all of which are ultimately resolved back into one's own nature (*svabhāva*), thereby uniting nature with its source.
This, moreover, subsumes the preceding nine practices; while the former were expedient means, this is the reality (*bhūtatā*). From the three gradual stages onward, it has been thus.
This is the untainted (anāsrava). Reaching this point, one finally attains purity. [End of the Ten Practices.
Below this are the ten stages of Dedication (pariṇāmanā). According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, dedication is precisely the making of vows.
This is because if there is practice without vows, the practice will surely be aimless; if there are vows without practice, the vows are merely empty formalities. Therefore, practice and vows—
By combining these two resources, one will finally enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. This method of dedication does not exceed three points:
namely, dedication to sentient beings, dedication to bodhi, and dedication to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

In the preceding stages of the ten abidings and ten practices, the mind for transcending the mundane world was predominant while the practice of great compassion was deficient; thus, it required the support of compassionate vows. Now, while remaining in the mundane world to benefit living beings, one must dedicate...
