Turning true wisdom toward the conventional, and turning discernment toward compassion, so that the conventional and the true are perfectly integrated and discernment and compassion are non-dual—
this is called the Ten Dedications, and is also called the Ten Vows.
Ānanda, when these good sons have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of Buddhahood, they will be pure, clean, and true, far removed from all lingering afflictions.

They shall deliver sentient beings while extinguishing the very notion of "delivering" them; turning their unconditioned minds toward the path of Nirvana, this is called the Dedication for the Protection of All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
This first phase of dedication free from signs and the subsequent stages are all dedications for the sake of sentient beings.
Ānanda, these good men who have already cultivated the ten practices, from the first practice through to the eighth, manifest the sense objects and the realms.
His supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) have reached their ultimate limit, lacking not even the slightest deficiency. Upon reaching the ninth stage, he fulfills the rules for attaining Buddhahood;

having thus accomplished the work of a Buddha, he reaches the tenth stage. Being pure and free from outflows (*anāsrava*), he is utterly pristine. Being one with true non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), he is quintessentially authentic.
Having perfected all things throughout the ten directions, within the realm he is no longer subject to the afflictions of the various states of existence, and without the realm...
To remain stuck in emptiness is to harbor a lingering affliction; therefore, one must transcend both the mundane and supramundane worlds simultaneously.
Emerging from this state to deliver sentient beings, at the very moment of delivering them, one perceives no sentient being to be delivered, thereby eliminating the very notion of "delivering.
Now, having delivered all sentient beings and not grasping at the mark of delivery, one turns back conditioned practices and enters the unconditioned mind. This is...
This is the turning toward the true cause. To turn one’s back on the path of birth and death and head toward the road to Nirvana is to advance toward the true fruit.
When a Bodhisattva dedicates merit in this manner, they deliver and liberate sentient beings without ever ceasing, yet they do not dwell upon the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
This is called "protecting and rescuing all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings. [To] deliver beings while maintaining [this state]...
To perceive the marks of those being saved is to cling to the notions of self and person; this merely adds shackles and chains and is not the method of dedication.
As the Great Master of Nanyue said: "If one swallows all Buddhas of the three periods of time in a single gulp, where else could there be any sentient beings to save?
This is true dedication. The four stages below this correspond to the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
To destroy that which is destructible and to remain far removed from all forms of detachment is called the "indestructible dedication.
This second indestructible dedication is also dedicated for the sake of sentient beings, because it previously eliminated the marks of crossing over [to nirvana].
"Extinction" (*nirodha*) means destruction. Because one destroys that which is destructible, it is called "destructible.

Since the preceding stage involved being detached from the marks of sentient beings, one is thereby detached from the four marks and five aggregates of sentient beings; hence, it is called "detachment from all things.

Now, this bodhisattva destroys what is destructible, and by extinguishing and eliminating even the mark of deliverance (*tāraṇa*), he does not maintain it; thus, he is far removed from all forms of detachment. Furthermore—
Even the mark of sentient beings does not exist. Once that which is subject to destruction is destroyed, that which is indestructible remains;

this is precisely the work of saving sentient beings. For although those in the higher stages save sentient beings, they do not cling to the marks of sentient beings—this is called the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Although one in these stages does not cling to marks, this does not hinder the work of saving sentient beings—this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This is the correct [view].
The simultaneous integration of compassion and wisdom is the middle way between the two benefits of self and others.
Because there are sentient beings to be delivered, one does not destroy the compassion that delivers them; therefore, it is called the "Undestroyed Dedication. Zhong says:

The preceding text asks, regarding the conditioned phenomena of the world, what could be undestroyed? One has never heard of empty space decaying or perishing; hence it is called the "Undestroyed Dedication."

In the preceding stage, there were no sentient beings to be saved; in this stage, there is no Buddha-way to be sought. The old commentary points to sentient beings [as the object], which is highly forced.
Fundamental enlightenment is profound and still; its awakening is equal to the awakening of a Buddha, and thus it is called the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
The four stages below are all dedicated toward the Buddha-way; however, this stage first clarifies that one’s own wisdom is identical to the Buddha-wisdom.

When residing within oneself, it is called "original awakening wisdom" (*mūla-bodhi-jñāna*); when residing within a Buddha, it is called "ultimate awakening wisdom" (*niṣṭhā-bodhi-jñāna*). This Bodhisattva-mind is manifested by the Buddha;
the ocean of awakening is serene and still, such that its mental essence is perfectly interfused and merged with that of all Tathāgatas, and the *dharmakāya* is level and uniform.
"Equal," "non-dual," and "perfectly complete. Just as all Buddhas dedicate in this way, I also dedicate in this way;
this is called the dedication equal to that of all Buddhas.
The essence of the refined truth is brilliantly manifested; the stage is like the Buddha-stage.
This is called the Dedication Reaching All Places (*sarvatragāminī-praṇidhāna*). This fourth dedication, "Reaching All Places," shares the same realm as the Buddha-realm.

Through the manifestation of the wondrous function of the essence of prior original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), the boundless realms contained within one's own causal-ground mind are entirely identical [to those of a Buddha].
The immeasurable lands manifested in the ground of fruition of all Buddhas exhaust the entire realm of the Buddhas.
May the power of the merit of these roots of goodness reach everywhere; this is called the dedication that reaches all places. ○ He said:
"The single moon universally appears in all waters; therefore, it is called reaching all places."
The worlds and Tathāgatas interpenetrate one another without obstruction; this is called the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
This fifth inexhaustible dedication achieves mutual fusion by building upon the preceding two stages.
That which was reached previously is the world; those Buddhas who were equated are the Tathāgatas. Yet, it is said that they are self-awakened.
The Buddha’s awakening distinguishes between his own ground and the ground of the Buddhas as if they were self and other; now, however, they are fused into one without division.
Thus, when speaking of the world as the Tathāgata, self and other are completely integrated.
By means of the world entering the Tathāgata, there are within a single pore immeasurable jewel-adorned lands, exquisitely and subtly decorated. By means of the Tathāgata entering the world, then...
Within each and every atom, there are immeasurable Tathāgatas turning the great wheel of Dharma.

When the world enters the time of the Tathāgata, it does not obstruct the Tathāgata, yet it immediately enters the Tathāgata. When the Tathāgata enters the time of the world, he does not obstruct the world, yet he immediately enters the world.
In this way, both the Buddha-body and the Buddha-realm each possess immeasurable adornments.
This fully manifests inexhaustible merit. When Bodhisattvas abide in this dedication, they attain ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries. These are:
the treasury of seeing the Buddhas without end, and the treasury of seeing the Dharma without end. All of these take the great practices and vows of Samantabhadra as their root;
the merits manifested by the adornments of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) are called the treasury of inexhaustible merit.
Virtue is dedicated therein. ○ The three stages below correspond to the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within the stage identical to that of the Buddha, pure causes arise individually within each stage; by relying on these causes, one manifests and takes up the path to *nirvāṇa*.
This is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accords with equality.
This sixth dedication of equality is also dedicated toward the Buddha-way. Since the Bodhisattva’s body and land are mutually fused, they are identical to the stage of Buddhahood.
Within this inexhaustible treasury, each and every thing gives rise to inexhaustible purity.
This is the cause. Furthermore, by relying on this pure cause, one realizes the pure fruit:

namely, that every single object is the luminous wisdom-body of Samantabhadra, and every single thing is the practice-gate of Samantabhadra. It is like gold fashioned into vessels; every vessel is gold. Thus, the roots of goodness are equal.
This is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accords with equanimity. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva may become a sovereign ruler over a great kingdom;
his majestic virtue is widely diffused and his fame resounds throughout the world. Holding a single parasol, he provides universal shade to the ten thousand regions.
By means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he gathers in all sentient beings. This is the pure [state] arising within each stage."
The cause of purity. Relying on this cause, it is manifested, thereby taking up the path to *nirvāṇa*. ○ Zhong says:
"Ground" refers to the ground of the second stage, the Stage of Cultivation (*bhūmi*). In that [stage], one merely plows and cultivates; here, however, it becomes a fertile field.
It gives rise to the cause of purity, just as fine grain grows within a fertile field.

Once the true roots have been established, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own fundamental nature. When this nature is perfectly accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings;
this is called the dedication of following the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.
This seventh section on the dedication of equal contemplation appears to dedicate [merit] to sentient beings, yet in reality it also dedicates it to the Buddha-way.
The roots of goodness of equality from the preceding stage are the true roots. Once these true roots are established, this root is entirely cultivation that is identical to nature (*dharmatā*).
Since this nature encompasses all sentient beings, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature.
However, since my faculties have already been perfected, all sentient beings are likewise fully perfected; thus, their nature is accomplished in its fullness.
Although the Bodhisattva perceives that both self and others are thus perfectly accomplished, this does not prevent him from continuing to deliver suffering and distressed sentient beings.
He continues to extensively practice the two kinds of giving, vowing that all sentient beings shall attain the treasury of great merit. This is called "conforming observation of all things as equal."
Sentient beings dedicate [their merit] to this. In the preceding stage, one accords with one's own mind to bring it into equality with the Buddha-mind;

in this stage, one accords with one's own mind to bring it into equality with the minds of sentient beings. When combined with the former, the principle that the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without distinction is revealed.
That is, all dharmas are free from all marks; being both identical with and detached from them, without attachment to either, is called the dedication of the mark of *tathatā*.
The three stages below this all constitute dedication to *tathatā*. The preceding [stages] of saving sentient beings and attaining Buddhahood encompass all myriad things.
"Dharma" refers to all dharmas. It is free from the marks of sentient beings and identical to the primordial Buddha; it is free from all marks.
This Bodhisattva dwells in both "being" and "leaving," yet remains unattached to both. To be unattached to "being" is to transcend existence.
"Not clinging to detachment" means transcending emptiness (*śūnyatā*). To transcend both emptiness and existence simultaneously is the Middle Way.

Since True Suchness (*tathatā*) takes non-clinging as its characteristic, it is called the "Dedication of the Characteristic of True Suchness. This clearly demonstrates that one has entered into the principle ever more deeply. ○ He said:
What was previously called "being far removed from all forms of detachment" refers to the ultimate limit of detachment; here, even detachment itself is [transcended].
It is non-attached. Regarding the "non-attachment" mentioned in the seventh stage, it refers to non-attachment toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This implies, moreover, that one is also non-attached toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The three stages below this correspond to the empty and non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Truly attaining that which accords with reality (*tathatā*), one is unimpeded throughout the ten directions; this is called the dedication of the liberation of non-binding.

This is the ninth dedication, the dedication of liberation. In the preceding stage, "leaving" refers to leaving both [subject and object] simultaneously, which is termed the characteristic of *tathatā*.
If one were to become attached to the characteristic of *tathatā*, one would again be bound by the characteristic of *tathatā*. Therefore, this Bodhisattva forgets even that *tathatā*.
This is called "truly attaining the Suchness. Since one has truly attained suchness, then all places are suchness;
what further obstruction could there be? Throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm, where could one go that is not free?
Because from the beginning there is neither bondage nor liberation, it is named the "Unbound Liberation Dedication. While the preceding stage was the non-obstruction of principle, this—
The "stage" (*pada*) refers to the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, and between phenomena and phenomena.
When the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are perfectly accomplished and the limits of the *dharmadhātu* are extinguished, it is called the "Infinite Dedication to the *Dharmadhātu*.
This is the tenth Infinite Dedication. Through the preceding non-attachment, one attains the full embodiment of these inherent virtues. No...

Obstructed, one nevertheless attains the great function of the inherent virtues. Since both essence and function are fully present, the inherent virtues are perfectly realized. The essence is nowhere not pervasive;
the function is nowhere not complete. Therefore, every single speck of dust and every single hair is equal to the Dharma-realm, without further limitation or measure.
The extinction of measure is itself immeasurability. Although it was previously as described, one was still within the bounds of the *dharmadhātu*;

the limitations had not yet been entirely dissolved. Now, as every sense organ and every object pervades the *dharmadhātu*, the sentiment of limitation is forgotten and one does not fall into any numerical categories;
therefore, it is called the "Dedication of Immeasurable Merit to the *Dharmadhātu*. According to the three virtues (*triguṇa*), there is no...
Adherence is precisely *prajñā*. Non-obstruction is precisely liberation. And the immeasurable is precisely the *dharmakāya*. To speak of these by combining them into ten points:

first, compassion does not obstruct wisdom; second, wisdom does not destroy compassion; third, the fundamental and the wondrous are merged in awakening; fourth, cause and effect share the same ground;
fifth, the environment and its inhabitants are mutually interfused; sixth, nature and cultivation are simultaneously identical.
7. The identity of self and others in their common faculty; 8. The simultaneous transcendence of both identity and difference; 9. The sovereign mastery of the ultimate and the conventional;
10. The perfect consummation of essence and function. This is why the *Avataṃsaka* states that when this stage is reached, the earth trembles, flowers rain down, and the devas sing praises.
How magnificent! Thus ends the tenth stage, the Ten Dedications.

From here below, the four stages of application (*prayoga*) are explained. According to the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-vāda*), the first three are termed the Stage of Provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*). "Provisions" (*sambhāra*) refers to equipment;
"provisions" (*āhāra*) refers to food. This means that since what has been accumulated is so great, the destination must necessarily be far away—just as for one traveling a thousand *li*.

One must necessarily gather provisions for three months; thus, one relies on the ten stages (*bhūmi*) to perfect internal virtue, the ten practices (*caryā*) to perfect the virtue of benefiting others, and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) to perfect the virtue of the mutual integration of self and others. Once these myriad virtues are complete, [one attains the fruit].
One may enter the realm of the noble ones (*ārya*). However, there still remains a subtle obstruction herein; therefore, the stage of application (*prayoga*) is established once again.
Were it not for the World-Honored One’s profound and exhaustive insight into the most secret depths, who could discern this? Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"To manifestly posit a slight object, claiming it to be the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only. The term "slight" [refers to this subtle obstruction].
"Things" (vastu) refers to subtle obstructions. Here, the term "distinct" (bie) is borrowed to mean "perfect" (yuan). Although the names are the same, their realities are different;

for the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching is only equal to this first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching. Indeed, it is the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching [that serves as the standard].

One immediately severs one grade of ignorance; from the second stage to the tenth stage, one severes one grade of ignorance at each stage, which is equal to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
Next, by severing one grade of ignorance from the first practice, one is equal to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Next, upon entering the second practice, one is equal to the Sublime Enlightenment (*miaojue*). From the third practice onward, those of the Separate Teaching do not yet even know [this].
How much more so regarding their subduing and severance? This is because the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) merely destroys eleven grades of ignorance.

Thus we know that the ordinary person of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) has already surpassed the sages of the Separate Teaching; how much more so for the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory stages (prayoga)?

Now, let us examine in detail the four kinds of preparatory stages in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: each possesses the meditative concentration that can be produced, the contemplation that is produced, and the dharmas that are the objects of observation.
This sutra has no such intention at all; it merely uses the two terms "mind" and "Buddha" to distinguish four stages. Therefore, it is not the same [as other systems]. Question:
This sutra establishes sixty saintly positions (ārya-sthāna). Why does it likewise divide them into ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and saints, similar to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*?

Answer: Bestowing and withholding, as well as identity and difference—both are unimpeded. If one considers the initial sudden awakening within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), [the distinction between ordinary and saintly is established].

Since this is the fundamental Buddha, it is of the same rank as the Sage. If one discriminates between their relative depth, then there is no hindrance to distinguishing between ordinary and sage regarding the vision of faith-and-understanding compared to true cultivation;
yet this ordinary person of the Perfect Teaching has already far surpassed the sages of the Separate Teaching.
Ānanda, these sons of good family have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds and subsequently accomplished the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
This clarifies that these preparatory practices serve as the superior advancement for entering the stages (*bhūmi*). Ānanda, these are the sons of good family who cultivate perfect penetration.
My son, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā) through the ten stages of Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Orientation—these constitute the entirety of the forty-one pure minds.

Yet, while the ten faiths appear to be cultivation, in reality they merely fulfill the mind of faith; the three levels of worthiness (trīṇi kula-putrāṇi) appear to be cultivation, but in reality they merely perfect the mind of understanding.
Neither constitutes true cultivation. Now, with faith fulfilled and understanding perfected, one is about to...
One enters true cultivation; thus, the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are successively accomplished.

It is not merely called "preparatory practice," but must necessarily be called "wondrous and perfect" because the Small Vehicle and the Shared Teaching both possess four types of preparatory practices that are neither wondrous nor perfect.
Therefore, the term "wondrous and perfect" is used as a heading to distinguish them from ordinary preparatory practices. The preceding text states:
The desire for the true is already not the true nature of *tathatā*. There are three gradual stages:

the first arising of the thought that desires the true proceeds from the true, wondrous, and perfect, and again gives rise to the true, wondrous, and perfect; this is the second arising of the thought that desires the true.

Now, these four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*) constitute the third arising of the thought that desires the true. Upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), the coarse thoughts that desire the true are severed; upon reaching the eighth stage...

Furthermore, one desires to sever even the subtlest thoughts of the true [nature], reaching up to the state of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi*), where the most subtle thoughts of the true [nature] are forever severed.
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, it takes the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) as the cause of differentiation and the stages from the first ground upward as the cause of equality.
The *Tongyi* (General Discussion) relies on this, stating that the four stages of application (*catvāraḥ prayogāḥ*) serve to eliminate the marks of the cause of differentiation; this is most correct.

One takes the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind; whether it has emerged or not yet emerged, it is like drilling for fire when one wishes to ignite the wood—this is called the Stage of Warmth (*uṣmagata*).

As previously stated, "awakening equal to the Buddha's awakening" refers merely to making a vow and aspiring toward it; there is still a sense of duality in this awakening, and one has not yet attained total integration.

Taking the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind, when one is about to advance toward the holy fruit, one takes that very Buddha-awakening as the causal mind of oneself and further applies effort and practice to seek authentic realization.
However, the vision of the Buddha has not yet been forgotten; though one desires to merge with it, one is unable to do so immediately.
Thus, it is as if emerging but not yet emerged—comparable to drilling for fire: one wishes to ignite the wood, yet it is not yet ablaze. It is merely...
There is only the sign of warmth; therefore, it is called the Stage of Warmth (uṣmagata). At this stage, the Buddha is precisely the mind.
Longya said: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: when you encounter smoke, do not stop. Only wait until the golden star appears;
then returning home is finally reaching the goal. This refers to exactly this.

Furthermore, by means of one's own mind, one attains what the Buddhas have traversed—whether relying or not relying [on external forms]. It is like ascending a high mountain until the body enters empty space;
yet if there remains even a slight obstruction below, it is called the "Stage of the Summit" (mūrdha-bhūmi).

Previously it was said that the ground is like the ground of the Buddhas; this too was a matter of aspiring through the arousal of vows, yet one had not yet been able to realize within one's own mind the state traversed by the Buddhas.

Now, for the first time, one takes one's own mind as the state traversed by the Buddhas. Nevertheless, because the view of a self has not yet been forgotten, although one relies [upon this], it cannot be called "relying.
It is like a person climbing a high mountain: although the body has entered the void, [the sense of self remains].
Though empty, the heels of the feet still touch the ground; there remains a slight obstruction, and one is not yet able to grasp the sun and moon while roaming through the eight directions.
Therefore, this is called the Ground of the Summit (Mūrdha-bhūmi). At this stage, the mind itself is the Buddha.

Mind and Buddha are identical; this is skillfully attaining the Middle Way. It is like enduring a person—one neither harbors resentment nor expresses it—and is thus called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).

This encompasses the two preceding stages. "That which is mind is that which is Buddha" means that mind and Buddha are identical. Nevertheless, they are spoken of as "functioning" and "accomplishment."

Yet two characteristics still remain; this is not the Middle Way. Upon reaching this state, the entire mind is Buddha and the entire Buddha is mind, without leaning toward either extreme, thereby skillfully attaining the Middle Way. However, what is called "skillful attainment" is still not yet true attainment.
It is like a person who practices forbearance: although they are capable of tolerance, they are not like ordinary people who harbor resentment; yet, they still...

One maintains endurance. Yet this is not like the sudden forgetting of the Perfected Person (zhiren). Regarding the matters endured, they are at the stage of being about to be forgotten but not yet forgotten;
compared to a Bodhisattva on the Stage of Endurance (Rendì), it is the stage of being about to realize but not yet realized. Therefore, it is named the Stage of Endurance.
This stage is "mind itself is Buddha."
When quantity is extinguished and one awakens to the Middle Way, both [subject and object] have nothing by which to be designated; this is called the Stage Supreme in the World (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Previously, it was said that one has "well-attained the Middle Way"; although mind and Buddha are not divided, there still exists a mind and a Buddha, and the distinction between cause and effect stages remains entirely within the realm of quantity.
Upon reaching this stage, however, mind and Buddha are mutually fused, and only then does quantity begin to dissolve—just as when one awakens from delusion.
The Middle Way is precisely the causal mind within the state of non-awakening. Awakening to the Middle Way is the resultant wisdom within the state of Great Awakening.
Once numerical distinctions have dissolved, one does not see one’s own mind below, nor does one see the Buddha-wisdom above;
yet, while delusion and awakening constitute the Middle Way, there is nothing for these two to refer to. That there is both delusion and awakening is something that worldly people still [recognize].
It can be pointed out and identified, yet it is not called "transcendence. Now, as numerical quantities dissolve, delusion and awakening both cease;

the Middle Way is forgotten, and one rises far above the common world. Therefore, it is named the "First Worldly Ground" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). As the saying goes: "Only heaven is above; there is no mountain equal to it.
If one advances further to ascend to the [first] ground, only then is it called "transcending the world" and surpassing wondrous enlightenment. Furthermore...
This is called the foremost state that transcends the world. ○ This stage is neither mind nor Buddha. Nanquan said: "Do not recognize the mind; do not recognize the Buddha.
Even if you were to recognize them, they would be objects, and the ancients called this the ignorance of the known. Mazu Daoshi said:

"It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing"—all of these refer to this very point. ○ Regarding the four additions of the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only), the dual characteristics of emptiness and existence have not yet been eliminated;
here, however, the dual characteristics of mind and Buddha have not yet been exhausted. Therefore, it is said that "distinct names are borrowed for the sake of the Perfect.
○ He [Heshang Moheyan] said: "The mundane world is like dust; the supramundane is like empty space. There is delusion and there is awakening."

The coarse particle is the middle way; the subtle particle is the limit of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Beyond these two, there is nothing to be designated, which is the "particle of the infinitesimal" (*paramāṇuraja*).
Once one transcends this stage, one enters the supramundane. It is like analyzing the infinitesimal particle: it becomes empty space itself.

○ From here below, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are elucidated. There are two meanings of "stage" (*bhūmi*): first, the sense of being "perfected and real," for a stage takes solidity and reality as its essence;
second, the sense of "generating and causing to arise," for a stage takes generation and arising as its cause.
This is because one cannot perfect virtues without abiding [in a stage], one cannot benefit oneself without accumulating virtues, and one cannot benefit others without benefiting oneself.

Thus, once all virtues have been perfected, spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) have been accomplished, and great vows have been fulfilled, he further establishes four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to refine and eliminate the measures of the emotional mind (*citta-pramāṇa*).
He must ensure that both mind and Buddha are forgotten, that not even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization remains, and that even the Middle Way does not persist;
only then does he ascend to the stages (*bhūmi*). This means that the previously accumulated dharmas reach their ultimate fulfillment. One.

All Buddha-dharmas arise based upon this. According to the preceding text, which takes the awakening of the stage of fruition as the mind of the causal stage, then from the Abiding in the Initial Resolve up to Equal Enlightenment all belong to the causal stage; only ultimate wondrous enlightenment constitutes the stage of fruition.
Question: Since, according to the Perfect Teaching, from the first abode up to Equal Enlightenment one is severing the ignorance of partiality, [how can they be considered the causal stage?]
One partially realizes the true reality. Why is it that one must reach this point and further employ four kinds of preparatory practices before entering the stages?

Answer: If one speaks in terms of sudden enlightenment, then the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause; thus, at the very moment of first generating the mind of awakening...
One immediately attains perfect enlightenment; how then can there be distinctions of stages? If we speak in terms of cultivation and realization:

since the ten bhūmis are called "true cultivation," it is evident that the stages prior to them are all "semblance cultivation. Since the state of Buddhahood is "true realization," it is evident that even the ten bhūmis are "semblance realization.
Thus, from the initial aspiration to the ultimate goal, although the principle is identical in its suddenness, there is a sequence of shallow and deep stages that unfold in order.

Chaos. The perfect fusion and the sequential arrangement do not obstruct one another. Furthermore, according to the sacred stages, the second abode in the original text is named "Cultivating the Ground" (Zhìdì).
One traverses this by means of the previously mentioned wondrous mind to complete the ground. Moreover, the fourth dedication states:

"The essence and truth are brilliantly manifested; the ground is like the Buddha-ground. Up to the four stages of preparatory application, each position is a true ground. These are all grounds based on causes.

Furthermore, "ground" (*bhūmi*) is also explained as meaning "step. This is because the ten grounds are indeed the true cause, and the mention of "grounds" prior to [the final realization] refers to the stages that serve as steps toward this true cause.
Now, these ten grounds should also be subsumed under the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
However, since the Buddha-ground alone is the true fruition, these ten grounds are the stages for progressing toward and realizing that true fruition.

Ānanda, these sons of good family have attained excellent penetration into great bodhi; their awakening penetrates that of the Tathāgatas and they exhaust the realm of the Buddhas—this is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
Ānanda, by means of these four preceding kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices, that son of good family then forgets both mind and Buddha;
the middle way no longer stands, and only then does he transcend the world and enter the true realm of the Buddha regarding unsurpassed bodhi.
Sentient beings within the three realms of existence and those of the two vehicles who have transcended the world cannot fathom this with their minds of objective knowledge;

it is not merely that they penetrate it, but that they skillfully attain such penetration. This is because it is realized through direct personal experience rather than being known through the comparative understanding of words and letters.
What is meant by "penetration"? It is the perfect fusion of the fundamental awakening of one’s own mind with the wondrous awakening of the Buddha-mind.

There is no duality. Yet this awakening penetrates to the Tathāgatas; from one Buddha, extending to hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, nay, as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—the entire sphere of their realms is all that which this awakening penetrates.
At this, great joy pervades the body, and it is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
One rejoices because of mindfulness of the Buddhas; one rejoices because of mindfulness of the Buddha-dharma, and so on until one enters...
Because all Bodhisattvas are equal in nature, they rejoice.
Diverse natures enter into sameness, and even that sameness is extinguished; this is called the Ground Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
This clarifies the second ground. Because the preceding awakening penetrates the Tathāgata, it constitutes the severing of the diverse natures of the nine realms.

(The ten dharma-realms consist of nine realms from the Bodhisattva downward, excluding the Buddha-realm itself. One enters the equality of Buddha-nature; this is called "entering the same through different natures.
If one merely realizes this equal Buddha-nature but is still unable to forget it, then the Buddha-realm remains an object of the mind.

Furthermore, within the mind of pure awakening, there remains a single subtle stain; therefore, this "sameness-nature" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) must also be extinguished before one can attain stainless purity.
For "other-nature" (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa) is the stain on the side of turbidity, while "sameness-nature" is the stain on the side of purity;
thus, both must be abandoned. Only then is it called the Ground of Freedom from Stain (vimalā-bhūmi). This is because, among the four stages of application (prayoga), it is not...
The mind is not the Buddha. Only when numerical distinctions are extinguished does one enter the sameness of different natures;
subsequently, even this sameness is extinguished. Advancing to realize the stainless state, one perceives further excellence and attains the noble stage of the second bhūmi.

According to the *Avataṃsaka* and *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, both symbolize being free from the defilement of breaking precepts; while their purports seem somewhat different, there is no need for forced interpretation.

The same applies here. ○ Zhong says: "In this stage of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), one realizes the most supreme Tathatā (Suchness) and severs the obstacle of wrong conduct (mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa).

Upon reaching this, the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) is attained. Subsequently, at the stage of the Vajra-mind, the perfection of meditative concentration (samādhi-pāramitā) is attained. Finally, at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (Miao-jue-wei), the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) is attained."
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity arises;

this is called the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*). This refers to the third ground. In the preceding stage, one had merely departed from defilement (*vimalā*) but had not yet reached the departure from that departure;

now, one is about to further distance oneself even from the "departure" of that departure. This constitutes the ultimate limit of purity. When purity reaches its ultimate limit, true awakening occurs.
This manifestation is what constitutes the arising of clarity. It is like an ancient mirror: once freed from defilement, if it is further polished, its natural radiance becomes even more manifest.

In the same way, when the subtle veils of emotional defilement regarding the identity or difference between the present and the primordial Buddha have been purified without remainder, the inherently existing capacity for illumination naturally reveals itself, unable to be suppressed or concealed. This is what is meant by "purity."

It is the ultimate penetration of the light-attainments (*ābhijñā*). Because radiance arises from this, it is named the "Radiant Stage" (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*). This refers to the internal brilliance that emits light.
When clarity reaches its peak and awakening is fulfilled, it is named the "Blazing Wisdom Stage" (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
This explains the fourth stage (*bhūmi*). In the preceding stage, illumination arose like a fire that has just begun to burn, yet it had not reached full completion.
Now, however, it is like a blazing fire that has become a great, fierce mass; all subtle afflictive obstructions are incinerated and severed.

Because awakening accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is called "full awakening" (*saṃbodhi*); thus it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). It is not called simply "wisdom" (*prajñā*), but rather "blaze."
"Wisdom" (hui) signifies wisdom that is like a flame; it possesses the supreme function of incinerating and severing [delusions].
This is what is meant by "the ultimate clarity is the Tathāgata. Zhong said: "The previous stage of 'Heat' (nuan) is like drilling wood for fire;
one desires to ignite the wood. Upon reaching the third stage, the fire emerges. At this stage, the wood is actually burning."
That which nothing—neither all things that are different nor those that are the same—can reach is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Dūramgamā-bhūmi*).
This clarifies the fifth ground. Now, the wisdom prior to the grounds is termed "different," while the wisdom of the grounds and above is termed "the same.

If there were differences that could be reached, then ordinary sentiments could surpass it; if there were sameness that could be reached, then the understanding of the sages could surpass it. Now, by virtue of...
It is pure and luminous. Through this luminosity, it becomes full; thus, both ordinary sentiments and saintly understandings are completely incinerated and severed.

All distinctions of difference and identity have long since been left far behind, so remote that they can no longer reach one another. Therefore, they cannot arrive; since even "arriving" is impossible, who could possibly surpass it?

Hence, it is named the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Durjayā*). ○ He [Heshang Moheyan] says: "The second ground is the simultaneous departure from both identity and difference; this refers only to sentient beings."
It possesses three types of equality with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; this, in general, encompasses all phenomena (*dharma*). In terms of essence (*tattva*), it is like space and existence.

In terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is like defilement and purity. In terms of truth (*satya*), it is like the ultimate and the conventional. In terms of the path (*mārga*), it is like the middle and the extremes. In terms of stages (*avasthā*)...

As with the provisional and the real, so it is regarding the teachings; as with the mundane world, all shadows of commonality and difference are utterly extinguished and severed, remaining entirely unrelated to one another—this is what is meant by "birth and extinction having ceased.
Thereafter, quiescent extinction manifests before one, and everything begins from this point. Who could surpass this?
Unconditioned True Suchness (tathatā) is by nature pure, luminous, and manifest;

this is called the Ground of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi). This clarifies the sixth ground. Indeed, from the stages prior to the grounds, one applies effortful practice, aspiring from the state of the Worthy (śaikṣa) toward the Sage (arhat/saint).
Upon entering the grounds, distinctions are dissolved and sameness is extinguished; clarity arises and awakening becomes full. Thereby, one transcends both sameness and difference, and yet...

It constitutes the ultimate application of effort, the most supreme and unsurpassed. Upon reaching the absolute limit of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) True Suchness (*tathatā*) finally manifests its nature;

therefore, this stage is named "Manifestation" (*abhimukhī*). For those of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle], the moment they resolve their minds, they immediately awaken to the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
Nevertheless, as the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) have not yet been shattered and the defilements of the mind have not yet been removed, regarding...
True Suchness (tathatā) still belongs to the realm of inferential knowledge; how could it be directly realized?

Now, by progressing from semblance cultivation to authentic cultivation, one exhausts the functional effort of the conditioned and approaches the stage of effortless practice (anabhoga-caryā). Therefore, at this stage, true suchness is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Only now does it begin to manifest. However, the great function of the entire reality of *tathatā* (suchness) still resides in the eighth and ninth stages;
it is only here that one reaches the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and truly manifests *tathatā*. ○ Hege said: "This stage is precisely the manifestation of quiescent extinction."
"Reaching the limit of the reality-limit (bhūtatathatā) is called the Far-Reaching Ground (dūraṃgamā-bhūmi).
This clarifies the seventh ground. On the preceding stages, the reality-limit has only just begun to manifest and has not yet been fully revealed;
how much less could one have traversed it to its end? Herein, one exhausts its very boundary. Ordinarily, when one looks toward it, its shore is not seen; now, having reached its limit—"
That which was previously unfathomable in its measure now pervades the entire realm and the entirety of space, manifesting itself everywhere—not merely before one's eyes.
While the manifestation of True Suchness (tathatā) is limited when realized partially, at the ultimate limit it is far-reaching, transcendent, and reaches the pinnacle;
therefore, this stage is named "Far-Going" (dūraṃgamā). Indeed, the limit of the ultimate limit is the limit of the limitless.

Since principle is boundless, how could practice ever approximate it? As previously stated, the five aggregates, six sense bases, and so forth, are all the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
even the seven great elements each pervade the entire dharma-realm. This is the primordial limit of true suchness.
Only this Bodhisattva can exhaust its full measure. Having exhausted the Buddha-realm in the preceding stage, he has now attained thorough penetration.
This exhaustion reaches the limit of true suchness (*tathatā*); it is the exhaustion that is fully complete.
The single mind of true suchness is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
This clarifies the eighth ground. Since the limits of the preceding stages have been exhausted, this stage fully attains its essence. Thus.
The mind is the Buddha-mind; both are completely merged and extinguished, leaving only the true Suchness, the fundamental mind, which is itself the single Dharma-realm of True Suchness.

From the root-faculties and the physical body to the vessel-world, every speck of dust and every hair is the very essence of True Suchness, even amidst the midst of one’s own deluded karmic activities.

The *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) which was previously attained is now finally realized through direct personal witness. This is what is meant by "thoroughly reaching the source of all dharmas," being unmoving and indestructible;
therefore, it is named the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). "Moving" implies change; here, in accordance with the principle of ultimate reality, there is not even the slightest variation.
The distinction between this stage and the preceding ones lies solely in the difference between having effort (*sābhoga*) and being effortless (*anābhoga*).
The manifestation of the function of True Suchness (tathatā) is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
This clarifies the ninth stage. In the preceding stage, one has already attained the entire substance of True Suchness; in this stage, one then brings forth the great function of True Suchness.
In the preceding stage, every single atom and every single hair-pore are all identical to True Suchness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; however, in this [stage], it is...
Each and every one mutually encompasses and enters the others; thus they are all-pervasive and all-encompassing.

From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vitarka*) onward, it is only upon reaching this stage that one is called "Excellent Wisdom" (*sādhumatī*), because for the first time one realizes the unobstructed wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

In the *Avataṃsaka*, this Bodhisattva is said to possess the four types of unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*), acting as a Great Dharma Master who expounds immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* phrases and meanings.

Therefore, it is called "manifesting the function of True Suchness" (*tathatā*). I maintain that while preaching the Dharma can indeed be described as manifesting a function, it is nonetheless but one function among the great functions.
The great functions do not exclude the preaching of the Dharma, yet how could the preaching of the Dharma exhaust the great functions?
Question: The realms of the seven practices manifest within one another; the environments and inhabitants of the five vehicles mutually interpenetrate. This is [as you have stated]. However—
"What is the difference between these? Answer: "The seven practices (saptāṅga-pratipad) involve this practice; the five stages of approach (pañca-abhimukha) involve this aspiration.
Since they have not yet reached direct realization, they are not the same."
Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and bring their merit to perfection;
therefore, this stage is also called the Stage of Cultivation (bhāvanā-avasthā).
This [phrase] generally concludes the preceding stages. The word "all" (*zhū*) seems to refer generally to the aforementioned stages;

however, since the Buddha, prior to the four stages of added effort (*prāyogika*), summarizes those as being beyond the forty-one minds, it is revealed that they are the various preparatory minds (*upāya-citta*) preceding the stage of cultivation.
This word "all" should properly extend from the four stages of added effort up to the ninth ground. Ānanda, these four...
Including the Bodhisattvas of the Ninth Ground: prior to this stage—from the Fourth through the Sixth Grounds—one completes the cultivation;
from the Seventh through the Ninth Grounds, one brings merit to perfection.
However, generally speaking, everything prior to this stage is collectively termed the "stage of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga*). From this point onward, the need for cultivation is slight, and...
The realizations of this stage are manifold.
The wondrous cloud of the compassionate shade covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*; hence it is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmameghā*) stage.
This clarifies the tenth stage. Now, the mind of compassion is like the shade, and wondrous wisdom is like the cloud; such is the [nature] of the Bodhisattva.

This is due to its qualities (*guṇa*). The ocean of *nirvāṇa* is the fruit-quality (*phala-guṇa*) of the Tathāgata. When a Bodhisattva reaches this stage, their compassion (*karuṇā*) is like a mass of clouds that provides shelter and moisture to all without exception;
their wisdom (*prajñā*) is like a cloud that fills everything without exception. With both compassion and wisdom perfected, they are on the very verge of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, they directly cover the great ocean of *nirvāṇa*, and thus it is named the "Dharma-Cloud Stage" (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). "Dharma" refers to the two [compassion and wisdom].
This contains both compassion and wisdom. "Clouds" signifies the encompassing of the aggregates (*skandhas*). It is not that the preceding stages lack wisdom and compassion;
however, it is here that one is said to be "in accord with *nirvāṇa*," being without even the slightest deficiency. This is what makes it superior.
Now, the reason it says "in accord with *nirvāṇa*" rather than "in accord with the virtues of a Buddha" is to prevent confusion with the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogi-bodhi*). 10.

The section on the *bhūmis* concludes. [Objection]: Examining the stages of the ten bhumis and ten abodes in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, they are all identical to the "abode" (*vihāra*) stages of this sūtra.
Based on this, Master Wuxing hastily disparages the *Avataṃsaka* as being a separate system. How could this sūtra possibly transcend the *Avataṃsaka*?

Why would its "ten abodes" be identical to the "ten bhumis" of that [sūtra]? [Response]: The *Avataṃsaka* emphasizes sequential arrangement (*pravibhāga*), whereas this sūtra emphasizes perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). Perfect...

If the essential principle encompasses all, then the first abiding (*prathama-vihāra*) should immediately encompass the first practice (*prathama-caryā*), the first orientation (*prathama-pratipatti*), and the first ground (*prathama-bhūmi*).

This would continue in this manner until the tenth abiding should likewise encompass the tenth practice, the tenth orientation, and the tenth ground. If this were so, then each set of ten would be identical;
how could it be limited merely to the identity of the four positions of the abidings and grounds? ○ He [Heze Shenhui] said: "This applies throughout the preceding stages."

The first gradual stage serves as the barrier between the pure and the defiled; the third gradual stage serves as the barrier between the real and the false; the seventh faith serves as the barrier between the ordinary being and the Buddha;

the first abode serves as the barrier between delusion and awakening; and the initial stage of the ten practices and the initial stage of the ten dedications serve as the barrier between the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Entering the stages constitutes the gateway between the mundane and the supramundane.

While the Tathāgata flows against the current, the Bodhisattva proceeds in accordance with it until they reach the point where awakening and the limit intersect; this is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

This clarifies the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Indeed, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), these are all the means employed by Bodhisattvas to advance toward the ocean of fruition.
As for the Tathāgata, he has already previously realized and entered the ocean of fruition of Wondrous Enlightenment; there is nothing further to be attained.
Yet, out of compassion for sentient beings whom he does not abandon, he turns the vessel of mercy against the current and emerges upstream. And as for this Bodhisattva...
The pursuit has not yet reached its consummation; one is now heading toward the ocean of fruition, entering by following the current.

At this point, where initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*) and wondrous awakening (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) meet at their two boundaries, the demarcations are perfectly aligned; hence it is called "entering the intersection. The initial stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s flow of Dharma;
this "entry into the intersection" is precisely when one connects with the Tathāgata’s flow of Dharma. It is like this:
It is like those who enter the sea to gather treasures: the first merchant has already obtained various jewels and, traveling against the current, reaches the mouth of the sea;
only then does the second merchant advance to take his own share, entering with the current and likewise reaching the mouth of the sea; the two ships arrive at exactly the same time.
However, the bow of the preceding merchant ship faces outward, while the bow of the following merchant ship faces inward.

Because their perceived boundaries meet and intersect, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), meaning that initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) is equal to wondrous enlightenment (*prajñā-bodhi*). Upon reaching this stage, one is without interval from the Buddha;
this is truly what is meant by "emptiness and enlightenment are perfectly complete," and "that which empties emptiness is extinguished. — *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng)
It says: "Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness; Wondrous Enlightenment is stillness within illumination. This is the basis for distinguishing between these two stages.

According to my humble analysis, "stillness within illumination" is precisely "sincerity and luminosity" (cheng-ming), while "illumination within stillness" is "luminosity and sincerity" (ming-cheng). That which proceeds from sincerity to luminosity is called "nature" (xing);

that which proceeds from luminosity to sincerity is called "instruction" (jiao). This is entirely identical in meaning, differing only in that the establishment of instruction distinguishes between the mundane and the supramundane.
Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), this awakening first attains the Vajra Mind.
This initial stage of Dry Wisdom is established here as a distinct position to clarify that wisdom is still differentiated at this point. Some schools merely merge it [into the preceding stages].
Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). If one takes only the fifty-five stages, then it is appropriate to combine them as such.
If one takes the twelve single and double stages, as well as the sixty noble stages, then it is fitting to distinguish them.

Ānanda, from the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) onwards, having passed through fifty-four stages up to Equal Enlightenment—although this is indeed the stage of Equal Enlightenment—if one examines it closely:
Only then does one first attain the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā*) within the Diamond Mind (*vajracitta*).

As for the preceding Dry Wisdom, it already employed the Diamond Mind to sever the ignorance of differentiated characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), thereby attaining a partial manifestation of radiance like the newly risen moon.

Upon reaching this [present] stage, one likewise employs the subsequent Diamond Mind to sever the ignorance of arising characteristics (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), and only then does one fully obtain the radiance.
It is perfected, like the moon on a clear night. However, the preceding stage of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā) has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma;
this [present] dry wisdom has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment. Therefore, both are termed "dry wisdom.
To illustrate this using the hexagrams of the *I Ching*: the initial stage of dry wisdom is like the hexagram Fu, where the single Yang line first returns.

The Ten Abidings correspond to the hexagram Lin (Approaching). The Ten Practices correspond to Tai (Peace). The Ten Transferences correspond to Da Zhuang (Great Strength). The Ten Grounds correspond to Guai (Decision).
Reaching the Wisdom of Dryness (*qianhui*) following Equal Enlightenment corresponds to Qian (Heaven). Upon reaching this stage, the yin is exhausted and the substance of yang is complete.

The Tongyi (General Discussion) states: "Regarding the two stages from the beginning to the end of the Wisdom of Dryness, those who have provided commentaries since antiquity have not [fully understood them]."
First: Scholars find it difficult to rely upon [the teachings], yet this is merely because they have not observed the source of the Buddha-dharma.

Sentient beings of the nine realms, by means of the three kinds of outflows, summon the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) and give rise to the two kinds of birth-and-death (*dvividha-jāti-maraṇa*). As for the five stages of dwelling:

the stage of dwelling in desire-attachment (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*), the stage of dwelling in form-attachment (*rūparāga-vāsabhūmi*), the stage of dwelling in formless-attachment (*ārūpyarāga-vāsabhūmi*), the stage of dwelling in all views (*sarvadṛṣṭi-vāsabhūmi*), and the stage of dwelling in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).

The three floods (*ogha*) are the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*). The first four afflictions constitute the floods of desire and existence;

they induce *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death) and are severed at the stage of the first faith (*prathama-śraddhā*). The ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is called the flood of ignorance;

it induces *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth and death) and is severed only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood. By this evidence, [it is clear that] the aforementioned stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*)...
On this stage, one employs the adamantine mind to first sever the two flows of desire and exit the cycle of birth-and-death characterized by segmented existence;

hence it is said that "the craving of desire is parched and dried up. When the faculties and their objects no longer meet, the remaining physical form manifests before one and will not continue into further rebirth. It is like clearing turbid water:
as the sand and silt settle of their own accord, the clear water appears before one; this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions. Its absence...

Regarding the "Flow of Ignorance": from the moment one enters the stage of faith, one has already resolved to sever it. However, because ignorance is so profound and thick, one must pass through fifty-four stages until the final thought-moment of the Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).

Only when the "mark of arising" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*) ignorance is finally dried up can it be said that this awakening has first attained the "Initial Ground of Dry Wisdom" within the Diamond Mind (*vajra-citta*).
At this point, the five abodes are completely exhausted and the two deaths are forever extinguished. Thus...

Entering wondrous enlightenment and emerging from the birth-and-death of transformation—this is what is meant by "removing the mud to reveal pure water," which is termed the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
This is the explicit textual evidence. Nevertheless, although the stages have a beginning and an end, contemplation has no sequence;
they are merely ordered according to the depth of the power of practice. Zhong says: Tongyi states that the first stage is the Ground of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
What is called "clear water appearing before one" is termed the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).

This stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*)—what is called "removing the mud so that pure water remains"—is termed the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). This thoroughly captures the intent of the Sūtra.

Regarding the point where the old commentary adds that [this stage] has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment (*tathāgata-pratimaṇḍita-samudra*), [the author] publicly maintains that it enters into and intersects with the limit of enlightenment (*bodhy-anta*).
These are the words [of the Buddha].
Thus, through these successive layers—twelve stages of both single and combined levels—one exhausts the wondrous enlightenment and accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way.
This clarifies the ultimate fruition of the Tathāgata. These various positions are: first, Dry Wisdom (Kāṣāya); second, Faith (Śraddhā); third, Abiding (Vihāra); fourth, Practice (Caryā).

Five stages of orientation (*mukha*); six levels of warmth (*ūṣmagata*); seven summits (*mūrdhan*); eight patiences (*kṣānti*); nine worldly dharma-stages (*laukika-agra-dharma*); ten grounds (*bhūmi*); eleven equalities (*samatā*);

twelve golds (*suvarṇa*). These are layered and mutually dependent. Among them, *kṣānti*, *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *laukika-agra-dharma*, *samatā*, and *suvarṇa* each have a single name and a single position; thus they are "single" (*dan*).

Faith (*śraddhā*), abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), orientation (*mukha*), and ground (*bhūmi*) each have a single name but multiple positions; thus they are "repeated" (*fu*). There are seven single positions and five repeated ones.

There are twelve positions in total, both single and combined, all of which are termed "causes," as they all lead toward the fruit. Upon reaching this point, the causes are perfected and the fruit is fulfilled;
only then is the task completed. In a single kṣaṇa, one realizes and enters wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), thereby accomplishing the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way.
What is called "wondrous enlightenment" is, in its essence, nothing other than the three Tathāgatagarbhas.

Its application does not transcend the four meanings and four marks. However, although those at the initial stage of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching share the same path of awakening as the Tathāgata, their original nature and its manifestation are not yet unified, and subject and object have not been forgotten; thus they have not yet fully perfected the subtle mystery, continuing this way until the stage of Equal Enlightenment.

Furthermore, while one may only be able to align with them, one has not yet been able to unify with them. Now, however, the ten profound marks of virtue (*daśa-guṇa*) and the ten profound functions of activity are simultaneously and fully perfected;
they exhaust the mystery and reach the ultimate subtlety, being inconceivable. This is what is called "unsurpassed."

Prior to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), all preceding stages are considered lower and subsequent stages are considered higher; thus, one knows that among the various stages within the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*), there is none that does not have a superior above it.
This stage, however, is the ultimate realization beyond which nothing further can be added.

Furthermore, while the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) of the previous [causal] path is the unsurpassed within the mundane world (*laukika*), this [present stage] is the unsurpassed within the supramundane (*lokottara*). The cause encompasses the fruit.
The Ocean: when the fruit thoroughly penetrates to the source of the cause, this is indeed the ultimate pinnacle.

As for the necessity of stating "the twelve single and double [categories]," it is because one exhausts the twelve transformations of the twelve classes of beings mentioned previously to achieve a single cycle of return; thus, by cultivating the cause, one realizes the fruit.

There are also twelve instances of both single and double [terms]. Master Zhong says: First is the single term "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*); next follows the double terms of the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and orientation;
after that, the single terms of the four preparatory practices (*prayoga-mārga*); following these singles, the double terms of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
after these doubles, the single term of "equal enlightenment" (*samyak-sambodhi*), continuing thus through to "wondrous enlightenment" (*miao-jue*). This consists of both single and double [terms].
They interpenetrate one another; hence it is called "layer upon layer.
These various stages are all observed through the ten profound metaphors of the diamond-like [wisdom] regarding phenomena as being like illusions, within the state of *śamatha*.
Through the *vipaśyanā* (insight) of all Tathāgatas, one purifies, cultivates, and realizes [the path], gradually entering deeper and deeper.

This generally clarifies the practice across all stages. From the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) to the resultant ground (*phala-bhūmi*), these various grounds all employ the adamantine jewel-like awakening as the sharp instrument for severing delusions, observing the ten kinds of profound metaphors of illusion.
That is to say: one contemplates all karma as being like an illusion; all phenomena as being like a mirage; all bodies as being like the moon reflected in water;
exquisite forms as being like space; exquisite sounds as being like an echo; all Buddha-fields as being like a city of the gandharvas; and the Buddha-activities as being like a dream.
The Buddha-body is like a shadow; the Reward-body is like a reflected image; the Dharma-body is like a magical transformation.

Not only are all conditioned phenomena empty, but even the unconditioned is like a dream or an illusion. Therefore, these are called profound metaphors. Having contemplated these ten kinds of profound metaphors, [one realizes this truth].

Within the fundamental concentration that is the very nature of *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas for pure cultivation and realization. Thus, *śamatha* is subtle and secret contemplation;
*vipaśyanā* is the illusory-like *samāpatti*. This adamantine jewel of awakening is precisely these two, and nothing else.
By employing this observation, one is able to arise from nature through cultivation and attain realization through cultivation.
Gradually entering deeper, one perfectly accomplishes the wondrous *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (meditative concentration).

Your inquiry regarding the sequence of practice for attaining the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* that constitute Bodhi is, in its general outline, as follows. ○ He said: "The preceding passage merely sets forth [the framework]."
Regarding the stages of practice: if one does not reveal the practical methods for application, it is like counting another's treasures—one possesses not even half a coin oneself.

Therefore, this section directly points to the universal method of cultivation. Having seen through both the beginning and the end, one simply employs the Vajra-like Illusory Samādhi to observe and penetrate deeply.
By observing that the faculties and their objects are illusory, one immediately enters the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*).

Observing that the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is like an illusion, one enters the Ten Faiths; continuing thus until observing that Equal Enlightenment (*samyaṅ-saṃbodhi*) is like an illusion, one enters Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*).
Therefore, it is said that one "gradually and deeply penetrates. ○ Furthermore, it says: "This section is the most critical point of direct instruction.
From the ordinary person below up to Equal Enlightenment above, all may practice this universally. Thus, Avalokiteśvara himself..."
Chan Yuan-tong’s opening statement is: "The illusory Vajra Samādhi. Mañjuśrī’s selection of the perfect penetration likewise says:
"Proclaiming the Vajra King, the inconceivable illusion, the true samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas.
After the fifty-five stages, the World-Honored One further uses this passage as a concluding summary, just like a pair of mandarin ducks embroidered upon a brocade.
Furthermore, he crossed the Golden Needle Bridge; this was truly an expression of his boundless maternal compassion.
Ānanda, it is because of these three progressive stages that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five ranks of the true path to Bodhi.
One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice false contemplation.

This emphasizes the initial resolve, desiring that people study what is fundamental below and attain what is realized above. Ānanda, my explanations of the true cause and the wondrous fruit have been set forth clearly in this manner.
Do you not fear that you might regard the three gradual stages as coarse and shallow, and thus find them insufficient to follow?
You do not realize that all these various [teachings] are likewise rooted in the three kinds of progressive cultivation and advancement.

Next, by employing these three progressive advancements, one is able to successfully accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi, ranging from faith up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
One does not include the two stages of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), for they are paths rather than the ultimate truth.
Nor does one include Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), for that is the destination rather than the path. Thus, the merit of the gradual process of advancement can indeed be [appreciated].
"How meager! I wish for you to cultivate this contemplation. For one who cultivates this contemplation is said to possess right contemplation and shall proceed directly toward Bodhi.
Any other contemplation is called false contemplation and remains far removed from Bodhi.
Thus we know that apart from the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), all that is practiced by the Three Vehicles belongs to false contemplation; how could it possibly be otherwise?"
Is it that only after following the Way can one be called "heterodox"? ○ He [Heze Shenhui] says: The fifty-five stages begin with *qianhui* (dry wisdom) and end with the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Recently, Master Jiaoguang composed the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse), yet he still follows the errors of Gushan by forcibly correlating the three gradual steps with the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), and treating the ten faiths as an expansion of the first abode (*prathamavihāra*). This is to say nothing of his audacity in altering the Buddha’s teachings.
[The Master] said: "This is most laughable! If it were as you say, then the true path to Bodhi would consist of only forty-five stages;

how then could there be fifty-five positions? This major section belongs, within the four actual dharmas of the sutra’s title, specifically to the explanation of the myriad practices of the bodhisattvas, teaching wondrous *dhyāna* so that they may know the successive stages and realize them perfectly."
[This section] is concluded. Within the first division, the section on the realization of the Way is finished.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet.
Having bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "What should this sutra be named? How should I and all sentient beings uphold it?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This sutra is named *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Śītata-Pāṇḍarā Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions*.
It is also named 'The Savior and Protector of Kinsmen and Causes, Delivering Ānanda and These [Others]...'"

In this assembly, the bhikṣuṇī Zhongxing has attained the bodhicitta and entered the ocean of universal knowledge. It is also called "The Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata.
It is also called "The Great Vaipulya Sūtra of the King of the Wondrous Lotus, the Dhāraṇī-Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
It is also called "The Consecrated Syllables, the Śūraṃgama of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas. You should uphold it with reverence.
This is the statement of the sutra’s title. Although the main body of the teaching has not yet concluded, the title is recorded prematurely because the formal structure of the sutra is complete:
it begins by revealing the secret cause, proceeds to open up the stages of cultivation and realization, and culminates in the ultimate fruit.

While the subsequent sections of the text still belong to the main body of the teaching, they serve specifically as auxiliary paths; therefore, there is no impediment to concluding the title at this point.
This is a sutra. At the beginning, Ānanda is made the primary interlocutor because the intention is to advance one of great learning into the Great Samādhi.
At the end, Mañjuśrī is made to request the title because this signifies that the entire sutra is held in total retention (dhāraṇī), which cannot be achieved except through fundamental great wisdom.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince (and so forth), addressed the Buddha, saying: "I venture to ask the Tathāgata:
what shall this sūtra be named? Once its name is known, how may I and all sentient beings uphold it without losing it?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Regarding the name you ask for this sūtra, this sūtra is named..."
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa: because it is without marks that can be perceived;
because it is the supreme Uṣṇīṣa-dharma realized by all Buddhas, it is called the Great White Parasol, as it covers and protects all sentient beings;

because the myriad phenomena of the forest and the ten thousand forms are all sealed by this single Dharma, it is called the Unsurpassed Jewel Seal; because it is the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, it is called Perfect Illumination.
The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because it leaves not a single thing behind, this name is established based on wisdom and principle.
It is also called "The Savior of Close Causes. "Close" refers to Ānanda; "Causes" refers to Caṇḍā.

By means of fearless radiance and secret mantras, it can deliver one from all calamities and cause them to attain the causal mind for Bodhi, thereby entering the ocean of the fruit of universal knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). This is based on...
This name is established based on its function. It is also called "The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization.

This is because it is that which all Buddhas have cultivated and realized—the true cause and true fruit—in which nothing is not fully perfected. This name is established based on both the person and the dharma.

It is also named *Mahāvaipulya-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-rāja*. Because its essence, attributes, and functions are pure from the very beginning and pervade the entire Dharma-realm, cause and effect interpenetrate such that nothing is not sovereign.
Thus, these two titles—*Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—are seen together within this single name.
Furthermore, it is the *Dhāraṇī-mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*, which gives birth to all things.
The Buddhas are so named because they maintain all dharmas; this is a designation established according to both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.
It is also called the "Mantra of Consecration," for this sutra flows forth from the Consecration Section (*abhiṣeka-kalpa*).
It is the Śūraṅgama of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas, for by cultivating this samādhi, one fulfills the myriad practices within a single mind, reaching ultimate firmness.

This is the establishment of names based upon teaching and practice. You should know that this sutra encompasses everything—manifest and secret, principle and wisdom, teaching and practice, person and dharma, and its functional efficacy. Because it possesses such various merits, it has various titles;
it is truly the unsurpassed, profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma, difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. You...
"You should maintain and uphold this with diligence, never allowing it to be neglected.

When these words were spoken, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Pañcara*, as well as the titles of the definitive meanings of this sutra; they suddenly awakened to *dhyāna* and attained progress toward the stages of sainthood.

(Examining the scripture from the beginning, it discusses sequentially; however, it only mentions *śamatha* and *samādhi* without yet mentioning *dhyāna*. It is only at this point that it first names it. Furthermore, the subsequent connection with the cultivation and advancement through the noble stages clearly indicates that where the noble stages are discussed, it is indeed speaking of *dhyāna*.
With the supreme and wondrous principle, the mind becomes empty and still, severing the six grades of subtle afflictions cultivated within the three realms.

This passage describes the benefits obtained by those present who were ready to receive the teaching. When the World-Honored One had finished speaking these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the secret heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) revealed by the Tathāgata.

This is none other than the mind that is without exterior, the essence that is pure, and the function that universally covers—all of which are fully encompassed within the three characters of the "Great White Parasol" (*Mahāsitātapatra*). These three characters can condense the entirety of this sutra.
Therefore, it is called the meaning of *pāṇḍarā*. Furthermore, having heard these five titles of this sutra, one realizes they all expound the ultimate truth through direct pointing;
they are definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) and not provisional (*neyārtha*). Thus, this is the Tathāgata’s sincere guidance for humanity:
