Yet they are mixed and blended among humans; for the most part, they belong to the class of the obstinate. One whose mind does not follow the classics of virtue and righteousness is called obstinate. Lacking benevolence and righteousness, being utterly evil and utterly foolish, they cannot be transformed into even a hair’s breadth of goodness.

As for those who bear the signs of retribution, having fully received their karmic recompense, they return to physical form and are born within the human realm, yet remain a hybrid of different species. The signs of retribution originate from licentiousness and depravity; their residual habits further manifest as strange anomalies.

Just as with an infant, whose mouth, eyes, and all bodily faculties atop the head are all abnormal, so it is with those of the fox-like class; once they have repaid their debts and regained their forms, they are born among the human realm.

They are mixed among the common and mediocre. (Formerly they were foxes; though they possess human forms, they merely distort their feelings and adorn their appearances, wagging their tails to beg for pity, using flattery to seek acceptance in the world. They cannot stand on their own feet with distinction, but rather achieve results by relying on others—these are the dull and mediocre.
As for those of the poisonous class, once their retribution is exhausted and they regain their form, they are born into the human realm, mixed among the cruel and fierce.

(Those with bee-like eyes and jackal-like voices are stubborn, cruel, harmful to living things, and devoid of compassion. Those of the *huí* (roundworm) class, once their retribution is exhausted and they regain their form, are born into the human realm, merging with those of a subtle category.
(Because the *huí* attaches itself to objects through its decaying breath, its residual habits are likewise lowly; though it may associate closely with humans, humans do not count it among their own.

Those of the *shí* (carnivorous) class, once their retribution is exhausted and they regain their form, are born into the human realm, merging with those of a yielding category. (Because they were arrogant toward others, they become objects of human loathing; having turned into the carnivorous class, although they possess human forms, they lack the spirit of a true man.)

They are those who are dejected and lacking in vigor. Those who conform to the "Ethical" (Lun) category, having fulfilled their retribution and regained their form, are born into the human realm and join the class of laborers.
(Because in past lives they carried heavy burdens for long distances, toiling without rest, they are now likewise driven by others, serving as oxen or horses, their toil never ceasing.

Those who correspond to the "Cultural" (Wen) category, having fulfilled their retribution and regained their form, are born into the human realm and join the class of scholars. (Because in former times they possessed intelligence and insight, yet did not attain the Truth, they belong to the class of scholars; they merely possess a small degree of...)

As for talent and emotion: they may comprehend texts and explain meanings, yet they concern themselves only with wind, clouds, moon, and dew; they are not writings that span the heavens and weave the earth. As for those auspicious signs: they are sufficient recompense and a restoration of form;

born into the human realm, they participate in the category of the luminous. (This is because, by the power of riding upon luminous mantras, they possess worldly wisdom and eloquence; it is not a brilliance that illuminates heaven and mirrors the earth. As for those who follow the natural order:

Having fully repaid their debts, they regain their human forms and join the ranks of the enlightened. (Because they relied upon humans for a long time in past lives, they are now also experienced in worldly affairs and understand human nature;
yet this does not mean they have attained universal penetration. Ānanda, all such beings have settled their karmic debts from former lives and returned to the human realm.

Since beginningless time, their karmic calculations have been inverted, leading them to give birth to one another and kill one another. Having failed to encounter the Tathāgata and hear the True Dharma, they remain [in this state].

Within the midst of worldly afflictions, they revolve according to the nature of phenomena; these types of beings are called "those to be pitied. (This concludes the summary of their pitiable state to serve as a warning to people.

Ānanda, all these sentient beings, in the past while in the human realm, committed karma leading to the three miserable realms and received retribution in those three realms. From hell they went to the hungry ghosts, and from the hungry ghosts to the animals; all must fully repay their karmic debts from former lives. If even a small portion remains unpaid, they cannot become human again.

All of this has proceeded from time immemorial: ignorance obscures the mind, afflictions obstruct the intellect, and karmic calculations lead to perversion. Bound by the debt of life, beings are born to one another as creditors seeking repayment and kill one another as debtors demanding their lives. These are all gatherings of unfavorable conditions; only upon meeting the Tathāgata can they be explained away.

Only by practicing the True Dharma can liberation be attained. Were these two not encountered, birth and killing would never cease. A human body is not long-lasting, and one would soon enter the three miserable realms. Indeed, it is extremely difficult to obtain and extremely easy to lose; having fortunately obtained it now—

Furthermore, there is much misfortune and little fortune; much suffering and little joy. If this is so, when will one be free from the afflictions of the mundane world (*saṃsāra*), and when will the cycle of rebirth cease? When speaking of this, the hearts of all Buddhas are moved with sorrow; therefore, it is called "pitiable. (The section on the human realm concludes.)

The following clarifies the destinies of the various *ṛṣis*. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "xian" (immortal) means "to transition. It refers to one who does not die despite aging, but transitions into the mountains.

While the karmas of the three lower realms all take the ten habitual tendencies as their cause, and even upon first attaining a human body one still carries the remnants of these ten types of residual habits, this realm of the *ṛṣis* has no connection whatsoever with the ten habitual tendencies. Now, as for the arising of the Way of the Immortals:

Feeling weary of and fearful toward sentient beings and impermanence, they imagine their own bodies to be eternally abiding. They falsely devise many paths, all of which are nothing other than aspirations for longevity and immortality.
They do not realize that this body is merely a deluded misapprehension within the true mind;
it is no different from those who rely upon grass or cling to wood. Now, because they fear death, they further falsely cultivate the quest for longevity; this is an error.
Furthermore, they err in their practice, becoming increasingly fragmented and distracted; lost in delusion, they do not know how to return. How deeply regrettable this is!

Ānanda, there are also followers who, instead of relying on Perfect Enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, separately cultivate deluded thoughts and fixate their mental images to preserve the physical form.
They roam in mountain forests and remote places where humans cannot reach; these are the ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
Ānanda, above the human realm, there is another class who advance from the human path in their cultivation; yet they do not rely upon the True Teaching of the Tathāgata.

Taking the fundamental, primordially pure essence—neither arising nor ceasing—as their primary cause for cultivation, they falsely cling to the body of the five aggregates, believing there is a nature that can be cultivated and a life-force that can be sustained, such that one may achieve longevity and abide long in the world.
This constitutes the separate cultivation of deluded thoughts. Although their varieties are many, the essential secret is this: to preserve mental images and to solidify the physical form.
To speak of "preserving mental images" is simply to employ various deluded thoughts; it cannot be compared to the dissolution of all mental states.
To speak of "solidifying the form" is simply to falsely identify with the physical body; it cannot be compared to ultimate, unshakeable stability. Once such false cultivation is perfected—
Thus, they roam in mountain forests and places beyond the reach of human tracks—such as the famous mountains, grottoes, and palaces, within blessed lands and pure capitals.
Of this kind, there are ten types of immortals (*xian*) in total. Zong says: "Compared to the heavens, they are inferior;
compared to humans, they are superior. This is the realm of the immortals. The worldly do not examine this and thus take the immortals [to be the ultimate state]."
"Excellent, Ānanda!
Those sentient beings who steadfastly take up their medicinal practice without ceasing, until the path of food is perfected, are called earth-walking transcendents."

"What are these ten kinds? Ānanda, among those sentient beings who cultivate deluded thoughts separately, there are some who firmly rely on medicinal substances such as *qiushí* (autumn-stone) and red lead.
They process and compound these ingredients, forming them into pills or cakes, which they consume without ceasing.
Thus, their digestive systems become perfected, their entire bodies grow robust and healthy, and their lifespans are extended; yet they have not yet attained [liberation]."
Those who can levitate are called earth-walking immortals (*bhūcarī-ṛṣi*). They are like Asita of the Western Regions or Peng Zu and Jianzi of this land.
How could they know that the nectar of immortality, the food of dhyāna-delight, the rice of the golden ox, and the cakes of Yunmen—by a single satiation of which one may forget a hundred hungers?
One who firmly cultivates medicinal herbs without ceasing, until the Way of medicine is perfected, is called a "Flying Immortal" (Khecarī).
Furthermore, there are those who firmly cultivate herbs such as purple *zhī*, yellow *jīng*, sweet flag (*xiāngpú*), pine, and cypress;

by long-term ingestion, their bodies become light and their gait becomes like flying, even ascending heights and leaping over ravines with such swiftness that nothing can compare—these are called "Flying [Immortals]."
"Immortals (xian). ○ These are, for example, the Master Mao and the Maiden Mao.

How could one know that the Agada medicine, when touched, causes the knots of the sense-faculties to dissolve so that one proceeds everywhere without obstruction; and when ingested, all myriad sufferings are eliminated and one’s lifespan becomes immeasurable?
Formerly, 'flying' (feixing) was taken to mean 'soaring upward' (feiju), which is incorrect, as 'traversing the void' (kongxing) occurs later."
To be as firm and solid as metal or stone, without ceasing, until the Way of transformation is perfected—this is called a *yóuxíng-xiān* (wandering immortal).

Furthermore, there are those who are firm and solid as metal or stone, like the smelting of the five metals and eight minerals, the cultivation of cinnabar and the joining of mercury, or the nine-fold Great Return (*jiǔzhuǎn dàhuán*);
they transform vermilion into gold and transform the ordinary body into the skeletal bones of an immortal—this is called a *huà* (transformation immortal).

When the Way is perfected, the physical body becomes light and subtle; traversing ten thousand *li* in an instant, one wanders everywhere without weariness, and is thus called a "Wandering Immortal" (*yóuxíng xiān*).

This refers to figures such as Lü Dōngbīn and Hé Xiānzhi. How could they have known that by opening their own precious treasury, they would realize this indestructible body, sporting with supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-lands, and being present everywhere—without even waiting for [external conditions]?
Having perfected the path of transformation, they travel about;
their movements and stillness are firm and stable, never ceasing. Their vital energy (*prāṇa*) and essence are fully perfected, and they are called *khecarī-ṛṣis* (Sky-faring Seers).

Furthermore, their movements and stillness are firm and stable, like stroking or manipulating [an object]; they circulate the vital energy and harmonize the body, moving and remaining still according to the proper time.
One must be diligent in every movement and posture. After practicing this for a long time without ceasing, the vital energy (*qi*) and essence (*jing*) become perfected.

This is what is called "refining the essence back into energy," "refining the energy back into spirit" (*shen*), and "refining the spirit back into the void. Thereupon, one undergoes transcendence and ascends on wings, roaming through the void.
This is called the practice of the Sky-Walking Immortal (khecarī). It is like Jingyang’s ascending his entire residence, or Li Ziqi riding the wind.
Yet, one must not realize that not relying on the breath, not relying on form or color, and not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind—this is the practice of true emptiness.
When the vital fluids are stabilized and flow without ceasing, such that the cultivation of virtue is perfected, one is called a *devacara-ṛṣi* (heaven-walking immortal).
Furthermore, there are those whose vital fluids are stabilized through practices such as exhaling the old and inhaling the new, stirring the celestial pond, or swallowing the jade nectar (*yùlì*).

If one continues this for a long time without ceasing, it can cause the water to ascend and the fire to descend, thereby forming the inner elixir (*neidan*). Once the essence is complete and solidified, the physical form becomes radiant and lustrous;
the skin is like snow and the countenance is like that of a child. Transcending the void, one travels to the heavens, and is thus called a "Heaven-Walking Immortal" (*tianxing xian*).
This refers, for example, to the Spirit-Man of Gushan. Yet, they fail to realize that the true nature of their own water is [the source].
It is empty, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and penetrating the ten directions. Its fluids, secretions, and froth all flow as a single current with the Fragrant Water Ocean;
they do not require solidification before they come into being.

Solidifying the refined essence without ceasing, one attains perfection through the absorption of its purest elements; this is called the "Practice of the Transcendent Immortal" (the character *xing* here is pronounced in the departing tone).

Furthermore, there is the practice of solidifying the refined essence by, for example, closing the eyes at dawn and facing the east to gather the solar essence and drink it, gathering the lunar radiance at night, and even partaking of the five stars and feasting on clouds and mists. Having absorbed these for a long time, the essence becomes...

The vital energy (*qi*) circulates in hidden penetration; dross and impurities depart day by day, while purity and emptiness arrive day by day. Thus, one is able to pass through metal and stone, tread upon water and fire without the slightest hindrance;
this is called the "Transcendent of Unimpeded Passage" (*tongxing xian*). This refers, for example, to the Five-Attainment Transcendents (*wutong xian*) and Zhuang Bo-mei.

Little do they realize that their own radiance illuminates both heaven and earth; it penetrates everywhere through the gates of the six sense organs, without waiting for the essence to be drawn in before it becomes pervasive.
They maintain firm and steadfast incantations without ceasing; when their ritual methods are perfected, they are called "Path-Practicing Immortals" (Caryācāraṇa).
Furthermore, there are those who maintain firm and steadfast incantations, such as using incantations for dates or writing talismans to cure illnesses, ward off poisons, and expel malevolent spirits.
They benefit all classes of living beings. Having maintained their incantations for a long time, they concentrate their spirits without wavering and thus also attain the Way.
Because they possess the aspiration for the Way to save the world, they are called Daoxing-xian (Immortals of Dao Practice). Examples include Yu Ji and Zhang Daoling.
How could one know that *Siddhārthapātra* (悉怛多般怛囉) is the mantra-heart that transforms the ordinary into the holy?
To not take this as the Way is not the Right Way.
With firm and unwavering mindfulness, one practices without ceasing until the visualization is perfected; such a person is called a *jyotir-yogin*.

Furthermore, there are those who, with firm and unwavering mindfulness, fix their minds below the navel, pass through the *mūlādhāra* (tail-gate), ascend the *vaṃśa* (climbing the spine), and reach the *brahmarandhra* (the crown of the head), where they pierce the summit and cause the spirit to emerge; practicing this for a long time without ceasing until the visualization is perfected, they too—
This is called "turning the light back to reflect. Such a person is named a "Walking Immortal" (xingxian). Figures such as Zhang Ziyang and Wei Boyang were of this sort.
How could they have known that the essence which is perfectly bright and pure—when one neither thinks of good nor thinks of evil—is the perfect illumination of the Dharma-realm?
Maintaining firm union without ceasing, until the resonance is perfectly realized, one is called a "refined-practice immortal" (*siddha*).
Furthermore, there is firm union like that of an infant and a maiden, wherein yin and yang are joined, taking from the *kan* trigram to fill the *li* trigram.

By binding the essence of the immortal embryo and maintaining this state for a long time without ceasing, the two aspects mutually resonate; thus one is able to produce the medicine and complete the elixir.
This is because within the human body there is a single point of true essence (*zhenjing*), which is precisely the primordial essence of the Great Unity (*Taichi*) prior to Heaven.
As Laozi said, "Within it there is essence," and as Guangchengzi said, "Do not shake your essence. Once this essence is attained—
He attained the Way immediately and was named Jingxingxian (The Immortal of Refined Conduct).
It is said that Lü Dongbin also enjoyed "harvesting the battle" [sexual cultivation], yet he did not realize that the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the fundamentally pure body of clarity.
Once it has received form, it moves and dwells together with it, never departing. Yet he abandoned it without a second thought, seeking instead the primal essence of Taiyi.

Sexual intercourse—what is it other than deluded thought? As for employing women as "cauldrons" (dingqi) and thereby indulging in lewdness, the Inner Teachings (Buddhism) certainly reject this as the discourse of demons, while the Way of the Immortals (Daoism) likewise despises it as an inferior practice.

This is merely catering to human lust; those who are deranged and confused may be led astray by such things, but upright men and gentlemen do not engage in them. Nevertheless, regarding the Daoist tradition...

The latter currents follow human desires, and thus people easily comply with them. The original intent of the Inner Teachings (Buddhism) subverts human desires, and thus people find it difficult to uphold.
Now, wealth, sensual beauty, and longevity are the great desires of humanity.

The Way [of Daoism] employs lead, mercury, and the alchemical cauldron to cast away the desire for wealth and beauty, and further utilizes the inner elixir of essence and breath to accord with the longing for life.

As for the mind, who would not delight in following it? Yet when it comes to the inner teachings—such as the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) and the holy life (*brahmacarya*)—these run counter to the heart’s craving for wealth and sensual pleasure.
Furthermore, they command one to contemplate the body as a venomous snake and to discard the body like mucus or spittle.

If one does not penetrate their profound depth, who could possibly believe them? Alas! Is it any wonder that among the gentry and those of wealth and status, those who speak of alchemy and elixirs are found everywhere?
Yet among those who observe the fasts and recite the Buddha’s name, not even one or two in a hundred do so.
Through firm resolve and transformative power, they practice without ceasing; having attained perfect awakening, they are called transcendental immortals (*vidyādhara*).

Furthermore, there is the "firm transformation" (*jiangu bianhua*). One awakens to and penetrates the principle of transformation, capable of great illusory manifestations that continue without ceasing for a long time.

Upon achieving perfect awakening, one can move mountains and overturn waters, becoming wondrously peerless in this world; such a person is called a "Transcendent of Ultimate Conduct" (*juexing xian*).
Examples include Liu Gen and Zuo Ci. The awakening within this context is like that of Zhuangzi’s contemplation of transformation (*guan hua*) and Tanzi’s realization of transformation (*da hua*).
This is not the true awakening found within Perfect Enlightenment. Formerly, Lao Chengzi studied illusion under Master Yin Wen.
The Master told him: "The vital energy of life and the forms of physical appearance—all are illusion.
That which is the beginning of creation and the end of yin and yang is called birth and death. To exhaust the constants and master the changes, one must shift and transform according to form."
This is what is called "phantasmagoria. Only when one knows that phantasmagoria is no different from birth and death can one begin to learn the art of phantasmagoria.
Since both you and I are phantasms, why is there any need to learn it? Lao Chengzi returned home and, employing the words of Yin Wen, meditated deeply for three months.
He was subsequently able to exercise mastery over existence and non-existence, reversing the order of the four seasons so that thunder arose in winter and ice was produced in summer.
Those who fly walk; those who walk fly. Throughout their lives, they do not cling to these techniques; therefore, the world has no tradition of them.

Although this is knowing that illusory transformation is the ultimate practice, one does not realize that the source from which illusory transformation arises is the absolute transcendence of all dualistic relativity.
This is what constitutes the ultimate practice.
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening; instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence and live for ten million years.
They dwell in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands, far removed from the realm of humanity. This, too, is merely the circulation of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra;
because they do not cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of immortals and others each cultivate their own specific gates, yet their conduct is collectively the same.
All of them refine their minds among human beings; however, they fail to realize that the true and eternal nature of the fundamental mind is beyond both birth and death.

Thus, they abandon the cultivation of perfect enlightenment and instead seek the principle of longevity within the confines of the physical body. Their lifespans likewise reach up to a thousand years.
"Ten thousand years! How could one know that this length is merely sufficient to surpass brevity? This life ultimately awaits extinction.
Although long and short differ, how could there truly be immortality? As for the place where they rest, it is not mixed with human habitation, nor is it in the heavens;
rather, it is in deep mountains or upon islands in the great ocean—simply places beyond the reach of human tracks. And so forth.
To claim that there is no distinction between worldly immortals and celestial beings is erroneous, for those who dwell in the heavens are mistaken.
To speak briefly, they too remain within the cycle of saṃsāra and the flow of deluded thoughts, because they do not cultivate the correct samādhi of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.
If one encounters a holy teacher, one may suddenly change course and likewise enter the wondrous *samādhi*.

If, however, one stubbornly clings to [worldly attachments] and refuses to let go, then once this celestial retribution is exhausted, one will once again change heads and faces and return to disperse among the various realms of existence;
what benefit would there be then? Indeed, though ten thousand may practice, not one attains [liberation]; even if one were to attain it, if it does not transcend *saṃsāra*, what is the use?

Just as those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Western Land attain a golden body in a single lifetime and shall not undergo the cycle of transmigration for vast eons—how painful it is, how painful it is, that there are those who lack the conditions for faith and do not believe! Question:

Those who cultivate the path of the immortals falsely claim that the teachings of Śākyamuni cultivate nature but do not cultivate life, and thus their numinous spirits remain in the shadows for ten thousand kalpas, unable to enter the state of sainthood. Is this true or not? Answer: Regarding what they say...

Regarding the teachings on nature (*xing*) and life-force (*ming*), both are not ultimately true. This is because "nature" refers to the spirit-soul within the body, while "life-force" refers to the root of life formed by the condensation of vital energy (*qi*) within the body.
Therefore, it is said that those who cultivate nature alone attain only the ghostly immortality of the *yin*-soul, lacking a long-lived physical form.
Only those who cultivate life-force concurrently attain a light, subtle, and long-lived body, thereby boasting of the perfection of both form and spirit.
How wondrous! Who would have known that the "nature" (dhātu) spoken of by the Buddha is the ocean of true suchness (tathatā) inherently possessed by every person;
it is the fundamental substance of immeasurable heavens and earths, and of immeasurable myriad phenomena.

One who realizes this nature is not only able to manifest immeasurable wondrous bodies, but can also manifest immeasurable heavens, earths, and myriad phenomena. As for those manifestations, how could they be merely...
One can cause it to abide for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years; though it be for kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges, it may likewise be made to abide.

Yet, when one wishes to withdraw it, it is withdrawn at once, so that not a single atom remains established. When one wishes to manifest it, it is manifested at once, such that the myriad dharmas are fully revealed. Thus, one attains great sovereign mastery.
Attaining great enjoyment is precisely what constitutes the *tathatā* (suchness) Buddha-nature. I request that you consult the preceding passages where the nature is revealed;
there, you will naturally realize that it was through ignorance that they falsely slandered it. [End of] the section on the various sages.

The following are the various celestial realms (*deva-gati*). These are fundamentally different from the realm of the immortals (*ṛṣi-gati*). Yet, worldly people do not distinguish between immortals and devas;
those who study the path of the immortals indiscriminately affiliate themselves with the heavens, even claiming that all the devas were originally their ancestral immortals.
Now, I shall briefly clarify this. Immortals possess human bodies and crave longevity; they most fear casting off the body to receive another. All the devas, however, cast such bodies aside.

To cast off one's former body and receive a celestial body—how could these possibly be of the same kind? Furthermore, the abodes of immortals, such as Mount Penglai and Mount Kunlun, are all not within the heavens;
even the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have no place for them to dwell, let alone the higher realms, let alone the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Thus we know that the celestial realm is the most honored and superior class within the [six] destinies, standing far apart from both immortals and ghosts.
They belong to the class of spirits.
Ānanda, there are people in the world who do not seek permanence, yet are unable to abandon their affection for wives and concubines;
within the midst of sexual misconduct, their minds do not wander, and they polish themselves until clarity arises. After the end of their lives, they will dwell near the sun and moon. Thus it is.
One class is named the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
this clarifies that it is the first heaven of the Desire Realm. Ānanda, above the realm of the immortals (*ṛṣi*), are there not what are called the various heavens?
These various heavens are none other than those who have all come from the human path through cultivation. All people of the world, by means of—
They do not seek supramundane liberation, but cultivate the fundamental principle of the mundane world. They merely hope for the fruits of worldly pleasure that eventually come to an end;
they do not rely on the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the basis for their cultivation, but instead take the ten wholesome actions as the basis for their cultivation.

Although such a person maintains the precept against sexual misconduct, they merely refrain from illicit sex while still engaging in "right" sexual conduct; they have not yet been able to renounce their wives and concubines.
Regarding affection and love, it is not their own physical beauty that causes them to flow outwardly or dissipate.

Not only does the body dare not transgress, but the mind likewise does not give rise to a single thought. Because desire is regulated and the will is largely withdrawn, the heart-mind is pure and unstained, its ground luminous.
Furthermore, by diligently cultivating the ten wholesome actions, after the end of life, one casts off the fleshly body and receives birth in heaven.

As for the body [of these gods] and the reward land (*vipākakṣetra*) where they dwell: it is located at the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, adjacent to the palaces of the sun and moon, and is named the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).

Because there are four kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Nation), Virūḍhaka (Increasing Growth), Virūpākṣa (Broad Eyes), and Vaiśravaṇa (Much Hearing)—each occupying one side of the mountain’s waist and each protecting one continent, it is called the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Regarding the term "heaven" (*deva*): it means "to rise to the summit" (*diān*), carrying the sense of emerging as the head above all other things.
There are three heavens, namely: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

As for the heavens of the desire realm, from the middle and summit of Mount Sumeru up to those dwelling in space, they all possess food and drink, sexual desire, and sleep; because they are fully endowed with these three desires, they are called the "desire heavens" (*kāmadeva*).
Their men and women marry and have wives and concubines just as humans do; however, among these devas, there are none who... [are not born spontaneously].

Their bodies are composed of bone and flesh, yet they are free from the impurities of excrement and urine. By retribution, they attain the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and their forms encounter no obstruction.

Thus, one knows that the celestial realm (*devagati*) is the most honored within the [five] destinies. The blessings of the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*) are all fundamentally brought about by the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).
Now, I shall distinguish them solely according to desire: these six are collectively termed the "Desire Heavens," and among them, sexual desire is the foremost.

First, regarding the gravity or lightness of sexual misconduct, the sequence of the lower and upper grades is distinguished. As for the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), they are the universal cause for the three realms;
this need not be further elaborated. The four characters "not seeking permanence" (*bùqiú chángzhù*) are likewise the universal cause for the three realms.
While the phrasing is restricted to this [section], their meaning extends to what follows. Those who fall from the human path into the hells and the three miserable states (*tridurgati*)...

This refers to the fact that the habit of lust is the foremost [obstacle]. For those in the human realm who ascend to become the various devas of the higher realms, the subduing of the habit of lust is foremost.
Furthermore, for those in the human realm who ascend to become sages and worthies, the severing of the habit of lust is foremost.
The harm caused by the habit of lust is no less than that of a vengeful thief or a venomous serpent. Be on guard! Be on guard!
Ah! Question: When the various devas undergo rebirth, how can this be superior to "longevity" (changsheng)? Answer: Longevity is like mending and washing old clothes;

in the end, it possesses no extraordinary excellence. Rebirth is like casting off tattered, filthy garments to exchange them for precious, elegant ones; the difference between superiority and inferiority is as vast as heaven and abyss.
It is especially because fools are habituated to attachment to the body and their base, inverted practices lead them to consider longevity as supreme.
Consequently, they have but a slight passion for their own wives; when dwelling in the Pure Abodes, they cannot experience full flavor, and after the end of their lives—
Surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon, they dwell at the summit of the human realm; such a class is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Even with one's own wife, one does not indulge excessively; lustful desire is slight. By refraining from sexual misconduct, one dwells in purity for much of the time.
Yet, when occasional thoughts of lust arise, one cannot attain the full flavor of that purity.
Compared to those mentioned previously, this is already twice as superior; after death, one likewise ascends by a factor of two, surpassing the realms of the Sun and Moon.
They dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; because they do not dwell in the air, they are still referred to as being among "humans.
This class is called the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa), and they are governed by Śakra Devendra.

These, together with the preceding heaven, are collectively termed "earth-dwelling" (bhūmi-vāsin), as they have not yet departed from the earth. However, these two heavens engage in sexual intercourse to form a union, no different from humans; it is only that—
Once the wind-energy is released, the desire to leak it ceases immediately; it is not like the human world where impurities flow and overflow.

these beings possess their own light. This class of beings is called the Suyāma Heaven.
This clarifies the third heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, there is a class of beings who do not give rise to lustful thoughts when they do not encounter objects of desire;
yet, upon encountering such objects, they engage in sexual union only once and thereafter feel no further longing.

Because they have already attained the full flavor of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and are gradually progressing toward the states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their movement is slight while their stillness is predominant; thus, they are twice as superior as those previously mentioned. amidst both movement and stillness, they are entirely devoid of lustful thoughts. Having already surpassed those with more stillness than movement, they are twice as superior.

Yet, when encountering objects that are extremely pleasing to the mind, they inevitably respond to the contact; though it comes upon them by force, they are unable to remain without a mind and refuse the stimulus. It is like...

This is called the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita). According to this [text], this heaven consists of an inner court and an outer court, totaling fifty tiers.
Each tier contains five hundred *koṭi* celestial palaces; there are forty-nine within the inner court and one in the outer court.

The Bodhisattva Maitreya dwells within the Great Maṇi Palace at its center. Beyond the two courtyards, there is furthermore the Heaven of Karmic Retribution (*karmavipāka*), which is produced by the fruits of tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*).
This is the Heaven of Aggregate Retribution (*saṃbhāra-vipāka-deva*). Those who practice the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) attain birth in that place.
Because it is tainted, it can be destroyed by the three calamities (*trividha-vyasanāni*). Although these [two heavens] are of the same general category, they are distinct.

However, when comparing the collective retribution [of this heaven] to the Outer Court, it is already like the distance between a celestial immortal and an ordinary mortal; how much more so for the Inner Court!

That what is now produced is outside the Outer Court, yet is described in general terms as "subtle and refined," suggests that the translator was overly concise and lacked sufficient detail in his analysis.
Otherwise, how could this heaven be so fortunate as to attain [such a state] through minor desires and inferior merit? And yet, suddenly—

They are born in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*). Such a class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations;

this is the fifth heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Whereas those in the previous [heaven] still possess a mind that responds to stimuli, these beings have no such responding mind when the objects of stimulation are presented before them.

Its flavor is like chewing wax; this is twice as superior as the former. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations.
In this heaven, laughter serves as sexual desire, and they delight in the emanations produced by themselves. [The text continues with: "Lying side by side."
As Sima Xiangru’s "Fu on the Love of Beauty" says: "The exquisite countenance offers itself; the jade-like body lies prostrate. And as the ancient poem says:
"A single turn of the head makes a hundred thousand lie prostrate. Both express this same meaning.
They possess no worldly mind, yet they engage in worldly affairs; amidst the interactions of daily activities, they clearly transcend them.

After their lives end, they are universally able to transcend both the realms of transformation and non-transformation. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
This is the sixth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, there are those whose minds aspire to the higher realms and who take no pleasure in the mundane world;

yet they merely conform to worldly conventions by taking a wife. When it comes to the time of sexual union, not only is it devoid of flavor, but their spirits wander to external realms, having no involvement whatsoever.
This is twice as superior as the former state; therefore, after death, they are universally able to transcend [the realm].

The fifth is the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*). Unlike the four lower heavens, which lack the power of transformation, this class of beings is named the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations because they regard mutual gazing as sexual desire;
they do not labor to transform objects themselves, but rather enjoy them with sovereign ease through what is transformed by others.
Ānanda, in these six heavens, although their forms move about, the traces of their minds still intermingle. From this point downward, it is called the Realm of Desire.
This is a summary of the six heavens. Ānanda, worldly people are driven by desire like a torrential flood or a runaway fire.
An intoxicated elephant or a mad monkey leaping and charging cannot be controlled; yet these gods of the six heavens of desire gradually exercise restraint over their minds and turn toward stillness.
Just as in the first heaven external movement ceases, in the second heaven internal movement also diminishes.

In the first three heavens, movement occurs only when encountering external objects; in the fourth heaven, one does not resist even when pressed by objects; in the fifth heaven, there is no flavor during the union;
and in the sixth heaven, although the forms unite, the mind transcends them, yet all are capable of such movement. Nevertheless, though the forms move, the traces of the mind still intermingle.

This is because in the first four heavens, the mental intermingling is still present due to the presence of flavor (*rasa*); whereas in the latter two heavens, it is merely a matter of the physical traces intermingling, as there is none [of that flavor].

Because they possess [sensual] flavor, all realms from this heaven downward are collectively named the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), as they share the same three objects of desire and are fully endowed with male and female characteristics.

Now, sexual desire is the very root of falling into bondage. While the six heavens of the Desire Realm ascend gradually through their relative lightness, the four *dhyānas* rise loftily by severing [desire].
Thus, if one does not abandon the mind of desire, even the higher realms cannot be hoped for; how much less can one aspire to [liberation]?
To transcend the triple world, one must cultivate *samādhi*. This is why Ānanda was necessarily prompted to give this teaching.

Tiantai says: Beyond the ten wholesome actions, the first three heavens each combine meritorious conduct with practice, while the latter three heavens each combine meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) with practice.
It is not merely that one should lightly regard sensual desire; those who seek rebirth in the heavens must know this.

The Śramaṇa Fang of Chengdu Zhaojue Temple identifies and examines Ānanda:
Among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, there are some who do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and possess no wisdom;
yet they are merely able to restrain their bodies from practicing sexual desire. Whether walking or sitting, they have no discursive thoughts, no passions arise, and they leave nothing behind.
In the desire realm, such a person should reflect: "My body is a companion to Brahmā; I am of this same class. This is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmapārṣadya*).
Below this, the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas of the form realm are explained; here, first, the first heaven of the first dhyāna is clarified.
Ānanda, among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, those who are deluded and practice in darkness each individually claim:
This is the true cultivation of the mind. However, it does not rely upon *dhyāna*; there is no *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, no wisdom, and no vajra-wisdom.
Rather, taking impure meditative concentration as the causal mind, one restrains that habit of lust and maintains physical celibacy.
Whether walking or sitting, at all times, all mental conceptions are absent, and no defiled attachment arises.

Now, even if one’s six desires are unrestrained and one forgets all worldly emotions, one cannot avoid committing physical transgressions. Only when this body is entirely distanced from such faults can the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) be perfected.

Because both body and mind are thus purified, there is no need for further seeking a dwelling place below; therefore, at the time of death, one is reborn in the Brahma-world by virtue of mindfulness, becoming a follower of Brahmā.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmapārisadya*). Compared to the defilements and turbidity of the Desire Realm, they are vastly superior.
Furthermore, they rise one level higher. Encompassing the subsequent eighteen heavens, although they are free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material form;

therefore, they are collectively termed the "Form Realm" (*rūpadhātu*). They are also collectively termed the "Brahma-world," signifying that they have already abandoned the defilement of desire. They are collectively designated as the "Four Dhyānas," signifying that they have already abandoned agitation and movement.
While the heavens of the Desire Realm are produced solely by the influence of the ten wholesome actions, these heavens are produced by both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and those actions.
It certainly brings about rebirth. However, this specifically refers to the six modes of practice of impure *dhyāna* meditation.
As for these six modes of practice: one feels aversion toward the desire realm as being suffering, coarse, and obstructive; and one takes delight in the form realm as being pure, sublime, and free.

This is the path by which ordinary beings suppress their afflictions and transcend the desire realm. Question: The heavens above also occasionally possess meditative concentration (*samādhi*); why is it that only this realm [is discussed here]?
Why is it called "dhyāna"? The answer is: as stated previously, although the body may move outward, the traces of the mind still remain intertwined.
From this stage upward, there is absolutely no contact with women; both body and mind are detached, with nothing further to be joined. Furthermore, there is neither eating nor sleeping.

The three desires were simultaneously forgotten. Gradually feeling hunger and fatigue, he immediately entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Upon emerging from concentration, he was satiated and his spirit was refined and lucid.
This is simply because he took the joy of meditation as his food and rest, thereby gradually departing from the coarse and heavy body and mind.

Furthermore, this heaven uniquely manifests the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*), while concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have not yet been revealed. The latter two heavens briefly manifest concentration and wisdom, as will be explained in the text.
This is self-perception.
Once the habit-energies of desire have been eliminated, the mind free from desire manifests; one takes pleasure in and accords with all forms of discipline.
Such a person is able to practice brahmic virtue at the appropriate time. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita).
This clarifies that in the second heaven of the first dhyāna, the precepts of this heaven are conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Although the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated in the preceding heavens, the mental characteristics have not yet reached manifestation. Here, however, being free from desire and pure, the mental characteristics emerge and manifest with clarity.
Regarding the categories of precepts for the various Brahma-conducts, one feels love and joy, and experiences pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) through compliance. This is precisely...
This is the characteristic shared with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When such a person approaches the end of life, their long-standing habitual practice does not falter;
they act in accordance with their mindfulness and manifest Brahma-virtue. Not only do they purify body and mind, but they also propagate virtuous transformation.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*), and they are able to assist and support the King of Brahmā.

With body and mind wondrously perfected, their majestic deportment flawless, and their pure prohibitive precepts augmented by clear awakening, such persons are timely able to preside over the Brahma hosts as Great Brahma Kings. This class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven.
This clarifies that this is the third heaven of the first dhyāna; in this heaven, precept and wisdom coexist.
Now, in the first heaven, one restrains the mind by means of grasping the body; in the next heaven, one manifests virtue through the mind.

This, however, is the marvelous state where body and mind are simultaneously integrated as one and non-dual, fulfilling the perfection of their respective measures. Thus, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, [all actions are unified].

It is wondrously perfect, yet his dignified deportment remains flawless. By means of these pure prohibitions and precepts, and further augmented by clear awakening, wisdom is generated from within meditative discipline;
this is the characteristic of being conjoined with wisdom. Because his wisdom surpasses that of the previous [heaven], he is fit to be the Lord of Brahma.
When such a person approaches the end of life, they will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven by virtue of their mindfulness, presiding over it.
The Brahma-multitude serves as the Great Brahma King; such is this class who constitute the Great Brahma Heaven. Their virtues are all sufficient to lead others.
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction, even though they do not yet possess the true, correct cultivation of the Three [Vows].
Samādhi. Within the pure mind, the various outflows (*āsrava*) do not move; this is called the First Dhyāna.

This collectively summarizes the three heavens and names them the First Dhyāna. Ānanda, these three heavens all surpass the various realms of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are likewise termed "superior flows.
Having already departed from the eight sufferings of the Desire Realm, they are not oppressed by affliction and distress. Although they are not...
Although this is the correct cultivation of true samādhi, it remains very far from the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama.
Nevertheless, because his mind of precepts is pure, even though the outflows have not yet been subdued, they are nonetheless suppressed and remain unmoving.

Having first attained meditative concentration, there is not a single moment of intermingling with discursive thoughts; therefore, it is collectively termed "the First Dhyāna. There are four categories of dhyāna. The first is...

1. Contemplation with outflows (*sāsrava-dhyāna*): this refers to the present four *dhyānas*. 2. Contemplation without outflows (*anāsrava-dhyāna*): this refers to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), and so forth.

3. Contemplation that is both with and without outflows (*sāsravānāsrava-dhyāna*): this refers to the six marvelous supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the clarities (*vidyā*). 4. Contemplation that is neither with nor without outflows (*naiva-sāsrava-naivānāsrava-dhyāna*):
this is the present Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama at the beginning of this sutra. The above three types of heavens are suspected of being incorrect.
Vertically divided: Now, if the celestial subjects, the celestial ministers, and the celestial sovereign each occupy a separate layer, how can there be a unified system?
Furthermore, if subjects and ministers are permitted to be so numerous while the celestial sovereign occupies only a single layer, filling the heavens, then everyone would be a sovereign;
who then could issue commands? Perhaps they are distinguished by the superiority or inferiority of their virtue, such that some serve as subjects, some as assistants, and some as sovereigns.

Therefore, they are enumerated as three. It is not the case that one heaven possesses all subjects and ministers while lacking a king, nor that one heaven possesses a king while lacking subjects and ministers.
Furthermore, in the first two heavens, both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are present; in the third heaven, there is no vitarka but only vicāra.
Because of the presence of vitarka and vicāra within, external fire calamities are induced, and thus the fire calamity destroys the First Dhyāna.
Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmā-puruṣas and perfects the Brahma-conduct. With a tranquil mind unmoving, from profound stillness light is produced.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā).
This is the first heaven of the second dhyāna. Ānanda, as for the next [heaven] of the second dhyāna, it is this Great Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmā-puruṣas.
Being able to fulfill the brahma-conduct (brahmacarya) until the mind is tranquil and unmoving, one reaches the ultimate state of stillness and clarity, whereby light arises.
However, this light is still inferior and has not reached its full measure. Such is one class of beings. Furthermore—
Ascending one level from the Brahma-heaven, it is called the Heaven of Limited Radiance (Parīttābha). This means that as the vast expanse of the universe becomes tranquil, celestial light is emitted;
however, it does not yet compare to the all-pervading, profound stillness [of higher realms]. This heaven is likely attained by cultivating further from within that previous heaven.
That is to say, by building upon prior practice and merely adding fullness, one ascends to this heaven. Question: How does this differ from the *śamatha* (calm abiding) of a Bodhisattva?

Question: What is the distinction in their illumination? Answer: Regarding the two attachments to self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*), not even a hair’s breadth has been moved. The distinction lies simply in this: by abandoning desire, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*); as the concentration deepens, illumination arises.
Furthermore, previously there was the coarse movement of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), which gave rise to the three consciousnesses;
now, with internal purity and single-mindedness, applied and sustained thought are absent, and one merely takes internal objects as its condition. This is how it differs from the First Dhyāna.
This is the third consciousness.
Light illuminates light in mutual resonance, shining forth without end. It reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, universally transforming them into lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light.
This is the second heaven of the Second Dhyāna. From the previous Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābhā*), they emit even more light;

light upon light ignites one another, shining forth inexhaustibly and illuminating the worlds of the ten directions until they take on the color of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*). Although this has reached its ultimate extent, it has not yet produced sound.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Infinite Light (*Apramāṇābhā*). However, it is not like the interior of pure lapis lazuli.
This contains a comparison to the Jewel Moon. According to this, although this heaven cannot outshine the entire great trichiliocosm, within its own realm it also covers a small chiliocosm;
that is, when one thousand sets of four continents throughout the ten directions are fully encompassed.

They inhale and sustain the circular radiance, accomplish the essence of the teachings, give rise to pure transformation, and apply themselves inexhaustibly. This class of beings is called the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Heaven of Luminous Sound).
This is the third heaven of the Second Dhyāna. Now, when light illuminates light, it forms a circular halo (*maṇḍala*).
By thus absorbing and maintaining this circular halo, one employs radiance in place of vocal sound to accomplish the substance of the teaching.
Thereby, one propagates the Brahma-teachings and initiates pure transformation, providing instruction according to the capacities of beings with inexhaustible application.
This class of beings is called the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven). This means that they do not rely on verbal expression, but take light as their "sound.
According to this, these devas have already transcended vitarka and vicāra (applied and sustained thought), and thus possess no speech; they perform the work of a Buddha solely by means of radiance.
Nevertheless, it is not that they are entirely without speech. For example, although worldly paper, ink, and written characters serve as [substitutes for]...
In teaching, how could one ever completely discard the use of speech?
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be assailed by any anxieties or hangings (where "hanging" means being unsettled; it may be a scribal error for the character for "sorrow").
Although they have not yet attained the true, correct Samādhi of the ultimate reality, within their pure minds, gross outflows have already been subdued; this is called the Second Dhyāna.

This summarizes that the names of these three heavens constitute the Second Dhyāna. Ānanda, when these three superior streams arise from meditative concentration, they emerge together with joy (*prīti*).
Because there is the joy of concentration, worldly sorrow and anxiety are extinguished; therefore, distress cannot oppress them.

Although this is not yet the formal cultivation of *samādhi* and remains far from the Great *Samādhi* of the *Śūraṅgama*, nevertheless, within the pure mind, the coarse outflows (*āsrava*) have already been suppressed.
Compared to the state of the first dhyāna, where the outflows remain and the mind cannot be made immovable, this represents a step forward;
therefore, it is collectively designated as the second dhyāna. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* identifies this as the second dhyāna.
This is called the dhyāna accompanied by joy (*prīti-sahagata-dhyāna*). These three heavens are collectively named the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Concentration (*samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*).

Anxiety (*daurmanasya*) is distinct from affliction (*duḥkha*). Affliction is coarse and heavy, pressing upon both body and mind; anxiety is subtle and light, involving only the sphere of thought and deliberation.

"The coarse outflows have already been suppressed" means that through the power of concentration, the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) have been suppressed. Because they have been suppressed...
5. Therefore, there is no vitarka or vicāra. Because the sixth consciousness has not yet been subdued, there is joy and bliss.
Since the internal waters of joy cause agitation, external water disasters arise; thus, the second dhyāna is destroyed by water. In the first three heavens, precepts are predominant;
in these [next] three heavens, meditative concentration is predominant.

Ānanda, when such devas and humans have perfected their radiant light into sound, and having uncovered the subtle through that sound, they give rise to refined practice and penetrate the bliss of cessation—
this class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parittasubha).

This is the first heaven of the third dhyāna, Ānanda. Since the celestial beings of the previous [heaven] took the radiant light as the substance of their teaching, "disclosing the light" (pī-kōng) is equivalent to "disclosing the sound" (pī-yīn). When the sound is disclosed, the wondrous principle reveals itself spontaneously.

However, there is still a mind of joy that is discursive and agitated, which can obstruct the bliss of meditative concentration. The beings of this heaven are able to rely upon this wondrous principle to develop and perfect their refinement.
They practice and penetrate the bliss of quiescence (*śānti*). Departing from the prior agitation of joy, they give rise to pure bliss that is tranquil and serene;

thus it is called "quiescence. Because the sixth consciousness is suppressed, this is a quiescence similar to that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), but it is not comparable to the manifestation of quiescence where both arising and ceasing have been extinguished.
This class of beings is named the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Paritta-śubhā devāḥ*). It is the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As soon as it becomes permeable and pure space first manifests, it is therefore called "Limited Purity" (Parīttaśubha). It is merely able to permeate and has not yet reached full accomplishment;
because it is still inferior, it is named Limited Purity.
Pure emptiness manifests before them, giving rise to boundlessness; body and mind become light and serene, achieving the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the gods of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha).
This is the second heaven of the third dhyāna. Because the six consciousnesses are suppressed, one appears to attain the emptiness of persons; thus, pure emptiness manifests before them.
While the previous stage merely attained purity, this stage further gives rise to emptiness, gradually becoming increasingly vast and expansive until it reaches the infinite.

Furthermore, while the former was characterized by pervasive stillness and focused solely on inner bliss, this stage attains pliancy throughout the body and mind, both internally and externally. Accumulated...
When that which was within is emitted outward and becomes vast and expansive, then quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) is already accomplished; it is pure emptiness, immeasurable.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha), and they ascend one level higher than the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha).

The body and mind of this world are entirely perfect and pure; having accomplished the virtues of purity, the supreme reliance manifests before them, and they return to the bliss of quiescent extinction.
This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven (the Heaven of Universal Purity).
This is the third heaven of the third dhyāna. In the preceding heavens, purity and bliss reside only within body and mind and have not yet been termed "pervasive.
Here, however, the world, body, and mind are unified; every point of contact is nothing but sublime bliss. This is called "universal and perfect purity."

Since the world, body, and mind are now perfectly pure, is this not the accomplishment of pure virtue? Nevertheless, although pure virtue has been accomplished, it is fundamentally not a place where one can entrust oneself or take refuge.
Yet these devas and humans immediately recognize this as the place where they shall entrust themselves for the rest of their lives;
with such a sublime entrustment manifest before them, they recognize this as the land of pure and ultimate bliss, and thus return to it.
Regarding the bliss of quiescent extinction, they consider this alone sufficient for establishing their bodies and sustaining their lives.

However, because the world previously failed to integrate, although it was pure, it was not all-pervasive. Now, having integrated it entirely, this class of beings is named the Śubhakṛtsna (All-Pervasive Purity) Heaven;
they have ascended one further level to the Apramāṇaśubha (Immeasurable Purity) Heaven.
Ānanda, these three superior types of practitioners possess great compliance; their bodies and minds are peaceful and secure, and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although they have not yet truly attained the genuine *samādhi*, within their peaceful and secure minds, they are fully endowed with joy; this is called the third dhyāna.
This summarizes the three heavens as the Third Dhyāna. Ānanda, these three superior streams accord with pure bliss and extend to immeasurable pervasiveness;

their accordance is truly great. Furthermore, in the first and second dhyānas, the mind possesses the sensation of joy (*prīti*), and thus there is much distraction and movement, preventing one from personally experiencing bliss with the body. Now, since the sensation of joy has been eliminated, the body and mind—

One dwells in peace and security, enjoying immeasurable and wondrous bliss. Although this is not yet the actual attainment of true *samādhi*, within this state of peace and security, joy is fully present.
Now, joy (*prīti*) is that which arises when the mind is active; bliss (*sukha*) is that which is integrated when the mind is tranquil.
If one were in a state of flighty or agitated mind, even if there were bliss, it would still merely be a factor of joy.
If one were in a state of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), even though there is joy (*prīti*), it would still be a factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*). Now, this joy emerges from tranquility;
therefore, it is called "joy apart from joy" and "bliss of wondrous bliss. Because it is joy apart from joy and the bliss of wondrous bliss, it is collectively designated as the Third Dhyāna.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Dichilun) identifies the Third Dhyāna as the "Dhyāna Conjoined with Bliss" (*sukhasahagata-dhyāna*). This...
These three heavens are collectively named the Stage of Sublime Bliss Free from Joy (*nirābhirati-sukha-bhūmi*).

Although the first two dhyānas possess the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*), they are obstructed by the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*); now, with joy extinguished and pure bliss remaining, they receive this name.

Furthermore, although these three heavens have already suppressed the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and thus lack the sensation of joy, they still possess the disturbance of inhalation and exhalation; consequently, they are externally affected by the calamity of wind.
The wind disaster destroys the third dhyāna.

Ānanda, furthermore, when gods and humans are no longer oppressed in body or mind, the causes of suffering have already been exhausted. Yet pleasure is not permanent; after a long time, it must inevitably give rise to destruction.
At that moment, the two mental states of suffering and pleasure are both suddenly abandoned; coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises. Thus it is.
The first class is named the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*).

This section below clarifies the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna, and this [heaven] is the first among them. Although there are nine heavens, within the retributive realms (*vipākagocara*) of the fourth dhyāna there are only three heavens;
the fourth, the Heaven of Non-Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), is a separate opening from the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven. This is so because...

The non-Buddhists report on the realms: beyond these four [heavens] are the five heavens of the Non-returners (anāgāmin), where noble sages cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a manner distinct from that of ordinary worldlings.
Ānanda, furthermore, the devas of the third dhyāna have already abandoned the afflictions of the initial painful dhyāna.
In the second dhyāna, sorrow and anxiety are exhausted; thus, neither can they oppress the body or mind.
Since the causes of suffering have already been eliminated, in the third dhyāna there is no suffering, only bliss. Yet even this bliss should not be accepted, for bliss is not permanent;
after a time it must inevitably decay, and once it decays, it becomes suffering. Having already departed from suffering, these devas likewise do not accept bliss. About to...
The two minds of suffering and pleasure are simultaneously and instantaneously relinquished. Since pleasure is no longer accepted, its destruction does not arise;

since suffering is transcended along with its destruction, the characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are extinguished. All calamities and afflictions of the lower stages are severed, and the nature of pure merit [remains].

They arise spontaneously; because they produce merit through renunciation, they are called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava). If one can see but cannot renounce pleasure, then birth will be destroyed.
If one can indeed renounce pleasure, then merit is produced. The distinction between this heaven and the preceding ones lies precisely in the interval between renouncing and not renouncing.
With a mind of equanimity perfectly integrated and resolute understanding purified, they attain wondrous compliance within unobstructed merit.
Reaching to the end of the future, this class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Love (Puṇyaprasava).
This is the second heaven of the fourth dhyāna. In the preceding [heaven], one was initially focused exclusively on equanimity (*upekṣā*), yet had not yet escaped partiality toward emptiness.

Now that this state has become fully matured, it gradually ceases to obstruct existence; this is called the perfect integration of the mind of equanimity. Previously, one took the abandonment of pleasure as purity.
Thus, since pleasant sensation is already empty and yet does not obstruct existence, this is called the purification of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Because superior purity gives rise to superior merit, there is no limit to that merit. Whatever one aspires to or seeks will not be contrary to one's intent;

one attains wondrous accordance and proceeds directly to the very end of the future. Although the experience of retribution is thus inexhaustible, it is nonetheless not the attainment of true permanence.
They dwell there. This class of beings is called the Puṇyaprasavā devas; that is to say, among all the devas, the merit of these devas alone is most beloved.
Ānanda, from this celestial realm, there are two diverging paths.
This clarifies that while one is in the third heaven of the four dhyānas, there are first of all two distinct paths. Ānanda, from this Heaven of Merit-Love (Puṇyaprasava), one ascends;
there are two diverging paths: one proceeds directly toward the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), and the other takes a circuitous route toward the Unconscious (Asaṃjñin).
Since the mental intentions and karmic actions of practitioners differ from one another, those who study must distinguish between them.
Yes. ○ He said: "The two divergent paths are, first, diligence and, second, annihilationism. One neither grasps at suffering or pleasure, nor does one loathe suffering or pleasure;
rather, by means of the four immeasurable minds, one cultivates merit and realizes the vast fruit."

This is called the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*). If one regards suffering and pleasure as things to be loathed, yet clings to a mind of equanimity, refining it without ceasing—such that the minds of suffering and pleasure are extinguished and a mind of loathing and renunciation arises—this is entirely the cause of birth and extinction.
From this point, having exhausted the path of equanimity, one attains the fruit of the "ashen heart" (*huīxīn*). That person considers themselves to be neither born nor extinguished.
How could one fail to realize that the cause of arising and ceasing can never manifest the nature that is free from arising and ceasing?
When first born into this heaven, they are not yet entirely without thought; it is only after half an eon (*kalpa*) that thought ceases, and after the other half of the eon, it arises once more.

If one dwells in the cultivation and realization of the immeasurable pure light of the preceding mind, wherein merit is perfectly luminous—such a class is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).
What are the two branches? First, if within the Heaven of Merit and Love (Puṇyaprasava), one develops a mind of equanimity that is perfectly integrated, from which [the following] is emitted:

The Measure of Pure Light (*Prabhāsvara*). Within this light, one cultivates only the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), thereby increasing and nourishing merit and virtue until they reach a state of fullness, brilliance, and perfection.
Through diligent cultivation and realization, one attains what is taken as the permanent abode. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*).
For when merit and virtue are perfected and radiant, the fruit of realization is vast; such is the meritorious retribution experienced by the various devas of the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).

This is the ultimate limit; therefore, it is named "Vipulaphala" (Extensive Fruit). One must understand that among the realms resulting from the retribution of the Fourth Dhyāna, there are only these three heavens.

The fourth, the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), is a distinction within the category of those who cherish merit, while the five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are merely different abodes for the noble ones who have attained the third fruit.

If, regarding the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one simultaneously feels aversion toward both suffering and pleasure, refining the mind of equanimity until it flows in an uninterrupted succession and fully masters the path of equanimity, then body and mind both cease;
the mental faculties become ashen and congealed, remaining so for five hundred kalpas. Because this person takes arising and ceasing as their cause, they [attain this state].
They are unable to give rise to the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. They cease during the first half-aeon and arise during the latter half-aeon;

such a class is called the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). Second, if within the Heaven of Merit-Love (*puṇyaprasava*), one abandons the mind that seeks pleasure and, being weary of both suffering and pleasure, applies oneself with diligence...
He investigates it with intensity, searching deeply and scrutinizing minutely, continuing without interruption and exerting diligent effort without ceasing.

He thoroughly masters the path of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and resolutely seeks its ultimate consummation. Not only does he relinquish pleasant sensations, but he also relinquishes the very mind that seeks equanimity;

by means of the meditative absorption of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*), he extinguishes the mind of equanimity itself. This continues until body and mind are reduced to ashes, becoming entirely obscured and darkened, merging into a single, profound stillness.
"Empty. It is like what is called withered wood or dead ashes. Its lifespan spans five hundred great kalpas;
though such is its length, one does not know that what is called "congealed ash" is not truly subject to birth and extinction.
Like a fish trapped in ice, or grass crushed by a stone—the subtle flow of arising and ceasing has never once ceased. This is indeed the person..."
Originally taking birth and extinction as the cause, you mistakenly relied upon the six consciousnesses—the very root of birth and death—as the fundamental cause for your cultivation.

You have forcibly caused the ashes to solidify; how could you possibly recognize the essential source of the consciousness’s brilliant clarity and thereby give rise to the perfect, profound, and non-arising, non-extinguishing nature?
Therefore, upon first being born in this heaven, you practiced meditative concentration for half a kalpa before finally attaining the cessation of thought. This is the retribution of this heaven.
When [the lifespan] is exhausted, after four hundred and ninety-nine intermediate kalpas and a half have passed, the mind of ideation arises once more.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of No-Ideation (Asaṃjñisattva-deva). Together with the Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), these form two branches.

According to this, while those in the Heaven of Vast Fruit weary of suffering and pleasure and further cultivate merit and wisdom, those in this heaven weary of suffering and pleasure and instead refine the mind of equanimity (upekṣā-citta). These two—
This is why the heavens branch out. When paths are laid out horizontally, they likewise do not divide vertically. Question:

What is the difference between this state of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the state of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)? Answer: Since the state of cessation has already ceased the sixth consciousness, [it differs from the state of non-perception].
Furthermore, it extinguishes the seventh defiled portion. The Non-conceptualization [Heaven] merely extinguishes the discrimination and views of the six consciousnesses;

yet even these various false views have not been fully exhausted, let alone others. Question: When both the body and the realm are empty, how does this differ from the four lower formless attainments?
Answer: They exist upon emerging from meditative absorption; therefore, they are not the same. Furthermore, according to the three realms, there are twenty-eight heavens in total.

Two are exclusively the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), five are exclusively the level of noble ones (*ārya*), and the remainder are all places where ordinary beings and noble ones dwell together.

As for the two that are exclusively the level of ordinary beings, they refer to the Great Brahmā Heaven (*Mahābrahmā*). Because he falsely claims to be the creator of celestial objects and human beings, and because of his arrogance and contempt, the noble ones [do not dwell there].

The worthy do not dwell here; this is the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva-deva), where only those non-Buddhists who have cultivated the meditative attainment of non-thought (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) are born, receiving the retribution of five hundred kalpas of mindlessness. As for the "five noble stages," these refer to the five lower types of Anāgāmins.
Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly objects of suffering or pleasure.
Although they are not the unconditioned, truly immovable stage, because the mind that seeks attainment has reached maturity in its application, they are called the Four Dhyānas.
This summarizes the four heavens as the Four Dhyānas. Ānanda, these four superior streams collectively cultivate dual equanimity;
therefore, they cannot be moved by the two worldly objects of suffering and pleasure. Since they cannot be moved, can one hastily designate them as the "Immovable Ground" (Acalā-bhūmi)?
Now, the eighth stage of the sages realizes true unconditionedness (asaṃskṛta), and is thus named the "Immovable."
The shaking of the earth signifies that this is truly the stage of immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Although this heaven is not comparable to that stage, those who possess a mind that seeks attainment and employ conditioned effort have reached a state of pure maturity; therefore, it is collectively designated as the "Fourth Dhyāna.
Indeed, it is called the True Immovable Stage because it extinguishes the sixth consciousness and exhausts the seventh. As for those who possess a mind that seeks attainment...
This merely serves to subdue the six consciousnesses. Thus, the boundaries between the noble and the ordinary are clearly demarcated without confusion. Regarding the aforementioned dhyāna heavens:
in the first dhyāna, the two consciousnesses of smell and taste are subdued, as there is no solid food (*kavadīkāra-āhāra*) there. In the third dhyāna, the first five consciousnesses are subdued.
Because the third dhyāna subdues the active functioning of the discriminating manovijñāna, one attains wondrous bliss. In the fourth dhyāna, the discriminating manovijñāna is subdued.
Because it is the seed [of equanimity], one attains wondrous relinquishment (*upekṣā*); this in total merely suppresses the sixth consciousness’s delusions of conceptual views (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
Thus, when compared with the "immovability at forty" of Mencius and the "immovability regarding life and death" of Zhuangzi, they fall short of the immovability of the Dhyāna heavens.
