Since they have already been separated by the vast gulf between heaven and abyss, how much more so could one wish to surreptitiously imitate the Tathāgata’s true samādhi, the immovable essence?
○ The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* designates the four dhyānas as "dhyānas conjoined with equanimity" (*upekṣā-sahagata-dhyāna*).
Ānanda, herein there are further five types of non-returning devas. Within the lower realms, they simultaneously extinguish the nine grades of habitual tendencies;

with both suffering and pleasure forgotten, they have no dwelling place below. Therefore, they establish their abodes within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).
This clarifies the reason why the five types of non-returners (anāgāmin) reside within the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) heaven.
Ānanda, within this Vast Fruit heaven, there are furthermore five abodes for the non-returners who have attained the third fruit.
This is because these third-fruit Anāgāmins have already completely severed the nine grades of afflictions of thought (saṃyojana) belonging to the five destinies of the lower realms. Therefore...

Because suffering is forgotten, there is no provisional dwelling in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, as one proceeds to sever the nine grades of each of the three higher stages, pleasure is forgotten, and thus there is no provisional dwelling in the three stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Only the fourth dhyāna possesses the purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*); this constitutes its homogeneous class (*sabhāga*).
Therefore, it alone establishes a permanent residence therein. Having dwelt here, one severs the seventy-two grades of [defilements] that are most...
With subtle greed, anger, ignorance, and pride, one aspires to become an Arhat. ○ In Sanskrit, *anāgāmin*;
this is translated here as "Non-returner," meaning that one will no longer undergo rebirth in the desire realm. It is also called the Five Pure Abodes.

*Vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) refers to the seeds of the afflictions of thought (*vicikitsā-kleśa*). The afflictions of thought refer to greed, anger, ignorance, and pride—subtle afflictions that arise spontaneously. They are not...
These are the coarse afflictions within the same category of discrimination. Because they are difficult to eliminate, they are divided into eighty-one grades for abandonment.
Specifically, the three realms are divided into nine stages: the desire realm constitutes one stage, while the form realm’s four dhyānas are divided into four stages.
The four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) consist of four spheres (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.), each sphere being divided into nine grades. Thus, there are nine times nine, totaling eighty-one.
Since the five non-returner heavens (*anāgāmin*) possess degrees of superiority and inferiority, how could they not be arranged according to the shallowness or depth of their severance of delusions?
This implies that the first four heavens seem to correspond to the sequential severance of the delusions of the four spheres of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). However...
The five heavens are like those that sever the afflictions of the four stages of the formless realm. However, the reason why the five heavens differ from the four dhyānas is this:
the five heavens belong to the noble ones (ārya), whereas the four dhyānas belong to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana). Ordinary beings suppress their afflictions but cannot sever them;
the noble ones sever their afflictions rather than merely suppressing them. This is the basis for their distinction. In the five heavens, one severs the afflictions.
Although one gradually abandons the four stages, one’s provisional residence remains only in the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) of the fourth dhyāna.

This is because the dhyāna accompanied by equanimity shares the same category (*sabhāga*) exclusively with the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*), whereas the three dhyānas below it do not share this category.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because there are five distinct grades of mixed cultivation of dhyāna, one is born in five [places]."
Regarding the Śuddhāvāsa deities: "mixed cultivation" refers to practicing by alternating between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

"Dhyāna" (meditative concentration) refers to the state where samādhi and prajñā are in equilibrium. As for the "five grades"—inferior, middling, superior, superior-excellent, and supreme—since all five heavens proceed from the inferior toward the superior, it appears there would be no discrepancy in dividing them according to these grades.
Ānanda, when both suffering and pleasure have vanished and the warring minds no longer intersect—such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*).

This clarifies that it is the first of the five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Ānanda, when a person has not yet eliminated suffering and pleasure, they loathe suffering and delight in pleasure;
these battle within the breast. How could the mind not be at war? Now, when both suffering and pleasure have vanished, the war [ceases].
The mind does not engage [in conflict]; it enters into purity and coolness. What affliction or agitation could there be? This class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha).

According to the five grades, they should be placed in the lower grade; according to the severance of delusions, they should have severed the nine grades of afflictions of thought within the stage of the joy and bliss born of seclusion in the first dhyāna.
○ He says: "The fighting mind" refers to the mind where suffering and pleasure battle one another; it does not [refer to the name of the heaven].
This refers to the mind contending with its objects.
The trigger and the catch operate alone; there is no ground for their interaction. A class of beings such as this is called the Heaven of No Heat (*Atapa*).

This is the second of the non-returning (*anāgāmin*) heavens. When one releases through mindfulness, it is called the "trigger" (*ji*); when one withdraws through mindfulness, it is called the "catch" (*kuo*).
This deity possesses only equanimity and mindfulness. Whether releasing and arising or withdrawing and ceasing, no other thoughts intermingle therein;
this is called the "single operation of the mechanism. Although previously the fighting mind did not engage, there was still a ground for engagement;
now, even that ground of engagement has been thoroughly refined away. Thus, the mind is like a crystal pitcher—cool, clear, and penetrating. What heat could there be?
There is. Such a class is called the Heaven of No Heat (*Atapa*). According to the five grades, it should be placed among the middle grades.
According to the severing of delusions, one should have severed the nine grades of afflictions of thought within the stage of the joy and bliss born of the second dhyāna.
○ Internally there is no mind capable of engaging [in passion], yet one still perceives externally that there is ground for engagement. When the mechanism functions alone, then one proceeds.

They come from nowhere; one investigates the locus where they meet, yet it is utterly unfindable. As for these two kinds of heavens, since the subtle dust upon which they depend is not being perceived, the faculties have nothing with which to pair.

In the worlds of the ten directions, their wondrous vision is perfectly clear and serene, with no further traces of dust or phenomena; all heavy defilements having been thus purified, this class of beings is named the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa).

This is the third stage of the Non-returner (Anāgāmin). Once the feverish distress has been eliminated, the inner mind becomes clear and translucent, giving rise to the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus).

Its range of vision pervades the worlds of the ten directions; everything encountered is wondrous. Because this sublime vision is perfectly clear and tranquil, one externally contemplates the objective realm.
There are no further obstructions; this is the sign of being free from dust. Internally observing the mind, there is no further stagnation; this is the absence of sedimentary defilement.
When both mind and objects are extinguished, all that is perceived is wholesome. This class of beings is called the Sudarśana Heaven (Heaven of Good Vision).

According to the five grades, it should belong to the superior grade. According to the severance of delusions, one should sever the nine grades of afflictions of volition within the stage of "sublime bliss free from joy" of the third dhyāna.
○ "Dusty images" refers to objective realms; "sinking defilements" refers to afflictions.
Reaching this point, the lands of the ten directions appear as faint traces, yet they are brilliantly pure.
With refined vision manifest before one, all things are forged without obstruction. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Good Manifestation (Sudṛśa).

This is the fourth heaven of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*). In the previous heavens, while the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) was perfected, its functional application had not yet reached supremacy.
In this heaven, that which was previously a subtle manifestation now appears before one; it is what is pervaded by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), accomplished according to the mind.
It is as if I alone were the smith tempering and forging [all things] without obstruction, just like Maheśvara, who creates and transforms according to his will. I.

All things are distinct, yet they differ specifically in their grasping for power and their deluded presiding over others. Such a class [of beings] clearly possesses the function of manifesting transformations;

they are named the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven (Good Manifestation Heaven). According to the five grades, they belong to the "Superior" grade; according to the severance of afflictions, [they are at this stage].
One should sever the nine grades of afflictions of volition within the stage of "pure equanimity and mindfulness" of the fourth dhyāna.

According to this, this heaven shares the same sphere as the fourth dhyāna; therefore, it is combined with the three preceding heavens and the subsequent one heaven to establish its residence in the Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit) realm.
As for "unimpeded forging," it means that by smelting and refining all afflictions, they do not act as obstructions, and one is able to give rise to the fourteen [unhindered powers].
Mastery over transformations is like a potter molding clay or a smith casting vessels; they change according to the mind.
Reaching this stage, one may vaguely say that all manifestations do not constitute afflictions (*kleśa*).

The reason this differs from the former [stage] is that while in the former both the grasping at self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, here one has not yet attained the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*). The old commentary, by—
To mold and cast all things as the creative transformation of the universe—this is not something known to Śakra-devānām-indra; it is not the business of ordinary beings.

To exhaustively investigate the myriad capacities of sentient beings, to penetrate to the ultimate nature of form and its essence, and to enter into the boundless—this kind of state is called Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate of Form).

"O Deva, this is the fifth heaven of the Non-returners (Anāgāmin). Now, the previous heavens were called 'Exquisite Vision' (Sudarśana) and 'Sublime Vision' (Sudṛśa); in these, vision still possessed form.
This [heaven], however, exhausts form until it reaches the subtlest limit. Moreover, it does not merely exhaust form; furthermore—"

One is able to exhaustively investigate the nature of the nature of form (*rūpa*). From what source does it arise? Then one knows that the nature of form is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the nature of emptiness is true form.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, it enters into the boundless.

By investigating in this manner, one finally knows the ultimate limit of form; thus it is named the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*). According to the five grades, it corresponds to the highest grade.
In accordance with the severing of delusions, one should sever the thirty-six grades of afflictions of thought within the four stages of the formless realm.
Ānanda, as for these heavens of the Non-returners, the various Heavenly Kings of the four levels of the fourth dhyāna merely hear of them with admiration, yet they are unable to know or see them.
It is like the vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the sacred path in this world today, which are all inhabited by Arhats.
Because they maintain [this state], they cannot be seen by the coarse people of the world.
This teaching demonstrates that these five heavens are the abodes of the noble ones (*ārya*) alone.

Ānanda, as for these five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), only those noble ones who have attained the third fruit are able to be born there and dwell therein. Although they do not depart from the single heaven of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*), those various...
The fourth dhyāna consists of the four celestial kings of the respective stages; even they merely revere the hearing of its name, yet do not know its location nor see its form.

If this is so for the celestial kings, how much more so for the devas and humans? The reason for this is that those who practice the fourth dhyāna cultivate the mundane, out-flowing concentrations (*sāsrava-vitarka*), whereas those of the five heavens cultivate the supramundane, non-out-flowing noble concentrations (*anāsrava-ārya-samādhi*). There is a vast difference between the coarseness and subtlety of these two in terms of severing delusions versus suppressing them.
Therefore, we merely revere their illustrious names, yet we do not know how they enjoy [their sustenance], nor do we see their primary and secondary environments (*āśraya* and *sambhoga*).
This ignorance and lack of vision is comparable to our present world, where vast wildernesses and deep mountains— such as the bamboo groves of Tiantai,
Mount Emei, and Mount Wutai— are all sites of the holy path, and in each of them there dwell Arhats.

"Abbot, it is simply that worldly, coarse people cannot see for themselves. What difference is there between the Five Indias residing within the Vast Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*) and the Dharma-hall residing within the mundane world?
If one examines the Five Indias closely, one will find that they have never been divided into five distinct layers."
It seems they merely reside in the Single Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), just as the Sages dwell among humans; one hears of them but does not see them.
If they were divided vertically into five levels, they would be so far apart from top to bottom that it would naturally be impossible to see them—so why even mention this?
Moreover, the Buddha initially spoke only of "within this," and did not yet speak of "above this"; this is especially worthy of proof. Formerly, Yunju Ying established [the monastery].
Mao Sanfeng did not attend the hall for ten days. Dongshan asked him, "Why have you not been attending the hall lately?
Mao replied, "Every day a celestial being brings me offerings. Dongshan said, "I thought you were a man of substance; it turns out you still hold such views as these.
When Yang arrived late that evening, Dongshan called out to him, "Do not think of good; do not think of evil."
"What is this? Yingshou returned to his hermitage and sat in tranquil meditation. The devas and humans searched for him, but after three days they could not find him, and so they ceased their search.
The fact that the Four Heavenly Kings did not see Wutian is just like the devas and humans not seeing Yunju.

Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it states that from the second dhyāna upward, there is no distinction between kings and ministers; the mention here of the "Four Kings" may be due to a respectful inference.
They are merely like kings in their preeminence.
Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without companions; they have not yet exhausted the burden of form. From here downward, it is called the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu).
This concludes the summary of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Ānanda, as for these eighteen heavens, they are all devoid of sensual desire;
therefore, they move alone without sexual union. Yet, because they still possess material form (*rūpa*), they have not yet exhausted the burden of the physical body.
From this Akaniṣṭha Heaven downward, reaching up to the Brahmakāyika Heaven, they are collectively designated as the Form Realm alone.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there are again two divergent paths.
If one develops wisdom through a mind of equanimity, and the light of that wisdom becomes perfectly penetrating, one then transcends the realm of dust and becomes an Arhat.
They enter the Bodhisattva vehicle; such a class is called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds.
This indicates that these noble ones stand out alone. Furthermore, Ānanda, from the aforementioned Ultimate Heaven (Akaniṣṭha), which dwells at the summit of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu)...
Therefore, it is called the Summit (*bhavāgra*). Because it is adjacent to the formless realm (*ārūpya*), it is called the limit of form (*rūpānta*).

From within this Summit, the limit of form, as one ascends further, there are two divergent paths. What are these two paths? They arise because those who have attained the three fruits differ in having either sharp or dull faculties;
for those with sharp faculties, if they give rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) while in a state of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), they contemplate...
When delusions are exhausted and the wisdom of emptiness is fulfilled, the light of prajñā becomes perfectly pervasive;

one may then transcend the formless realm, exit the triple world horizontally, and enter directly into the Bodhisattva vehicle. Such a class of practitioners is called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds."
This means turning back the mind that delights in the higher realms and loathes the lower ones, thereby emerging suddenly from the triple world;
and turning back the mind that abandons the Great and grasps the Small, thereby swiftly entering the Mahāyāna. Yet, how could such faculties be found in great abundance?

It is clear that those of dull faculties also transcend the three realms through the vertical progression by means of a mind of equanimity that delights in the higher and loathes the lower, thereby being born in the formless realm, gradually severing [defilements] and gradually realizing [the fruits].
This is also discussed in sequential order; thus, for convenience, it directly refers to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

In reality, however, both the *bṛhatphala* (Vast Fruit) of ordinary worldlings and the *asaṃjñi-samāpatti* (non-conceptual attainment) of non-Buddhists are both adjacent to the realm of emptiness (*ākāśānantya*).
Both may ascend to enter the Four Heavens. ○ He said: Regarding the two divergent paths, one is the realization that form is emptiness;
the other is the loathing of form to enter emptiness.
If one abides in a mind of equanimity, having accomplished the relinquishing of aversion, they perceive the body as an obstruction; by dissolving this obstruction, they enter into emptiness.
This class of practitioners is called the Sphere of Infinite Space.
The following clarifies the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), of which this is the first. All four heavens advance through cultivation based on the pervasive emptiness (*ākāśa*).

First, one detests form and relies on emptiness. Second, one detests emptiness and relies on consciousness (*vijñāna*). Third, the three—form, emptiness, and consciousness—are all extinguished, and one relies on the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatā*).
Fourth, relying on the nature of consciousness, one exhaustively investigates until extinction; yet, this does not attain true extinction. This is [the first heaven].
All these are superior wholesome fruits of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), yet they do not transcend saṃsāra nor constitute the path of the noble ones (*ārya-mārga*).
Speaking of the first heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one cannot find there a Great Arhat.

If, prior to this, one has abandoned the mind and accomplished the abandonment of aversion, perceiving the body as a substantial obstruction and lacking mastery, one then cultivates emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

By contemplating [the body] until the body is extinguished and returns to non-existence, this is called "dissolving obstructions to enter emptiness. It is because one loathes the physical body as if it were a prison and desires to escape from it;
by loathing form and relying on emptiness, one is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space, which is termed the "Concentration of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Indeed, if one does not realize that the nature of form is true emptiness, but instead exerts oneself in dissolving obstructions, how can such a person know how to relinquish existence?
To return to non-existence—how is this any different from fleeing from a mountain peak only to plunge into a ravine? ○ Changshui says:

There are two ways of abandoning the mind. First, if one uses the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to sever afflictions and enter emptiness, this is the *sukha-vihārin* Anāgāmin.
Second, if one uses the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) at the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhat-phala*) to suppress afflictions and enter emptiness, this refers to ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists.
When all obstructions have been dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; therein remains only the *ālaya-vijñāna* in its entirety and a subtle portion of the *manas*.
This class of beings is called the Sphere of Consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*).
This is the second heaven of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Since the various obstructions of the preceding heavens have dissolved and ceased to exist, one does not rely upon form (*rūpa*).
In this heaven, even the non-obstruction of emptiness (*ākāśa*) is extinguished, so one does not rely upon space.
Within it, only the eighth *ālayavijñāna* remains in its entirety, along with a minute portion of the seventh *manas-vijñāna*.

Subtle. This is because if form and emptiness were present, the full portion of the manas would be present as well; now that form and emptiness have been exhausted, only half of the manas enters into the subtle.
Because one detests emptiness and relies upon consciousness, one is reborn in the Sphere of Consciousness, which is called the "Consciousness-Sphere Samādhi.
While there, one naturally considers oneself to be free from both form and emptiness, [realizing] the true nature.
Furthermore, how could one know that delusion is actually identical to the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*)? Question:

As for the *manas* and the *ālayavijñāna*, if even Arhats have not yet fully realized them, how can ordinary beings, outsiders, or Anāgāmins know of them? Answer: These were seen directly by the Buddha’s eye and given their names;
it is not that he granted that they [the other classes of beings] knew them. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Sentient beings dwell in various stages (*bhūmi*). Only...
The Tathāgata knows this as it truly is:
when emptiness and form have both vanished and the consciousness-mind has utterly ceased, the ten directions are tranquil and there is nowhere to go. Such is one class [of beings].
This is named the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
It is the third heaven among the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). Since the perception of space has already vanished in the preceding heaven, only consciousness remains.

In this heaven, one becomes weary of consciousness; by relying on profound meditative power (*samādhi*), both types of manifesting consciousness are suppressed and do not function. Thus, the mind of consciousness is entirely...

It ceases. One sees only the worlds of the ten directions as utterly silent and void, and no longer proceeds further—to that which is called the realm of profound obscurity and the land of dark silence.
Herein, non-Buddhists cling to it as the "Principle of Obscurity" (tamas-tattva), while Laozi and Zhuangzi call it the "Mysteriously Perfected" (hun-cheng);
all are situated here. Because they weary of consciousness and seek to return to nothingness, their retribution is birth in the state of non-existence.

This is called the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*). It is merely the previous stage advancing into a deeper concentration where both the subject that perceives and the object perceived subside, and it is temporarily termed "total cessation.
How could this be the same as what is meant by an Arhat’s severing of both active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*)?
The nature of consciousness is unmoving; by extinguishing it through exhaustive investigation, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible.
It is as if existing yet not existing, as if exhausted yet not exhausted. This class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

This is the fourth heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). In the preceding heavens, while the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the consciousness-mind have ceased, the seeds of the consciousness-nature (*vijñāna-dhātu*) have not yet perished;
therefore, the nature of consciousness remains firm and steadfast, never wavering. In this heaven, one relies forcefully upon the power of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
One exhausts it, desiring to reach its end; one investigates it, desiring to penetrate through it. Yet, it is ultimately impossible to exhaust it.

Within this inexhaustibility, one forcibly attempts to express it, determined to fully exhaust the nature of consciousness before ceasing. Thereupon, the two consciousnesses are like a dying lamp, half-extinguished and half-bright.
This is truly because they are pressed by the meditative absorption of cessation; thus, they seem to exist yet do not exist, resembling a lamp [at the point of extinction].
It is half-extinguished. Since the substance of the seeds does not move, it is as if exhausted yet not exhausted, resembling a lamp that is half-illuminated.
Because it exists as if it did not exist, it is not characterized by perception (*saṃjñā*); because it is as if exhausted yet not exhausted, it is not characterized by non-perception (*asaṃjñā*).
Such a class of beings, born through retribution in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, is called "Neither-Perception."

This is the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*). When a practitioner reaches this point, it may be said that they have attained the ultimate limit. Yet, how could one know that they have still not escaped the three realms (*tridhātu*)?

Such individuals exhaust the void but do not fully realize the principle of emptiness; though they proceed from the heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), their noble path remains incomplete. Such is the nature of this class of beings.

They are called "dull-witted Arhats who do not turn their minds [toward enlightenment]. If they come from among the non-Buddhist heavens of the Unconscious, they exhaust the realm of emptiness without returning;
deluded, leaking, and without hearing [the Dharma], they then enter the cycle of rebirth.
This generally clarifies the ground from which the noble and the ordinary emerge or fall. These celestial beings: those of the first heaven exhaust form and return to emptiness;

those of the second heaven exhaust emptiness and return to consciousness; those of the third heaven exhaust the mind of consciousness and return to non-existence; those of the fourth heaven exhaust the nature of consciousness and return to extinction.
The former two exhaust the objective realm, while the latter two exhaust the mind. This is intended so that both mind and object may [be transcended].

It is empty; thus it is collectively termed "exhausting emptiness. If one exhausts emptiness in such a manner, how could this not fail to reach the principle that the nature of form is true emptiness within the Perfect and Sudden teaching?

Indeed, the principles of the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena—are both not understood, yet one falsely desires to give rise to a mind to dissolve, empty, extinguish, and exhaust them.
How can one know that in the end, one will be unable to dissolve, empty, extinguish, or exhaust them? Therefore:
Those who have come from the five non-returner heavens, exhausting the realm of emptiness to enter this heaven, still possess a fundamentally upright mind;
they are called Arhats of dull faculties with unturned minds. They are the opposite of the aforementioned Great Arhats with turned minds.
Only after eighty thousand kalpas have elapsed will their afflictions of thought be completely severed, and they too shall transcend the three realms. As for those from the Heaven of No-Thought...
As for the non-Buddhist devas who exhaust the realm of emptiness and enter this heaven, their fundamental origin is false.

Because they are deluded regarding the tainted heavens and mistake them for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), after eighty thousand kalpas have passed and their retribution is fully exhausted, they have no place of refuge.

They still enter into the cycle of saṃsāra; how can one not stand in awe of this? Question: Previously, at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), it was determined that the afflictions of thought (kleshas) were completely severed.
I do not understand what is cultivated and severed by these persons within the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti). Answer: The previous explanation was based on those of sharp faculties.
How could those of dull faculties be the same? When those of dull faculties are in the five heavens, they abandon the first four categories of afflictions just as those of sharp faculties do.

Upon reaching the fifth heaven, they no longer possess a mind of longing for the higher and aversion to the lower; instead, they merely apply effort to eliminate obstacles and seek rebirth in the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
They expect to sever the remaining afflictions in those heavens. Since each of the four levels of the four formless realms contains nine grades [of afflictions], it reaches...
It is not perception; it is only at the end of the kalpa that it is exhausted.
Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm, body and mind are extinguished, and the nature of stability manifests before one. There is no form resulting from karmic fruit.
From this point until the end, it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). (This passage of the sutra was erroneously misplaced later; it is now corrected and moved to its proper position.)
This summarizes the formless realms. Ānanda, regarding these four heavens of the formless realm: in the first two heavens, there is entirely no body or objective sphere;

thus, the body is extinguished. In the latter two heavens, the active manifestation of consciousness is suppressed; thus, the mind is extinguished. In both cases, body and mind are extinguished together.

Therefore, when the meditative state (*samādhi*) manifests, there exists the "matter resulting from concentration" (*samādhija-rūpa*). This matter is utilized with sovereign mastery according to the transformed environment and inhabitants;
it is not like the physical bodies and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) of the desire and form realms, which are all matter produced by the retribution of karma.

Beginning from the Sphere of Infinite Space and ending with the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, these are collectively termed the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Thus, the three realms are fully encompassed.

Thus it is. Regarding the designation "formless" (*ārūpya*): it refers merely to relying on meditative concentration for a period of two hundred thousand kalpas, during which time the provisional support and the supported (the environment and the body) temporarily cease to exist;
it does not mean that the aggregates are truly empty or that karmic fruits are forever severed.
Ānanda, these various heavens and their respective devas are all ordinary beings receiving the retribution for their karmic fruits;

once that retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth. Those celestial kings, however, are bodhisattvas who dwell in *samādhi*, gradually advancing and turning toward the ranks of the sages;
this is the path upon which they practice. (This section was misplaced earlier; it is now corrected and moved here.)
This passage generally concludes that the gods and humans of the three realms, as well as their celestial lords, sages, and ordinary beings, are each distinct.

Ānanda, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, those among these heavens who have ministers and subjects are "celestial humans" (devamanuṣya);

those who have sovereigns and rulers are "celestial kings" (devendra). These various celestial humans are all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who, while in the causal stage, cultivated the ten [virtuous actions].

They skillfully employ the eight meditative absorptions, yet repay them with the six realms of desire and the four dhyānas. Once these exchanges are exhausted, they enter the cycle of saṃsāra once more;

this is what is meant by "when one's momentum is spent, the arrow falls back down. If those are the kings of the various heavens, they are bodhisattvas who have taken up provisional positions for further cultivation and do not fall into saṃsāra.
For example, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, those in the first bhūmi act as kings of Jambudvīpa.
In the second bhūmi, one becomes a Wheel-Turning King; in the third bhūmi, a king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; in the fourth bhūmi, a king of the Yāma Heaven;
and so on, up to the tenth bhūmi, where one becomes a king of the Mahesvara Heaven. Question: The higher realms are devoid of evil. How can this be?
Question: Why is it that some fall directly into the three miserable realms? Answer: The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) contains various seeds that are not lost over distant eons.
These ripen in succession and cannot be bypassed; therefore, when the rewards of celestial merit are exhausted, one falls spontaneously according to those ripened seeds.
This is why the Tathāgata earnestly exhorts one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha in order to seek a transverse exit [from saṃsāra].
All of this arises from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened mind of clarity; through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms manifest.

Within these delusions, *pudgalas* (which means "those who repeatedly take on rebirth," referring here to those in the intermediate state) sink and drown according to their karmic inclinations among the seven destinies, each following its own kind.

This summarizes that all three realms are illusory. Taken together, these twenty-eight heavens of the three realms all arise from the failure to realize the originally existing wondrously enlightened mind of clarity;
through the accumulation of delusion upon delusion, the three realms are falsely produced.
Once the karmic retribution of the intermediate devas and humans is exhausted, they cannot avoid again sinking into the seven destinies, cycle after cycle.
They undergo birth and take up existence within the various realms; these *pudgalas* continue from one kind of birth to another without finding rest.
If one can thoroughly realize the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind, then the three realms will become entirely empty and the seven destinies will all cease.

In that moment of realization, one transforms into supreme awakening. How, then, could there still be the suffering of sinking into accumulated delusions? [The Section on the Heavenly Destinies Concludes.]
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms—(though the three realms are mentioned collectively, they actually reside only within the desire realm)—there are four classes of asuras.

(Asura means "non-god," because although they possess celestial blessings, they lack celestial conduct; they are also called "not upright," because while the husbands are ugly, the wives are beautiful; they are also called "without wine," because their anger prevents the harmonious breath required for brewing, so that wine cannot be produced).
If, among the realm of ghosts, they rely on the power of dhāraṇīs and enter the void by means of supernatural powers, these are asuras.

Born from eggs, they are subsumed within the realm of ghosts (*preta*). (Regarding the "ghost path" mentioned as their prior cause: it refers to those who originally resolved their minds within the ghost realm to protect and uphold sūtras, mantras, dhyāna, and precepts.

By the power of these dharmas, they travel by supernatural power into the empty space and dwell as neighbors to the three *yakṣa* devas. Because they are egg-born, fly through the air, and share the same causes and conditions as ghosts, they are subsumed under the category of ghosts.
If, among the devas, their merit declines and they fall, the place where they settle is adjacent to the sun and moon. These *asuras* emerge from wombs and are subsumed within the realm of humans.

[Included in the human realm. (Among the gods, these were their previous lives. While they were among the gods, some had diminished their merit, or their heavenly blessings were exhausted, and thus they were all demoted and cast down. They dwell adjacent to the sun and moon and are born from a womb; therefore, they are included within the human destiny. There is an Asura King who upholds the world;
his power penetrates all and he is fearless, able to contend for authority with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
This Asura exists through transformation and is included within the celestial destiny. (Of the four [destinies], this is the most superior; therefore, it is called...)

"O King, those who separately govern the world drive and employ spirits and deities to bring about calamities or bestow blessings. Those whose power penetrates all without fear possess a vast strength that reaches through both humans and devas, such that they have nothing to dread. Since they can preside over misfortune and fortune, yet their exclusive authority does not equal that of the various heavens, they frequently become angry and contend with them.

The Sūtras state that their manifested bodies are sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas* in height; when they shake Mount Sumeru with their hands, the various heavens tremble with fear, and Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings constantly engage them in battle.

As for the statement here that the Brahmā King also contends, it may be that when Śakra is defeated, the Brahmā King and those below him all provide assistance. Because the power of their merit from birth by transformation is equal to that of the heavens, they are included within the realm of the devas. "Ānanda, there are others..."
A certain class of inferior asuras is born in the heart of the great ocean; they sink into the mouths of underwater caverns and roam only through the void, returning to dwell in the waters at dusk.

These asuras exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). (Mount Sumeru enters the water for eighty-four thousand *yojanas*. The asuras reside in four tiers; this is one such class.

Because they dwell at the bottom of the water, they are moisture-born beings. Due to their inferiority, they are included among the animals. A sutra states: "The food and clothing of asuras appear spontaneously; their crowns, sashes, and garments are made entirely of the seven treasures, and are fresh...")

Their purity is equal to that of heaven. Whatever food and drink they consume arises according to their thoughts, all of which possess a hundred flavors. However, whenever they eat, the very last mouthful transforms into green mud; therefore, they are not equal to humans. (The section on the asura realm concludes.
The detailed explanation of the seven realms of existence is completed.)

Ānanda, these hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras—having minutely examined these seven realms, they are all but the signs of conditioned existence arising from a state of stupor.
They are born through deluded thought and follow after karma through deluded thought.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind that is fundamentally unconditioned, they are all like flowers in the sky; originally they have no point of attachment, being nothing but a single falsehood, and nothing more.
The Root Source.

This concludes the summary of delusion. Ānanda, if one investigates these seven realms of existence, such as the hells, with meticulous detail, they are all manifestations of the delusion of dullness, giving rise to conditioned karma; and furthermore, this is due to false conceptualization.
The causes of delusion and karma lead one to take birth according to deluded thoughts and to receive retribution according to deluded thoughts.

Delusion, karma, and suffering—these three are like a cluster of akṣa fruits. Yet, there is the wondrousness of not being bound by karmic results; the perfection of neither falling into emptiness nor clinging to existence;
the clarity that is not obscured by the hindrances of delusion; and the non-action that does not depend on the cultivation or realization of acceptance or rejection. Thus, it is identical with...
That which is called the "original mind" exists within this very mind, appearing exactly like a flower in the sky, entirely without foundation or basis;
it is nothing but a uniform delusion. How could there be any root, stem, or thread of reality to be found?
○ All seven realms of existence are illnesses, and this Great Samādhi of the Sūtra is the medicine. This is why the Tathāgata so profoundly elucidates the nature of these ailments.
The intention is to urge them to use the medicine quickly.
Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and undergo this cycle of saṃsāra for immeasurable kalpas without attaining true purity;
all this is due to following the impulses of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. If they turn away from these three, then birth will no longer arise through killing.

Regarding theft, sexual misconduct, and so forth: there are those with names in the realm of ghosts and spirits, and those without names in the heavenly realms. As existence and non-existence mutually influence one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
If one attains the wondrous arousal of samādhi, then there is wondrous, eternal stillness; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even this absence of duality ceases.
Since there is not even "non-killing," "non-stealing," or "non-sexual misconduct," how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?
This refers to prescribing medicine according to the illness and thereby exhorting the cultivation of the Great Samādhi. Above, it was stated that there is no root or continuity;

yet here, it again points specifically to the root of the illness. This is because although delusion has no substance and its arising is indeed without cause, the principle of delusion nevertheless accords with [the nature of reality].
Because it is not non-existent, I point to it once more. Ānanda, that which I call the wondrous, perfect, luminous, and unconditioned fundamental mind exists within every person;
each and every one possesses it without exception. Yet, alas, these sentient beings do not recognize this mind.
Though they possess it, they remain oblivious to it—like holding a lamp while searching for its light, or wearing a jewel on one’s chest while wandering about begging. Thus they undergo [suffering].
In this saṃsāra, throughout immeasurable kalpas, one has not attained true purity. The desire realm is inherently impure;
even the form and formless realms, which are considered pure by their own nature, still harbor latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and are thus not truly pure.
When one examines the origin of this state, how could there not be a cause? It is those three evils—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—that afflict sentient beings.
To follow along with the three evils and practice them without realizing it, so that one falls into the three miserable realms—this is not at all surprising.

As for those who possess even a slight degree of spiritual capacity, they turn away from these three evil paths and instead hold it precious to refrain from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, thereby giving rise to the three virtues.
How could one know that by possessing these very qualities, one might instead commit the three evils? This is certainly the case.
This is the realm of ghosts. To achieve the three wholesome states without [wholesome roots] is likewise merely the realm of devas.
Thus, by taking what exists and making it non-existent, one ascends from below to above; by taking what does not exist and making it existent, one falls from above to below.

This incessant overturning and seizing is precisely the nature of saṃsāra. As for that from which saṃsāra arises, how could one know it were not from failing to contemplate the wholesome? Failing to contemplate the wholesome...
Evil is one's original face; this is precisely what is called the "original mind.
To recognize the original mind, there is no other method than this single gate of the Samādhi of the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-organ, which penetrates the essence and responds to the faculty.
If one attains the wondrous arousal of this Samādhi, then the three virtues of the nature of hearing will manifest simultaneously—how wondrous! And...
There are no bonds of the seven destinies; it is eternal. There is no arising or ceasing within the seven destinies; it is quiescent. There is no wandering through the seven destinies; it is still.
Thus, if one is able to turn the hearing inward and abide constantly in this nature, then the three evil realms that exist will become non-existent, and the three good realms will likewise be absent.
Being free from both, it is said that "existence and non-existence are both non-existent. This constitutes first attaining the emptiness of persons and emerging [from them].
This is the threefold realm. Even the non-existence of these two [extremes] is likewise extinguished; thus it is said, "The absence of duality is also extinguished.
This constitutes the liberation of the Dharma, by which one transcends the Two Vehicles.

At this time, there is not even the non-killing, non-stealing, or non-lustfulness [of the precepts], for even gold dust does not remain in the eye. Minor ailments are already absent, let alone serious illnesses.

And yet they continue to follow the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Thus, if one wishes to recognize the fundamental mind and escape the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), it is truly not possible without practicing the Great Samādhi.
○ Hei says: From the preceding section up to this point, the emphasis has again been placed on maintaining the precepts as the conclusion for the seven destinies.
It was stated above that "all [rebirths] result from following and conforming to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct," which has already been revealed.

This reveals the fundamental cause of falling back into the state of illness. One might fear that people will doubt this, asking: "If those in the heavenly realms uphold these three precepts, why are they not exempt from falling back?
It should be understood that this is not a fault of upholding the precepts, but rather a fault of upholding them with a tainted (sāsrava) mind.
Within the untainted (anāsrava) training, not even a speck of dust can stand; therein, there is no such thing as "upholding precepts," let alone "violating them. This is the correct [view].
The words regarding the severance of the three karmas are most poignant. For this sutra emphasizes the precepts from beginning to end; how could it possibly offer ambiguous or wavering teachings?

Ānanda, if one does not sever the three karmas, each will have its own private attachments. Because of these individual attachments, these private interests form a collective affinity; it is not that they do not exist.

The locus of concentration arises from one's own delusion; this arising of delusion has no cause and cannot be traced back to its origin. You must exert yourself in practice if you wish to attain Bodhi. To do so, you must eliminate the three delusions;
if these three delusions are not exhausted, even if you should obtain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they will all be merely worldly, conditioned functions.
If habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not eliminated, you will fall into the path of Māra. Though you may wish to remove delusion, you will instead increase your hypocrisy. Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
To say that they are to be pitied is a fabrication you have created yourself; it is not the fault of Bodhi.
To speak thus is called the correct teaching; if anyone speaks otherwise, they are speaking as the Māra King.
This concludes the response to the question and serves as an exhortation for authentic cultivation.

Ānanda, you asked whether hell has a fixed location or whether it arises spontaneously, with each individual receiving their retribution according to the specific karma they have produced. From my own perspective, I shall explain this.
The creation of karma is a private matter; the receiving of retribution is a shared matter. Since it is called "shared," it is not that there is no fixed location.
Yet, from where does this fixed location come? It is fundamentally what is summoned and evoked by one's own delusion.
Since that which is produced is delusory, it truly has no cause; therefore, its point of origin cannot be investigated. Thus, you—
Now, as you strive in practice with the desire to attain Bodhi, by what path should you follow? Indeed, the three evil realms and the three good realms are all collectively karma.
Yet, because one fails to realize that these three are the root of bondage and the source of obstacles to wisdom, they are also termed the "three delusions.
In your practice, you must eliminate these three delusions; it is not merely...
One eliminates the three [afflictions], yet one also eliminates the absence of those three. Why is this? Because the three delusions must be exhausted without exception.
If one were to eliminate only worldly evils while not eliminating worldly virtues, then the state of mutual opposition would remain unexhausted.
Even if one attains supernatural powers—such as those of celestial immortals—these are all mundane, conditioned functions that merely suppress active manifestations without...
The seeds are removed, yet the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are not extinguished; when they encounter conditions, they arise again, and one ultimately falls into the path of Māra.

Once fallen into the path of Māra, even if there is a person of clear vision who wishes to eliminate their delusions, that person will instead claim for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Yet you have doubled your falsehoods, relying on superficial penetration to create karma; thus you have strayed far from perfect penetration and turned your back on the city of Nirvana.
You have wasted your efforts in vain, turning them instead into causes for evil. The Tathāgata says you are truly pitiable.

Furthermore, since you first asked about the true reality of the Buddha-body, why is it that there are still the various realms of existence? Is it not because you are blaming the Buddha for the existence of these realms?
Is it so? Now you know that all these various delusions are created by yourself; thus, it is clear that they are not the fault of Bodhi.
Since Bodhi is without fault, how could the essence of the Buddha be at fault? Indeed, one must not fail to sever the three karmas, nor must one fail to eliminate the three delusions.
If, in the final age, one were to urge people to distance themselves from these three...
As for "the seeds," this refers to what the Buddha taught. If one praises these three types [of seeds] as being unimpeded, that is merely the speech of Māra.
Such a person still clings to visual discernment; do not allow the clamor of the masses to confound the Sage. It would be like mistaking fish eyes for pearls. Alas!
Such is the wondrous nature of samādhi, yet people are unwilling to exert themselves toward it. How grievous are the sufferings of the seven realms of existence!
"Such as they are, yet they do not contemplate wearying of them and seeking liberation. 'Sentient beings, sentient beings,' I can do nothing for them; it is all over.
[End of the exhortation to leave the seven destinies.]
The second major section, concerning the root of beginningless birth-and-death transmigration, is hereby concluded.
At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to rise from the Dharma seat, he took up a seven-jeweled desk upon his lion throne and turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain.

Leaning forward once more, he addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying: "You who are still in training—whether Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—who have today turned your minds toward the Great Bodhi and the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment, listen.

I have now explained the true practice. (Note: Regarding the parenthetical remark: "You who are in training" refers to those for whom the four aggregates [of form, sensation, perception, and formations] have already been destroyed, leaving only the fifth aggregate, consciousness.

Since coarse external demonic realms—including devas, ghosts, and spirits—no longer reach them, this discourse on the demonic distortions of the five aggregates is spoken specifically for those in training; therefore, they are singled out.)
Dharma, you still do not recognize the subtle demonic activities that arise during the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
When such demonic realms manifest before you, you fail to recognize them; your purification of mind is not authentic, and you fall into false views.

Whether it be the *skandha-māra*, the celestial *māra*, possession by ghosts and spirits, or encounters with malevolent demons, your mind remains obscured, leading you to mistake a thief for your own son. Furthermore, regarding...

[In the] middle [of their practice], they consider a small attainment to be sufficient. Like the bhikṣu who had not heard the teachings in the fourth dhyāna, he falsely claimed to have realized the state of an arhat.
When his heavenly retribution was exhausted, the signs of decline appeared before him. Having slandered the arhats, he underwent further existence and fell into the Avīci Hell.
You should listen attentively; I shall now explain this to you in detail for you. Ānanda rose from his seat, as did those in the assembly who were still in training (śaikṣas).
...he joyfully prostrated and humbly awaited compassionate instruction.
From this point downward, the various demonic realms are detailed and distinguished. The practitioner (the "one who meets the occasion") knew only to request meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

however, the subtle demonic realms that arise within that concentration were beyond the reach of his intellectual power, and thus he did not inquire about them. Since the Buddha had already guided him through the great concentration, [he proceeded as follows].
The victory or defeat of Māra’s armies is truly related to the formation or destruction of the Great Samādhi; the stakes are not trivial.
Therefore, moved by profound compassion, he paused and then remained, speaking of his own accord without waiting for a question. At that moment, the Tathāgata had finished preaching the Dharma.
As he was about to conclude his session upon the Dharma-seat, his true compassion remained inexhaustible;
thus, he leaned forward from his couch, resting his hands upon the armrests, and turning toward the mountain-like assembly once more, he addressed the great multitude and Ānanda, saying:

"You disciples in training—pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who today turn your minds toward the Great Vehicle: I have now expounded the method of true cultivation and pointed out the single gateway of 'returning the hearing.'"

However, you still do not recognize that for those who cultivate the nature of *śamatha* and the two types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are many subtle demonic activities within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

These demonic visions appear suddenly, unknown and unperceived, all of them so harmonious with the human mind that they prevent you from discerning whether they are deviant or authentic. If, within your breast, there is even a hair’s breadth of...
If your deviant mind has not been completely washed away, they will seize upon this single hair’s breadth of an opening and be able to hook you into falling into false views.

What are these various demons? They may be your own internal demons (*antarāya-māra*), such as the ten kinds within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which manifest from within your own initial state of mind;

at that stage, there are as yet no external demons. As for the ten kinds within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), although one has already summoned external demons, [they remain within the internal aggregates].
They may still enter within one’s body, yet the demon has not yet manifested its form.

Whether it be a celestial demon (*devaputra-māra*), or possession by a ghost or spirit, or encountering a *chimei* (goblin), these constitute the ten types within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
At the very moment the demon manifests, it is essential to possess the "eye that distinguishes dragons from snakes"; only then will one not be deluded by them. If your "Dharma-eye" is not...
To mistake this for the transformation of one's own body is to recognize a thief as one's son; it causes the family treasure to be plundered.
Whether one identifies oneself as a sage or recognizes a demon as a sage, both are cases of recognizing a thief as one's son.

Furthermore, there are ten kinds of mental demons arising from the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) and ten kinds of view-demons arising from the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness); these all lack external objects and exist only as [internal projections].
This is due to one's own mind harboring wrong views and considering a mere trifle sufficient. To illustrate this with a single example:

consider a monk of the fourth dhyāna who, having heard nothing of the Dharma, cultivates only the state of non-perception as his ultimate goal. He claims for himself that he has realized the Unsurpassed Way.

Yet, once his celestial retribution is exhausted, the signs of decline appear before him; the faculty of perception and thought arise once more, and he realizes he was never actually enlightened from the start.

"Sages! You have instead slandered the Arhats; you have encountered future existence for yourselves, yet you claim that the Buddha’s statement regarding those who do not undergo future existence is false.
Because you have slandered the Dharma, you shall consequently fall into hell. Such is its poison—how can you not stand in awe? You all should turn your minds toward Great Bodhi;
how could you possibly remain ignorant of its benefits and harms? Therefore, I act on your behalf..."

This is a detailed analysis; it is not a superficial treatment. Thereupon, Ānanda rose and paid his respects, and together with those in the assembly who were still in training, they joyfully prostrated themselves and again listened to the Tathāgata’s compassionate instructions.
The World-Honored One had once pointed out the path of true cultivation, yet Ānanda and the others had not yet personally traversed it, and thus they did not know [it].
Along the way there will be hardships and obstructions. The World-Honored One is one who has traversed this path;

having personally experienced every peril, difficulty, and misfortune, he now turns back from his seat to remain, pointing out each encounter along the way so that you may recognize them for yourself and prepare for unforeseen circumstances.
It is like a compassionate mother who, when her beloved child travels far away, gives him instructions regarding the road at the moment of departure.
Regarding the matters of benefit and harm therein, I have instructed you to cherish and protect yourselves in every possible way; the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible compassionate intent is likewise so.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly: "You should know that within this world of outflows, there are twelve classes of sentient beings."
Fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous; this perfected essence of the mind is non-dual and indistinguishable from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

It is due to your deluded thoughts that you mistake the principle for error. From ignorance and craving, birth arises; as this process of birth unfolds, universal delusion ensues. Thus, the nature of space emerges, and as delusion continues without ceasing, transformation occurs.
Since there is the arising of worlds, these lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions are not free from outflows;

they are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization. You should know that empty space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great sky.

How much more so for all worlds that exist within space? If even one of you were to give rise to true realization and return to the source, the worlds of the ten directions would all be dissolved and vanish;
how then could the lands existing within space fail to tremble and shatter?
These words explain the cause by which Māra agitates them. The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly:

"Do you know the reason from which Māra comes to afflict you? You should all know this: the essence of the fundamentally awakened mind of sentient beings in the world is wondrously bright and perfect;
it is originally no different from that of the Buddhas. One may say that sentient beings are themselves the Buddhas."

It may be said that the Buddha is none other than sentient beings. This is because, through the slightest movement of deluded thought, one becomes confused regarding this principle of awakened perfection and thus incurs faults.

Consequently, the aspect of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*) constitutes ignorance (*moha*), and the aspect of transformation (*pariṇāmalakṣaṇa*) constitutes craving (*tṛṣṇā*); these are the two types of ignorance.

In an instant, it arises. Once it has arisen, the essence of awakening becomes universally deluded; this delusion constitutes the nature of emptiness—what is called "dark obscurity becoming emptiness.

Since the entire dharma-realm is thus collectively deluded into a state of stubborn emptiness, this delusion continues to transform without ceasing, thereby giving rise to worlds—what is called "establishing worlds based upon emptiness. Thus, the ten directions exist.
The myriad subtle lands are all established by deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Conceptualization is the general essence; it is precisely fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Through delusion, it gives rise to the "sentient" aspect of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*);

through stubbornness, it gives rise to the "insentient" aspect of the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Thus, they are all established by that [conceptualization]. You should know that empty space arises within your own mind.
It is merely like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so for all the worlds that exist within space?
One can see that they are illusory and ephemeral, easily subject to dissolution and extinction.

Furthermore, all the people in the world exhaustively give rise to delusions without ceasing, chasing after sounds and pursuing forms; not a single person has given rise to the truth. If you [disciples]...
Within the assembly, there was one person who dwelt in the Great Samādhi and entered the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*).

As the true manifested and the false was shattered, he realized the truth and returned to the source. At that moment, this empty space of the ten directions should have been pulverized instantly, entirely dissolving away;
how much more so the lands contained within that space—how could they not have been shaken and split asunder? This is because internally...
Movement is an external stimulus; this is true of all things. Why, then, should one harbor doubts regarding Great Samādhi? Question:
From antiquity to the present, there have been no few who have manifested the Truth. For what reason does the world remain exactly as it was before? Answer:
The world is fundamentally the result of the collective karma of sentient beings. When one person manifests the Truth, that one person’s world perishes. If everyone in the world were to do so...
If a person within this realm were to give rise to the truth, then the entire world would be utterly dissolved. Yet, how could such a thing occur?

This is why this world remains as it was, exactly as before. ○ Daokai said: "The sages of this land say that when 'harmony and centrality' are realized, heaven and earth find their proper places and the myriad things are nourished. The sages of the Western Land say that when one person gives rise to the truth..."

Returning to the source, the worlds of the ten directions would all be extinguished; yet when the Great Sage Confucius presided over and nurtured the world through the Spring and Autumn Annals, he did not cause the world to perish.
Likewise, when Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood, he did not cause the world to perish.
Thus we know that one who preserves the principle need not necessarily manifest the phenomenal event. ○ He said: "Sentient beings cannot be exhausted; the worlds cannot be exhausted. One.
When a person gives rise to the truth, the multitudes again experience a congealing of their bonds; though there may be a temporary trembling, it soon returns to a state of solidification.
You who cultivate dhyāna and adorn yourselves with samādhi—O Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and all the great Arhats free from outflows!
The mind and its objects merge in perfect harmony; wherever one dwells, there is profound stillness.

All Māras, as well as ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas (namely, those of the Heaven of No-Thought), see their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason. The great earth quakes and splits open;

waters (such as river essences and ocean essences) and lands (such as mountain forests and local deities) surge and fly upward. Even the powerful ghost kings and flying yakṣas are all struck with terror and awe. Ordinary people, being mired in darkness, do not perceive this.

They have undergone transformation and corruption. They have all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the extinction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Yet they remain attached to these worldly defilements;

how then could you cause them to shatter that place? For this reason, ghosts and spirits, as well as the devas, Māras, and various malevolent demons, all come to harass you during your time in samādhi.
These words mean that the demons will be provoked to distress. Now, when a single person awakens to the truth, the ten directions dissolve and perish;

the lands tremble and split apart, and the palaces of the demons are the first to suffer its effects. You who cultivate dhyāna—amidst walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—[must remain vigilant].
Strictly maintain *samādhi*. Whether through "hearing back" (*praty-śravaṇa*) or through "resting," remain neither obscured nor interrupted, without the slightest leakage.
At the very moment of manifesting the truth, you will find your affinity with all the Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats free from outflows;
your minds will merge perfectly, blending into one. Thus, you shall abide in profound stillness, pure and unmoving. You—

He remained unmoving, yet Māra was shaken. Thereupon, from the celestial Māras above down to the spirits and ghosts, and all the ordinary devas, saw their palaces collapse and crack without cause, and the great earth tremble and split apart without cause.
Thus, among the māra-kings dwelling in water, on land, or in the air—whether stationary or soaring—there were none who were not struck with terror; only...

Ordinary beings of the lower realms are bewildered and unaware; they see the great earth shaking, yet they merely hear distorted rumors that the yin and yang have lost their measure, or false reports that the divine turtle is moving its eyes, without experiencing any alarm or fear.

Indeed, those terrifying Māras and others are none other than beings who have attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), but have not yet realized the single power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
This is so. Since you possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), you must know that this was brought about by the power of your meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Moreover, as they all cling to these worldly afflictions (*saṃsāra*) and will surely obtain their own dwelling places, how could you willingly cause them to be torn apart?
Since I did not allow you to tear them apart, I certainly did not permit it when you entered into *samādhi*. Those beings were likewise [prevented].
They come to harass and disturb him, desiring to disrupt his meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). This is why Māra arrives just as he has first attained the summer retreat (*varṣa*).
Yet, although those Māras may be filled with great rage, within his afflictions (*kleśa*) and within your wondrous awakening (*pratyavekṣā-jñāna*), they are like wind blowing against light.

It is like a blade cutting through water; they do not touch one another at all. You are like boiling water, and he is like solid ice. As the warmth gradually approaches, the ice will melt away before long.
To rely merely on your supernatural powers is to be but a guest; it leads only to the accomplishment of disorder and confusion.

This is because you are the master of the five aggregates within your own mind. If the master is deluded, the guest gains the advantage. Therefore, while practicing *dhyāna*, awaken to the truth and remain free from doubt.
Then those demonic activities will be powerless against you. As the five aggregates dissolve and enter into clarity, all those various evils will be forced to absorb the dark, stagnant energy.

Since clarity can destroy darkness, they will perish on their own as they draw near; how then would they dare remain to disturb your meditative concentration? This is so unless you have not yet attained clear awakening.
Deluded by the aggregates, you, Ānanda, would surely become a son of Māra and achieve the state of a demonic person, like Mahā-Pragāpati;

such a one is truly insignificant and inferior. She merely used a spell against you, violating the Buddha’s code of discipline; among the eighty thousand practices, she destroyed but a single precept.

Because the mind is pure, you have not yet sunk into ruin; yet this [state] will destroy your entire body of precious awakening, like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering confiscation of their property—utterly dispersed and fallen, beyond all hope of rescue.
This statement regarding the method for warding off demons means that if one awakens to it, there will be no fault; if one remains deluded, one will succumb to evil.

Nevertheless, even so, the practitioner need not fear them. Although those various demons possess great power and may give rise to fierce anger, they are ultimately but things within the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*).
How could they compare to you, who are among those of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi*), profoundly still and empty, pervading everywhere?
Throughout the ten directions, even if they were to attempt to harm you, it would be like the wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water;
in the end, they could never cause the light or the water to move or be damaged. Not only can they not inflict harm, but you, on the contrary, are able to transform them.
You are likened to boiling water, while they are likened to solid ice. If the boiling water comes near the solid ice...
When ice is confronted by warm air, it naturally melts away. Why should I fear them?
Furthermore, although they rely on the supernatural power of their fivefold abhijñās, they are in fact restless and never at rest; they cannot remain for even a moment and are merely guests.
That which brings about the destruction and disturbance of meditative concentration does not lie with these guests, but entirely with you.

The master within the five aggregates of the mind—if this master lacks clarity within his heart and mistakes the thief for his son, then the guest will take advantage of the opening to enter, causing affliction and disorder.

If the master remains in *dhyāna* right where he is, alert and lucid, refusing to be coarse or negligent, then even though those demonic affairs may be powerful, they will have no way to move you. What can they do?
What do you mean? It is like a thief who has plundered a master's house. If the master remains deep within his quarters unmoving, the thief cannot fathom him;
the closer he draws, the more terrified he becomes. This is what the common saying means when it says, "A strong thief fears a weak master.

If the master fails to maintain his composure and flees in a state of panic, he will rarely escape being captured by the thief. As for the phrase "he can do nothing with you," it refers to this very principle.
It is not that you possess the power to overcome them; rather, it is simply because clarity can dispel darkness.
For you abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), your dark vapors have already been dissipated, and you have entered the Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*).
They, however, are all subject to gloomy vapors and dwell in a realm of stupor and obscurity. To approach the light from the darkness is just like an owl entering the day, or a *rākṣasa* facing...
The Yang [principle] will naturally cause it to dissolve and perish, its spirit lost as it departs. How could it remain long enough to disturb your meditative concentration?

It is true that only those who have attained awakening are free from delusion. Conversely, if one does not attain clear understanding, one will inevitably be bewildered by the Yin [principle], becoming attached to or terrified by, and feeling love or hatred for, those illusory realms, thereby losing the capacity to perceive the underlying principle.
Not only are you unable to transform him, but you have instead fallen into his class. You, Ānanda, are like this;
you will surely become a son of Māra and complete the work of a demonic person. Consider, for example, the case of the Mātanga woman:

she was a person of such lowly and inferior status that even if she were able to cast a spell upon you, it would merely break a single precept, and the harm would still be minor. Moreover, your mind remains pure and untainted.
...to the point of drowning in ruin. How could such a Māra-king be compared to Tathāgatā? You are the son of a Māra and have achieved the state of a Māra-man;
he, however, shall destroy your entire body of precious awakening, utterly ruin your fruits of the Path, and cast you into the Avīci Hell.
It is like a high minister’s family suddenly being confiscated by the Heavenly King: not only would they lose [their wealth], but...
When one’s official post is terminated and their very person cannot escape physical execution, they will drift and wander in misery with no means of rescue or relief.
Such are the harms wrought by Māra; how can one fail to be alarmed and to exercise vigilant discernment?

From here below, the characteristics of the five demonic realms (*pañca-māra-gocara*) are detailed. In the preceding section, it was understood that the movement of demons arises from the intensity of meditative concentration;

thus, one is not startled by the initial onset of demons and remains free from affliction through prevention. It was also understood that the production of disorder arises from the confusion of the subject;
thus, one remains unshaken by the ultimate manifestation of demons and maintains firm self-guarding. Nevertheless, as for the characteristics of the manifested realms—
It is overly prolix and lacks detailed analysis; it is not certain that one will not become confused by it. Therefore, I shall now provide a detailed and systematic differentiation.

Although this discussion concerns demons (*māra*), the essential principles for the practical application of cultivation are contained herein. Students must not fail to apply their full effort to this.

Ānanda, you should know this: when you sit at the site of enlightenment (the physical site is the eight-cornered altar; the principle site is the focused turning-back of hearing so that the mind does not wander), all discursive thoughts will dissolve.

When those thoughts are exhausted—that is, profound stillness—then all states of being free from thought (as the *Awakening of Faith* says, the substance of the mind is free from thought, equal to the realm of empty space) will manifest as total clarity and alertness.
Unmoved by motion or stillness, memory and its absence will be as one. (When consciousness suddenly arises as memory, it is like a reflection appearing in a mirror.)

Suddenly it ceases and becomes forgotten, like an image vanishing within a mirror while the substance of the mirror remains as before; therefore, it is said to be "as one. One should dwell in this state and enter *samādhi*, like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness.

A person with a distracted mind, facing only the objects currently appearing before them, perceives only a single area of light and is unaware that all other places are dark—just as when one faces the light of a lamp in a room at night while the space outside is boundless and pitch-black.

Now, if one suddenly disregards the current objects before one and focuses exclusively on the infinite *dharmadhātu* within hearing, once this concentration is accomplished, the current objects will entirely vanish, and only then will one realize that the ten directions are all [empty].

Darkness. It is like blowing out the lamp in a room until the room itself seems to vanish; from heaven to earth, everything becomes total darkness. Thus it is said: "It is like a person with clear vision situated in great, profound darkness.
