When the Dragon Cage Pond blew out the lamp and manifested the Bright Mountain, it was precisely this samādhi that was entered.

(○ Furthermore, the mountains, rivers, and other objects clearly perceived before one's eyes are produced by the illusion of ignorance (*avidyā*). Both the seer and the seen are the workings of ignorance. Because this accumulated vision is centered in the eye, there is light when the eyes are open and darkness when they are closed.)

If you see [objects] without being liberated from the sense organs and their objects, and your light remains entirely within darkness, yet you cling to this as real, when will there be an opportunity for awakening? It is like a person in a dream who does not know it is a dream; they see only what is bright before them and call it clear perception, having no realization at all that they are in a state of deep sleep and darkness.

How could they ever wake up? Now, those who enter *samādhi* must suddenly abandon the illusory body and illusory objects before them without a single thread of attachment. Exert yourself in "hearing-internalization" (*pratyāśravaṇa*). Only within this state will you realize the boundless darkness;

you will be just like the person in the dream who realizes it is a dream, abandons that dream-scene, and no longer clings to it, exerting effort to seek awakening. Only then will you realize that you were oppressed by deep sleep and darkness, and mired in confusion. This is the subtle essence of the spirit.

Purity. (To be pure and unmixed in its essence while free from discursive thought is called "essence" (*jing*). To be utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects is called "wondrous" (*miao*). To transcend both emptiness and existence simultaneously is called "pure" (*jing*)).

When the mind has not yet emitted light, this is termed the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). (A dark room covered over is called a "domain" (*qu*). A wall that confines and obstructs is called a "space" (*yu*)).

If the eyes become clear and bright, the ten directions open up through and through (pervading one world-realm or even up to a small thousand-fold world system), and there is no longer any darkness; this is termed the exhaustion of the aggregate of form. (It is like five layers of clothing: one has first removed the uppermost layer). This person then...

One is able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). (Ordinarily, the turbidity of the kalpa occurs when the human lifespan reaches one hundred years; it governs the five turbidities and is termed an "evil age. Now, this refers to when the obscured darkness becomes emptiness and the binding of darkness becomes form;

at that moment, one enters the turbidity of the kalpa. Since immeasurable kalpas past, one has long slumbered within the darkness of birth and death. However, because the substance of this turbidity entirely depends upon the profound obscurity of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), when the aggregate of form is exhausted, the obscured darkness immediately opens up and one transcends the turbidity of the kalpa.

One contemplates its origin: false attachment and solidified deluded thoughts serve as its root. (It is the stubborn clinging and firm entanglement of deluded emotions and ignorant conceptions regarding the external four great elements.)

One stubbornly clings to [the earth element] as being real and external to the body, and one stubbornly clings to the four internal great elements as the dwelling place of the mind. Because of this firm entanglement that cannot be unraveled, this dark substance of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is formed.

All eleven types of form constitute the aggregate of form; they all belong to the delusion of solidity. (Regarding the phrase "observing its origin": the commentator says that it must necessarily be exhausted before one can observe it, but this is not necessarily so. It merely explains the origin of the aggregate of form, supplementing what was omitted in the preceding section.)
This describes the characteristics of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) from its beginning to its end.
Ānanda, you should know that what I call "Māra" does not go beyond form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. First, regarding the aggregate of form:

when you sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), focus intently on the practice of "returning the hearing," causing all discursive thoughts to dissolve. This is what is meant by "at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. As for those thoughts...
When [thoughts] have thus ceased, this is called "transcending thought. This state of transcending thought is like empty space;

at all times it is alert and never obscured, hence it is termed "vivid lucidity" (*jīngmíng*). Thus, it has no concern with the realms of movement and stillness, yet movement and stillness do not shift it;
it has no involvement with the consciousness of recollection and forgetfulness, yet recollection and forgetfulness are as one. This is precisely what constitutes "striking through to completion."
For even a brief moment, you should abide in this state of brilliant clarity free from thought. You will then be able to enter the Samādhi of the Perfect Illumination of the Ear-faculty.
This state of meditative concentration is like a person with clear vision situated in a vast, profound darkness:

that which is not seen by the eyes is certainly dark, and that which is seen by the eyes is also dark. That which is seen by the eyes is certainly dark, and the eye that is able to see is also [dark].
It is dark. Because this mind of essential purity and wondrous clarity is shrouded by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it has been unable to emit light;
therefore, all that is seen before one’s eyes is only darkness. This appearance of darkness is precisely the nature of the confinement of the aggregate of form, which is like a house or building;
thus it is called the "confined space of the aggregate of form. This is the sign that the aggregate of form has not yet been shattered.
Furthermore, if the light of the mind is allowed to radiate forth, all obstructions will be penetrated;

what is seen by the physical eyes will become vivid and clear, the ten directions will open wide, and the preceding darkness will be transformed entirely into light, penetrating inwardly through the five viscera.
Externally, mountains and rivers are transparent; from the heavens to the human realm, all are as clear as the palm of one's hand.

When the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, this is the sign that the aggregate of form has been shattered. One who has shattered the aggregate of form is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

This is because the turbidity of the kalpa is formed by the binding of darkness within the dark gloom of emptiness; once one is detached from this aggregate of form, it originally possesses no substance.
Thus, when it is exhausted, one ultimately transcends it. Looking back from this point, I have finally come to know the origin of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*):
its fundamental root is none other than solidified deluded thought (*dṛḍha-vikalpa*). It is like a woodcutter who must first clear away the covering soil before the primary roots can be seen;
now that the *kalpa*-turbidity has opened, observing the origin of the aggregate of form is likewise a matter of natural principle. ○
Question: Since all forms are still perceived, why do you say they are "exhausted"? Answer: Within the perfectly interfused Middle Way, how could one exhaust form to produce emptiness?

It is simply that the aggregates (skandhas) are exhausted so that they no longer act as a covering. This is truly because the True Mind is fundamentally able to manifest form in accordance with conditions.
Yet form is not different from mind; it is fundamentally luminous and penetrating, like a pearl that emits light which in turn illuminates the substance of the pearl itself.

It is only because of beginningless delusion that one takes oneself to be an object, resulting in universal obstructions and barriers. Furthermore, by identifying objects as the self, one gathers the faculty of vision within the eyes.
Consequently, one sinks forever into darkness and completely loses the luminosity that pervades all realms. How could this be anything less than ignorance of one's own fundamental nature?
Luminosity. Furthermore, it is not that the manifestation of darkness is not perceived. At that time, even those who are still in training (śaikṣa) know it through inference (anumāna);

One day, suddenly, as the colored clouds of the physical aggregate dispersed, he personally realized his original luminosity.

The "intermediate" refers to the point of intersection. This is because the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) universally encompasses the four lands;

Within one world-system; within one world-system, one realm; within one realm, one continent; within one continent, one country; within one country, one town.

At the moment when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has not yet opened, the intensity of the "returning hearing" is profound; the radiance of the mind flows forth, sometimes penetrating nearby.

How can one not be cautious and vigilant, and apply further scrutiny? Regarding the four lands:

After a short while, this body passes through walls and barriers without any obstruction whatsoever; this is called the "light of the mind" (cittaprabhā).

It leaks forth and overflows even before objects that are solid and obstructive to the eyes, occurring specifically because the intensity of one's diligent cultivation has reached its limit, resulting in a temporary state of such ethereal integration.

It is not the same as a realization of the Sage. If you do not conceive the thought that this is a sagehood, it is called a "wholesome state"; if you conceive the understanding that it is sagehood, [it becomes an obstacle].

even the teachings spoken are merely those uttered by them. How could it be that at the very beginning of their manifestation, they would immediately dispatch a real person?
"O Ānanda, people come to cause confusion and delusion!

These ten kinds of visionary states appearing during *dhyāna* are all manifestations resulting from the interaction between the mind and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Thus these matters appear.
Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these conditions, they fail to recognize them for what they are and say:"
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood; one will fall into the Avīci Hell.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the Age of Dharma Decline, you should proclaim this meaning so that Māras and heavenly demons find no opportunity to exploit you. Protect and sustain it, and thereby achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
This is a summary of the ten characteristics of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), intended to urge you to protect them.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of objects that appear within *dhyāna* are all the practitioner’s own meditative contemplation clashing and contending with solidified false conceptualization (*abhiniveśa-vikalpa*).
Whether one prevails or suffers defeat, these ten matters manifest; for instance, when a favorable object appears, it is immediately—
This is because the power of contemplation is superior to deluded thought; it appears for a moment and then vanishes. Conversely, deluded thought is superior to the power of contemplation;
as they emerge and enter one another alternately, they cannot be mutually integrated. This is why Māra seizes these intervals to enter. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded;
they do not examine their own level of realization to see how it compares to that of the Buddha, nor do they compare their spiritual practice to that of the Buddha.
Thus, merely encountering these temporary conditions for manifestation, one remains deluded and fails to awaken; one then claims to have ascended high into the realm of the sages.
This is to claim realization where there is none, and to claim attainment where there is none—it constitutes a great falsehood, leading to a fall into the Avīci Hell.
This is what is meant by "first ascending to heaven, and later falling to earth. Such are the demonic signs of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Alas! Thus ends the teaching of the Tathāgata.

I shall enter parinirvāṇa now; how much more so after this time? When the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is diminished and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) prevails, you all should rely upon the teachings of the Tathāgata today.

After the Tathāgata’s passing, until the midst of the Semblance Dharma, you must extensively propagate this meaning to those who practice meditation and contemplation in the future, causing them to understand it clearly, and do not let the celestial Māras [obstruct them].
Having attained these skillful means, you shall thereby provide assurance, sustain, conceal, and protect this Great Samādhi, and together bring the Unsurpassed Way to fulfillment.
I now entrust this to you; you must exert yourselves!

Ānanda, when those good sons practice samādhi within śamatha (the simultaneous cultivation of cessation and contemplation—specifically the contemplation of entering the stream through the ear-door and the cessation of forgetting objects), they reach the point where the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted.

Regarding the ten realms mentioned above, whether one has fully traversed them or not, it is essential to clearly recognize them so as not to be deluded by them. When the功夫 (kōngfú, spiritual effort) reaches its culmination, the aggregate of form will naturally reach its end.

Hereafter, all shall be explained according to this principle. They perceive the minds of the Buddhas as images appearing in a clear mirror; yet, if they harbor the notion of attainment, [they remain bound].

Yet they are unable to employ them. It is like a person suffering from sleep paralysis: their hands and feet are perfectly intact, and their sight and hearing are unconfused (a metaphor for having attained some realization), yet because their mind has been contacted by an external malevolent spirit, they cannot move (a metaphor for being unable to employ it). This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

If the affliction of sleep paralysis ceases, then the aggregate of sensation is exhausted; the mind leaves the body and looks back at its own face, moving freely whether departing or staying, with nothing further to detain it.

Obstruction. (This refers to the ability to manifest the function of sovereign mastery. One should know that this is not the same as passing away while seated and being unable to return; the latter merely involves passing away while seated by relying on meditative power within the preceding state of profound darkness.

This is why Jiufeng did not permit the Head Seat Tai to do so. In this case, both form and sensation are opened, and both essence and function are complete; coming and going are unimpeded. Dongshan Faqing and others were such individuals.

This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Observing its origin, one finds that empty, luminous delusion constitutes its root. (The aggregate of sensation has no substance.)
"Because there is illumination where there is nothing, it is called 'illusory luminous delusion' (*vibhrama-vikalpa*).
This describes the characteristics of the beginning and end of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Ānanda, when that virtuous man is practicing great samādhi..."
When the preceding ten objects are no longer confused, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, and one’s stage corresponds to the first faith (*śraddhā*).
This exhaustion of the aggregate of form is like a person with clear vision who, having been in a vast dark room, now finds it entirely filled with light;

they perceive the minds of all Buddhas as clearly as images appearing in a bright mirror. Indeed, the minds of all Buddhas are none other than my own wondrously enlightened, luminous mind. Toward sentient beings...
Seeking outwardly, one can never see it; now, seeing it within the opening of one's own mind, one realizes it was originally not outside.
Is this not intimate and clear? Since it is one's own mind and yet is seen directly, if there is something attained, it is truly the attainment of its essence.
It is simply that one has not yet been able to give rise to its sovereign function in accordance with that essence. This is an analogy.

It is like a person who, while asleep, is possessed by a nightmare; though they clearly perceive the objects of their waking state, because their mind is defiled by adventitious evils, they are overwhelmed and unable to move.
The color-aggregate (rūpa-skandha) has already opened, yet the state of being covered by the feeling-aggregate (vedanā-skandha) is likewise so.
This is called the realm of the feeling-aggregate: having a body, one is unable to use it. Thus it is said.

This is the realm of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), a place of confinement and obscuration. Now, the mind is fundamentally not confined within the body; yet, due to beginningless attachment and delusion, it is confined where it was not.
While alive, it is confined within the manifest aggregate; at death, it is confined within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). There is no time when it is not confined within the body.

How could there be a separation from the body and a state of freedom? If the affliction of being haunted by a nightmare ceases, then that mind departs from the body and is able to look back upon its own face; whether it goes outside the body or remains within it, it is free and at ease.
It regards this body as a traveler’s inn, no longer lingering or obstructed by it. This is what is meant by "being able to use" [the mind]. This is the reception.

The exhaustion of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is the mark [of liberation]. Now, the *skandha* of sensation is the root of the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). The view of a self-body is the root of all views.
Once sensation is exhausted and one is detached from the body, the view of a self-body is liberated; thus, one is able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Viewed from this perspective, it can be seen that the fundamental mind does not reside within the body; rather, it is merely the *skandha* of sensation that falsely functions as reception, and is empty.
Explanation: It receives because it is empty; it receives without error because it is luminous. This is the origin of the aggregate of reception (*vedanā-skandha*);
its fundamental root is merely empty-luminosity-wandering-thought (*śūnyatā-prakāśa-vikalpa*). How can the practitioner fail to examine this closely? ○ Zhong says:
The "ejecting of the spirit" (*chushen*) in the schools of immortals is somewhat similar to what is taught in this sutra, yet they are actually different. That...
If one seeks it with a mind, this cannot be attained by the mind; that [state] is what they themselves call "sublime function," whereas this [state] does not involve the formation of a holy mind.
In the previous section on the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), when one was able to emerge from obstruction for a brief moment, this was the stage of "desiring to emerge.

When one saw afar and flew forth upon reaching the limit of proximity, this was the stage of "gradually emerging. This present stage is the freedom of going forth, where there are no longer any lingering obstructions.
How wondrous is this emergence! Subsequently, within the aggregate of thought (saṃjñā-skandha), the mind detaches from the form, like a bird escaping its cage.

To ascend through the stages of sagehood and attain the body born of mastery (manomaya-kāya) is the most wondrous of wonders. Regarding this, there is the teaching of the "yin spirit" and the "yang spirit."

Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there are two locations where yin and yang have not yet been differentiated. That which is described as the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) resembles a yang-spirit;

that which is described as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is beyond the reach of those yin and yang. The former belongs to the essence of deluded thought (*vikalpa*), while the latter is the cultivation of the samādhi of right awakening (*samyak-bodhi*);

their roots and sources are fundamentally different. In sum, one destroys the two aggregates of form and sensation, while the three—perception, mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—abide [therein].

Yet, since it has not been broken, what is there to marvel at? To give rise to such a sense of wonder and claim to have realized the state of a sage would surely cause the works of Māra to surge forth.
Ānanda, when that good man is in this state, he will attain a great radiance; his mind will become luminously clear, yet internally restrained.
This is excessive. Suddenly, in that state, an inexhaustible compassion arises. Thus, even upon seeing mosquitoes and gadflies, one regards them as if they were newborn infants;

a heart of pity arises, and tears flow involuntarily. This is called the suppression and overcoming of excess through effortful application. If one realizes this for what it is, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization.
Once one awakens to this and is no longer deluded, it will naturally subside after a long time. If one takes this to be a sign of saintly attainment, then there is [error].
The demon of sorrow enters his heart and viscera; upon seeing others, he feels grief and weeps boundlessly. He loses right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) and shall fall into ruin.
These following ten sections clarify the signs of the receptivity aggregate (*vedanā-skandha*) being about to break or not yet broken; herein, first, internal suppression is clarified.

He gives rise to compassion. Ānanda, when that son of good family is within this stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)—having already opened it but not yet broken through the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*)—he attains a great radiance.
The ten directions open up clearly; there is no longer any darkness or obscurity. His mind becomes luminously enlightened.
He realized that all sentient beings equally possess this wondrous principle of luminosity, yet they suffer in vain through drowning and delusion.
He then reproached himself for his own persistent confusion, lamenting that he had not awakened early enough to deliver living beings.

Suppressing his inner passions to an extreme degree, he suddenly attained a state of tranquil emptiness, from which an inexhaustible compassion arose; such was his realization that even the most minute creatures, like mosquitoes and gadflies, were clearly perceived within it.
It is like regarding others as one's own children; out of pity for their ignorance and compassion for their falling away, one involuntarily sheds tears.
While this is also a form of "compassion of the same essence" (*samatā-karuṇā*), it arises because one’s meditative effort has suppressed [the afflictions] too excessively.

Such a state is not appropriate within the midst of correct meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Only when the practitioner recognizes this as an error and attains awakening will they be free from fault; otherwise, it is not the same [as true equanimity].
This is the Great Compassion of the same essence realized by the Sages. If one can awaken to this as delusion and not be further confused by it, this is what is called "enlightenment.
Through gradual enlightenment and gradual cessation, one returns to right mindfulness; then, the compassion that was internally suppressed will naturally subside after a long time.
If, however, one forms a conception of holiness and claims for oneself that one has already attained the Great Compassion of all Buddhas, then there is...

The demon of sorrow takes advantage of this interval to enter; upon seeing the person, it causes them to grieve and weep incessantly, whereby they lose their right concentration (*samādhi*) and give rise to immeasurable inverted and false thoughts, falling downward into ruin. As for "suppressing those who have gone too far":

the original intent was to arouse compassion and exert effort to break through the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), but by suppressing oneself excessively, one loses gentleness and kindness, and conversely—
This brings about the occasion for being possessed by demons.

Ānanda, furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, a superior sign manifests before them.
Being moved to an excessive degree, they suddenly give rise to boundless courage within that state; their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal [to the task].
Regarding the Buddhas: it is said that one can transcend three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* in a single thought-moment. This is called "transcending by means of effortful exertion.

If this is realized through awakening, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization. Once one has attained clear understanding and is no longer deluded, [the affliction] will naturally subside after a long time.

If one takes this to be a sign of saintliness, then a mad demon will enter one’s heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, one will boast and harbor an incomparable arrogance, such that one’s mind ultimately... does not ascend.

He sees the Buddha, but looking downward he does not see anyone; he loses his right concentration and is about to fall into ruin (since views are the root of the aggregate of sensation, all that follows describes the dissolution of the aggregate of form).

This explains how one invites mad demons. Ānanda, furthermore, when those sons of good family who practice the Great Samādhi see that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already dissolved—like shedding an outer garment—and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, like seeing an inner garment;

at this time, the bright mirror of the Buddha-mind reflects superior signs appearing before them. Although they have consistently heard that the mind and the Buddha are non-dual, they have never yet personally [realized it].
I have seen it. Now that I have finally beheld it all at once, I am moved beyond measure and have given rise to great valor.
This sharp and keen resolve of mine is already equal to that of all Buddhas; I declare that without passing through the kalpas of a *saṃgha*, I shall attain Buddhahood on this very spot.

This was originally intended to advance toward the destruction of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha). Yet, you suddenly became arrogant, harboring thoughts equal to those of a Buddha, reaching the point of overstepping proper boundaries, being coarse and negligent, exceeding your station, and transgressing ritual decorum.

How could you have known that although principle may be realized all at once (tunwu), matters must be eliminated gradually? Within the process of spiritual cultivation (yònggōng), how can such arrogance and transgression be tolerated?
You must surely reflect upon yourself and recognize your error; only then will you be free from blame. This is certainly not the same as the state of a Sage.

To realize this is to attain the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. If one can awaken to this and remain undeluded, then this transgressive mind will naturally subside after a long time.
However, if one forms a conception of holiness and claims that directly taking responsibility for it constitutes being a sage, [one is mistaken].
Then a fierce demon will take advantage of an opening to enter one's heart and inner being.

Encountering people, one will boast of oneself, possessing an incomparable arrogance such that one thinks, "From the heavens above to the heavens below, I alone am supreme. One will inevitably lose right concentration and fall into ruin.
Question: The Sudden Teaching does not establish stages; it is said that one transcends directly and enters [enlightenment] at once. How does this differ from the present case? Answer:

That [Sudden Teaching] was intended for those of lofty mind who contemplate the realm of the sages, yet who are themselves limited and struggling; it is merely the administration of medicine according to the illness.

It is not that the principle of perfect interfusion (yuanrong) is used to obstruct the sequential progression (xingbu). Please examine carefully the meaning of the "stages of faith" and the "stages of persons" in the School of the Lineage (Zongmen), and then [you will understand] the Sudden.

When teaching others, how could one completely abandon the conventional stages? Alas! Even for a sage who has shattered the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)—one who claims that what takes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought—this is still called "rashness and transgression," for it invites mad demons into ruin.

As for those of today who claim to have attained the "point beyond the top" and mimic [ancient masters] by reviling the Buddhas and scolding the Patriarchs, they do not know how many aggregates they themselves have shattered.

Having attained no particular stage of realization, you nevertheless dare to speak with great arrogance and boast of yourself. Your pride runs wild, and you remain complacent, unaware of your fearfulness.
The Sages have provided clear and explicit teachings; why do you not reflect upon them?
Furthermore, within that samādhi, O sons of good family, they see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear.
They have no new realization before them, yet they have lost their former ground; their power of wisdom has declined, and they fall into a state of desolation within the middle stage.

Seeing nothing at all, a great parching thirst suddenly arises in their hearts, which they constantly dwell upon without distraction throughout all times, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind while lacking wisdom, thereby losing oneself. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization.

If you take it as a sign of sainthood, then the demon of recollection will enter your heart and viscera. Morning and evening it will seize the mind (the illness lies in the word "seize"), suspending it in a single place.
You will lose right concentration and fall into ruin (this is a partiality toward meditative absorption).

This clarifies the summoning of the demon of recollection. Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, O sons of good family, when the sensation aggregate manifests as the form aggregate dissolves, the sensation aggregate has not yet been shattered.
There is no new realization from before, and the form aggregate having already been exhausted, one loses the former dwelling place.

At this juncture, you should simply maintain the equilibrium of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). By entering the stream and losing the objective referent, you will eventually achieve success.
Yet, looking back, your intellectual power has declined and weakened; unable to illuminate and see clearly, you fall between the two pillars with nothing to rely upon.

Entering the center, you lose your footing; both before and after, you are utterly confused, turning around with nothing to behold. Furthermore, you again employ the mind of concentration exclusively, completely lacking...
Irrigated by the waters of wisdom, my mind suddenly became parched with craving. Moment by moment, I contemplated deeply and dwelt in profound recollection, not daring to engage in any activity.

Maintaining this undistracted recollection as the very function of diligent effort toward breaking through and receiving [realization], this is called cultivating and treating the mind by relying exclusively on the power of concentration (*samādhi*).
It lacks the wisdom that perceives the essential emptiness of the body of sensation.
Thus, one loses one's own skillful means. If one realizes that wisdom is deficient while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is excessive, one should return to *samāpatti* (equipoise);

in this way, one may avoid fault, though it is certainly not a realization of the holy. If one takes this to be a holy realization—claiming that this sunken mind in a state of recollective concentration is naturally the proof of sainthood—then the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*) will take advantage of the interval to enter, seizing the mind day and night and suspending it [in agitation].

If one fixes [the mind] on a single point, one loses its original stability and falls into ruin. Question: The ancients said that if one places the mind on a single point, there is no task that cannot be accomplished.
How does this differ from the present case? Answer: That was a medicinal countermeasure for those with excessive distraction;
it was not a matter of exclusively suspending the mind as a form of diligence. Furthermore, how much difference is there between the characters "to grasp" (cuō) and "to suspend" (xuán)?
It requires effort and involves a degree of lack of ease. When compared with one who has settled the mind in a single place, the distinction between them is clear and decisive.

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, O sons of good family, you will see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become luminous, such that the power of wisdom surpasses the concentration itself.
They lose their vigor because they harbor various superior natures within their hearts; having already suspected their own minds to be Vairocana, they consider a small attainment to be sufficient.
This is called losing the constant discernment of the mind through attachment to intellectual views. Awakening, however, entails no fault.
This is not true realization. If you mistake it for such realization, then the demon of inferiority and easy contentment will enter your heart and innermost being.
You will see others claiming, "I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth," and you will lose your right concentration, falling into ruin (this is a partiality toward wisdom).

This clarifies the summoning of the demon of contentment. Furthermore, during that state of meditative concentration, O sons of noble family, when the experience of the dissolution of form manifests, the power of wisdom exceeds the power of concentration.
One loses the sharpness of wisdom and, harboring within one's heart and mind various superior natures, claims that buddha-nature is inherently complete and requires no cultivation.
[He] achieves [this]. He then suspects himself, thinking, "I am already Vairocana; where else could there be another Vairocana?
Is it still necessary to seek further progress? Thereupon, taking little as sufficient, he no longer advances.
This is what is meant by the object of one's mental application becoming too exalted: having lost constant scrutiny, one is unable to constantly examine oneself.
How does one's own virtue compare to the virtues of a Buddha? It is merely that one is immersed in one’s own knowledge and views, believing them to be the very knowledge and vision of a Buddha;
thus, clinging to one's innate nature while abandoning cultivation, one arrives at this state.

If one can achieve introspection and awakening, realizing with certainty that the five aggregates are not yet entirely empty, how could one possibly equal the functional power of a Buddha’s virtues? Only then can one return to being free from fault. Otherwise, it is not so.

The realization of the Sage can thus be known. If one takes the *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) as the attainment of sainthood and ceases cultivation without further progress, then a certain type of inferior demon—easily satisfied with minor gains—will attach itself to them by way of similarity and enter their very heart and viscera.

It will cause them to utter great delirious words, saying, "I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)," and claiming, "I have attained it; I have attained it. Thus they become possessed.

If one possesses the two attachments to persons and phenomena, how could there be such a thing as the ultimate truth? To lose right concentration and thereby fall into ruin is an inevitable consequence.
Question: The masters of old have said that the mind is fundamentally the Buddha and does not require cultivation to be realized.
Why is this? The answer is: this is a remedial medicine prescribed for those who, clinging solely to cultivation, neglect their own spiritual nature.
Nevertheless, there are also such expressions as "causing one to undergo a great death," "advancing further on the tip of the staff," and "exhausting the present moment."
How could this ever mean that cultivation and realization have been abandoned?

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, good sons, they see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear, yet they have not yet attained a new realization.

Therefore, the mind has already perished. (This is identical in all respects to the section on "partial concentration. Surveying the two limits—that is, the ground where the center collapses—one naturally encounters hardship and danger.
Suddenly, within the mind, an inexhaustible sorrow arises, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison;
the heart has no desire to live, and one constantly seeks someone to end one's life so as to attain liberation early. This is called failing in skillful means during practice. Awakening.

This will result in no fault; however, it does not constitute proof of sainthood. If you mistake this for such realization, then a portion of the demon of constant sorrow and anxiety will enter your heart and viscera.

Grasping a sword in hand, he will cut his own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of his life-span. Alternatively, one may become constantly sorrowful and flee into mountain forests, unable to bear the sight of others.
Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), one shall surely fall into ruin.

This clarifies the summoning of the demon of sorrow. Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, O sons of good family, when the experience of the dissolution of form manifests, the new realization that breaks through sensation has not yet been protected, while the old mind that broke through form has already perished.
Surveying these two boundaries of form and sensation, one does not cling to the village ahead nor attach to the shore behind, like one standing on a precipice, fearing a fall.
Falling into ruin, seeing this peril, the mind gives rise to great anxiety; excessive worry leads to ignorance, which in turn results in madness.
It is like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking poisonous medicine; one loathes life and seeks death, desiring only the thought of liberation.

This anxiety originally arises from the practice of being cautious and fearful, which is itself a form of cultivation; however, when it becomes excessive, there is no longer any way to find relief or consolation.
Thus, it has come to this. If one could but understand that the Great Way is exceedingly level—simply letting go—is there any fault or cause for anxiety?
Furthermore, how can excessive worry constitute the realization of a sage? If one were to persistently hold that worry is itself the state of a sage...
If one refuses to relax and release oneself, the demon of constant anxiety and sorrow will take advantage of the opportunity to enter.
One may then seize a sword or blade to cut oneself, flee to the mountains and forests to avoid people, suffer from violent insanity, or lose right concentration (*samādhi*).
And thus one falls into ruin. The Patriarch said: "The Great Way is vast and remote; why be so busy? He also said:
"In silent stillness, one knows for oneself that the ground is secure; in carefree ease, who would let their belly grow bloated? And he further said: "Relax the four elements."
Do not grasp at things and so forth; through immeasurable skillful means, one may forget all sorrow. How could one allow Māra to find an opportunity? Zong said:
Because new realization has not yet been attained, the mind has already perished, and thus the demon of anxiety arises. Since there is no new realization before one, [the demon finds its chance].

When one loses their former dwelling, the "demon of recollection" (*smṛti-māra*) arises. What is the distinction between them? The first type sees that both the preceding and succeeding states have been simultaneously relinquished;

they neither wish to maintain the former nor wish to move toward the latter, and thus seek a separate path from between them. For this reason, day and night they constrain the mind, harboring thoughts and fixating on them, whereby the demon of recollection enters.
The second type also sees that both the preceding and succeeding states have been simultaneously relinquished, yet they wish to maintain the former.
Furthermore, when one is about to fall back from the desire realm, two thoughts arise simultaneously, and one does not know which will prevail. Because of this, one's calculations become unsettled;
wandering in confusion and distressed, one fears that Māra has entered.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, noble sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
Abiding in purity, once their minds have become tranquil and secure, there suddenly arises within them an infinite joy; their hearts are filled with such rapture that they cannot restrain themselves.
This is called "light ease" (praśrabdhi) without wisdom, a form of self-restraint. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy.
If one takes it to be a holy realization, then a portion of the demon of "delightful joy" will enter one's heart and viscera, causing one to laugh upon seeing people by the side of the road.
They sing and dance by themselves, claiming to have attained unimpeded liberation; yet they lose their meditative absorption and are destined for downfall.

This clarifies how one invites the demon of joy (*nandī-māra*). Furthermore, during that concentration, O sons of good family, when the perception of form has subsided and the perception of sensation manifests, while dwelling in purity and the mind has attained stability, suddenly an infinite joy arises within the heart.
One experiences joy and cannot stop oneself; this is called attaining lightness and ease by chance.

Lacking the power of wisdom to restrain oneself, one might observe with the eye of wisdom and realize that this is but a shallow realization—what cause for deep rejoicing? Thus, the wind of joy will naturally subside.
It still results in no blame, because this is not the same as the realization of a sage.
If one claims that delighting in the Way is what the mind of a sage ought to do, and thus rejoices without ceasing, then the demon of joy will take advantage of the interval to enter.

Such a person laughs upon seeing others, dances and sings within themselves, claiming that the mountain of knives and the mass of fire are all simply sites of practice (bodhimaṇḍa), and that wine shops and brothels are nothing other than liberation.
How could you know that within the pure mind not even a hair’s breadth of form stands? Once right concentration is lost, how can one avoid falling into ruin?

Furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) vanish and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear; they then consider themselves sufficient.

Suddenly, groundless and great *māna* (pride) arises. (*Māna* is one of the seven types of pride; it is the general category of all prides. The seven prides are: *māna*, *atimāna*, *mānātimāna*, *asmimāna*, *abhimāna*, *ūnamāna*, and *mithyāmāna*).

Thus, even up to: *māna* (conceiving oneself superior to those who are inferior, or equal to those who are equal—this is *māna*), *atimāna* (conceiving oneself equal to those who are superior, or superior to those who are equal—this is *atimāna*), as well as *mānātimāna* (conceiving oneself superior to those who are superior—this is *mānātimāna*), or *adhimāna* (claiming to have attained what has not been attained, or considering oneself much superior to those who are inferior—this is *adhimāna*), or...

The pride of inferiority (the state of regarding oneself as lowly and insignificant in the presence of those who are vastly superior, thereby failing to show respect or seek [instruction], thus becoming stubborn and inferior) may arise simultaneously with other states;

even then, one still holds the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt within one’s heart, let alone those of lower rank such as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. This is called "seeing superiority while lacking the wisdom to save oneself.
If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization. If one interprets this as a sign of sainthood, then a portion of the great demon of *māna* (arrogance) has entered.

In their hearts and minds, they do not revere stupas or temples, but instead destroy scriptures and images. They say to the donors: "These [images] are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood;

the scriptures are but leaves from trees, or perhaps layers of flowers. The physical body is eternally real and true, yet you do not show it respect, while instead you honor clay and wood—this is truly a perversion.
Those who have deep faith follow them in destroying and breaking [the objects], burying and discarding them in the ground. Thus they harbor doubts.
They delude sentient beings, causing them to enter the Avīci Hell and lose their right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), leading inevitably to their downfall.

This clarifies how they invite the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*). Furthermore, during that state of meditative absorption, when the various good sons perceive the manifestation of the dissolution of form into sensation, they immediately become complacent and arrogant, failing to seek the seal of approval from their teachers. Suddenly, without cause—
Great conceit arises; they hold themselves in high esteem while disparaging others, with haughty gait and inflated air.

This extends even to mere pride and the pride of inferiority, all erupting simultaneously. Within their minds, even a Tathāgata would be held in contempt, let alone those below the level of a Śrāvaka.
Compared to the previous case of biased wisdom, this is more deluded, and its faults are even more severe. They merely claim that from the beginning...
"To be equal to the Buddhas" means here to surpass all Buddhas. The arising of pride always stems from viewing oneself as superior;
it is only through a lack of wisdom that this affliction persists. If one possesses the wisdom of introspection, one perceives that all phenomena are equal and devoid of high or low.
If one does not perceive even a single sentient being toward whom one could feel pride, how much less so regarding the various sages?

This is precisely the non-sagely realization of ego-inflation (*māna*), which everyone knows. If one persists in this delusion without reforming it and instead takes it to be the realization of a sage, then the demon of arrogance will seize the opportunity to enter the mind.

Suddenly, one will neglect pagodas and temples without paying them homage, and destroy scriptures and images without a second thought, even going so far as to tell patrons that Buddha images are merely made of gold, copper, earth, or wood, and that Buddhist scriptures are... [merely paper].
To heap up leaves and flowers while failing to show reverence to one’s own living Buddha, yet instead venerating mere earth and wood—what is the purpose of this?
If a donor places their faith in such things, they will surely destroy and bury [the true object of veneration]; thus they mislead themselves and others, and their transgression is grave.
They shall enter the Avīci Hell as swiftly as an arrow; this is their own loss of right concentration and their willing descent into ruin. Who can hold them accountable?

Question: Linji’s refusal to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda, Danxia’s burning of the wooden Buddha, Deshan’s statement that the entire Tripitaka is like wiping away snot and spittle, and Yantou’s remark that the words of the patriarchs are like worn-out straw sandals—are these not instances of great arrogance?
Answer: These were acts taken because they clung to seeking [the truth] externally without realizing one's own mind, and because they clung to words and teachings.
To those who are unwilling to advance in their practice, these stern and urgent words are spoken to rouse them; they are, in fact, an expression of pure, genuine compassion.
If the Patriarchs truly possessed a mind of arrogance, they would not have avoided the *naraka* hells themselves—how much less could others do so?
In recent times, this kind of demon has become ubiquitous everywhere; they speak nonsense at will and boast with great words without shame, deceiving both themselves and others.
Humans are ignorant of heaven and ignorant of earth; when reading the sutra to this point, they should likewise be struck with awe and know to feel fear. ○ Zhong says:
There are seven types of pride (*māna*); the sutra omits "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*).

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, sons of good family may perceive the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becoming clear and bright.

Within this state of refined spirit and clarity—this being precisely what the Buddha first pointed out as the fundamental source of the clarity of consciousness—they achieve a perfect realization of the subtle principle and attain great accord. Suddenly, their minds give rise to immeasurable lightness and tranquility;
they claim to have become sages and attained great mastery. This is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom; yet, upon true awakening, it vanishes.
This is a fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization. If you mistake this for such realization, then a portion of the "delusive demon of lightness and purity" will enter your heart and viscera.
You will then consider yourself satisfied and no longer seek further progress. Such individuals mostly become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead future generations and fall into the Avīci Hell.
Having lost right concentration, they shall surely sink into ruin.

This is called "summoning the light Māra. Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, O sons of good family, when the sensation of form arises as it dissolves, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has already been shattered;

thus, one attains lucidity and vigor. As the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) is about to be exhausted, one is able to perfectly realize the subtle principle and obtain the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*);
thus, one attains great compliance, such that whatever one directs toward is as one wishes. Yet, suddenly...
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) means being free from all heaviness and rigidity; it is "light. It means a vast awakening and mastery; it is "ease.
Having given rise to pliancy, one then considers oneself satisfied, believing one has become a sage and attained great liberation.

One does not realize that this is merely a temporary awakening and a transient manifestation of such a state—wherein one perceives body and mind as being like clouds or shadows, having left behind coarseness and turbidity to attain lightness.
Clear your ears! Practitioners must realize that this lightness and purity is merely temporary; you must urgently expel it, for only then can you be free from fault.
How could there be any realization of sainthood? Why then should you be self-satisfied? If you remain deluded and fail to awaken, you will sit fixedly within the cave of lightness and purity.

If one refuses to wade through the mud and water but instead strives forward with diligence, then demons will attach themselves to such a person, causing them to become complacent and self-satisfied, ultimately becoming a monk of no renown.
Not only do they bring ruin upon themselves, but they also mislead many others;
furthermore, filled with regret and slandering the Buddha, they fall into the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration, descending into the abyss.

Furthermore, within that samādhi, O sons of good family, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear and manifest, one attains a nature of empty luminosity amidst this enlightened clarity.
Suddenly, within that state, one turns toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect, and enters exclusively into emptiness.

When the realization of emptiness manifests before one, and even if a mind arises that conceives of long-term annihilation, there is no fault provided one awakens to this state; it is not yet a holy realization.
If one treats it as a holy realization, then an "emptiness-demon" will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to slander the observance of precepts and label them as the "Lesser Vehicle."

When a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness, what is there to be maintained or transgressed? Such a person constantly drinks wine and eats meat, and extensively engages in sexual misconduct with faithful lay donors.
By means of demonic power, they captivate those people so that no suspicion or slander arises; the ghostly mind has long since entered them.
Some consume excrement and urine, along with alcohol and meat, thereby violating the Buddha’s precepts and erroneously leading others into sin (it is likely "leading people into sin").
They lose right concentration and shall surely fall into ruin.
This clarifies the summoning of the phantom-demon of emptiness (*śūnyatā-māra*).

Furthermore, when those sons of good family within that samādhi reach the stage where form dissolves and sensation manifests, the ten directions open up like a cave, becoming suddenly and brilliantly clear. Within this luminous awakening, they attain the nature of empty luminosity.
In a state of profound stillness, no dharma can be apprehended. The mind suddenly turns toward eternal extinction.

One perceives that there is neither action nor reception, and one dismisses cause and effect as non-existent; yet both cause and effect are empty. One sees only the empty mind manifest before oneself, while all else is severed and extinguished.
This is entirely due to grasping at a false clarity, which leads to this state. If one realizes that this emptiness is evil—
If one grasps at emptiness as being non-ultimate emptiness, then there is no fault. However, how could the emptiness of annihilation be a realization of the sages?
If one takes this to be a saintly understanding and clings to it without changing, then the demon of emptiness will enter the mind, causing one to cling to emptiness and slander the precepts.
They claim that drinking alcohol and eating meat are entirely empty; that practicing filth and engaging in sexual misconduct are none other than the Way.

They regard those who uphold the precepts as followers of the Lesser Vehicle and as being attached to them, while they regard those who break the precepts as followers of the Great Vehicle and as having attained thorough awakening.
Furthermore, since the ghost has entered for a long time, it cannot distinguish between fragrance and filth; it even equates excrement and urine with wine and meat.
By violating the rules of discipline (*vinaya*), it leads people into transgression. It is certain that such a being will lose right reception (*samyak-samādāna*) and fall into ruin. Question:
As for those such as Master Zhi, Kumārajīva, the Three Chariots, Xiǎnzǐ, the Wine Immortal, and Bùdài—how are they to be understood? The answer is:
these were all great Bodhisattvas who manifested in response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to perform Buddha-work and to untangle the entanglements and loosen the bonds of sentient beings.
How could this be called the denial of cause and effect?

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, O sons of good family, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, one relishes its empty luminosity.

(Previously, one had merely attained the nature of empty luminosity; now, one becomes addicted to and delights in it. This enters deeply into the marrow of the heart, and suddenly an infinite love arises within the mind.

When this love reaches its peak, it gives rise to madness, which is then greed and desire. This is called "the state of concentration being peaceful and compliant as it enters the mind, yet lacking wisdom to sustain itself," leading to error.

Entering into various desires, one incurs no fault upon awakening; it is not considered a holy realization. If one takes this for a holy realization, then the Mara of Desire will enter one's heart and innermost being, constantly preaching that desire is the path to Bodhi.
Such a person transforms laypeople into practicing desire with equanimity—“equanimity” here meaning “the common way.
Those who engage in sexual misconduct are called "sons and disciples who uphold the Dharma. By the power of spirits and ghosts, they will gather followers during the Final Age.
These common fools numbered in the hundreds—thus reaching one hundred, two hundred, or even five or six hundred, up to many millions.

(Considering the subsequent phrase regarding the king’s difficulty, it appears that "common fools" specifically refers to women; yet how could such a profusion of sexual misconduct occur? The Buddha’s words are not false; such things will surely come to pass in the depths of the future Dharma-ending age.
The demon’s mind grew weary and he departed from their bodies. Deprived of their majestic power, they fell into the king’s difficulties, misleading and confusing the masses.
They are born and enter the Avīci Hell; they lose their correct meditative absorption and shall fall into ruin.

This clarifies how one invites the Mara of Desire. Furthermore, when those sons of good family within that concentration experience the manifestation of the dissolution of form into sensation, they perceive a sense of empty luminosity and become attached to its flavor. Clinging to it without relinquishing it, this attachment penetrates deep into their very marrow; thus their minds—
Suddenly, infinite craving arises. Because of the flavor, craving is born; when craving reaches its peak, it becomes madness. Consequently, right desire is transformed into lustful desire.
This is because, within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), a subtle touch (*praśrabdhi*) arises, which is experienced with such mastery that it is beyond all analogy.

There are those who say that what exceeds sensual pleasure is precisely the source of sexual desire. This clarifies that these are the wondrous tactile sensations experienced within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which settle peacefully and accord with the mind.
However, lacking the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) to maintain them, one may mistakenly enter into various forms of lust.
One should properly employ the power of wisdom to observe them, accepting nothing at all; by relinquishing and transcending them, one may avoid such transgressions.

How could this be regarded as proof of sainthood? If one remains deluded and does not abandon it, yet takes it to be the realization of a sage, then the Mara of desire enters the mind, causing one to preach that desire is the Way, to practice desire oneself, and to incite others to practice desire.
The number of foolish women gathered to satisfy one's own desires reaches a full ten million; yet, that upon which one relies is Mara.
They possess only the power of ghosts. When the Māras grow weary and depart, their supernatural powers immediately vanish. Because they entice the ignorant, they are clearly cast into secular law;
because they mislead others, they sink into the dark realm of Avīci. Wandering and wasting away, they lose right concentration and fall into ruin—how can they be saved?
The preceding section was categorized under the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*); this section is categorized under the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*).
Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifestations that appear during *dhyāna* are all caused by the interaction of the mind with the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).

[The term "interaction" (*jiaohu*) has the same meaning as in the previous section, though the phrasing differs slightly; for instance, when one attains radiant clarity, up to the attainment of the nature of empty luminosity, it is because the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) has surpassed deluded thought (*vikalpa*). When boundless compassion arises, up to the birth of limitless attachment, it is because deluded thought has surpassed the power of contemplation.

Therefore, these phenomena manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these conditions, they remain confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming:
To claim to have attained the state of a sage constitutes a great falsehood and results in falling into the Avīci Hell.

You all should likewise carry the words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them throughout the Dharma-ending age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity;
maintain and protect these teachings so that they may lead to the attainment of the Unsurpassed Way.
This is a summary of the ten characteristics of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Ānanda, these ten kinds of objects manifested during *dhyāna* are all produced by the mutual assault and combat between the aggregate of sensation and the application of the mind. It is only because sentient beings are stubborn and deluded [that they fail to see this].
Unwilling to reflect upon or examine themselves, when they encounter such circumstances, they fail to recognize even the names of these conditions.
Unaware that this is a transgression, they falsely claim to have attained sainthood; having committed a great lie, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
To claim attainment only to fall into hell—this is truly pitiable. You all should likewise transmit my words from today to others.
Come! May this cause all sentient beings to attain awakening, so that the celestial Māras shall retreat from their abodes.

In the age of the Final Dharma, may all be preserved, protected, and brought to the realization of the Unsurpassed Way. Ānanda, exert yourself! According to these ten types, the works of Māra have already been accomplished;
they are not merely the initial provocations as described previously. This is why they differ from those of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). Nevertheless...
It is merely said that demons arrive in accordance with their kind and enter the human mind in darkness, causing one to fall into delusion without realizing it;
however, this does not yet involve the celestial demons who dispatch their essences to fly into people, which is why it differs from the *xiang-yin* (the aggregate of perceptions).

Ānanda, when that son of good family practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet ended, his mind separates from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.

He is already able to achieve this and, from this ordinary body, ascend through the sixty sacred stages of a Bodhisattva (the fifty-five stages, with the stage of Dry Wisdom added before and the stage of Sublime Enlightenment added after, making fifty-seven; together with the three preceding gradual stages, they exactly total sixty). [Question: Why is it that from an ordinary body one can thus traverse these stages? [Answer: This refers to the Perfect [Teaching].

The Sudden [Vehicle] possesses the most acute faculties. Without taking realization as a substantial attainment, one ascends through the various stages in this very ordinary body, thereby manifesting that perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential progression. This is exemplified by those such as Sudhana and the Dragon Girl; it is not like the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), where one takes realization as a substantial attainment, traverses three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and only thereafter attains the fruit.

One attains the "body born of mental mastery" (*manomaya-kāya*). This is metaphorically described as being as swift and unimpeded as the movement of a wish-fulfilling gem. There are three types: 1. The Body Born of Mental Mastery Consisting of the Joy of Entering Samādhi: This refers to the mind being tranquil and unmoving. It corresponds to the stage of semblance from the first to the seventh faith, which is the position of entering emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

2. The Body Born of Mental Mastery Consisting of the Self-Nature of Dharmas: This refers to universally entering Buddha-fields, taking the Dharma as its self-nature. It corresponds to the eighth faith and beyond within the stage of semblance, which is the position of emerging into the provisional (*upāya*). 3. The Body Born of Mental Mastery Arising Spontaneously from All Categories... [text ends]

The "body born of mental attention" (*manomaya-kāya*) refers to realizing the Dharma realized by the Buddha; this corresponds to the stages of the nine faiths and ten faiths, which constitute the middle stage of cultivation. Those who study the arts of immortality often regard the emergence of the "yang-spirit" (*yang-shen*) as a supreme achievement, yet they do not realize that within the tradition of Śākyamuni, even the three types of *manomaya-kāya* at the shallow stages are wondrously transcendent and beyond compare—let alone the ten bodies of the deep stages.

To look back with false claims that these are merely "yin-spirits" (*yin-shen*) is truly the speech of one devoid of knowledge. Moving wherever one goes without obstruction is like, for example, a person...

When one is in deep sleep and speaks in a dream, although this person has no distinct cognition, the words formed possess rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing those who are not asleep to fully understand their meaning.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). If all stirring thoughts are exhausted...

Floating thoughts are eliminated. Within the awakened, luminous mind, it is like removing dust and grime. When the cycle of birth and death is illuminated from beginning to end as a single continuum, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Examining its origin, one finds it to be a pervasive delusion.
This is considered its fundamental basis.
This passage describes the characteristics of the beginning and end of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception).

Ānanda, when that virtuous man, practicing *samādhi*, has exhausted the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation), his delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are already exhausted, and his discriminating attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*) is also exhausted; however, the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) remain.
It has not yet been eliminated. The innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) still persists, and the outflows (*āsrava*) have not been exhausted.

It is only upon reaching the stage of the seventh faith, where one no longer undergoes future existence, that the outflows are truly exhausted. Since this [stage] falls within the second or third faith, the outflows are not yet exhausted.

Nevertheless, although one does not attain the exhaustion of outflows—and thus lacks the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) and eighteen transformations of the four fruits—one has already exhausted the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and no longer clings to it.
Because of these physical characteristics, the mind is able to depart from its form, like a bird escaping from a cage, moving freely wherever it intends.
Having already achieved this, one traverses the sixty sacred stages of a bodhisattva from this ordinary body;

whereas those who follow the Separate Teaching (biejiao) must attain only a single portion after many lifetimes and kalpas to reach each stage, one here is able to traverse them all instantaneously with an ordinary body.
This is what is meant by "perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential progression. Thus, one attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), moving everywhere without obstruction;
it is swift without haste, arriving without traveling. These are all the signs of having exhausted the [coarse] aggregates.

Nevertheless, although one has attained the mind-made body, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered; it is just like when the affliction of a nightmare has ceased, yet one has not yet awakened from deep sleep.

It is like speaking in one's sleep. Although this person speaking in their sleep does not know for themselves what they are saying, the words uttered nonetheless form a melodic cadence and possess a logical sequence, such that those who are awake can all understand their speech.
This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
It is because one is shrouded by sensation (*vedanā*) that, although one's seeing and hearing are comprehensive, they are entirely useless—like being paralyzed during a nightmare.

One who is shrouded by perception, while having more utility than the former, is still unable to fully illuminate birth and death—like a nightmare having subsided yet still speaking in dreams; these are not the words of one who has awakened. [End of section.]

There is nothing known. This is the sign that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been destroyed. Now, the luminous awareness is like a mirror, and floating thoughts are like dust.

The dust moves while the mirror remains still. If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating thoughts are eliminated, then within the essence of the mind of luminous awareness, it will be like a bright mirror set upon its stand, receiving not a single speck of dust. When the dust is cleared away, the nature of the mirror is naturally luminous.

When the perceptions are eliminated and the awakened clarity is naturally pure, one is then able to know from where the birth of the uniform, segmented life-and-death within the triple world comes, and to where its death goes;
thus, there is a complete illumination from beginning to end. This is the sign that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been shattered.
Although perception occupies the middle position among the five aggregates, both the two preceding it and the two following it depend upon it.
These are false imaginings, differing in their coarse and subtle degrees; how much more so for all the root and secondary afflictions?

Apart from this aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), they ultimately have no substance. Therefore, when perception is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of afflictions. Thus one contemplates the origin of this aggregate of perception.

Thus, pervasive conceptualization (yǒngtōng wǎngxiǎng) serves as its foundation. For conceptualization is capable of fusing and transforming, causing the mind to follow objects and objects to follow the mind.
It is like imagining sour plums, which causes saliva to flow from the mouth; it can penetrate through material obstructions. Therefore, it is called pervasive conceptualization.
Such is the characteristic of the beginning and end of the aggregate of conceptualization (xiǎng yīn).

Ānanda, when that son of good family’s aggregate of perception (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and he has not encountered perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration (samādhi) becomes luminous.
Within this samādhi, his mind comes to cherish perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful methods.

At that time, a celestial Māra, waiting for such an opportunity, dispatches his essence to possess another person. (The term "dispatching" [fei] means sending swiftly, like the "fei" in "fèi qiè" or "fèi piào"; "essence" [jing] refers to the Māra's followers, various ghosts and demons; "possessing another person" means taking possession of someone else.)

This is because those who have exhausted their karmic retribution cannot penetrate the core of one's heart; thus, they delude others by means of bystanders. They speak of the sutras and the Dharma, yet the person does not realize they are possessed by a māra.

They claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa (the person referred to is the one upon whom they have attached themselves). They come to the place of that seeker of skillful means, the good son, where they arrange seats and preach the Dharma.
For a brief moment, their form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see them, or they may become a Cakravartin king.
[The Buddha] explained: "Sometimes [the demon] appears as a woman, or as a bhikṣuṇī; or he may appear in a dark room with his body emitting light.

This person—being a seeker of skillful means—is deluded and confused, mistaking him for a bodhisattva. They place faith in his teachings, which agitate their minds and cause them to violate the Buddhist precepts while secretly practicing lust.

(These three phrases describe the demon’s delusion of the practitioner; this is the core intent. For when the practitioner’s threefold training is flawless and they advance with the speed of flight, the palaces of Māra tremble with fear, and thus he devises schemes to disturb them, seeking only to break their precepts.)"

If one leads others toward lust, both concentration and wisdom will be drawn into the depraved; the body becomes a child of Māra, and Māra finds peace and security. If one’s wisdom is strong, this very thing becomes a mirror for illuminating Māra, allowing one to observe his spiritual transformations at will, which are unfathomable.

Yet, by simply observing how he destroys precepts and entices others with lust, one knows he is Māra; how could one possibly be deluded by him? He delights in speaking of disasters, auspicious signs, and strange anomalies;

sometimes he says the Tathāgata has appeared in such-and-such a place, or speaks of the kalpa-ending fires, or of wars and weapons, terrifying people and causing their wealth and property to waste away without cause.
Disperse! This is called the "Strange Ghost," who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb this person. Once his heart is satisfied, he departs from the person’s body.

Both the disciple and the master—the seeker of skillful means and the teacher of the Dharma—shall together fall into royal peril (for using demonic speech to delude the masses, the king’s law must execute them).

You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter saṃsāra; if you are confused and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. (The afflictions of thought are the root of the aggregate of perception; the ten types [of demons] described below all arise from this.)
[This arises] from the activation of craving).

The following ten sections clarify the signs of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) being about to break or not yet having broken; herein, first, it clarifies how craving leads to becoming a strange ghost.
Ānanda, when that good man’s aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) has already been exhausted, his seeing and hearing become all-pervasive and empty.
It is subtle and wondrous, detached from bodily functions. In the interim, one is not deluded by the ten objects of perception and does not encounter perverse thoughts.
By means of this empty, subtle, and perfect concentration (*samādhi*), one illuminates the realm where sensation is exhausted.
When the practitioner is within this *samādhi*, it is precisely right to let not a single thought arise and press forward. Alas, how can the mind still crave perfect luminosity? At this point—

Regarding the illumination through perfect concentration: one gives rise to a single heart of attachment, desiring to cause the awakened mind to be perfectly bright and luminous, such that there is nothing it does not know and understand, and that all skillful means are accomplished without exception.

Desiring to deliver sentient beings through the practice of teaching and transformation, one thus exerts oneself with sharp thought and greedily seeks after skillful means. This single instance of greed is precisely the root of stirring up demons.
At that time, the celestial Māra, seeing that [the practitioner] had attained the profound state of the exhaustion of sensation (vedanā-kṣaya-samādhi), became personally uneasy.

He then waited for an opportunity to exploit his craving for skillful means and immediately dispatched a malevolent spirit (*piśāca*). This spirit entered another person, who was then able to spontaneously recite the scriptures and the Dharma without cause.
This was because those who seek skillful means are themselves deluded by skillful means; as for the person possessed by the spirit, he did not...
Possessed by Māra, he claimed that he himself had already attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
He came before those seekers of skill, spread out his seat, and preached the Dharma; fearing they might not believe him, he further employed supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi*) to subdue them.

Why, then, is "unchanging" (*avikāra*) added? Thus, we know that there is no further alteration; it simply refers to this principle of causeless spontaneity (*svabhāva*), which remains unshaken through the passage of time. Let the student examine this carefully.
This is what is called the first heterodox school establishing the doctrine of causelessness.
These two types of causelessness were both established by heterodox practitioners of former ages; they are doctrines that contradict reason and oppose the truth.
How is it that, at the moment the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to open up, one falsely calculates and falls into this? It is because they do not understand the good.

Evil arises according to one's karma. One falsely calculates that before eighty thousand kalpas there was spontaneous existence, and after eighty thousand kalpas there will be spontaneous non-existence;
thus one forms a theory of annihilationism, which is subsumed under wrong views. ○ He said:
