Among the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions, there is a distinct school of teachers who propound causelessness (*ahetuvāda*). It is not that these practitioners have suddenly fallen into this [annihilationist] view.
This person establishes for themselves the theory of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).
Ānanda, when these good sons within *samādhi* concentrate their clarity and stabilize their minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. It is such a person who, amidst this perfect and eternal reality, gives rise to conceptual speculation. This person—
They fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
This clarifies the second calculation of universal permanence. Ānanda, within this samādhi (and so forth), it is the fundamental source of constant agitation;
although one may exhaustively reach the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), it remains shrouded, and its subtle, hidden flux has not yet been perceived.

Regarding those who have not yet attained pervasiveness or permanence, they prematurely calculate that pervasiveness and permanence exist; such persons fall into the four heterodox theories of pervasive permanence.

Although all four types arise from calculations based on the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), the first three all involve investigating other phenomena, distinguishing the duration of kalpas according to the breadth or narrowness of those phenomena; only the fourth is devoid of this.
While these [other views] are also mentioned, they do not speak of the duration of the kalpas; this is their distinction. Changshui says:

"The arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) continues without interruption, and is thus called 'constant. Furthermore, the four types [of permanence] they calculate pervade all phenomena, and are thus called 'universal' (yuan).
Wēnnǚng says: "'Universal' is synonymous with 'round' (yuan). Therefore, the name 'universal constancy' (biàncháng) is established here, and later it is concluded as 'round constancy' (yuáncháng)."

First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects; finding no cause for these two realms, they cultivate the practice until they can know the births and deaths of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions over twenty thousand kalpas.
They perceive that all these beings circulate in an endless cycle, never being lost or scattered, and thus reckon them to be permanent.
What are the four theories of universal permanence? First, this person’s perceptions break through their habitual conduct and manifest.

Riding upon the opening of this mind, they then investigate the inner mind and external objects to the very limit, seeking from what origin they originally arise. Thus, they perceive two locations: the mind and its objects.
All arise without cause. However, the phenomena they investigate are coarse and narrow; thus, the scope of their vision is limited.
Even when investigating the cultivation of the mind and its objects to beyond twenty thousand kalpas, they remain in a state of dark ignorance regarding what lies beyond.
They can only know that within these twenty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings cycle through birth and death without ever being lost.
Therefore, they do not reckon that there is no cause beyond the kalpas, and thus do not hold it to be annihilated; rather, they reckon only the continuity within the kalpas to be universally eternal.
This differs from the previous reckoning and constitutes the first theory of universal permanence.

Second, this person exhaustively investigates the source of the four great elements. Believing that the four natures are eternally abiding, they cultivate the practice until they can know the births and deaths of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas;
they perceive that all these are fundamentally constant and have never been lost, and thus reckon them to be permanent.

Second, this person’s perception of breaking through conditioned formations manifests; riding upon this opening of the mind, they see that all phenomena are formed from the combination of the four great elements.
Therefore, they apply their intention to exhaustively investigate them, reaching the ultimate source, and thus perceive the fundamental nature of the four great elements.

It is originally and eternally abiding. By practicing in reliance upon this, one is eventually able to penetrate and illuminate that, although sentient beings within forty thousand kalpas undergo birth and death, the substance of the four great elements is constant and eternal, having never been dispersed or lost from the beginning;
thus, they again reckon it to be permanent. Because the phenomena investigated are somewhat more detailed and extensive, their illumination of the kalpas is twice as great.
This constitutes the second type of the doctrine of universal permanence.
Third, this person exhaustively investigates the fundamental origin and locus within the six sense faculties, the manas, the grasping, and the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Because its nature is eternally constant, through cultivation one is able to know that all sentient beings within eighty thousand kalpas circulate without loss;
they are fundamentally and permanently abiding, and thus it is reckoned as permanent.

Third, after this person’s mind has opened through practice, they thoroughly investigate the six consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the seventh consciousness of *manas* and the eighth consciousness that appropriates [the body].
They take these eight consciousnesses of the mind and seven consciousnesses of the intellect...
Regarding the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) among the six consciousnesses, he exhaustively investigates its fundamental source.
Yet, he does not realize that it is still shrouded by the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). This so-called fundamental source is merely the *saṃskāra-skandha* itself;
it is limited to the seventh stage and has not yet reached the eighth. Consequently, he falsely claims it to be truly permanent and, relying upon this, practices until he is able to observe it.
Throughout eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings die here and are born there, yet their fundamental nature remains eternally abiding.
This is because the sixth and eighth consciousnesses both take the seventh consciousness as the root source of their arising and ceasing;

therefore, they mistakenly reckon this root source of arising and ceasing to be an eternally abiding nature. It is like seeing a thin stream and calling it still water—such people have not yet even caught sight of the eight consciousnesses.

If even the flow of the True and Constant is thus, how much more so the wondrous nature of Bodhi! What is called the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas, the deluded call the "original person.

It is precisely because the Dharma-gate of the Eight Consciousnesses which he has investigated is profound, vast, detailed, and pertinent—ten times greater than the previous four elements—that the number of kalpas he knows is also ten times that of the former person; thus he constitutes the third universal [stage].
This is the Constant Discourse. Question: Since the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) has not yet been opened, how can one suddenly exhaust the eight consciousnesses?

Answer: The eight consciousnesses are merely the dharma-gates used for further cultivation after this person’s mind has opened. As for "thoroughly penetrating" (*cheda*) versus "not yet thoroughly penetrated," one is permitted to speak of "exhausting" them only when they have been thoroughly exhausted.
This is, for example, like a śrāvaka exhausting the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; he merely exhausts birth and death, but how could he penetrate the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*)?
Furthermore, there are four points. This person, having exhausted the source of ideation, finds that within the fundamental principle (*li*) there is no longer any flowing, ceasing, or movement.

The mind of ideation, characterized by arising and ceasing, has now been eternally extinguished. Within this principle, it naturally becomes non-arising and non-ceasing; yet, because they have measured this through their own minds, they reckon it to be permanent.
Fourth: Once this person has exhausted the source of perception (*saṃjñā*), there is no further principle for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) to arise.
They then conclude that these various movements, transitions, and modes of arising and ceasing all belong to the mind of perception;

now that they have been eternally extinguished, the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing naturally belongs to mental formations (*saṃskāra*). Without further investigation or observation, they recklessly take this to be permanent. This is [the view of permanence].
Even the first [of these views] is shallow and inferior; how much more so the second and third? Therefore, one cannot establish a kalpa-length that can be known.
Measuring what is knowable, it certainly does not reach twenty thousand kalpas. This is the fourth "Theory of Universal Permanence.
○ Wénlíng states that the "principle of life" (*shēnglǐ*) is the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); otherwise, the phrase "even more so" (*gèng wú*) would be impossible to explain.
If the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) no longer exists, how could there be further false conceptualizations below it?

Because of this calculation of permanence, one loses right universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the second type of non-Buddhist doctrine: the theory of the established perfect permanence.
Because of this calculation of permanence, one perceives what is not all-pervasive as all-pervasive, and what is not truly eternal as truly eternal.
Thus, one falls into false awakening and loses right awakening; this is called the second type of externalist who establishes the doctrine of pervasive permanence.
How is it that at the moment the skandha of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to open, one falsely calculates and falls into this? This...

All four [of these views] take arising and ceasing to be the perfect and eternal; they are subsumed within the category of extreme views. Regarding the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, which suddenly exhausts the eight consciousnesses:

now, at the point where the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ended, one fails to understand the subtle arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and falsely conceives it to be permanent.
How could this be "suddenly exhausting" [the eight consciousnesses]? If one truly understood the eight consciousnesses, how could such a divergent conception arise?

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who maintain a firm and concentrated upright mind—(the character "firm" being substituted for "stable," which is superior to the former)—Māra finds no opportunity.
Exhausting the root of all living beings, one contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

Within this state of self and other, those who give rise to conceptual calculations fall into the four inverted views, specifically the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
This clarifies the third pair of dualistic calculations: permanence and impermanence.

Furthermore, within samādhi, O sons of good family, after you have visualized the manifestation of all conditioned activities, you should contemplate your own body as well as the bodies of others and the lands of sentient beings.
Those who give rise to false and deluded discrimination fall into the four kinds of inverted, heterodox views of the non-Buddhists:

the doctrine that some things are impermanent while others are permanent. This is because within the nature of equality, there is fundamentally no self or other, yet they falsely conceptualize self and other;
within the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, there is fundamentally no biased attachment, yet they falsely cling to the two extremes. Furthermore, regarding the Śūraṅgama...

O King, it is only when all matters are ultimately firm and stable that one attains perfect enlightenment. To now calculate by dividing the eternal from the impermanent is therefore to fall into perverted views.

First, this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate *ātman* (the "Lord Principle" among the twenty-five categories of the non-Buddhists, meaning that all phenomena are his possessions and that this spirit is their sovereign).

From this, they reckon that their self pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and unmoving; that all sentient beings are born and die within the center of their own heart, and thus their own mind...
This nature is called "constant. Within that process of arising and ceasing, what is the true nature of impermanence?

What is meant by the discourse on the constant and the impermanent? First, this person contemplates this wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions, profoundly still and transparent, its magnitude equal to empty space, and considers all dharmas to be derived from this spirit.
The Lord is called the Ultimate Divine Self (paramātman). From this arises the conceit:
"My mind pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and unmoving; thus all sentient beings are born and die within my own mind."
The mind is without arising or ceasing; is this not permanence? Sentient beings undergo arising and ceasing; is this not impermanence?
The mind that is without arising or ceasing is itself permanent; sentient beings who possess birth and death are themselves impermanent.
This is a single instance of inverted view.
Second, this person does not contemplate their own mind, but contemplates throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Where they see places where kalpas are destroyed, they call it the nature of ultimate impermanence; where they see places where kalpas are not destroyed, they call it ultimate permanence.
This is the second instance of observing others while neglecting oneself:

such a person does not observe their own mind, but instead observes the lands of the ten directions, reckoning everything from the third dhyāna downward—where the three calamities reach—as impermanent, and reckoning everything from the fourth dhyāna upward—where the three calamities do not reach—as permanent. How could they know that what is called "permanent" is not truly so?
If that which is called impermanent is also not of the nature of a seed-lineage (*gotra*), these two are inverted views.

Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as subtle, refined, and profound. (The non-Buddhists postulate three types of self-characteristics: first, the subtle self; second, the vast self.)

There are three [types of] self: the great, the small, and the subtle. This is the subtle self (*sūkṣma-ātman*). "Essential" (*praṇīta*) means it is not mixed; "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) means it is not coarse; "minute" (*aṇu*) means it is not attached; "dense" (*ghana*) means it is not manifest. It is like a minute particle that circulates throughout the ten directions;
its nature does not shift or change. It can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant. Its indestructible nature is called the permanence of the self-nature (*ātmatva-nityatā*).
All death and birth flow forth from this self and are thus called the nature of impermanence (*anityatā*).
This means setting aside the observation of others to observe oneself. Third, this person does not observe the external world, but observes their own mind.
They see that this mind is subtle, refined, and profound; it is as difficult to perceive as a minute speck of dust. Nevertheless, it wanders throughout the ten directions.
Yet its fundamental nature is originally without change or alteration. The mind is the master of the body; it is able to cause this body to arise and perish.
That which is unchanging and possesses an indestructible nature is the permanence of my own nature (*ātman*).
That all bodies subject to birth and death flow forth from my nature is their impermanent nature. How could one know the mind that is being contemplated?
That which is as fine as a mote of dust is the mark of the subtle, pure, and constantly agitated state.

As long as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not been shattered, how could one suddenly perceive the true mind? To reckon permanence as false is to reckon impermanence as false as well; these are the three inverted views.

Fourth: This person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations flows constantly, they reckon it to have the nature of permanence;
whereas form, sensation, perception, and so forth, having now ceased and been extinguished, they name them impermanent.

This contemplation involves dualistic reckoning regarding the four aggregates (*skandhas*). As for the "four": this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has already ceased, yet they see the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flowing secretly;
seeing this very aggregate of formations constantly flowing before their eyes, they reckon it to be permanent. They then reckon the other three aggregates to have already been extinguished.
They then reckon this to be impermanent; these are the four inverted views.
Because they calculate that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the third heterodox school’s doctrine of partial permanence.
Because of these four types of speculative calculation, although the self and others are not fixed, they collectively constitute a doctrine of one part being impermanent and one part being permanent.
By holding this dualistic view, they fall into the ranks of the heterodox and lose sight of Bodhi; therefore, it is called the third heterodox school.

The theory that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent arises when the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is about to open up, yet one falls into this through false conceptualization;
it is truly regrettable. This is also subsumed under the category of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). He said:

"The difference between this and the four types of 'universal permanence' is that while the latter calculates everything to be eternally constant, this calculates that within oneself and others, there is only one part that is real."
It is always thus.
Furthermore, among the sons of good family within *samādhi*, when they stabilize and concentrate their correct minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, observing that source of constant agitation within profound stillness. Within this state of differentiation (of which there are four: the state of the three periods of time, the state of seeing and hearing, and the state of "that" and "self"...)
[The stage of] arising and ceasing (the stages of arising and ceasing). Those who engage in such conceptualization fall into the four theories of finitude.
This clarifies the fourth [theory]: the calculation of the finite and the infinite.

Furthermore, O sons of good family, within samādhi, when the manifestations of all practices appear, those who give rise to false conceptualizations regarding these four stages of existence will likewise fall [into error].
This enters into the four types of heterodox (tīrthika) theories concerning the finite and the infinite. Regarding the fact that the scriptural text does not mention the "infinite":
it may be due to an abbreviation of the text, or it may be intended to include [the infinite] by implication. He [He Shao] says: "The former two types of views reckon [the self] as truly eternal;
this type reckons it as vast."
First: This person calculates that the fundamental source of the mind (the *saṃskāra-skandha*) functions in a ceaseless flow. Calculating the past and future, they call it "finite";
calculating the continuous mind, they call it "infinite."
What are the four theories of finitude? First, this person observes that the present skandha of formations flows on without interruption.
Consequently, they reckon that what has passed in the past is already extinguished and what is yet to come in the future is not yet seen; thus, they designate these as "finite.
They maintain that only the present mind continues in an uninterrupted succession, which they designate as "infinite. This is a false construction established within the midst of the boundless.
This is the ultimate limit—namely, to carve and paint empty space. How could one know that the Way of Bodhi has no past, future, or present?
Second, when such a person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas, they see sentient beings; yet prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, there was silence, with nothing heard or seen.
That which is devoid of hearing and seeing is called "boundless" (*ananta*); that which is the locus of sentient beings is called "bounded" (*anta*).
This is the opposite of the previous calculation; it refers to what is known as a "reversal of mutual interdependence" or an inverted calculation.

The previous calculation held that the past and future are "bounded," resembling the calculation of the locus devoid of hearing and seeing; it held that the present is "boundless," resembling the calculation of that which possesses hearing and seeing.

This refers to the locus of perception. Now, calculating that within a kalpa there is a locus where hearing and seeing occur, it is considered "finite," because it is limited by the number eighty thousand.
Calculating that outside a kalpa there is no locus where hearing and seeing occur, it is considered "infinite," because it is without end and cannot be measured or known.
○ Wuxing says: "The subsequent eighty thousand kalpas should likewise be as before."
Now, fearing it may be too brief, there are three points:
this person calculates that their own self possesses universal knowledge and attains the nature of boundlessness. All those people appear within the scope of my knowledge;
yet I have never known the nature of their knowing. Thus, they are said not to possess a mind of boundlessness, but rather to possess a nature of limitation.
Third, this person calculates that their own self-soul (*ātman*) perceives forms when forms come and hears sounds when sounds come, knowing all things without exception.
They claim for themselves alone the attainment of infinite nature, such that all sentient beings appear within the scope of their universal knowledge;
yet they see only those individuals and are never aware that these beings possess a distinct existence apart from themselves.
If you understand it thus, then that person fundamentally never attained a mind that is boundless; they merely possess a nature that is finite. How could you know this?
It is simply that you do not see for yourself; it is not that the person's nature is finite. Furthermore, you are not a person—how can you know whether a person has limits?
In the preceding and following passages, "limits" (*bian*) were defined by the existence or non-existence of a physical substance; here, it refers to boundaries (*ji*).
Existence and non-existence are called extremes.
Fourth, this person exhaustively investigates the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and, through mental deliberation, considers all sentient beings within a single body.
He calculates that all things are half-born and half-extinguished, thereby clarifying that everything within this world is such that one half has limits and one half is limitless.

Fourth, this person exhaustively investigates the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), yet failing to realize that the phenomenal realm has not yet been emptied, he consequently asserts it to be true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the nature of quiescent extinction, those who follow the path of the conceptual mind recklessly speculate that within the bodies of sentient beings, everything prior to the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) belongs to arising, while everything subsequent to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of mental formations) belongs to cessation.
Extending this logic to all things in the world, they claim that everything is half-arising and half-ceasing; thus, arising is finite, and cessation is... [infinite].

If it were infinite, then one half would be finite and the other half infinite. The underlying intention is to take the emptiness and stillness of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as the supreme nature of boundless limits.
Based on this speculative reckoning of finitude and infinity, they fall among the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fourth type of non-Buddhist who establishes the doctrine of finitude.

Based on these four kinds of conceptual reckonings—whether [the world] is infinite or finite—they all fall into the ranks of the externalists (tīrthikas) and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is because within the nature of Bodhi, there are no distinct stages and no boundaries. This is called the fourth externalist school that establishes the doctrine of finitude.
It is a pity that they fall into this through false reckoning just as the activity-aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) is about to open.
End. This is included among the category of false views.

Furthermore, O sons of good family within samādhi, if you maintain a firm and concentrated right mind, Māras will find no opportunity; you shall exhaustively investigate the fundamental nature of all living beings.

Contemplating that profound clarity as being fundamentally subject to constant agitation, those who give rise to conceptual calculations within their knowledge and views fall into four kinds of perverse "undying" confusion (*amara-vikṣepa*).

(According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, non-Buddhists reckon that the heavens are eternally abiding and thus name them "undying. One who answers questions with evasive ambiguity can be reborn in those heavens;

therefore, when questioned, they respond with secret terminology that should not be fully disclosed, or they provide indefinite answers. This is called "perversion and confusion" (*kuṭila-vikṣepa*): to be perverse is to be stubborn and unyielding to principle; to be confused is for the mind to lack a central point of correctness. Now, examining this closely, the first and fourth [of these four] statements are both ambiguous.

Their distracted minds prevail; ultimately, they do not accord with principle and are also characterized by pretension. The second and third [types] are likewise one-sided; their minds are mostly pretentious and ultimately do not center on what is correct, as they all lead to disorder.

Regarding "pervasive conceptualization and false discourse": these four types belong to pervasive conceptual grasping (*parikalpita*), hence they are called "pervasive conceptualization. "False" means deceptive and unreal. To grasp a rope as a snake is the height of delusion.
This clarifies the fifth type of deceptive, confused, and empty discourse.

Furthermore, O good sons, when the practice of the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) manifests, if one gives rise to inverted calculations based on what is known and seen within that state of concentration, such a person falls into the four kinds of inverted, "immortal" (un-dying) deceptive and confused pervasive conceptualizations of empty discourse. This refers to the aforementioned calculation of permanence.

To claim that [the world] is both impermanent and not impermanent, or both finite and infinite—before even reaching a state of confusion—this is to say it is both permanent and impermanent, and both finite and infinite; this is a total perversion, the very height of sophistry.
First, this person contemplates the source of transformation: that which is a place of shifting flux is called "change";
seeing the place of continuity is called "permanence"; seeing the place where there is something seen is called "arising"; and not seeing the place where there is seeing is called "cessation."
The point at which the causal nature of the continuity is uninterrupted is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*).

Within the midst of that very continuity, the point where it is separated [from its preceding state]—(for whatever is called "continuity" necessarily involves a succession of before and after, and there must necessarily be points of deficiency in the interval; just as there is a lack between the two breaths of inhalation and exhalation at their junction;

this deficiency is "decrease")—is called "decrease" (*hāni*). Each respective place of arising is called "existence" (*bhāva*). Each respective place of cessation is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).

Observing through principle as a whole, yet seeing distinctly with the mind. (To observe as a whole means to contemplate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). To see distinctly means to give rise to eight distinct meanings. There are those who seek the Dharma.
When someone comes to inquire about its meaning, he replies: "I am now both arising and ceasing; both existent and non-existent; both increasing and decreasing.

(In his reply, he briefly cites six meanings, answering each by balancing two opposing positions. At all times, he confuses their speech, causing the person before him (the one who inquired about the meaning) to lose track of the words and phrases.
What are the four kinds of evasive equivocation? First, such a person contemplates the origin of transformation.
Regarding the upward migration into the sphere of infinite space, they call it "transformation. Regarding the intermediate continuity in the sphere of nothingness, they call it "permanence";
this is not the principle of remaining unchanging in accordance with conditions. They name that which is perceived within eighty thousand kalpas as "birth."
That which is not perceived beyond eighty thousand kalpas is called "extinction" (*nirodha*); this is not the principle that the cause ceases because the fruit has arisen.
That where continuity is uninterrupted is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*); that which is separated in the interim is called "decrease" (*hāni*);
this is not the principle of neither-increasing-nor-decreasing (*an-utpanna-aniruddha*). Each respective place of arising is called "existence" (*bhava*); each respective place of cessation...
To name it "non-existence" is not the principle of simultaneously discarding both existence and non-existence.

When observing the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) through the comprehensive perspective of principle and applying the mind to distinguish its eight aspects, if a seeker of the Dharma should come and question me regarding these meanings, I would answer them by blending the two pillars of discourse:
that arising and ceasing are indeterminate, existence and non-existence are indeterminate, and increase and decrease are indeterminate.
From time to time he confused his speech, causing those who were inquiring about the meaning to lose track of the passages and sentences;

or, because of such deceptive confusion, they found it difficult to remember them themselves, so that they lost what they had heard as soon as they heard it; or, because of his inability to resolve whether a point was right or wrong.
Instead, they come to doubt the sutras and treatises they have long practiced, losing their own tenets and falling into total forgetfulness.
This is one type of confusion that exceeds even that of affectation.
Second, this person contemplates the mind with precision and finds that it has no location whatsoever; because there is nothing to grasp, they realize the truth.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying simply "non-existence. Apart from this non-existence, there is nothing further to be said.

Second, there are those who contemplate the mind in a state of non-existence; from this state of non-existence, they find a point of entry and then cling to the view that all phenomena are non-existent. When people come to question them, they respond with only the single word "non-existent" (wu), having nothing else to say beyond that. This kind of pretension is largely characterized by confusion. To truly understand Zhaozhou— To recognize Zhaozhou, one must look at his "Mu. This "Mu" is not a mere negation; it is the very pivot of the great matter. If you can grasp it, then the myriad phenomena are all right here before you. If you cannot grasp it, you will wander through birth and death for ten thousand kalpas. Do not seek it in words or phrases; do not seek it in the mind or consciousness. It is not something to be grasped or rejected. It is not something to be attained or lost. It is the original face of your own self. If you can see it clearly, you will know that the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all the patriarchs have never been anything other than this. If you cannot see it clearly, you will be like a person looking at their own face in a mirror yet failing to recognize themselves. Therefore, you must investigate this "Mu" with all your heart and soul. Do not let it pass for a mere word; do not let it become a dead concept. Only when you can break through this barrier will you realize that the entire universe is the single word "Mu," and the single word "Mu" is the entire universe. At that moment, you will be free from all delusions and attain liberation. This is what is meant by "seeing the Buddha-nature. Do not doubt it. Practice it! Practice it! To recognize Zhaozhou, one must look at his "Mu. This "Mu" is not a mere negation; it is the very pivot of the great matter. If you can grasp it, then the myriad phenomena are all right here before you. If you cannot grasp it, you will wander through birth and death for ten thousand kalpas. Do not seek it in words or phrases; do not seek it in the mind or consciousness. It is not something to be grasped or rejected. It is not something to be attained or lost. It is the original face of your own self. If you can see it clearly, you will know that the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all the patriarchs have never been anything other than this.

If you cannot see it clearly, you will be like a person looking at their own face in a mirror yet failing to recognize themselves. Therefore, you must investigate this "Mu" with all your heart and soul. Do not let it pass for a mere word; do not let it become a dead concept. Only when you can break through this barrier will you realize that the entire universe is the single word "Mu," and the single word "Mu" is the entire universe. At that moment, you will be free from all delusions and attain liberation. This is what is meant by "seeing the Buddha-nature. Do not doubt it. Practice it! Practice it!
There are no words. As for why this differs from that, in what place does one recognize the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox?
Thirdly, such a person contemplates their own mind and finds that each has its own locus; because of this, they attain realization. When someone comes to question them, [they respond accordingly].

He answered with only a single word, saying simply, "It is. (Note: When examining the scriptural text, this is identical in structure to the previous section; it differs from the phrase "What is it? [How is it?]. If one were to force an interpretation of the word "is" [shì], it would ultimately remain unintelligible.
Thus, we know for certain that it must be an error for the character "have" [yǒu]). Aside from this, there was nothing further to be said.
Third: This person contemplates the mind from the standpoint of existence (*bhava*). Having thus found an entry point through existence, they then cling to the view that all phenomena exist.
When encountering others who come to question them, they answer with only the single word "existence," and beyond this, they have nothing else to say.
This type of person is also characterized by excessive pretension and confusion. One must understand that if it were truly so...
One who has truly attained the ground possesses a way of emergence and livelihood whether they speak of existence or non-existence.
Fourth, such a person perceives both existence and non-existence; because their objective sphere is fragmented, their mind is likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them:

He replied: "To say 'it both exists and does not exist' is itself to say 'it neither exists nor does not exist. Within this state of neither existing nor not existing, it is not the case that it both exists and does not exist.
This is entirely evasive and confused; there is no room for further interrogation."

Fourth: This person, having seen that each thing exists individually and also seeing that they are mutually non-existent, finds the objects of perception to be fragmented and the perceiving mind to be deluded. Therefore, whenever asked, he answers:
"Existence is itself non-existence, just as ice is itself water; non-existence is itself existence, just as water is itself ice."
Furthermore, their knowledge and views are confused and entangled; they are obscure and hazy, lacking any internal standard of measure.

Consequently, they all descend into perversity and disorder, making it impossible to subject them to exhaustive inquiry. This particular type is even more characterized by disorder than by perversity.
By means of such speculative reckoning, they resort to evasive equivocation and empty nothingness, falling into the ranks of external paths and becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fifth type of external path: the fourfold nature of perversion, the evasive equivocation of immortality, and the pervasive false theorizing.
As the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to open, be careful not to fall into this through false views. These four types are subsumed within wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, if they stabilize and concentrate their right minds, Māras will find no opportunity; they will exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
Observing that profound clarity which is constantly agitated at its source—the inexhaustible flow (which is the aggregate of formations)—one gives rise to conceptual calculations.
Such a person falls into the error of conceiving of a post-mortem existence and develops a perverted resolve.
This clarifies the sixth [type of] reckoning that there are characteristics within the future limit (*aparānta*).

Furthermore, O sons of good family, while in *samādhi*, when the current activities of all formations (*saṃskāra*) appear to reach their end, one falsely gives rise to conceptualization regarding the inexhaustible flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), perceiving these formations as having characteristics.
Together with the three aggregates previously extinguished, they are all taken to possess characteristics. Such a person then falls into the [view of] external...

To think that there are signs after death is a perverted conception. If one truly awakens to non-arising and realizes that what is initially born is fundamentally subject to extinction, then even before birth there is nothing but emptiness and no signs; how much more so after death?
How could one falsely reckon that there are signs?
Some fixate upon the body itself, saying, "Form is the self. Others perceive the self as encompassing and pervading the entire realm, saying, "The self possesses form.
Or they see that the objects before them (the forms currently present) revolve and respond according to the self (this refers to its functional activity), saying, "Form belongs to the self.

Or again, they perceive the self as persisting through the continuity of formations, saying, "The self is within form. All such calculations claim that after death there remains a mark of existence. Thus, following...
The Cycle has sixteen aspects. What is meant by the aspect of existence after death?

The practitioner may either stubbornly cling to and nourish their own body, saying, "Form is the self," or they may perceive the nature of the self as perfect and capable of universally containing all lands, thinking, "The self is great and form is small. Thus they speak of the self.
There is form. Or, seeing forms before one's eyes, one follows their movement and application, thinking, "Form belongs to me.

Or again, one thinks that the self depends on the continuity within formations (*saṃskāra*), and since formations are identical to form, and form is vast while the self is small, one says, "I am within form.
Thus, by extrapolating from the existence of the present birth toward the existence of future death, one gives rise to false conceptualization.
There are characteristics after death. As it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it is with the other three aggregates.
Inferring by means of these four, there are sixteen characteristics in a cycle; these constitute four of the sixty-two views.
From this point on, one may alternatively conceive of ultimate affliction and ultimate enlightenment as two natures proceeding side by side, each without mutual contact (*sparśa*;
"contact" here meaning obstruction).

Furthermore, from this they further calculate that afflictions are ultimately [afflictions] and all defiled phenomena are ultimately [defiled], while bodhi is ultimately [bodhi] and all pure phenomena are ultimately [pure].
Since the four aggregates are permanent, they know that the two natures of affliction and bodhi proceed side by side, each not obstructing the other.
Thus, the ordinary person is definitively an ordinary person, and the sage is definitively a sage; there is absolutely no transforming the ordinary into the sage.
Regarding the matter of transforming afflictions into bodhi, it is entirely due to clinging to the fixed existence of marks;
thus, one recognizes death as being invariably constant in this way, and is likewise deluded regarding the principle of "the unchanging following conditions."
Because they speculate that there is existence after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.

This is called the sixth type of non-Buddhist doctrine, which establishes [theories] within the five aggregates (though the general summary of the five aggregates concludes with the preceding four, and although it appears among the first four, its meaning pertains specifically to the *saṃskāra-skandha*);
it is the inverted theory of the mind concerning the signs of existence after death.

As the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to open, be careful not to fall into this through false conceptualization. This is also subsumed within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright; thus Māras find no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the fundamental nature of all living beings.
Observing that profound clarity as a source of constant agitation, one who gives rise to conceptual calculations within the previously eliminated states of form, sensation,
and perception will fall into the inverted resolve of perceiving "signlessness" after death.
This clarifies the seventh [view]: reckoning that there is no characteristic after death.

Furthermore, O good sons, while in samādhi, when the manifestations of the dissolving activities appear, if one gives rise to conceptual calculations regarding the three aggregates that were previously eliminated and extinguished, such a person falls into the heterodox view that there is no characteristic after death; their resolve is inverted. This is the same as the aforementioned calculation.
Because they are diametrically opposed in nature, existence transforms into non-existence.

This is because, looking upward at the unextinguished *saṃskāra-skandha*, one perceives it as inexhaustible and consequently reckons that the preceding three aggregates and all phenomena are likewise inexhaustible;
yet, seeing that the preceding three have already ceased, one perceives them as signless and consequently reckons that the *saṃskāra-skandha* and all phenomena are likewise signless.

Seeing that form (*rūpa*) ceases, one realizes that the physical body has no underlying cause. Contemplating that perception (*saṃjñā*) ceases, one realizes that the mind has nothing to which it is attached.

Knowing that sensation (*vedanā*) ceases, one realizes there is no further connection; the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) dissolves (referring to the cessation of form, sensation, and perception).

Even if the processes of conditioning (*saṃskāra*)—referring to the aggregate of formations—should still persist, in the absence of sensation and perception, they are identical to grass and trees (meaning that without sensation and perception, formations also cease). Thus, even when these physical constituents (referring generally to the four aggregates) are present before one, they cannot be apprehended.
After death, how can there still be various marks? By investigating and examining this, one finds that after death, marks are absent. Thus it cycles through eight instances of the absence of marks.
What is meant by the absence of marks after death? Form constitutes the body, perception constitutes the mind, and feeling then connects and sustains both.
Regarding form and mind: when this person perceives the cessation of form, the physical body has no further basis.
When they contemplate the cessation of perception, the mind has nothing to which it is bound. When they know the cessation of sensation, there is no longer any further connection.

When the three aggregates (*skandhas*) have thus been extinguished, even if there remains the subtle physiological activity of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), since form, sensation, and perception are already absent, it is likewise [extinguished].
Grasses and trees are equally devoid of cognition, yet they both return to annihilation; this is an inference based on annihilation.
Furthermore, regarding the substance of these four aggregates (*skandhas*) as it appears in the present life, even now no characteristics can be apprehended;
how then could there be any further characteristics after death? This is an inference of death based on life. By means of such investigation and comparison...
[Commentary: After death, there is no mark. Thus they circulate; there are eight non-marks (*animitta*). For each aggregate (*skandha*), one calculates two non-marks—present and future.
Because there are four aggregates, there are thus eight non-marks. Question: How does this differ from the meaning of "the existence at birth has extinction" and so forth in the previous explanation?
Answer: That [previous explanation] refers to emptiness within existence itself; the wood, for instance, has no arising of its own.

The single continuity from beginning to end is the Buddha’s orthodox teaching. This refers to that which existed in the past but is now absent, and that which perished in the present but will not exist hereafter.
[Your view] is entirely a deluded and false calculation based on arising and ceasing; how vastly different it is from the former! It is as distinct as heaven and earth.
From this, some may calculate that the causes and effects of nirvana are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total annihilation.
Furthermore, from this they may further calculate that the causes and effects of nirvana are all cultivated based on the present aggregates (*skandha*) and realized through subsequent aggregates.
Since the aggregates (*skandhas*) are ultimately unfathomable, what existence can there be for cultivation or realization? Therefore, both the cause and fruit of *nirvāṇa* are empty.

Furthermore, cause and fruit encompass worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), while *nirvāṇa* encompasses supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*). If the cause and fruit of *nirvāṇa* are empty, then all phenomena are empty;
they are merely names that ultimately revert to annihilation. Thus, one proceeds by means of the three aggregates as the superior cause.
The aggregates perish together. Based on these four aggregates, they falsely calculate that all phenomena likewise perish.
Because of this speculative reckoning that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ranks of the external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox teaching: the inverted theory of the mind within the five aggregates that asserts there is no sign after death.

As the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to open, be careful not to fall into this through false conceptualization. This, too, is subsumed within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

When considered together with the previous calculation of existence, how could one know that within the nature of Bodhi, not a single speck of dust is established and not a single dharma is discarded?
It is wondrous emptiness and wondrous existence; wondrous existence and wondrous emptiness. It is neither cessation nor annihilation, nor is it something that undergoes cessation or annihilation.
Indeed it is so.
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, such that Māras find no opportunity to interfere.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, contemplating that profound, pure, yet eternally restless source. While abiding in the midst of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), dualistically calculating both existence and non-existence.
Their own essential nature is thus destroyed. This person falls into the perverted doctrine that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence.
This is the eighth pair of views, which calculates both existence and non-existence as being neither.

Furthermore, O sons of good family, within samādhi, when you contemplate the manifestation of the exhaustion of formations, while formations still persist, you see that the aggregate of formations has not yet been extinguished, and its domain remains clearly present.
Furthermore, when both feeling and perception cease, one observes that the preceding three aggregates have already been extinguished and their essence and characteristics are entirely empty.

Thereupon, one dualistically calculates existence and non-existence: calculating existence regarding what remains, and calculating non-existence regarding what has ceased. These self-characteristics mutually subvert one another;

the existence of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) subverts the non-existence of the preceding three, while the non-existence of the preceding three subverts the existence of the aggregate of formations. By subverting non-existence, one establishes "not non-existent."
To negate existence is to establish non-existence; such a person falls into the heterodox view of "neither existing nor non-existing after death," giving rise to inverted theories.
Within the realm of form and perception, they see both existence and non-existence; within the flux of conditioned formations, they observe both non-existence and not-non-existence.

What is meant by "the mutual destruction of their own essential characteristics"? When this person, amidst the aggregates of form, sensation, and perception, is precisely at the moment of the cessation of objects, they see that although the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) still exists, it is likewise identical to cessation and non-existent.

It is like looking at a bright, pure object through a medium of darkness; it becomes identical to the darkness and is no longer bright. Within the shifting flow of formations, while they are precisely in a state of agitation...

Regarding the locus of movement: although the preceding three [states] are absent, they are likewise identical to movement and yet not non-existent. It is like looking at the reflection of stillness within moving water;

that reflection is likewise identical to movement and is not stillness itself. By mutually negating one another, they establish a state of "neither-nor"; this is precisely the mutual negation of their own essential nature and characteristics.

Thus they circulate, exhausting the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*). Regarding the eight aspects of neither-existence-nor-non-existence, whenever they encounter a single condition, they all claim that after death there is either existence or non-existence.
Thus they circulate, traversing the four aggregates and conceptualizing them; for each aggregate, they calculate these two negations.

Combining the four aggregates (skandhas) results in eight states that are neither [existent nor non-existent]. Thus, according to whichever single condition one encounters, all become "neither both" (ubhayānta-vivarjita).
Because it is not non-existent, it is said that there is a mark after death; because it is not existent, it is said that there is no mark after death.
This merely exhausts the four aggregates.

Furthermore, by calculating that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are by nature subject to flux and transformation, the mind gives rise to penetrating realization: that they are neither existent nor non-existent, and that both the void and the real are beyond determination.
(Flux refers to constant movement; transformation refers to change.)
Furthermore, proceeding from the eightfold negation of correct reckoning, he turned to further reckonings, asserting that all phenomena are without exception thus:

their nature is subject to change and error, and by analogy, they all exist or do not exist after death, mutually refuting and displacing one another. Thereupon, his mind gave rise to penetrating awakening.
Thus they increase and broaden their wrong views and erroneous understandings, ultimately arriving at the position that both existence and non-existence are negated.
With neither the void nor the real to rely upon, how could there ever be any certainty?

Because of such conceptualization, they conclude that everything after death is non-existent; their vision of the future becomes clouded and obscure, leaving nothing to be said. Consequently, they fall into the ranks of the heterodox paths.

This deludes the nature of Bodhi. This is called the eighth heterodox school’s inverted theory of mind within the five aggregates, which posits that after death there is "neither existence nor non-existence.

Based on this calculation, they extrapolate from the state of being alive to the state after death, asserting that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, persisting until the end of the future.

At the limit of the profound and the obscure, where the Way is neither attained nor un-attained, and all is ineffable—for this very reason, one falls into deviant perceptions and becomes deluded regarding the true nature. This is called the eighth heterodox school:

the inverted doctrine of the mind which posits that after death, one exists as "neither [existent nor non-existent]" within the five aggregates. This is truly because they have not yet attained true, penetrating knowledge.

I have observed and, through tentative conjecture, composed this treatise. If one were truly a seer of the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya), it would not matter whether one asserts that the Way exists or does not exist;
both would constitute sublime discourses. This [position] is likewise subsumed within the category of false views (mithyādṛṣṭi).
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, such that Māras find no opportunity,

they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, subsequently, they harbor speculative calculations regarding its non-existence, these people fall into the seven theories of annihilationism.

This clarifies the ninth [false] calculation: the annihilationism of the seven realms. Furthermore, O sons of good family, within samādhi, when the various formations (*saṃskāra*) are manifesting at their exhaustion, one perceives the place where these formations cease moment by moment; this is termed "the subsequent non-existence.
Based on this, they falsely calculate that even if one is born in the seven realms of humans or devas, all will ultimately be annihilated. Such a person falls into the path of the externalists.
The seven theories of annihilationism. Although this annihilationism resembles the seventh [view], the underlying conceptualization differs.

That [view] calculates that because there is nothing in the present, there will likewise be nothing after death; this [view], however, merely calculates that there is annihilation after death and nothing beyond.

Some reckon it as the extinction of the body (the humans and devas of the desire realm); some as the extinction of desire (the first dhyāna); some as the extinction of suffering (the second dhyāna); or some as the extinction of ultimate bliss.

(In the third dhyāna,) there is the cessation of pleasure and equanimity. (In the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments,) one cycles in this manner until the seven limits are exhausted, whereby [the afflictions] are extinguished before one's eyes.
Once extinguished, there is nothing more.
What are the seven theories of annihilation? Such a person calculates the nature of these aggregates (*skandha*) to be like water without a source:

some streams exhaust themselves after flowing for a short distance, while others exhaust themselves after flowing for a long distance. Those that flow for a short distance perish right here in the human realm; those that flow for a long distance... [perish] far away.
Just as [the formless realm] is extinguished only at its highest point (bhavāgra), so too does one's own body undergo extinction, reaching the ultimate abandonment and cessation.

Thus, through this cycle, the seven locations—the four continents, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, plus the four formless attainments—are exhausted;

they manifest before one and ultimately return to extinction. Once extinguished, there is no further rebirth; there remains only the present aggregates (skandhas) and the intermediate state (antarābhava).

It would be entirely non-existent with respect to the subsequent aggregates (*paścima-skandha*). This is also how the latter-day followers of the Confucian school in this land feel when they loathe hearing the doctrine of transmigration (*saṃsāra*);
yet they merely calculate that [existence] ceases immediately upon the human stage, and still do not allow for the existence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Based on this speculative reckoning that there is annihilation after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the ninth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory established within the five aggregates that there is annihilation after death.
How could one know that the true nature of Bodhi is constant and uninterrupted throughout all eternity?
This, too, is included among the views of extremes.
Furthermore, within samādhi, when sons of good family maintain a firm and concentrated right mind, Māra finds no opportunity; they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

If one contemplates that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source and subsequently engages in speculative calculations regarding subsequent existence, such a person falls into the doctrine of the five nirvāṇas.
This clarifies the tenth calculation, which posits five nirvāṇas. Furthermore, within *samādhi*, O sons of good family, you should contemplate as follows:
When all formations (*saṃskāra*) are manifesting, that which is called "subsequent existence" (*paścāt-bhava*) arises at every moment within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

To engage in such conceptual calculation (*vikalpa*) is because one observes that the aggregate of formations continues in succession from moment to moment, with each new moment constituting an existence;

thus, one calculates that there must be a real fruit of future existence and that it will certainly not perish into non-existence. Such a person falls into the five heterodox theories of *nirvāṇa*. Five.
As for *nirvāṇa*, it does not depend upon the extinction of the ashes; rather, within the very place where one is currently born, they reckon this to be the fruit.
There are five such reckonings. This reckoning is fundamentally different from the sixth [reckoning], which concerns the marks of existence after death.

That reckoning concerns the marks of existence following death, whereas this reckoning holds that the very place of current birth is the eternally abiding ultimate fruit. The old [tradition] says that [the latter] flows forth from that [former].
This is utterly groundless.

(The word "or" [或] is an indefinite particle; it indicates that it is not a single person who universally conceptualizes all five locations, but rather each person, according to their own perception, conceptualizes only one location.

Taking the realm of desire—as for example, when Taoist practitioners claim that Jade Emperor (Yùhuáng) universally presides over the thirty-three heavens as the Mysterious Capital (Xuándū), the realm of Upper Purity (Shàngqīng), free from birth and death, unaware that this is actually none other than Śakra, the Lord of the Six Desires)—as the primary basis of transformation (parāvṛtti). (Transformation means shifting from the cycle of birth and death to rely upon nirvāṇa.)

Therefore it is said: "Because one observes the perfect clarity of the transformed basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and gives rise to a longing for it. Alternatively, it may refer to the first dhyāna, because its nature is free from sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

(In the first dhyāna, suffering and affliction do not oppress; thus it is called "free from sorrow. This is an error where the character for "suffering" [duḥkha] has been dropped below. According to the context, the four characters "for the sake of the correct transformation of the basis" should appear between these two phrases, but they have been omitted by the redactor of the scripture.

Alternatively, it may refer to the second dhyāna, because the mind is free from suffering (*duḥkha*). (In the second dhyāna, anxiety and distress do not oppress; thus it is called "free from suffering. This is likewise an error where the character for "sorrow" [daurmanasya] has been dropped above. Alternatively, it may refer to the third dhyāna, because of the following of extreme joy (*prīti*).

Therefore, by means of the four dhyānas, both suffering and pleasure have perished; because they do not undergo the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra, they become deluded regarding the outflow-tainted heavens and conceive the notion that these are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding these five abodes as secure, they take them to be the supreme pure refuge. Thus they cycle through them until they reach the ultimate limit of these five abodes.
What are the five theories regarding nirvāṇa? Some take the six heavens of the desire realm as the true realm of nirvāṇa, claiming that one may turn back from birth and death by relying upon them.

Because those beings first obtain the divine eye and universally observe the celestial radiance—which is perfectly bright and beautiful, surpassing that of the sun and moon—they conceive a heart of longing and attachment; thus, they reckon this place to be the manifest nirvāṇa. Or...
One takes the first dhyāna as the primary basis for transformation, because the suffering and affliction of the first dhyāna cannot oppress it;
or one takes the second dhyāna as the primary basis for transformation, because the anxiety and longing of the second dhyāna cannot oppress it;
or one takes the third dhyāna as the primary basis for transformation, because joy is fully perfected in the third dhyāna; or one takes the fourth dhyāna as the primary basis for transformation.

In the fourth dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure are abandoned; it is not destroyed by the three calamities, and because one does not undergo the birth and death of saṃsāra, these are all heavens with outflows (sāsrava).

To mistake that which has outflows for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and to falsely calculate it as the fruit of liberation and mastery, is to erroneously confuse it with the true self of nirvāṇa. This occurs because [those beings] have slightly departed from the instability of the lower realms.
They thus reckon these five places to be secure; this is a mistaken conflation of them with the true bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

Because they have slightly departed from the turbid impurities of the lower realms, they reckon these five places to be superior, pure refuges; this is a mistaken conflation of them with the true purity of *nirvāṇa*.
In this way, they cycle through false reckonings, holding only these five places to be the ultimate and final fruit. This...

They mistakenly and indiscriminately conflate this with the true permanence of *nirvāṇa*. Amidst that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure, they falsely reckon it as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. How great indeed is such perversion!

Based on this calculation, they conceive of five kinds of nirvana in the present life (because they experience happiness in the present without awaiting a future birth), thereby falling into the ranks of external paths and becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the tenth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of establishing five kinds of nirvana in the present within the five aggregates.
"How could one know that Bodhi and Nirvana are still so remote? This, too, is subsumed under wrong views.
Generally speaking, the ten types [of wrong views] do not go beyond the four characters: annihilation (斷), permanence (常), emptiness (空), and existence (有).

The first five belong to annihilation and permanence; the latter five belong to emptiness and existence. The first is the view of annihilation; the second is the view of permanence; the third is the view of both [annihilation and permanence]; the fourth is...
The fourth and fifth [views] expand upon both [existence and non-existence]. The sixth clings to existence; the seventh clings to emptiness; the eighth clings to the negation of both;
the ninth expands upon ultimate annihilation-emptiness; and the tenth expands upon ultimate stagnation in existence.
If one further subsumes emptiness and existence under annihilation and permanence, they remain nothing more than these two views of annihilation and permanence.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of delusory insights in *dhyāna* (as previously stated: "the manifestation of objects in *dhyāna* is when celestial Māras seize the opportunity"; here it is said:
"delusory insights in *dhyāna* arise from the mind itself as a deep affliction") all result from the interaction of the mental faculty with the *saṃskāra-skandha* (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Thus, they manifest as such "awakenings" (which are actually false understandings). Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; failing to reflect upon themselves, they encounter these manifestations as they appear before them.
Taking delusion for liberation, they claim for themselves to have attained the state of a sage; having committed this great falsehood, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
You must take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them to future generations, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning.
Do not allow the demon of the mind to give rise to deep affliction within itself. Maintain and protect [the practitioner], subduing and dispelling false views.

Teach their body and mind to awaken to the true meaning, so that they do not encounter byways on the Unsurpassed Way (where "branch" refers to what emerges from a tree trunk, and "fork" refers to what emerges from the side of a path).
Do not let the mind pray for little and consider it sufficient; rather, act as the pure guiding finger of the Great Awakened King.

This is an exhortation to provide protection. Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings arising from *dhyāna* all result from the interaction and mutual combat between the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) and the mind’s application.
Therefore, such false awakenings manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and find it difficult to give rise to correct awakening;
they are deluded and easily produce false understandings. Furthermore, they do not examine their own cultivation and realization to see where they have reached.
Regarding this stage: when this demon of the mind manifests before you, you may mistake delusion for understanding and dare to act with self-will, passing judgment and establishing doctrines.
Furthermore, you might presumptuously claim the rank of a sage, thereby committing a great falsehood and falling into the most grievous hells.
You must ensure that the words of the Tathāgata spoken today are transmitted after my parinirvāṇa, so that all sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age may hear them throughout.
Having realized this meaning, one’s delusion and understanding become distinct; do not allow the demons of one's own mind to create their own calamities.
By maintaining and protecting the True Dharma, one eliminates and extinguishes false views.
For all such as these, it is taught that the body and mind awaken to the true definitive meaning, transcending entirely the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

Only after [realizing] emptiness and existence may one directly cultivate and directly realize the Unsurpassed Way without encountering bypaths; for to encounter bypaths is to fall into the paths of externalists.
Furthermore, do not allow the mind’s seeking to be satisfied with a mere trifle, thereby limiting oneself with the vision of a "dwarf mouse" or a "jiao-liao" bird;
for to seek little and be content is to fall into the stage of the Two Vehicles. These two— [the aforementioned errors].
These are all the perils encountered along the way to the ultimate fruit. When the mind and eyes open wide and clear, one is no longer deluded by them;
thus, one becomes capable of acting as a guiding pointer for sentient beings toward Buddhahood. As for the responsibility of teaching and instructing, you must exert yourself in this!

One must know that when the mind is correct, affairs are correct; when the mind is deviant, affairs are deviant. If one has not yet attained the realization of the One Mind, then whatever one encounters will be false.
Right practice becomes wrong practice, and the Buddha-gate transforms into the Mara-gate. If one realizes the single mind, then there is nothing that does not lead to benefit:
wrong practice becomes sublime practice, and the heterodox school is itself the orthodox school.

This is just like the single method of the non-Buddhist who scorches his body with the five heats; if one understands it, then Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa becomes the gateway to the flame of non-discriminative wisdom.
If one is deluded regarding this, then the Nirgranthas (Jains) will produce the fiercely burning interpretation of great false views. Thus, in the Dharma there is neither false nor correct;

the Way lies in transformation and adaptation. ○ He said: These ten kinds of frantic interpretations all arise from mistakenly identifying the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as the wondrous true nature of *tathatā*.
Therefore, these divergent views exist. The first, the theory of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), is a mistaken identification of the essence...

Awakened wondrous clarity is neither cause nor condition. The second and third views—the theories of universal permanence and partial permanence—are errors arising from misidentifying the profound stillness and eternal abiding.
The fourth view—the theory of finitude and infinitude—is an error arising from misidentifying the pure original nature as being all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
The latter six types of views erroneously identify the Tathāgatagarbha, thereby giving rise to the dualistic views of emptiness and existence.
The seventh [view], which asserts that there is nothing after death, and the ninth, which asserts annihilationism, both erroneously identify the empty Tathāgatagarbha.
The sixth, which asserts that there is something after death, and the tenth, which manifests as the view of nirvāṇa, both erroneously identify the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
The fifth, which is equivocation, and the eighth, which is the "neither-is-nor-is-not" position regarding what exists after death, both erroneously identify the Tathāgatagarbha.
To be free from all marks is itself all dharmas. As the former masters said: "How many people have been led astray within the Buddha-dharma! Is this not so?
Ānanda, when those good sons cultivate *samādhi* and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted, the natures of all worlds become profoundly pure and serene.

Agitated, the *sabhāgatā* (the commonality of existence; that is, the basis for shared birth—where "basis" indicates the root of birth and "mechanism" clarifies the beginning of movement; their meaning is one)—suddenly collapses and splits asunder.

The deep and subtle net-knots (also referring to the *saṃskāra-skandha* [the aggregate of formations]. It is called "deep and subtle" because it is obscure, hidden, profound, and minute; it is called a "net-knot" because it is the essential nexus of arising and ceasing).

The *pudgala* (translated here as "one who repeatedly takes on rebirth"; this refers to the intermediate state body). The profound channels through which karma is requited—the resonance and response (that is, cause and effect)—are suspended and severed.

Regarding the Heaven of Nirvana, one is about to attain great awakening, like the crowing of a rooster after midnight (the nature-heaven of Nirvana is shrouded by the five aggregates and is as dark as a long night. As each aggregate manifests, it is like the crowing of a rooster once; thus, the manifestation of the aggregate of form is like the first crow of the rooster).

It crows. When the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) manifests, it is like the second crowing of a hen; when the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) manifests, it is like the hen’s final crowing. Looking toward the east, there is already a refined radiance. The six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping.

(According to the *Yuan-tong*, this corresponds to the time when "that which is heard" has been exhausted and the six [faculties] have dissolved. Internally and externally, there is profound clarity; one enters that which has nothing to enter.

One deeply penetrates the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions and the fundamental source of their receiving life. (This refers to the "various threads of life," which is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha*. It is clearly distinct from what preceded it.)

Because it is the universal characteristic, it is said that one has profoundly penetrated [the truth]: by observing that all categories arise from grasping at the source, they cannot be summoned; throughout the ten directions, one has already attained their sameness.

(The "realm" refers to the realm of sentient beings. There are two interpretations of "sameness": first, "one" means unity. This refers to the dissolution of the sixfold combination, returning to the single brilliant essence. Second, "one" means emptiness. This refers to the fact that once the faculties and objects are exhausted, there remains only the single nature of emptiness. This is the state where the six have been dissolved but the "one" has not yet been realized;

the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle is precisely aligned with this. The brilliant color does not sink; the profound and secret is revealed. (Regarding "the brilliant color does not sink": it is like the clear sky, which can be discerned.)

It is form (*rūpa*). To "reveal what is obscure and secret" means, for example, to clearly see objects within the darkness. This is the manifestation of consciousness through the elimination of the formations (*saṃskāra*). It is like removing all outer garments only to see the inner undershirt pressed against the body.

This is called the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). If, among the various summonings (referring to the classes of beings; since all twelve [bases] can draw one toward rebirth, they are called "various summonings"), one has already attained identity within them, the six gates are dissolved, and their integration and opening are perfected, such that seeing and hearing penetrate one another’s domains and their mutual functions become pure throughout the ten directions.

The world, as well as body and mind, become like *vaiḍūrya* (a gemstone of deep blue and extreme hardness that cannot be destroyed by any precious blade, though only spirits possessing supernatural powers can fashion it into tools);

they are transparent and luminous from within and without. This is called the exhaustion of the *vijñāna-skandha*. As for the "exhaustion of formations" (*saṃskāra-kṣaya*), this occurs at the stage of the seven levels of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), which is equivalent to a Small Vehicle *arhat*.

The "exhaustion of consciousness" (*vijñāna-kṣaya*) occurs at the initial mind of the stage of the ten levels of faith reaching their fullness; only then does one enter into perfect penetration (*pariṇata*). Thus, we know that whenever it is said that an *arhat* attains perfect penetration, it refers to the first *bhūmi*, because the perfect *vihāras* are equal to the distinct stages (*pratyeka-bhūmi*); these are the *arhats* of the Mahāyāna. This is so.
A person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life. When one observes its origin, it is found that formless unreality and inverted false imaginings constitute its root.
This is a general description of the characteristics of the consciousness aggregate from beginning to end. Ānanda, that virtuous man cultivates samādhi...
Regarding the "ground": through the aforementioned firm and concentrated right mind, one does not fall into the ten [false] reckonings.
