When one's cultivation reaches its ultimate penetration, the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) naturally comes to an end.

Once the formations are exhausted, then all the natures of ordinary beings in the world—namely, that which serves as the basis for co-arising, characterized by profound clarity or agitation—suddenly shatters its subtle and deep-seated bonds and knots, and all fetters are cast off.
The deep roots [of cyclic existence] are suddenly dissolved, like ice melting into water.

Once the mainstays and bonds are severed, the profound conduits through which one receives birth and repays karma across the various realms of the three worlds—where this causes that to respond—are all suspended and utterly cut off.
Because birth-and-death with distinct segments has ceased, the sky of the nature of *nirvāṇa* is about to be clearly and fully realized, as if...
The roosters cried out in confusion, and as dawn was about to break, he rose and looked toward the east; the first light of day had already begun to appear.

Previously, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) had not yet been exhausted, and the six sense faculties still wandered restlessly. Now that the aggregate of formations is exhausted, there is no longer any further flux.

Then the six sense faculties first attain emptiness and stillness, no longer wandering or running wild. Thereupon, the internal faculties and external objects transform into a single flavor of profound, luminous reality;
internally, one no longer perceives a faculty that enters, and externally, one no longer perceives an object that is entered.
Once the faculties and objects have dissolved, the karmic consciousness first reveals itself, and one deeply penetrates the twelve classes of sentient beings.
Each [of these] receives its life-force from its original source; this is no longer like the previous state where the origins of each life-force were unpenetrated.
Having observed these origins, one is further able to maintain and uphold the primary source of birth. Thus, among the twelve classes of beings, they cannot be drawn or summoned to take birth.
Upon reaching this stage, the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) is severed, and one realizes the *sarvatraga-tathatā* (all-pervading suchness) throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the realm of emotion (*vedanā-dhātu*), we have already attained its sameness. However, this is merely the first glimpse of the Buddha-realm;
it is like seeing the first light of dawn breaking in the east, which is already able to reveal things hidden within the darkness.

Yet the Buddha-realm thus perceived is like observing objects at the break of day, not yet like the great brightness filling the sky where nothing remains unpenetrated. This is because there remains one further layer.

The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is circumscribed and its domain covers it; hence it is called the "circumscribed domain of the aggregate of consciousness. This is the characteristic of this aggregate of consciousness when it has not yet been exhausted.
If, among the various classes of beings, one can neither summon them nor attain their commonality throughout the ten directions, [then this aggregate remains].
Furthermore, by employing the power of *vajra*-wisdom, one dissolves the six gates so that what was divided is joined and what was obstructed is opened;
thus, all attain accomplishment. Then the six faculties—seeing, hearing, and the rest—are like neighboring houses communicating with one another, such that they may function interchangeably.
The faculty of the eye can perform the Buddha-work of the ear, and the same applies to the other four [faculties]. Completely detached from sense organs and objects, they are pure and unimpeded.
The world and the body-and-mind become transparently clear within and without, like vaidūrya; they form a single, perfectly fused, pure, and enlightened jewel-consciousness.
This is no longer a manifestation of hidden mysteries, but is the sign that the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) has been exhausted.
For the turbidity of receiving life originates in the *vijñāna-skandha*; once the *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted, the continuity between matter and mind is severed.
These [afflictions] have also been completely severed and exhausted. Therefore, this person attains transcendence over the turbidity of lifespan.

Reaching this point, one finally perceives that the source of receiving life is entirely a phantom-like void, a state of hazy unreality; it is collectively termed inverted deluded thought, which constitutes the very root of this consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha).
Since the consciousness-aggregate is fundamentally rooted in a phantom-like void, how could it be mistaken?
By recognizing this, one gives rise to the ten kinds of grasping that follow. ○ The *Tongyi* says: "The body, mind, and world are all transformations of the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Now, observing that they return to the nature of consciousness, it is said that 'one has already attained their identity. ○ Master Tiantai says:

This is the accomplishment through opening and closing. The ancient interpretation held that the faculties (*indriya*) are joined without being divided and the realms (*dhātu*) are opened without being separated;

however, this meaning is still not exhaustive. I, the ignorant one, say that as for "joining," although the gates of the faculties (*indriyamukha*) are arranged as six, the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have never been anything other than one.
Returning to the source is like a vessel, a ring, a hairpin, and an armlet—all of which are originally one piece of gold.
As for "opening," although the six sense faculties are fused into one, in each single location they are never not six; from the essence, function arises, and every door interconnects.
This is like how a single piece of gold is fashioned into various vessels, rings, hairpins, and armlets. This mastery over opening and closing is called [the faculty of the mind].
[The text] states: "It is accomplished. However, since the subsequent section is still within the consciousness, why is it also said that the faculties are "separated" and "joined"?
It is because one merely speaks of "joining" and "separating," rather than "accomplishing. This is like suddenly joining and suddenly parting, or suddenly opening and suddenly closing;
they cannot be used interchangeably. Therefore, in the sixth section as well, one merely attains conformity through their mutual interchangeability.
Ānanda, you should know that these good sons have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and returned to the source within consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Although they have extinguished arising and ceasing, their subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected. (Since the aggregate of formations has been emptied, this constitutes the extinction of arising and ceasing; yet because they still rely upon the source of consciousness, this quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.

This aggregate of consciousness is what was referred to in the first fascicle as the "luminous essence of seeing. It is because the *ālaya-vijñāna* is already very close to the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), yet there still remain two kinds of deluded perceptions—both common and specific—that it is said to be "not yet perfected.")
This is the first cause for the grasping at causes. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the front pillar, and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the rear pillar.
The locus where the ten types of grasping arise is precisely between these two; therefore, all ten types of grasping are headed by this category.
Ānanda, you should know that when this virtuous son of noble family who practices concentration has already investigated and clearly perceived [this].

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is empty. When the emptiness of formations gives rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*), the preceding forms of activity vanish and submerge into the ocean of consciousness.
Since these originally surged forth from the ocean of consciousness, they naturally return to their source and revert to their origin.

This constitutes the cessation of the turbid arising and ceasing of birth and death, transcending the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*), and transforming into [the state of] change-and-decay (*anyathātva*).
Birth and death still persist. Within this final state of quiescence, not even a trace of the essence of arising and ceasing remains;

yet that which is purely the wondrous, singular flavor of tranquil permanence is still not fully perfected. This is precisely the sign that the consciousness-aggregate (vijñānaskandha) has not been shattered and remains shrouded.

One can cause one's own faculties to contract, join, open, and separate; furthermore, one attains universal awareness with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions, and through this pervasive realization, enters the perfect source.
Generally, whenever an attachment arises, it must first be triggered by beholding extraordinary signs within Great Samādhi. Now, one practices emptiness.
As for the manifestation of consciousness: it can cause the six sense organs of one's own body to join those that are separated and open those that are joined;

thus, the six organs approach mutual functioning. Furthermore, it causes its awareness to merge seamlessly with the pervasive awareness of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, like a thousand lamps in a single room whose light interpenetrates without duality. Then, what distinction remains between the internal and the external?

It is through this luminous clarity that one is able to enter the Perfect; therein all categories are universally contained. It is by entering the Origin that the myriad transformations find their beginning.
Indeed, when the four aggregates are utterly dispelled, one finds one’s final resting place here, just as when the various waves have ceased.
They vanish into the sea; is this not a most extraordinary sign? Yet, it remains within the realm of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

If one establishes a cause of true permanence regarding that which has returned [to its source] and gives rise to a resolute conviction, such a person falls into the attachment to the "cause of causes."

He became a companion to Śvikaḷa (translated here as the "Yellow-Headed Heretic"), who had returned to the *tattva* of darkness (*tamas*). Regarding this *tattva* of darkness: from darkness arises intellect (*buddhi*); from intellect arises the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*); from the ego-consciousness arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*);

from the five subtle elements arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); and from the five gross elements arise the eleven sense organs. Among these twenty-three factors, the divine self (*puruṣa*) is the sovereign. Thus, they claim that all phenomena arise from the *tattva* of darkness, while the divine self is that which experiences these phenomena.

Consequently, he became deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and lost his true knowledge and vision. As for the cause upon which he relied, he falsely established a single cause as the fundamental cause.
This is the ground [of delusion]. Indeed, true causes do not exist; everything that exists is but delusion.
Now, entering into the perfect and primordial source is certainly attaining one's place of return. Nevertheless, it ultimately is not the true and eternal.
This is because consciousness is but a phantom image of ignorance, formless and void, ultimately lacking reality—just as when a person dreams.
Relying upon and taking refuge in a place of support, one falsely gives rise to feelings of celebration; how could there be anything truly real here?

When a practitioner encounters this, they should further employ the power of vajra-wisdom to grind away what lies before them. If, within that which is taken as a refuge, [one still harbors attachments...]

Establishing a cause that is true and eternal, one gives rise to a superior and wondrous understanding, yet does not seek further progress. Such a person falls into the attachment to the "cause of causes.
Here, "cause" (yin) means "that which is relied upon" (yi). Originally, it is not something that can be relied upon; yet they falsely calculate the mind that relies as being the object relied upon.
Having fallen into this attachment, they are like the Yellow-Headed Heretics who establish the *tattva* (the ultimate principle) and take refuge in the *tattva*.

They become companions for those of their own kind, yet they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi; they do not know the true fruit, have lost their wisdom and insight, and do not know the true cause.

This is called the first establishment of a mind that grasps at attainment; it constitutes a fruit toward which one has taken refuge, yet it is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of external paths.

Such being the case, this is called the first establishment of a mind that possesses the notion of "having something to attain," resulting in a fruit that has something to which one returns; thus it is directed [toward the mundane].

The faculties were once separated, yet now they are joined; the perfect penetration is drawing near. Yet now, that which was perfect has become partial, and that which was penetrating has become obstructed;

thus, one has instead moved further away from the goal. Previously, one was about to attain great enlightenment within the heaven of Nirvana, but now one turns one's back on the city of Nirvana and cannot see it.
Previously, the awakened mind was about to emerge, and one was about to become a child of the Buddha; now, one has instead given rise to the ways of external paths.
[They] sow [the seeds of delusion] and thereby sever the Buddha-nature. How could they know that the fulfillment of Bodhi ultimately results in non-attainment?
○ He said: This is a mistaken recognition of having obtained the fundamental wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable.
Ānanda, furthermore, there may be a son of good family who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth-and-death;
yet, regarding this state of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), his subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.

If he regards that which he has returned to as his own self-substance, then throughout the entirety of the void realm, among all sentient beings within the twelve categories, they are all seen as a single flow within his own body.

When one gives rise to the conviction that there is a "producer," such a person falls into the dualistic grasping of "agent" and "non-agent. Maheśvara (the Māra King at the Peak of Form) manifests boundless bodies to become his companion.
Thus, they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the second [stage]:

establishing the mind as the agent, whereby the fruit of the agent's activity is accomplished. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to the "I" of the Greatly Arrogant Heaven.

The Pien-yüan School (the fifteenth of the non-Buddhist schools of the Western Regions). They assert that all sentient and insentient things within the triple world are born from Maheśvara. As for Maheśvara:

empty space is his head, the great earth is his body, water is his urine, mountains are his excrement, all sentient beings are the worms within his belly, wind is his breath, and fire is his warmth. This is roughly equivalent to what is said in this region regarding Pangu giving birth to heaven and earth.

This second conception is the grasping at the capable and the incapable. Ānanda, furthermore, when the consciousness-aggregate manifests within the emptiness of formations, if one merely conceives of that consciousness-aggregate which is the locus of refuge as being the nature of that which provides refuge and support;

Now, further regarding the view that the self is the intrinsic substance: one claims that all sentient beings flow forth from the substance of the self, thereby giving rise to a notion of supreme excellence.
One then clings to the idea that the self can produce them, while they cannot produce themselves. Such a person falls into the dualistic clinging to "the producer" and "the non-producer.
This is precisely like Maheśvara, who manifests the bodies of boundless sentient beings and then claims—
"All sentient beings are born from me; they are of the same kind. Thus, Śūra became his companion.

Because of this, he became deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost his true knowledge and vision. It is like looking at a bubble arising within the ocean and not realizing that one's own body has not yet emerged from that bubble.
This is called the second [delusion]: establishing the mind that "I am the agent."

To claim that one can accomplish the fruits of one's own affairs is to oppose perfect penetration and turn one’s back on Nirvana. It gives rise to the state of Mahesvara, characterized by great arrogance;
one looks down upon all things, believing they are born from oneself, thereby cultivating the seeds of a pervasive self and a perfect self.

How could such a person know that the fulfillment of Bodhi is the spontaneous creation of the mind? The former was calculating the "object" (the perceived); this is calculating the "agent" (the perceiver).

He said: "This is a mistaken identification of the ten directions as being solely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), and of the nature of consciousness as flowing forth immeasurable Tathāgatas and so forth.

Furthermore, good son, though you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness and already extinguished birth and death, within this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected."

If, regarding that to which one has returned and upon which one relies, one suspects that one’s own body and mind flow forth from it, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it—
then, with respect to that ground from which everything flows forth, one should form the understanding that it is the true, eternal body, free from arising and ceasing.
Amidst arising and ceasing, they prematurely calculate that there is permanence; thus they are deluded regarding non-arising and likewise confused about arising and ceasing.

Dwelling securely in this immersion, those who conceive such a superior understanding fall into the dualistic attachment to permanence and impermanence, taking the Lord God (Īśvara) as their companion.

Having become confused about the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost their true knowledge and vision, this is called the third [stage]: establishing causes based on the mind to produce deluded conceptualized effects.
This violates and distances one from perfect penetration, turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.
This is the third calculation, the attachment to permanence and impermanence.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the manifestation of the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) occurs, if one takes joy in having a place of refuge within that consciousness-aggregate, one will then suspect that one’s own body and mind flow forth from within it, and that even the worlds of the ten directions arise from within it. Thus one calculates:
This place from which arising flows forth is precisely the essence of true non-arising. Yet, while situated within birth and death, one prematurely calculates it to be eternally abiding.
Thus, one is both deluded regarding the truly non-arising nature and confused about the presently manifesting phenomena of birth and death.
Dwelling in this delusion, one gives rise to a false conviction, taking the impermanent to be permanent. Such a person falls into the dualistic attachment of permanence and impermanence. Since—
To reckon that he can produce me is identical to reckoning that Maheśvara can produce all things; therefore, they reckon Maheśvara as their companion.

This is truly because Maheśvara is also not a permanent deity, yet the non-Buddhists do not know this and consequently cling to him as the fundamental source for the production of heaven and earth (just as, in our own tradition, the Great Ultimate produces the Two Forms). From this arises delusion.

Regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi, they lose their true knowledge and vision; this is called the third establishment of causes based on the mind, which results in the formation of false conceptualizations.

That is to say, relying on the source of consciousness, they falsely conceptualize it as being eternally abiding. This contradicts perfect penetration and turns one's back on Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.

While the former conceptualization held that the "self" is perfect and gives rise to phenomena, this conceptualization holds that those phenomena are perfect and give rise to the self; hence it is called "inverted."
How could one know that it is only upon the fulfillment of Bodhi that one is permitted to teach that all phenomena are consciousness-only?

This [view] and the previous attachment both arise from consciousness, yet what they calculate differs. The former held that consciousness itself is the self (*ātman*) capable of producing all things;
this holds that the self emerges from consciousness and is true and eternal—this is their distinction. Question: The myriad...
"The Dharma is consciousness-only; this is what the Tathāgata has taught. How is it that here [in your position] everything falls into external seeds? Answer:

In our internal teaching, the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only, arising through conditions and transformations, all like dreams or illusions; they do not truly arise. Therefore, one does not establish [the duality of] knowing and seeing, nor does one give rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
Now, you say that you establish a mind that is the "attained" (*prāpya*), establish a mind that is the "agent" (*kartṛ*), and establish a mind that is the "causal basis" (*hetvāśraya*).

All of these are instances of establishing knowledge upon what is already known and seen. Furthermore, while the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) correctly clarifies that there are no phenomena external to consciousness, this [view] reckons that consciousness can produce other phenomena;
it is thus utterly inverted. How could these two be conflated? ○ He [Hegel? says:
This is an erroneous recognition that everything from the physical body outward—the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is all an object within the wondrously luminous true mind.
This is similar to the first kind; however, while that takes the source of consciousness as its point of return, this further takes that point of return as the productive cause.

Furthermore, good son, although you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death, your subtle and wondrous state within quiescent extinction has not yet reached full perfection.

If, regarding the objects of knowledge (which are the objects of the returning knowledge, and which also constitute the aggregate of consciousness), one establishes a conviction based on the notion that this knowledge is all-pervasive and complete—such that all grasses and trees in the ten directions are called sentient beings and are no different from humans;

and that when grasses and trees become humans, those humans, upon death, return to becoming grasses and trees in the ten directions—one who gives rise to such a superior conviction without discrimination falls into the attachment of "knowing the unknowable" (claiming that insentient things possess knowledge). Furthermore, [if one claims] that insentient things have knowledge...

In reality, they are fundamentally ignorant; therefore it is said that they "cling to the knowledge of non-knowledge. (2) The two *pāṣaṇḍas* cling to all-encompassing awakening (*bodha*—that is, knowledge).

They form a companion group, deluding themselves regarding the Buddha’s *bodhi* and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth calculation: the mind that considers itself perfectly awakened.
It achieves a false and erroneous fruit, strays far from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of *nirvāṇa*, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted knowledge.
This fourth calculation is the cognition of non-cognition. Furthermore, son of good family, when the emptiness of consciousness (*vijñāna*) manifests,
if one perceives within the observed aggregate of consciousness that its cognitive nature is omnipresent and nowhere not pervasive, and that it is perfect and encompasses all objects,
one will then falsely establish a view based on this pervasive and perfect cognition, claiming that all phenomena arise through the transformation of cognition.
Know that there is no difference; phenomena (*dharma*) likewise have no difference. Thus, even insentient things such as grasses and trees may be called sentient;
how, then, does the sentience of humans differ from their insentience? Grasses and trees can become human beings, and when humans die, they return to being grasses and trees.
Without discriminating between the sentient and the insentient, all things everywhere possess cognition. One should develop a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding this.
Such a person falls into the attachment of knowing and not-knowing. They become companions to the Pāṭhaśailas, who maintain that all things possess consciousness.
Thus they lose the Way of Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth type of externalist.

By reckoning "perfect knowledge" as the causal mind, their result will ultimately be empty, erroneous, and unaccomplished; they merely distance themselves from perfect penetration and turn their backs on Nirvana.
...and thus gave rise to this category of inverted cognition. To take ignorance for knowledge is what is called inverted cognition.
How could one know that when perfect Bodhi is attained, the worlds of the ten directions will, by a mere thought, be transformed into supreme enlightened awareness?
Question: Regarding National Preceptor Gwan’s teaching that sentient beings and insentient things share a single essence, [Chong]...
The National Preceptor has spoken of insentient things attaining Buddhahood; how does this differ from the present [teaching]? Answer:

The inner teaching (Buddhism) maintains that through delusion regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) is formed. From this karma-consciousness, the two divisions of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) arise, thereby distinguishing between sentient beings and insentient things, each established separately. Once awakening is attained, the karma-consciousness is transformed and becomes True Suchness.
Thus, sentient and insentient beings are of one identical, perfectly interfused, and pure jewel-like awakening;
they universally constitute a single Buddha-land, which is called the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land. The entire body is the land, and the entire land is the body.
How could there then be distinctions such as grasses, trees, and humans, or humans being grasses and trees? This is what is taught in the inner teachings.
"The insentient preach the Dharma" refers to the time after consciousness has been shattered and all has become a single mind.

At this stage, however, the karmic consciousness still persists and the subject-object duality remains; they have not yet been fused into a single entity, which is a false conceptualization. Question:
In the preceding text, it was stated that grasses, trees, metals, and stones can all manifest as demons and bring about calamities. Are these not sentient beings? Answer: This is...
The spirits that rely on grass and cling to wood possess consciousness; it is not that the grass and wood themselves originally possessed consciousness. It is said:
"If an old maple tree transforms into a feathered immortal, or withered wheat transforms into a butterfly, this is a transition from the insentient to the sentient."
"The virtuous woman transformed into a chaste stone; the earthworm transformed into a lily. These are cases of passing from the sentient to the insentient;
what, then, is the meaning of this? Answer: "These are transformations occurring due to a particular resonance.

It is not that the aged maple or the withered wheat were originally sentient, nor is it that the virtuous woman or the earthworm were originally insentient. This is so for those who have not yet broken through the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*)."
Those who falsely claim that heaven and earth share the same root and that all things are one body are merely of the same class as the *pāṭha* and *kṣapaṇaka* heretics.

Formerly, when the Elder Huìtáng was discussing the Way with Xià Yígōng, they reached the point where all phenomena are realized as oneself and where sentient and insentient beings constitute a single body.
At that time, a dog was lying beneath the incense table; [the Master] pressed down upon it...
Changchui struck the dog and then struck the incense table, saying, "The dog has sentience, so it departs; the incense table lacks sentience, so it remains.
How can sentience and insentience suddenly become one? Xia was unable to answer.
Changchui said, "As soon as you enter into deliberation, you have already fallen into superfluous dharmas. When did you ever realize that all dharmas are the self? ○ Heze said:
This is the mistaken perception of the appearances of the floating dust and the vessel-world; one should contemplate that these transform into supreme enlightened awareness.

Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned formations to the point of emptiness, you have already extinguished birth and death; yet, within this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous essence is not yet perfected.

If, within the state where the faculties are interfused and mutually interchangeable—(the single character "zhong" [middle] sufficiently reveals the subtle wonder of this mutual interchangeability, which was previously contained but not yet manifested)—one has already attained conformity.
Thus, they were spontaneously transformed. All things came into being: they sought the light of fire, delighted in the purity of water, and craved the circulation of wind.
Observing the *rajas* (the earth element)—which constitutes the vessel-world and all material forms, for everything is produced by this *rajas*—they each venerated it.

Through these various *rajas* (the four great elements), they gave rise to their fundamental cause (*mūla-hetu*). "Giving rise to" means production; "creating" means fashioning; "fundamental cause" refers to the root source. [They] erroneously reckoned that the four great elements are what produce all things.

This is the root source for producing all things. They establish the view of permanence. Such people fall into the attachment to birth as being non-birth (falsely calculating that they can produce the myriad dharmas, yet in reality they cannot produce them).

Together with the various Kāśyapas (a specific clan name) and the Brahmins (the general caste name), they diligently exert their minds and bodies, serving fire and venerating water, seeking to transcend birth and death.
Thus they become companions who are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true insight. This is called...
The fifth [delusion] is attachment to veneration. With a deluded mind following external objects, one establishes false causes for seeking and falsely hopes for fruits.
This is to be far removed from perfect penetration and to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted transformation (the principle of inverted transformation).

This is the fifth calculation regarding the arising and non-arising [of consciousness]. Furthermore, son of good family, when the manifestation of the emptiness-consciousness occurs, for one whose aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is exhausted, the six gates are dissolved and the various faculties function interchangeably. Although one has not yet attained this mutual functioning, [the seeds are present].
Within the perfectly interfused state where the sense organs function interchangeably, one has already attained the ability to act according to the mind and will;

this refers to the eighteen types of meditative transformations, such as water emerging from the upper part of the body and fire from the lower part—indeed, all Arhats possess such supernormal powers and transformations.
Nevertheless, they have only just attained the capacity for such compliance; the subtle wonder of the mutual functioning of the organs remains yet contained within them.
Before it has yet been aroused, the practitioner, within the state of compliance, completely transforms various arising attachments;
they falsely claim that all transformations arise from the four great elements. Thus, they turn their backs on the luminous fire of their own inherent nature.
Yet they seek the light of fire; they turn their backs on the nature of their own water which is pure, yet delight in the purity of external water;
they turn their backs on the nature of their own wind which circulates everywhere, yet crave the circulation of external wind;

they turn their backs on the nature of their own earth where there is no phenomenon that does not arise, yet they focus exclusively on the element of earth as the sole agent capable of producing all things, thus engaging with water and earth as external objects.

Fire, water, wind, and earth—each is venerated as such. Taking these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to be the fundamental root of all arising and creation, they establish these four elements as the true sovereigns that govern all things, asserting that they are eternally abiding and indestructible.
They falsely reckon that these can give rise to the myriad phenomena, yet in reality, they cannot. Such people fall into the attachment to the "arising of the non-arisen. All [of them...]
Kāśyapa, there are those who, along with brahmins, exert themselves physically and mentally to serve fire and water in their quest for liberation from birth and death.
They come to become companions [in this delusion], confusing the true fruit and losing the true cause. This is called the fifth attachment to false delusions:
honoring and serving perverted practices while being bewildered by the spirit of awakening; [seeking it] through the material objects of the four great elements rather than through the cause.
Based on calculation, one establishes false seeking for causes; hoping for results where there are no results, one seeks with false expectations for effects.
Thus, perfect penetration grows ever more distant and one turns one's back on the clarity of *nirvāṇa*, giving rise to the various types of inverted transformations of principle.

How could one know that the mind is the source of transformation and consciousness is the seed of transformation? That the four great elements are what is produced and transformed, while in reality they are not the producer or the transformer?
How transformative this is! ○ He said: "This is a mistaken recognition that all seven elements are the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.

Furthermore, good man, you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, within this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected."

If, regarding the perfect luminosity (which is the *vijñāna-skandha*), one calculates that the luminosity within it is empty, and—falsely denigrating the cessation of all transformations—takes this eternal cessation as a basis for reliance and develops a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward it as the refuge, such a person falls into the attachment of "seeking a refuge where there is no refuge.

They will become companions among the *śūnyatā-devas* (gods of space) in the Heaven of No-Thought (here referring briefly to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception to encompass the four formless realms, not the non-perception of the fourth dhyāna). Thus they lose the Buddha’s Bodhi.
One loses all knowledge and insight; this is called the sixth "perfectly void and heartless" state, which results in the fruit of empty ruin.
It is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of annihilationism.
This is the sixth calculation, which returns to the state of having no refuge.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the emptiness-consciousness manifests, if one perceives the perfect clarity of the aggregate of consciousness and consequently calculates that the body of indistinct, void, and non-existent within that clarity is the ultimate nature of emptiness, one will then destroy all manifestations of phenomena, desiring to reduce the body to ashes and extinguish it in the dust so that not even a speck of dust remains. Thus he says:
"Permanent cessation" serves as a basis for reliance; taking this permanent cessation as a basis, one regards it as a place of refuge and rest.

One who gives rise to such a superior and wondrous understanding falls into the attachment of "taking that which has no refuge as a refuge. This is because permanent cessation is empty and is likewise an illusory phenomenon, not a real place of refuge.
For this reason, those among the various classes of beings in the four heavens of emptiness take the celestial hosts of those heavens as their companions.

They are deluded regarding Bodhi and have lost their wisdom and insight. This is called the sixth [type of practitioner], who takes the formless and the void as the cause and takes annihilation, emptiness, and non-existence as the fruit.
They oppose perfect penetration and turn their backs on Nirvana, thereby producing the seeds of annihilationism.
How could they know that perfect Bodhi is the spontaneous, true void and wondrous existence? Question: How does this differ from the two vehicles discussed later?
What is the difference? Answer: Both discard existence and take up emptiness; their views and understandings are identical. However, their initial intentions differ.

This [approach] is that of the ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists, who suppress afflictions to take up emptiness. That [approach] is that of the noble lineage, which eradicates afflictions to take up emptiness.

The Confucian scholars here in this land refute Buddhism, constantly claiming it leads to "voidity" (*kōmō*) or "annihilationism" (*dannetsu*). How could they know that annihilationism and voidity were already condemned by the Buddhas of old?

"You belong to the lineage of Māra; why then wait for the sharp rebukes of the Confucians? ○ He said: "This is a mistaken recognition that emptiness and the three realms of existence are all fundamentally non-existent."

Furthermore, good son, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize their emptiness and has already extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected—should they regard the Perfect and Constant:

(looking back over what precedes, within this single realm, the terms "Perfect," "Primordial," "Fusion," "Clarity," and "Constant" each signify a specific meaning. "Primordial" signifies that all dharmas ultimately return [to the source]; "Fusion" signifies that the myriad transformations are contained therein;

"Clarity" signifies that the entire substance is transparent and luminous; "Constant" signifies ultimate firmness and stability. Each of these relates to the original text, which can be seen by careful examination. However, because they are equally the pervasive ocean of consciousness, they are all termed "Perfect. Moreover, they are all alike in being similar to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

[This is] a characteristic. Because practitioners do not understand that [what they see] is a semblance and not the reality, each gives rise to different calculations and different attachments according to what they perceive. [They claim] the body is solid and eternally abiding, identical to the essence (the essence is, in fact, the nature).

(As with seeing-nature transforming into what is called the essence of seeing, etc. it is round and long, never tilting or receding. One who develops a resolute conviction in this will fall into the attachment of grasping at "life" and "non-life.
Such a person becomes a companion to the various asuras who seek long life; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision.
This is called the seventh attachment to the source of life. It establishes a cause of solid delusion and leads to the fruit of enduring toil.
This violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of delusive extension.
This is the seventh calculation: that greed is not greed. Furthermore, son of good family, when the manifestation of the consciousness of emptiness occurs:

If, regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one perceives its perfect constancy and likewise perceives the constancy of the nature of seeing, one then desires that life itself be constant.

Consequently, one seeks to make the body firm and enduring so that it may abide eternally in the world, identical to the perfect constancy of that nature, never falling or passing away—much like the practitioners of the Immortal school who cultivate both life and nature together, achieving the sublime excellence of both form and spirit. Thus, one gives rise to this superior and wondrous understanding.

They give rise to false attachments and remain in this world, unaware that this body is like a plantain tree, a flash of lightning, or a drop of dew—fundamentally ungraspable and not to be clung to as permanent.
Because they cling to what should not be clung to, these people follow their attachment rather than non-attachment;
seeking long life, they become companions to those peerless sages who likewise seek long life.
Deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and having lost their true knowledge and vision, this is called the seventh attachment: taking the aggregate of consciousness as the source of longevity.

They establish a solid false cause and pursue a long-lasting false fruit; thus they oppose perfect penetration, turn their backs on Nirvana, and give rise to the seeds of delusory thoughts that prolong existence.
How could they know that the Dharma-body is eternal throughout past and present, indestructible and...
This is indeed the nature of decay. ○ An external text says: "The Creator toils me with life, grants me rest through old age, and brings repose through death.
Therefore, the character for "toil" (勞) should remain as it is; there is no necessity to substitute it with the character for "hardship" (牢).
○ A long life is inherently not worth coveting; moreover, the nature upon which one relies is merely the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), which is already but a semblance of permanence.

It is not truly eternal. The life-force that it accompanies is entirely subject to birth and death, empty and illusory; even if it endures for many kalpas, it will ultimately fall into voidness and extinction.
How could it be real, true, and permanently abiding? Formerly, Lü Dongbin visited Huanglong, who said, "Even if you last for eighty thousand kalpas, you are merely a ghost guarding a corpse.
Dongbin attained great enlightenment, and there is a verse concerning the smashing of his gourd and the breaking of his lute.
Alas! Āṣāḍha, an ancient sage, was thus rebuked by the Buddha.
Are not those who carry water-jars today and lecture on the arts of the bedchamber likewise sinners like him? That scholars and officials are deluded and fail to awaken is truly pitiable.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) into emptiness and already extinguished the cycle of birth and death, one may yet not have perfected the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*śānti*).

Observing that life-force is interpenetrating—wherein consciousness, vitality, and warmth sustain one another without interruption (taking consciousness as the primary factor here, this refers to the consciousness-aggregate [vijñānaskandha] interpenetrating all forms of life)—one might nevertheless retain the defilements (*kleśa*) for fear they would be entirely consumed.
Thus, at this juncture, one sits within a lotus palace, extensively transforming the seven treasures and greatly increasing precious jewels.
Those who indulge their minds and give rise to such superior understanding fall into the attachment to "the real within the unreal.

They become companions of the Kiṃkaras (a class of celestial beings belonging to the Realm of Desire). They lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the eighth stage:

giving rise to the cause of perverse thinking and establishing the fruit of blazing dust. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, giving birth to the lineage of celestial Māras.

This eighth view maintains that the true is truly non-existent. Furthermore, son of good family, when the consciousness of emptiness manifests, since one takes consciousness as the source of life (*jīvamūla*), one observes this life-force by naming it the "sustainer" (*saṃdhāraka*) of both form and mind.
Yet, the afflictions (*kleśa*) do not emerge to move the mind or enslave the body; thus, the source of life is fundamentally coextensive with the afflictions. Therefore, [the practitioner] exists...

They exist together, and with their death, they perish together. Thus, fearing that once the defilements are exhausted, the source of life will necessarily be severed, they falsely conceive a plan to retain these defilements so as not to let them be completely extinguished.
Furthermore, taking advantage of the moment when the consciousness manifests at the end of this practice, they effect a total transformation according to their own minds;
thus, they indulge at will in the creation of various objects of desire—precious jewels and beautiful women—and therein they become dissolute. On the contrary, [the practitioner]...
They give rise to resolute conviction, regarding this as the practice of a great Bodhisattva.

How can this compare to a Bodhisattva who truly perceives the source of life, entering the dust of worldly toil to deliver sentient beings? Because they falsely reckon this to be the true Bodhisattva practice, they do not know it is not true;

thus they fall into the attachment to "true" and "untrue," while seeking to reach the summit of the Heaven of Sovereignty over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), which is able to transform the realms of desire.
Taking those who seek self-entertainment as one's companions, both the correct fruit and the correct cause are utterly lost.

This is called the eighth cause for giving rise to perverse thoughts, which establishes the fruit of blazing afflictions. Now, when first seeking perfect penetration, it was said that the complete exhaustion of conditioned thoughts is the cause;
yet now, one conversely takes the indulgence of perverse thoughts as the cause. This is to be far removed from perfect penetration.
Originally seeking *nirvāṇa*, one takes the non-establishment of even a speck of dust as the fruit; now, conversely, you take the blazing intensity of worldly toil (*rajas*) as the fruit.
This is to turn one's back on the city of *nirvāṇa*. Such things "gather according to their kind"; it is certain that you will give birth to the seeds of celestial Māras.

How could you know that when the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, perfect *bodhi* is attained? Indeed, this does not preclude seeking [the Way] within brothels or wine shops.

Maitreya, one seeks Samantabhadra in the willow alleys and flower-lined streets! Long ago, Udraka Rāmaputra, by means of worldly wisdom, suppressed the afflictions of the lower realms and attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), possessing the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). At that time, the sovereign held him in high esteem and welcomed him into the palace.
There, the women of the court prostrated themselves, touching his feet in worship. When Udraka touched the hand of a woman, he immediately gave rise to—
Through craving, one loses supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Thus it is said: "As soon as a single thought of desire arises, one immediately loses the five supernormal faculties.

How could there be one whose perverse thoughts and worldly passions blaze so fiercely yet does not fall into decline? As for Kumārajīva’s taking of a wife or Sengzhe’s indulgence in lust, their underlying motivations are unfathomable;
furthermore, these cases cannot be cited as precedents for general discussion.

Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize emptiness, you have already extinguished arising and ceasing; yet, within this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.

Within the light of life (which refers to the *vijñāna-skandha*, or the "light of destiny"), you still distinguish between the refined and the coarse, and discern the true from the false, as cause and effect respond to one another.

One seeks only for resonance and response—cultivating the path as the cause is called "resonance" (gan), and realizing cessation as the fruit is called "response" (ying)—yet turns one's back on the path of purity, namely, the vision of suffering and the abandonment of its origin.

Having realized cessation and cultivated the path, they abide in cessation and rest; no longer advancing further, those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the category of śrāvakas of fixed nature.
They become companions to those monks who have heard nothing and to those of overweening pride, and thus they lose the Buddha’s bodhi.
They lose their knowledge and vision; this is called the ninth state where the perfect essence accords with the mind to achieve the fruit of quiescence.

It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness. (He said: "The previous eight were all mistaken entries onto bypaths; these two, however, merely come to rest at the conjured city.")

This is the ninth type: the śrāvaka who clings to fixed characteristics. Furthermore, son of good family, when practicing the manifestation of emptiness and consciousness, by thoroughly investigating the aggregate of consciousness, one deeply clarifies the fundamental source from which sentient beings receive their life-force.

Within this clarity regarding life, one sees that this consciousness contains both tainted and untainted seeds; thus, one makes a definitive discernment regarding these seeds of suffering and its origin.
This is with outflows (*sāsrava*); this is coarse; this is counterfeit. This is the seed of cessation and the path; this is without outflows (*anāsrava*); this is refined; this is authentic.
These two types clearly illustrate cause and effect, establishing a definitive correspondence between them. One seeks only the stimulus of the cause to summon the response of the fruit.
Through actual cultivation and actual realization, the sole requirement is to swiftly transcend birth and death, rather than following a "cultivation of non-cultivation. No...

To realize this realization is to turn one's back on the path of purity. Regarding that which is called the vision of suffering and the abandonment of its origin, the realization of cessation and the cultivation of the path—one dwells in quiescent extinction and immediately rests there.
One does not give rise to a joyful aspiration for the bodhisattvas' playful mastery of supernormal powers or the purification of buddha-fields.
Thus, one remains attached to the illusory city and does not proceed toward the place of jewels. In this regard—
Those who develop such superior resolve will fall into the category of śrāvakas of fixed nature— dull-witted arhats who do not turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna—

and will become companions to those monks who lack learning, to śrāvakas attached to the Dharma, and to those who claim to have realized what they have not realized and attained what they have not attained.
They will remain utterly deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi and will lose the correct knowledge and vision.
This is called the ninth fulfillment of the causal mind that seeks resonance through dedicated application. It achieves the fruit of cessation that universally accords with profound stillness;

yet this is but the nirvana with remainder. Being limited to the stage of the seventh faith and still shrouded by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), it does not even reach the ground of the cause for perfect penetration—how much less could it reach the ground of the fruit of nirvana without remainder? I see that such a person is bound by emptiness.

They merely give rise to the class of those entangled in emptiness; although they are not yet actual demons, in terms of their attachment to the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), they are in reality no different from the various demons.

Furthermore, good son, you may have exhausted the emptiness of all natures and already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.

If, within this perfectly integrated, pure, and luminous awakening, you develop an investigation into its profound subtlety and thereby establish yourself in nirvana without proceeding further, [you will remain there].

Those who give rise to such a resolute conviction fall into the fixed nature of the *pratyekabuddhas*—the class of those who seek awakening through conditions alone (the peers of the *pratyekabuddhas* and *viveka-buddhas*) and do not turn their minds back [toward the Great Vehicle].
They become their companions, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth stage:

the "Perfectly Harmonious Mind" (*yuanjue minxin*)—where "perfect" (*yuan*) means perfect fusion, "awakening" (*jue*) means luminous awareness, and "harmonious mind" (*minxin*) means purity—which achieves the fruit of profound clarity. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on it.

The City of Nirvana. To give rise to an awakening that is perfectly luminous yet fails to transform the seeds of perfection (meaning one cannot dissolve through what has been realized, but instead clings to the empty, pure reflection of the perfect circle;
this is what the Patriarchal House calls "sentiment forming within the breast of a hidden man").

This is the tenth reckoning: the fixed-nature Pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, son of good family, when the consciousness of emptiness manifests, if one contemplates the perfect fusion of the six sense bases into one, the purity of breaking through existence to return to emptiness, and clearly perceives the awakening-clarity of the life-source (*jīvamūla*), thereby developing a profound and subtle investigation, one becomes a Solitary Realizer (*pratyekabuddha*). Thus, observing the transformation of phenomena, one develops deep...
The Pratyekabuddha attains a profound and wondrous awakening by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination.

Taking that very point where the profound and wondrous awakening arises as the place of Nirvana and rest, they cling to it firmly and refuse to let go. They remain stagnant on the single path of perfect clarity and fail to proceed to the Precious Abode.
This is what is meant by the saying: "When the water is clear and the moon is full, the practitioner of the Way feels sorrow. Regarding this:
If one gives rise to such resolute conviction, that person will fall into the fixed category of a *pratyekabuddha*. Compared to a *śrāvaka*, they are slightly superior by one step.
They shall be the companions of those belonging to the same class as the various *pratyekabuddhas* and *vivekajinas* who do not turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi, they remain utterly deluded; regarding right knowledge and vision, they have lost them entirely.
This is called the tenth [stage], wherein by means of the perfectly integrated, awakened, bright, and pure mind, one brings to fruition the result of profound and subtle investigation.
That which they call "perfect enlightenment" (yuanjue) is merely a state of conformity; it is truly far removed from perfect penetration (yuantong).
That which they call "luminous stillness" (zhanming) is merely the awakening to an object; it is truly contrary to nirvana.
Although they possess enlightened clarity, they are unable to dissolve and transcend what has been awakened to; how can this compare to the constant [practice] of the Bodhisattvas?

Awakening does not abide; therefore, it gives rise to the perfected seed of non-transformation. Although this is not yet the true demon itself, in terms of its attachment to the dharma-attachment (*dharmagrāha*), it is in reality no different from the various demons.

Once, a monk asked Caoshan, "What is it like when the bright moon is suspended in the sky? Caoshan said, "It is still but a man standing on the steps. The monk said, "I beg the Master to lead him upward."
Jiē (Tang). He said: "We shall meet after the moon has set. Question: Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are all world-transcending sages;
for what reason are they also listed among the ranks of Māra? Answer: This sutra takes perfect penetration as its primary principle.

If there is even the slightest trace of attachment or stagnation, it constitutes a violation of perfect penetration. Those who fall into this state become entangled in divergent branches and dull stagnation, which harms the fundamental matter.
"Jun: 'If he were not a Māra, what would he be? However, I have distinguished him by his fixed nature; this refers only to those who do not turn their minds [toward enlightenment].
