This clarifies that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is a deluded thought of pervasive fusion. Now, you possess thoughts and considerations, which is what is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As soon as these thoughts and considerations stir, all your eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body are made subject to their service.

If your physical body were not of the same nature as these thoughts and considerations, then the body would be real while the thoughts would be empty; since the empty and the real would be discordant, for what reason would [the body] follow them?

Is it not because one is impelled by mindfulness? Therefore, whatever various images are grasped before one’s eyes must first be moved by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), after which the various sense faculties (*indriya*) subsequently apprehend them.
This sufficiently demonstrates that this body is in correspondence with mindfulness, never separated from it for even a moment.
It is just like a performer of song, dance, or acrobatics who follows the beat of another: when the beat is slow, the steps are slow; when the beat is rapid, [the steps are rapid].

The steps are hurried. The five faculties are likewise in relation to the mind (*manas*). When the mental ground arises, the bodily wheel moves; when the mental ground ceases, the faculties and their objects become tranquil.
Thus, when waking, one encounters forms, which constitutes ideation (*saṃjñā*); when sleeping, one communes with the spirit, which constitutes dreaming.
Both ideation and dreaming have the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their essence. Due to these ideations, the mind wavers and becomes deluded.
The emotions suddenly lose their tranquil true mind; this is why the aggregate of thought is called "pervasive delusive ideation.

To say it is "pervasive" means that this thinking mind, within the five sense organs, is perfectly pervasive and penetrating, unlike the various organs which are obstructed and not pervasive, or limited and not penetrating.

The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and migrates in secret. As nails grow and hair sprouts, vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles. Day and night they alternate, yet there is never any realization of this.
Ānanda, if this were not you, how could your physical form undergo change? If it must be truly you, why do you have no awareness of it?
Thus, your various formations (saṃskāras) ceaselessly flow from moment to moment; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden false conception.
This clarifies that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is a subtle and hidden delusion. Now, the nature of the aggregate of formations is transformation;
thus it is also called the principle of transformation. This principle of transformation flows and shifts without ceasing, moving on and on, subtly and incessantly displacing itself.
Within the single human body, fingernails grow and hair emerges; this is the transition from youth to maturity. Vital energy wanes and the face becomes wrinkled;
this is the transition from vigor to old age. Birth follows birth and death follows death, succeeding one another day and night before us—what is called moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*).
It does not pause, yet there is not a single person who can perceive it; how subtle its secret movement is!
Ānanda, if this aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) were not your body, how could it cause your nails to grow and your hair to lengthen?

It can be seen that it is not separate from you. If this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) were truly your body, why does it undergo change day and night without you ever being aware of it?
It can be seen that it is not identical to you. That it is neither "not you" nor "you"—these two states cannot be definitively established.

It is clear enough that these are empty and false, and not real. Thus, as for your present conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*), which shift and flow from moment to moment without ceasing—subtle and difficult to perceive, hidden and difficult to know—it is truly because subtle and hidden delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) constitute their basis.
Is this not what is called the "fourth subtle and hidden delusive thought"? Generally speaking, [this applies to] sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*).
These three aggregates (*skandhas*), although all belong to the mind, are each intended in the text to demonstrate their pervasive connection with the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
Feeling (*vedanā*) enables the physical body to experience objects; perception (*saṃjñā*) can direct the body; and formations (*saṃskāra*) can transform the physical substance.

Nevertheless, while it is said that these three aggregates pervade the physical body, the essential point is actually to demonstrate that the body belongs to the category of mental factors (*caitasika*).
It does not exist as a reality.

Furthermore, that which is your brilliant clarity (this refers to the fundamental source of the clarity of consciousness), where it is profound and unmoving (profound like still water; all of this points to the eighth consciousness.

Although in the state of delusion the aggregate of consciousness encompasses all seven [consciousnesses], within the stage of cultivation and severance, the first four aggregates have been exhausted. Since there is no longer any coarse or shifting movement, what need is there to mention the [first] seven? One should know that this refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness. and is called "constant. Regarding this—
The body does not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. If it were truly essential and genuine, it would not tolerate the cultivation of delusion.
For what reason, then, did you all once in years past behold a singular object; though many years passed, there was neither memory nor forgetting of it?
Yet later, upon suddenly beholding that same former anomaly again, the memory was vividly present, never having been lost. Thus, within this essence that is lucid, profound, and unmoving, thought—

"Regarding the mindfulness that receives perfuming, what calculation can there be? (This means it is 'incalculable,' indicating that while this [mindfulness] is the verification of not forgetting a single object, in reality, the seeds held are immeasurable and the accumulated habits are boundless.

Ānanda, you should know that this stillness (referring to the state of being still and unmoving) is not real; it is like a rapid current appearing tranquil from a distance—the rapid flow is not seen, but it is not that there is no flow at all.
If it were not the source of perception (this perception is the root of the four preceding false conceptions, hence it is called the 'source of perception'),..."
It would be better to undergo delusive habituation than for your six faculties to function in mutual interchange; this delusion will never cease.

Therefore, within your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, there is a deep-seated habituation (*chuanxi*). (*Chuan* means to thread together; *ji* means the subtlest degree. "Deep-seated habituation within" refers to not forgetting what one has seen upon encountering an object.)

As each thought-moment is perfumed, there is a profound clarity within that is "entangled" (wangxiang) and void (xuwu). This is the fifth inverted state: subtle and refined conceptualization (where "entangled" means appearing as if non-existent, and "form" means appearing as if existent).

This clarifies that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is a subtle and refined ideation. That which is purely singular and unmixed, yet horizontally and vertically illuminates all things, is called "vivid clarity" (*jīngmíng*).
That in which floating thoughts have already ceased and all disturbances have come to rest is called "serene and unshakable" (*zhànbùyáo*).
Both of these refer to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Furthermore, you now take this state of vivid clarity and serene stillness as...
If it were truly eternal, then your single body would not transcend the six faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
The nature within these faculties is precisely the eighth substantial reality. If it were indeed pure and true, it would be neither mixed nor false;
it should not be subject again to the perfuming of mixture and falsehood. For what reason, then, do you forget things that you once beheld in years past?
A long time has passed, yet when it is beheld again, it appears exactly as before.
This is because, although the initial perfuming occurs through the first six consciousnesses, their retention without loss is the function of the eighth.
Thus, the sixth is like a minister who collects revenues, the seventh is like an official who transmits them, and the eighth is like a steward of the treasury. From a single object...

Do not falsely speculate on this. For within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, one is still able to remember and maintain the immeasurable varieties of habitual tendencies from many kalpas;
these are perfumed moment by moment in a manner beyond calculation—how much more so than the many years of the present life alone?
Ānanda, you should know that this profound stillness which does not waver becomes true when permeated by the True, and becomes false when permeated by the delusive;
it is certainly not the nature of the eternally true and immovable. It is like a rapid torrent of water:
from a distance, it appears tranquil and serene. This is merely because the current is so swift that its movement is not perceived; it is not that the water truly does not flow.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise thus: it is not truly unmoving, for it is the root source of the preceding four types of deluded conceptualization;
therefore, it receives the perfuming of deluded habits. If it were not the root source of deluded conceptualization, how could it receive the perfuming of the deluded habits of the preceding four?
Now, since the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is neither certain nor truly real, it still belongs to the realm of deluded habituation.

If so, when will this delusion finally be extinguished? It must wait until the time when the six sense organs function interchangeably, after the barriers between the faculties have been opened and merged;
only then can these false thoughts be eliminated. Otherwise, they can never be extinguished. Therefore, at present...
Among the six sense faculties of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, there is a subtle habitual permeation.
As it is said, "one does not forget what one has seen," and every thought-moment is perfumed; this appears real yet is empty, appears existent yet is non-existent.

Thus, within the profound clarity, there is a formless and vacuous state—nothing more than the fifth subtle, refined, and inverted conception. "Inverted" means that which is inverted from the wondrously perfect.
It exists as the true, pure, and wondrous mind. "Subtle" refers to the subtle *ālayavijñāna*.
"Essential thought" refers to the source of the consciousness's brilliant clarity. How can anything not have deluded imagination (*vikalpa*) as its basis?

Since it is said that the nature within the faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is the substance of the eighth [consciousness], and while the essence of consciousness is delusive, one nevertheless specifically extracts it from the faculties.
"Where does this nature reside? The Sixth Patriarch said: "Consciousness is itself awakening; what need is there for transformation?
That which destroys a nation and ruins a family depends on you; that which transforms a family into a nation likewise depends on you. Zhong said:

"It goes without saying that those of the Two Vehicles do not know the eight consciousnesses, yet they take the state of profound stillness and immovability to be the wondrous nature of True Suchness. This is as if taking the earth..."

The superior Bodhisattvas have destroyed and ceased the delusion of the abiding aspect (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), which is able to eliminate the two consciousnesses of the evolving and manifesting [aspects].

Yet they have not yet departed from the state of profound stillness and non-trembling. As for the delusion of conjunction inherent within that state of profound stillness and non-trembling, which serves as the root of birth and death—that is the delusion of the arising aspect (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*).
Only the Tathāgata can perceive it through his illumination and point directly to it. As it is said:
The four lines on the "swift-flowing water" describe this state with complete thoroughness. This is the stillness resulting from the division of the four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);

however, while that [previous passage] refers generally to the *vijñānaskandha*, this refers specifically to the limit of the *vijñānaskandha*. At the moment when the stillness enters and merges with stillness, it lies dormant as if formless;
yet when perfumed by conditions, it arises again. This must continue until the six sense-faculties function interchangeably and the *vijñānaskandha* is exhausted. This is the delusion.
Only through contemplation can they be extinguished; this is the realm of the Buddhas.
Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are formed by five kinds of false imaginings (*vikalpa*);
this is a summary concluding that the five aggregates are but false imaginings. Ānanda, as for these five aggregates, they arise from a single moment of delusion.
Deluded, they accept this and grasp at this, using it to conceal themselves; therefore, these are collectively called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Although they differ in terms of depth and shallowness, or coarseness and subtlety, in essence, they are all produced by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and do not inherently exist within the true mind.
If one perceives the five aggregates as having existence, that is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*); if one perceives the five aggregates as empty, [that is the world of the vessel].

This is precisely the mundane world of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). If one realizes the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), this is the world of the Middle Way, the primary meaning, and perfect enlightenment (*samyag-bodhi*).
Apart from these three worlds of the five aggregates, there is not a single dharma that can be established or posited as either conventional or ultimate.
All that is expounded by the teachings of the One Lifetime and One Period has no other expedient means besides this; those who are deluded regarding this...
To be an ordinary person; to awaken to this is to become a Buddha—it depends solely on one’s own recognition.

○ Feeling and perception are listed together among the five aggregates (skandhas), yet all five aggregates possess both feeling and perception; therefore, it is said that the five delusive thoughts constitute them.

If you now wish to know the depth and shallowness of the causal realms—[note: the character "yin" (cause) appears in both old and new commentaries; both involve forced interpretations. I, the fool, consider it an error for the character "yin" (aggregate/skandha)]—then:
only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form; only contact and separation constitute the limit of feeling;

only recollection and oblivion constitute the limit of perception; only cessation and arising constitute the limit of mental formations; and the profound entry into union with the profound constitutes the limit of consciousness.
This answers the previous question regarding what constitutes the "realm" (*dhātu*) of the five aggregates (*skandha*). As for the realms of the aggregates, there are both shallow and deep levels.

Do you now wish to know the shallow and deep dimensions of these aggregate-realms? For instance, within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), that which possesses characteristics is form, while that which lacks characteristics is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Ordinarily, one knows only that form possessing characteristics is the limit of the aggregate of form, yet one does not realize...
The emptiness of signlessness (*animitta-śūnyatā*) is likewise the limit of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

For when one is detached from all signs of form and settles the mind in empty purity, this is called the "limit of one form. Thus, it is known that while form is exhausted, emptiness is not yet exhausted;

both remain within the limit of the aggregate of form, and all forms of patience regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*) are not ultimate. Within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the faculties and their objects...
Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the meeting of [the sense faculty and its object]; non-meeting of the faculty and object is called separation (*viśleṣa*).

Ordinarily, one understands only the experiencing of the two types of objects—the agreeable and the disagreeable—as the limit of sensation (*vedanā*), yet one does not realize that the non-experiencing of these two types of objects is likewise the limit of sensation.
That is to say, although one has severed all attachments and grasping, one does not forget the state of weary detachment (*vidūṣaṇā*) and remains within the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Therefore, after teaching the departure from illusion, the Buddha further taught the departure from that very departure. Thus we know that while contact may be exhausted, if detachment is not fully perfected, one has still not emerged from the limits of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*);
consequently, all forms of renunciation (*pratikūla-vairāgya*) are not ultimate. Within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), there is...

Take mindfulness as the marker. There is neither mindfulness nor forgetfulness. People only know that being mindful of all phenomena is the limit of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), but they do not know that not being mindful of all phenomena is likewise the limit of conceptualization.

For if one eliminates various thoughts while failing to eliminate non-mindfulness, one remains dwelling within the state of stillness and mindfulness. Therefore it is said: "Both having mindfulness and lacking mindfulness alike lead back to delusion."
I am perplexed. Furthermore, it is said: "Do not say that 'no-mind' (amūlacitta) is truly the Way; even no-mind still leaves one separated by a further barrier.

From this we know that even if one has fully memorized [the teachings] yet has not fully forgotten them, one has still not transcended the limits of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha); for as long as there is anything at all, it is not the state of total non-perception (asaṃjñā).
None of these are ultimate. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the coarse activity of the distracted mind during the stage of delusion constitutes the characteristic of arising;

the subtle activity of the concentrated mind during the stage of cultivation constitutes the characteristic of cessation. People know only the coarse activity of the distracted mind, which is likened to a torrential stream.
To reach the limit of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) yet not know the subtle operation of the concentrated mind is like the analogy of a wild horse;
this too is the limit of conditioned activity. For subtle activity resembles extinction but is not truly extinguished; it remains a subtle, restless shifting.
This can be verified by one in meditative concentration, who cannot avoid the growth of nails and hair. Thus we know that while birth is exhausted, extinction is not.
Furthermore, one has not yet transcended the limits of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Indeed, all states of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) are not ultimate.

Within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), taking "entry" as a profound entry means that the flow of formations has been extinguished and one has submerged into the ocean of consciousness.

Taking "non-entry" as merging with the profound stillness means that because the current is so swift, its flow is not perceived; people merely recognize that the aggregate of formations has just dissolved, while the [aggregate of] consciousness...

When the ocean first enters [the state of stillness], its stage corresponds to the seventh level of faith (*śraddhā*). To equate this with the four fruits of the Śrāvaka path is merely to recognize the limit of consciousness;

it does not realize that the ocean of consciousness has long been still and that its domains are gradually opening. When the stage corresponds to the ten levels of faith and one awaits entry into the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) to realize perfect penetration, this too is merely the limit of consciousness.
For although the merging of the profound stillness may seem to add to the clarity of vision, it remains as it was.

Within the realm of consciousness, none are exempt from being transmuted by the four most subtle characteristics. Thus, one knows that although the profound stillness is entered, the merging with that profound stillness is not yet perfected;
ultimately, one has not transcended the boundaries of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

This is what is meant by "clear light shining into the eyes while one remains as if lost in one's own home"; all the luminous and pure *dharmakāya* remains, for now, incomplete. Because of these aggregates and realms—

Comparing these levels in their entirety from shallow to deep: one who knows only that form is form, yet does not know that emptiness is also form, understands the shallow level of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
One who knows that both emptiness and form are equally form understands the deep level of the realm of form.
In this manner, it extends even to knowing only that the profound entry is consciousness (*vijñāna*), yet not knowing that the merging with the profound is also consciousness.

Those who know that the realms of consciousness merge with the profound stillness are those who understand the shallowness of the realm of consciousness. Those who know that both the entry into stillness and its merging with stillness are all consciousness are those who understand the depth of the realm of consciousness.
Reaching this point, one may say that the five layers of deluded thought have been fully exhausted in their scope.
Master Zhong said: "The upper character 'zhan' (tranquil) refers to the practice; the lower character 'zhan' refers to the fundamental substance.
This means that by employing the practice of clarity and tranquility to enter the flow and revolve the source, one approximates union with the perfectly tranquil substance.

People know that when the mind flows outward and chases after sensory dust, it divides your tranquil and perfect nature into consciousness; yet they do not realize that even this 'tranquility entering and merging with tranquility' is likewise consciousness."
To its ultimate limit. Why is this? Because although there is profound clarity within, the subtle flow [of consciousness] has not yet been severed.

These five aggregates fundamentally arise in successive layers; their arising is due to the existence of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and their cessation proceeds from the removal of form (*rūpa*). In principle, they are suddenly realized through awakening.

"Awakening brings about their simultaneous dissolution; yet phenomena are not removed instantaneously, but are exhausted through successive stages. I have already shown you the knots in the *kṣapa* cloth;
what is there that you do not understand? Why do you inquire again? You should take this root-source of deluded thought and allow your mind to attain thorough penetration."

This is transmitted for the sake of all practitioners in the future age of the Dharma’s decay, to enable them to recognize the nature of delusion, to develop a profound weariness with their own arising,
to know that there is nirvana, and not to cling to the three realms.
This answers the previous question regarding whether the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are eliminated all at once or gradually severed.
You asked whether the severance of the five aggregates is sudden or gradual, and whether there is both principle and phenomenon involved.
Now, as for the fundamental root of these five aggregates, they originally arise one layer upon another in successive order. Their arising proceeds from a single moment of non-awakening (*avidyā*).

This awakened mind is transformed into the consciousness of karma (*karma-vijñāna*). From this consciousness, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise; from volitional formations, perception (*saṃjñā*);

from perception, sensation (*vedanā*); and from sensation, form (*rūpa*). This is how birth arises from the existence of consciousness. As for its cessation: first one eliminates form, and next one eliminates sensation.
Next, one eliminates perception; next, one eliminates formations; and finally, one eliminates consciousness. This cessation proceeds from form downward.
Birth, however, proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, like putting on a garment; cessation proceeds from the coarse to the subtle, like taking off a garment.
Such is the sequence of birth and cessation. If one were to discuss the order of cessation alone, the principle and the phenomenon would indeed differ.

The principle of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is complete; it originally arises from a single thought of deluded imagination. Therefore, beneath a single word, the ground of the mind opens up.

Riding upon that one awakening, doubts and delusions are instantly eliminated—just as when one is startled by a stump in the dark and mistakes it for a ghost, running frantically through the wilderness, yet once someone points it out to them, the notion of a ghost vanishes entirely. If one were to break through...

This matter is now clearly explained: one must dismantle [the five aggregates] by breaking through their five successive layers. Therefore, within a single moment of thought, they cannot be eliminated all at once;

the mind can only be brought to its end through a gradual process. It is like the perception of a ghost: though it may have been entirely dispelled, how could one suddenly turn back from a long journey?
One must necessarily retrace the path ahead before returning to one’s original place. Such is the dismantling of the five aggregates.
And thus one enters the First Abode (*prathamā-bhūmi*). This is fundamentally the same principle as the previous explanation of entering perfect penetration by untying the six knots.

Therefore, from "the union of form and emptiness" up to "entering the profound stillness," one unties the first three knots; from "entering the profound stillness" up to "merging with the profound stillness," [one unties the remaining knots].
This refers precisely to the untangling of the latter three fetters. Previously, I showed you how to untangle the knots of the *kapāsa* cloth in successive order;

the correspondence between the dharma and the metaphor is perfectly clear. Why do you not understand? You should realize this very principle through that analogy; only then will you have properly grasped the Buddha’s instruction.
"Why do you neglect that and instead ask about this? My instruction to you is complete with this.
You should thoroughly understand each of these five aggregates (skandhas) and know that their very root is entirely nothing but false conceptualization."
If one causes the mind to become open and unobstructed, so that it is not deluded by these [five aggregates], then the path of self-benefit lies herein.

Furthermore, if one transmits this to future generations so that all practitioners during the Dharma-ending age may recognize the emptiness and falsity of the five aggregates, they will develop a profound weariness with their own arising.
By recognizing what is false, they will know that there is the nature of the fruit of Nirvana.
Truly. To weary of birth means that one no longer clings to the pleasures of the cycle of birth and death within the three realms;
therein lies the path of benefiting others. Ānanda, exert yourself! Question: What is the meaning of sudden awakening and gradual elimination? Answer:
It is like the fierce winds of the great ocean suddenly ceasing—this is sudden awakening. The waves gradually subside—this is gradual elimination. It is like a child...
The sudden emergence of the various faculties is sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*). The gradual perfection of one’s strength and capacity is gradual elimination (*jianchu*).
This is like the sudden appearance of the morning sun, which is sudden enlightenment; and like the gradual dissipation of frost and dew, which is gradual elimination.

It is like the sudden growth of spring bamboo shoots, which immediately reaches the height of its mother—this is sudden enlightenment; and like the branching and spreading of leaves, ascending joint by joint—this is gradual [elimination].

They must be eliminated. If one attains sudden enlightenment without gradual elimination, there will be understanding without practice; one will cling to principle while remaining deluded regarding phenomena.
This is ultimately not the correct cultivation of true samādhi. These four lines are the essential instructions transmitted by the thousand Buddhas.
This is the grand regulation that shall not change for ten thousand generations. [The Section on the True Doctrine concludes.
Third Question of the Section on Dissemination:
Since this sutra and the Lotus Sutra follow the same path, [should we apply] the passages from the *Lotus Sutra* concerning the exhortation and praise for its dissemination?

Each chapter contains [such passages], yet why is this text for circulation so very brief? Answer: At the initial stage of establishing the *Dharmapada* (Lotus Sūtra) by way of refuting other teachings, doubts were deep and faith was shallow;
therefore, the washing away of doubtful sentiments was detailed, while the elucidation of principle and practice was concise.
Now that this sūtra has long been revealed, doubts have dissolved and faith is settled; thus, the elucidation of principle and practice [is expanded].
To be detailed: the washing away of lack of faith is the concise [teaching].

Ānanda, suppose there were another person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a heart that never wasted its intent. What do you think? Would this person...
"By this cause and condition of giving to the Buddha, would one not obtain much merit?

This first raises up the merit to allow for comparison. "Ānanda, if there were another person here who were to take these seven treasures, filling the entirety of the void of the ten directions until it was overflowing—such that the wealth were inexhaustible—and were to take these seven treasures..."
To offer to as many Buddhas as there are atoms is for the field of merit to be inexhaustible. To serve and make offerings with a sincere heart is for the mind not to be in vain;
thus, one’s mindfulness is inexhaustible. What do you think? Is the merit gained by this person through such offerings to the Buddhas great or not?
One need not ask to know that it is indeed great.
Ānanda replied, "Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to the Buddha;
even by relinquishing his body, he attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King. How much more so now, when the space before us is already exhausted and the Buddha-lands are filled everywhere?"
Even if one were to bestow precious jewels for an entire kalpa, even the most exhaustive calculation could not equal it. How could there be any limit to such merit?
This comparison establishes its immeasurability. Ānanda replied, "As the Buddha has said, the empty space of the ten directions is inexhaustible;
if filled with precious jewels, they would be boundless. According to what I have heard, in the past there was a sentient being..."
To give seven coins to the Buddha is an exceedingly minor merit; yet after relinquishing his body, he still obtained the retribution of becoming a Wheel-Turning King.
How much more so when one fills the entirety of space before them—reaching to the limits of the ten directions—with precious jewels offered to the Buddha-fields?

Even the power of thought cannot fathom such an act. Compared to that, how can the gift of seven coins be considered? By taking that case as an analogy for this, one may understand [the magnitude of the former].
"Is there yet another limit to this merit?
Ānanda replied, "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not speak falsely.
Because the effort expended in propagating this sutra hereafter will be minimal, while the merit gained from the extinction of sins will be immense, it is difficult to fathom."
This is for the sake of inspiring faith; therefore, he first clarifies that the Buddha has no speech that is unreal or untrue, so as to cause others to believe it with certainty.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, when establishing the precepts, first prohibit false speech.
If the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were to speak with falsehood themselves at the outset, this would certainly not be the case. Therefore, one knows that their words are without falsehood."
Since there is no falsehood, you should not fail to believe my words today with earnest sincerity.

Furthermore, if there is another person whose body is burdened by the four grave offenses (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying) and the ten *pārājika* offenses (which are the ten evil deeds;

translated as "abandonment," for they are like the severest of the five punishments and represent the utmost gravity of retribution), that person will, in an instant, pass through this world, other worlds, and the Avīci Hell, continuing until the exhaustion of ten...

Throughout the intermediate and immediate [kalpas], there is nowhere he has not passed through. If one can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-door and reveal it to those of later learning during the final kalpa, that person’s karmic obstacles will be extinguished at that very moment.
The causes for the suffering of hell they were to undergo will be transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss.
The merit they obtain shall surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten thousandfold, a hundred millionfold, and even a billionfold. As it is said:
This extends even to the point where it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy;
this speaks to the vastness of the merit obtained from propagating the sutra. Furthermore, suppose there is a person whose body is burdened with the four grave offenses and the ten evil deeds.
The causes of evil have reached their limit; in a mere instant, one passes through the hells of the ten directions. The fruits of evil have reached their limit.

If this person who is about to fall into hell can, for even a moment, give rise to the resolve to enter deeply through this single gate of the perfect penetration of the Great Samādhi, they will be able to instruct those of later generations—during an age when the sages are distant and demons are powerful, and when beginners find it difficult to advance and easy to retreat.

When such a person beholds this individual’s karmic obstacles, they shall be extinguished by this single thought, just as snow is melted by hot water or grass is consumed by fire, leaving nothing but ashes and vapor. Moreover, it does not merely eliminate evil karma;
it can further transform suffering into joy, causing the very hells one is destined to undergo to become a land of peace and bliss.
And as for being reborn therein—how great is that bliss! Moreover, it is not merely that heavy offenses are extinguished;

one also attains merit that surpasses all others. Compared to the merit obtained by those who previously made offerings of the seven treasures to the Buddhas, this merit is hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of times greater—even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy. How great is that merit! This is truly because:

This sutra opens the precious treasury of the Tathāgata’s secrets; it enables one to obtain the innate, all-pervading family treasure and to achieve the Buddha-fruit in which the atoms of all lands are mutually integrated.
Therefore, it cannot be equaled by material gifts, offerings based on grasping at signs, or the fruits of conditioned phenomena.
If even a single thought of propagating this sutra can bring about such results, how much more so for those who propagate it over a long period?
The greatness of a single thought does not exceed a single phrase or a single verse, yet it can still achieve such results;

how much more so for a single phrase, half a volume, or even an entire sutra? If those with heavy offenses can still achieve such results, how much more so those with light offenses or no offenses at all?
Even for those who possess great merit and abundant virtue, their karmic rewards are so exceptionally sublime that they can hardly be measured.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra as I have extensively explained it, [their merit] would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
This reveals that the merit of those who are free from transgression in upholding this sutra and reciting this dharani is inexhaustible.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this Śūraṅgama Sūtra and uphold this Śūraṅgama Dharani, I shall praise such persons with my eightfold voice and fourfold eloquence;
they shall extinguish the aforementioned sins and obtain the aforementioned blessings, even throughout the exhaustion of kalpas.
Even this cannot be fully recounted. Now, merely by upholding and reciting [this teaching], one attains the wisdom derived from hearing;
if its merit is already such as this, how much more so for those who advance to the stages of reflection and cultivation!
Relying on my teachings and practicing the Way according to those instructions, one will directly achieve Bodhi, and no further demonic activities will arise.
As for those who practice through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, they rely on the words within my teachings and practice the Way according to my instructions;

they attain sudden enlightenment while gradually eliminating [afflictions], entering deeply through a single gate. From the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the attainment of Buddhahood, throughout this interval...
There are no further complications or devious turns; it is like water rushing into a ravine or an arrow piercing the void. No demonic obstacles shall arise to hinder its progress.
Furthermore, why worry about halting within the "Transformation City" of the Lesser Vehicle or being delayed by the gradual stages of realization?
Thus, although this circulation of the text is brief in its written form, when one investigates its words and meaning, its significance is profound.
Even if one were to compile them into volumes numbering in the hundreds, they could not exceed this [work]. Is this not because it gathers the vast through its conciseness, leaving nothing out?
Thus, the saying that "I am the Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma" is truly beyond reproach.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;
all those in the world—devas, humans, asuras, and the bodhisattvas and followers of the two vehicles from other directions;

the holy seers and youths (the title "holy" is specifically added to "seer" to denote those who, while belonging to the class of seers, practice the inner teaching and aspire to attain the wondrous fruit of *kumārabhūta*); and the powerful spirits and ghosts who have first resolved their minds upon enlightenment (the phrase "who have resolved their minds" is specifically added to "spirits and ghosts").

This demonstrates their resolve to protect the Dharma and their possession of great supernormal powers and profound fearlessness. These two groups are both capable of propagating, protecting, and circulating [the teachings]. Since the eight classes of beings have not yet been fully encompassed, they are added here.
Having said this, they were all greatly rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and departed.
This was established by the scribe of the sutra to clarify the joy and celebration of the Dharma assembly.

After the Buddha had finished preaching this *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, the great assembly present—from the bhikṣus down to the ghosts and spirits—having heard the orthodox teaching, attained their fundamental, wondrous, and perfect mind;

and further hearing the instructions for its circulation, they knew its ultimate, far-reaching benefit. In the near term, they were free from the anxiety of falling into evil realms; in the long term...
Possessing the hope of realizing the truth, they experienced extraordinary joy and great delight. They prostrated before the Buddha and departed to return to their respective abodes.
Each returned to the immovable *bodhimaṇḍa* within their own mind, where they would either practice cultivation or propagate the teachings;
they were not like worldly people who, upon leaving the assembly, fall into distraction.
Zhong Bojing said: This *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* Sūtra is the sovereign king of samādhis, fully embodying the myriad practices and encompassing all dhāraṇīs.
It perfumes and cultivates the path of *śamatha*, revealing to sentient beings that the wondrous lies in transcending through a single gate.
Because Ānanda was limited by his extensive learning and had not yet perfected his power of the Way, Kāśyapa (the Buddha) took his false views as a cause to point directly to the human mind. (7)

When the bases are dismantled, the dust on the precious mirror is polished away and its original luminosity manifests spontaneously. Through the tenfold manifestation, the cataracts are scraped off with a golden probe and illusory shadows vanish accordingly.
By rejecting攀緣 (*pán-yuán*, objective clinging), it is shown that the mind is not the [deluded] mind; by revealing true awakening, it is shown that even seeing is free from seeing.
Having thus manifested the real and dismantled the false, one still speaks of the real by means of the false, exhausting the realms of the *āyatanas* and *dhātus*.
The realms are categorized into four sections; both causal conditions and spontaneity are set aside. Earth, water, fire, and wind are unified and collectively termed the "Seven Greats.
The Middle Way of the True and the Conventional is the perfect fusion of the Three Truths. This is the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, which encompasses and gives voice to the ten voids.
According to the minds of sentient beings, it manifests all phenomena, such that even one and many are mutually identical. Great.
Small things mutually accommodate one another: the jeweled lands appear upon the tip of a hair, and the turning of the Dharma wheel occurs within a speck of dust.

For those who have attained non-obstruction, perverted perceptions are dissolved over billions of kalpas; for those who do not follow conceptual discrimination, the wild mind ceases and is itself Bodhi.

For those of the Perfect and Sudden capacity, the secret cause has already been clarified; now, for those of middling and lower capacities, the wondrous practice must be set forth. Thus, the "Returning of the Long-Dwelling Guest" is opened.

The path of the home refers to the gate through which the Heavenly King bestowed the dwelling. It examines the fundamental cause of all sages and, based on the teaching of realization, explains the initial expedient means.
In accordance with the essence of the teachings of this region, it selects the faculty of hearing as the foremost perfect penetration.
Next, to collect the mind, one should once again uphold the precepts. Following the former World-Honored One, he proclaimed the pure and luminous instructions;
the manifested Nirmāṇakāya Buddha expounded the secret gāthās. With the three trainings fully perfected, that which is realized is not partial.

All delusions vanish; what need is there to wait for the "not-true"? Furthermore, by meticulously investigating the seven destinies and how birth is received according to karma, [one perceives] the suffering...
This illustrates the sixfold intersection. It shows how habitual tendencies invite retribution and reveals the fifty stages of *dhyāna*.

It provides deep protection against the demons of craving and false views, and possesses eighty thousand methods for liberation. It serves as an antidote to the afflictions of worldly toil, maintaining and shielding the practitioner while exhorting them to propagate the teaching.
From beginning to end, it is nothing other than the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization; whether refuting or establishing, it remains so.
Without departing from the eternally abiding true mind, lutes, harps, and *konghou* zithers, upon meeting skillful fingers, and forests, groves, ponds,

and marshes all proclaim the sound of the Dharma, causing even those of the icchantika class to abandon their *mleccha* ways and, from within *samādhi*, attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Either they establish themselves in the stages of the noble ones through their own true nature, or they transcend from mutual interpenetration to reach the final mind, sitting in the Great Dharma-Assembly and ascending to Unsurpassed Enlightenment. All matters are ultimately firm and solid;

they extensively open the many skillful means of the Bodhisattvas, traversing the worlds of the ten directions with effortless spontaneity, together entering the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments. Its...
The teaching has reached its consummation.
